The session resumption approach fails because subagent context is isolated and not captured in the coordinator's session history. The full restart with retry approach is the explicit anti-pattern: it discards all prior work and relies on non-deterministic model outputs to regenerate results, which is both wasteful and unreliable.

The key principle is that recovery requires persisted state, not just persisted conversation history. State must be written to durable storage at known locations so any component can load it independently on resume. Learn more about multi-agent orchestration patterns at Agent SDK and Claude Code Sub-agents.
option_feedback: Restarting the full pipeline from scratch is the anti-pattern this question is designed to avoid. Relying on output consistency to "quickly regenerate" prior work is unreliable since language model outputs are non-deterministic, and this approach wastes all previously completed compute. It also ignores the core requirement of resuming from the point of failure rather than restarting completely.

Structured state persistence using manifest files is the documented pattern for crash recovery in multi-agent systems. Each agent writes its state to a known location, and the coordinator reads the manifest on resume to reconstruct progress, inject completed findings into agent prompts, and skip already-finished work. This provides deterministic recovery without restarting the entire pipeline.

While a heartbeat database could track agent liveness, it does not preserve the actual findings and outputs that completed agents produced. On restart, the coordinator would know which agents finished but would have no access to their results, requiring those agents to re-run anyway. This approach conflates tracking agent status with preserving agent output, which are two separate problems.

Named session resumption restores a prior conversation's context for the coordinator itself, but subagents operate with isolated context and do not automatically inherit the coordinator's session history. After a crash, subagent state (completed findings, sources searched) is not preserved in the coordinator's session, so this approach does not solve the problem of knowing which subagents finished and what they produced.

question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

Your CI/CD pipeline runs automated code reviews on every pull request. After three months in production, your team notices that developers are routinely dismissing an entire category of findings without acting on them. Exit surveys reveal that developers consider the "code comment accuracy" findings unreliable: the reviewer flags comments as inaccurate even when they correctly describe the code's intent at a higher level of abstraction. Meanwhile, findings in other categories (security vulnerabilities, null pointer risks) are being acted on consistently. Your manager asks you to fix the comment accuracy category without disrupting the other categories that are working well. What is the most effective prompt change to address this?
options: Replace the vague instruction "check that comments are accurate" with a specific criterion such as "flag a comment only when the described behavior directly contradicts what the code actually does, not when the comment summarizes intent at a higher level of abstraction."
Temporarily disable all comment accuracy findings from the pipeline output until the team can retrain the underlying model on a labeled dataset of correct and incorrect comment accuracy judgments.

Add a general instruction to the system prompt telling Claude to "only report findings when confidence is high" and "be conservative when unsure whether a comment is inaccurate," applying this guidance globally across all review categories.

Add a severity threshold instruction stating that comment accuracy issues should only be reported when they are classified as "critical" or "high" severity, and instruct Claude to downgrade any comment accuracy finding that lacks a direct code example to "low" severity so it is filtered out.
answer: Replace the vague instruction "check that comments are accurate" with a specific criterion such as "flag a comment only when the described behavior directly contradicts what the code actually does, not when the comment summarizes intent at a higher level of abstraction."
explanation:
The core principle tested here is that explicit categorical criteria outperform vague or confidence-based instructions when reducing false positives in a specific review category. The exam guide states this directly: instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" fail to improve precision compared to defining exactly which issues to report and which to skip.

The correct fix narrows the definition of a reportable comment accuracy issue to a precise, verifiable condition: the comment's described behavior must directly contradict what the code does. This eliminates the false positive pattern (flagging high-level abstractions) without touching the security and null pointer categories. The change is surgical and categorical, not a global dial-down of confidence.

The anti-pattern in this question is the confidence-based instruction ("only report when confidence is high"). This is a classic false positive reduction attempt that fails in practice because it does not give the model a concrete rule for distinguishing genuine issues from acceptable abstractions. The model was already "confident" in its incorrect comment accuracy findings, so lowering a confidence threshold does not help.

Severity-based filtering and category disablement are also distractors: the former is a proxy that avoids defining the actual problem, and the latter discards value rather than fixing the root cause. The right approach is always to define explicit, testable criteria for what belongs in each finding category before reaching for infrastructure changes or global suppression.

For further reading on designing explicit review criteria and reducing false positives, see Prompt Engineering and the Claude Code Overview.
option_feedback: Explicit categorical criteria directly define the boundary between what should and should not be flagged, eliminating the ambiguity that causes false positives. This approach targets only the failing category without touching the working ones, and it gives the model a precise rule rather than a judgment call, which is why it outperforms confidence-based or general conservatism instructions.

Disabling the category entirely removes value from the pipeline and model retraining is out of scope for this certification and unnecessary when prompt refinement is the appropriate first intervention. Retraining is a heavyweight solution that should only be considered after prompt engineering has been exhausted, and it does not address the root cause of imprecise criteria.

General conservatism instructions like "only report high-confidence findings" fail to improve precision because they do not define what makes a finding high-confidence in the specific context of comment accuracy. This approach also applies globally, risking suppression of valid findings in the security and null pointer categories that are already performing well.

Severity-based filtering is a proxy workaround rather than a fix for the underlying imprecision. It does not define what constitutes a genuine comment inaccuracy versus an acceptable abstraction, so the model will still generate the same false positives and then attempt to self-classify their severity, which is itself unreliable without explicit criteria defining what makes a comment finding reportable in the first place.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with MCP servers.

Your developer productivity agent has a synthesis subagent responsible for combining findings from codebase exploration into structured summaries. During testing, you observe that the synthesis subagent is frequently making direct web search calls to look up documentation for unfamiliar APIs it encounters, rather than flagging those gaps for the coordinator to investigate. Additionally, when it encounters an ambiguous function signature, it attempts to run Bash commands to execute test calls against the codebase. These behaviors are causing incorrect assumptions to appear in summaries and occasionally triggering unintended side effects in the development environment.

You have 18 tools available across your agent system, and the synthesis subagent currently has access to all of them. What change would most directly address the observed reliability issues?
options: Reduce the total tool count available to the synthesis subagent from 18 to a fixed cap of 5 tools chosen at random from the available set, since research shows that fewer tools improve selection reliability regardless of which tools are included.

Configure tool_choice to "any" for the synthesis subagent so it is required to call at least one tool per turn, then add a PostToolUse hook that intercepts Bash and web search calls and returns an error instructing the subagent to delegate those requests instead.

Add explicit instructions to the synthesis subagent's system prompt prohibiting it from calling web search or Bash tools, and specify that ambiguous signatures should be noted as gaps rather than investigated directly.

Restrict the synthesis subagent's tool access to only the tools required for its role (such as Read and Write for loading context and persisting summaries), routing web lookups and execution requests through the coordinator to appropriate specialist subagents.
answer: Restrict the synthesis subagent's tool access to only the tools required for its role (such as Read and Write for loading context and persisting summaries), routing web lookups and execution requests through the coordinator to appropriate specialist subagents.
explanation:
The root cause of the synthesis subagent's misbehavior is over-provisioning: giving it access to 18 tools when its role only requires a small subset. When agents have access to tools outside their specialization, they tend to misuse them, especially when those tools seem like reasonable shortcuts for the task at hand.

The correct architectural principle is scoped tool access: each subagent should receive only the tools needed for its specific role. A synthesis subagent that consolidates findings needs tools like Read (to load context) and Write (to persist summaries), not Bash or web search tools. When those tools are simply absent from its allowed set, cross-specialization misuse becomes impossible regardless of the subagent's reasoning.

The prompt-based prohibition distractor represents a common anti-pattern: relying on probabilistic compliance through instructions when deterministic enforcement through tool scoping is available and more reliable. The arbitrary tool cap distractor correctly identifies that fewer tools improve reliability but misses the critical point that the specific tools must match the subagent's role. The hook-based approach is problematic because PostToolUse hooks fire after execution, meaning Bash side effects may already have occurred before any corrective feedback reaches the subagent.

For complex verifications that the synthesis subagent genuinely needs (such as fact-checking a specific claim), the recommended pattern is to provide a scoped cross-role tool like verify_fact for the common case, while routing deeper investigations through the coordinator to specialist subagents. This preserves separation of concerns while avoiding unnecessary round-trips for high-frequency needs.

Learn more about tool distribution and scoped access patterns at Tool Use and Agent SDK.
option_feedback: Reducing tool count does improve selection reliability, but the specific tools provided must match the subagent's role. Arbitrarily capping at 5 random tools could remove tools the synthesis subagent legitimately needs (like Read) while retaining tools it should not have (like Bash). The principle is role-appropriate scoping, not arbitrary reduction.

While PostToolUse hooks can intercept and provide feedback after tool execution, they fire after the tool has already been called, meaning Bash commands may have already produced side effects before the hook can redirect the subagent. Preventing access through scoped tool assignment is more reliable than intercepting calls after they have been initiated.

Prompt-based prohibitions rely on probabilistic LLM compliance rather than deterministic enforcement. If the synthesis subagent retains access to web search and Bash tools in its allowed tool set, it may still invoke them when it reasons that doing so would improve its output, especially in novel situations not covered by the instructions.

Giving each subagent only the tools needed for its specific role prevents cross-specialization misuse. When the synthesis subagent lacks web search and Bash tools, it cannot attempt those actions regardless of how it reasons about the task, eliminating the observed side effects and incorrect assumptions at the source. This is the principle of scoped tool access applied to subagent design.

question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

Your CI/CD pipeline runs automated code reviews using Claude. Each review request sends the full diff to Claude and asks for findings in a structured JSON format. The pipeline parses Claude's response and posts inline comments on the pull request. In production, you observe that roughly 1 in 8 requests results in a JSON parsing error that crashes the comment-posting step, forcing engineers to re-trigger the pipeline manually. The failures are random across different PR sizes and file types, and the JSON structure varies between runs even when the prompt is identical. You need a reliable fix that guarantees schema-compliant output on every request. What change most directly solves this problem?
options: Pre-fill the assistant message with the opening brace of the expected JSON object and add a stop sequence matching the closing brace, so Claude generates only the interior fields and the pipeline wraps them into a complete JSON object.

Define a review findings extraction tool with a JSON schema and configure the request to use tool_use, then parse structured output from the tool_use response block rather than from Claude's text output.

Add a retry loop that catches JSON parsing exceptions, appends the error message to the prompt, and re-sends the original request to Claude until a valid response is received or a maximum of three attempts is exhausted.

Switch the output format instruction in the system prompt from "respond with JSON" to a more explicit template with labeled placeholders and an example of the exact JSON structure you expect Claude to produce.
answer: Define a review findings extraction tool with a JSON schema and configure the request to use tool_use, then parse structured output from the tool_use response block rather than from Claude's text output.
explanation:
Tool use with a JSON schema is the correct architectural solution for guaranteed schema-compliant structured output. When you define an extraction tool and configure the request to call it, the API enforces the schema definition and eliminates JSON syntax errors entirely. Parsing from the tool_use response block, rather than from Claude's free-form text, removes the source of the random formatting failures described in the scenario.

The exam guide draws a clear distinction: "Tool use (tool_use) with JSON schemas as the most reliable approach for guaranteed schema-compliant structured output, eliminating JSON syntax errors." This is contrasted with prompt-based approaches (templates, examples, pre-filling) which are probabilistic improvements, not structural guarantees. The random failure pattern across different PR sizes is a classic symptom of relying on free-form text generation for structured output.

The retry-with-error-feedback distractor is a real and useful pattern, but it addresses a different problem: correcting semantic validation errors when the required information exists in the source but was formatted incorrectly. It does not fix the root cause of syntax failures from unstructured generation, making it an anti-pattern when applied to this specific problem.

Note that eliminating syntax errors via tool use does not prevent semantic errors (for example, line items that do not sum to a stated total). Semantic validation requires additional application-layer checks even after adopting tool use. See Tool Use for schema design guidance and Prompt Engineering for when other techniques are more appropriate.
option_feedback: Pre-filling and stop sequences can help constrain output format, but they do not provide schema validation or guarantee syntactically correct JSON. Claude may still produce malformed field values, mismatched brackets within the body, or truncated output if generation stops unexpectedly. This technique also requires fragile string manipulation on the pipeline side and does not scale reliably to variable-length review outputs.

Tool use with a JSON schema is the documented approach for guaranteed schema-compliant structured output. When Claude is forced to respond via a tool call, the API enforces the schema and eliminates JSON syntax errors entirely. Parsing from the tool_use response block instead of free-form text removes the source of the random formatting failures.

Retry-with-error-feedback is useful for correcting semantic validation errors or structural mismatches, but it does not address the root cause of random JSON syntax failures from free-form text generation. Each retry still relies on Claude producing valid JSON from unstructured output, so failures will continue to occur at a similar rate, just with added latency and cost per affected request.

Providing a more explicit template and example improves output consistency in many cases, but it still relies on Claude reproducing the format correctly from natural language instructions. This is a probabilistic improvement, not a structural guarantee, so random syntax failures will persist even if their frequency decreases. The failures described require an architectural change, not just a prompt refinement.

question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

A developer joins the team responsible for the document analysis subagent. This subagent's job is to scan a large repository of research papers, locate all files matching the pattern `**/*.pdf`, and then search within those files for mentions of a specific author's name before passing relevant excerpts to the synthesis subagent. The developer observes that the subagent is currently using a single Bash tool call with a combined shell pipeline to accomplish both steps. The subagent occasionally misses files or returns garbled output when the repository structure changes. Which approach to tool selection would make this workflow most reliable and maintainable?
options: Use Grep alone with a recursive flag and the `**/*.pdf` glob pattern embedded directly in the Grep invocation, since Grep can both locate files and search their contents in a single operation, reducing the number of tool calls the subagent needs to make.
Use Glob to find all files matching the `**/*.pdf` pattern, then pass the resulting file list to Grep to search within those files for the author's name, keeping each operation in its dedicated tool.

Use a single Bash tool call with a shell pipeline combining `find` and `grep` commands, but add error handling flags to the pipeline so partial failures in one stage do not silently corrupt the output passed downstream.

Use Read to iterate through every file in the repository directory, inspect each file's path programmatically to filter for PDFs, and then scan the loaded content for the author's name, avoiding shell tool calls entirely to improve portability across environments.
answer: Use Glob to find all files matching the `**/*.pdf` pattern, then pass the resulting file list to Grep to search within those files for the author's name, keeping each operation in its dedicated tool.
explanation:
The built-in tools in Claude Code have distinct, well-defined purposes: Glob is for file path pattern matching (finding files by name or extension pattern such as **/*.pdf), while Grep is for content search (finding files whose contents match a pattern, such as an author name). Using each tool for its intended role produces reliable, composable workflows that remain stable when repository structure changes.

The anti-pattern here is consolidating both operations into a single Bash pipeline. While Bash is a general-purpose escape hatch, combining file discovery and content search in one shell command creates a brittle dependency on the exact shell environment and makes it harder to isolate failures. The exam guide explicitly distinguishes Grep for content search from Glob for file path pattern matching, and recommends using Read as a fallback only when Edit fails due to non-unique text matches, not as a file discovery mechanism.

Similarly, attempting to use Grep alone for both file discovery and content search conflates two separate concerns, and iterating through all files with Read is an inefficient anti-pattern that ignores the purpose-built tools available. The correct approach is to sequence Glob and Grep: Glob produces the file list, Grep searches within that list.

For more on built-in tool selection and when to use each, see the Claude Code Overview and Agent SDK documentation.
option_feedback: Grep is the tool for searching file contents for patterns, not for file path pattern matching by name or extension. Embedding a glob pattern inside a Grep invocation conflates the two operations and produces unpredictable results when file discovery based on naming patterns is needed. Glob is the correct tool for the file discovery step.

Glob is designed specifically for file path pattern matching by name or extension, while Grep is designed for searching file contents for patterns like author names. Using each tool for its intended purpose produces reliable results regardless of repository structure changes, and separates concerns so failures in one step are easy to diagnose and fix independently.

Wrapping a combined shell pipeline in error handling addresses symptoms rather than the underlying design issue. A single Bash call conflates two distinct operations (file discovery and content search) that have dedicated built-in tools, making the subagent harder to debug and more brittle when repository structure changes in ways the shell command does not anticipate.

Loading every file with Read to perform path filtering and content scanning is a highly inefficient anti-pattern for large repositories. Read is designed for loading the full contents of specific known files, not for discovering or filtering files by name pattern. This approach also bypasses the purpose-built Glob and Grep tools, which handle these operations reliably and efficiently at scale.

question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

Your CI/CD pipeline uses Claude to generate structured code review findings. Each finding is returned as JSON with fields including "file_path", "line_number", "issue_description", "severity", and "category". The pipeline posts these findings as inline PR comments automatically.

After several weeks in production, you notice that approximately 30% of findings have the "severity" field set to "critical" even when the underlying issues are minor style inconsistencies. Developers are losing trust in the review system because the severity classifications are inconsistent and often feel arbitrary. You have already confirmed that your JSON schema enforces severity as a required enum field with values: "critical", "high", "medium", "low".

A colleague suggests that since tool use with a JSON schema already eliminates syntax errors, the severity miscalibration must be a prompt engineering problem that cannot be addressed through schema changes. How should you evaluate this suggestion, and what is the most effective way to address the severity miscalibration?
options: The colleague is incorrect: the schema itself is the problem. Replace the severity enum with a free-text string field so the model can express nuanced severity in natural language, then add a post-processing step that maps the free-text descriptions to severity levels before posting PR comments.

The colleague is correct that schema changes cannot help, but the fix is to add a confidence score field to the schema and filter out any findings where the model reports low confidence in its severity classification, routing those to human review before posting PR comments.

The colleague is partially correct: tool use eliminates syntax errors but not semantic errors. Add concrete code examples for each severity level to the prompt alongside the existing schema, so the model has calibration anchors rather than inferring severity from the enum values alone.

The colleague is correct: schema enforcement already covers all output quality issues. Switch to tool_choice set to "any" instead of forced tool selection so the model has more flexibility when choosing severity, which will naturally produce more calibrated classifications across the enum values.
answer: The colleague is partially correct: tool use eliminates syntax errors but not semantic errors. Add concrete code examples for each severity level to the prompt alongside the existing schema, so the model has calibration anchors rather than inferring severity from the enum values alone.
explanation:
The core distinction here is between schema-enforced syntax correctness and prompt-driven semantic correctness. Tool use with a JSON schema guarantees that the severity field will always contain one of the valid enum values ("critical", "high", "medium", "low") and will never be missing or malformed. This is what the exam guide means when it states that "strict JSON schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but do not prevent semantic errors."

Severity miscalibration is a semantic error: the model selects a syntactically valid value but chooses the wrong one. The fix requires giving the model calibration guidance in the prompt, such as concrete code examples for each severity level. For instance, showing that a missing null check in an authentication path is "critical" while a variable naming inconsistency is "low" gives the model anchors to generalize from, rather than leaving it to infer meaning from enum labels alone.

The distractor involving tool_choice: "any" is an anti-pattern because it conflates tool selection configuration with output value calibration. Changing whether the model must call a tool has no effect on how it populates fields within a tool call that is already happening. Similarly, replacing a structured enum with free text undermines the entire purpose of schema-enforced output and would create downstream parsing fragility.

The confidence score approach is a common but misapplied pattern for this problem. Confidence scores are useful for routing uncertain extractions to human review, but they do not correct systematic miscalibration where the model is confidently wrong. Addressing root-cause calibration through prompt examples is more effective than routing workarounds.

For more on schema design and the limits of structured output enforcement, see Tool Use and Prompt Engineering.
option_feedback: Replacing a constrained enum with a free-text field reintroduces the very inconsistency that structured output is designed to prevent. The post-processing mapping step would require its own calibration logic and would be fragile to varied natural language descriptions. The existing enum structure is sound; the issue is that the model lacks guidance on which values apply to which types of findings.

Adding a confidence score field addresses triage routing but does not fix the underlying miscalibration. If the model consistently overclassifies minor issues as "critical" with high confidence, filtering by confidence would not catch those findings. This approach treats a symptom rather than the root cause, and self-reported model confidence scores are not reliably calibrated proxies for actual classification accuracy.

Tool use with a JSON schema guarantees that the severity field will always contain a valid enum value, but it cannot enforce that the chosen value is semantically correct for the given finding. The schema enforces structure; the prompt must supply the meaning. Adding concrete code examples for each severity level gives the model calibration anchors that reduce arbitrary classification, directly addressing the root cause without any schema changes.

Changing tool_choice to "any" affects whether the model must call a tool, not how it classifies severity within an already-called tool. The model is already calling the tool and populating the severity field with valid enum values. Loosening tool selection constraints does nothing to improve semantic calibration of the values chosen, and the colleague's claim that schema enforcement covers all output quality issues is incorrect.

question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

Your web search subagent occasionally encounters timeouts when querying external sources. When this happens, the subagent currently catches the exception and returns an empty result set with a success status to the coordinator, reasoning that an empty response is better than surfacing an error. You begin noticing that the coordinator consistently produces reports with unexplained coverage gaps on certain subtopics, but the coordinator's logs show no errors and all subagents reported success. What is the fundamental problem with the current error handling approach, and what change would most directly fix it?
options: The subagent is not logging timeout events to a shared monitoring system, so the coordinator has no visibility into failures during the research run. The fix is to write timeout events to a centralized log that the coordinator polls between subagent calls, allowing it to detect failures and reissue queries to the affected subagent before synthesizing results.

The subagent is silently suppressing failures by returning empty results as success, which prevents the coordinator from distinguishing access failures from valid empty results and blocks any meaningful recovery. The fix is to return structured error context including the failure type, the attempted query, and any partial results so the coordinator can make informed decisions about retrying, rerouting, or annotating coverage gaps.

The subagent is not setting the MCP isError flag when returning error conditions, so the coordinator's tool result processing does not recognize the failure. The fix is to set isError to true on the tool result whenever a timeout occurs, which causes the coordinator to automatically halt the workflow and prompt the user for guidance before continuing.

The subagent is returning results too slowly, causing the coordinator to time out before receiving the response. The fix is to implement exponential backoff with automatic retries inside the subagent so that transient network issues resolve before results are returned, and the coordinator always receives a complete response within the expected window.
answer: The subagent is silently suppressing failures by returning empty results as success, which prevents the coordinator from distinguishing access failures from valid empty results and blocks any meaningful recovery. The fix is to return structured error context including the failure type, the attempted query, and any partial results so the coordinator can make informed decisions about retrying, rerouting, or annotating coverage gaps.
explanation:
The core issue in this scenario is a classic silent failure anti-pattern: the subagent catches an exception and returns an empty result with a success status, making it impossible for the coordinator to distinguish between two fundamentally different situations: a valid empty result (no sources matched the query) and an access failure (a timeout prevented retrieval). Because both look identical to the coordinator, it cannot take any corrective action.

The correct fix is to return structured error context through the MCP tool result, including the isError flag, the failure type (transient timeout), the attempted query, and any partial results. This gives the coordinator the information it needs to make intelligent recovery decisions: retry the query, reroute to an alternative source, proceed with partial results, or annotate the final report with a coverage gap indicating which subtopic could not be fully researched.

The exam guide explicitly identifies two anti-patterns to avoid: silently suppressing errors by returning empty results as success, and terminating entire workflows on single failures. The correct pattern sits between these extremes: subagents handle transient failures locally when possible, and when they cannot, they propagate structured error context rather than hiding the failure. The coordinator then decides how to proceed based on the error metadata it receives.

Automatic retry logic inside the subagent is a useful complement but does not replace structured error propagation. If all retries fail, the subagent must still report the failure with context rather than returning empty success. Similarly, the isError flag alone is insufficient without accompanying metadata about what failed and what was attempted. Learn more about error handling patterns in the Agent SDK and MCP Tools documentation.
option_feedback: Centralized logging is a useful operational practice but it is not the correct mechanism for communicating subagent failures to the coordinator during an active research run. The coordinator should receive failure information directly through the tool result response, not by polling an external log. This approach also introduces unnecessary coupling and latency, and does not address the core problem of the subagent misrepresenting failure as success in its returned result.

Returning empty results as success is a documented anti-pattern because it hides the distinction between a genuine empty result (no matching sources exist) and an access failure (a timeout prevented retrieval). When the coordinator cannot tell these apart, it cannot retry, reroute, or flag the gap, leading to silently incomplete reports. Structured error context with failure type, attempted query, and partial results is the correct fix because it gives the coordinator the information it needs to recover intelligently.

While setting the isError flag is part of correct MCP error reporting, the claim that this automatically halts the workflow and prompts the user is incorrect. The coordinator receives the flagged error and decides how to respond based on its own logic, which may include retrying, proceeding with partial results, or annotating gaps. Additionally, the isError flag alone does not convey the failure type, attempted query, or partial results that the coordinator needs to make an intelligent recovery decision.

The described problem is not about response latency or coordinator timeouts; it is about the subagent suppressing failure information entirely. Implementing retries inside the subagent may help with transient issues, but if all retries fail, the subagent still needs to propagate structured error context to the coordinator rather than returning empty success. Retries alone do not fix the fundamental problem of silent failure suppression.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with MCP servers.

Your developer productivity agent integrates with three MCP servers: a code_search server for semantic code queries, a dependency_graph server for tracing module relationships, and a test_runner server for executing test suites. During a codebase exploration session, an engineer asks the agent to "find all callers of the authenticate() function and check whether their tests pass." The agent calls code_search to locate callers, then invokes test_runner for each caller's test suite. In the logs, you notice that test_runner occasionally returns the same response structure for two very different situations: when the test infrastructure itself is unreachable (network timeout to the CI backend), and when a module simply has no associated test files. In both cases, the agent treats the response as "no tests found" and moves on without any recovery attempt or note to the engineer. What is the most significant architectural problem with this behavior, and what change would best address it?
options: The agent should use sentiment analysis on the tool response content to infer whether the absence of results reflects an error state or a genuine finding, then escalate to the engineer whenever its confidence in the interpretation falls below a threshold.

The tool conflates access failures with valid empty results, preventing the agent from distinguishing a retriable infrastructure problem from a legitimate "no tests exist" outcome. The test_runner tool should return distinct structured responses: a success response with an empty results array when no tests exist, and an error response with isError set, an errorCategory of "transient", and isRetryable set to true when the CI backend is unreachable.

The agent lacks retry logic for all tool calls, so it should implement exponential backoff around every test_runner invocation and treat any non-successful response as a transient failure worth retrying up to three times before reporting the result to the engineer.

The dependency_graph server should be updated to pre-validate that test files exist for each module before the agent invokes test_runner, so that test_runner is only called when tests are confirmed to be present and infrastructure availability issues surface as dependency_graph errors instead.
answer: The tool conflates access failures with valid empty results, preventing the agent from distinguishing a retriable infrastructure problem from a legitimate "no tests exist" outcome. The test_runner tool should return distinct structured responses: a success response with an empty results array when no tests exist, and an error response with isError set, an errorCategory of "transient", and isRetryable set to true when the CI backend is unreachable.
explanation:
A core principle of MCP tool design is that access failures and valid empty results must be structurally distinguishable. When a tool returns the same response shape for "no data exists" and "I could not reach the backend," the agent has no reliable basis for deciding whether to retry, escalate, or proceed. This is the distinction the exam guide calls out explicitly: distinguishing access failures from valid empty results in error reporting so the coordinator can make appropriate decisions.

The correct fix is to update test_runner to use the MCP isError flag pattern for infrastructure failures, paired with structured metadata: an errorCategory of "transient" and an isRetryable: true field. A genuine empty result (no test files found) should return a success response with an empty results array. This gives the agent unambiguous signals: retry or escalate on errors, report findings on success.

The blanket retry anti-pattern fails because it treats valid empty results as errors, wasting resources and potentially confusing the engineer with false "retry succeeded" signals. The sentiment analysis anti-pattern is especially problematic because it replaces structured error contracts with unreliable probabilistic inference, which is never appropriate for tool response handling. Shifting error detection to an upstream tool introduces unnecessary coupling and does not address the root cause in the tool that actually experiences the failure.

For more on structured error response design for MCP tools, see MCP Tools and Tool Use.
option_feedback: Using natural language or sentiment analysis to infer error state from tool output is an anti-pattern. Tool responses are structured data, and the agent should not rely on probabilistic interpretation to determine whether a failure occurred. This approach would be unreliable and would not address the root cause, which is that the tool itself returns structurally identical responses for two distinct outcomes.

When an MCP tool returns the same structure for a connectivity failure and a valid empty result, the agent loses the information it needs to make appropriate recovery decisions. A transient infrastructure failure warrants a retry or escalation, while a genuine absence of tests is a valid finding the agent should report. Separating these two outcomes using the isError flag, errorCategory, and isRetryable fields gives the agent the context to act correctly in each case.

Applying blanket retry logic to all tool responses conflates two fundamentally different situations: a valid empty result does not need retrying and retrying it wastes time and resources. Retrying a "no tests found" response will simply return the same empty result. The real problem is that the tool's response structure does not distinguish between the two cases, so the agent cannot know when retrying is appropriate.

Shifting responsibility to a different MCP server does not fix the underlying issue: test_runner still returns ambiguous responses when its CI backend is unreachable. Pre-validation by dependency_graph would not help if the test infrastructure fails after validation passes, and it introduces unnecessary coupling between two unrelated servers rather than fixing the error response design of the tool that actually has the problem.

question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

Your CI/CD pipeline uses Claude to extract structured code review findings from pull requests. Each finding includes fields for file_path, line_number, issue_description, and suggested_fix. After deploying the pipeline, you notice that approximately 20% of findings have a suggested_fix value that references variables, function names, or imports that do not exist anywhere in the submitted pull request diff. Developers are dismissing these findings because the suggested fixes are nonsensical, eroding trust in the entire review system.

You add a post-extraction validation step that checks each finding's suggested_fix against the actual diff content. When a finding fails this check, you want to implement a mechanism that improves output quality on a second attempt. Which approach most effectively addresses this problem?
options: Add a system prompt instruction telling Claude to only reference identifiers that are explicitly visible in the provided diff, and re-run all extractions from scratch using the updated prompt rather than implementing any per-finding retry logic.

Automatically discard any finding that fails the post-extraction validation check and proceed with only the validated findings, treating the invalid suggestions as unrecoverable errors that cannot be corrected through retry.

Send a follow-up request to Claude that includes the original diff, the failed finding, and a specific validation error message explaining which referenced identifiers were not found in the diff, so Claude can produce a corrected suggested_fix grounded in the actual code.

Increase the temperature setting for the extraction request so Claude explores a wider range of possible fixes, making it more likely to produce a suggested_fix that matches identifiers actually present in the diff.
answer: Send a follow-up request to Claude that includes the original diff, the failed finding, and a specific validation error message explaining which referenced identifiers were not found in the diff, so Claude can produce a corrected suggested_fix grounded in the actual code.
explanation:
The core pattern tested here is retry-with-error-feedback: when post-extraction validation identifies a specific failure, the most effective recovery is a follow-up request that includes the original source document, the failed extraction output, and a precise description of the validation error. This gives Claude the context it needs to correct the specific problem rather than regenerating blindly.

A key judgment call in this scenario is recognizing that the failure mode is hallucination of non-existent identifiers, not missing information in the source. The exam guide distinguishes these two cases explicitly: retries are effective when the source document contains the needed information but the model produced structural or grounding errors, and retries are ineffective when the required information simply does not exist in the provided document. Because the diff contains real code, a grounded suggested_fix is achievable through targeted retry.

The distractor involving temperature increase represents a common anti-pattern: using a randomness parameter to address a grounding problem. Higher temperature increases output diversity but does not improve factual grounding, making it likely to produce different hallucinations rather than correct ones. The silent-discard option conflates recoverable and unrecoverable failures, discarding cases where retry would succeed. The prompt-update-only option is a valid long-term improvement but does not implement the per-finding feedback loop that enables precise correction of already-identified failures.

For more on validation and retry patterns in structured extraction, see Prompt Engineering and Tool Use.
option_feedback: While improving the system prompt is a valid long-term measure, re-running all extractions from scratch to address failures that have already been identified is inefficient. More importantly, this approach does not implement a targeted feedback loop: it applies a general instruction change rather than providing Claude with the specific validation error for each failed finding, which is what enables precise self-correction on retry.

Discarding failed findings without attempting recovery conflates two distinct failure modes: cases where information is absent from the source document (where retries are ineffective) and cases where the model hallucinated references despite the information being present (where retries with specific error feedback can succeed). Since the diff contains the actual code, a grounded fix is possible and silent discard wastes an opportunity for correction.

Retry-with-error-feedback is the documented pattern for correcting structural or grounding errors in extraction output. By including the original document (the diff), the failed extraction, and a specific description of what went wrong (the referenced identifiers are absent from the diff), the follow-up request gives Claude the precise information it needs to produce a grounded correction. This is effective because the information needed for a valid fix does exist in the diff; Claude simply hallucinated references on the first attempt.

Increasing temperature makes output more random and exploratory, which is the opposite of what is needed when the problem is hallucination of non-existent identifiers. Higher temperature would increase variance in outputs but would not ground the suggested_fix in the actual diff content, making hallucination of invalid references equally or more likely on subsequent attempts.

question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

Your CI/CD pipeline runs automated code reviews on every pull request. Developer adoption has been strong, but your team lead reports that engineers on the payments service have stopped acting on review findings entirely. When you investigate, you find that the payments service has a 71% dismissal rate compared to 18% across other services. Digging into the dismissed findings, you notice they cluster around a specific category: "sensitive data exposure." The review prompt currently instructs Claude to "flag any code that could potentially expose sensitive information." You pull a sample of dismissed findings and see that Claude is flagging standard logging statements that use a custom internal logger already configured to redact PII, treating them identically to genuine hardcoded credential issues. What is the most effective change to the review prompt to address this problem?
options: Add a general instruction telling Claude to apply conservative judgment and only flag sensitive data issues when confidence is high, so borderline cases like logging statements are filtered out before appearing in review output.

Replace the single sensitive data exposure category with three subcategories (hardcoded credentials, unencrypted transmission, and logging exposure) and instruct Claude to score each subcategory independently, so the overall finding rate is distributed across more granular labels.

Add explicit criteria defining what constitutes a genuine sensitive data exposure finding, including a boundary that excludes calls to the internal PII-redacting logger, so Claude distinguishes between verified exposure risks and compliant logging patterns.

Temporarily disable the sensitive data exposure category entirely for the payments service until a better prompt is written, then re-enable it once the false positive rate has been reduced to match other services.
answer: Add explicit criteria defining what constitutes a genuine sensitive data exposure finding, including a boundary that excludes calls to the internal PII-redacting logger, so Claude distinguishes between verified exposure risks and compliant logging patterns.
explanation:
The core principle tested here is that explicit categorical criteria outperform vague or confidence-based instructions when the goal is reducing false positives in a specific category. The prompt "flag any code that could potentially expose sensitive information" is too broad: it gives Claude no way to distinguish a compliant, PII-redacting internal logger from a genuine exposure risk.

The fix is to add a specific boundary condition directly in the prompt criteria, for example: "Do not flag calls to the internal SecureLogger class, which is configured to redact PII before output. Flag only patterns where sensitive values are passed to standard output mechanisms, hardcoded in source, or transmitted without encryption." This is the kind of explicit, categorical distinction that the exam guide identifies as the most effective technique for precision improvement.

The confidence-based filtering anti-pattern (telling Claude to "be conservative" or "only flag high-confidence issues") fails because it does not resolve the underlying ambiguity. Claude still does not know the internal logger is safe, so its confidence on those calls may remain high, and the false positives persist. The exam guide explicitly identifies general confidence instructions as ineffective compared to specific categorical criteria.

Splitting into subcategories is a structural change that does not address the information gap. Disabling the category entirely trades false positives for missed detections and is only appropriate as a temporary measure alongside active prompt improvement, not as a standalone resolution when the specific failure pattern is already understood.

For further reading on designing explicit review criteria and reducing false positives, see Prompt Engineering and the Claude Code Overview.
option_feedback: General confidence-based filtering instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" are documented as ineffective at improving precision compared to specific categorical criteria. Claude has no basis for knowing that the internal logger is safe, so confidence-based filtering does not resolve the underlying ambiguity and will produce inconsistent results.

Splitting into subcategories changes the reporting structure but does not give Claude the information it needs to correctly classify the internal logger calls. Without an explicit boundary condition explaining that the internal logger performs redaction, Claude will continue flagging those calls, now under the "logging exposure" subcategory, producing the same false positives in a relabeled form.

Explicit criteria that define the boundary between reportable and non-reportable patterns directly address the root cause: Claude cannot distinguish compliant logging from genuine exposure without knowing that the internal logger already handles redaction. Adding a specific boundary condition eliminates the false positive category while preserving detection of actual risks like hardcoded credentials.

Disabling an entire finding category removes all detection capability for that category, including genuine risks like hardcoded credentials that the payments service may still introduce. While temporarily disabling high-false-positive categories can be appropriate to restore trust, it should accompany prompt improvement work, not replace it as the primary fix when the specific false positive pattern is already understood.

question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

Your CI/CD pipeline runs an automated Claude Code review on every pull request. After a developer pushes a second commit to address feedback from the first review run, the pipeline triggers again and posts a full new set of comments. Developers are complaining that issues already fixed in the second commit are being flagged again as new findings, and that issues raised in the first review but not yet addressed are being duplicated in the comment thread. What change to your pipeline design would most effectively eliminate this problem?
options: Run two independent Claude instances on each commit and only post findings that appear in both runs, using consensus to filter out issues that are inconsistently detected across review passes.
Configure the pipeline to delete all previous PR comments before each new review run, so that only the most recent set of findings is visible in the pull request at any time.
Include the findings from the prior review run in the context provided to Claude, and instruct it to report only issues that are new or that remain unaddressed since the last review.
Switch the pipeline to use the Message Batches API so that all review runs for a pull request are consolidated into a single batch job, producing one unified comment set per PR.
answer: Include the findings from the prior review run in the context provided to Claude, and instruct it to report only issues that are new or that remain unaddressed since the last review.
explanation:
When Claude Code runs automated reviews on successive commits to the same pull request, each run operates without memory of prior runs by default. Without prior context, Claude will re-flag issues that were already reported and may even re-flag issues that the developer already fixed, generating duplicate comments that erode developer trust.

The correct approach is to include prior review findings in the context of each re-review run and instruct Claude to report only issues that are new or that remain unaddressed. This is explicitly documented as a CI/CD best practice: "Including prior review findings in context when re-running reviews after new commits, instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues to avoid duplicate comments."

The consensus filtering anti-pattern (requiring findings to appear in multiple independent runs) addresses a different problem entirely: reducing false positives within a single review. Applying it across commits would suppress intermittently detected bugs and does nothing to prevent re-reporting of previously raised issues. Deleting prior comments is a surface-level workaround that destroys the review history developers depend on. The Message Batches API is designed for latency-tolerant, non-blocking workloads and is inappropriate for blocking pre-merge checks; it also does not solve the context-awareness problem.

For more on integrating Claude Code into CI/CD workflows, see Claude Code Overview and Claude Code CLI.
option_feedback: Running multiple instances for consensus is a technique for reducing false positives from a single review pass, not for eliminating duplicate comments across successive commits. This approach would suppress findings that are only caught intermittently, potentially hiding real bugs, and would not prevent the same issues from being re-reported on each new commit push.

Deleting prior comments before each run discards the historical record of what was already addressed and what remains open, making it harder for developers to track progress. This approach treats a symptom (duplicate visible comments) rather than the root cause (Claude lacking awareness of prior findings), and removes valuable context that reviewers and authors rely on during code review.

Passing prior review findings as context and instructing Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues is the documented approach for re-review runs. This prevents duplicate comments by giving Claude the information it needs to distinguish between issues that have been resolved and issues that are genuinely new or persistent.

The Message Batches API is designed for latency-tolerant, non-blocking workloads and does not support multi-turn tool calling within a single request. More importantly, batching review runs together does not solve the root problem: each run still lacks awareness of what prior runs already reported, so duplicates would persist within the consolidated output.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with MCP servers.

Your developer productivity agent integrates with three MCP servers: a legacy issue tracker that returns timestamps as Unix epoch integers, a modern code review service that uses ISO 8601 strings, and a deployment pipeline tool that encodes build status as numeric codes (0 = success, 1 = pending, 2 = failed). Engineers report that when the agent synthesizes information across all three tools in a single response, it frequently misinterprets timestamps and misrepresents build statuses. For example, it conflates a Unix timestamp like 1700000000 with a build status code, and it struggles to compare dates across the two different timestamp formats. You need to ensure the agent always receives normalized, consistent data regardless of which combination of tools it calls. What is the most appropriate architectural approach to address this?
options: Update the system prompt to instruct the agent on how to interpret each tool's output format, explaining that the legacy tracker uses Unix epochs, the code review service uses ISO 8601, and numeric codes represent build statuses with specific meanings.
Replace the three separate MCP tools with a single unified wrapper tool that internally calls each service and normalizes all output formats before returning a consolidated response to the agent.

Add few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating correct interpretation of each format combination, showing the agent how to handle Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings, and numeric status codes when they appear together in tool results.

Implement PostToolUse hooks that intercept each tool's output and normalize the data before the agent processes it, converting Unix timestamps and ISO 8601 strings to a consistent format and mapping numeric status codes to descriptive strings.
answer: Implement PostToolUse hooks that intercept each tool's output and normalize the data before the agent processes it, converting Unix timestamps and ISO 8601 strings to a consistent format and mapping numeric status codes to descriptive strings.
explanation:
PostToolUse hooks are the correct architectural tool for this scenario because they intercept tool results after execution but before the model processes them, enabling deterministic data transformation at the infrastructure layer rather than relying on the model to correctly interpret inconsistent formats at inference time.

The exam guide explicitly identifies this pattern: "Implementing PostToolUse hooks to normalize heterogeneous data formats (Unix timestamps, ISO 8601, numeric status codes) from different MCP tools before the agent processes them." This is a direct application of the principle that hooks should be chosen over prompt-based approaches when business rules require guaranteed compliance. When three tools return incompatible data representations, normalization must happen deterministically on every call, not probabilistically based on instructions or examples.

The system prompt and few-shot approaches are anti-patterns here because they shift the normalization burden to the model's inference process. The model may handle familiar format combinations correctly but will occasionally fail when values from different tools appear together in ambiguous contexts, exactly the failure mode described in the question. The unified wrapper approach is over-engineered and conflates normalization with tool interface design, creating unnecessary coupling.

The key architectural principle is: use hooks for transformations that must be guaranteed on every invocation, and reserve prompt-based guidance for behaviors that are advisory or context-dependent. Learn more about hook patterns and tool result handling in the Agent SDK documentation.
option_feedback: Relying on system prompt instructions to guide format interpretation is a probabilistic approach that does not guarantee consistent behavior. The agent may correctly apply the instructions in most cases but will occasionally misinterpret values, especially when multiple heterogeneous formats appear together in a single context window. This does not provide the deterministic normalization that the cross-tool synthesis problem requires.

Consolidating tools into a single wrapper changes the tool interface and eliminates the agent's ability to selectively call individual services based on context. This approach also violates the principle of tool separation and would require significant refactoring of the MCP server layer. It conflates the normalization concern with the tool interface design, creating a tightly coupled solution when a lightweight interception mechanism already exists for exactly this purpose.

Few-shot examples improve the agent's ability to generalize to similar patterns but still depend on probabilistic inference at runtime. When three tools with incompatible formats are called together, the agent must still reason about which format applies to each value, creating opportunities for confusion. This approach addresses the symptom through prompt engineering rather than eliminating the inconsistency at the data layer where it originates.

PostToolUse hooks are designed exactly for this scenario: they intercept tool results after execution and before the model processes them, allowing deterministic transformation of heterogeneous data formats into a consistent representation. This guarantees normalization on every invocation regardless of which tools are called, without relying on the agent to correctly interpret inconsistent formats at inference time.

question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

Your multi-agent research system has been running in production for several weeks. The coordinator agent delegates research tasks to a web search subagent, a document analysis subagent, and a synthesis subagent. You notice that the synthesis subagent frequently produces reports that attribute findings to the wrong sources, merge statistics from different studies without distinguishing their origins, and occasionally cite URLs that were never part of the research. You review the coordinator's implementation and find that after the web search and document analysis subagents complete their work, the coordinator calls the synthesis subagent with a prompt that says: "Synthesize the research findings on this topic and produce a comprehensive report with citations." No additional content is passed in the prompt. What is the most likely root cause of the attribution and citation errors in the synthesis output?
options: The synthesis subagent has access to too many tools, causing it to re-run its own web searches that return different results than the original web search subagent retrieved, leading to source divergence in the final report.

The synthesis subagent does not receive the actual findings from the prior subagents in its prompt, so it has no source material to work from and generates plausible-sounding but fabricated citations.

The web search subagent and document analysis subagent return their findings in incompatible formats, causing the synthesis subagent to misparse the structured data and scramble source attributions when combining results from both subagents.

The coordinator's system prompt does not explicitly instruct the synthesis subagent to preserve citation formatting, so the subagent reformats source references during synthesis and loses fidelity to the original URLs and statistics.
answer: The synthesis subagent does not receive the actual findings from the prior subagents in its prompt, so it has no source material to work from and generates plausible-sounding but fabricated citations.
explanation:
In multi-agent systems built with the Claude Agent SDK, subagents do not automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history or the outputs of other subagents. Each subagent operates with an isolated context that contains only what is explicitly provided in its prompt. When the synthesis subagent receives a generic instruction like "Synthesize the research findings" with no actual findings attached, it has no grounding material and will generate plausible-sounding but fabricated content from its training data, including invented citations.

The correct pattern is to include complete findings from prior subagents directly in the synthesis subagent's prompt. This means the coordinator must collect the structured outputs from the web search and document analysis subagents, then pass that content explicitly when invoking synthesis. For citation integrity, the findings should be structured to preserve claim-source mappings: each finding paired with its source URL, document name, and relevant excerpt, so the synthesis subagent has accurate attribution data to work from rather than having to reconstruct it.

The fabricated URLs are a key diagnostic signal here. Format mismatches or tool over-provisioning would produce errors with real source material; hallucinated URLs that were never retrieved indicate the subagent had no access to the actual research content at all. This is the classic symptom of missing explicit context passing in a multi-agent pipeline.

Learn more about subagent context passing and spawning patterns at Agent SDK and Claude Code Sub-agents.
option_feedback: While over-provisioning tools is a real concern in multi-agent systems, the described symptoms (wrong source attribution, merged statistics, fabricated URLs) are characteristic of a subagent generating content without grounding in actual retrieved findings. If the synthesis subagent were conducting its own searches, it would at least cite real URLs it found rather than fabricated ones, and the issue would be framed as duplicate or divergent search results rather than citation hallucination.

Subagents do not automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history or the outputs of sibling subagents. When the synthesis subagent receives only a generic instruction with no findings passed explicitly in the prompt, it has no access to the actual research content and must generate citations from its training data, producing hallucinated or misattributed sources. This is the documented behavior: context must be explicitly provided in the subagent's prompt.

Format incompatibility between subagent outputs is a real integration challenge, but it would only apply if the synthesis subagent were actually receiving those outputs. Since the coordinator passes only a generic instruction with no findings content, there is nothing to misparse. Format normalization problems manifest as garbled or merged data from real sources, not as completely fabricated URLs that were never retrieved during the research session.

Formatting instructions in the system prompt can influence how citations are rendered, but they cannot compensate for the absence of actual source material. If the synthesis subagent had received the real findings with accurate URLs and statistics, a formatting issue would produce incorrectly formatted citations, not fabricated URLs that were never part of the research. The root cause is missing input content, not missing output formatting guidance.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with MCP servers.

Your team uses a long-running Claude agent session to explore a large legacy payment processing codebase. An engineer spent two hours building up session context: the agent mapped the transaction routing layer, identified deprecated API call sites, and traced data flow through several middleware components. The engineer then closed the laptop overnight. The next morning, they reopen the session and ask the agent to continue investigating the fee calculation module. The agent begins referencing "typical patterns in payment systems" and describes middleware behavior in generic terms rather than citing the specific classes and method names it had identified the previous day. The session has become unreliable. What is the most effective approach for the engineer to continue this investigation productively?
options: Resume the existing session using the --resume flag with the session name, then provide the agent with the names of the specific files and modules examined yesterday so it can re-anchor its understanding without re-exploring the full codebase.

Start a new session and inject a structured summary of the prior session's key findings (specific class names, data flow paths, deprecated call sites) into the initial context, then continue the investigation from that foundation.

Resume the existing session and instruct the agent to re-read all files it analyzed yesterday, then re-run its earlier Grep and Glob queries so it can rebuild its understanding of the codebase from scratch before continuing.

Continue in the existing session and use the /compact command to summarize the conversation history, which will consolidate the accumulated context and restore the agent's ability to reference specific classes and methods it identified previously.
answer: Start a new session and inject a structured summary of the prior session's key findings (specific class names, data flow paths, deprecated call sites) into the initial context, then continue the investigation from that foundation.
explanation:
The exam guide identifies a key judgment call in session management: choosing between session resumption and starting fresh with an injected summary. The guidance is to prefer resumption when prior context is mostly valid, but to start a new session with a structured summary when prior tool results are stale.

In this scenario, the agent is already exhibiting the classic symptom of context degradation: it references "typical patterns" and generic behavior instead of the specific classes and methods it discovered. This indicates the session's internal state can no longer reliably surface the earlier findings, making resumption counterproductive. The right move is to extract the valuable knowledge from the prior session into a structured summary and inject it into a fresh session's initial context.

The /compact distractor is a common anti-pattern here. While /compact is useful for reducing context window pressure during an active session, it cannot recover lost specificity in a session that has already degraded. Similarly, re-exploring the codebase from scratch within the same degraded session wastes the prior work rather than preserving it.

The resumption distractor (using --resume with file names) represents the correct approach for a different scenario: when a session is paused but still healthy and the engineer wants to re-anchor after a break. The distinction is whether the session context is mostly valid (resume) or has already degraded to unreliable output (start fresh with summary).

Learn more about session management patterns at Claude Code CLI and Claude Code Overview.
option_feedback: Resuming the existing session and providing file names as re-anchors is the correct approach when prior tool results are still valid and the session context is mostly intact. However, the scenario describes a session that has already degraded to producing generic answers rather than specific findings, indicating the session state is no longer reliable. In this case, resuming the degraded session and feeding it file names is less effective than starting fresh with a structured summary of the actual findings.

When prior tool results have become stale and the session is producing generic answers instead of referencing specific discovered artifacts, starting fresh with an injected summary is more reliable than resuming. The summary preserves the valuable findings from the prior session while giving the new session clean, accurate context to reason from, avoiding the degraded state of the old session.

Instructing the agent to re-explore the entire codebase from scratch within the degraded session does not address the root cause, which is that the session context has become unreliable. This approach wastes time duplicating prior work and still leaves the agent operating within a compromised context window rather than starting fresh with a clean, accurate foundation.

/compact reduces context usage by summarizing conversation history, but it cannot restore accurate references to specific code artifacts that the session has already lost track of. Compacting a degraded session may further compress or lose the precise details (class names, method signatures, data flow paths) that the investigation depends on, rather than recovering them.

question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

You are building a multi-agent research system using the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: one searches the web, one analyzes documents, one synthesizes findings, and one generates reports. The system researches topics and produces comprehensive, cited reports.

Your multi-agent research system has grown to include several MCP servers: a web search server, a document retrieval server, an academic database server, and a citation formatting server. Your team wants to add a new Jira MCP server so the report-generation subagent can automatically create project tickets for follow-up research tasks identified in the final report.

A junior engineer on your team proposes building a custom Jira MCP server from scratch, reasoning that a custom implementation will let the team control exactly which Jira fields and workflows are exposed to the agent. You have found an existing, well-maintained community MCP server for Jira that covers the operations your team needs.

What is the most appropriate approach for integrating Jira into the system, and why?
options: Configure the Jira MCP server at user scope in each developer's personal configuration file so that individual team members can customize which Jira operations their local agent instance exposes.
Build a custom Jira MCP server so that only the specific ticket creation and field mapping operations the team needs are exposed, reducing the risk of the agent misusing broader Jira functionality.

Defer adding Jira integration until the team has evaluated whether the community server's tool descriptions are detailed enough, since inadequate descriptions will cause the agent to ignore the Jira tools in favor of built-in alternatives.
Use the existing community Jira MCP server rather than building a custom one, reserving custom server development for workflows that community servers cannot support.
