Aggregating dismissed findings by detected_pattern produces a ranked list of the actual patterns driving false positives, enabling surgical prompt improvements.

The exam guide explicitly calls out the detected_pattern field as the mechanism for tracking which code constructs trigger findings and enabling systematic analysis of dismissal patterns. This is the feedback loop design principle: structured metadata in the output enables data-driven prompt iteration rather than guesswork.

Confidence-based filtering is a well-documented anti-pattern in this context. It reduces visible finding volume without improving the underlying prompt quality, and LLM self-reported confidence scores are poorly calibrated for distinguishing genuine issues from false positives. The exam guide specifically warns against relying on self-reported confidence scores as proxies for case complexity or finding quality.

Free-text rationale fields provide qualitative insight but cannot be aggregated systematically at scale. Subtype taxonomies describe the nature of the finding rather than the code construct that triggered it, so they do not surface the structural patterns causing false positives. Only a structured detected_pattern field with consistent categorical values enables the kind of quantitative dismissal analysis needed to drive targeted improvements.

For more on structured output design and feedback loop patterns, see Tool Use and Prompt Engineering.
option_feedback: Confidence-based suppression is an anti-pattern for this problem: it reduces finding volume but does not reveal which patterns are causing false positives or help improve the underlying prompt. Self-reported LLM confidence scores are also poorly calibrated and do not reliably distinguish genuine coverage gaps from false positives, so this approach masks the symptom without addressing the root cause.

Subdividing findings by coverage type describes what kind of test is missing rather than what code construct triggered the finding. Knowing that dismissed findings are mostly "missing unit test" subtypes does not reveal whether the false positives come from private methods, generated code, test utilities, or other specific patterns. This approach shifts the taxonomy without capturing the structural code characteristics that drive the false positive rate.

While a rationale field provides some qualitative insight, free-text reasoning is difficult to aggregate systematically across hundreds of dismissed findings. Unlike a structured detected_pattern field with consistent categorical values, rationale text requires manual reading and subjective interpretation, making it impractical for the systematic pattern analysis needed to drive targeted prompt improvements at scale.

A detected_pattern field captures the specific code construct that caused each finding, such as "private helper method," "test utility function," or "abstract base class." When developers dismiss findings, aggregating dismissed findings by detected_pattern reveals exactly which code patterns the current prompt over-flags, enabling precise, targeted prompt improvements rather than broad rewrites based on guesswork.

question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

Your CI pipeline generates test cases for every pull request using Claude Code. After running the system for three weeks, you review the output and find that Claude consistently produces tests covering only the "happy path" for new functions, missing edge cases like null inputs, empty collections, and boundary values. You have already tried updating the CLAUDE.md instructions with a detailed prose description of edge case categories, but the output remains inconsistent: some runs include edge cases thoroughly while others ignore them entirely. What is the most effective next step to improve the reliability of edge case coverage across all runs?
options: Provide 2 to 3 concrete examples in the prompt showing a sample function alongside its complete test suite, including annotated edge case tests, so Claude can generalize the expected pattern to new functions.

Add a confidence threshold instruction to the prompt telling Claude to only generate tests it is highly confident are correct, and to skip any test scenario where it is uncertain about expected behavior.

Restructure the pipeline to run three independent Claude Code test generation passes on each function and then merge only the test scenarios that appear in at least two of the three outputs, using consensus to filter for reliability.

Switch to running Claude Code in plan mode before each test generation session so it produces an explicit outline of all test scenarios for review before writing any test code, adding a manual approval gate to the pipeline.
answer: Provide 2 to 3 concrete examples in the prompt showing a sample function alongside its complete test suite, including annotated edge case tests, so Claude can generalize the expected pattern to new functions.
explanation:
When Claude produces inconsistent output despite detailed prose instructions, the most effective intervention is providing concrete input/output examples. Natural language descriptions of transformations like "include edge cases" are interpreted differently across runs because the model must infer what counts as an edge case from abstract categories. A concrete example showing a real function alongside its complete test suite, with edge case tests explicitly present, gives Claude a pattern to generalize rather than a rule to interpret.

This is the core principle behind few-shot prompting for iterative refinement: when instructions alone produce inconsistency, examples anchor the expected output format and content. Two to three well-chosen examples covering null inputs, boundary values, and empty collections are far more effective than expanding the prose description of those same categories.

The confidence threshold anti-pattern is a common but ineffective response to inconsistency. Asking Claude to self-filter based on confidence does not address the interpretive ambiguity causing the inconsistency and tends to reduce coverage of the less common scenarios (edge cases) that are the exact target of improvement. Similarly, multi-pass consensus filtering would systematically suppress the infrequently generated edge case tests, worsening the problem it attempts to solve.

Plan mode is appropriate for complex, open-ended architectural decisions, not for improving the consistency of a well-scoped repeatable task. Adding a manual approval gate also undermines the automation goals of a CI pipeline.

For more on iterative refinement techniques including input/output examples and test-driven iteration, see Claude Code Overview and Prompt Engineering.
option_feedback: When prose descriptions produce inconsistent results, concrete input/output examples are the most effective technique for communicating expected transformations. By showing a sample function paired with a complete test suite that explicitly includes edge cases, Claude can generalize the pattern to new functions rather than relying on ambiguous natural language instructions that are interpreted differently across runs.

Asking Claude to self-filter based on internal confidence is an anti-pattern for this problem. This approach would likely reduce edge case coverage further, since edge cases by definition involve less common behavior that Claude may feel less certain about. The root cause is inconsistent pattern interpretation, not overconfident test generation.

Running multiple passes and requiring consensus would suppress edge case tests, since edge cases are by nature less likely to be generated consistently across independent runs. This approach penalizes exactly the coverage the team wants to improve and adds significant latency and cost to the CI pipeline without addressing the underlying inconsistency.

Plan mode is designed for complex architectural decisions and large-scale changes, not for improving the consistency of a well-defined repeatable task like test generation. Adding a manual approval gate also contradicts the goal of automated CI feedback and does not address the root cause of inconsistent pattern application.

question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

Your CI/CD pipeline runs automated code reviews on pull requests. A senior engineer reports that the review output for a 22-file PR touching the authentication module, the payment processing service, and the shared utility library is inconsistent: some files receive detailed, actionable feedback while others get only surface-level comments. More troubling, the review flags a null-check pattern as a potential bug in the authentication module but approves identical null-check patterns in the payment service. The pipeline runs a single pass that sends all 22 files to Claude simultaneously. How should you restructure the review architecture to address these consistency problems?
options: Run three independent full-PR review passes simultaneously and report only findings that appear in at least two of the three passes, using consensus to filter inconsistent results and improve overall reliability.

Increase the token budget allocated to the single-pass review by switching to a model with a larger context window, giving Claude more capacity to attend to all 22 files simultaneously without quality degradation.

Require developers to split large PRs into smaller submissions of five or fewer files before automated review runs, enforcing a PR size policy so the single-pass architecture can operate within its reliable range.

Split the review into two passes: a per-file pass where each file is analyzed independently for local issues, followed by a separate cross-file integration pass that examines data flow and shared contracts across all 22 files.
answer: Split the review into two passes: a per-file pass where each file is analyzed independently for local issues, followed by a separate cross-file integration pass that examines data flow and shared contracts across all 22 files.
explanation:
When a single-pass review processes many files simultaneously, attention dilution causes two related problems: uneven depth across files and contradictory findings where the same code pattern is evaluated differently depending on where it appears in the input. The fix is a multi-pass architecture that separates concerns.

The first pass analyzes each file independently, ensuring every file receives the same focused attention regardless of PR size. The second pass examines cross-file integration concerns such as shared data contracts, API compatibility, and data flow across module boundaries. These two passes are complementary: local issues (null checks, error handling, input validation) are best caught in isolation, while integration issues (inconsistent type expectations between the authentication module and the payment service) require a holistic view.

The consensus-voting approach is an anti-pattern: it does not fix the attention problem and actively suppresses findings that only emerge in one pass due to that same dilution. A larger context window is similarly ineffective because attention quality, not context capacity, is the limiting factor. Enforcing PR size limits addresses the symptom at the cost of developer workflow without improving the underlying review system.

Learn more about multi-pass review design and CI/CD integration at Claude Code Overview and Prompt Engineering.
option_feedback: Requiring consensus across multiple full-PR passes suppresses valid findings rather than fixing the root cause. A real bug that only surfaces in one pass due to attention dilution would be filtered out, reducing recall rather than improving consistency. This approach masks the problem instead of solving it.

A larger context window does not resolve attention dilution. The issue is that attention quality degrades when many files compete for focus in one pass, not that the files exceed the context limit. Switching to a higher-capacity model without changing the review architecture leaves the fundamental consistency problem unaddressed.

Imposing a PR size limit shifts the burden to developers and changes team workflow without improving the review system itself. It also does not address the cross-file integration analysis that a multi-pass architecture provides, and it treats the symptom (large PRs) rather than the architectural root cause (single-pass attention dilution).

Splitting into focused per-file passes and a separate integration pass directly addresses both symptoms: inconsistent depth (each file gets dedicated attention) and contradictory findings (the same pattern is evaluated in isolation per file, then cross-file interactions are assessed separately). This is the documented multi-pass architecture for large reviews.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with MCP servers.

Your developer productivity agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases. The agent has access to a single analyze_code tool whose description reads: "Analyzes code and returns useful information about it." Engineers report that the agent frequently produces low-quality results: when asked to summarize what a module does, the agent returns raw data points instead of a narrative; when asked to verify whether a specific claim about the code is accurate, the agent returns a summary instead; and when asked to extract configuration values from a config file, the agent sometimes returns a summary or a verification result instead of the extracted values. The tool's implementation actually supports three distinct operations internally, but all three share the same entry point and description. What is the most effective structural change to address this pattern of mismatched outputs?
options: Keep analyze_code as a single tool but expand its description to include all three operation modes, listing each mode by name and describing what it returns, so the model can select the correct mode by including the mode name in its tool call arguments.

Implement a pre-processing classifier that inspects each user request before it reaches the agent, routes it to a specialized sub-prompt tuned for that operation type, and then calls analyze_code with a structured payload indicating which operation to perform.

Split analyze_code into three purpose-specific tools (such as summarize_content, extract_data_points, and verify_claim_against_source), each with a description that defines its distinct input contract, expected output format, and the scenarios where it should be used instead of the alternatives.

Add few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating the correct tool call for each request type (summarization, extraction, verification), so the model learns to match request phrasing to the appropriate internal operation via pattern recognition.
answer: Split analyze_code into three purpose-specific tools (such as summarize_content, extract_data_points, and verify_claim_against_source), each with a description that defines its distinct input contract, expected output format, and the scenarios where it should be used instead of the alternatives.
explanation:
Splitting generic tools into purpose-specific tools is the correct structural response when a single tool wraps multiple distinct operations that differ in their input contracts, output formats, and usage contexts. The exam guide explicitly identifies this skill: "Splitting generic tools into purpose-specific tools with defined input/output contracts (e.g., splitting a generic analyze_document into extract_data_points, summarize_content, and verify_claim_against_source)."

The core principle is that tool descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection. When a description is ambiguous or covers multiple operations, the model lacks the signal needed to predict which behavior will result from a call. Purpose-specific tools allow each description to define a clear boundary: what inputs are expected, what the output will look like, and when to use this tool versus a similar alternative.

The "expand the description with modes" option is a common but flawed approach. It increases description complexity without eliminating the fundamental ambiguity, and it forces the model to parse a compound description and correctly populate a mode parameter, which is less reliable than matching a focused, single-purpose description.

The "few-shot examples" option represents an anti-pattern for this problem: applying a prompt-layer fix to a structural tool design problem. Examples help with edge cases and format consistency, but they do not substitute for a well-designed tool interface when the root cause is ambiguous boundaries between operations.

For further reading, see Tool Use and the Agent SDK documentation.
option_feedback: Adding operation modes to a single tool description increases the cognitive load the model must resolve at selection time and introduces ambiguity about which mode argument to pass. When operations have genuinely distinct input types, output contracts, and usage boundaries, consolidating them into one tool with a mode parameter produces less reliable selection than purpose-specific tools with independent descriptions, because the model must parse a compound description rather than match a clear, focused one.

Building a separate routing classifier adds significant infrastructure complexity to work around a tool design problem that can be solved directly. This approach also bypasses the model's natural language understanding by replacing tool description matching with a brittle keyword classifier, creating a maintenance burden whenever new request phrasings emerge. Fixing the tool interface is the proportionate, lower-complexity solution before introducing additional pipeline stages.

When a single generic tool wraps multiple distinct operations, the model cannot reliably select the correct internal behavior because the description provides no signal about which operation to invoke or what output to expect. Splitting into purpose-specific tools with well-defined input contracts, output formats, and boundary explanations gives the model the information it needs to route each request correctly. This directly addresses the root cause: ambiguous tool boundaries, not implementation bugs.

Few-shot examples can improve consistency for known phrasing patterns, but they do not fix the underlying structural problem: a single tool with an ambiguous description that gives the model no principled basis for distinguishing operations. Examples teach pattern matching for the cases shown but do not generalize reliably to novel phrasings. The root cause is inadequate tool interface design, not insufficient training signal in the prompt.

question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to backend systems through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

Your customer support agent uses a coordinator that delegates billing dispute investigations to a specialized billing subagent. The coordinator invokes the billing subagent after the web search subagent has already retrieved the customer's account history and recent transaction records. In production, you observe that the billing subagent consistently ignores the transaction records already retrieved and re-fetches the same data using its own MCP tool calls, adding 8-12 seconds of unnecessary latency per case and occasionally retrieving stale data between the two fetches.

A senior engineer reviews the coordinator's subagent invocation code and finds that the Task tool prompt sent to the billing subagent contains only: "Investigate this billing dispute and identify whether a refund is warranted." The transaction records retrieved by the web search subagent are stored in the coordinator's conversation history but are not included in the billing subagent's prompt.

What is the most direct fix for this behavior?
options: Include the transaction records retrieved by the web search subagent directly in the Task tool prompt sent to the billing subagent, alongside the dispute instructions.

Restructure the pipeline so the billing subagent runs before the web search subagent, eliminating the dependency on prior subagent outputs and allowing it to fetch transaction records independently as the first step.

Configure the billing subagent's AgentDefinition to include a shared_context flag that enables it to read from the coordinator's conversation history at invocation time, avoiding the need to pass data explicitly in each prompt.
Add an instruction to the coordinator's system prompt specifying that subagents should use data already retrieved by prior subagents before making their own tool calls, to avoid redundant fetching.
answer: Include the transaction records retrieved by the web search subagent directly in the Task tool prompt sent to the billing subagent, alongside the dispute instructions.
explanation:
The root cause of the redundant fetching is a fundamental property of multi-agent systems: subagents have isolated context and do not inherit the coordinator's conversation history or outputs from sibling subagents. The only information a subagent receives is what the coordinator explicitly includes in its Task tool prompt.

When the coordinator invokes the billing subagent with only a brief instruction and no data, the billing subagent has no way to know that transaction records already exist. From its perspective, it must fetch everything it needs. The correct fix is for the coordinator to embed the retrieved transaction records directly in the Task tool prompt, passing the data as explicit context alongside the investigation instructions.

The distractor involving a shared_context flag represents an invented feature that does not exist in the Agent SDK. The system prompt distractor fails because coordinator-level instructions do not propagate into subagent prompts. The pipeline reordering option is an anti-pattern that trades one inefficiency for another without addressing the isolation property.

This pattern of explicit context passing is essential for all multi-agent handoffs: structured findings from prior agents (account history, transaction records, search results) must be serialized into the downstream subagent's prompt to avoid redundant work and data staleness. See Claude Code Sub-agents and Agent SDK for more on subagent context management.
option_feedback: Subagents do not automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history or outputs from sibling subagents. The only context a subagent receives is what is explicitly included in its Task tool prompt. Embedding the already-retrieved transaction records directly in the prompt eliminates redundant fetches and ensures the billing subagent operates on the same data the coordinator already has.

Reordering the pipeline to make the billing subagent run first does not resolve the underlying problem and introduces a different inefficiency: the transaction records would still be fetched twice (once by billing, once by web search) and the billing subagent would lack any account history context that the web search subagent was intended to provide. This is a restructuring anti-pattern that avoids the real fix.

There is no shared_context flag or automatic history inheritance mechanism in the AgentDefinition configuration. Subagents always operate with isolated context and cannot read the coordinator's conversation history at invocation time. Any data a subagent needs must be explicitly included in its Task tool prompt by the coordinator.

Coordinator system prompt instructions do not propagate into subagent context. Subagents operate with isolated context and only receive what is included in their specific Task tool prompt. Instructing the coordinator to tell subagents to reuse prior data does not work because subagents cannot access the coordinator's conversation history regardless of instructions.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with MCP servers.

A senior engineer on your team frequently invokes a codebase exploration skill that runs a series of Grep, Glob, and Read operations across the repository to map out module boundaries and dependency chains. The skill produces several hundred lines of file listings, import graphs, and annotated summaries before returning a final structured overview. After each invocation, the engineer notices that subsequent requests in the same session behave inconsistently: Claude references stale file paths from the exploration output, conflates findings from different invocations, and occasionally loses track of the task the engineer was working on before running the skill.

The engineer wants to add a parameter prompt so that when they type the skill name without any arguments, Claude asks them which module or subsystem to scope the exploration to. They also want to ensure the exploration output stays completely isolated from the rest of their working session.

Which skill frontmatter configuration achieves both goals?
options: Set context: fork and add the target module as an allowed-tools restriction, so the skill only reads files matching the module path and automatically scopes itself without requiring a separate parameter prompt.

Omit context: fork so the main session retains the full exploration output for follow-up questions, and add an argument-hint field to prompt for the target module, relying on the session's context window to keep exploration findings and active work separate.
Set context: fork and add an argument-hint field describing the target module or subsystem, so the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context and prompts for scope when invoked without arguments.

Set context: fork and define a required input field in the skill's SKILL.md body, instructing Claude to refuse execution and ask for the module name if the field is absent from the invocation command.
answer: Set context: fork and add an argument-hint field describing the target module or subsystem, so the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context and prompts for scope when invoked without arguments.
explanation:
Claude Code skills support a set of SKILL.md frontmatter fields that control execution behavior and developer experience. Two fields are directly relevant here: context: fork and argument-hint.

context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, meaning its output (file listings, import graphs, annotated summaries) does not accumulate in the main conversation history. This prevents the stale-path and context-conflation problems described in the scenario. Without this setting, every exploration invocation adds hundreds of lines to the session context, degrading subsequent response quality.

argument-hint is the dedicated frontmatter mechanism for prompting developers when they invoke a skill without arguments. When the engineer types the skill name alone, Claude presents the hint text and waits for the scope parameter before executing. This is the correct, purpose-built approach rather than embedding refusal logic in the SKILL.md body, which would rely on probabilistic LLM instruction-following.

The allowed-tools field controls which tools the skill may call during execution (for example, limiting a skill to file write operations to prevent destructive actions). It has no role in runtime parameter collection or scoping, making the option that conflates it with parameter prompting a plausible but incorrect distractor.

Omitting context: fork while adding argument-hint addresses only one of the two goals and perpetuates the exact interference pattern the engineer is trying to eliminate. This is the explicit anti-pattern: assuming the context window will naturally separate verbose skill output from active work.

Learn more about skill frontmatter configuration at Claude Code Overview and CLAUDE.md Configuration.
option_feedback: The allowed-tools frontmatter field restricts which tools the skill can invoke during execution, not which file paths or modules are in scope. It cannot serve as a parameter prompt mechanism. Using it this way conflates tool access control with runtime parameter collection, which are separate concerns addressed by separate frontmatter fields.

Omitting context: fork is the anti-pattern the scenario describes: verbose exploration output accumulates in the main session, causing Claude to reference stale paths and conflate findings across invocations. Relying on the context window to naturally separate exploration output from active work does not prevent the interference described, and is explicitly what context: fork is designed to avoid.

The context: fork frontmatter option runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, preventing its verbose output from polluting the main conversation. The argument-hint field prompts the developer for a required parameter when the skill is invoked without arguments. Together these two frontmatter fields directly address both goals described in the scenario.

While context: fork correctly isolates skill output, asking Claude to refuse execution based on instructions in the SKILL.md body is a prompt-based approach that relies on probabilistic LLM compliance rather than the dedicated frontmatter mechanism designed for this purpose. The argument-hint frontmatter field is the documented way to prompt developers for required parameters at invocation time.

question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to backend systems through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

Your customer support agent currently has access to all five MCP tools: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human, and a newly added update_account tool for modifying contact details, notification preferences, and payment methods. Production logs show the agent is performing well on billing disputes and returns, but you notice it occasionally calls update_account during refund workflows to "proactively update the customer's preferred refund method," even when the customer made no such request. The agent also sometimes calls process_refund during account update requests when it infers the customer might want a refund based on complaint language. You have 18 additional tools planned for upcoming quarters across billing, shipping, and fraud detection. What is the most effective architectural change to address the current misuse and prepare for this growth?
options: Replace the five individual tools with two consolidated tools: a transaction_operations tool that internally routes between customer lookup, order lookup, and refund processing, and an account_operations tool that handles all account modifications, reducing the number of tool choices the agent must make.

Implement a pre-tool-use hook that inspects each tool call, detects cross-domain invocations by comparing the active workflow context against a hardcoded mapping of allowed tools per workflow type, and blocks disallowed calls with an error message redirecting the agent to the appropriate tool.

Partition the agent into role-specific subagents, each with a restricted tool set matching its function: a transaction subagent with get_customer, lookup_order, and process_refund, and an account subagent with get_customer and update_account, with escalate_to_human available to both, and a coordinator routing requests to the appropriate subagent.

Add explicit instructions to the system prompt prohibiting the agent from calling update_account during refund workflows and from calling process_refund unless the customer explicitly requests a refund, and include few-shot examples demonstrating correct tool selection for each request type.
answer: Partition the agent into role-specific subagents, each with a restricted tool set matching its function: a transaction subagent with get_customer, lookup_order, and process_refund, and an account subagent with get_customer and update_account, with escalate_to_human available to both, and a coordinator routing requests to the appropriate subagent.
explanation:
The core principle tested here is scoped tool access: giving each agent only the tools it needs for its specific role. When an agent has access to tools outside its domain, it will occasionally misuse them, particularly when customer language contains signals that activate unintended tool associations. The exam guide states that "giving an agent access to too many tools degrades tool selection reliability by increasing decision complexity" and that "agents with tools outside their specialization tend to misuse them."

The correct architectural response is to decompose the single agent into role-specific subagents with restricted tool sets. A transaction subagent handles order and refund operations; an account subagent handles contact and payment modifications. Each subagent only sees the tools relevant to its function, making cross-domain misuse structurally impossible rather than probabilistically discouraged. This pattern also scales predictably: new billing, shipping, and fraud tools can be assigned to purpose-specific subagents without inflating the decision space for existing agents.

The prompt-based restriction option is a classic anti-pattern for tool scoping problems. Instructions reduce misuse rates but cannot enforce them, and reliability degrades as tool count grows. The tool consolidation option moves in the wrong direction by bundling distinct operations together, making descriptions less precise. The hook-based runtime inspection option solves the symptom rather than the cause and creates a maintenance burden as the tool catalog expands.

For more on tool distribution and scoped access patterns, see Tool Use and Agent SDK.
option_feedback: Consolidating tools into broad multi-purpose tools hides the action boundaries from the model and makes tool descriptions harder to write clearly, which tends to worsen selection reliability rather than improve it. The underlying issue is that the agent has access to tools outside its current task scope, which consolidation does not resolve since both domains remain accessible in a single call.

While hooks can enforce business rules, using them to replicate tool access scoping through runtime inspection adds significant complexity compared to simply restricting which tools each agent can see. This approach also requires maintaining a separate workflow-to-tool mapping that must be updated as tools are added, creating ongoing maintenance burden without addressing the architectural root cause of over-provisioning.

Restricting each subagent to only the tools relevant to its role directly prevents cross-domain tool misuse by making out-of-scope tools unavailable rather than relying on the model to avoid calling them. This also scales well: as new tools are added, they can be assigned to the appropriate specialized subagent without increasing decision complexity for any single agent.

Prompt-based restrictions reduce misuse probabilistically but cannot guarantee correct behavior, especially as tool count grows. The exam guide specifically identifies over-provisioning agents with too many tools as degrading tool selection reliability, and prompt instructions do not address that root cause. With 18 additional tools planned, this approach will become increasingly unreliable.

question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to backend systems through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

Your customer support agent has been deployed for three weeks. Reviewing the escalation logs, you notice a pattern: when customers express frustration or use emotionally charged language (phrases like "this is ridiculous" or "I've been waiting forever"), the agent immediately invokes escalate_to_human without attempting to investigate or resolve the issue. In many of these cases, the underlying problem turns out to be a straightforward order status question or a standard return that the agent is fully capable of handling. Meanwhile, the agent regularly attempts to autonomously resolve cases involving genuine policy gaps, such as requests for competitor price matching, where your policy documentation is silent. What is the most effective way to recalibrate the agent's escalation behavior to address both patterns?
options: Implement a self-reported confidence scoring system where the agent rates its confidence before each response, and automatically route to a human agent whenever the score falls below a calibrated threshold.

Replace sentiment-based escalation triggers with explicit policy-based criteria, and add escalation instructions that cover policy gap scenarios, with few-shot examples demonstrating when to escalate versus resolve autonomously.

Lower the sentiment detection threshold so only extreme frustration triggers escalation, and add a step where the agent attempts one resolution before escalating, regardless of the nature of the request.

Train a separate binary classifier on historical escalation outcomes to predict which incoming requests need human handling, and route requests through the classifier before passing them to the main agent.
answer: Replace sentiment-based escalation triggers with explicit policy-based criteria, and add escalation instructions that cover policy gap scenarios, with few-shot examples demonstrating when to escalate versus resolve autonomously.
explanation:
Sentiment-based escalation is a well-documented anti-pattern in customer support agents. Emotional language does not reliably indicate case complexity: a frustrated customer with a routine order status question deserves resolution, not a handoff. Replacing sentiment triggers with explicit, policy-grounded escalation criteria removes the unreliable signal and replaces it with a decision rule the agent can apply consistently.

The second failure mode in this scenario, attempting to autonomously resolve policy gap cases, is equally important. When policy documentation is silent on a specific request (such as competitor price matching), the agent lacks the authority to make a binding decision. The exam guide identifies "escalating when policy is ambiguous or silent on the customer's specific request" as an explicit escalation trigger that should appear in the agent's system prompt.

Adding few-shot examples alongside explicit criteria is the most effective way to calibrate this behavior. Examples demonstrate the reasoning behind edge-case decisions, helping the agent generalize to novel situations rather than matching only pre-specified keywords. Self-reported confidence scores and sentiment thresholds both substitute unreliable proxies for the underlying decision logic, while a separate ML classifier is disproportionately complex for a problem that prompt refinement can address directly.

For more on escalation design and few-shot calibration, see Prompt Engineering and Agent SDK.
option_feedback: Self-reported confidence scores from LLMs are poorly calibrated and do not reliably correlate with actual case complexity or policy authority. An agent may express high confidence when attempting to resolve a genuine policy gap and low confidence when handling a routine return. This approach substitutes one unreliable signal (sentiment) for another (self-reported confidence) without addressing the root cause.

Sentiment is an unreliable proxy for case complexity. Frustrated customers with simple problems should be helped, not escalated. Meanwhile, policy gaps (like competitor price matching when policy only addresses own-site adjustments) are a legitimate escalation trigger because the agent lacks the authority to make exceptions. Replacing sentiment triggers with explicit, policy-grounded criteria and adding few-shot examples directly addresses both miscalibration patterns at once.

Tuning a sentiment threshold still relies on emotional tone as the primary escalation signal, which remains an unreliable proxy for actual case complexity. Requiring one resolution attempt before escalating also does not address policy gap scenarios, where the agent should escalate immediately rather than attempt an unauthorized resolution and potentially set a precedent.

Building a separate classifier requires labeled historical data, ML infrastructure, and ongoing maintenance, none of which are warranted when the simpler fix of refining escalation criteria and adding few-shot examples has not yet been attempted. This is an over-engineered solution that also does not directly address the policy gap scenario, where the issue is a missing decision rule rather than a prediction problem.

question:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.

Your team has been using Claude Code for several months and recently noticed inconsistent behavior: some developers receive context-aware suggestions that respect your internal API naming conventions, while others get generic suggestions that ignore those conventions entirely. After investigation, you discover that one senior developer placed the API naming rules in a file at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on their own machine, believing this would apply to all teammates working on the same repository. New team members who clone the repository and run Claude Code never see these rules applied. What is the most accurate explanation for this behavior, and what change would resolve it for the entire team?
options: Claude Code does not automatically load CLAUDE.md files placed in the repository root. The rules need to be added to a .claude/config.json file with a "rules" array so that Claude Code discovers and applies them consistently across all developer environments.

The inconsistency occurs because Claude Code only loads CLAUDE.md files when developers explicitly run the /memory command at the start of each session. Team members who skip this initialization step will not have the naming conventions applied, regardless of where the file is located.

The behavior is caused by a conflict between the user-level file and the absence of a project-level override. Claude Code merges all CLAUDE.md files it finds, so the correct fix is to add a project-level CLAUDE.md that explicitly declares "override: true" to suppress any user-level settings that differ between team members.

User-level CLAUDE.md files at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md are scoped to a single user's machine and are not shared via version control. Moving the API naming rules to a project-level CLAUDE.md at the repository root (or .claude/CLAUDE.md) ensures all developers receive them when they clone the repository.
answer: User-level CLAUDE.md files at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md are scoped to a single user's machine and are not shared via version control. Moving the API naming rules to a project-level CLAUDE.md at the repository root (or .claude/CLAUDE.md) ensures all developers receive them when they clone the repository.
explanation:
The CLAUDE.md configuration hierarchy in Claude Code has three distinct scopes: user-level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project-level (.claude/CLAUDE.md or the repository root CLAUDE.md), and directory-level (subdirectory CLAUDE.md files). The critical distinction is that user-level files exist only on one person's machine and are never committed to version control, making them invisible to teammates.

A common misconfiguration is placing team-wide instructions at user scope, assuming they will propagate to all developers. This produces exactly the symptom described: the developer who authored the rules sees them applied, while new team members who clone the repository do not. The fix is straightforward: move shared conventions to a project-level file so they travel with the repository.

The /memory command is a diagnostic tool for verifying which memory files are currently loaded, not for triggering their discovery. CLAUDE.md files are loaded automatically at session start based on the hierarchy. Options describing non-existent mechanisms like .claude/config.json rules arrays or override: true directives are fabricated and do not reflect documented Claude Code behavior.

For more on the CLAUDE.md hierarchy and scoping, see CLAUDE.md Configuration and the Claude Code Overview.
option_feedback: This option describes a configuration mechanism that does not exist in Claude Code. Claude Code does not use a .claude/config.json with a "rules" array for this purpose. CLAUDE.md files placed at the project root or in the .claude/ directory are automatically loaded by Claude Code without any additional configuration file.

The /memory command is used to inspect which memory files are currently loaded and to diagnose configuration issues, not to trigger loading of CLAUDE.md files. Claude Code automatically discovers and loads applicable CLAUDE.md files at session start based on the file hierarchy; no explicit initialization command is required.

Claude Code does not support an "override: true" directive in CLAUDE.md files. While Claude Code does load multiple CLAUDE.md files from the hierarchy simultaneously, there is no documented flag to suppress or override files at other levels. The root issue is simply that user-level files are not shared via version control, not a merge conflict requiring a special directive.

The CLAUDE.md hierarchy has distinct scopes: user-level (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) applies only to that individual's machine and is never committed to version control. Project-level CLAUDE.md files live inside the repository and travel with it, making them available to every developer who clones the project. Moving the rules to project scope directly resolves the inconsistency.

question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

Your CI/CD pipeline runs automated code reviews on every pull request. After three months in production, your team notices that developers are dismissing the pipeline's security findings at a much higher rate than its performance findings. Exit interviews with engineers reveal that the security category frequently flags code patterns that are actually safe in your codebase's specific execution context, while performance findings are almost always actionable. Your manager asks you to improve the security category without touching the performance category or adding infrastructure. Your current security prompt instruction reads: "Flag any code that could introduce security vulnerabilities, including input handling, authentication, and data exposure."

What change to the review prompt would most effectively reduce false positives in the security category while preserving detection of genuine issues?
options: Split the security category into subcategories (input handling, authentication, data exposure) and add a separate confidence threshold to each subcategory, so findings in each area are only surfaced when the model rates them above a per-subcategory confidence level.

Add a confidence threshold instruction to the prompt, such as "only report security findings when you are highly confident the issue is a genuine vulnerability," to filter out uncertain findings before they reach developers.

Replace the vague instruction with explicit criteria that define which patterns to flag versus skip, such as specifying that input handling findings should only be reported when untrusted external input reaches a sink without sanitization, rather than flagging all input handling patterns broadly.

Temporarily disable the security category entirely to restore developer trust, then reintroduce it after retraining the model on codebase-specific examples of true positives and false positives to improve its baseline detection accuracy.
answer: Replace the vague instruction with explicit criteria that define which patterns to flag versus skip, such as specifying that input handling findings should only be reported when untrusted external input reaches a sink without sanitization, rather than flagging all input handling patterns broadly.
explanation:
The core principle tested here is that explicit categorical criteria outperform vague instructions or confidence-based filtering for reducing false positives in automated code review. When a prompt says "flag any code that could introduce security vulnerabilities," the model interprets "could" broadly, catching safe patterns that superficially resemble vulnerable ones. The fix is to replace that vague instruction with a testable condition: for example, requiring that untrusted external input must reach a sink without sanitization before flagging an input handling issue.

The exam guide explicitly identifies this as a key skill: "writing specific review criteria that define which issues to report versus skip rather than relying on confidence-based filtering." General instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" fail because LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated for domain-specific patterns. A model can be highly confident about a false positive if the pattern superficially matches its training signal for vulnerabilities.

The anti-pattern in this question is confidence-based filtering, which appears in two distractor forms: a simple threshold instruction and a subcategory-plus-threshold structure. Both fail for the same reason: they delegate the boundary decision to the model's self-assessment rather than providing an explicit, externally defined criterion. The "disable and retrain" option is a disproportionate response that bypasses the proportionate first step of prompt improvement.

For further reading, see Prompt Engineering and the CI/CD scenario in the Claude Code Overview.
option_feedback: Subcategory structure combined with confidence thresholds adds complexity without addressing the root cause. Confidence-based filtering is unreliable for reducing false positives because the model's self-reported confidence does not correlate with whether a pattern is actually a vulnerability in this codebase's execution context. The problem requires explicit criteria defining what constitutes a reportable finding, not finer-grained confidence filtering.

General confidence-based filtering instructions like "only report high-confidence findings" do not improve precision because the model lacks calibrated self-assessment for domain-specific security patterns. The model may be highly confident about patterns that are false positives in this specific codebase context, so a confidence threshold does not address the underlying issue of overly broad categorical criteria.

Explicit categorical criteria directly address the root cause: the current instruction is too broad, causing the model to flag safe patterns that match the general description. By defining concrete conditions for when to report versus skip (for example, requiring untrusted input to reach a sink without sanitization rather than flagging all input handling), the prompt gives the model a testable boundary that reduces false positives without disabling detection of genuine vulnerabilities.

Disabling the security category and waiting to retrain the model is disproportionate when the problem can be addressed through prompt refinement. The exam guide identifies temporarily disabling high-false-positive categories as a tool for restoring developer trust while improving prompts for those categories, but the primary fix is improving the prompt criteria rather than disabling the category and waiting for model retraining, which is an out-of-scope operation.

question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to backend systems through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

Your customer support agent handles multi-concern requests, but production logs reveal a critical failure pattern: when customers submit requests involving both a billing dispute and a return request simultaneously, the agent sometimes processes the refund for the return before completing the billing investigation. In one incident, a customer received a partial refund that was later reversed when the billing investigation revealed an outstanding balance that offset the return amount, resulting in a confusing customer experience and a manual correction by your finance team.

Your current implementation uses prompt instructions that tell the agent to "always investigate all issues before taking any action." Despite this instruction, the failure occurs in roughly 8% of multi-concern cases. You need to eliminate this ordering failure entirely. What architectural change would most reliably prevent the agent from calling process_refund before all investigative tool calls have completed?
options: Add a sentiment analysis check after each tool call that detects whether the customer's original message expressed urgency, and if urgency is detected, require the agent to pause and confirm with a supervisor before calling process_refund on any multi-concern case.

Decompose the multi-concern request into two sequential sub-conversations: first spawn a subagent that handles only investigation (get_customer, lookup_order), then pass its findings to a second subagent that handles only action (process_refund, escalate_to_human), so the action subagent never has access to investigation tools.

Strengthen the system prompt by adding explicit numbered steps (1. investigate all concerns, 2. summarize findings, 3. take action) and include a few-shot example showing the agent completing all investigations before any refund call.

Implement a programmatic gate that tracks which investigative tools have returned results and blocks process_refund from being called until get_customer and lookup_order have both completed for all concerns in the request.
answer: Implement a programmatic gate that tracks which investigative tools have returned results and blocks process_refund from being called until get_customer and lookup_order have both completed for all concerns in the request.
explanation:
The core principle tested here is the distinction between prompt-based guidance (probabilistic compliance) and programmatic enforcement (deterministic compliance). The exam guide states explicitly: "When deterministic compliance is required (e.g., identity verification before financial operations), prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate."

A programmatic gate that tracks prerequisite completion and blocks downstream action tools is the correct architectural response when financial correctness requires guaranteed ordering. This is fundamentally different from adding more prompt instructions or examples, which can only reduce the failure rate, not eliminate it. The 8% failure rate in the scenario persists despite existing prompt instructions, confirming that prompt-level guidance has already been tried and is insufficient.

The subagent decomposition option is plausible but over-engineered for this problem: it adds latency and coordination complexity while still relying on correct orchestration sequencing rather than enforcing the ordering constraint at the tool level. The sentiment analysis option is a classic anti-pattern: it conflates customer emotional state with workflow correctness, which are unrelated concerns.

For multi-concern requests specifically, the exam guide recommends "decomposing multi-concern customer requests into distinct items, then investigating each in parallel using shared context before synthesizing a unified resolution." A programmatic gate enables exactly this pattern by ensuring all parallel investigations complete before any action tool is unblocked.

Learn more about programmatic enforcement patterns and hook-based workflow control at Agent SDK and Tool Use.
option_feedback: Sentiment-based escalation is an anti-pattern that does not address the root cause of the ordering failure. Customer urgency sentiment is unrelated to whether the agent has completed all necessary investigative steps before taking action. This approach would either over-escalate routine urgent cases or under-protect non-urgent cases where the ordering failure is equally likely to cause financial errors.

While separating investigation and action into distinct subagents enforces tool access boundaries, it introduces unnecessary latency and coordination overhead for a problem that can be solved within a single agent using a programmatic gate. Additionally, this approach requires the coordinator to correctly sequence the subagent invocations, which itself relies on correct orchestration logic rather than eliminating the ordering risk at the tool call level where the failure actually occurs.

Strengthening prompt instructions and adding few-shot examples can improve compliance rates but cannot eliminate failures entirely. The existing 8% failure rate already occurs despite a prompt instruction covering this exact ordering requirement, demonstrating that prompt-based guidance is insufficient when deterministic compliance is needed for financial operations. Adding more examples reduces but does not eliminate the non-zero failure rate.

When deterministic ordering is required for financial operations, programmatic enforcement is the only reliable approach. A gate that tracks completed investigative steps and blocks action tools until prerequisites are satisfied provides a 100% compliance guarantee, eliminating the 8% failure rate that prompt instructions cannot prevent. This directly addresses the architectural gap between probabilistic prompt compliance and deterministic workflow enforcement.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with MCP servers.

Your team has built a Claude Code skill that scans an unfamiliar codebase for architectural patterns, generates a detailed dependency graph, and produces a verbose multi-section analysis report. Engineers invoke this skill at the start of new assignments to orient themselves before writing code. After several weeks of use, engineers report that after running the skill, their subsequent requests in the same session produce lower-quality responses: Claude references the analysis report's terminology inconsistently, conflates findings from the exploration phase with the current coding task, and sometimes hallucinates file paths that appeared in the analysis but no longer exist. A senior engineer suggests the skill configuration is the root cause. What frontmatter configuration change to the skill's SKILL.md would most directly address this issue?
options: Add `context: fork` to the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter so the codebase analysis runs in an isolated sub-agent context, returning only a summary to the main session rather than accumulating all exploration output in the shared conversation history.

Add `allowed-tools: []` to the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter to restrict the skill from using any file system tools during execution, forcing it to produce a concise output that does not overwhelm the session context with exploration artifacts.

Add `argument-hint: "Enter the root directory path to analyze"` to the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter so engineers provide a scoped path, limiting the analysis to a smaller portion of the codebase and reducing the volume of output that accumulates in the session.

Move the skill from `.claude/skills/` to `~/.claude/skills/` under a different name so each engineer maintains a personal variant, preventing the shared skill's accumulated context from affecting teammates who have not run the analysis on the same codebase.
answer: Add `context: fork` to the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter so the codebase analysis runs in an isolated sub-agent context, returning only a summary to the main session rather than accumulating all exploration output in the shared conversation history.
explanation:
The reported symptoms (inconsistent terminology, conflation of exploration findings with coding tasks, hallucinated file paths from a prior analysis) are classic signs of context pollution: verbose skill output has accumulated in the main conversation history and is interfering with subsequent requests in the same session.

The context: fork frontmatter option in a skill's SKILL.md is specifically designed for this scenario. When set, the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context, so all of its tool calls, intermediate reasoning, and verbose output remain in a separate context boundary. Only the final summary result is returned to the main session, keeping the primary conversation clean for the coding tasks that follow.

The allowed-tools frontmatter option controls which tools the skill may invoke during execution, not how its output is scoped to the session. Restricting tools would break the skill's analysis capability. The argument-hint option prompts for missing invocation parameters and has no effect on context isolation. Moving a skill to user scope changes its availability across teammates but does not affect the session context behavior for any individual engineer.

The exam guide explicitly identifies context: fork as the correct mechanism for "isolating skills that produce verbose output (e.g., codebase analysis) or exploratory context (e.g., brainstorming alternatives) from the main session." This is the canonical use case the option was designed to address. Learn more about skill frontmatter configuration at Claude Code Overview and CLAUDE.md Configuration.
option_feedback: The context: fork frontmatter option runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context, which prevents the verbose exploration output (dependency graphs, multi-section analysis, file path references) from accumulating in the main conversation history. The main session receives only the summary result, keeping the conversation context clean for subsequent coding tasks.

Setting allowed-tools to an empty list would prevent the skill from reading files, running grep, or using any other tools it needs to perform codebase analysis. This would break the skill's core functionality rather than isolating its output from the main session context, making it an incorrect approach to the stated problem.

The argument-hint frontmatter option prompts engineers for a required parameter when they invoke the skill without arguments, but it does not change how the skill's output is handled or whether it accumulates in the main conversation context. Scoping the analysis path might reduce output volume slightly but does not prevent exploration artifacts from polluting subsequent coding interactions.

Moving the skill to user scope addresses who can access the skill but does not change how the skill's output is handled within any individual engineer's session. Each engineer would still experience the same context pollution problem in their own session after running the analysis, because the root cause is the skill's output accumulating in the shared conversation history, not the skill's scope.

question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests like returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to backend systems through MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

Your customer support agent handles complex, multi-issue cases that often require calling several MCP tools in sequence: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, and escalate_to_human. During a routine audit of extended sessions (cases involving 15 or more tool calls), you notice a troubling pattern: in the final third of these long sessions, the agent begins referencing policy details that were superseded three months ago, misidentifies order statuses it correctly identified earlier in the same session, and occasionally contradicts its own earlier findings within the same case. Shorter sessions (under 8 tool calls) show none of these issues. What is the most effective strategy to address this reliability problem in extended sessions?
options: Have the agent maintain a running scratchpad file recording confirmed facts (customer ID, verified order statuses, applicable policy determinations) and instruct it to reference this file before each tool call or policy decision in the session.

Restart the agent session after every 10 tool calls and inject a structured summary of the case facts gathered so far, so each continuation begins with fresh context rather than an accumulating history of tool outputs.

Reduce the verbosity of each MCP tool's response by trimming fields irrelevant to the current case type, so the context window fills more slowly and the agent retains accurate recall of earlier findings for a longer portion of the session.

Implement a session confidence monitor that tracks how often the agent self-reports uncertainty in its responses, and automatically escalate to a human agent when the uncertainty rate crosses a threshold during a session.
answer: Have the agent maintain a running scratchpad file recording confirmed facts (customer ID, verified order statuses, applicable policy determinations) and instruct it to reference this file before each tool call or policy decision in the session.
explanation:
The observed pattern (accurate early in sessions, degraded accuracy late) is a classic symptom of context degradation in extended interactions. As tool results and conversation history accumulate, earlier findings are pushed toward the middle of the context window, where the lost-in-the-middle effect causes models to process information less reliably than content at the beginning or end of the input.

The most targeted fix is a scratchpad file: a persistent external record of confirmed facts that the agent writes to as it resolves each sub-question and reads from before making subsequent decisions. Unlike in-context recall, which degrades as the window fills, the scratchpad remains accurate regardless of session length. The agent references the file explicitly rather than reconstructing facts from a long, attention-diluted history.

Trimming verbose tool outputs (reducing fields per response) is a complementary optimization that slows the rate of context fill, but does not eliminate degradation for genuinely long sessions. Session restarts with injected summaries are a heavier-weight alternative that works, but introduces discontinuity and summarization risk. Confidence-based escalation is an anti-pattern here because the agent's failures are confident errors, not expressed uncertainty, making self-reported confidence a poor signal for this specific failure mode.

For more on scratchpad-based context management and subagent delegation strategies for extended sessions, see Claude Code Overview and Agent SDK.
option_feedback: A scratchpad file externalizes critical findings outside the context window, allowing the agent to retrieve accurate, previously confirmed information rather than relying on degraded in-context recall. This directly counters the mechanism causing the observed failures: the agent is "forgetting" or misrecalling facts it established earlier because those findings have been pushed toward the middle of a long context, where attention is weakest.

Periodic session restarts with injected summaries can help manage context length, but introduce coordination overhead and risk losing nuanced case context during the summarization step. This approach is more disruptive than necessary when a targeted persistence mechanism can address the recall problem without breaking session continuity or requiring periodic reconstruction of case state.

Trimming verbose tool outputs is a valuable optimization that slows context exhaustion, but it does not eliminate the degradation problem for genuinely extended sessions. Once the context window fills regardless of trimming, the same recall failures will recur. This approach delays the symptom rather than addressing the underlying mechanism of context-dependent recall degradation.

Self-reported confidence scores are an unreliable proxy for actual accuracy degradation. The observed failures (referencing outdated policies, misidentifying order statuses) are not cases where the agent expresses uncertainty; they are cases where the agent confidently produces incorrect outputs. Routing on self-reported uncertainty would miss the specific failure mode identified in the audit.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

You are building developer productivity tools using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with MCP servers.

Your team has deployed a coordinator agent that delegates codebase exploration tasks to specialized subagents: a structure-mapping subagent, a dependency-tracing subagent, and a pattern-detection subagent. Engineers report that when they ask the agent to "help understand this legacy authentication module," the coordinator consistently routes the request through all three subagents in fixed order, regardless of what the engineer actually needs. For simple questions like "what does this function return?", the agent still spawns all three subagents, waits for all results, and then synthesizes a response, leading to unnecessary latency and verbose output that buries the answer. For complex questions about cross-module dependencies, the fixed pipeline sometimes terminates before fully tracing all relevant call chains because the structure-mapping subagent's output didn't surface enough entry points for the dependency tracer to follow. What is the most likely root cause of both failure modes?
options: The coordinator's system prompt contains too many procedural step-by-step instructions, which causes the agent to follow a rigid execution script instead of reasoning about the task, and the fix is to rewrite the prompt to remove all structured guidance.

The coordinator is configured to always route through the full subagent pipeline rather than analyzing each query's requirements and dynamically selecting which subagents to invoke based on what the question actually demands.

The subagents are receiving insufficient context in their prompts, causing each one to operate on incomplete information and produce outputs that do not adequately inform the next subagent in the pipeline sequence.

The pattern-detection subagent's tool access is too broad, causing it to consume context budget on irrelevant file patterns and leaving insufficient capacity for the dependency-tracing subagent to complete its analysis on complex queries.
answer: The coordinator is configured to always route through the full subagent pipeline rather than analyzing each query's requirements and dynamically selecting which subagents to invoke based on what the question actually demands.
explanation:
The two failure modes described (over-invoking for simple queries and under-serving complex ones) share a single architectural root cause: the coordinator uses a fixed pipeline that always routes through all subagents rather than dynamically selecting subagents based on what each query actually requires.

The exam guide identifies this as a core coordinator skill: "designing coordinator agents that analyze query requirements and dynamically select which subagents to invoke rather than always routing through the full pipeline." A coordinator that evaluates each query first can invoke only the pattern-detection subagent for a simple function lookup, while adaptively chaining structure-mapping and dependency-tracing subagents (and potentially re-invoking them with refined queries) for complex cross-module analysis.

The anti-pattern in this question is the option suggesting the fix is to remove all structured guidance from the coordinator prompt. This overcorrects in the wrong direction. The real fix is to replace procedural step-by-step instructions with goal-oriented prompts that specify research objectives and quality criteria, enabling the coordinator to reason about subagent selection rather than following a script. Removing all structure would make the coordinator less reliable, not more adaptive.

The context-passing distractor is plausible because subagent context management is a genuine concern in multi-agent systems, but it targets a different failure mode (information loss between handoffs) rather than the routing decision that causes both symptoms described in the scenario.

For more on coordinator-subagent patterns and dynamic task delegation, see Agent SDK and Claude Code Sub-agents.
option_feedback: While overly procedural coordinator prompts can contribute to rigid behavior, removing all structured guidance is an anti-pattern that would leave the coordinator without any direction. The correct approach is to replace step-by-step procedural instructions with goal-oriented prompts that specify quality criteria and let the coordinator reason about which subagents to invoke. Removing all structure entirely would degrade coordinator reliability rather than fix the routing problem.

Both failure modes (over-invoking subagents for simple questions and under-serving complex ones) share a common root cause: the coordinator does not analyze query requirements before deciding which subagents to invoke. A coordinator that dynamically selects subagents based on query complexity and type would invoke only the relevant subagent for simple lookups and would adaptively chain or re-invoke subagents for complex dependency traces as intermediate findings reveal new investigation paths.

Insufficient context passing between subagents is a real failure mode in multi-agent systems, but it does not explain why simple questions trigger the full pipeline unnecessarily. The described symptoms (over-invocation for simple queries and incomplete tracing for complex ones) both point to a coordinator routing problem rather than a context handoff problem. Improving context passing would not fix the coordinator's failure to match subagent selection to query requirements.

Tool access scope and context budget consumption are valid concerns in multi-agent systems, but they do not explain the over-invocation behavior on simple queries or the systematic routing of all requests through the full pipeline. This explanation addresses a resource contention symptom rather than the architectural routing decision that causes both observed failure modes.

question:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

You are using Claude Code to accelerate software development. Your team uses it for code generation, refactoring, debugging, and documentation. You need to integrate it into your development workflow with custom slash commands, CLAUDE.md configurations, and understand when to use plan mode vs direct execution.

Your team uses Claude Code to generate boilerplate service classes for a microservices project. Each service requires a standard structure: a constructor, a logger initialization block, a health check method, and a graceful shutdown handler. After several iterations, you notice that Claude consistently produces the constructor and logger correctly, but the health check and shutdown handler vary significantly across generations: sometimes they are missing entirely, sometimes they use incompatible patterns, and sometimes the shutdown handler references an undefined logger variable. You have already written a detailed prose description of the expected structure in your prompt. What is the most effective next step to improve generation consistency for the problematic components?
options: Provide two or three concrete example service classes as input/output pairs in the prompt, showing the exact health check and shutdown handler implementations you expect, so Claude can generalize the pattern rather than interpret prose descriptions.

Switch to plan mode before each generation so Claude produces a structural outline of the service class for you to review and approve before writing any code, catching missing components before they appear in the final output.

Add a confidence threshold instruction to the prompt, asking Claude to self-report a score from 1 to 10 for each generated component and regenerate any section it rates below 7 before returning the final output.

Expand the prose description in the prompt with additional paragraphs explaining the health check and shutdown handler requirements in greater detail, including the rationale for each design choice, to help Claude better understand the intent.
