After investigation, you discover that the testing standards, fixture documentation, and valuable test criteria were all added to one engineer's personal Claude Code configuration rather than to the repository. The team lead wants to fix this distribution problem while also making the configuration easier to maintain as testing standards evolve across different service layers. What is the most effective approach to address both the distribution problem and long-term maintainability?
options: Create a project-scoped skill in .claude/skills/ containing all testing standards and fixture documentation, configured with context: fork so the skill runs in an isolated context and engineers invoke it explicitly before each test generation task.

Create a single comprehensive CLAUDE.md file at the project root containing all testing standards, fixture conventions, and review criteria concatenated under section headers, relying on Claude to infer which sections apply based on the file being reviewed.

Move the testing standards into a shared internal wiki and instruct each engineer to manually copy the relevant sections into their personal Claude Code configuration at the start of each sprint to keep it synchronized with current standards.

Move the testing standards and fixture documentation into a project-level CLAUDE.md committed to the repository, then split the growing configuration into focused topic files in .claude/rules/ to keep each area maintainable independently.
answer: Move the testing standards and fixture documentation into a project-level CLAUDE.md committed to the repository, then split the growing configuration into focused topic files in .claude/rules/ to keep each area maintainable independently.
explanation:
The root cause of inconsistent test generation is that configuration was placed in user-level personal settings rather than in project-level configuration committed to version control. User-level settings (such as ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) apply only to the individual engineer and are never shared with teammates via version control. Project-level configuration (a CLAUDE.md at the repository root or in .claude/) travels with the repository and is automatically available to every developer who clones or pulls.

The second part of the problem is long-term maintainability. A single monolithic CLAUDE.md becomes difficult to update as standards grow across testing, fixtures, API conventions, and deployment rules. The recommended pattern is to split the configuration into focused topic-specific files in .claude/rules/ (for example, testing.md, fixture-conventions.md, deployment.md). Each file covers one area and can be updated independently without risking unintended changes to other sections.

Skills are the wrong tool here because they require explicit invocation and are designed for on-demand task workflows, not always-loaded universal standards. A monolithic CLAUDE.md solves distribution but creates a maintainability anti-pattern. Manual synchronization from a wiki perpetuates the original distribution failure.

For more detail on CLAUDE.md hierarchy and modular organization, see the CLAUDE.md Configuration documentation and the Claude Code Overview.
option_feedback: Skills are designed for on-demand invocation of specific task workflows, not for always-loaded universal standards that should apply automatically to every test generation request. Requiring engineers to explicitly invoke a skill before each task introduces a manual step that can be forgotten and does not match the intended use of CLAUDE.md for persistent project-wide conventions. The context: fork option isolates skill output from the main session but does not help with automatic convention application.

While a project-level CLAUDE.md does solve the distribution problem, consolidating all conventions into one monolithic file under section headers creates a maintainability burden as standards grow. Relying on Claude to infer which sections apply is also less reliable than explicit path-scoped rules. The exam guide specifically identifies splitting large CLAUDE.md files into focused topic files in .claude/rules/ as the recommended approach for maintainability.

Requiring engineers to manually synchronize personal configurations from a wiki replicates the original distribution problem rather than solving it. Personal configurations are not version-controlled or shared automatically, so any engineer who misses the update step will still receive inconsistent test generation. This approach also creates ongoing maintenance overhead with no guarantee of consistency.

Project-level CLAUDE.md files committed to version control are distributed to all team members automatically when they clone or pull the repository, which directly resolves the inconsistency caused by user-level configuration. Splitting the configuration into focused topic files in .claude/rules/ (such as testing.md, fixture-conventions.md, and api-standards.md) keeps each section independently maintainable as standards evolve, avoiding a monolithic file that becomes hard to update.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer asks the agent to update a configuration constant that appears identically in six places across a legacy file. The agent's Edit tool call fails with a "non-unique match" error, and the agent retries the same Edit call three times with no success. What should the agent do instead?
options: Use Read to load the full file, then use Write to save the file with all instances updated.
Retry Edit with a shorter search string to increase the chance of a match.
Use Bash with a sed command to perform the replacement across the file.
Use Grep to locate the line numbers, then call Edit once per line number.
answer: Use Read to load the full file, then use Write to save the file with all instances updated.
explanation: The guide explicitly states that when Edit fails due to non-unique text matches, Read + Write is the reliable fallback for file modifications.
option_feedback: The guide explicitly states that when Edit fails due to non-unique text matches, Read + Write is the reliable fallback for file modifications.
It doesn't solve the root problem — a shorter string is even more likely to match multiple locations.
It introduces a tool outside the documented built-in selection pattern for this scenario.
It misunderstands Edit's mechanism, which matches on unique text, not line numbers.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer asks the agent to "find all React test files in the frontend package." The agent responds by using Bash to run a recursive find command with a filename filter, which works but takes noticeably longer than necessary and produces unstructured output. Which built-in tool should the agent have used instead?
options: Glob, using a pattern like frontend/**/*.test.tsx
Grep, since test files often contain the word "test" in their content
Read, applied iteratively across all files in the frontend directory
Bash, but with a more optimized find command
answer: Glob, using a pattern like frontend/**/*.test.tsx
explanation: Glob is designed for file path pattern matching — finding files by name or extension patterns.
option_feedback: Glob is designed for file path pattern matching — finding files by name or extension patterns.
Grep searches file content, not file names, so it's the wrong tool for locating files by naming convention.
Read is for loading file contents, not discovery, and would be extremely inefficient.
Bash can technically accomplish this but bypasses the purpose-built tool designed for this exact pattern-matching task.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

Your coordinator agent repeatedly issues exploratory tool calls just to discover what documentation and datasets are available in a connected MCP server before it can plan delegation to subagents, adding several round trips before real research begins. The MCP server maintains a stable catalog of available document summaries and schemas. What change would most directly reduce this overhead?
options: Expose the catalog of available content as an MCP resource so the coordinator can view it without exploratory tool calls.
Instruct the coordinator via system prompt to "minimize exploratory calls before delegating."
Increase the coordinator's max_tokens so it can process more exploratory results per turn
Add a caching layer that stores the coordinator's most recent exploratory tool call results.
answer: Expose the catalog of available content as an MCP resource so the coordinator can view it without exploratory tool calls.
explanation: MCP resources are the documented mechanism for exposing content catalogs (document summaries, schemas) so agents gain visibility into available data without needing exploratory tool calls — directly addressing the root cause.
option_feedback: MCP resources are the documented mechanism for exposing content catalogs (document summaries, schemas) so agents gain visibility into available data without needing exploratory tool calls — directly addressing the root cause.
It is a probabilistic prompt-based nudge that doesn't eliminate the structural need for discovery calls.
It addresses token capacity, not the number of round trips required.
It only helps on repeated identical queries and doesn't prevent the initial round of exploratory discovery calls.

question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

Your document analysis subagent connects to an MCP server holding thousands of research papers. Before analyzing anything, it issues 8-10 exploratory tool calls just to list available documents, their titles, and topics, adding significant latency before real analysis begins. The document set changes only weekly. What is the most effective change to reduce this overhead?
options: Expose the document catalog (titles, topics, summaries) as an MCP resource so the subagent can view it without exploratory tool calls.
Instruct the subagent via system prompt to limit itself to 2 exploratory tool calls maximum.
Increase the subagent's max_tokens so exploratory results are processed in fewer turns.
Have the coordinator pre-fetch all document contents and inject the full text into every subagent's prompt.
answer: Expose the document catalog (titles, topics, summaries) as an MCP resource so the subagent can view it without exploratory tool calls.
explanation: MCP resources are the documented mechanism for exposing content catalogs (e.g., document summaries) to reduce exploratory tool calls, giving the agent visibility into available data upfront.
option_feedback: MCP resources are the documented mechanism for exposing content catalogs (e.g., document summaries) to reduce exploratory tool calls, giving the agent visibility into available data upfront.
It arbitrarily caps calls without addressing the root cause and risks the agent missing relevant documents.
It addresses token capacity per turn, not the number of round trips required for discovery.
It is wasteful and unnecessary — injecting full text for every document (rather than a catalog) bloats context far beyond what's needed for planning.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer productivity team is deciding how to integrate two systems: (1) a standard, widely-used issue tracker, and (2) a proprietary internal deployment-approval system unique to the company with no external equivalent. How should they approach MCP server sourcing for each?
options: Use a community MCP server for the issue tracker; build a custom MCP server for the proprietary deployment-approval system.
Build custom MCP servers for both systems to ensure consistent internal support.
Use community MCP servers for both, since community options exist for every integration need.
Use a custom server for the issue tracker to allow deeper customization, and skip integrating the proprietary system.
answer: Use a community MCP server for the issue tracker; build a custom MCP server for the proprietary deployment-approval system.
explanation: This directly reflects the guide's principle: reserve custom MCP server development for team-specific workflows (like a proprietary deployment-approval system with no standard equivalent) while relying on existing community servers for standard integrations like issue trackers.
option_feedback: This directly reflects the guide's principle: reserve custom MCP server development for team-specific workflows (like a proprietary deployment-approval system with no standard equivalent) while relying on existing community servers for standard integrations like issue trackers.

question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

Debugging becomes difficult because coordinator logs no longer show why certain analysis passes ran, and error handling behaves inconsistently between the two paths. What change best addresses this?
options: Require all inter-subagent communication to route through the coordinator, which manages delegation, error handling, and information flow.
Add logging directly inside the web search subagent to capture its calls to the document analysis subagent.
Merge the web search and document analysis subagents into one combined subagent to eliminate the direct call.
Give the document analysis subagent its own independent error-handling logic to match the web search subagent's behavior.
answer: Require all inter-subagent communication to route through the coordinator, which manages delegation, error handling, and information flow.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

An engineer asks the agent to trace a bug across three files. The agent runs Grep to find the function, then Read on the relevant file, but its final answer only references the Grep output and ignores the file contents that Read returned, producing an incomplete trace. What most likely explains this?
options: The Read tool result was not added to conversation context before the model generated its final response.
Grep and Read were called with an incorrect tool_choice setting of "any".
The agent should have used Glob instead of Grep to locate the function.
The model's context window is too small to hold both tool outputs.
answer: The Read tool result was not added to conversation context before the model generated its final response.
explanation: Correct agentic loop implementation requires that tool results be added to context between iterations so the model can incorporate new information into its reasoning; if the Read result wasn't appended, the model would only have visibility into the earlier Grep output.
option_feedback: Correct agentic loop implementation requires that tool results be added to context between iterations so the model can incorporate new information into its reasoning; if the Read result wasn't appended, the model would only have visibility into the earlier Grep output.
It misapplies tool_choice, which governs whether/which tool is called, not context retention.
It is a valid tool-selection point but doesn't explain why returned data was ignored.
It is implausible for two tool outputs and isn't supported by the log evidence.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

An engineer built a codebase-exploration agent whose loop terminates as soon as Claude's response includes any explanatory text, on the assumption that text means the answer is ready. Logs show the agent frequently stops after explaining what it's about to search for, without actually executing the Grep or Read calls it just described. What should be changed in the loop's termination logic?
options: Terminate only when stop_reason is "end_turn", and continue executing requested tools and appending results whenever stop_reason is "tool_use".
Strip explanatory text from responses before evaluating whether to stop the loop.
Require Claude to omit all text and return only tool calls until the task is finished.
Terminate the loop once a Grep or Read tool has been called at least one time.
answer: Terminate only when stop_reason is "end_turn", and continue executing requested tools and appending results whenever stop_reason is "tool_use".
explanation: Task Statement 1.1 knowledge covers inspecting stop_reason ("tool_use" vs "end_turn") to control loop continuation, since a "tool_use" response can include explanatory text alongside the tool call.
option_feedback: Task Statement 1.1 knowledge covers inspecting stop_reason ("tool_use" vs "end_turn") to control loop continuation, since a "tool_use" response can include explanatory text alongside the tool call.
Stripping text doesn't address the actual bug, which is using text presence rather than stop_reason as the signal.
This restricts legitimate model behavior instead of fixing the flawed termination check.
Stopping after one tool call regardless of stop_reason would cut off multi-step exploration prematurely.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

You're debugging an agent built with the Claude Agent SDK that uses Read, Grep, and a custom MCP linting tool. Logs show that after each tool call, the agent's next request to the API omits the previous tool's output, so the model repeatedly re-requests the same file contents it already retrieved. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The loop is not appending tool results to conversation history before sending the next request, so the model has no memory of prior findings.
The model is hallucinating tool results and needs stricter tool descriptions.
The Grep tool is returning empty results, causing the model to retry.
The agent needs a larger max_tokens value to remember previous outputs.
answer: The loop is not appending tool results to conversation history before sending the next request, so the model has no memory of prior findings.
explanation: Tool results must be appended to conversation history between iterations so the model can incorporate new information into its reasoning on the next turn (Domain 1, Task Statement 1.1).
option_feedback: Tool results must be appended to conversation history between iterations so the model can incorporate new information into its reasoning on the next turn (Domain 1, Task Statement 1.1).
Hallucination isn't indicated here; the model is re-requesting data it never actually received in context.
Empty Grep results wouldn't explain repeated re-fetching of the same file via Read.
max_tokens controls output length per turn, not whether prior tool results persist across turns.

question:

The synthesis subagent receives two credible sources reporting different market growth figures (18% vs 24% CAGR) for the same industry segment. The final report shows only the 24% figure with no mention of the discrepancy. A reviewer later discovers the 18% figure in the underlying document analysis output. What should the synthesis process have done instead?
options: Annotate both figures in the report with their respective source attributions rather than selecting one value.
Average the two figures to produce a single blended estimate for the report.
Discard both figures since conflicting statistics indicate unreliable sources.
Use the figure from whichever source was retrieved first in the pipeline.
answer: Annotate both figures in the report with their respective source attributions rather than selecting one value.
explanation: Conflicting statistics from credible sources should be annotated with source attribution rather than arbitrarily selecting one value (Domain 5, Task Statement 5.6, Knowledge of).

question:

The document analysis subagent returns findings as free-form paragraphs summarizing each paper's conclusions. When the synthesis agent combines these into a report, several claims are stated without any indication of which source they came from, forcing reviewers to manually re-check every paper. options: Require the document analysis subagent to output structured claim-source mappings (source URL/document name, relevant excerpt) that downstream agents preserve.

question:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

Your pipeline auto-approves any extraction with a model-reported confidence above 0.9, with no human review. Six months later an audit finds the model was consistently over-confident on a newly introduced document template, and the errors went undetected until customers noticed. What should have been in place to catch this?
options: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to measure ongoing error rates and detect novel error patterns.
A fixed confidence threshold that is periodically raised as the model version is updated.
A rule that reprocesses every document a second time using a different prompt.
A monthly review of only the extractions the model flagged as low-confidence.
answer: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to measure ongoing error rates and detect novel error patterns.
explanation: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions is the mechanism for ongoing error rate measurement and catching novel error patterns like a new template the model doesn't handle well.
option_feedback: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions is the mechanism for ongoing error rate measurement and catching novel error patterns like a new template the model doesn't handle well.
Raising a static threshold doesn't detect new failure modes hidden within the "high-confidence" bucket.
Reprocessing with a different prompt doesn't systematically measure error rates or catch drift over time.
Reviewing only low-confidence items misses errors in the high-confidence bucket, which is exactly where this failure occurred.

question:

options: Calibrate field-level confidence thresholds against the labeled validation set, then route low-confidence or ambiguous/contradictory-source extractions to human review.

Randomly sample 10% of all extractions for review regardless of confidence score.

explanation: Field-level confidence scores calibrated using a labeled validation set is the documented method for setting review thresholds, and low-confidence or ambiguous/contradictory-source extractions should be prioritized for limited reviewer capacity.
option_feedback: Field-level confidence scores calibrated using a labeled validation set is the documented method for setting review thresholds, and low-confidence or ambiguous/contradictory-source extractions should be prioritized for limited reviewer capacity.

question:

During a long-running legacy system exploration, the agent process crashes after 40 minutes. options: Have each exploration agent export its state to a known location, and have the coordinator load a manifest on resume to determine what was already completed.

Switch from subagent delegation to a single monolithic agent to avoid multi-process crash points.

explanation: Structured state persistence via per-agent state exports and a coordinator-loaded manifest is the documented crash recovery mechanism for long codebase exploration sessions.
option_feedback: Structured state persistence via per-agent state exports and a coordinator-loaded manifest is the documented crash recovery mechanism for long codebase exploration sessions.

question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

The document analysis subagent hits a rate-limit error mid-task and immediately returns "analysis unavailable" with no other detail. The coordinator retries the entire research pipeline from scratch three times, tripling latency and cost, before eventually succeeding. What change to the subagent's error response would most effectively let the coordinator avoid unnecessary full-pipeline retries?
options: Return structured error context including failure type, what was attempted, and any partial results already gathered.
Have the subagent silently return an empty result set marked as successful so the pipeline continues.
Terminate the entire workflow immediately whenever any subagent encounters an error.
Increase the subagent's internal retry count so rate-limit errors are retried indefinitely before reporting failure.
answer: Return structured error context including failure type, what was attempted, and any partial results already gathered.
explanation: Structured error context (failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives) lets the coordinator decide whether to retry narrowly, substitute an approach, or proceed with partial results, per Task Statement 5.3.
option_feedback: Structured error context (failure type, attempted query, partial results, alternatives) lets the coordinator decide whether to retry narrowly, substitute an approach, or proceed with partial results, per Task Statement 5.3.

Terminating the whole workflow on a single failure is the opposite anti-pattern and wastes work already completed.
Unbounded internal retries don't address the coordinator's inability to make an informed recovery decision and can still stall the whole pipeline.

question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

Two web search subagent calls both return zero results: one because the API timed out before completing the search, the other because the search completed successfully but no matching articles exist. Both are logged identically as "no results found," and the coordinator treats both cases the same way, sometimes citing a topic as unresearched when it was actually just timed out. options: Have subagents distinguish access failures (needing retry decisions) from valid empty results in their error/response reporting.

explanation: Explicitly distinguishing access failures from valid empty results is called out in Task Statement 5.3 as necessary so the coordinator can make appropriate downstream decisions.
option_feedback: Explicitly distinguishing access failures from valid empty results is called out in Task Statement 5.3 as necessary so the coordinator can make appropriate downstream decisions.
Blanket retries waste effort on genuinely empty (successful) results and don't fix the ambiguous labeling problem.
Treating a legitimate empty result as an exception conflates a valid outcome with a failure, worsening the ambiguity.

question:

question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

A customer requests a price match against a competitor's current sale. Your refund policy only documents matching your own site's past promotions and is silent on competitor matching. Logs show the agent approximates a matching discount and applies it as if policy explicitly allowed it. What is the correct handling?
options: Escalate since policy is silent on this specific request, rather than approximating a resolution.
Apply the closest documented discount rate since the customer's intent is similar to a covered case.
Deny the request outright since competitor price matching is not explicitly permitted.

answer: Escalate since policy is silent on this specific request, rather than approximating a resolution.
explanation: Policy gaps, not just complex cases, are an explicit escalation trigger, and silent/ambiguous policy areas should be escalated rather than resolved by approximation (Domain 5, Task Statement 5.2, Knowledge of / Skills in).
option_feedback: Policy gaps, not just complex cases, are an explicit escalation trigger, and silent/ambiguous policy areas should be escalated rather than resolved by approximation (Domain 5, Task Statement 5.2, Knowledge of / Skills in).
Approximating an unlisted discount fabricates a policy exception the agent isn't authorized to grant.
Denying outright assumes an answer policy doesn't actually provide, which is itself an incorrect resolution.

question:

question:

Your pipeline concatenates a 40-page contract into a single extraction prompt. Audit results show the model reliably extracts clauses from the first and last few pages but frequently misses obligations defined in pages 15-25. What is the most effective way to address this pattern?

question:

question:

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

While automating a repetitive refactor, the agent needs to change a function signature that appears twice in a file with surrounding code that is nearly, but not exactly, identical in both locations. The agent's Edit calls repeatedly fail because the anchor text isn't unique. What is the most reliable resolution?
options: Read the entire file's contents, then Write the complete file back with both instances corrected.
Use Glob to find all files with the same function name and edit each individually.
Ask the agent to guess which instance is intended and apply Edit to only one.
Increase the anchor text length slightly and retry Edit indefinitely until it succeeds.
answer: Read the entire file's contents, then Write the complete file back with both instances corrected.
explanation: This directly reflects the documented skill of using Read followed by Write as a fallback when Edit cannot find unique anchor text.
option_feedback: This directly reflects the documented skill of using Read followed by Write as a fallback when Edit cannot find unique anchor text.
It misapplies Glob, which is for file path pattern matching, not fixing a non-unique match within one file.
It risks silently missing a required change.
It isn't a documented pattern and could loop indefinitely without resolution.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

An agent is asked to trace how a utility function is used throughout a legacy codebase, but the function is re-exported under different names from three separate wrapper modules. A single Grep search for the original function name misses most usages. What is the most effective next step?
options: First identify all exported names for the function via the wrapper modules, then run separate Grep searches for each name.
Increase the Bash timeout so the search can run against the entire repository at once.
Switch to Glob to locate all wrapper module files by filename pattern.
Ask the user to manually supply every alias under which the function might be called.
answer: First identify all exported names for the function via the wrapper modules, then run separate Grep searches for each name.
explanation: The guide specifically describes this pattern: tracing function usage across wrapper modules by first identifying all exported names, then searching for each name across the codebase.
option_feedback: The guide specifically describes this pattern: tracing function usage across wrapper modules by first identifying all exported names, then searching for each name across the codebase.
It doesn't address the root issue, which is search scope by name, not timeout.
It locates files by name pattern, not the content usages themselves.
It is a fallback that avoids using the agent's own tool capabilities.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer commits .mcp.json to the repository so the whole team can use a shared GitHub MCP server. Code review flags that the file contains a literal personal access token in plaintext. Rotating the token would require every teammate to manually edit the file. What is the correct fix?
options: Replace the literal token with ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in .mcp.json and have each developer set that variable in their own environment.
Move .mcp.json to ~/.claude.json so the token is stored per-user instead of in the repo.
Add .mcp.json to .gitignore and ask each developer to recreate the file locally with their own token.
Encrypt the token within .mcp.json using a team-shared symmetric key checked into the repo.
answer: Replace the literal token with ${GITHUB_TOKEN} in .mcp.json and have each developer set that variable in their own environment.
explanation: Environment variable expansion (e.g., ${GITHUB_TOKEN}) in .mcp.json is the documented mechanism for credential management without committing secrets, letting the shared server config stay version-controlled while each developer supplies their own token locally.
option_feedback: Environment variable expansion (e.g., ${GITHUB_TOKEN}) in .mcp.json is the documented mechanism for credential management without committing secrets, letting the shared server config stay version-controlled while each developer supplies their own token locally.
It abandons project-level sharing entirely, undermining the goal of team-wide availability via version control.
It loses the benefit of a shared, version-controlled server definition entirely.
It still commits a decryptable secret to the repo, which is the exact risk being avoided.

question:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

Your extraction system defines three schemas (invoice, receipt, purchase order) as separate tools, but document type isn't known before processing. Logs show that on ambiguous documents, the model sometimes responds with a clarifying question instead of calling any extraction tool, breaking the pipeline. What's the most effective configuration change?
options: Set tool_choice to "any" so the model must call one of the extraction tools rather than returning text.
Set tool_choice to "auto" and add a system prompt reminder to always extract data.
Force tool_choice to the invoice schema tool as a default fallback.
Merge all three schemas into one tool with an "unclear" enum field.
answer: Set tool_choice to "any" so the model must call one of the extraction tools rather than returning text.
explanation: Setting tool_choice: "any" guarantees the model calls one of the available tools rather than returning conversational text, which directly fixes the observed failure mode.
option_feedback: Setting tool_choice: "any" guarantees the model calls one of the available tools rather than returning conversational text, which directly fixes the observed failure mode.
It is exactly the setting causing the problem, since it permits text-only responses.
It forces the wrong tool when the document type is genuinely unknown, risking a bad extraction.
It is a reasonable schema redesign but doesn't address the immediate configuration bug and is a bigger change than warranted.

question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

Your document analysis subagent repeatedly calls a list_documents tool followed by get_document_metadata for each result, just to figure out which documents are relevant before doing any real analysis—consuming 4-5 calls before real work starts. What change would most directly reduce this overhead?
options: Expose the document catalog (titles, summaries, metadata) as an MCP resource instead of requiring sequential list/metadata tool calls.
Increase the subagent's tool call budget so it can make more exploratory calls per session.
Merge list_documents and get_document_metadata into a single tool call.
Have the coordinator pre-filter documents before delegating to the subagent.
answer: Expose the document catalog (titles, summaries, metadata) as an MCP resource instead of requiring sequential list/metadata tool calls.
explanation: Exposing a content catalog like document summaries as an MCP resource gives the subagent visibility into what's available without needing exploratory tool calls at all.
option_feedback: Exposing a content catalog like document summaries as an MCP resource gives the subagent visibility into what's available without needing exploratory tool calls at all.
It doesn't reduce overhead, it just permits more of it.
It is a reasonable tool-design improvement but still requires an active tool call each time, unlike a resource the agent can reference directly.
It shifts the problem to the coordinator rather than solving the underlying access pattern, and isn't the documented mechanism for this issue.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A developer configures both a Jira MCP server and a GitHub MCP server in the same project. When asked to "close out the ticket for this bug fix," the agent calls the GitHub MCP server's close_issue tool instead of the intended Jira ticket-closing tool, since both servers expose similarly named tools. What is the most likely explanation for this behavior?
options: Tools from all connected MCP servers are discovered at connection time and made simultaneously available, so overlapping tool names/descriptions across servers can cause misrouting.
Claude Code only loads tools from the first MCP server listed in .mcp.json, so the GitHub server is being read incorrectly.
The agent cannot access two MCP servers in the same session, so it fell back to a cached tool from a prior session.
MCP resources take priority over MCP tools when both are configured, causing the wrong tool to be invoked.
answer: Tools from all connected MCP servers are discovered at connection time and made simultaneously available, so overlapping tool names/descriptions across servers can cause misrouting.
explanation: It is correct. Tools from all configured MCP servers are discovered at connection time and available simultaneously to the agent — meaning overlapping or ambiguous tool descriptions across servers (not just within one server) can cause the same misrouting problems.
option_feedback: It is correct. Tools from all configured MCP servers are discovered at connection time and available simultaneously to the agent — meaning overlapping or ambiguous tool descriptions across servers (not just within one server) can cause the same misrouting problems.
It is factually wrong: Claude Code loads tools from all configured servers, not just the first.
It misstates MCP behavior — multiple servers can be active concurrently.
It confuses resources (content catalogs) with tools (actions); there is no such priority rule in the guide.

question:

options: Configure the shared web search server in project-scoped .mcp.json with ${API_KEY} expansion, and the experimental server in that researcher's user-scoped ~/.claude.json.
Add both servers to .mcp.json but comment out the experimental one for other developers.
Configure both servers in ~/.claude.json so neither is shared with the team.
Configure both servers in .mcp.json and rely on the researcher not sharing their branch.
answer: Configure the shared web search server in project-scoped .mcp.json with ${API_KEY} expansion, and the experimental server in that researcher's user-scoped ~/.claude.json.
explanation: This matches the knowledge that project-level .mcp.json is for shared team tooling while user-level ~/.claude.json is for personal/experimental servers, and that tools from all configured servers are simultaneously available to the agent.
option_feedback: This matches the knowledge that project-level .mcp.json is for shared team tooling while user-level ~/.claude.json is for personal/experimental servers, and that tools from all configured servers are simultaneously available to the agent.
It misuses .mcp.json's intended scope and JSON doesn't reliably support "commented out per-user" behavior.

question:

Giving it full web_search access fixed the immediate friction but introduced new problems: duplicated searches already done by the search agent and inconsistent source formatting. What's the best long-term architecture?
options: Provide the synthesis agent a narrowly scoped verify_fact tool for simple lookups, routing complex verification needs through the coordinator to the web search agent.
Keep full web_search access on the synthesis agent since it resolved the immediate friction.
Remove all tool access from the synthesis agent so it can only use provided context.
Merge the synthesis and web search agents into a single agent to eliminate handoffs.
answer: Provide the synthesis agent a narrowly scoped verify_fact tool for simple lookups, routing complex verification needs through the coordinator to the web search agent.
explanation: This matches the skill of providing scoped cross-role tools for high-frequency needs (e.g., a verify_fact tool for the synthesis agent) while routing complex cases through the coordinator.
option_feedback: This matches the skill of providing scoped cross-role tools for high-frequency needs (e.g., a verify_fact tool for the synthesis agent) while routing complex cases through the coordinator.

question:
Scenario: Code Generation with Claude Code

Your team configured a single Claude Code agent with Bash, Write, and a deployment MCP tool available for all tasks, including simple code-generation requests. Logs show the agent occasionally invokes the deployment tool while just drafting a new function, based on unrelated context in the conversation. What change would best prevent this?
options: Scope tool access per task type, restricting the deployment tool to sessions or skills where deployment is actually the intended action.
Add a confirmation prompt before every deployment tool call regardless of task context.
Rely on the model's judgment to avoid calling deployment tools when the task doesn't mention deployment.
Remove the deployment tool from the agent entirely so it can never be used.
answer: Scope tool access per task type, restricting the deployment tool to sessions or skills where deployment is actually the intended action.
explanation: This aligns with the skill of giving agents only the tools needed for their role, with limited cross-role tools for specific high-frequency needs, and with configuring allowed-tools in skill frontmatter (Task Statement 3.2) to restrict tool access during specific workflows.
option_feedback: This aligns with the skill of giving agents only the tools needed for their role, with limited cross-role tools for specific high-frequency needs, and with configuring allowed-tools in skill frontmatter (Task Statement 3.2) to restrict tool access during specific workflows.

question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

Your process_refund MCP tool returns {"error": "Operation failed"} whenever a refund exceeds the policy limit. Logs show the agent responds by repeatedly retrying the call with slightly reworded parameters, then eventually tells the customer "something went wrong" instead of explaining the policy limit. What change to the tool's error response would most directly fix this?
options: Return {"errorCategory": "business", "isRetryable": false, "message": "Refund exceeds $500 policy limit; escalate to a supervisor."}
Return an HTTP 500 status code so the agent's retry logic backs off exponentially.
Add a confidence field to the error response so the agent can judge whether to retry.
Return {"error": "Operation failed", "errorCode": 42} so the failure is at least machine-readable.
answer: Return {"errorCategory": "business", "isRetryable": false, "message": "Refund exceeds $500 policy limit; escalate to a supervisor."}
explanation: Uniform, generic errors like "Operation failed" prevent the agent from distinguishing a policy violation from a transient failure, which is exactly why it keeps retrying — this maps to the guide's point that generic responses "prevent the agent from making appropriate recovery decisions." Including errorCategory: "business", isRetryable: false, and a human-readable description lets the agent stop retrying and give the customer an accurate, policy-based explanation.
option_feedback: Uniform, generic errors like "Operation failed" prevent the agent from distinguishing a policy violation from a transient failure, which is exactly why it keeps retrying — this maps to the guide's point that generic responses "prevent the agent from making appropriate recovery decisions." Including errorCategory: "business", isRetryable: false, and a human-readable description lets the agent stop retrying and give the customer an accurate, policy-based explanation.
It addresses transport-level retry behavior but doesn't tell the agent why it failed.
It introduces a confidence score, which isn't the documented error-handling pattern and doesn't explain the business rule.
It adds a numeric code but no retryability signal or customer-facing explanation, so the agent still can't act appropriately.

question:
Scenario: Multi-Agent Research System

Your web search subagent's tool occasionally fails: sometimes due to a rate-limited API (transient), sometimes due to a malformed query the coordinator passed in (validation), and sometimes because a source requires paid access the system lacks (permission). Currently all three return {"success": false}. Which fix lets the subagent decide correctly whether to retry locally or propagate the failure upward?
options: Return errorCategory, isRetryable, and a human-readable description so the subagent can distinguish transient failures from validation and permission errors.
Have the subagent always retry the tool call three times before giving up, regardless of failure type.
Add a fallback tool that scrapes a secondary search engine whenever the primary tool returns false.
Instruct the coordinator in its system prompt to interpret any "success": false as a transient error.
answer: Return errorCategory, isRetryable, and a human-readable description so the subagent can distinguish transient failures from validation and permission errors.
explanation: Task Statement 2.2 (Domain 2) explicitly distinguishes transient, validation, permission, and business errors, and calls for errorCategory/isRetryable/description fields so the agent can make appropriate recovery decisions—directly matching this scenario.
option_feedback: Task Statement 2.2 (Domain 2) explicitly distinguishes transient, validation, permission, and business errors, and calls for errorCategory/isRetryable/description fields so the agent can make appropriate recovery decisions—directly matching this scenario.
It wastes calls retrying non-retryable validation/permission errors, which the guide flags as "wasted retry attempts" it aims to prevent.
It adds architecture complexity without fixing the missing error signal.
It hardcodes an incorrect assumption that all failures are transient, which is precisely the "uniform error response" anti-pattern the task statement warns against.

question:
Scenario: Developer Productivity with Claude

A custom MCP tool used by a developer-productivity agent queries an internal dependency-graph service. When the service is briefly unavailable, the tool returns the same error shape as when a requested module simply doesn't exist in the graph. The agent sometimes retries permanently-missing-module lookups repeatedly. What should the tool's error response include to fix this?
options: Structured error metadata distinguishing a transient service-unavailable error (retryable) from a valid "module not found" result (not an error, and not retryable).
A moduleExists boolean computed by a separate validation tool call before every graph query.
A longer default timeout so the service is less likely to appear unavailable.
A hard cap on the number of MCP tool calls per session.
answer: Structured error metadata distinguishing a transient service-unavailable error (retryable) from a valid "module not found" result (not an error, and not retryable).
explanation: This reflects the guide's distinction between access failures needing retry decisions and valid empty results representing a successful query with no matches — "module not found" isn't a failure at all and should never be retried, while service unavailability is transient and retryable.
option_feedback: This reflects the guide's distinction between access failures needing retry decisions and valid empty results representing a successful query with no matches — "module not found" isn't a failure at all and should never be retried, while service unavailability is transient and retryable.
It adds an extra round-trip instead of fixing the response contract.
It may reduce apparent unavailability but doesn't address the conflation of two different result types.
It limits total calls but doesn't stop the agent from wasting calls on a fundamentally non-retryable case.

question:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

An extraction tool queries a reference lookup service to validate extracted vendor names against a master database. When the lookup service is unreachable, the tool returns null for matched_vendor, identical to what it returns when the vendor name genuinely has no match in the database. Engineers notice validation reports treating outage periods as "unknown vendor" spikes. What should change?
options: Return a distinct error object for lookup-service failures, separate from a null value that represents a legitimate no-match result.
Have the extraction pipeline suppress null results entirely so they never appear in reports.
Fall back to fuzzy string matching whenever the lookup service returns null.
Log all null results at the same severity level so they can be reviewed manually in bulk.
answer: Return a distinct error object for lookup-service failures, separate from a null value that represents a legitimate no-match result.
explanation: This is the core distinction called out in Task Statement 2.2: an access failure (service unreachable) must be reported differently from a valid empty/no-match result, since conflating them corrupts downstream analysis, as seen here with outages misclassified as "unknown vendor" trends.
option_feedback: This is the core distinction called out in Task Statement 2.2: an access failure (service unreachable) must be reported differently from a valid empty/no-match result, since conflating them corrupts downstream analysis, as seen here with outages misclassified as "unknown vendor" trends.
It hides the problem rather than fixing the signal, and would also destroy legitimate no-match data.
It is a workaround that doesn't address the root cause of ambiguous error signaling.
It treats both cases identically, which is the very problem the fix needs to eliminate rather than reinforce.

question:

The agent responds identically to all three cases, sometimes telling customers a policy violation is a "temporary issue" and prompting them to retry. Increase the tool's timeout threshold so gateway timeouts occur less frequently.

explanation: Uniform error responses like "Operation failed" prevent the agent from distinguishing transient errors from validation, business, or permission errors, which is exactly the failure mode described. Structured metadata (errorCategory, isRetryable) lets the agent know when to retry, when to explain a policy violation, and when to escalate.
option_feedback: Uniform error responses like "Operation failed" prevent the agent from distinguishing transient errors from validation, business, or permission errors, which is exactly the failure mode described. Structured metadata (errorCategory, isRetryable) lets the agent know when to retry, when to explain a policy violation, and when to escalate.
It doesn't fix the missing information at the source.

question:

Logs show the agent responds to a temporary database timeout the same way it responds to a customer submitting an invalid order number — apologizing and telling the customer to "try again later" in both cases, even when the second case needs a corrected input, not a retry. What is the root cause?
options: A uniform "Operation failed" response gives the agent no way to distinguish a retryable transient failure from a validation error requiring different input.
The agent's system prompt does not instruct it to apologize differently depending on the tool that failed.
The tools should be consolidated into a single tool to reduce the number of possible failure messages.
The agent needs a longer timeout configured on the database connection.
answer: A uniform "Operation failed" response gives the agent no way to distinguish a retryable transient failure from a validation error requiring different input.
explanation: The guide states that uniform error responses like generic "Operation failed" prevent the agent from making appropriate recovery decisions, and that transient errors (timeouts) require different handling than validation errors (invalid input).
option_feedback: The guide states that uniform error responses like generic "Operation failed" prevent the agent from making appropriate recovery decisions, and that transient errors (timeouts) require different handling than validation errors (invalid input).
It treats the symptom as a prompting issue when the actual defect is missing information in the tool response itself.

question:

question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

Your automated PR review analyzes each modified file individually, producing high-quality local feedback. However, it consistently misses bugs caused by inconsistent function signatures between a modified API handler and its three callers in other files, since each file is reviewed in isolation. What change would best address this gap?
options: Add a separate cross-file integration pass after the per-file passes to examine data flow between modified files.

The web search subagent's tool returns {"success": false} for both rate-limit errors (retryable) and malformed-query errors (non-retryable, since the query itself is invalid). The coordinator currently retries both identically, and 30% of retries on malformed queries fail predictably every time. What is the most effective fix?
options: Add an isRetryable flag and error category to the tool's response so the subagent can skip retrying non-retryable failures.
Have the subagent cache prior queries so repeated malformed queries are detected client-side.
Increase the number of retry attempts allowed before the coordinator escalates.
Instruct the coordinator in its system prompt to "use judgment" when deciding whether to retry.
answer: Add an isRetryable flag and error category to the tool's response so the subagent can skip retrying non-retryable failures.
explanation: This matches the guide's point that returning structured metadata (including retryable/non-retryable distinctions) prevents wasted retry attempts, since malformed-query errors will never succeed no matter how many times they're retried.
option_feedback: This matches the guide's point that returning structured metadata (including retryable/non-retryable distinctions) prevents wasted retry attempts, since malformed-query errors will never succeed no matter how many times they're retried.

options: Return an isRetryable: false flag with a description for missing-field cases (since the field is absent from the source, not the result of a fixable format issue), reserving retries for genuinely recoverable errors like corruption.
Remove the isError flag entirely and always return partial results marked as successful.
Increase the number of retry attempts so missing-field cases eventually succeed.
Have the tool guess and fabricate a plausible value when a field is missing, rather than returning an error.
answer: Return an isRetryable: false flag with a description for missing-field cases (since the field is absent from the source, not the result of a fixable format issue), reserving retries for genuinely recoverable errors like corruption.
explanation: This matches the guide's point that retries are ineffective when required information is simply absent from the source, versus genuine format/structural errors that retries can fix; a retryable flag lets the agent stop wasting attempts on unrecoverable cases.
option_feedback: This matches the guide's point that retries are ineffective when required information is simply absent from the source, versus genuine format/structural errors that retries can fix; a retryable flag lets the agent stop wasting attempts on unrecoverable cases.
It removes useful failure signaling entirely and risks silently treating incomplete data as valid.

question:
Scenario: Customer Support Resolution Agent

Your agent calls lookup_order to retrieve shipping status, but on the next turn it asks the customer to repeat the order number and re-fetches identical data instead of using what was already returned. question:

question:

question:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

Your extraction pipeline processes invoices from vendors using inconsistent units, and validation logs show 18% of quantity fields contain fabricated standard units (e.g., "12 units") when source text used informal phrasing like "a dozen" or "roughly half a case." What change would most directly reduce this hallucination pattern?
options: Add few-shot examples showing correct extraction from informal measurement phrasing into standardized fields.
Increase the model's max_tokens to allow more reasoning before producing the final answer.
Add a post-processing regex step that flags any quantity field for manual review.
Switch the quantity field from optional to required in the JSON schema.
answer: Add few-shot examples showing correct extraction from informal measurement phrasing into standardized fields.
explanation: Few-shot examples reduce hallucination in extraction tasks by demonstrating how to handle informal measurements correctly (Domain 4, Task Statement 4.2).
option_feedback: Few-shot examples reduce hallucination in extraction tasks by demonstrating how to handle informal measurements correctly (Domain 4, Task Statement 4.2).
More reasoning tokens don't address a lack of demonstrated handling for informal phrasing.
A regex flag increases review burden but doesn't fix the underlying extraction accuracy.
Making a field required increases fabrication risk rather than reducing it, since the model must fill it even when uncertain.

question:
Scenario: Structured Data Extraction

Your extraction pipeline flags "unclear" values whenever a document uses non-standard phrasing, even when the requested fact is clearly present. The prompt currently instructs the model to "only extract values you're confident are correct." Analysts report the false positive rate on the unclear flag is unacceptably high. What should you change first?
options: Replace the confidence-based instruction with explicit criteria specifying the exact conditions under which a value should be marked "unclear" versus extracted normally.
Increase the number of retries allowed before a field is marked unclear.
Switch the "unclear" enum value to a lower-priority field so it appears less often in reports.
Ask the model to double-check its own extraction in a follow-up turn within the same session.
answer: Replace the confidence-based instruction with explicit criteria specifying the exact conditions under which a value should be marked "unclear" versus extracted normally.
explanation: Vague confidence-based instructions like "only extract values you're confident are correct" don't improve precision the way specific, explicit criteria for the ambiguous case do.
option_feedback: Vague confidence-based instructions like "only extract values you're confident are correct" don't improve precision the way specific, explicit criteria for the ambiguous case do.
Retrying is meant for correctable format/structural errors, not for fixing ambiguous flagging criteria.
Reordering the field's visibility hides the problem rather than fixing the underlying criteria.
Self-review in the same session retains reasoning context and is less effective than independent review or clearer criteria at catching this kind of issue.

question:
Scenario: Claude Code for Continuous Integration

Your automated PR review agent is instructed to "be conservative and only report high-confidence findings." Developers still report a 35% false positive rate on style-related comments, causing many to ignore the bot entirely. The prompt gives no other guidance on what counts as a valid issue. What change would most effectively reduce false positives?
options: Replace the vague conservatism instruction with explicit criteria defining which categories to report (e.g., bugs, security) versus skip (e.g., minor style, local patterns).
Add a stronger instruction telling the model to "only report issues you are 100% certain about."
Lower the model's temperature setting to make outputs more deterministic.
Ask the model to rate its own confidence from 1-10 and filter out anything below 8.
answer: Replace the vague conservatism instruction with explicit criteria defining which categories to report (e.g., bugs, security) versus skip (e.g., minor style, local patterns).
explanation: Explicit categorical criteria address the root cause, since vague instructions like "be conservative" don't reliably improve precision compared to specific, concrete rules (Domain 4, Task 4.1).
option_feedback: Explicit categorical criteria address the root cause, since vague instructions like "be conservative" don't reliably improve precision compared to specific, concrete rules (Domain 4, Task 4.1).
This is just a stronger version of the same vague conservatism instruction and doesn't add concrete criteria.
Temperature affects randomness, not the model's understanding of what qualifies as a reportable issue.
Self-reported confidence scores are not a reliable substitute for explicit categorical criteria.

question: A support resolution agent handles password resets, shipping-status questions, and goodwill-credit requests. CSAT is dropping because every ticket triggers order lookup, fraud review, policy retrieval, and a manager-style reasoning pass. Compliance still requires evidence before issuing credits. Which architecture best improves latency without weakening the risky cases?
options: Run all tickets through the full investigation path, then cache the final assistant response for similar future tickets.
Use deterministic triage to send low-risk intents to short workflows, while credit requests enter a tool-verified review path with approval gates.
Replace the live agent with nightly batch processing so every ticket can be scored at lower cost before any reply is sent.
Create separate specialist agents for every support category and require unanimous agreement before any customer-facing message is sent.
answer: Use deterministic triage to send low-risk intents to short workflows, while credit requests enter a tool-verified review path with approval gates.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Use deterministic triage to send low-risk intents to short workflows, while credit requests enter a tool-verified review path with approval gates, because: the support system needs fast handling for routine intents and stronger controls for customer-impacting credits.

A good agentic architecture does not make every ticket pay the cost of the hardest ticket. Password resets and shipping-status questions can often be handled by narrow workflows with limited tools and fast completion criteria. Goodwill credits are different: they require account evidence, policy checks, and often human or policy approval before a side effect occurs.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Run all tickets through the full investigation path, then cache the final assistant response for similar future tickets. - Caching can reduce repeated prompt cost for stable context, but final responses tied to customer state can become stale or unsafe. It leaves simple support intents stuck behind fraud and policy work they do not need.

Replace the live agent with nightly batch processing so every ticket can be scored at lower cost before any reply is sent. - Batch processing fits offline, independent workloads. A customer waiting in chat needs immediate progress, and some cases require interactive clarification.

Create separate specialist agents for every support category and require unanimous agreement before any customer-facing message is sent. - Multi-agent review may improve difficult decisions, but applying it to resets and status checks wastes latency and creates avoidable coordination failure points.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Match agent depth to risk, reversibility, and evidence needs.
Cost optimization should preserve stronger validation for side-effecting support actions.
Batch or multi-agent patterns are not automatically better for live customer workflows.

question: A customer-support agent calls a billing lookup tool before answering refund questions. When the billing API fails, the tool currently returns only the string "something went wrong." Claude sometimes retries expired cards, asks customers irrelevant questions, or drafts an answer without account evidence. What tool-result design best supports safe recovery?
options: Return the raw stack trace so Claude can infer the bug source and decide whether to keep retrying.
Tell Claude in the system prompt to avoid answering refund questions whenever a tool sounds uncertain.
Return typed errors such as retryable, user-fixable, permission-denied, and not-found, with safe next actions for each case.
Suppress failed tool results from the conversation so Claude focuses on the policy article and avoids confusing error details.
answer: Return typed errors such as retryable, user-fixable, permission-denied, and not-found, with safe next actions for each case.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Return typed errors such as retryable, user-fixable, permission-denied, and not-found, with safe next actions for each case, because: the agent needs a structured recovery signal before it can safely answer account-specific refund questions.

Tool use is a contract between the model and the application. If the billing lookup fails, the application should send a tool result that clearly represents the failure and enough metadata for the next step. A timeout might allow a bounded retry; a permission-denied error may require internal escalation; a not-found result may require customer verification.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Return the raw stack trace so Claude can infer the bug source and decide whether to keep retrying. - A stack trace is developer-oriented and may not map to customer-safe actions. It also risks leaking unnecessary internals into a support transcript.

Tell Claude in the system prompt to avoid answering refund questions whenever a tool sounds uncertain. - This depends on the model interpreting vague wording consistently. A production support agent should receive structured evidence about why a lookup failed and what recovery is allowed.

Suppress failed tool results from the conversation so Claude focuses on the policy article and avoids confusing error details. - The missing account lookup is itself important evidence. Hiding it makes unsupported refund answers more likely because the model loses the reason it should pause.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Tool errors should be represented as data, not only prose.
Recovery logic depends on distinguishing retryable, user-fixable, authorization, and not-found failures.
Account-specific answers should not proceed when the required tool evidence is absent.

Troubleshooting tool use - Anthropic Docs - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use

question: A support team wants every pull request that changes refund prompts to run Claude Code against regression transcripts before merge. The run must be non-interactive, avoid editing production files, respect repository permissions, and produce concise review notes for maintainers. Which CI design best matches that requirement?
options: Run Claude Code locally after merge so maintainers can inspect failures once the refund prompt is already deployed.
Give Claude Code write access in CI so it can automatically patch prompts and push fixes whenever transcripts fail.
Ask developers to paste transcript results into chat manually because CI cannot run agentic checks without a person present.
Run Claude Code headlessly in the pull-request workflow with read-limited permissions, fixed transcripts, and posted review artifacts.
answer: Run Claude Code headlessly in the pull-request workflow with read-limited permissions, fixed transcripts, and posted review artifacts.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Run Claude Code headlessly in the pull-request workflow with read-limited permissions, fixed transcripts, and posted review artifacts, because: CI needs a repeatable non-interactive check that informs maintainers before customer-facing prompt changes merge.

Claude Code headless mode is intended for programmatic usage such as automation and CI. For this support-agent use case, the run should be bounded: fixed regression transcripts, limited permissions, deterministic output expectations, and artifacts that reviewers can inspect. That gives maintainers useful signal without letting an automated process silently change production behavior.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Run Claude Code locally after merge so maintainers can inspect failures once the refund prompt is already deployed. - Post-merge review is too late for a regression gate. It detects customer-support failures after the risky change has entered the main branch.

Give Claude Code write access in CI so it can automatically patch prompts and push fixes whenever transcripts fail. - Auto-fixing may be useful in some controlled workflows, but this requirement asks for review notes. Granting write access expands the blast radius of a failed evaluation.

Ask developers to paste transcript results into chat manually because CI cannot run agentic checks without a person present. - Manual checks are inconsistent and easy to skip. Claude Code supports headless operation for automation, which is the natural fit here.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Headless Claude Code supports non-interactive automation and CI workflows.
CI agents should have the minimum permissions needed for the gate they perform.
Review artifacts are safer than silent mutation when humans own merge decisions.

question: A support resolution agent automatically flags potential refund abuse. Reviewers find many false positives when customers use angry phrases like "you charged me twice" or "this is fraud." The business wants fewer wrongful fraud escalations without missing real abuse. What prompt-and-output change is most appropriate?
options: Require cited account evidence for each fraud indicator, include an uncertainty field, and route unsupported cases to manual review.
Tell Claude that angry language is usually a fraud signal and ask it to be more conservative with refunds without requiring evidence.
Remove the fraud category from the output and let all disputed-charge tickets go directly to refund approval.
Ask the model to output only a confidence score, then escalate cases where confidence exceeds a fixed threshold.
answer: Require cited account evidence for each fraud indicator, include an uncertainty field, and route unsupported cases to manual review.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Require cited account evidence for each fraud indicator, include an uncertainty field, and route unsupported cases to manual review, because: the failure is unsupported fraud labeling from language cues rather than verified account behavior.

Reducing false positives usually requires changing what the model must prove. In this case, a valid fraud escalation should be tied to concrete evidence such as repeated chargebacks, mismatched identity signals, or policy-defined abuse patterns. An uncertainty field and manual-review path prevent the agent from forcing a binary answer when the retrieved evidence is incomplete.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Tell Claude that angry language is usually a fraud signal and ask it to be more conservative with refunds without requiring evidence. - This amplifies the problematic shortcut. Customers often use strong words when they believe billing failed, and the agent would punish tone rather than facts.

Remove the fraud category from the output and let all disputed-charge tickets go directly to refund approval. - This avoids one error by creating another. Real abuse still needs detection, and automatic approval may cause financial loss.

Ask the model to output only a confidence score, then escalate cases where confidence exceeds a fixed threshold. - Confidence without evidence is not a reliable production signal. The support team needs reasons and source-backed indicators, not a number detached from the account record.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

False-positive reduction depends on observable evidence and calibrated fallback paths.
Customer emotion is a weak proxy for fraud or abuse.
Confidence scores should not replace grounded criteria in high-impact routing.

question: A long-running support case spans three days and includes two order lookups, a warranty exception approved by a supervisor, and several casual chat turns. After compaction, the agent sometimes forgets which approval ID justified the exception. Which TWO practices best protect reliability while keeping context manageable?
options: Ask Claude to write a more detailed natural-language summary that repeats approval identifiers whenever the conversation approaches the context limit.
Persist the approval ID, order numbers, policy version, and source timestamps in structured case state outside the compacted transcript.
Keep every raw chat turn in the active prompt so the model can rediscover the exception during each response.
Compact routine conversation into a short case summary while reloading exact evidence records when the agent needs to act.
answer: Persist the approval ID, order numbers, policy version, and source timestamps in structured case state outside the compacted transcript.
Compact routine conversation into a short case summary while reloading exact evidence records when the agent needs to act.
explanation:
✅ The correct options are: Persist the approval ID, order numbers, policy version, and source timestamps in structured case state outside the compacted transcript and Compact routine conversation into a short case summary while reloading exact evidence records when the agent needs to act, because: exact support evidence must survive compaction while ordinary dialogue can be summarized.

Compaction is useful, but it is not a database. Approval IDs, order numbers, policy versions, and source timestamps are action-critical facts; losing or paraphrasing them can lead to an unsupported warranty exception. A structured case state or durable session store keeps those facts exact, while a compact narrative summary keeps the prompt lean.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Ask Claude to write a more detailed natural-language summary that repeats approval identifiers whenever the conversation approaches the context limit. - More summary text may still drop a key identifier or blur who approved what. The risk is precision loss, not merely lack of detail.

Keep every raw chat turn in the active prompt so the model can rediscover the exception during each response. - Full-history prompting wastes context on casual turns and can still bury the important approval ID. Retrieval of exact records is a better fit for later action.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Summaries are useful for narrative continuity, but exact approvals and identifiers need durable storage.
Reload source evidence before customer-impacting actions.
Context management is about preserving the right facts, not keeping every token active.

Compaction - Anthropic Docs - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction

question: A retailer wants to automate return-label approval for unopened accessories within 30 days, domestic shipping only, no fraud hold, and no prior exception on the order. All fields are available through existing APIs, and the policy rarely changes. Customers may still write messy explanations. Which design is the best fit?
options: Use a free-running agent loop that inspects the full conversation and decides when it has enough evidence to approve labels.
Send every request to a specialist subagent team so policy, fraud, shipping, and tone can be debated independently.
Use a deterministic workflow to fetch required fields and apply the rule, invoking Claude only for exception summaries or unclear customer text.
Ask Claude to classify each case from the customer message first, then call APIs only when its confidence is below threshold.
answer: Use a deterministic workflow to fetch required fields and apply the rule, invoking Claude only for exception summaries or unclear customer text.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Use a deterministic workflow to fetch required fields and apply the rule, invoking Claude only for exception summaries or unclear customer text, because: the approval rule is stable, structured, and directly checkable through existing APIs.

Not every support automation should become an open-ended agent. Here the policy is fully specified: date window, product condition, domestic shipping, fraud hold, and prior exception. A deterministic workflow can call the needed APIs, apply the rule, and produce consistent outcomes. Claude remains useful for interpreting messy prose, drafting customer-friendly explanations, or summarizing exceptions for humans.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Use a free-running agent loop that inspects the full conversation and decides when it has enough evidence to approve labels. - This adds judgment where the system already has a checkable rule. The agent might stop early or overread customer wording.

Send every request to a specialist subagent team so policy, fraud, shipping, and tone can be debated independently. - The rule does not need deliberation. Multi-agent coordination would slow a high-volume return flow without adding meaningful reliability.

Ask Claude to classify each case from the customer message first, then call APIs only when its confidence is below threshold. - The customer message is not the source of truth for order age, fraud hold, or exception history. Confidence gating would put weak evidence ahead of authoritative fields.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Stable business rules with structured inputs usually belong in deterministic workflows.
Agent loops are strongest when the next action requires judgment, exploration, or tool selection.
Natural-language messiness does not override authoritative system data.
