question:
In a multi-agent research system, specialist agents return claim reviews to a coordinator. The coordinator expects each review to include `claim_id`, `verdict`, `source_ids`, `quoted_spans`, and `needs_human_review`. Downstream dashboards also group results by claim ID, so one missing field can corrupt more than one report section. The coordinator also triggers chart generation from the same structured reviews.

Which TWO changes best address the failure?
options: Keep Markdown but add three examples showing the preferred heading order and citation style
Define a schema with required claim fields, allowed verdict enums, and source-span arrays
Let the coordinator normalize any specialist phrasing into the closest known verdict during synthesis
Validate each review before aggregation and retry or reject only the fields that fail
answer: Define a schema with required claim fields, allowed verdict enums, and source-span arrays
Validate each review before aggregation and retry or reject only the fields that fail
explanation:
✅ The correct options are: Define a schema with required claim fields, allowed verdict enums, and source-span arrays and Validate each review before aggregation and retry or reject only the fields that fail, because: the coordinator needs both a strict handoff contract and an enforcement step before synthesis.

The issue is not that the Markdown is unattractive; it is that downstream automation cannot trust it. A schema defines the legal shape of a specialist review, including required claim IDs, constrained verdicts, and source-span arrays that can be matched to records. Validation then prevents malformed reviews from entering the synthesis step.

Targeted retries are important because they keep the workflow efficient and honest. The system can repair missing structure without forcing a verdict that the evidence does not support.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Keep Markdown but add three examples showing the preferred heading order and citation style - Examples guide formatting but do not enforce required fields, types, or allowed verdicts.

Let the coordinator normalize any specialist phrasing into the closest known verdict during synthesis - This pushes ambiguity downstream. The coordinator might silently convert an uncertain phrase into a stronger verdict.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Structured outputs are contracts for downstream automation.
Validate before aggregation, not after synthesis has already used bad data.
Preserve uncertainty with explicit statuses instead of free-form wording.

question:
A multi-agent research system is preparing a competitive landscape report. One specialist finds that an executive biography on a company site conflicts with a regulator filing about the executive's current role. The coordinator can mark only the affected table cell as pending. Those unaffected findings are time-sensitive.

What should the coordinator do next?
options: Pause all agents until the report owner resolves the executive-title conflict
Prefer the regulator filing automatically because official filings are always more current than company pages
Publish the company-site title with a footnote that another source disagrees
Escalate the title conflict with both sources while continuing independent research tasks
answer: Escalate the title conflict with both sources while continuing independent research tasks
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Escalate the title conflict with both sources while continuing independent research tasks, because: the unresolved decision is localized and should not freeze unrelated evidence collection.

A strong coordinator distinguishes blocking uncertainty from independent work. The executive-title conflict needs a human decision because two plausible sources disagree and the final report should not silently choose. But product screenshots, pricing pages, and integration notes can continue because they do not depend on the title.

The handoff should include both sources, source dates if available, affected report sections, and the exact choice the owner needs to make.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Pause all agents until the report owner resolves the executive-title conflict - This treats a localized blocker as a global stop. It protects the disputed title but wastes the research window.

Prefer the regulator filing automatically because official filings are always more current than company pages - Official does not always mean current for this exact fact. The system should not invent a universal tie-break rule.

Publish the company-site title with a footnote that another source disagrees - A footnote is not enough when the report owner needs to decide the governing source before publication.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Escalate the narrow decision that needs ownership.
Continue independent work when it does not rely on the blocker.
Handoffs should identify affected outputs, not just conflicting sources.

Multiagent orchestration - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/multiagent-orchestration
Session operations - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/session-operations

question:
A company is deciding whether to expand a multi-agent research system from internal analysts to client-facing weekly briefings. The prototype produces polished summaries, and analysts like the writing quality. The dashboard will be reviewed after every prompt, tool, and source-index change, so it needs signals that can show regressions rather than one-time launch confidence. Leaders want the dashboard to support a go or no-go release call across releases.

Which dashboard best reflects objective reliability for this research system?
options: Average coordinator confidence, average summary length, analyst satisfaction, and number of sources retrieved
Golden-eval accuracy, citation-support audit rate, disagreement surfacing, validation failures, and open risk counts
Total tokens used, number of agents spawned, final report readability, and time to first draft
Reviewer comments per report, number of rewritten paragraphs, and the coordinator's final uncertainty note
answer: Golden-eval accuracy, citation-support audit rate, disagreement surfacing, validation failures, and open risk counts
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Golden-eval accuracy, citation-support audit rate, disagreement surfacing, validation failures, and open risk counts, because: those signals measure the concrete defects that would make client-facing research unsafe.

The prototype's writing quality is not the same as publication readiness. A useful dashboard measures whether the system answers representative tasks correctly, whether citations support claims, whether specialist disagreement reaches the coordinator or reviewer, and whether schema or validation failures are increasing after changes. Open risk counts prevent unresolved gaps from being hidden by polished prose.

This is especially important for multi-agent research because each layer can make the final answer sound more coherent while losing provenance or uncertainty along the way.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Average coordinator confidence, average summary length, analyst satisfaction, and number of sources retrieved - These are weak proxies. Confidence, length, and source count can rise while citation quality falls.

Total tokens used, number of agents spawned, final report readability, and time to first draft - These are operational metrics, not reliability metrics. They say little about whether claims are supported.

Reviewer comments per report, number of rewritten paragraphs, and the coordinator's final uncertainty note - Helpful review signals, but too indirect and too late to serve as the main readiness dashboard.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Readiness dashboards should track the actual failure modes.
Fluency and confidence are not evidence of research reliability.
Multi-agent synthesis needs provenance, validation, and disagreement visibility.

question: A CI assistant can call two internal tools, both currently named `workflow_status`: one reads check results and one reruns failed jobs. In headless runs, Claude sometimes reruns jobs when it only needed to summarize the failing check. Which redesign best improves tool selection without relying on a longer prompt?
options: Keep both names but add examples to the system prompt showing when reruns are allowed.
Merge the read and rerun paths into one tool with an optional `action` string and mode flag.
Rename tools by effect and require typed branch, commit SHA, workflow ID, and rerun-reason fields.
Disable the rerun tool in every headless job and ask maintainers to rerun checks manually.
answer: Rename tools by effect and require typed branch, commit SHA, workflow ID, and rerun-reason fields.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Rename tools by effect and require typed branch, commit SHA, workflow ID, and rerun-reason fields, because: the CI assistant needs the tool boundary itself to distinguish read-only inspection from a side-effecting rerun.

Good tool design makes the operation obvious through the name, description, and input schema. A read-only status tool should not be confused with a mutation tool that changes CI state.

Typed fields such as commit SHA and workflow ID give the wrapper concrete values to validate before a job is rerun. The rerun reason also makes the side effect auditable later.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Keep both names but add examples to the system prompt showing when reruns are allowed - Examples can improve selection, but they leave two similarly named tools with different effects. In a headless CI path, prompt guidance should support the tool contract, not compensate for a confusing one.

Merge the read and rerun paths into one tool with an optional `action` string and mode flag - This blurs the read/write boundary and makes a dangerous operation look like a mode on a generic utility. Optional strings are weaker than a narrow schema when downstream automation has side effects.

Disable the rerun tool in every headless job and ask maintainers to rerun checks manually - Manual reruns may be appropriate for some branches, but a blanket ban throws away useful automation. A better design keeps the capability while making selection and validation precise.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Tool names and descriptions should expose the real operation, especially read versus mutation.
Typed inputs help CI wrappers verify branch, commit, and workflow identity before acting.
Prompt examples are helpful, but they do not replace a well-designed tool schema.

question: A release pipeline starts a headless Claude Code diagnosis before dependency tests finish. Later, a second CI job should continue the same conversation and ask Claude to incorporate the final logs. The runner may process multiple release branches on the same machine, and the resumed job depends on the same MCP and tool permissions. Which TWO practices best preserve continuity without assuming hidden state?
options: Start a fresh headless run and paste the prior assistant summary into the new prompt as context.
Capture the session identifier from the first run and resume that session in the follow-up job.
Rely on `--continue` to find the right conversation from whichever checkout the runner uses next automatically.
Pass required settings, MCP configuration, and allowed tools again when the resumed job depends on them.
answer: Capture the session identifier from the first run and resume that session in the follow-up job.
Pass required settings, MCP configuration, and allowed tools again when the resumed job depends on them.
explanation:
✅ The correct options are: Capture the session identifier from the first run and resume that session in the follow-up job and Pass required settings, MCP configuration, and allowed tools again when the resumed job depends on them, because: one choice identifies the conversation to continue while the other recreates the runtime boundary the CI job needs.

Session resumption is useful for multi-stage CI because the second job can continue the diagnostic conversation instead of reconstructing it from a lossy summary.

The CI script should also treat runtime configuration as explicit input. If the resumed run depends on MCP servers, settings, or tool permissions, those must be supplied rather than assumed.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Start a fresh headless run and paste the prior assistant summary into the new prompt as context - A summary can help, but it is not the same as resuming the saved session. Important tool results or unresolved details may be missing from the pasted text.

CI resumption should identify the intended session directly, not by habit or recency.
Resuming conversation state is separate from re-supplying launch-time configuration.
Multi-stage automation should make continuity auditable through explicit IDs and flags.

Headless mode is designed for running Claude Code from scripts and automation. A pull request reviewer should not depend on an operator being present to approve prompts.

question: A Claude Code pull-request reviewer flags many “security regressions” that later turn out to be harmless refactors. Reviewers still want Claude to catch real risk, but noisy comments are slowing merges and weakening trust in the automation. Security owners have asked for evidence they can audit. Which output contract best reduces false positives?
options: Require Claude to include a numeric confidence score, rule tag, and hide comments below 70 percent.
Require file-line evidence, violated rule, diff or test support, and abstain when evidence is missing.
Ask Claude to write shorter comments so maintainers can dismiss false alarms faster.
Run the reviewer twice and post only findings that both independent runs phrase similarly in comments.
answer: Require file-line evidence, violated rule, diff or test support, and abstain when evidence is missing.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Require file-line evidence, violated rule, diff or test support, and abstain when evidence is missing, because: a CI reviewer should publish only claims that maintainers can verify against concrete evidence.

False positives often come from plausible interpretations that are not grounded in the changed lines or actual test output. Requiring evidence makes each comment auditable.

An explicit abstain value matters because the safest outcome for an unsupported security claim is often no automated comment, not a confident-sounding guess.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Require Claude to include a numeric confidence score, rule tag, and hide comments below 70 percent - Confidence is not the same as proof. A score can look rigorous while still hiding whether the finding is tied to the diff, a rule, or a test failure.

Ask Claude to write shorter comments so maintainers can dismiss false alarms faster - Short comments may be less annoying, but they do not improve correctness. The merge queue needs fewer unsupported findings, not faster triage of the same noise.

Run the reviewer twice and post only findings that both independent runs phrase similarly in comments - Two runs can converge on the same mistaken pattern. Agreement is weaker than requiring concrete changed lines, a rule, and supporting evidence.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Reduce false positives with evidence requirements and abstention paths.
Self-rated confidence is a weak routing signal for automated review comments.
CI review output should be easy for humans and scripts to audit.

question: A Claude Code CI job writes migration-risk notes after scanning changelogs and internal upgrade guides. During long runs, later comments cite “the docs” but lose which versioned page and log line supported each claim. The summary is consumed after context compaction and by a separate release reviewer. What design best preserves provenance through compaction and review?
options: Ask Claude to keep a running prose summary of all sources it remembers using in the run.
Place all changelogs before code files in the prompt so source material appears earlier.
Remove citations from CI comments and keep only the migration recommendation for readability.
Persist source URL, version, locator, retrieval time, and claim ID with each generated note.
answer: Persist source URL, version, locator, retrieval time, and claim ID with each generated note.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Persist source URL, version, locator, retrieval time, and claim ID with each generated note, because: reviewers need every migration-risk claim tied to durable evidence, not just remembered source categories.

Compaction and long CI sessions can compress away details that later become important. A separate provenance record keeps the page, version, locator, and claim relationship available for audit.

The CI comment can stay readable while still linking each recommendation to a claim ID and source evidence. That is different from asking the model to remember where a claim came from.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Ask Claude to keep a running prose summary of all sources it remembers using in the run - A summary is useful for orientation, but it can merge sources and drop exact locators. It is not a reliable provenance store for migration decisions.

Place all changelogs before code files in the prompt so source material appears earlier - Reordering context can improve attention during a call, but it does not preserve page versions or line references after later context changes.

Remove citations from CI comments and keep only the migration recommendation for readability - Readability matters, but deleting citations makes the note harder to audit. The release reviewer needs a path back to the evidence.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Provenance should be stored as durable metadata when claims affect CI or release decisions.
Context ordering helps attention; it does not replace citation retention.
Claim IDs make generated notes traceable even after compaction or handoff.

question: A team wants Claude Code CI repairs to follow repository conventions: preferred test targets, branch naming, and files that must not be edited. Only a link to the team wiki, because repository memory should stay empty for CI jobs.
Stable repository conventions and CI repair rules, while keeping secrets and local runner details out.
Only the current release emergency instructions, because long-lived rules make Claude less adaptive.
answer: Stable repository conventions and CI repair rules, while keeping secrets and local runner details out.
explanation:

Secrets, tokens, and temporary runner paths are a different category. They belong in CI configuration, environment variables, or local settings rather than shared project memory.

All conventions, tokens, and runner paths, so every CI job starts with complete instructions - This confuses completeness with safety. Shared memory is not the right place for credentials or runner-local paths.

Only a link to the team wiki, because repository memory should stay empty for CI jobs - Avoiding repository memory leaves Claude without immediate project conventions. A link is weaker than concise, versioned instructions in the checkout.

explanation:

Structured output is the right boundary when downstream automation depends on exact fields. The workflow can still include a human summary, but ticket routing should consume validated JSON rather than a markdown table.

question:

Which session workflow best fits this follow-up?
options: Branch the existing session so header exploration reuses gathered logs without overwriting the original patch path.
Resume the original session and ask Claude to replace the retry-timing patch with the header fix if it seems better.
Start a completely new session with no prior logs so the second diagnosis is uncontaminated.
Continue the latest session from the runner and rely on the final pull request diff to show both attempts.
answer: Branch the existing session so header exploration reuses gathered logs without overwriting the original patch path.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Branch the existing session so header exploration reuses gathered logs without overwriting the original patch path, because: the team needs shared evidence with separate investigation histories.

Branching is useful when a follow-up should start from an existing conversation but try a different approach. It keeps the first retry-timing patch path available for audit.

The alternative header hypothesis can reuse logs and files, which avoids the cost of rebuilding context from scratch. The two paths can then be compared before maintainers choose the safer fix.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Resume the original session and ask Claude to replace the retry-timing patch with the header fix if it seems better - This can muddy the record of why the first patch was proposed. The request is not just to continue; it is to explore an alternative without overwriting the first path.

Start a completely new session with no prior logs so the second diagnosis is uncontaminated - Fresh context has value for review, but this scenario explicitly wants the already gathered evidence. Starting from nothing wastes useful CI context.

Continue the latest session from the runner and rely on the final pull request diff to show both attempts - The latest session may not be the right one, and a diff is a weak audit artifact for reasoning history. The team needs separate session lineage.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Resume when continuing the same line of work; branch when exploring an alternative from shared context.

question:

options: Ask Claude to compare the returned check names with the names it expected from repository memory before posting.
Treat any successful tool call as authoritative and let branch protection reject the merge if checks changed later.
Retry the same tool three times and use the first response that reports all required checks as green.
Verify the response matches the request, current commit SHA, required-check set, conclusions, and freshness before recommending merge.
answer: Verify the response matches the request, current commit SHA, required-check set, conclusions, and freshness before recommending merge.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Verify the response matches the request, current commit SHA, required-check set, conclusions, and freshness before recommending merge, because: a successful tool call is not enough when stale green data can approve the wrong commit.

Tool-result validation has two layers here. First, the workflow should know which tool request the result answers. Second, the returned data must semantically match the merge decision being made.

Checking commit SHA, required-check membership, allowed conclusion values, and retrieval freshness prevents a previous commit's successful checks from being reused as current approval evidence.

Ask Claude to compare the returned check names with the names it expected from repository memory before posting - This can catch missing jobs, but it does not bind the result to the current commit. A stale response can still contain the right names.

Treat any successful tool call as authoritative and let branch protection reject the merge if checks changed later - Branch protection is a backstop, not a reason for the assistant to publish unsupported advice. The recommendation itself should be based on validated evidence.

Retry the same tool three times and use the first response that reports all required checks as green - Retrying without semantic checks can amplify stale-success risk. The workflow needs validation criteria, not just repetition.

question:
A Claude Code CI job generates a deployment-risk record for each pull request. The wrapper validates the record against a JSON schema and then checks business rules: every blocking item must include a file path, evidence snippet, and owner team. Operators want faster recovery for small defects and clearer escalation when the evidence itself is inconsistent. They also need retry logs that explain why a record was held.

What retry strategy is best?
options: Retry the entire prompt until the record passes schema validation or the token budget is exhausted.
Accept the first schema-valid record and leave business-rule conflicts for human reviewers after deployment.
Retry recoverable field defects with targeted instructions, capped attempts, and hold or escalate semantic conflicts.
Remove validation and ask Claude to self-review its deployment-risk record before returning the final answer.
answer: Retry recoverable field defects with targeted instructions, capped attempts, and hold or escalate semantic conflicts.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Retry recoverable field defects with targeted instructions, capped attempts, and hold or escalate semantic conflicts, because: validation failures do not all deserve the same broad retry loop.

A missing or malformed field can often be repaired from the existing context, so a targeted retry is efficient. The retry should name the exact defect and keep a bounded attempt count.

Semantic conflicts are different. If logs still show an unresolved migration error, the workflow should not keep asking for a nicer deployment-risk record until one passes. It should hold, escalate, or require new evidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Retry the entire prompt until the record passes schema validation or the token budget is exhausted - This wastes work and can mask contradictions. Passing the schema does not prove the record is semantically safe.

Accept the first schema-valid record and leave business-rule conflicts for human reviewers after deployment - The business-rule check exists to prevent bad routing before deployment. Deferring the conflict defeats the gate.

Remove validation and ask Claude to self-review its deployment-risk record before returning the final answer - Self-review may help as an extra step, but it cannot replace deterministic schema and business validation in CI.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Separate schema defects, business-rule conflicts, and unavailable evidence.

Rewrite the parser wrapper to prefer whichever currency amount appears immediately before the tax label in the rendered text. - That is an invented fix without investigation. question: An extraction team labels grant applications as nonprofit, school, or vendor. Optimize the prompt for fewer unknown labels so downstream analysts spend less time on manual review.
Define category-specific evidence rules, negative examples for employer-only mentions, required source fields, and an unknown path for insufficient support.

answer: Define category-specific evidence rules, negative examples for employer-only mentions, required source fields, and an unknown path for insufficient support.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Define category-specific evidence rules, negative examples for employer-only mentions, required source fields, and an unknown path for insufficient support, because: it turns the ambiguous employer-contact case into observable evidence rules plus a supported way to abstain.

A useful extraction rubric does two jobs: it teaches Claude what evidence counts, and it gives reviewers a repeatable basis for accepting or rejecting a label. The unknown path is part of quality, not a failure of confidence.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Tell Claude to use common sense and choose the most likely category whenever the document sounds business-related. - This reinforces the false-positive pattern. A company name in a contact field is not evidence of commercial vehicle use, and common-sense phrasing is too subjective for repeatable review.

Optimize the prompt for fewer unknown labels so downstream analysts spend less time on manual review. - This may lower queue volume while increasing bad labels. Unknown exists to protect the dataset when required evidence is missing.

Rubrics should use observable criteria, not vibes or self-rated certainty.
Near-miss negative examples are valuable when false positives come from plausible but insufficient cues.

question: A climate-report extractor must capture facility temperature exceptions. Summarize the entire report into one narrative paragraph before extraction so the model can focus on fewer tokens.
Split the report into equal token chunks and accept the first chunk result that returns a valid temperature field.
answer: Pre-extract candidate exceptions with page anchors, place them beside the target schema and decision rules, and keep links back to the full report.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Pre-extract candidate exceptions with page anchors, place them beside the target schema and decision rules, and keep links back to the full report, because: the missed appendix fact must be elevated into the working set while keeping provenance back to the original report.

The failure is not that Claude lacks a large enough context window; it is that the decisive exception was poorly positioned relative to the decision. A robust extraction workflow creates a focused working set of candidate exceptions, source anchors, and decision rules before producing the final structured field.

Keep the report in its original order and add an instruction that appendix details may override table defaults. - This states the rule but does not improve the model’s access to the buried exception. It is a tempting prompt-only fix for a context-organization problem.

Summarize the entire report into one narrative paragraph before extraction so the model can focus on fewer tokens. - Compression may make the input shorter, but it can also discard exact exception wording and provenance. The extracted value would be harder to audit.

Lost-in-the-middle mitigation is about evidence placement, not just bigger context.
Keep source anchors when summarizing or chunking critical documents.

question:

Retry only recoverable schema defects with the original source snippet, preserve validated fields, and route absent or unsupported renewal evidence to review.

question:
Claude Code generates migration tasks from failing test logs. A downstream script opens tickets only when a task has a package name, owner, severity enum, repro command, and source evidence. Human reviewers need a predictable incomplete state when the source logs are insufficient. The ticket schema is also consumed by dashboards, so silent coercion would spread bad labels beyond the initial migration queue.

What output strategy best supports this pipeline?
options: Ask Claude to write JSON in a fenced code block and retry the whole prompt whenever the parser fails.
Return Markdown plus a best-effort JSON appendix so humans can read the summary even when automation fails.
Use regex cleanup to coerce Claude's output into the expected shape, then let TypeScript type checks catch any bad fields later.
Use a JSON Schema with required fields, enum values, evidence arrays, and targeted retries only for schema or validation failures.
answer: Use a JSON Schema with required fields, enum values, evidence arrays, and targeted retries only for schema or validation failures.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Use a JSON Schema with required fields, enum values, evidence arrays, and targeted retries only for schema or validation failures, because: the downstream ticket creator needs a validated contract, not merely JSON-shaped prose.

Structured output should define the fields automation depends on: package, owner, severity, repro command, and evidence. Enum constraints prevent unsupported labels, required fields catch missing commands, and validation-specific retries keep recovery focused. If evidence is absent, the item should fail validation or be marked incomplete rather than repaired by guesswork.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Ask Claude to write JSON in a fenced code block and retry the whole prompt whenever the parser fails. - This may produce parseable text, but it does not enforce the field contract. Whole-prompt retries are blunt and can repeat semantic omissions.

Return Markdown plus a best-effort JSON appendix so humans can read the summary even when automation fails. - Humans may like it, but the automation boundary becomes unreliable. The script needs validated fields first.

Use regex cleanup to coerce Claude's output into the expected shape, then let TypeScript type checks catch any bad fields later. - Cleanup can convert bad output into convincing bad data. Validation should happen before tickets are opened.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Structured output is about enforceable contracts, not just JSON formatting.
Use enums and required fields for values downstream systems depend on.
Retry only recoverable validation defects; do not guess missing evidence.

📌 References:

Structured outputs - Claude Platform Docs - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
Get structured output from agents - Claude Code Docs - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/structured-outputs

question:
A team is designing a Claude Code workflow for routine dependency migrations. Most steps involve reading package files, searching for imports, editing source, and running tests. The lead engineer wants to avoid building tools that merely rename existing file operations, while still giving Claude a reliable way to retrieve ownership data. The workflow may run weekly, but the source tree and test commands remain directly accessible in the checked-out repository.

Select TWO statements that best describe when to use built-in versus custom tools here.
options: Use built-in Claude Code Read, Glob, Grep, Edit, and Bash tools for local source analysis and test-driven edits.
Create a custom tool when Claude must query the internal ownership service with typed inputs and return owner IDs the repository does not contain.
Create a custom MCP server for every recurring refactor so Claude uses the same tool name each time instead of reading files directly.
Avoid built-in Bash for tests and expose each test command as a separate MCP prompt so prompts can control execution more safely.
answer: Use built-in Claude Code Read, Glob, Grep, Edit, and Bash tools for local source analysis and test-driven edits.
Create a custom tool when Claude must query the internal ownership service with typed inputs and return owner IDs the repository does not contain.
explanation:
✅ The correct options are: Use built-in Claude Code Read, Glob, Grep, Edit, and Bash tools for local source analysis and test-driven edits and Create a custom tool when Claude must query the internal ownership service with typed inputs and return owner IDs the repository does not contain, because: local code work is already covered, while external ownership data needs a controlled integration boundary.

The decision is not whether the workflow is important; it is whether Claude needs a capability the built-in tools do not provide. Reading files, searching imports, editing, and running tests are native Claude Code activities. Querying an internal service introduces external data, authorization, and typed output requirements, so a custom tool or MCP integration can be the right boundary.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Create a custom MCP server for every recurring refactor so Claude uses the same tool name each time instead of reading files directly. - Repetition alone does not justify a tool. A slash command, skill, or documented workflow may be enough when all work is local.

Avoid built-in Bash for tests and expose each test command as a separate MCP prompt so prompts can control execution more safely. - Prompts do not execute commands. Test execution should be handled through actual tools and permission controls.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Built-in Claude Code tools are usually enough for local repository inspection, editing, and tests.
Custom tools make sense for external systems, typed contracts, and controlled side effects.
MCP prompts are reusable prompt templates, not action endpoints.

📌 References:

Tools reference - Claude Code Docs - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
Give Claude custom tools - Claude Code Docs - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/custom-tools

question:
A release engineering group wants Claude Code involved in nightly branch readiness checks. The current process is stable: checkout branch, install dependencies, run unit tests, run integration tests, collect artifacts, and publish a report. When a failure is ambiguous, however, engineers spend hours reading traces before deciding who should fix it. The architecture must therefore make routine success boring while making unusual failures easier to investigate and assign.

What architecture best balances reliability and agentic judgment?
options: Use a deterministic workflow for checkout, build, test, and report generation, with Claude Code invoked only for ambiguous failure analysis.
Replace the pipeline with one autonomous Claude Code agent that decides which build, test, and reporting steps to run each time.
Create separate agents for checkout, dependency install, unit tests, integration tests, and summary writing, all coordinated by a manager.
Ask developers to run the existing script manually, then paste failures into Claude only after the release branch is already blocked.
answer: Use a deterministic workflow for checkout, build, test, and report generation, with Claude Code invoked only for ambiguous failure analysis.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Use a deterministic workflow for checkout, build, test, and report generation, with Claude Code invoked only for ambiguous failure analysis, because: the known sequence should stay repeatable while Claude handles the uncertain interpretation step.

This is the agent-versus-workflow tradeoff in a code-generation setting. Stable build and test steps are easier to audit when they remain scripted. Claude Code adds the most value when the pipeline reaches a noisy failure that needs source inspection, hypothesis generation, or ownership reasoning. Keeping those boundaries separate makes the nightly check both debuggable and useful.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Replace the pipeline with one autonomous Claude Code agent that decides which build, test, and reporting steps to run each time. - The steps are already known. Letting an agent rediscover them adds variability to a release gate.

Create separate agents for checkout, dependency install, unit tests, integration tests, and summary writing, all coordinated by a manager. - This turns deterministic tasks into coordination overhead. More agents do not automatically mean more reliability.

Ask developers to run the existing script manually, then paste failures into Claude only after the release branch is already blocked. - That loses early automation benefits and delays analysis. The workflow can call Claude at the right failure point instead.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Use workflows for known, repeatable sequences.
Use agents for ambiguous decisions that benefit from tool use and reasoning.
Multi-agent topology should earn its coordination cost.

📌 References:

Run Claude Code programmatically - Claude Code Docs - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless
How the agent loop works - Claude Code Docs - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop

question: A research coordinator has eight specialist agents summarizing the same technical standard. The final synthesis is missing one late appendix requirement even though a subagent found it. The prompt already includes the full transcript from every specialist. What context change best reduces the risk of another missed requirement?
options: Increase the model context window and keep every specialist transcript in chronological order for synthesis
Build a claim ledger with source spans, unresolved items, and deduplicated specialist findings
Ask each specialist to write shorter prose summaries before the final synthesis begins
Have the final writer reread only the highest-confidence specialist report for each section
answer: Build a claim ledger with source spans, unresolved items, and deduplicated specialist findings
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Build a claim ledger with source spans, unresolved items, and deduplicated specialist findings, because: the system lost a source-backed requirement inside too much uncurated agent history.

The right fix is to change what reaches the synthesis step. A claim ledger turns many transcripts into a working set of evidence: each candidate requirement, its source span, the agent that found it, duplicates, and any unresolved status. That preserves the appendix requirement in a form the final writer can inspect instead of hoping it notices a late paragraph in a long conversation.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Increase the model context window and keep every specialist transcript in chronological order for synthesis - More room can still bury the important appendix under repeated tool output and commentary. Long context helps only when relevant material remains findable.

Ask each specialist to write shorter prose summaries before the final synthesis begins - Summaries save tokens, but prose compression may drop the exact source span the final writer needs to verify.

Have the final writer reread only the highest-confidence specialist report for each section - Confidence is not the same as evidence coverage. The specialist who found the late appendix could be excluded by this shortcut.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Curate context into source-bearing artifacts, not raw transcripts.
Lost facts often need better ordering and structure, not just more tokens.
Keep unresolved claims visible until synthesis explicitly handles them.

📌 References:

Context editing - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing
Manage tool context - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context

question: A research assistant answers daily analyst questions about a stable internal taxonomy. Most questions are simple lookups, but a few require fresh source review when an entry is missing or a cited page changed. Analysts complain about slow responses and rising costs. Which routing design best balances latency, cost, and reliability?
options: Send every question to five independent agents and publish the majority answer
Use one fast agent for all requests and skip retrieval unless the answer sounds uncertain to users
Batch all analyst questions overnight so expensive research runs only once per day
Serve verified taxonomy hits quickly and trigger deeper review only for misses, stale sources, or conflicts
answer: Serve verified taxonomy hits quickly and trigger deeper review only for misses, stale sources, or conflicts
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Serve verified taxonomy hits quickly and trigger deeper review only for misses, stale sources, or conflicts, because: the workload contains many routine lookups and a smaller set of cases that deserve slower research.

A good production architecture does not spend the same amount of reasoning on every request. Stable taxonomy hits can be answered from verified data with low latency. Misses, stale entries, and conflicting evidence should enter a deeper path where agents retrieve sources, compare evidence, or ask for review. That gives analysts speed for common questions without hiding the cases where reliability needs more work.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Send every question to five independent agents and publish the majority answer - This treats cost as unlimited and may still miss source-quality problems. Majority vote is not a freshness check.

Use one fast agent for all requests and skip retrieval unless the answer sounds uncertain to users - Self-uncertainty is a shaky router. Some low-evidence answers sound fluent and confident.

Batch all analyst questions overnight so expensive research runs only once per day - Batch mode fits delayed independent workloads, not interactive analyst support with same-day needs.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Route by observable conditions such as cache hits, source age, and conflicts.
Use multi-agent depth where it buys reliability.
Batch processing is not a universal latency solution.

📌 References:

Prompt caching - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
Batch processing - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing

question: A team adds a CI job that runs Claude Code after research prompt changes. The job should detect missing citation fields without giving the run broad repository access, depending on a developer chat, or requiring an operator to answer follow-up questions. Which setup is most appropriate?
options: Run `claude -p` with narrow inputs, allowed read tools, JSON output, and a schema gate that fails CI
Launch an interactive Claude Code session and let the reviewer ask for missing context during CI
Allow all tools so the agent can search the whole repository when citation fields are absent
Ask Claude to write a prose review and rely on maintainers to notice citation warnings later
answer: Run `claude -p` with narrow inputs, allowed read tools, JSON output, and a schema gate that fails CI
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Run `claude -p` with narrow inputs, allowed read tools, JSON output, and a schema gate that fails CI, because: CI needs a bounded, non-interactive check that can make citation-field failures machine-actionable.

Headless Claude Code is useful when the task is scripted: provide the relevant diff or fixtures, restrict tools to what the check needs, request structured output, and let CI validate the result. For a citation-field check, the important behavior is not a conversational review; it is a repeatable pass/fail signal when required fields are missing or malformed.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Launch an interactive Claude Code session and let the reviewer ask for missing context during CI - CI jobs should not wait for a chat. Ambiguous input should fail with a clear result instead of hanging.

Allow all tools so the agent can search the whole repository when citation fields are absent - Extra access adds risk and noise. A citation contract can be checked with scoped inputs and read-only permissions.

Ask Claude to write a prose review and rely on maintainers to notice citation warnings later - Human-readable prose is easy to miss. The gate should fail automatically when required citation fields are absent.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Headless runs should be scripted, bounded, and non-interactive.
CI gates work best with structured output and explicit failure conditions.
Tool permissions should match the narrow job, not the whole repository.

📌 References:

Run Claude Code programmatically - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless
Permissions - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions

question: A medical research triage pipeline marks abstracts as `practice_changing` for human analysts. Review shows too many positives when abstracts mention outcomes but do not compare against the required standard of care or provide a passage supporting that comparison. Which TWO changes best reduce false positives?
options: Require a quoted comparison passage and mark the item `needs_review` when that passage is absent
Raise the confidence threshold for `practice_changing` and keep the same label definitions
Evaluate against a labeled set that includes near-miss outcome-only abstracts as negatives
Ask a second agent to approve all positive labels before analysts see them in the queue
answer: Require a quoted comparison passage and mark the item `needs_review` when that passage is absent
Evaluate against a labeled set that includes near-miss outcome-only abstracts as negatives
explanation:
✅ The correct options are: Require a quoted comparison passage and mark the item `needs_review` when that passage is absent and Evaluate against a labeled set that includes near-miss outcome-only abstracts as negatives, because: one change fixes the evidence contract at runtime while the other measures the exact boundary that was failing.

The false positives come from confusing any outcome mention with a practice-changing comparison. Requiring a quoted passage forces the model to point to the evidence that satisfies the comparator criterion. The `needs_review` path prevents unsupported positives from being promoted just because the abstract feels promising. The labeled near-miss set then checks whether the change works on the cases most likely to fool the system.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Raise the confidence threshold for `practice_changing` and keep the same label definitions - Confidence filtering does not add the missing comparator requirement. Confident false positives can still pass.

Ask a second agent to approve all positive labels before analysts see them in the queue - Review can be useful, but duplicated vague criteria can reproduce the same error. The reviewer needs evidence rules and eval feedback.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Reduce false positives with explicit evidence requirements.
Give the model an abstain or review label for unsupported cases.
Use near-miss negatives to test classification boundaries.

📌 References:

Reduce hallucinations - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations
Define success criteria and build evaluations - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests

question: An MCP server supports a research workspace used by several analyst agents. It needs to expose static source packets, a callable search against a licensed index, and a reusable "compare two claims" prompt. Which design best clarifies the boundaries for Claude? The analysts also want permission reviews to distinguish read-only context from actions that call external services.
options: Expose one `research` tool that accepts a mode parameter for packets, search, and comparison
Put the source packets into prompts so Claude can ask for the packet it wants by name
Expose packets as resources, licensed search as a tool, and claim comparison as a prompt
Make every capability a resource and let Claude infer when it should execute search-like behavior
answer: Expose packets as resources, licensed search as a tool, and claim comparison as a prompt
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Expose packets as resources, licensed search as a tool, and claim comparison as a prompt, because: each MCP surface has a different job in the research workspace.

Static source packets are context, so resources are the cleanest way to expose them. A licensed search call is an action with inputs, authorization, and returned results, so it belongs behind a tool schema. A repeatable comparison routine is a prompt pattern, which makes it reusable without pretending it is a data object or an external operation.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Expose one `research` tool that accepts a mode parameter for packets, search, and comparison - A broad mode-switching tool is harder to describe, authorize, and validate. It hides the reason each capability exists.

Put the source packets into prompts so Claude can ask for the packet it wants by name - Prompts are recipes for interaction. Static source packets should remain readable resources.

Make every capability a resource and let Claude infer when it should execute search-like behavior - A resource is not the right boundary for parameterized search. Search needs a callable tool contract.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

MCP resources expose readable context.
MCP tools expose callable actions with schemas.
MCP prompts package reusable interaction patterns.

📌 References:

Resources - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/resources
Tools - https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools

question: A market research system uses twelve agents to analyze product categories. Running all agents in parallel is fast, but reports contain contradictory market-size figures because each agent normalizes currencies differently before synthesis. The CFO wants faster reports only if numbers remain auditable. What topology is best?
options: Keep all agents fully parallel and ask the final writer to choose the most plausible figure
Parallelize independent evidence collection, then use a shared normalization step and conflict gate before synthesis
Run every category sequentially through one senior agent so no agents disagree with each other
Ask each agent to include a confidence score and publish figures above the finance threshold
answer: Parallelize independent evidence collection, then use a shared normalization step and conflict gate before synthesis
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Parallelize independent evidence collection, then use a shared normalization step and conflict gate before synthesis, because: the slow part can stay parallel while the numeric consistency risk gets a single auditable control point.

The problem is not that parallel agents exist; it is that they each apply currency normalization differently. Independent collection can still happen concurrently. Once evidence is gathered, market-size figures should pass through a common normalization rule and a conflict gate that catches inconsistent units, exchange rates, or source assumptions before the final writer synthesizes the report.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Keep all agents fully parallel and ask the final writer to choose the most plausible figure - Plausibility is not an audit trail. The CFO needs consistent calculation evidence, not a prose tie-break.

Run every category sequentially through one senior agent so no agents disagree with each other - Sequential work reduces speed and may only hide disagreement. It does not create a measurable normalization control.

Ask each agent to include a confidence score and publish figures above the finance threshold - Confidence does not validate currency conversion or source comparability.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Parallelize independent research, not dependent reconciliation.
Shared transformations are reliability boundaries for numeric synthesis.
Conflict gates can preserve speed while protecting auditable claims.

📌 References:

Parallel tool use - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use
Multiagent orchestration - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/multiagent-orchestration

question: A Claude Code task must update a monorepo research pipeline with separate retrievers, rankers, and citation validators. The repo has many old experiments, benchmark folders, and abandoned prototypes. The team wants the agent to understand the active path before editing. What exploration workflow is best?
options: Paste every retriever and validator file into the prompt so no dependency is missed
Ask a subagent to summarize the whole repository and edit whichever file appears most central afterward first
Start by editing the ranker because ranking usually controls research quality most directly
Read project guidance, trace active entry points, inspect relevant tests, then narrow searches to touched modules
answer: Read project guidance, trace active entry points, inspect relevant tests, then narrow searches to touched modules
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Read project guidance, trace active entry points, inspect relevant tests, then narrow searches to touched modules, because: the repo contains stale experiments and the agent needs the live research path before changing behavior.

In a large codebase, context quality matters more than raw file volume. Project guidance can name conventions and active directories. Entry points and configs reveal which retriever, ranker, and validator paths actually run. Tests show the expected contract. After that, targeted searches can inspect nearby modules without dragging old experiments into the working context.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Paste every retriever and validator file into the prompt so no dependency is missed - This can bury the active path under obsolete files and duplicated patterns.

Ask a subagent to summarize the whole repository and edit whichever file appears most central afterward first - A summary is not enough to justify edits. The agent needs traceable evidence from active code and tests.

Start by editing the ranker because ranking usually controls research quality most directly - The premise may be true in some systems, but this repo requires exploration before selecting the change point.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Start large-codebase work from guidance, entry points, and tests.
Old experiments are context noise unless the live path references them.
Targeted search beats wholesale context stuffing.

📌 References:

Set up Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases
Common workflows - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/common-workflows

question:
A multi-agent research system ranks vendor security advisories for a weekly briefing used by incident-response leads. The current rubric asks agents to identify items that are "important, credible, and actionable." Analysts say the top-ranked items are often well-written blog recaps rather than primary advisories, and different agents disagree about what "important" means. They want examples that help agents reject tempting but weak evidence without making every item a manual-review case.

Which TWO rubric revisions would most improve reliability for this ranking task?
options: Add a seniority score for the writing source so polished advisories rank above terse primary security bulletins
Define severity with observable fields such as affected product, exploit status, patch availability, and primary-source link
Ask each agent to explain its private reasoning in more detail before assigning a final rank
Include negative examples that demote secondary recaps lacking primary advisory evidence
answer: Define severity with observable fields such as affected product, exploit status, patch availability, and primary-source link
Include negative examples that demote secondary recaps lacking primary advisory evidence
explanation:
✅ The correct options are: Define severity with observable fields such as affected product, exploit status, patch availability, and primary-source link and Include negative examples that demote secondary recaps lacking primary advisory evidence, because: the first makes the rubric inspectable and the second blocks the fluent-secondary-source shortcut.

The current rubric relies on adjectives that different agents can interpret differently. Observable fields make ranking decisions easier to compare and review: product impact, exploit status, patch availability, and primary-source evidence are facts the system can check. Negative examples then teach the exact failure boundary, showing that polished blog recaps should not outrank primary advisories when they lack direct support.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Add a seniority score for the writing source so polished advisories rank above terse primary security bulletins - This rewards presentation instead of authority and could make blog recaps look better than primary advisories.

Ask each agent to explain its private reasoning in more detail before assigning a final rank - More prose does not repair vague criteria. It can make inconsistent ranking sound more convincing.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Rubrics should use observable criteria, not quality adjectives alone.
Negative examples help models learn near-miss boundaries.
Research ranking should prefer source authority and evidence over fluency.

📌 References:

Define success criteria and build evaluations - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests
Claude prompting best practices - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

question:
A multi-agent research system produces comparative reports from hundreds of pages of procurement rules. The final writer receives a long prompt containing every extracted passage in source order, then a short instruction at the end: "prioritize mandatory exclusion rules over optional scoring guidance." In recent reports, the writer accurately summarizes early background material and late formatting instructions, but it misses several mandatory exclusion rules located near the middle of the evidence bundle. Human reviewers will inspect only the exceptions, which means the final writer's prompt must make mandatory exclusions visible before a mistake reaches review.

Which redesign most directly mitigates the lost-in-the-middle failure?
options: Chunk the evidence by decision category and place mandatory exclusion summaries plus source spans next to each synthesis task
Keep the same evidence order but add a stronger final sentence telling the writer not to miss mandatory exclusion rules
Ask three final writers to independently synthesize the whole bundle and merge overlapping conclusions
Summarize all middle passages into one paragraph so the final prompt becomes shorter
answer: Chunk the evidence by decision category and place mandatory exclusion summaries plus source spans next to each synthesis task
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Chunk the evidence by decision category and place mandatory exclusion summaries plus source spans next to each synthesis task, because: the missed rules are buried in the middle and need to be repositioned into focused working sets.

Lost-in-the-middle problems are often layout problems. If a final writer receives hundreds of pages in source order, critical material can sit far from the instruction that depends on it. Grouping evidence by decision category and placing mandatory exclusion facts near the relevant synthesis task makes those facts easier to use. Keeping source spans prevents the chunking step from turning precise procurement rules into unverifiable summaries.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Keep the same evidence order but add a stronger final sentence telling the writer not to miss mandatory exclusion rules - Urgency is not retrieval. The buried evidence remains buried.

Ask three final writers to independently synthesize the whole bundle and merge overlapping conclusions - Parallel writers can repeat the same context-position failure, and merging may blur provenance.

Summarize all middle passages into one paragraph so the final prompt becomes shorter - Shorter context can still be lossy. Procurement exclusions need exact source support, not a compressed blob.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Reorder and chunk long context around the decision being made.
Keep critical evidence close to the instruction that uses it.
Preserve source spans when summarizing regulated material.

📌 References:

Context windows - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows
Context editing - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing

question:
A research team uses Claude Code to maintain prompts, schemas, and fixture files for a multi-agent literature review system. A proposed improvement asks Claude to find stale fixture IDs inside the repository and check whether each ID still exists in a licensed article registry. If the registry is unavailable, the system should report a typed external-validation failure rather than pretending the local scan answered the whole question.

Which tool strategy is best?
options: Build one MCP tool that reads repository files, edits fixtures, queries the registry, and writes the final report
Use only built-in file tools and ask Claude to infer registry validity from fixture names
Use built-in search for local fixture discovery and a narrow custom registry lookup tool for external validation
Convert all fixture files into MCP resources and let Claude compare IDs without calling a registry
answer: Use built-in search for local fixture discovery and a narrow custom registry lookup tool for external validation
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Use built-in search for local fixture discovery and a narrow custom registry lookup tool for external validation, because: only the registry check needs a domain-specific authenticated boundary.

The best architecture separates ordinary local work from the external dependency. Claude Code's built-in file and search tools are appropriate for finding fixture IDs in the repository. A custom or MCP-backed lookup is appropriate for the licensed registry because it needs authentication, typed results, rate-limit behavior, and clear error states. This avoids building a large custom tool for work the environment already supports.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Build one MCP tool that reads repository files, edits fixtures, queries the registry, and writes the final report - That mixes local inspection, mutation, external calls, and reporting into one broad tool, making permissions and validation muddy.

Use only built-in file tools and ask Claude to infer registry validity from fixture names - Local names cannot prove current external registry status. The authoritative source must be checked.

Convert all fixture files into MCP resources and let Claude compare IDs without calling a registry - Resources expose context, but they do not answer whether an external ID still exists today.

📚 Key Concepts to Remember for the Exam:

Prefer built-in tools when they already fit the local task.
Add custom tools for external APIs, typed validation, or controlled side effects.
Avoid broad tools that merge unrelated responsibilities.

📌 References:

Tools reference - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
Give Claude custom tools - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/custom-tools

question:
A multi-agent research system produces a nightly evidence table for a clinical operations team. The required process is stable: ingest approved sources, extract claims into a schema, validate required fields, run a citation-support check, and publish only rows that pass. The team also wants failed rows to carry a reason code so analysts know whether the issue was missing evidence, schema failure, or citation mismatch.

What orchestration change best fits this workload?
options: Keep the coordinator loop but add a prompt reminding it to avoid unnecessary searches
Add more specialist agents so the coordinator has better advice before deciding each step
Use batch processing for the whole pipeline and accept whichever rows finish first
Move the fixed stages into a deterministic workflow and reserve agents for extraction or exception analysis
answer: Move the fixed stages into a deterministic workflow and reserve agents for extraction or exception analysis
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Move the fixed stages into a deterministic workflow and reserve agents for extraction or exception analysis, because: the nightly process has known gates and should not depend on an open-ended coordinator loop to decide when to stop.

Agentic loops are valuable when the system must choose the next action based on uncertain observations. This pipeline is different. The stages are known, the validation gates are mandatory, and publication has a clear condition. A deterministic workflow can enforce ingest, extraction, field validation, citation-support checking, and publish eligibility in order. Agents remain useful inside stages where judgment is needed, such as claim extraction or exception analysis.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Keep the coordinator loop but add a prompt reminding it to avoid unnecessary searches - A reminder does not enforce ordering or completion. The loop can still search too long or publish too early.

Add more specialist agents so the coordinator has better advice before deciding each step - The bottleneck is control flow, not lack of agent advice. More specialists can increase coordination noise.

question:

explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Persist a decision and evidence ledger with source IDs, exact snippets, timestamps, and unresolved assumptions across compactions, because: resumed agents need durable source facts rather than summary-level memory when modifying claims.

Compaction is useful for keeping long work manageable, but it is lossy. The pricing error happened because the exact tool result and quote were available only in the old conversation, while the resumed agent saw a shortened summary. A durable ledger gives later agents the authoritative record: source ID, exact snippet, retrieval timestamp, current claim, decision history, and unresolved assumptions. That lets the system compact conversation safely while preserving facts that should not be paraphrased away.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Make each compacted summary longer and ask the coordinator to preserve all business-critical details - Better summaries still compress evidence. They are not a reliable substitute for exact snippets and metadata.

Prevent all compaction so every resumed agent can inspect the complete original conversation - This ignores context limits and can make resumed work harder to navigate. Durable evidence storage is more practical.

Reviewers also complain that previous escalations arrived as vague “please check” comments without the exact decision being requested.

options: Escalate deployment-routing changes with owner ambiguity, incomplete rollback evidence, or unavailable validation, and include the pending approval decision.
Allow the change whenever Claude reports high confidence and the configuration diff is small and easy to review.
Require manual approval for every repository-settings pull request created by Claude.
Route only failed local checks to humans and let passing configuration changes merge automatically after a short summary.
answer: Escalate deployment-routing changes with owner ambiguity, incomplete rollback evidence, or unavailable validation, and include the pending approval decision.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Escalate deployment-routing changes with owner ambiguity, incomplete rollback evidence, or unavailable validation, and include the pending approval decision, because: the review gate should follow operational impact and evidence limits, not confidence or diff size.

A deployment-routing change can be small and still risky. It affects which artifact reaches staging across multiple services, and the scenario gives three escalation triggers: unclear ownership, undocumented rollback, and partial validation outage.

The handoff should also be decision-ready. Instead of a vague “please check,” reviewers need to know whether they are approving the route change, assigning an owner, deferring until validation returns, or rejecting the proposal.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Allow the change whenever Claude reports high confidence and the configuration diff is small - Confidence and diff size miss the operational blast radius. A tiny config change can redirect a deployment.

Require manual approval for every repository-settings pull request created by Claude - This overcorrects by slowing routine reversible updates. The scenario asks for automation plus selective escalation.

Route only failed local checks to humans and let passing configuration changes merge automatically - Passing local checks do not prove owner approval, rollback readiness, or staging behavior across services.

Human handoffs should state the decision being requested.

question:

explanation:

The original `history` tool is too vague. It hides the service being queried and accepts free-form input, which invites invalid calls and branch-scope mistakes. As more history tools are added, that ambiguity becomes more expensive.

question:

Create a draft guide, run a separate evidence-check pass against functions and examples, then revise only failed sections with a validation report.
Ask a second agent to rewrite the final guide in a different tone so reviewers can compare two independent versions side by side.
Generate a short guide with fewer details so there are fewer claims for reviewers to validate.

explanation:

The main issue is not Markdown quality. It is unsupported examples and missed incompatibilities. A prompt chain should separate generation from evidence checking so the review stage is not simply defending the first draft.

Targeted revision is also important. If example links are unsupported, the workflow should show that failure and repair those sections, not silently regenerate the entire guide and hide what changed.

question:

options: Use a bounded investigate-plan-patch loop that requires fresh evidence, focused verification, and escalates on stale data or repeated non-convergence.
Keep editing and rerunning until the mobile suite passes, because passing tests prove the patch is correct enough for merge.
Disable patching entirely and restrict Claude to writing summaries for human mobile engineers during every flaky-test incident.
Launch separate agents for logs, device history, UI diffs, and patching, then accept the first patch with a passing run.

explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Use a bounded investigate-plan-patch loop that requires fresh evidence, focused verification, and escalates on stale data or repeated non-convergence, because: the assistant should keep autonomy only while evidence remains current and the fix stays tied to the failure.

The workflow has two classes of failures. Obvious renamed identifiers can be patched and verified quickly. Intermittent device timeouts require stricter stop conditions because stale device history can make a failure disappear without proving the patch helped.

A bounded loop gives Claude room to investigate, plan, patch, and verify, but it stops when attempts do not converge or evidence freshness is insufficient. That prevents unrelated UI edits from being treated as successful fixes.

❌ Why the Other Options Are Wrong:

Keep editing and rerunning until the mobile suite passes, because passing tests prove the patch is correct - Flaky tests can pass for reasons unrelated to the patch. Unlimited loops invite drift.

Disable patching entirely and restrict Claude to writing summaries for human mobile engineers - This throws away useful repairs for straightforward failures that can be verified.

Launch separate agents for logs, device history, UI diffs, and patching, then accept the first patch with a passing run - Parallel work does not remove the need for evidence freshness and convergence checks.

Fresh evidence matters when external systems can return stale status.

question: A sanctions-screening extractor processes archived account packets over several hours. Start a fresh session after every restart so stale tool results are absent, then rerun all packets from the beginning.
Persist a checkpoint per packet with source version, tool-result status, validation outcome, and next action, then resume only from records whose prerequisites are current.
Cache all watchlist tool outputs for the full extraction window so resumed workers get consistent answers for every packet after any restart.
answer: Persist a checkpoint per packet with source version, tool-result status, validation outcome, and next action, then resume only from records whose prerequisites are current.
explanation:
✅ The correct option is: Persist a checkpoint per packet with source version, tool-result status, validation outcome, and next action, then resume only from records whose prerequisites are current, because: recovery depends on durable run state and source freshness, not on whatever the conversation last contained.

Long-running extraction jobs need resumable artifacts outside the model’s short-term reasoning. A checkpoint that records packet identity, watchlist version, validation result, and next action lets the system resume precisely after a restart and rerun only the stale or incomplete pieces.

Resume from the longest available transcript and ask Claude to summarize which packets were already processed before continuing. - A transcript is not a source-version ledger. It can preserve old reasoning while hiding whether the watchlist or tool result has expired.

Start a fresh session after every restart so stale tool results are absent, then rerun all packets from the beginning. - Fresh context avoids one risk but wastes completed validated work and still lacks checkpointed source metadata.
