-
Anthropic — Run agents in parallel → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents
option_feedback: One agent invoked three times still needs someone to decide what each query covers — the partitioning problem, unsolved — and it serializes three searches that currently run at the same time, so the topic now costs the sum of the three rather than the longest.

Partitioning the corpus rather than the brief keeps each agent searching for everything, so three full-brief searches are still paid for; it only changes which copy of a document each agent finds. Worse for this store, document classes do not align with sub-topics, so the material on any one sub-topic is now split across three agents that never see each other's results.

Duplication is created at delegation, so that is where it has to be removed: distinct assignments with stated exclusions mean the same document is not retrieved three times. The exclusions are also what create the boundary risk, and the fix for that is not to blur the assignments again but to give the seams an owner. The coordinator holds the whole brief and, once the findings are back, is the only component positioned to ask the cross-cutting question — at the cost of one extra round rather than of tripled retrieval on every run.

A shared retrieval list is inter-subagent state that hub-and-spoke deliberately does not provide, and making it work means either routing every retrieval through the coordinator mid-flight or serializing the three agents. It also settles overlap by first-come-first-served, so which agent gets a document that is genuinely relevant to two sub-topics is decided by timing.

question:
In a coordinator-led research system, a developer proposes letting the document-analysis subagent call the web-search subagent directly whenever it meets a citation it cannot resolve, instead of returning to the coordinator. Measurements support the proposal: it removes two round trips per unresolved citation, and unresolved citations occur in about 40% of papers. Two facts about how the system is operated are also on the table. On-call engineers reconstruct failed runs solely from the coordinator's message log; subagents emit no telemetry of their own. And each run has a token budget the coordinator enforces by deciding what to delegate next.

Which consequence is the strongest argument against the design?
options: Latency becomes harder to predict, because the number of searches per paper now depends on how many citations that paper fails to resolve, and how long they take depends on how many the search agent can serve at once
The coordinator's synthesis step must now merge two kinds of search findings — the ones it commissioned and the ones the analysis agent commissioned — with no way to tell them apart

The coordinator stops being the single place where inter-agent messages, failures and context can be observed and controlled, because the messages on that path never reach the log the on-call engineers read
The document-analysis subagent's own results become harder to reproduce, because two papers processed on different days may have had different search results folded into them
answer: The coordinator stops being the single place where inter-agent messages, failures and context can be observed and controlled, because the messages on that path never reach the log the on-call engineers read
explanation:
This question tests hub-and-spoke architecture, and specifically why the coordinator being the single communication path is load-bearing rather than incidental.

All Four Options Are Real Consequences

This is a "strongest argument" question, not a true/false one. Every option describes something that genuinely happens under the proposal. The task is ranking them against the two operational facts the stem supplies.

The Two Facts Decide It

-
On-call engineers reconstruct failed runs solely from the coordinator's message log; subagents emit no telemetry.

-
The coordinator enforces the token budget by deciding what to delegate next.

A direct subagent-to-subagent channel makes those messages invisible to the only log anyone reads, and spends budget the coordinator never authorised. In a 40%-of-papers path, that is a permanent blind spot in both observability and cost control — the coordinator stops being the place where inter-agent traffic can be seen or governed.

Why the other options are incorrect

Unpredictable latency (A) — true, and it is a genuine operational cost. But variable latency is tolerable and measurable; an unobservable failure path is neither. The stem gives no latency requirement.

Merging two kinds of findings (B) — a real integration wrinkle, and solvable by tagging provenance on the findings. It is a synthesis inconvenience, not a loss of control.

Reproducibility of the analysis agent (D) — true of any live web search, whether commissioned by the coordinator or the subagent. The proposal does not introduce this; it already exists.

Key Takeaway

In hub-and-spoke designs the coordinator owns inter-agent messaging, failure handling, observability and budget. Direct spoke-to-spoke channels save round trips by removing the only place the system can be watched and controlled.

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK overview → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview
option_feedback: Variable latency is a consequence worth planning for, but it is a scheduling problem with ordinary answers — a per-paper cap, a timeout — and it would exist in the same form if the coordinator issued the same follow-up searches on the subagent's behalf.

This is a real cost and it is the mildest of the three, because it has a cheap fix: tag findings with their commissioning agent. It is also downstream of the loss of the single control point — the merge is only ambiguous because the coordinator did not see the second set of searches happen.

Both operational facts in the stem point at the same thing. A search commissioned subagent-to-subagent produces no entry in the coordinator's log, so a run that fails inside one of those calls cannot be reconstructed by the people on call — and since the coordinator enforces the token budget by deciding what to delegate, spend it never sees is spend it cannot control. The 40% figure makes this worse rather than better: the invisible traffic is the common path, not the exception. The other options name real costs, but only this one follows from the loss of the single control point; the others would arise in much the same form if the coordinator had issued every one of those searches itself.

This is a real cost, and it is not specific to the proposal: search results vary between days whether the search is commissioned by the coordinator or by a subagent. Reproducibility here is a property of the corpus and the search backend, not of who issued the call.

question:
A research coordinator runs unattended on a schedule with no interactive approval path. It has three subagent definitions with clear descriptions, and it never delegates: every run is answered from its own reasoning. Investigation confirms that the tool used to spawn subagents is absent from the coordinator's allowed tools, which are Read, Grep, Glob and WebSearch. Two constraints govern the fix. The security runbook requires that any unattended job hold the smallest grant that lets it do its work, and the three subagents between them need Bash, Write and WebFetch — none of which the coordinator is permitted to hold.

Which change fixes the delegation failure within the runbook's constraint?
options: Grant the coordinator Bash, Write and WebFetch alongside the spawning tool, and let it do directly whatever a subagent fails at
Run the job with permission prompts bypassed, auto-approving every tool call the coordinator and its subagents make
Add the spawning tool to the coordinator's allowed tools, and give each subagent definition its own tool list containing only what that subagent needs
Move the three subagent definitions into markdown files on disk for the scheduler to discover at session start
answer: Add the spawning tool to the coordinator's allowed tools, and give each subagent definition its own tool list containing only what that subagent needs
explanation:
This question tests two easily-confused ideas: the tool that spawns subagents, and the tool lists that scope them.

Why It Never Delegates

Delegation is itself a tool call. If the spawning tool (the Agent/Task tool) is not in the coordinator's allowed tools, the coordinator has no mechanism to delegate — so it answers from its own reasoning, exactly as observed. Good subagent descriptions cannot help: descriptions drive selection, and there is nothing to select with.

Why Least Privilege Is Still Satisfied

The runbook's constraint is the second half of the question. Each AgentDefinition carries its own tool list, and a subagent runs with that list — not with the parent's. So the coordinator gets the spawning tool and nothing more, while Bash, Write and WebFetch live only in the individual subagents that need them.

The coordinator therefore never holds the dangerous grants; it merely delegates to agents that do, each scoped to its own job. Delegation is restored and the smallest-grant requirement is honoured.

Why the other options are incorrect

Grant the coordinator everything (A) — directly violates the runbook by concentrating Bash, Write and WebFetch in the single long-running unattended component, and undermines the reason to delegate at all.

Bypass permission prompts (B) — the classic trap in unattended runs. Auto-approving every call is orthogonal to the actual defect (a missing tool) and hands blanket authority to a scheduled job with no human in the loop.

Move definitions to markdown files (D) — changes where definitions are stored, not what the coordinator is allowed to do. Discovery was never the problem; the spawning capability was.

Key Takeaway

The parent needs the spawning tool to delegate at all; each subagent's own tool list is where least privilege is enforced. Scope capability per subagent rather than accumulating it in the coordinator.

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Configure permissions (Agent SDK) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions
option_feedback: This gives the coordinator the union of every subagent's permissions, which is the largest grant on the table rather than the smallest, and it does so to buy a fallback the stem did not ask for. Delegation would start working, but the runbook is what rules the option out: Bash, Write and WebFetch would sit permanently in an unattended job that never needs to run them itself.

Bypassing prompts makes the delegation succeed and discards the constraint entirely: every tool becomes available to every component of an unattended job. It answers "how do I stop being blocked" rather than "what should this job be allowed to do".

Delegating is a tool call, so the spawning tool has to be in the coordinator's allowed list or every delegation attempt goes to a permission layer that, in an unattended run, nothing answers. The runbook constraint is satisfied by where the subagents' tools are declared: each subagent definition carries its own tool list, and a subagent's grant is not the parent's grant. So the coordinator ends up holding one additional tool — the one that spawns — while Bash, Write and WebFetch exist only inside the subagents that need them.

Both definition styles work, and definitions supplied in code take precedence over markdown files of the same name. Relocating them changes nothing about the coordinator's own grant, which is what stops delegation from happening.

question:
A coordinator invokes its synthesis subagent with "Synthesize the research findings into a cited report." The search and analysis subagents have already returned their findings to the coordinator: roughly 60 KB of extracted passages, each carrying the document it came from, the page and the publication date. The synthesis subagent's reports come back generic and uncited. Two constraints apply. Every claim in the final report must carry the source it came from, and the synthesis subagent's context has to leave room for the report itself.

Which change fixes the reports?
options: Put the accumulated findings in the coordinator's system prompt for its subagents to inherit
Give the synthesis subagent the search and document tools and let it gather the material it needs for itself
Have the coordinator condense the 60 KB into a two-page brief in its own words and pass that brief in the synthesis subagent's prompt
Pass the findings in the synthesis subagent's prompt as structured items that keep each passage with its document, page and date
answer: Pass the findings in the synthesis subagent's prompt as structured items that keep each passage with its document, page and date
explanation:
This question tests subagent context isolation, and specifically that the invocation prompt is the only channel into a subagent.

Why the Reports Are Uncited

A spawned subagent starts with its own definition prompt plus the task prompt it was given — and nothing else. It does not inherit the parent's conversation or system prompt. "Synthesize the research findings into a cited report" refers to findings the synthesis subagent has never seen, so it writes generically and cites nothing. It is behaving correctly given its actual inputs.

Why Structure, Not Just Inclusion

Passing the material fixes half the problem; how it is passed fixes the rest. The two constraints point in opposite directions — every claim must carry its source, and context must leave room for the report — so the handoff should carry each passage together with its document, page and date as discrete structured items.

Attribution then survives the handoff as data rather than as prose the writer must re-derive, and the coordinator can select which passages to include rather than shipping everything.

Why the other options are incorrect

Findings in the coordinator's system prompt (A) — rests on a false premise. Subagents do not inherit the parent's system prompt; the material would never arrive.

Give the synthesis agent the research tools (B) — makes it redo work already completed and paid for, fills its context with raw retrieval instead of the report it exists to write, and re-opens the door to uncited claims.

A two-page brief in the coordinator's words (C) — the closest wrong answer, and it does respect the context budget. But condensing into prose is precisely the step that destroys per-passage attribution: page numbers and dates dissolve, and the requirement that every claim carry its source can no longer be met.

Key Takeaway

Subagent context is isolated — whatever it needs must be placed in its invocation prompt deliberately. When a downstream requirement depends on metadata, pass structured items that keep content and metadata together.

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Manage tool context → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context
option_feedback: Subagents do not inherit the parent's system prompt, so findings placed there never reach them. This is the common misconception about how context flows in a coordinator-subagent system.

Re-gathering material the system already holds doubles the search cost and returns a different set of sources than the ones the report is meant to synthesize, so the citations would point at documents the analysis step never examined.

This is the plausible answer and it is the one the citation requirement rules out. A brief in the coordinator's own words is a summarization step placed exactly where provenance is lost: the passages become paraphrase, the page numbers and dates drop out, and the synthesis agent is then asked to cite sources it can no longer see. It is the right move only when attribution does not survive to the deliverable.

A subagent starts with its own system prompt and the prompt string the coordinator passes it — no parent conversation, no parent tool results, no parent system prompt — so anything it must reason over has to be in that prompt. The citation requirement determines the shape: passages carried as structured items keep claim and source bound together through synthesis, which is what lets the report attribute each statement. Structuring them is also what keeps the payload affordable, because the metadata is a field per item rather than prose the model has to re-derive.

question:
A coordinator researches a topic in five subagent invocations. Three of them — market size, regulatory posture and competitor set — are independent of one another. The fourth summarizes the customer interviews that the competitor-set subagent surfaces, and the fifth drafts a risk register that quotes the regulatory findings. End-to-end latency is roughly five times the duration of a single search, and the team wants it down without giving up the five-way decomposition or accepting a thinner result.

Which change gives the largest latency reduction that the dependencies allow?
options: Emit all five invocations in a single response, and have the two dependent subagents fetch what they need from the coordinator when they reach it
Emit all five invocations in a single response, and re-run the two dependent ones afterwards if their inputs turn out to have changed
Keep the five sequential turns and give the two dependent subagents a faster model
Emit the three independent invocations in a single response, then the two dependent ones in a second response once their inputs are back
answer: Emit the three independent invocations in a single response, then the two dependent ones in a second response once their inputs are back
explanation:
This question tests parallel subagent invocation, and specifically that parallelism is bounded by the dependency graph, not by ambition.

Read the Dependencies First

Five invocations, but they are not five independent units. Market size, regulatory posture and competitor set depend on nothing. The interview-summary subagent needs what the competitor-set subagent surfaces. The risk register quotes the regulatory findings. So the graph is three-then-two, and the fastest legal schedule is exactly that: one response carrying the three independent invocations, then a second response carrying the two dependents once their inputs exist.

Parallel subagents are launched by emitting multiple invocations in a single response. Latency drops from five sequential searches to roughly two waves — the maximum the dependencies permit without thinning the result.

Why the other options are incorrect

All five at once, dependents fetch what they need (A) — the dependents launch before their inputs exist. There is nothing to fetch yet, so they either block or proceed on nothing.

All five at once, re-run dependents if inputs changed (B) — "changed" is the wrong word: the inputs did not exist at launch. This runs two subagents on absent data and then pays to run them again.

Sequential with a faster model (C) — keeps all five round trips and attacks the wrong term. It also trades quality on two steps for a fraction of the latency that restructuring gives for free.

Key Takeaway

Group parallel invocations by dependency: everything independent goes in one response, dependents follow once their inputs return. Parallelism is limited by the graph, not by the number of subagents.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Run agents in parallel → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Parallel tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use
option_feedback: A subagent cannot reach back into the coordinator mid-run; its context is fixed at the moment it is invoked. Dispatching all five together means the interview-summary and risk-register agents run with their inputs missing and produce exactly the generic output the team is trying to avoid.

The two dependent invocations do not have inputs that "turn out to have changed" — they have no inputs at all when dispatched, so the re-run is not a contingency but the only run that could produce anything. This pays for five invocations, then pays again for two, to arrive at the same two stages as the correct answer.

A faster model shortens two of five sequential steps and leaves the chain intact, so the multiplier survives. It also trades result quality for latency at exactly the two steps whose output the report depends on most.

Invocations emitted together in one response are dispatched together, so the three independent aspects finish in the time of the slowest rather than the sum of the three. The remaining two cannot start before their inputs exist, so they stay in a second response — which turns a five-deep chain into two stages and preserves both the decomposition and the quality of the dependent work.

question:
A research coordinator's prompt is a numbered procedure: call the search subagent, then the document-analysis subagent, then the synthesis subagent, then the report subagent, in that order, every time. When a source is unreachable or a question needs no document analysis, the coordinator either stalls on the failed step or runs the remaining steps on empty input and produces a thin report.

What is the most effective change?
options: Move the full procedure into each subagent's system prompt, so every agent knows its place in the sequence
Convert the procedure into code that calls each subagent in the fixed order, skipping any step whose inputs are missing
Extend the numbered procedure with conditional branches for each failure case observed so far, and add more as they arise
Instruct the coordinator to work toward the stated research goal against explicit quality criteria
answer: Instruct the coordinator to work toward the stated research goal against explicit quality criteria
explanation:
This question tests coordinator prompt design: goals and quality criteria versus step-by-step procedure.

Why the Procedure Fails

A numbered sequence encodes one assumed shape of the world — every source reachable, every question needing document analysis. Reality supplies neither. The coordinator stalls on a step it cannot complete, or executes the remainder on empty input, because the prompt tells it what to do rather than what to achieve.

Goals Plus Criteria

Stating the research goal and explicit quality criteria gives the coordinator something to reason against: if a source is unreachable, find another route to the same goal; if document analysis has nothing to analyze, skip it and satisfy the criteria another way. Coordinator prompts should specify goals and quality bars, not procedures — the model is the component that can adapt, and a rigid script is precisely what prevents it.

Why the other options are incorrect

Procedure into every subagent prompt (A) — spreads a brittle script across five components. Subagents execute their own task; knowing their position in a sequence does not let anyone recover from a failed step.

Convert to code with skip-if-missing (B) — the strongest distractor, and it does fix stalling. But it hard-codes the same fixed order in a different language, and "skip when inputs are missing" cannot invent an alternative route to the goal. It removes adaptability rather than adding it.

Conditional branches per failure case (C) — patches the failures observed so far and is permanently one incident behind. Branch count grows without bound while novel failures keep arriving.

Key Takeaway

Coordinator prompts should state goals and quality criteria, not numbered procedures. Fixed sequences work only where the workload's shape is genuinely fixed.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Subagents execute their assignments; they neither choose the sequence nor observe the run as a whole. Duplicating the procedure into them adds context without giving any component the ability to adapt.

Encoding the same fixed order in code makes it more rigid, not less: the coordinator loses even the ability to reorder or omit steps by judgment. A fixed pipeline implemented in code fits work whose shape is the same for every input, which is precisely what this workload is not.
Each branch fixes one observed case and the prompt grows with every incident, while the next unanticipated situation fails the same way. It postpones the problem rather than removing it.

A procedural prompt makes the coordinator's competence a function of the cases its author anticipated. Stating the goal and the criteria that make a result acceptable gives it a target to reason toward, so it can skip a step that adds nothing for this query, retry a different way when a source fails, and stop when the criteria are met. That adaptability is the reason to use a model-driven coordinator rather than a fixed pipeline.

question:
A support agent escalates a disputed charge to a human specialist. The specialist works in a separate queue tool that already displays the customer record and the full order history, and does not receive the conversation transcript. The handoff form accepts 1,500 characters. During the conversation the agent told the customer that the disputed amount would be credited within five working days.

Which TWO items should the handoff package contain? (Select TWO.)
options: The verified customer identifier, the order and the amount in dispute
The raw conversation transcript from the beginning of the exchange, truncated to fit the character limit
What the customer has already been told, including the five-working-day credit commitment
A list of the tools the agent called while investigating, in the order it called them
The root cause the investigation established, and the recommended action
answer: What the customer has already been told, including the five-working-day credit commitment
The root cause the investigation established, and the recommended action
explanation:
This question tests handoff design, and specifically that a good package carries what the receiver lacks — nothing more.

Start From What the Specialist Already Has

The queue tool already displays the customer record and full order history. Under a 1,500-character limit, re-sending any of that is spending the budget on information the specialist is already looking at.

Two things the specialist genuinely cannot see:

What the customer was promised — the agent committed to a credit within five working days. Nothing in the queue tool records that. If the specialist does not know, they may contradict it, and the customer experiences a broken promise.

The investigation's conclusion — the root cause established and the recommended action. This is the work product of the entire conversation; without it the specialist re-derives everything from scratch and the handoff saves nothing.

Why the other options are incorrect

Customer identifier, order and amount — genuinely important facts, and precisely the ones the queue tool already displays. Duplicating them consumes the character budget without adding information.

Truncated raw transcript — the lowest-density option available. Truncation drops the end of the exchange, which is usually where the commitments and conclusions live.

List of tools called, in order — process telemetry. Useful for debugging the agent; it tells the specialist nothing about what to do for this customer.

Key Takeaway

A handoff package carries the conclusions and the commitments — what the receiver cannot obtain elsewhere. Data already visible in the receiver's own tools, and raw process logs, are both wasted budget.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK overview → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview

-
Anthropic — Common workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/common-workflows

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: This is the right content for a handoff into a system that cannot look the customer up, and this queue tool can: the customer record and order history are displayed to the specialist already. Spending a constrained package on it crowds out the two things only the agent knows.

A transcript is unstructured, the specialist does not receive the conversation in the first place, and truncating one to 1,500 characters keeps the opening pleasantries and discards the conclusion. It also forces the reader to re-derive the root cause rather than being handed it.

The package exists to carry what the receiving system does not already have. The specialist's queue tool shows the customer record and the order history, so restating identifiers spends the character budget on data already on screen. What is not on screen is, first, the commitment the agent made — a specialist who settles this case on different terms contradicts the company in front of a customer who was given a date — and second, the conclusion the investigation reached and what the agent recommends, which are the two things no system holds and which the specialist would otherwise have to derive again.
A tool-call list conveys activity rather than findings. It tells the specialist that something was looked up, not what it showed or what the agent concluded from it.

The package exists to carry what the receiving system does not already have. The specialist's queue tool shows the customer record and the order history, so restating identifiers spends the character budget on data already on screen. What is not on screen is, first, the commitment the agent made — a specialist who settles this case on different terms contradicts the company in front of a customer who was given a date — and second, the conclusion the investigation reached and what the agent recommends, which are the two things no system holds and which the specialist would otherwise have to derive again.

question:
A customer's opening message raises three matters: a charge that appears twice on last month's statement, an item that arrived damaged, and a request to change the delivery address on an order that has not yet shipped. The deployment is measured on first-contact resolution and sits below its 80% target. Two facts about the tools matter here. The unshipped order enters its carrier handover in 40 minutes, after which the address can no longer be changed by any tool the agent holds. The billing lookup that would settle the duplicate charge takes about three minutes to return, and the damaged-item claim requires the customer's photographs to be reviewed, which takes longer still.

How should the agent handle the contact?
options: Investigate all three matters in parallel against the account context already established, and answer once
Change the delivery address first, reply immediately to confirm it, and open a second contact for the charge and the damaged item
Ask the customer which of the three is most urgent, and work through them in the order they give
Change the delivery address first, then investigate the charge and the damaged item, and answer all three in one reply
answer: Change the delivery address first, then investigate the charge and the damaged item, and answer all three in one reply
explanation:
This question tests multi-concern sequencing under a hard deadline, with first-contact resolution as the competing objective.

One Irreversible Deadline, Two Slow Investigations

The address change is the only matter with an expiry: 40 minutes to carrier handover, after which no tool the agent holds can help. It is also fast. The billing lookup takes ~3 minutes and the damaged-item claim longer — but neither expires.

So the ordering is forced: act on the deadline first, then investigate the two that can wait. Doing the address change first costs almost nothing and removes the only irreversible risk in the contact.

Why Not Reply Immediately

The deployment is measured on first-contact resolution and is below target. Splitting into a second contact for the charge and the damaged item guarantees a second contact — the metric moves in the wrong direction by design. Since neither remaining matter expires, one reply covering all three is both achievable and what the objective rewards.

Why the other options are incorrect

Investigate all three in parallel, answer once — tempting because it optimizes FCR. But it treats the address change as just another investigation; if the parallel work overruns 40 minutes, the one irreversible action is lost.

Address first, reply immediately, open a second contact — protects the deadline and then throws away the metric the deployment is judged on, for no gain: nothing forced the split.

Ask the customer to prioritize — pushes an operational decision the agent is better equipped to make onto the customer, spends a round trip, and risks the customer not choosing the expiring item.

Key Takeaway

Sequence by irreversibility first, then batch the rest into a single reply. Deadlines dictate order; the resolution metric dictates how many contacts it takes.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — How the agent loop works → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop

-
Anthropic — Common workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/common-workflows

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: This is the right instinct with the ordering left to chance. Investigating three matters in parallel and answering once is exactly the pattern first-contact resolution rewards, but the billing lookup and the photograph review are the slow ones, and a reply composed after both of them may land after the carrier handover has closed the address change for good.

Confirming the address immediately protects the deadline and then throws away the reason for decomposing the message: the remaining two matters become a second contact, which is the definition of a first-contact resolution failure and asks the customer to track two threads.

Asking the customer to triage adds a round trip in front of a 40-minute deadline and asks them to know something they cannot — that one of the three has a cutoff. The agent is the party that knows the constraint.

Decomposition is right and it is not sufficient on its own: one of the three items has a hard deadline that the other two do not, and the address change is also the cheapest of the three to execute. Doing it first converts the deadline from a risk into a completed action, after which the slower investigations can run against the customer context already established and be answered together. First-contact resolution is preserved because the customer receives one reply covering all three.

question:
A support agent calls three backend tools built by different teams. One returns timestamps as Unix epoch seconds, one as ISO 8601 strings, and one reports order state as a numeric code. The agent quotes wrong dates to customers and describes shipped orders as pending. Two of the three services belong to other teams that ship on a quarterly train and have declined a mid-quarter change; a fourth backend, with its own conventions, is being added next month. The team wants the misreadings to stop before that fourth backend arrives.

Where should the handling go?
options: In a validation step that compares each customer-facing response against the raw tool results and rewrites any date or status the agent stated incorrectly
In the system prompt, as a conversion table listing each tool's formats and the target representation
In the three backend services, each normalized at the source to emit ISO 8601 timestamps and a shared status vocabulary
In a PostToolUse hook that rewrites each tool result into one date and status representation before the model reads it
answer: In a PostToolUse hook that rewrites each tool result into one date and status representation before the model reads it
explanation:
This question tests PostToolUse hooks, and specifically that normalization belongs between the tool and the model.

Where the Defect Actually Is

The model is reading three incompatible representations and reporting what it sees. It is not misbehaving — it is being fed epoch integers, ISO strings and numeric status codes with no shared vocabulary. A PostToolUse hook rewrites each tool result into one date and status representation before the model reads it, so the model only ever sees consistent data, deterministically.

Why the Constraints Point Here

Two of the three services ship quarterly and have declined a mid-quarter change, and a fourth backend with its own conventions arrives next month. The hook is the only option that works this quarter and extends to backend four by adding one mapping — no other team's roadmap involved.

Why the other options are incorrect

Source normalization in the three services — architecturally the cleanest answer and explicitly unavailable: two teams have declined. It also leaves the fourth backend to negotiate separately, and does nothing before next quarter.

Conversion table in the system prompt — moves date arithmetic and status decoding into probabilistic generation, on customer-facing values, and spends context on every request for work a hook does silently and exactly.

Post-hoc response validation — inspects the model's prose after the fact and rewrites what it judges wrong. Detecting a misstated date in free text is far harder than converting a field, and the model still reasons on bad data throughout the turn.

Key Takeaway

Normalize tool results in a PostToolUse hook so the model sees one consistent representation. Source-side fixes are better when available; hooks are what you own when other teams' schedules are not yours.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Automate actions with hooks → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide

-
Anthropic — Hooks reference → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks

-
Anthropic — Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks
option_feedback: Checking the agent's prose against the raw results means detecting a wrong date inside generated text, which is harder and less reliable than transforming a structured field, and it acts after the misreading has already shaped the agent's reasoning for the rest of the conversation.

A conversion table asks the model to perform lookups and arithmetic correctly on every response, with the failures landing in customer-facing statements about money and delivery dates, and it grows by one entry each time a backend is added.

Fixing formats at the source is the better long-run answer where it is available, and here it is not: two of the three services belong to teams that have declined the change until the next quarterly train, and the fourth backend has not been built yet. Choosing it means the customer-facing errors continue for a quarter and recur each time a new backend is integrated.

Normalizing between the tool returning and the model reading puts one transformation in the team's own code, on a path they control, and applies it to every tool the agent calls — including the fourth backend, whose conventions can be added the day it appears. The model never encounters an epoch integer or a status code, so there is nothing left to misinterpret and no per-tool instruction to keep in step.

question:
A support deployment built on the Agent SDK has agreed on a gate: once an order's state is "shipped", the agent must not call update_shipping_address. The carrier can no longer reroute at that point, but the order service still accepts the write, so the record changes, the parcel does not, and the customer is told an address change succeeded. A PreToolUse hook will inspect the call and block it. About forty conversations a day reach this point, and in most of them the customer can still be helped: there is a create_reroute_request tool for parcels already in transit.

The team is now deciding what the hook returns when it fires. What should it return?
options: Deny the call and return nothing further, leaving the agent with only the fact that it did not go through
Deny the call and return a reason naming the shipped state and pointing at create_reroute_request instead
Allow the call and have a PostToolUse hook append a note to the result explaining that the change was not applied
Deny the call and end the turn, handing the conversation to the human queue for someone to handle the address
answer: Deny the call and return a reason naming the shipped state and pointing at create_reroute_request instead
explanation:
This question tests what a PreToolUse denial should return — not whether to deny.

Denial Is Only Half the Design

The block is settled: after "shipped", the write must not go through. The open question is what the hook hands back. A hook can deny with a reason, and that reason enters the model's context as the explanation for why the call failed.

Naming the shipped state tells the agent why, and pointing at create_reroute_request tells it what to do instead. In most of those forty daily conversations the customer can still be helped, so the difference between a bare denial and an informative one is the difference between forty dead ends and forty reroute requests.

Why the other options are incorrect

Deny and return nothing — enforces correctly and strands the agent. Knowing only that something failed, it guesses, retries, or apologizes — and the reroute path that would have helped goes unused.

Allow, then annotate in PostToolUse — the record has already changed by the time the note is appended. The parcel does not move, the database says it did, and the note arrives after the damage.

Deny and hand to the human queue — treats an expected, forty-a-day, automatable branch as an exception. It escalates cases the agent could resolve itself with one alternative tool.

Key Takeaway

Deny with a reason and an alternative. A blocked call is a decision point for the model, and the hook's response is what determines whether it recovers or stalls.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Hooks reference → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks

-
Anthropic — Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks

-
Anthropic — Automate actions with hooks → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide
option_feedback: A bare denial is deterministic and uninformative. The model observes a call that did not succeed and no statement of why, so its likely next moves are to retry the same call with slightly different arguments or to tell the customer the system is unavailable. Neither is true, and the reroute path the team already built is never reached, so a control that was supposed to protect the customer degrades the answer they get.

A denial cancels the tool call and feeds the denial reason back to the model, which makes that reason the only channel the hook has for shaping what happens next. A reason that states the constraint and names the tool that does apply converts a dead end into a recovery: in the same turn the agent can explain why the address cannot be edited and open a reroute request. The gate stays deterministic — the write never reaches the order service, and a PreToolUse denial holds regardless of the permission mode the session is running in — while the conversation keeps a route to resolution. Enforcement and recoverability are not in tension here; the reason string is what delivers both.

PostToolUse runs after the tool has executed and cannot undo it, so by the time the note is appended the address write has already landed in the order service. The model then reads a result asserting that the change was not applied while the record says otherwise — precisely the divergence between record and reality that the gate exists to prevent, now with a contradiction added.

Ending the turn converts every occurrence of a routine, recoverable constraint into human work: roughly forty conversations a day, most of which the agent could finish with a reroute request. Escalation should be a decision made from the state of the case, not the automatic consequence of one blocked call, and abandoning the turn also drops anything else the customer raised in the same conversation.

question:
A CI team runs two Claude-driven jobs. The first reviews every pull request against four aspects — correctness, error handling, test coverage and documentation — and has just gained a fifth, a data-migration check that applies to roughly one PR in six and is expensive to run. The second job investigates intermittently failing tests, where what to examine next depends on what the previous step found; its output is used in incident reviews, so the team needs a record of what was examined.

Which decomposition fits each job?
options: Keep a fixed chain for the four standing aspects and let the model decide per PR whether the fifth applies; use dynamic decomposition for the investigation, with each step and its result recorded as it runs
Use dynamic decomposition for both jobs, letting each skip or follow whatever the run turns up
Use a fixed chain for both jobs, extending the investigation's chain with a new step each time an unfamiliar failure mode is seen
Fixed chain for the four standing aspects with the fifth gated on a precondition evaluated in code; dynamic decomposition for the investigation, with each step recorded as it runs
answer: Fixed chain for the four standing aspects with the fifth gated on a precondition evaluated in code; dynamic decomposition for the investigation, with each step recorded as it runs
explanation:
This question tests matching decomposition strategy to workload shape — and it deliberately contains two workloads with opposite shapes.

Job One Is Fixed; Job Two Is Not

The PR review runs the same four aspects on every PR: known steps, known order, every time. That is a fixed chain. The fifth check applies to roughly one PR in six and is expensive, so it needs a precondition evaluated in code — a deterministic gate (does this PR touch migrations?) rather than a judgment call. Cheap, reliable, and it never runs the expensive check on the other five.

The flaky-test investigation is the opposite: what to examine next depends on what the last step found. That is dynamic decomposition. Because its output feeds incident reviews, each step and its result must be recorded as it runs — with a variable path, the executed sequence is the only audit trail available.

Why the other options are incorrect

Model decides per PR whether the fifth applies — very close, and correct on the investigation half. But it hands a deterministic, cheaply-checkable precondition to a probabilistic judgment, on an expensive check: some PRs get it unnecessarily, some migrations get missed.

Dynamic for both — spends orchestration reasoning on a review whose four steps never vary, and loses the predictability a standing PR check should have.

Fixed chain for both — cannot represent an investigation whose next step is unknown, and the "add a step per unfamiliar failure" habit grows a chain that is always one incident behind.

Key Takeaway

Fixed chains for fixed-shape work, dynamic decomposition where each finding reshapes the next step — and gate expensive optional steps in code, not by model judgment.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows

-
Anthropic — Run agents in parallel → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: This is right about both jobs and wrong about the gate. Letting the model decide whether the migration check applies makes the gate's coverage vary between runs on a check that exists precisely to catch a rare, expensive class of mistake — and the condition that triggers it can be read off the diff without asking anyone.

Applying dynamic decomposition to a review whose aspects are fixed adds planning overhead to every PR and makes coverage vary between runs, which is what undermines a gate's value. The fifth aspect's conditionality is not a reason to make the other four adaptive.

A fixed chain for an open-ended investigation locks in one hypothesis path, and growing it by one step per newly seen failure mode means the job only ever handles failures that have already happened once. It also does not satisfy the record-keeping requirement any better than the adaptive version does.

The two jobs are separated by whether the shape of the work is known before it starts, and each job's second constraint decides how far that goes. The review's shape is known, so a fixed chain gives it consistent coverage — but "one PR in six" is a property of the diff, not a judgment call, so the expensive fifth step belongs behind a deterministic precondition rather than behind a model decision that would vary between runs. The investigation's shape is not known, so each finding has to determine the next step; the incident-review requirement is satisfied by recording the steps as they are taken, which is a logging decision rather than a reason to force the work into a fixed sequence.

question:
Two days ago a developer used Claude Code to analyze a service ahead of a library migration, and the session recorded detailed findings about the modules involved. Since then a large refactor has landed on the main branch, moving or rewriting most of the files that session read. The developer wants to continue the migration work.

What is the most reliable way to proceed?
options: Run /compact on the earlier session before continuing in it, summarizing the outdated file contents away
Continue in the earlier session and list the files that have changed for targeted re-analysis
Start a new session and open it with a structured summary of the earlier conclusions and the current state
Fork the earlier session and continue the migration on the new branch, leaving its analysis intact on the original
answer: Start a new session and open it with a structured summary of the earlier conclusions and the current state
explanation:
This question tests session resumption, and specifically when accumulated context has become a liability rather than an asset.

How Much of the Session Is Still True

A resume is worth it when most of what the session knows still holds. Here a large refactor has moved or rewritten most of the files that session read, so the majority of its detailed findings now describe code that no longer exists.

Resuming carries all of that into the new work as confident, specific, wrong context — the expensive failure mode, because stale detail is indistinguishable from current detail from inside the session. A fresh session opened with a structured summary of the conclusions and the current state keeps the durable part (what was decided, what the migration is trying to achieve) and drops the perishable part (what line 240 of a since-rewritten module used to contain).

Why the other options are incorrect

/compact the old session — compaction summarizes; it does not fact-check. The outdated file contents are compressed into an outdated summary, and staleness survives in more confident form.

Resume and list the changed files — the right move when a handful of files moved. Here "most" changed, so the list approaches the whole analysis and the session spends more effort correcting itself than a clean start would cost.

Fork the session — forking branches the context, and the context is the problem. Both branches inherit the same stale findings.

Key Takeaway

Resume when context is mostly current; start fresh with a structured summary when the ground has moved. Conclusions travel well across a reset — file-level detail does not.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Manage sessions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions

-
Anthropic — Work with sessions (Agent SDK) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions

-
Anthropic — CLI reference → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference
option_feedback: Compaction condenses history; it does not distinguish the still-true parts from the invalidated ones. The summary it produces preserves stale specifics in shortened form, which is harder to detect than the originals.

Telling a resumed session which files changed is the right move when the prior context is mostly still valid and a few files moved. Here most of what the session read has changed, so the targeted re-analysis would be larger than the original exploration and would sit alongside a majority of stale findings.

When most of a session's tool results no longer describe the code on disk, the resumed conversation is a large body of confidently stated but obsolete detail, and the model has no way to tell which parts still hold. Starting fresh and injecting a summary of the conclusions that survived the refactor gives the new session accurate context of a size it can act on, without stale file contents to contradict what it reads now. This is a one-off, deliberate summary of the conclusions that survived the refactor, written knowing what still holds — not a mechanical compression of a history whose specifics are the thing that matters.

Forking creates a second conversation that begins with a copy of the same outdated analysis. Preserving the old branch has value for comparing approaches, but it does not make either branch's stale file contents correct.

question:
A developer-productivity agent reaches the team's issue tracker through one MCP tool, search_issues. Tool selection is not the problem: the agent picks this tool when it should. Roughly a fifth of its calls are rejected by the server, because status arrives as "in progress" when the tracker accepts only open, in_review and closed, and updated_since arrives as "last week" when the field expects a calendar date. The tool's description is three sentences and accurately says what the tool does; both parameters are declared as plain strings with no further detail. After a rejection the agent usually apologizes to the developer or retries with another guess.

Which change most directly removes these failures?
options: State the permitted status values and the required date format in the agent's system prompt
Normalize the arguments inside the server's handler, mapping phrases such as "in progress" and "last week" onto the accepted values, and log what it rewrote
Constrain and document the parameters in the tool's input schema: an enum for status, and a description with an example date for updated_since
Return the server's rejection to the model as a tool error naming the offending field
answer: Constrain and document the parameters in the tool's input schema: an enum for status, and a description with an example date for updated_since
explanation:
This question tests where a parameter contract belongs. Note carefully what the stem rules out: selection is not the problem, and the description is already accurate.

The Description Is Not the Contract

A description says what a tool does. The input schema says what its arguments must look like — and that is what is failing here. status is a closed set of three values, so it belongs in an enum, which makes "in progress" structurally impossible rather than merely discouraged. updated_since needs a format and a concrete example date in its parameter description.

Both live in the schema the model reads on every call, so the fix reaches every consumer of the tool at the point of use.

Why the other options are incorrect

Permitted values in the system prompt — puts a per-tool contract in a per-agent location. It patches this deployment, must be repeated for every other consumer, and drifts as the tracker's vocabulary changes.

Normalize in the server handler — a real technique that removes the rejections, and the strongest distractor. But it guesses at intent ("last week" from whose timezone?), silently accepts malformed input as correct, and leaves the model with a permanently untrue picture of the contract.

Return the rejection as a tool error — worth doing, and it is a recovery mechanism rather than a fix. The agent still makes the bad call first, and a fifth of calls remain a round trip that a schema constraint prevents outright.

Key Takeaway

Encode parameter constraints in the input schema — enums for closed sets, formats and examples in per-parameter descriptions. Descriptions drive selection; schemas drive correct invocation.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference

-
Anthropic — Strict tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use
option_feedback: Prompt text sits away from the point of use: it is present for every call the agent makes, it has to be restated for each tool the server grows, and it competes with everything else in the prompt for attention. It also leaves the schema still advertising an unconstrained string, so the model is told one thing by the field it is filling in and another by the prompt, which is a weaker position than not having said anything.

Server-side normalization hides the contract instead of communicating it. "Last week" has to be resolved against some clock and time zone the model never specified, so a misreading returns confident, wrong results rather than an error; each new phrasing the model invents needs another mapping rule; and every other client of the server is left guessing in the same way. The log records what the server rewrote, not that the rewrite was wrong — nobody reading it knows which window the model meant — so a visible rejection is traded for a silent misreading.

The input schema is the thing the model is filling in when it builds a call, so it is where a parameter contract belongs. An enum removes the invalid status strings from what the model can produce and, in the same stroke, tells it what the valid ones are; a parameter description that states the date format with a concrete example does the same for updated_since. Anthropic's tool-definition guidance treats per-parameter descriptions as part of the work that most determines tool performance, and offers input_examples for exactly these format-sensitive cases. The fix also travels with the tool, so every client of the server benefits without repeating anything.

A round trip per malformed call spends a request and the developer's waiting time to convey information that could have been in the schema from the start, and it corrects rather than prevents — the same fifth of calls goes wrong in every session, indefinitely. Returning actionable errors is worth doing as a backstop for what a schema cannot express; it is not a substitute for expressing what a schema can.

question:
A research system exposes one MCP tool, analyze_document, used for three different jobs: pulling named data points out of a paper, producing a plain summary, and checking whether a specific claim is supported by a given source. Its output shape differs depending on which job the model had in mind, so downstream parsing is unreliable, and the model picks it for tasks none of the three jobs fits.

What is the best redesign?
options: Add an operation parameter to the existing tool, constrained to an enum of the three jobs it performs
Require each subagent to state which of the three jobs it intends before it calls the tool
Split it into three tools — extract data points, summarize, verify a claim — each with its own contract
Validate the tool's output against a schema permitting all three shapes, retrying on a mismatch
answer: Split it into three tools — extract data points, summarize, verify a claim — each with its own contract
explanation:
This question tests tool granularity: one tool should do one job with one output contract.

Two Symptoms, One Cause

analyze_document does three jobs, and both reported problems follow from that. The output shape varies because three jobs legitimately produce three different shapes, so downstream parsing cannot be reliable. And the model mis-selects it because a tool that does "analysis" broadly matches almost any document task.

Splitting into three tools — extract data points, summarize, verify a claim — gives each a single purpose, a single stable output contract, and a description precise enough that selection becomes accurate. Downstream parsers get one shape per tool.

Why the other options are incorrect

An operation enum parameter — the near-miss, and it does fix selection within the tool. But one tool still returns three different shapes depending on the argument, so the parsing problem survives untouched. It is one tool wearing three hats with a label naming which.

Require subagents to state intent first — an unenforced convention that changes no interface. The output shape still varies and the tool is still over-broad.

Schema permitting all three shapes, retry on mismatch — formalizes the ambiguity as valid. Every consumer must branch on which shape arrived, and retrying does not converge on a shape that was never specified.

Key Takeaway

One tool, one job, one output contract. Multi-purpose tools produce unstable outputs and fuzzy selection; splitting fixes both at once.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use
option_feedback: An enum parameter makes the output shape predictable from the argument the caller passed, and it leaves one description that has to cover all three jobs at once, so the model still reaches for the tool in situations that none of the three fits.
A declared intention is a prompt convention with no enforcement behind it, and it does not change the tool's contract or its access granularity.

Three jobs with three output contracts are three tools. Splitting them gives each a description narrow enough that the model can tell when it applies, and gives downstream code one predictable shape per tool instead of a shape that depends on what the model was thinking. A tool that means three things cannot be described precisely, which is why it is both mis-selected and unparseable.

A permissive union schema accepts every shape, so validation catches nothing, and retrying a call whose shape was never constrained repeats the same gamble. It adds latency without adding a guarantee.

question:
A support agent escalates far too often. Every escalation the team samples was triggered by a customer using the word "urgent", including cases the agent could have resolved. The team has already rewritten the escalation tool's description to state that urgency alone is not a reason to escalate, and added few-shot examples showing urgent requests being resolved autonomously. Both changes reduced the rate only slightly.

What should the team examine next?
options: The escalation tool's input schema, adding a required field in which the agent names the trigger it acted on
The order in which the tools are listed in the request, with the escalation tool no longer first
The temperature and sampling settings, which may be making the agent's tool selection unstable between runs
The system prompt, for wording that ties urgency to human handling and competes with the tool descriptions
answer: The system prompt, for wording that ties urgency to human handling and competes with the tool descriptions
explanation:
This question tests where to look next when tool-level fixes have already been tried and barely moved the number.

Read What Has Already Failed

The team rewrote the tool description and added few-shot examples — the two standard remedies — and both barely helped. That pattern is diagnostic: something with more weight is pulling the other way. The system prompt sits above tool descriptions in influence, and if it contains wording tying urgency to human handling, the agent is obeying the stronger instruction while the description argues against it.

Auditing the system prompt for that conflict is the next step, because no amount of description polish wins an argument against it.

Why the other options are incorrect

A required trigger field in the schema — genuinely useful diagnostics: it would record what the agent believed it was acting on. But naming a trigger does not stop the escalation, so the rate stays where it is.

Tool ordering in the request — position in the tools array carries no priority semantics. Reordering changes nothing about selection.

Temperature and sampling — would explain inconsistency. The observed behavior is highly consistent — every sampled escalation traced to the same word — which points at instruction conflict, not sampling variance.

Key Takeaway

When description and few-shot fixes both fail, look upward: system-prompt wording outweighs tool descriptions, and a contradiction there defeats work done at the tool level.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Modifying system prompts → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/modifying-system-prompts

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use
option_feedback: The team already knows the trigger from its sample — every escalation followed the word "urgent". Recording it in the tool's arguments documents the decision after it has been made rather than changing which decisions get made.
Tool ordering in the request is not what drives selection, and reordering would not explain why the effect is specific to one word in the customer's message.

Sampling settings would produce scattered, inconsistent selection errors. The pattern here is highly consistent and correlates with a specific keyword, which points at the prompt rather than at randomness.

Instructions in the system prompt are keyword-sensitive: a line such as "urgent matters may need human attention" creates an association between a word the customer types and a tool, and that association can outweigh a well-written tool description. When the description has already been fixed and examples have already been added with little effect, the remaining place where the unwanted association can live is the prompt itself.

question:
The MCP tools behind a support agent return "Operation failed" for every failure. Three failures from yesterday's log are representative: a 30-second timeout against the order service; a refusal because the order fell outside the 30-day return window; and a rejected argument, where the agent sent a date as "03/04" and the tool expects ISO 8601. The redesigned error response must let the agent decide between retrying, explaining to the customer, and correcting and re-calling — without any of that decision depending on interpreting prose.

Which TWO fields does that decision depend on? (Select TWO.)
options: A human-readable description of what went wrong, phrased so it can be repeated to the customer
errorCategory, drawn from a fixed set: transient, validation, permission, business_rule
The name of the offending argument and the format that was expected
isRetryable, a boolean stating whether another attempt could succeed
retryAfter, the number of seconds to wait before another attempt
answer: errorCategory, drawn from a fixed set: transient, validation, permission, business_rule
isRetryable, a boolean stating whether another attempt could succeed
explanation:
This question tests error-response design, with a precise constraint: the branch must not depend on interpreting prose.

The Branch Needs Two Machine-Readable Facts

The agent must choose between retrying, explaining, and correcting-then-re-calling. Two fields carry that decision:

errorCategory from a fixed set — transient → retry; business_rule → explain to the customer; validation → fix the argument. The category is the branch.

isRetryable — states directly whether another attempt could succeed, so the agent never retries a refusal or abandons a recoverable timeout.

Together they are enumerable and unambiguous — no prose parsing anywhere in the decision.

Why the other options are incorrect

Human-readable description — belongs in a good error response, and the agent needs it after deciding, to speak to the customer. But reading it is exactly the prose interpretation the requirement forbids as a decision input.

Offending argument and expected format — the most tempting distractor. It is what makes the validation branch actionable, but it is payload, not the branch: it only matters once the category has already said "validation."

retryAfter — refines the timing of a retry the branch has already chosen. Useful, not decisive.

Key Takeaway

Machine-readable category plus a retryability flag drive the branch; human-readable detail and field-level specifics are what the chosen branch acts on.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: A customer-safe description belongs in the response and it is not what the branch depends on: it is what the agent says after the branch has been chosen. Making it the decision input puts the agent back to interpreting prose, which is what the redesign is replacing.

The decision is a branch, so it has to be driven by fields whose values are enumerable rather than by text the agent must interpret. The category is what selects the branch — transient means try again, validation means fix the argument, business_rule means explain, permission means escalate — and the retryable boolean makes the most consequential part of that branch explicit rather than inferred, so the agent does not spend attempts on the return-window refusal, which will never succeed however many times it is sent.

The argument name and expected format are exactly what the validation branch needs once it has been selected — they are what makes the correction possible for the "03/04" case. They do not tell the agent that this is a validation failure rather than a policy refusal, which is the decision in question.

The decision is a branch, so it has to be driven by fields whose values are enumerable rather than by text the agent must interpret. The category is what selects the branch — transient means try again, validation means fix the argument, business_rule means explain, permission means escalate — and the retryable boolean makes the most consequential part of that branch explicit rather than inferred, so the agent does not spend attempts on the return-window refusal, which will never succeed however many times it is sent.
A wait interval refines a retry that has already been decided on. It is useful on transient failures and meaningless on the other three categories, so it cannot be what selects between them.

question:
A support agent reaches the order service through an in-house MCP server. When the service answers 503, the server's lookup_order handler returns an ordinary result whose text is "Order service unavailable, try again later." Two consequences have shown up in review: the agent has more than once relayed that sentence to a customer as though it were the order's status, and the run's failure metrics record none of these events, because nothing in the response separates it from a successful lookup. The agent has a cached order summary it is allowed to fall back on once it knows a lookup has failed.

How should the handler report the 503?
options: Return a normal result whose text begins with ERROR:, and have the client string-match that prefix
Raise a JSON-RPC protocol error from the handler, putting the failure on the protocol's error channel
Return the 503 status code as the result content and let the model interpret what the number means
Return a tool result with isError set, whose content names the service failure and the order that could not be read
answer: Return a tool result with isError set, whose content names the service failure and the order that could not be read
explanation:
This question tests error channel selection — four plausible ways to report a 503, only one with the right semantics.

What Each Symptom Requires

Two failures are documented. The agent relayed the error sentence to a customer as order status, so the failure must be distinguishable from a successful result. And metrics recorded nothing, so it must be countable.

A tool result with isError set does both. The flag marks the result as a failure the model can reason about, the content names the service failure and the unreadable order, and the run's metrics can count error-flagged results without parsing anything. The agent then knows the lookup failed and can fall back to its cached summary — which the stem says it is allowed to do once it knows.

Why the other options are incorrect

ERROR: prefix with client string-matching — a convention, not a contract. Any wording drift breaks the match silently, and the result still travels the success channel.

JSON-RPC protocol error — the closest wrong answer. Protocol errors signal that the call mechanism failed. Here the call succeeded and the upstream service returned 503 — a legitimate tool outcome. Misusing the protocol channel also tends to abort rather than hand the model something to reason with.

Return the bare 503 — asks the model to infer semantics from a number, with no indication that the result is an error at all. Both symptoms survive.

Key Takeaway

Report tool failures as tool results with isError set and descriptive content. Reserve protocol errors for genuine protocol faults; never let a failure ride the success channel.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: A prefix convention is an agreement about wording, and nothing enforces it: any rewording of the message breaks the client's match, and the model still receives what looks like an ordinary successful result, so relaying the text to the customer remains available to it.

The protocol error channel carries the cases the specification assigns to it — an unknown tool, arguments that do not match the schema, a server that cannot service the request at all. A tool that ran and failed is none of those, and reporting it there moves the failure outside the tool result, which is where the agent's own recovery path lives.

A bare status code is data without an interpretation attached. The model has to know that 503 denotes a failure rather than an order field, and the response is still a successful result as far as the client and the metrics are concerned, so neither of the two reported problems is addressed.

MCP separates two reporting mechanisms, and a service that was reached and answered 503 is a tool execution error — the kind the specification puts inside the result with isError set. That keeps the failure on the path the model already reads, so the agent sees a lookup that failed rather than a sentence of prose it might repeat, and can do the one useful thing available to it and fall back on the cached summary. Because the flag is a field rather than a phrasing, the client and the run's metrics can branch on it without interpreting text, which is what puts these events back into the failure counts.

question:
The report-writing subagent in a research system has a general fetch_url tool that retrieves any URL and returns the page. Two problems have accumulated. The compliance rule for these reports is that they may cite only documents from the vetted corpus, and reviewers keep finding citations to pages that were merely linked from corpus material. Separately, one fetch of a long HTML page can consume a large share of the subagent's context, so it gets through only a few documents per run. Every corpus document already has an identifier and an extracted plain-text version in the index.

Which change best fits these constraints?
options: Add a handler-side allowlist to fetch_url that rejects URLs outside the approved domains, and return the rejection as an error the subagent can read
Replace fetch_url with load_document, which takes a corpus identifier and returns the indexed text, plus a search tool returning those identifiers
Have fetch_url strip navigation, scripts and boilerplate from each page before the result is returned
Have the coordinator check every citation against the corpus once the report is drafted, re-running the subagent when one fails
answer: Replace fetch_url with load_document, which takes a corpus identifier and returns the indexed text, plus a search tool returning those identifiers
explanation:
This question tests tool design against two constraints at once — a compliance boundary and a context budget — where only one option satisfies both.

One Redesign, Two Problems

A general fetch_url tool is the cause of both symptoms. It can reach anything linked from corpus material, which is how uncited-corpus pages became citations; and it returns whole HTML pages, which is how a few documents exhaust the subagent's context.

Replacing it with load_document, taking a corpus identifier and returning the indexed plain text, closes both. Documents outside the corpus have no identifier, so out-of-corpus citation becomes structurally impossible rather than policed. And indexed text is a fraction of raw HTML, so far more documents fit per run. The paired search tool returning identifiers keeps discovery working. Everything needed already exists in the index.

Why the other options are incorrect

Handler-side domain allowlist — enforces compliance and does nothing for context: pages are still fetched as full HTML. It also allowlists domains, while the rule is about vetted documents — an approved domain can host unvetted pages.

Strip boilerplate before returning — the mirror image: helps context, ignores compliance. Any linked page is still reachable and citable.

Post-hoc citation checking by the coordinator — detects violations after a full run and pays for a re-run, while the context problem is untouched throughout.

Key Takeaway
