When a tool's shape causes the problem, redesign the tool rather than filtering its output. Identifier-based access over a vetted corpus enforces scope structurally and trims context at the same time.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Manage tool context → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: A domain check narrows what can be fetched while leaving the subagent to guess URLs, because nothing in the tool tells it what the corpus contains, and each rejected guess costs a turn. Domain-level matching also does not tie a fetch to the vetted revision: an approved domain can serve a page that has changed since it was indexed. The context cost of a full HTML page is untouched.

Both problems are properties of what the tool is able to express. A tool whose input is a document identifier cannot reach anything outside the corpus, so the compliance rule is carried by the interface rather than checked after the fact, and the identifier pins each citation to the indexed revision a reviewer will open. Returning extracted text instead of a page removes the markup that was eating the context budget. The paired search tool is what keeps the constrained interface usable: identifiers have to come from somewhere, and discovery is a separate, equally well-defined job. This is the general pattern in Anthropic's tool-writing guidance — purpose-built tools that return high-signal content, rather than thin wrappers around a general-purpose capability.

Stripping boilerplate addresses the size problem and only the size problem. The subagent can still fetch anything it finds a link to, so the citations reviewers are objecting to keep appearing, and a cleaned live page is still not the indexed document the corpus rule refers to.

A post-draft check finds violations after the tokens have been spent writing around them, and its remedy is re-running work already done. It also gives the subagent no way to comply while working: it learns which citations were unacceptable only after producing a draft built on them, and nothing in the loop tells it what it should have fetched instead.

question:
An extraction service processes a mixed stream. Four extraction tools are defined, one per document type, and a document's type is not known until the model has read it. Downstream systems require a structured record from every document; a prose reply breaks the pipeline. A sample of last week's stream shows roughly 6% of the input is neither of the four types — scanned separator sheets, blank pages, and the occasional fax cover — for which there is no valid record. Under the current setting those documents come back as prose explaining that no record could be produced, and the pipeline rejects the batch.

Which configuration fits this workload?
options: {"type": "auto"}, with a prompt instruction to return a JSON object with a null record when the document matches none of the four types
{"type": "any"} with the four extraction tools, and a post-hoc filter that discards records whose fields are mostly empty
{"type": "any"} with a fifth tool defined for documents that match none of the four schemas, taking a reason and any legible identifiers
{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"} for the first turn, followed by a turn with tool_choice omitted so the model can correct the type if it was wrong
answer: {"type": "any"} with a fifth tool defined for documents that match none of the four schemas, taking a reason and any legible identifiers
explanation:
This question tests tool_choice in a pipeline with a hard structural requirement and a real 6% of inputs that fit none of the defined schemas.

Force a Tool, and Give the Remainder Somewhere to Go

Downstream requires a structured record from every document, so {"type": "any"} is right: it guarantees a tool call rather than prose, while letting the model pick which of the types applies after reading the document.

The 6% is the design problem. Forcing a tool call with only four document-type tools defined means separator sheets and fax covers must be crammed into a schema that does not fit them. Defining a fifth tool for unmatched documents — taking a reason and any legible identifiers — gives that 6% a truthful, structured destination. The pipeline receives a valid record for every document, and the unmatched ones are explicitly labelled rather than mislabelled.

Why the other options are incorrect

"auto" plus a prompt instruction — leaves prose possible on any turn, and prose is exactly what breaks the pipeline. The structural requirement deserves a structural guarantee.

"any" plus a post-hoc empty-field filter — the strongest distractor: correct on tool_choice, wrong on the remainder. The 6% is force-fitted into a wrong schema first, then discarded — so the pipeline silently loses documents instead of accounting for them.

Force extract_invoice, then a free turn — asserts a type before the document has been read, on a stream where type is unknown until reading. Every non-invoice pays a correction round trip.

Key Takeaway

Use "any" when every turn must produce structure, and define a tool for the "none of the above" case. Forcing tool use without an escape hatch converts unclassifiable inputs into wrong records.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Tool reference (tool_choice) → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Structured outputs → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: "auto" leaves the model free to answer in prose, which is the failure the pipeline already suffers. An instruction to return a null record asks for the format as a request rather than as a constraint, so every response that ignores it still breaks the batch — and the 6% with no valid record are exactly the documents on which the model is most likely to fall back on explaining itself in text.

Forcing a tool call without a destination for unclassifiable input forces the model to extract a separator sheet against one of the four schemas, which is fabrication with a schema wrapped around it. A downstream emptiness filter then has to distinguish a fabricated sparse record from a genuinely sparse real document, which is a harder problem than the one being avoided.

Two requirements are live at once: the pipeline cannot absorb prose, which rules out any setting that lets the model answer in text, and 6% of the stream has no valid record, which means the model needs a way to say so inside the mechanism rather than outside it. "any" guarantees a tool call and leaves the choice among schemas to the only component that has read the document; adding a fifth tool for unclassifiable input gives that 6% a structured destination, so the separator sheets arrive as data the pipeline can route rather than as a parse failure.

Naming one tool commits to a document type before the document has been read, and the follow-up turn with tool_choice omitted lets the model answer in prose — reintroducing exactly the failure the stem describes for the 6%.

question:
A two-person platform team supports thirty engineers using Claude Code. Two integrations are wanted. The first is read and write access to the company's Jira Cloud instance, for which a maintained server is already published in the connector directory. The second is the internal deployment-freeze calendar, which exists nowhere outside the company and is served by an internal HTTP API. The binding constraint is the platform team's capacity for ongoing maintenance, not the initial build.

How should the two integrations be provided?
options: Write one in-house MCP server covering both Jira and the freeze calendar, so there is a single server to configure and support
Fork the published Jira server and add freeze-calendar tools to the fork, so both integrations ship as one component
Add the published Jira server, and put the current freeze windows in CLAUDE.md rather than building a second server
Add the published Jira server for the tracker, and write and maintain a small custom server for the freeze calendar
answer: Add the published Jira server for the tracker, and write and maintain a small custom server for the freeze calendar
explanation:
This question tests build-versus-adopt for MCP servers, and names the deciding constraint explicitly: ongoing maintenance capacity, not build effort.

Two Integrations, Two Different Answers

Jira Cloud has a maintained published server in the connector directory. Adopting it means someone else absorbs API changes, auth updates and bug fixes — the recurring cost that a two-person team supporting thirty engineers cannot afford to duplicate.

The freeze calendar exists nowhere outside the company, so no published server can exist. It has to be built, and it is small: one internal HTTP API behind a few tools.

Adopt where a maintained option exists; build only what is genuinely unique. That is the split that minimizes the constrained resource.

Why the other options are incorrect

One in-house server covering both — takes on permanent maintenance of a Jira integration that someone else already maintains, in exchange for one fewer entry in a config file.

Fork the published Jira server — the worst outcome for the stated constraint: the fork inherits every upstream change as a merge, forever, and the freeze calendar has no relationship to Jira's codebase.

Freeze windows in CLAUDE.md — turns live operational data into static text that is stale the moment a window shifts, and someone must remember to edit it. It avoids a small build by introducing a manual process and wrong answers.

Key Takeaway

Adopt maintained servers for common systems; build custom servers only for what is unique to your organization. Weigh ongoing maintenance, not initial build.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp

-
Anthropic — Connect to MCP servers → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart

-
Anthropic — Connect to external tools with MCP (Agent SDK) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/mcp
option_feedback: Building a Jira integration in-house means re-implementing something that already exists and then tracking Jira Cloud's API changes indefinitely, with two people. The tidiness of a single server buys very little: servers are configured independently and their tools arrive in the same pool either way, so the consolidation removes no work the team is actually short of, while adding the one kind of work it is short of.

A fork stops receiving upstream fixes as updates and starts receiving them as merges, and the company-specific tools are now entangled with a codebase the team does not control, so every upstream release becomes a rebase against internal code. It carries the same maintenance burden as building the Jira integration in-house and adds a divergence problem on top of it.

Freeze windows are data that changes, and CLAUDE.md is instruction text loaded at the start of every session: nothing keeps it current, and a stale window is worse than no window, because Claude will state it with the same confidence as a correct one. It also cannot answer a question about a date that is not in the file, which is the thing a calendar integration is for.

The two integrations differ in the way that settles the decision. Jira is a standard, externally maintained API surface that a published server already tracks, so adopting it costs a configuration entry and the approval on first use; the freeze calendar is specific to this company, so nobody else will ever build or maintain it. Splitting along that line spends the team's scarce maintenance capacity only on the piece it alone can supply, and leaves the piece that drifts with a vendor's API to the people who follow that vendor. Both end up as ordinary configured servers whose tools are discovered together when the client connects, so the agent sees one combined toolset regardless.

question:
An agent connected to a team's issue-tracker MCP server spends several turns per task probing for which projects, labels and workflow states exist, and often falls back to the built-in Grep tool, searching a nightly repository mirror of the tracker for information the server could answer live. Two facts constrain the fix: the tracker's label and workflow-state vocabulary changes several times a week as teams reorganize, and the mirror the agent greps is up to 24 hours stale, so answers drawn from it are sometimes wrong rather than merely slow.

Which TWO changes address these behaviors? (Select TWO.)
options: Expose the tracker's current projects, labels and workflow states to the agent as an MCP resource
Add the current project, label and state vocabulary to the project's CLAUDE.md so it is loaded at the start of every session
Remove Grep from the agent's allowed tools, leaving the stale mirror unreachable
Raise the agent's maximum number of turns to give the exploration room to complete
Expand the MCP tools' descriptions to state what each one answers and what it returns, including the queries the built-in search cannot answer
answer: Expose the tracker's current projects, labels and workflow states to the agent as an MCP resource
Expand the MCP tools' descriptions to state what each one answers and what it returns, including the queries the built-in search cannot answer
explanation:
This question tests MCP resources and tool descriptions as complementary fixes for two distinct behaviors.

Two Behaviors, Two Fixes

Probing for vocabulary — the agent burns turns discovering which projects, labels and states exist. That is reference context, and exposing it as an MCP resource lets the client supply it directly. Because the vocabulary changes several times a week, a resource served live is always current.

Falling back to Grep on a stale mirror — the agent reaches for the mirror because it does not know the server can answer live. Tool descriptions that state what each tool answers and returns, including the queries the built-in search cannot serve, fix the selection error at the point where selection happens.

Why the other options are incorrect

Vocabulary in CLAUDE.md — the closest wrong answer. It puts the data in front of the agent, but CLAUDE.md is static text edited by hand, and the vocabulary changes several times a week. It would ship confidently wrong labels between edits, and load in every session whether relevant or not.

Remove Grep — removes a generally useful tool to prevent one misuse, and leaves the agent with no fallback while still not telling it the server can answer.

Raise the turn limit — budgets more turns for exploration that should not be necessary. Cost rises, the cause is untouched.

Key Takeaway

Serve reference vocabulary as an MCP resource rather than baking it into static memory, and use tool descriptions to tell the model what each tool answers — including what the built-in tools cannot.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp

-
Anthropic — Connect to external tools with MCP (Agent SDK) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/mcp

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
option_feedback: A resource gives the agent the catalog in one read instead of several probing calls, and it is read at the time it is used — which is what the several-changes-a-week vocabulary requires. Descriptions are the other half: a tool that does not say what it answers loses selection to a tool the model understands well, so stating what each tool returns, and naming the queries the built-in search cannot answer, is what makes the live server the more attractive option rather than merely the available one.

This puts a fast-moving catalog in an always-loaded file: it is stale within days, it costs tokens in every session whether the tracker is touched or not, and it has to be regenerated and committed by hand each time a team reorganizes.

Removing Grep stops the symptom by removing a capability the agent needs for the repository itself, and it leaves the agent with nothing when the MCP server is unavailable. The goal is for the MCP tool to be the better answer, not the only one.
More turns lets the wasteful exploration run to completion. It does not make the exploration unnecessary, and it does nothing about answers drawn from the stale mirror.

question:
An engineer asks a codebase agent to find every call site of a deprecated helper across a 400,000-file monorepo and explain how each caller uses it. The helper is defined in one module and re-exported through two wrapper modules, one of which renames it. A first attempt has already been made: grepping the helper's original name returned 11,800 matches, most of them a common English word inside comments and unrelated identifiers, and reading even a fraction of them exhausted the session.

Which approach finds all of the call sites without that volume?
options: Grep for the import specifier of the defining module to find the modules that import it, then read those modules and repeat the search for anything they re-export
Grep for each name the helper is exported under — the original and the two re-export names — restricted to call syntax, then read the matched files
Glob for files under the directories that contain the defining module and the two wrappers, then read each file that matched
Grep for the original name, then read only the files whose matches are import statements
answer: Grep for each name the helper is exported under — the original and the two re-export names — restricted to call syntax, then read the matched files
explanation:
This question tests search strategy on a monorepo, where the naive approach has already been tried and its failure quantified.

Why 11,800 Matches Happened

The helper's original name is a common English word, so searching for the bare name matches comments and unrelated identifiers across 400,000 files. Two refinements fix it together:

Search every name it is called by — the original plus both re-export names, one of which renames it. Any search for a single name structurally misses the renamed re-export's call sites.

Restrict to call syntax — matching the name as an invocation eliminates the prose and identifier noise that produced most of the 11,800.

Then read only the matched files. Complete coverage, tractable volume.

Why the other options are incorrect

Follow imports of the defining module — a sound-looking dependency walk that answers a different question: which modules import the helper, not which lines call it. Transitive re-export chains make it laborious, and it still requires the call-site search at the end.

Glob by directory, read every file — directories are not the unit of interest; call sites live throughout the monorepo, not near the definition. It reads far too much and still misses distant callers.

Grep the original name, read only import-statement matches — narrows to imports rather than calls, and searching only the original name misses everything reached through the renamed wrapper.

Key Takeaway

Search for every alias a symbol is exported under, and constrain the pattern to how it is used. Re-exports and renames are what make single-name searches quietly incomplete.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Tools reference → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference

-
Anthropic — Set up Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: This is the defensible alternative and it is one hop short. Searching for the module specifier finds direct importers, including the two wrappers — but the wrapper's own importers refer to the wrapper, not to the defining module, so the search has to be repeated for each wrapper, then again for anything that re-exports a wrapper. It is correct only if run to a fixed point, and the option stops after one repetition.

The 11,800 matches come from searching a common word across everything, so the two things that have to change are what is searched for and how the match is constrained. The alias set is finite and known — the original plus the two re-export names — and restricting the pattern to call syntax excludes prose and unrelated identifiers, which brings the result set down to the callers. Reading only the matched files then keeps the work proportional to the number of call sites rather than to the repository.

Glob matches paths and names, not contents. Callers are scattered across the monorepo and rarely live near the module they import, so this returns the definition and its wrappers and almost none of the call sites.

Reading only import matches identifies which files import the helper directly and stops there, so the call sites reached through a renamed wrapper are never examined — and no caller's usage is explained, which is half of what was asked.

question:
A developer asks an agent to change a default timeout inside the function retry_with_backoff. The literal appears five times in the 300-line file: three times inside that function, in three blocks generated from the same macro so that the surrounding lines are byte-identical, and twice in two other functions that must not change. The target is the third of the five in file order. Edit reports that the text it was given is not unique.

What is the appropriate way to complete the change?
options: Edit a unique line elsewhere in the target block to insert a temporary marker, Edit using the marker as the anchor, then Edit the marker away
Use Bash with a stream editor to substitute the third occurrence in the file
Retry the Edit with replace-all enabled, then Edit the two unintended occurrences back to their original values
Read the file, then Write it back with the change applied to the intended occurrence
answer: Read the file, then Write it back with the change applied to the intended occurrence
explanation:
This question tests what to do when Edit legitimately cannot disambiguate — a case its uniqueness guarantee is designed to surface.

Why Edit Fails Here, Correctly

Three occurrences sit in macro-generated blocks whose surrounding lines are byte-identical. No amount of extra context makes the target unique, because the context genuinely is not unique. Edit refusing is the tool working: it will not guess which of three identical sites you meant.

Reading the file and writing it back with the change applied to the intended occurrence resolves it deterministically. The full content is in hand, the third occurrence in file order is unambiguous once you can see positions, and the two other functions are preserved exactly.

Why the other options are incorrect

Temporary marker, three edits — clever, and it does work. But it makes three modifications where one suffices, and leaves the file in a state containing a stray marker in between; an interruption at the wrong moment leaves it there.

Bash stream editor on the third occurrence — positional substitution with no uniqueness verification, outside the session's normal edit-and-review path. It is exactly the blind mechanism Edit's failure was protecting against.

Replace-all, then revert two — deliberately corrupts two functions that must not change, then relies on repairing them correctly. Every intermediate state is broken and one missed revert ships a defect.

Key Takeaway

When Edit reports a non-unique match on genuinely identical text, fall back to Read-then-Write. Do not defeat the uniqueness check with blind substitution or by breaking and repairing the file.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Tools reference → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference

-
Anthropic — Common workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/common-workflows

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: This is the ingenious answer and it is three writes where one will do, each of which can fail. It also depends on there being a unique line inside the target block to carry the marker, which is precisely what the macro-generated blocks do not offer — and if such a line existed, it would have served as the anchor directly.

The stem supplies the index, so the objection is not the arithmetic but the blindness: a stream-editor substitution rewrites the file without the agent ever reading back what it produced, so nothing confirms that the line it changed was the one inside the intended function. What the editor counts is also the third match of a text pattern rather than the third occurrence of the literal, so any longer value containing the same digits shifts the count silently, and a miscount lands in one of the two functions the developer said must not change.

This writes the wrong value into two functions and then relies on a second operation to undo it, leaving the file briefly incorrect and the undo dependent on the same non-unique matching that failed in the first place.

Edit needs an anchor that identifies one location, and this file cannot supply one: the three candidate blocks are byte-identical by construction. Reading the file and writing back its complete corrected contents states the final state explicitly instead of deriving it from a pattern match, and at 300 lines the cost of doing so is small. The agent has read what it is writing, so the change it makes is the change it verified.

question:
A senior developer has Claude Code reliably following the team's naming conventions, test layout and commit style, plus a personal preference for terse commit bodies and a rule about which editor's formatting to assume. A new teammate clones the repository and finds Claude follows none of it. On the teammate's machine /memory lists the project CLAUDE.md and one rules file; on the senior developer's machine it lists those plus a file under their home directory. The team wants the shared conventions to apply to everyone and has said the personal preferences must not be imposed on the team.

What explains this, and what is the fix?
options: The conventions are in a user-level CLAUDE.md; have the new teammate import it with @~/.claude/CLAUDE.md from the project's CLAUDE.md, so both machines load the same content
The conventions are in a CLAUDE.local.md, which is gitignored; rename it to CLAUDE.md and commit it so that it reaches the whole team
The conventions are in a subdirectory CLAUDE.md that loads only when Claude reads files there; move it to the repository root so it loads for every session
They are in a user-level CLAUDE.md, personal to that machine; move the team-relevant subset into the project CLAUDE.md and commit it
answer: They are in a user-level CLAUDE.md, personal to that machine; move the team-relevant subset into the project CLAUDE.md and commit it
explanation:
This question tests the CLAUDE.md hierarchy, and the diagnostic evidence is sitting in the /memory output.

Read the Diagnostic

On the teammate's machine /memory lists the project CLAUDE.md and one rules file. On the senior developer's machine it lists those plus a file under their home directory — ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the user-level memory file. That file applies to all of that developer's projects and is personal to that machine, so it is never shared through version control. Everything living only there is invisible to the team.

Why the Fix Is a Split, Not a Move

The file holds two kinds of content, and the team's requirement separates them: the naming conventions, test layout and commit style are team standards and belong in the project CLAUDE.md, committed. The terse-commit-body preference and the editor-formatting rule are personal and must not be imposed, so they stay at user level. Moving the team-relevant subset satisfies both halves.

Why the other options are incorrect

Import ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md from the project file — imports resolve on each developer's own machine, so teammates would import their own (absent or different) file. It also drags the personal preferences along, which the team explicitly ruled out.

It is a gitignored CLAUDE.local.md — contradicted by the evidence: /memory locates the extra file under the home directory, not the project root.

It is a subdirectory CLAUDE.md — also contradicted. Subdirectory files live inside the repo and would appear on the teammate's clone.

Key Takeaway

User-level CLAUDE.md is personal and machine-local; project CLAUDE.md is committed and shared. When one file holds both kinds of content, split it along that line rather than importing or relocating wholesale.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — How Claude remembers your project → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory

-
Anthropic — Claude Code settings → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings

-
Anthropic — Commands → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands
option_feedback: An import in a committed file pointing at a path in someone's home directory resolves to each developer's own file, so the teammate would import whatever they happen to have, or nothing. Even if it resolved as intended, it would carry the personal preferences to the whole team, which the team has ruled out.

A local project file is gitignored and applies to one project, not to every project the senior developer works in — which is what the two /memory listings show. Committing it would also publish the personal preferences wholesale.

A subdirectory file lives in the repository and would have reached the teammate when Claude worked on files in that directory, and it would not apply across all of that developer's projects. Neither symptom fits.

The listing on each machine identifies the source: the senior developer has an extra memory file under their home directory, which is loaded for every project on that machine and travels with the person rather than with the repository. The fix has to respect the second constraint as well as the first, so it is a split rather than a move: the naming, test-layout and commit-style conventions belong in the committed project file where every clone loads them, while the editor assumption and the terse-commit preference stay personal.

question:
A service's root CLAUDE.md runs to 340 lines, about 200 of which are a hand-maintained listing of the HTTP endpoints, their parameters and their response shapes. Endpoints change several times a week. The repository also generates an OpenAPI specification from the handlers on every commit, at a fixed path. Developers report that Claude confidently cites endpoints removed a month ago and does not know about ones added last week.

What should the team do with the endpoint listing?
options: Move the listing into a separate file and pull it into CLAUDE.md with an @import
Move the listing into a path-scoped rule under .claude/rules/ covering the handler directory
Keep the listing, and add a CI check that fails the build whenever it diverges from the generated specification
Remove the listing, keep the conventions the code cannot state, and point at the generated specification so Claude reads the endpoints there
answer: Remove the listing, keep the conventions the code cannot state, and point at the generated specification so Claude reads the endpoints there
explanation:
This question tests what belongs in CLAUDE.md, and specifically that derived facts should be pointed at rather than copied.

Two Kinds of Content in One File

The 340-line file mixes two things. Roughly 140 lines are conventions and rationale the code cannot state for itself — genuine memory content. The other 200 lines are a hand-maintained copy of information the repository already generates on every commit.

That copy is the defect. Endpoints change several times a week and the listing is updated by hand, so it is wrong most of the time — and Claude cites it confidently because a memory file reads as authoritative. Removing the listing and pointing at the generated OpenAPI specification means Claude reads current endpoints from the artifact that is regenerated automatically, and never sees a stale copy at all.

Why the other options are incorrect

@import the listing from a separate file — imports are expanded and loaded at launch, so the same 200 stale lines still enter every session. Better filing, identical staleness and identical cost.

Path-scoped rule over the handler directory — improves when the listing loads, and leaves it hand-maintained and wrong. It also loads precisely when someone is editing handlers, which is exactly when accuracy matters most.

CI check that fails on divergence — the strongest distractor: it does keep the copy accurate. But it makes every endpoint change a two-file change with a build break as the enforcement, permanently maintaining a duplicate of a generated artifact. The copy has no reason to exist.

Key Takeaway

Keep in CLAUDE.md what the code cannot say for itself; point at generated artifacts for everything derivable. Hand-maintained duplicates of generated data go stale between commits and are cited with full confidence.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — How Claude remembers your project → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices

-
Anthropic — Set up Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases
option_feedback: An import is a file-organization change, not a context change: imported files are expanded and loaded at launch alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them. The same 200 lines enter every session and the same removed endpoints are asserted. The root file reads better and nothing about the reported problem moves.

Path scoping genuinely cuts the token cost, since the rule enters context only when Claude reads files matching its patterns. But it is still a hand-maintained duplicate of generated data, so it still drifts — and the moment it now loads is precisely when Claude is editing the API, which is where a wrong endpoint list does the most damage rather than the least.

This keeps the duplicate and pays for it twice. Every API change must now also edit CLAUDE.md to get through CI, on a surface that changes several times a week, and the 200 lines still occupy every session's context. It buys accuracy the repository already provides for free in the generated specification, and it makes a memory file part of the build's failure surface.

The listing is a second copy of something the repository already states authoritatively, and CLAUDE.md is read as standing fact at the start of every session, so a stale copy is asserted with exactly the confidence of a correct one. Deleting it removes the drift and the roughly 200 lines being spent on every session at once, and naming the generated specification's path means Claude reads the current endpoints at the moment it needs them, at the cost of one file read. What is left in CLAUDE.md is what the code cannot tell Claude on its own — conventions, pitfalls, decisions. This is the same line Claude Code's own CLAUDE.md checkup draws when it proposes trims: cut what is derivable from the codebase, keep the rationale and the conventions.

question:
Claude Code applies the team's error-handling conventions for one developer and not for another in the same repository. The investigating developer needs two different things: an inventory of which instruction files exist on each machine across user and project scope, so the two setups can be compared and the missing file edited; and, once a change is made, confirmation that the file actually reached the context of a running session rather than merely existing on disk.

Which commands serve these two needs?
options: /memory alone, which lists the CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md and rules files across user and project scope
/memory to enumerate and open the instruction files across scopes, and /context to confirm what this session loaded
/context for both, reporting on the session that is running rather than on the files on disk
/doctor to compare the two installations and their configuration, and /memory to open whichever file the comparison identifies
answer: /memory to enumerate and open the instruction files across scopes, and /context to confirm what this session loaded
explanation:
This question tests two diagnostic commands that answer two genuinely different questions.

Files on Disk vs Context in the Session

The developer needs both halves, and each command supplies one:

/memory enumerates the instruction files across user and project scope — CLAUDE.md, CLAUDE.local.md, rules — and opens them for editing. That is the inventory needed to compare two machines and find the file one of them is missing.

/context reports what the running session actually loaded. Existing on disk and reaching the context window are different things, and only /context confirms the second.

The pairing matters because the failure mode being investigated — conventions applying for one developer and not another — can live at either layer.

Why the other options are incorrect

/memory alone — correct about what /memory does, and it stops at the file system. After editing, the developer still has no confirmation that the change reached a session, which is explicitly the second stated need.

/context for both — reports on the running session only. It cannot enumerate the files that exist on the other machine, nor open one for editing.

/doctor plus /memory — /doctor checks installation and configuration health and proposes trims; it is not a two-machine comparison tool, and it does not report per-session loading.

Key Takeaway

/memory inventories and edits instruction files across scopes; /context confirms what the current session actually loaded. Use both when a file exists but its effect is missing.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — How Claude remembers your project → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory

-
Anthropic — Commands → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands

-
Anthropic — Explore the context window → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window
option_feedback: /memory tells you which files exist and where, which is the first half. It does not report which of them the current session loaded, so a rule that exists on disk and did not load looks identical to one that did.

The two needs are different questions and they have different answers. /memory enumerates the CLAUDE.md and related memory files across user and project scope and lets you open any of them for editing, which is what comparing two machines and fixing the gap requires. Whether a file was actually loaded into the session that is running is a separate fact — a file can exist, be listed, and still not be in context — and /context is the view that reports it.

/context reports what the running session loaded and how the window is being used. It is not an inventory across scopes and it does not open files for editing, so it cannot support the comparison the developer starts with.
/doctor checks the health of an installation and its configuration. It may surface a problem, and it is not how the memory files in effect are enumerated, nor does it establish what a session loaded.

question:
A team's database-migration runbook is a 180-line section of the project CLAUDE.md: ordering rules, the backfill pattern, the rollback steps. It is needed perhaps twice a month, at the point where a developer is planning a migration and before any migration file has been opened. Two complaints have come out of review: every session pays for those lines, and Claude sometimes applies migration-specific rules — batch sizes, backfill phrasing — to unrelated code. The runbook must stay available to the whole team through the repository.

Where should it go?
options: Stay in CLAUDE.md, under a heading stating that the runbook applies only to database migrations
Move into a separate file in the repository, referenced from CLAUDE.md with an @import
Move into a project skill under .claude/skills/, described so Claude loads it when a migration comes up
Move into a path-scoped rule under .claude/rules/ covering the migrations directory
answer: Move into a project skill under .claude/skills/, described so Claude loads it when a migration comes up
explanation:
This question tests the cost model behind CLAUDE.md, rules and skills — three homes with three different loading behaviors.

Match Loading to Usage

The runbook is a multi-step procedure, needed about twice a month, at planning time — before any migration file has been opened — and it must stay shared through the repository.

A project skill matches all three facts. Skill bodies load only when the skill is used, so the other sessions stop paying for 180 lines. It is invoked by relevance to the conversation, which is what "before any file has been opened" requires. And living in .claude/skills/ it is committed and shared like any repository content.

Why the other options are incorrect

Stay in CLAUDE.md with a scoping heading — the heading is prose; the lines still load in every session. Both complaints — the cost and the bleed of migration rules into unrelated code — survive intact.

Separate file pulled in with @import — imports expand at launch, so the content still enters every session. This is organization, not deferral.

Path-scoped rule over the migrations directory — the closest wrong answer, and it does defer loading. But path rules trigger when Claude reads files matching the pattern, and the runbook is needed while planning, before any migration file exists to trigger it.

Key Takeaway

CLAUDE.md loads always; path rules load when matching files are touched; skills load when invoked. A procedure needed occasionally and before any file is opened belongs in a skill.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Extend Claude with skills → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills

-
Anthropic — How Claude remembers your project → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory

-
Anthropic — Extend Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/features-overview
option_feedback: A heading tells a human reader when a section applies; the content is loaded either way. The 180 lines still enter every session, and instructions that are present are instructions the model can draw on, which is exactly the bleed into unrelated code that the team is reporting.

Imported files are expanded and loaded into context at launch alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them. The root file gets shorter while the per-session cost and the bleed stay exactly where they were; only the layout on disk has changed.

A skill's body loads only when the skill is used, so the runbook costs almost nothing until a migration is actually on the table — which is the documented line between a fact that belongs in always-loaded memory and a procedure that does not. Because only the skill's short description sits in context the rest of the time, the migration-specific wording is no longer available to bleed into unrelated work, which is the second complaint. And a skill committed under .claude/skills/ travels with the repository like any other file, so the whole team has it without anyone setting anything up.

A path-scoped rule loads when Claude reads a file matching its patterns, which would fix both the cost and the bleed, but it arrives too late to be useful here. The runbook is wanted while the migration is being planned — before a file in the migrations directory has been written or opened — so a rule keyed to that directory is not in context at the one moment the developer needs it.

question:
A team's codebase-mapping skill walks a service and reports its module boundaries. It works, and running it fills the session with thousands of lines of intermediate exploration, after which the developer's actual task has noticeably less room. Two things are true of how it is used: the developer acts on the map immediately, in the same conversation, referring back to specific module names while implementing; and the same map is worth having on later days, when the exploration would otherwise be repeated.

Which change best fits both?
options: Add context: fork to the skill's frontmatter, running the exploration in an isolated subagent context
Add context: fork, and have the skill's final step also write the map to a file in the repository
Have the skill write its map to a file and return only the file's path, leaving the main conversation to read the file when it needs a module name
Add allowed-tools naming the read-only tools the skill uses, and set a paths glob so it activates only in that service
answer: Add context: fork, and have the skill's final step also write the map to a file in the repository
explanation:
This question tests context: fork, and the trap is that forking alone solves only one of the two stated needs.

What Forking Does

context: fork runs the skill in an isolated subagent context. The thousands of lines of intermediate exploration stay there, and only the resulting map returns to the main conversation — which is exactly what protects the developer's working room.

Why Forking Alone Is Not Enough

The second fact is that the same map is worth having on later days. A fork's context is discarded when it ends, so tomorrow's session would repeat the entire exploration. Having the skill's final step also write the map to a file in the repository makes it durable and shareable, without costing the current conversation anything.

Both requirements are then met: today's session gets the map inline (so the developer can refer to module names while implementing), and later sessions read the file instead of re-exploring.

Why the other options are incorrect

context: fork alone — solves the context pollution and leaves the map ephemeral. Every future run pays the full exploration cost again.

Write to a file and return only the path — protects context and breaks the first stated fact: the developer acts on the map immediately, in the same conversation. Returning only a path forces a re-read to use anything, turning every module lookup into a file operation.

allowed-tools plus a paths glob — pre-approves tools and narrows activation. Neither field affects where the exploration's output accumulates, so the context problem is untouched.

Key Takeaway

Use context: fork to keep a skill's intermediate work out of the main conversation, and write durable output to a file when the result has value beyond this session.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Extend Claude with skills → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills

-
Anthropic — Extend agents with skills (Agent SDK) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/skills

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents
option_feedback: This is right about the context problem and silent about the second requirement. The map returns to the conversation and lives only there, so the next day's session starts with nothing and the walk is repeated.

Forking is what solves the stated problem: the file reads and searches happen in a context the main conversation never sees, and what returns is the map rather than the transcript of producing it. That satisfies the first requirement, because the map itself lands in the conversation and stays available while the developer implements. The second requirement is a different problem — durability across days — and it is solved by the skill also writing the map down, which costs one extra step and saves the whole exploration on the next occasion.

Returning only a path keeps the main conversation small and puts the map behind a read on every reference, so the developer's immediate implementation work pays a round trip each time they need a module name — and the exploration output still accumulates in whatever context ran it, unless it is also forked.

Neither half of it touches either requirement. Pre-approving read-only tools removes permission prompts during the skill's turn, and read-only exploration produces exactly as much output, so the context cost is unchanged; a paths glob only narrows when Claude loads the skill on its own, so on the runs where it does fire the same thousands of lines still land in the conversation, and nothing is written down for the next day.

question:
A team is packaging its database-migration workflow as a skill. Review produces two requirements. A developer typing the skill's name in the slash-command menu should see which arguments it expects before sending it. And the skill's own file-writing steps must not stop for a permission prompt part-way through a run — while the pre-approval must not silently persist into the developer's subsequent messages, because the same session is used for ordinary work afterwards.

Which TWO frontmatter fields address these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: arguments
disallowed-tools
argument-hint
allowed-tools
disable-model-invocation
answer: argument-hint
allowed-tools
explanation:
This question tests skill frontmatter, and hinges on a precise property of allowed-tools.

Two Requirements, Two Fields

argument-hint — displays the expected arguments in the slash-command menu as the developer types the skill's name, before sending. That is exactly the stated need: discoverability at the moment of invocation.

allowed-tools — pre-approves the named tools for the invoking turn, so the skill's file-writing steps run without stopping for a permission prompt. Crucially, the grant clears on the next message, which satisfies the second half of the requirement: the pre-approval does not silently persist into the developer's subsequent ordinary work in the same session.

Why the other options are incorrect

arguments — the tempting near-miss on naming. The field that renders the hint in the menu is argument-hint; picking by the more obvious-sounding name is the trap here.

disallowed-tools — removes tools during the skill. That is the field for restricting capability, the opposite of clearing a permission prompt out of the way.

disable-model-invocation — controls whether Claude may invoke the skill on its own initiative. Relevant to invocation policy, irrelevant to both stated requirements.

Key Takeaway

argument-hint surfaces expected arguments in the menu; allowed-tools pre-approves tools for the invoking turn and clears afterwards. allowed-tools grants — it never restricts.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Extend Claude with skills → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills

-
Anthropic — Configure permissions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions

-
Anthropic — Commands → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands
option_feedback: The arguments field declares named arguments for substitution inside the skill's body. It governs how values are referenced once they have been supplied, not what a developer is shown before supplying them.

disallowed-tools removes the named tools from Claude's available pool while the skill is active — a restriction, not a pre-approval, and like allowed-tools it clears when the developer sends the next message. Listing Write there would stop the skill's file-writing steps outright rather than stop them prompting, and listing anything else leaves the prompts exactly where they are.

argument-hint supplies the autocomplete hint, so a developer typing the skill's name sees what it expects rather than guessing. allowed-tools pre-approves the named tools for the turn that invokes the skill, which is what keeps a multi-step file-writing procedure from pausing on a permission dialog — and the grant clears when the developer sends their next message rather than persisting into the ordinary work that follows, which is the second half of the requirement.
