disable-model-invocation controls whether Claude may invoke the skill on its own. Neither requirement is about who triggers it.

question:
A team moves its Terraform conventions out of the root CLAUDE.md into .claude/rules/terraform.md with the frontmatter paths: ["**/terraform/**/*.tf"]. The Terraform files live at services/<name>/terraform/*.tf across eleven service directories. A developer starts a session, immediately runs the command that lists loaded instruction files, sees no sign of the Terraform conventions, and reports the rule as broken. A second developer, three hours into a session spent editing services/billing/terraform/main.tf, reports that Claude is applying the conventions correctly.

What is happening?
options: The glob does not match: a leading **/ cannot match services/billing/terraform/main.tf, so the rule never activates and the second developer is seeing conventions still cached from the old root CLAUDE.md

A path-scoped rule loads when Claude reads or edits a file matching its patterns, so a session that has not yet touched a Terraform file has not loaded it — both reports are consistent with the rule working as designed
Rule files load only after the session's first tool call, so the first developer's listing was taken too early and would show the rule after any tool use
A rule scoped by path takes the place of the project's instructions while it is active, so it is listed separately from them and the first developer was reading the wrong list
answer: A path-scoped rule loads when Claude reads or edits a file matching its patterns, so a session that has not yet touched a Terraform file has not loaded it — both reports are consistent with the rule working as designed
explanation:
This question tests path-scoped rule loading, and it is a diagnosis question: both developers' reports are true and consistent.

The Trigger Is File Involvement

A rule with paths frontmatter loads when Claude reads or edits a file matching its patterns — not at session start. The first developer listed loaded instructions immediately, before touching any .tf file, so the rule correctly had not loaded. The second developer spent three hours editing services/billing/terraform/main.tf, so the rule loaded and the conventions applied.

Nothing is broken. The two reports are the same mechanism observed at two different moments, which is precisely the behaviour path scoping exists to provide: instructions arrive when they are relevant and cost nothing when they are not.

Why the other options are incorrect

The glob does not match — it does. **/terraform/**/*.tf matches services/billing/terraform/main.tf; a leading **/ matches any number of leading directories. The "cached from the old CLAUDE.md" claim also has no mechanism behind it.

Rules load after the first tool call — invents a trigger. Loading is tied to matching files, not to tool use in general; a session doing non-Terraform work never loads it however many tools it calls.

A path rule replaces the project instructions — rules are additive. Nothing supplants CLAUDE.md while a rule is active, and there is no separate list to have been reading.

Key Takeaway

Path-scoped rules load on file match, not at startup. A rule missing from a fresh session's listing is expected behaviour, not a broken glob.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — How Claude remembers your project → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory

-
Anthropic — Explore the context window → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window

-
Anthropic — Set up Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases
option_feedback: This is the right instinct — a mis-specified glob is the other common cause of exactly this report — and the pattern here is well-formed for these paths. It also has to explain the second developer, and it cannot: instructions are not cached from a file the team removed, and a rule that never activates cannot be what is being applied.

Two reports are on the table and only one explanation fits both. Path scoping makes a rule conditional on the files being worked with, so a session that has just started and touched nothing Terraform-shaped has no reason to have loaded it — the first developer's listing is accurate. The second developer has been editing a matching file for three hours, so the rule is loaded and applied. The glob is worth checking before accepting this, and it does match: **/ matches the intervening services/billing/ segments.

There is no general delay of that kind. Rules without path scoping load at the start of the session alongside the project's instructions; what defers this one is its patterns, not the timing of any tool call.
Instruction sources are additive rather than replacing one another. A path-scoped rule adds its content to what is already loaded when its patterns match.

question:
A stack trace points to a function that dereferences a value without checking whether it is null. The fix is one conditional and the developer knows what it should be. The service is failing in production now. Before starting, the developer greps and finds the same unchecked pattern in three sibling handlers that have not yet failed, and the file has no tests.

How should this be approached?
options: Use direct execution for the identified fix, review the diff, and raise the three siblings as separate follow-up work
Use direct execution and have the agent apply the same conditional to all four handlers in one pass
Enter plan mode so the four handlers and the missing tests can be assessed together before anything is edited
Use direct execution for the identified fix, and add the null-check convention to CLAUDE.md in the same change so the pattern is applied consistently later
answer: Use direct execution for the identified fix, review the diff, and raise the three siblings as separate follow-up work
explanation:
This question tests plan mode versus direct execution, and specifically that scope discipline is part of the answer.

A Known One-Line Fix in a Live Incident

The developer knows the fix, it is one conditional, and the service is failing in production now. Plan mode's value is deciding what to do when that is unclear; here it is not. Direct execution plus a diff review is the proportionate path, and reviewing the diff keeps the human gate where it belongs.

Why the Siblings Wait

The three sibling handlers share the pattern and have not failed. Fixing them in the same change turns a one-line incident fix into a four-handler change, in a file with no tests, under production pressure. They are real work — raised as separate follow-up, where they can be done with tests and unhurried review.

Why the other options are incorrect

Fix all four in one pass — expands the blast radius of an urgent change into untested code. Three of the four sites are not causing the incident and can safely wait.

Enter plan mode to assess everything — the right instinct at the wrong moment. Planning the siblings and the missing tests is worth doing; doing it while production is down delays a known fix.

Add the convention to CLAUDE.md in the same change — a good idea bundled into an incident fix. It mixes an unrelated concern into the diff being reviewed under time pressure.

Key Takeaway

Direct execution for known, scoped fixes; keep the incident change minimal and raise the adjacent work separately. Plan mode earns its cost when the approach is genuinely uncertain.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Choose a permission mode → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes

-
Anthropic — Common workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/common-workflows

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Plan mode earns its overhead when the work is large, spans many files, or has several defensible approaches. This one has a known cause, a known file and a decided fix, and a live incident setting the priority — so the shortest path to a reviewable diff is to make the change and read it. The three siblings are a real finding and a different piece of work: they are not failing, they are unverified by tests, and folding them into an incident fix enlarges the diff that has to be reviewed under time pressure.

The three siblings look identical to a grep and have not been examined; one of them may dereference a value that cannot be null, where the added conditional is dead code, or may need a different fallback. It also turns a one-line reviewable fix into a four-site change during an incident, with no tests to catch a mistake.
There is nothing to explore for the failing handler, and planning the sibling sweep and the missing tests holds up a fix the developer has already decided on while the service is failing.

Recording the convention is worth doing and it is not part of this change: it does not fix the defect in production, and mixing a standards edit into an incident diff makes the diff harder to review and to revert.

question:
An engineer is using an agent to add a feature to an unfamiliar service. The first phase maps the service — dozens of files read, many searches — and the second phase implements the change. By the time implementation begins, the agent gives vaguer answers and starts describing "the typical pattern for this kind of service" instead of the specific classes it found earlier.

Which change best preserves the agent's working context through both phases?
options: Run discovery in a dedicated exploration subagent, so only its summary of findings returns to the conversation
Run /compact once discovery is finished, starting the implementation phase from a summarized history
Do discovery in one session and implementation in a second, fresh session started afterwards
Run the discovery phase in plan mode, leaving files unmodified while the agent explores the service
answer: Run discovery in a dedicated exploration subagent, so only its summary of findings returns to the conversation
explanation:
This question tests context management across a two-phase task, and the symptom names the cause.

Why Answers Get Vaguer

Dozens of files read and many searches fill the context with raw discovery material. By implementation time the specific classes found earlier are competing with everything else that was read, and the agent drifts toward generic patterns — "the typical pattern for this kind of service" — because the specifics have been diluted.

Isolate the Discovery, Keep the Findings

Running discovery in a dedicated exploration subagent puts the file reads and searches in a separate context that absorbs the volume. Only the summary of findings returns to the main conversation, so implementation begins with the conclusions — the specific classes and boundaries — and a largely clean window. The expensive-but-bulky part is done where its bulk does not matter.

Why the other options are incorrect

/compact after discovery — the closest wrong answer, and it does reclaim room. But compaction summarizes lossily after the material has been ingested and paid for, and what it drops is unpredictable — often the specific class names the second phase needs.

Two separate sessions — the fresh session starts with no findings at all, so the discovery must be re-explained or re-run. It solves the context problem by discarding the work.

Discovery in plan mode — prevents modifications, which was never the issue. Everything read still lands in the same context window, so the dilution happens identically.

Key Takeaway

Send high-volume exploration to a subagent and bring back only its findings. Isolation prevents the context pressure; compaction merely responds to it after the fact.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Run agents in parallel → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents

-
Anthropic — Explore the context window → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window
option_feedback: The degradation comes from the volume of raw exploration output sitting in the main conversation. Delegating discovery to a subagent moves that volume into a context the main agent never sees: the subagent absorbs the file reads and searches and returns a condensed set of findings, so the implementation phase starts with a small, accurate picture rather than a crowded one.

Compaction reduces size by summarizing what is already there, and the specifics most worth keeping — class names, the call paths that were traced — are exactly what a summary tends to generalize away. It mitigates the symptom after the cost has been paid.

A fresh session solves the crowding by discarding the findings, so the second session has to rediscover the service or be re-briefed by hand. Handing off deliberately through a written summary can work; simply starting over does not.
Plan mode governs whether the agent may modify files while it explores. It does not change how much exploration output accumulates in the conversation, which is the actual cause here.

question:
A developer needs a function that normalizes inconsistent customer address records. Three attempts at describing the transformation in prose produced three different interpretations of abbreviations, missing fields and mixed casing. Reviewing what happened, the developer finds that the disagreements fall into two groups: about thirty abbreviation cases where they have a spreadsheet of real records with the desired output already filled in for six of them, and a question they have not settled at all — whether a record missing a postal code should be rejected or passed through with the field empty, which depends on a downstream system nobody has asked yet.

What is most likely to resolve this efficiently?
options: Provide two or three of the filled-in pairs covering the awkward abbreviations, and settle the postal-code question separately
Provide all six filled-in input/output pairs and let the model infer the postal-code behavior from how the examples treat other missing fields
Ask Claude to interview the developer about the requirements and surface the cases they have not considered, then write the function from the answers
Break the request into a sequence of smaller requests, describing one normalization rule at a time in prose
answer: Provide two or three of the filled-in pairs covering the awkward abbreviations, and settle the postal-code question separately
explanation:
This question tests few-shot examples versus prose, plus a second lesson: some disagreements are not the model's to resolve.

Two Groups, Two Different Problems

The developer's own analysis splits the failures:

The thirty abbreviation cases are a specification problem the developer has already solved — there is a spreadsheet with the desired output filled in. Two or three filled-in input/output pairs, chosen to cover the awkward cases, communicate the transformation far more precisely than a fourth prose attempt. Examples excel exactly where prose keeps producing different interpretations.

The postal-code question is not answered anywhere. It depends on a downstream system nobody has asked. No example can encode a decision that has not been made, so it has to be settled separately — with the downstream owners.

Why the other options are incorrect

All six pairs, infer postal-code behavior — the trap. Providing more examples is reasonable, but asking the model to infer an unsettled business rule from unrelated missing fields invents a requirement. The developer would then discover the invented choice downstream.

Have Claude interview the developer — a strong technique when the developer does not know what they have not considered. Here they have already identified both groups precisely; the unknown is external, and interviewing cannot supply it.

One prose rule at a time — more of the approach that failed three times, at higher round-trip cost, while the unsettled question remains unsettled.

Key Takeaway

Use worked examples where you can already show the answer; escalate genuinely undecided requirements to whoever owns them. Do not let examples silently invent a business rule.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Prompt engineering overview → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview

-
Anthropic — Prompting best practices → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

-
Anthropic — Common workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/common-workflows
option_feedback: The two groups are different problems and only one of them is a communication problem. For the abbreviation cases the developer knows the answer and has it written down, and a handful of input/output pairs states it exactly where three rounds of prose did not. The postal-code case is not underspecified language but an undecided requirement, and no example can convey a decision that has not been made — it has to be settled with the downstream system first, or the function will encode a guess.

This treats an undecided requirement as an inference problem. The model will infer something consistent-looking from how other missing fields are handled, and that inference becomes the behavior nobody chose — which is harder to catch later than an explicit gap, because the code looks deliberate.

The interview pattern is valuable when the developer has not worked out what they need, and here that is true of exactly one question out of thirty-one. Running it over the whole transformation re-opens cases that are already decided and written down.
Rule-by-rule requests still express each rule in the prose that is causing the ambiguity, and they make the interactions between the rules harder to see.

question:
A CI pipeline runs Claude Code non-interactively to review pull requests and must post each finding as an inline comment on a specific file and line. Two proposals are being compared. One asks the model to write its findings to findings.json in the workspace with the Write tool, and has the job read that file. The other requests structured output from the CLI directly. The team's constraints: a run that produces malformed findings must fail loudly rather than posting a partial set, and the job runs in a container whose workspace is discarded when the process exits.

How should the invocation be configured?
options: Have the model write findings.json with the Write tool, and have the job read and validate it against the expected structure before posting
Request JSON output with --output-format json, and parse whatever object structure the response contains
Request JSON output with --output-format json together with --json-schema describing the finding structure the pipeline expects
Keep the default text output and have the prompt format findings as a markdown table the pipeline can split on
answer: Request JSON output with --output-format json together with --json-schema describing the finding structure the pipeline expects
explanation:
This question tests headless output configuration, with two constraints that decide it.

Fail Loudly, and Do Not Rely on the Workspace

--output-format json returns a structured envelope on stdout — no file, which matters because the container's workspace is discarded on exit. Adding --json-schema describing the expected finding structure makes the output validated against that schema, so malformed findings fail at the boundary rather than being posted as a partial set. Both constraints are satisfied by the invocation itself, with nothing to parse defensively.

Why the other options are incorrect

Write findings.json, job reads and validates — depends on a workspace the stem says is discarded, and validation is hand-rolled downstream after the model has already finished. It reintroduces the file-based indirection the second proposal exists to remove.

--output-format json alone, parse whatever arrives — the near-miss. It gets the envelope but not the guarantee: without a schema, a structurally wrong findings payload parses as valid JSON and gets posted. The "fail loudly" constraint is unmet.

Default text output plus a markdown table — pipeline correctness now depends on prose formatting, split on delimiters. Any drift in the table's shape silently corrupts the posted comments.

Key Takeaway

In CI, request --output-format json and pair it with --json-schema so malformed output fails at the boundary. Structured output beats file hand-offs in ephemeral containers.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Run Claude Code programmatically → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless

-
Anthropic — CLI reference → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference

-
Anthropic — Get structured output from agents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/structured-outputs
option_feedback: This is a real pattern and it is the weaker of the two here. Writing JSON with a file tool is the model composing a JSON document, with the same fence, preamble and trailing-comma failure modes as any generated text, and the validation happens in the job after the fact. It also depends on a workspace the container discards, so a run that exits early leaves nothing to read.

--output-format json returns a fixed envelope — result, session identifier, usage metadata — with the review itself inside it as prose. The pipeline ends up with JSON wrapped around free text rather than findings it can iterate over.

The schema is what makes the structure a property of the invocation rather than of the model's compliance: the CLI validates the output against it, so a run that cannot produce conforming findings fails at the point of generation instead of handing the job something to discover later. That is what the loud-failure requirement asks for, and it removes the workspace question entirely, since the findings come back on the process's own output rather than through a file in a container that is about to be destroyed.

A markdown table is a formatting instruction with no enforcement. Column counts, escaping and stray commentary vary between runs, and the runs that vary fail silently by producing rows the splitter mangles rather than rejects.

question:
An automated reviewer runs on every push to a pull request. After a developer pushes a fix, the next run posts the same findings again alongside new ones, so long-running branches accumulate dozens of duplicate comments. Two measurements are in front of the team. A full-PR review costs roughly six minutes and a meaningful share of the CI budget, and the busiest branches see forty pushes. And a sample of resolved pull requests found that 20% of previously reported findings had been fixed by a later commit without the reviewer ever confirming it, so reviewers were re-checking them by hand.

What is the appropriate change?
options: Have the reviewer look only at the diff introduced by the newest commit, which removes the repetition and cuts the per-run cost on long branches
Give the review the previous findings as structured items with file, line and status, and ask for only new or unaddressed issues
Have the pipeline hash each comment's text and suppress any comment whose hash has been posted before
Run the full review only on the first push and on the final push before merge, and run a diff-only review on the pushes in between
answer: Give the review the previous findings as structured items with file, line and status, and ask for only new or unaddressed issues
explanation:
This question tests re-run design for an automated reviewer, with two measurements that rule out the obvious answers.

The Reviewer Needs Memory, Not a Smaller Window

Giving the review the previous findings as structured items — file, line, status — and asking for only new or unaddressed issues fixes both measured problems. Duplicates stop because the reviewer knows what it already said. And because it re-checks the prior findings against the current code, the 20% that were quietly fixed get confirmed as resolved rather than left for reviewers to verify by hand.

Why the other options are incorrect

Review only the newest commit's diff — the most tempting option: it removes repetition and cuts cost. But a finding fixed by a later commit lives in code the newest diff does not touch, so the 20%-silently-fixed problem gets worse, not better. Issues spanning commits also fall outside every individual diff.

Hash and suppress previously-posted comments — suppresses the comment while the underlying finding's status stays unknown. Trivial rewording defeats the hash, and resolved findings are still never confirmed.

Full review on first and last push only — a cost compromise that leaves the middle 38 pushes reviewed shallowly and still says nothing about which prior findings were fixed.

Key Takeaway

Carry prior findings into each re-run as structured state and ask for new-or-unaddressed. Narrowing the review window suppresses duplicates by suppressing coverage.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Code Review → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review

-
Anthropic — Claude Code GitHub Actions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/github-actions

-
Anthropic — Run Claude Code programmatically → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless
option_feedback: This is the cost-driven answer and it buys the saving by blinding the reviewer to everything outside the newest commit — including whether an earlier finding was addressed, which is the second problem the team has. Problems introduced by the interaction between commits also go unreported.

The reviewer repeats findings because each run starts with no knowledge of what was already reported, so supplying the prior findings is what makes "new or still outstanding" a question it can answer. Structuring them by file, line and status is what lets it be answered per finding rather than by comparing prose, and it is what converts the second measurement into value: a reviewer that is told what was previously reported can state that an issue is now fixed, which is the 20% reviewers are currently re-checking by hand.

Text hashing catches only byte-identical comments. The same finding worded slightly differently on the next run hashes differently and posts again, so the duplicates persist in a less predictable form, and nothing confirms fixes.

This reduces how often the duplication happens without changing why it happens, and it leaves the pushes in between with the same blindness as option A. The first full review still repeats itself at the end.

question:
An automated reviewer reports stale comments in pull requests. Most of what it flags turns out to be fine — comments that are terse, or that describe intent rather than mechanics, but that say nothing untrue. The flagged comments come back with the same stated confidence as the findings reviewers act on. The team added the instruction "be conservative and report only high-confidence issues", which changed the volume slightly and the accuracy not at all.

What is most likely to raise precision for this category?
options: Have the reviewer attach a confidence score to each comment finding, and post only those above a threshold
Review fewer files per run, giving the model more attention for each individual file
Replace that instruction in the review prompt with a specific criterion: flag a comment only when it contradicts what the code does
Instruct the reviewer to re-read each comment finding and confirm it before including it in the review
answer: Replace that instruction in the review prompt with a specific criterion: flag a comment only when it contradicts what the code does
explanation:
This question tests criteria design, and the stem has already eliminated the instruction-based fix.

"Be Conservative" Is Not a Criterion

The team tried "report only high-confidence issues" and it changed volume slightly and accuracy not at all. That is the expected result: the instruction adjusts a threshold on a judgment the model was already making, without telling it what makes a stale comment stale.

The category needs a decidable test. "Flag a comment only when it contradicts what the code does" is checkable against the code itself — and it excludes exactly what is being over-flagged: comments that are terse, or that describe intent rather than mechanics, but say nothing untrue. Precision rises because the criterion partitions the cases correctly, not because the model is asked to be more careful.

Why the other options are incorrect

Confidence score plus threshold — the stem forecloses it: the false positives arrive with the same stated confidence as the findings reviewers act on. Filtering on that signal cannot separate them.

Fewer files per run — treats this as an attention problem. The flags are not careless; they are correct observations against an unstated standard. More attention produces more of them.

Re-read and confirm each finding — self-review against the same vague criterion. The model re-derives the same judgment and confirms it.

Key Takeaway

Replace conservatism instructions with a specific, decidable criterion. Vague standards produce confident wrong findings, and confidence filtering cannot fix a definition problem.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Prompting best practices → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

-
Anthropic — Prompt engineering overview → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview

-
Anthropic — Code Review → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review
option_feedback: Uncalibrated self-reported confidence does not separate these cases: the stem states that the false positives carry the same stated confidence as the findings reviewers accept, so any threshold either keeps both or discards both.

This addresses attention dilution, which produces uneven depth across files. The failure here is consistent and systematic — one category is wrong in a specific way on every run — which points at the criterion rather than at capacity.

"Be conservative" gives the model no new information about which cases count — it is asked to be more careful about a boundary that was never defined. A categorical criterion moves the decision from a feeling to a test the model can apply: does the comment assert behavior the code contradicts? Terse and intent-describing comments fail that test and stop being reported, while genuinely wrong comments still are.
Re-reading applies the same undefined standard a second time. Without a test for what makes a comment stale, a confirmation step has nothing to check the finding against.

question:
A code review bot posts findings in five categories. Four are acted on most of the time. The fifth, performance, is confirmed as a non-issue by the author in roughly six of seven cases — and in the two cases over six months where it was right, it caught regressions that would have cost real money in production. Developers have started skimming past all of the bot's comments, including the accurate categories. Management has asked that the performance analysis not simply be switched off.

What should the team do while it reworks the performance criteria?
options: Keep the four trusted categories on pull requests, and route performance findings to a weekly digest its owners triage
Keep posting performance findings on pull requests but only when the finding includes a measured benchmark delta, and suppress the rest
Keep posting all five categories on pull requests, and lower the severity label on performance findings to informational
Keep posting all five categories, ordered so that security and correctness findings appear above the performance ones
answer: Keep the four trusted categories on pull requests, and route performance findings to a weekly digest its owners triage
explanation:
This question tests what to do about a low-precision finding category that is nonetheless valuable — under an explicit constraint that it may not be switched off.

Protect the Trusted Channel

The real damage is contagion: developers have started skimming past all the bot's comments, including the four accurate categories. So the immediate priority is to remove the noisy category from the PR channel and restore trust there.

But performance caught two regressions in six months that would have cost real money, and management has ruled out disabling it. Routing performance findings to a weekly digest triaged by its owners keeps the analysis running and reviewed, by people whose job it is, without spending the pull-request channel's credibility. Both constraints are met while the criteria get reworked.

Why the other options are incorrect

Require a measured benchmark delta — a reasonable-sounding filter that is really a criteria rewrite in disguise, and it would suppress most genuine findings too: a code-review agent generally cannot produce measured benchmarks, so the category goes nearly silent — effectively the switch-off management rejected.

Lower the severity label — the comments still appear in pull requests at the same volume. Skimming does not distinguish severity labels; the contagion continues.

Reorder so security appears first — cosmetic. Six-in-seven noise remains in the channel, just further down the page.

Key Takeaway

When one category poisons a trusted channel, move it to a channel matched to its precision rather than suppressing or reordering it. Protect the credibility of the findings people act on.

option_feedback: Two things have to be true at once: the pull-request stream has to stop teaching developers that the bot's output is not worth reading, and the analysis has to keep running so the rare genuine regression is still caught. Moving the category out of the pull-request flow does both — the four trusted categories recover their signal, and the performance findings go to people whose job makes triaging a six-in-seven false-positive rate worthwhile, which is not the position a PR author is in.

This is the most attractive alternative and it is a criteria change made without the evidence to support it. Nobody has established that a measured delta separates the two genuine catches from the false positives — that is the analysis the team has not done yet — and a filter chosen on intuition can as easily suppress the two findings that mattered.

A lower severity label on a finding that is usually wrong is still a wrong finding on the pull request. It reduces the urgency of the noise rather than the noise, and the skimming habit is a response to volume.
Ordering does not reduce the number of wrong comments. Developers still scroll past them, and the habit of dismissing the bot's output is what has to be broken.

question:
An extraction pipeline pulls study metadata out of research papers. Papers with numbered inline citations extract correctly; papers with an end bibliography, or with methodology described inside the narrative rather than in a labeled section, return those fields empty although the information is present. A survey of the corpus finds six recurring layout families and a long tail: about 30% of papers use a layout that appears only once or twice. The prompt budget allows roughly two short examples per request without pushing out the document itself.

What is the most effective change?
options: Add two examples to the extraction prompt, chosen for structural contrast — an end-bibliography paper and a narrative-methodology paper
Classify each paper into one of the six layout families first, then extract with a prompt written for that family, and treat the long tail with the current prompt
Add one example per layout family, six in all, and shorten the document excerpt sent with each request to make room
Expand the prompt's prose description of where each field is usually located within a paper
answer: Add two examples to the extraction prompt, chosen for structural contrast — an end-bibliography paper and a narrative-methodology paper
explanation:
This question tests few-shot example selection under a real budget: roughly two short examples per request.

Choose Examples for Contrast, Not Coverage

The failures are structural — papers with an end bibliography, and papers with methodology in the narrative rather than a labeled section. Two examples chosen for structural contrast, one of each, demonstrate the two extraction behaviors that are actually missing.

Selecting for contrast also generalizes better than selecting for frequency. A paper from the long tail — 30% of the corpus, appearing once or twice — resembles one of these two structural situations far more often than it resembles nothing, so two well-chosen examples reach cases that no per-family enumeration could.

Why the other options are incorrect

Classify into six families, then extract per family — builds a classifier plus six prompts to maintain, and by construction leaves 30% of the corpus on the current failing prompt. Substantial machinery, no coverage of the long tail.

Six examples, shorten the document excerpt — spends the budget in the wrong place. Trimming the source document to fit more examples removes the very text the fields must be extracted from.

Expand the prose description — describing where fields "usually" appear is what the current prompt already does. The failures are structural variation, which examples demonstrate and prose describes only approximately.

Key Takeaway

Pick few-shot examples for structural contrast across the failure modes, not one per observed variant. Two well-chosen examples generalize further than six representative ones.

option_feedback: The budget allows two examples, so they have to be chosen for what they teach rather than for coverage. Two structurally opposite papers — one whose references sit in an end bibliography, one whose methodology is described in the narrative — show what makes a passage count as the reference list or the methodology when no label marks it, and that is what transfers to a layout the model has never seen. Coverage by enumeration cannot reach the long tail by construction.

A router is the reasonable-looking alternative and it optimizes the part of the corpus that is already tractable. Six family-specific prompts leave the long tail on the prompt that is failing today, and the classifier needs the same structural understanding the extraction lacks — so the problem is moved rather than solved, at the cost of a second model call per document.

Six examples do not fit, and the option pays for them by truncating the document — removing the very text the missing fields are in. It also spends the entire budget teaching six specific layouts rather than the discrimination that transfers.
More prose about likely locations is the approach that produced this result. Structure is what examples convey better than descriptions, which is why the fields are empty despite being described.

question:
A team is adding few-shot examples to the prompt behind its automated test-generation job. Two failure modes are measured over 200 pull requests. The generated tests are inconsistent in shape — some name the behavior under test, some do not, some include setup, some assume it. And the job's judgment about coverage is wrong in both directions: it reports the team's in-house fixture pattern as missing coverage in about half the cases where it appears, and it passes over genuinely untested error branches in about a fifth of the pull requests that contain one. The prompt budget allows four examples.

Which TWO things should the examples demonstrate? (Select TWO.)
options: Four examples of the in-house fixture pattern being correctly recognized as coverage
The exact shape expected of a generated test: name, setup, action and assertion
Tests copied verbatim from those the job generated and the team merged in the previous release
The widest range of frameworks and file layouts the repository contains that four examples will cover
A matched pair: the in-house fixture pattern accepted as coverage, and a superficially similar case that is a genuine gap, each with the reasoning for the judgment
answer: The exact shape expected of a generated test: name, setup, action and assertion
A matched pair: the in-house fixture pattern accepted as coverage, and a superficially similar case that is a genuine gap, each with the reasoning for the judgment
explanation:
This question tests example design against two measured, distinct failure modes — with only four example slots.

One Failure Is Shape, One Is Judgment

Shape — generated tests vary in naming, setup and assertions. That is an output-format problem, and the direct fix is an example demonstrating the exact expected shape: name, setup, action, assertion.

Judgment — the job misjudges coverage in both directions: it flags the in-house fixture pattern as missing coverage half the time, and misses genuine error-branch gaps a fifth of the time. A two-directional error needs a matched pair: the fixture pattern correctly accepted as coverage, and a superficially similar case that is a genuine gap — each with the reasoning. The pair teaches the discriminating boundary, which is precisely what is being confused.

Why the other options are incorrect

Four examples of the fixture pattern accepted — spends the entire budget on one direction of the error. It would reduce false "missing coverage" flags while making the missed-gap direction worse, by teaching that fixture-like code is always covered.

Verbatim merged tests from last release — real and passing, but not selected to demonstrate anything. Good output is not the same as instructive output.

Widest range of frameworks and layouts — optimizes for breadth when neither measured failure is about framework variety. It dilutes four slots across a dimension that is not failing.

Key Takeaway

Match examples to measured failure modes: one for output shape, a contrastive pair for a boundary the model confuses in both directions.

-
Anthropic — Code Review → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review

Examples weighted entirely toward one direction teach suppression: the job learns to stop reporting things that look like the fixture pattern, which raises the second error rate — the genuine error branches it already misses one time in five.

The shape problem is a format problem and examples written in the intended form communicate it more reliably than a specification of it, which is what the first two examples buy. The judgment problem is not one-sided — the job over-reports in one direction and under-reports in the other — so what has to be demonstrated is the boundary, not either side of it. A matched pair with the reasoning attached shows where the line falls, and the reasoning is what lets the model apply it to a pattern the examples never mention.
Merged tests carry whatever inconsistency the job already produces, which is precisely what the examples are meant to correct. Examples should show intended behavior, not historical behavior.

Four examples spent on breadth demonstrate four framework surfaces and neither of the two things that are failing. Range coverage is what a small example budget cannot buy, and it pushes the model toward matching the instances shown rather than generalizing from them.

The shape problem is a format problem and examples written in the intended form communicate it more reliably than a specification of it, which is what the first two examples buy. The judgment problem is not one-sided — the job over-reports in one direction and under-reports in the other — so what has to be demonstrated is the boundary, not either side of it. question:
An extraction service asks the model to return a JSON record per document. About 8% of responses fail to parse: some arrive wrapped in markdown fences, some carry a sentence of commentary before the object, a few have a trailing comma. A separate 3% parse cleanly but are missing a field the downstream system requires — the source documents do state that value, so the omission is the model's rather than the document's. Two proposals are on the table. One prefills the assistant turn with an opening brace and sets a stop sequence at the closing brace, which is cheap and needs no schema work. The other defines a tool whose input schema is the record structure and reads the record from the tool call.

Which proposal should the team adopt?
options: Prefill the assistant turn with "{" and stop on the matching close, then validate the parsed object against the record structure in the pipeline
Define a tool whose input schema is the record structure, including its required fields, and read the record from the tool call
Prefill the assistant turn with "{" and pass the output through a JSON repair library before parsing
Instruct the model to return only valid JSON with no fences or commentary, and strip fences before parsing
answer: Define a tool whose input schema is the record structure, including its required fields, and read the record from the tool call
explanation:
This question tests structured-output mechanisms, and the deciding factor is the second failure class.

Two Failure Classes, Only One Addressed by Prefill

The 8% parse failures — markdown fences, leading commentary, trailing commas — are all syntax, and prefill-plus-stop-sequence handles them adequately. That is the cheap proposal's genuine strength.

The 3% is what decides the question. Those responses parse cleanly but omit a field the downstream system requires, and the source documents do state the value. Prefill constrains where the output starts and stops; it has no notion of required fields, so it cannot address this class at all.

A tool whose input schema is the record structure, including its required fields, addresses both: the schema eliminates the syntax class by construction, and required fields make the omission a schema violation rather than a silent gap. This is the canonical structured-output approach for exactly this reason.

Why the other options are incorrect

Prefill plus downstream validation — validation detects the 3% after generation; it does not prevent it, and the pipeline still needs a remedy for every record it rejects.

Prefill plus a JSON repair library — repairs syntax, which prefill already largely solved, and does nothing about a missing field. A repair library cannot invent a value it was never given.

Instruct the model to return valid JSON only — the weakest option: an instruction with a non-zero failure rate against a requirement the schema enforces structurally, plus fence-stripping as a workaround.

Key Takeaway

Tool use with a JSON schema is the reliable structured-output method: it eliminates syntax errors and enforces required fields. Prefill-and-stop only shapes the envelope.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Structured outputs → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference
option_feedback: Prefilling is a real technique and it is genuinely effective against the 8%: it eliminates fences and commentary outright, and the stop sequence bounds the object. It does nothing about the 3%, because nothing in the mechanism knows which fields are required — validation in the pipeline detects the missing field after the response has been paid for and returns the pipeline to a retry it has no structured basis for. It also does not prevent a trailing comma inside the braces.

Only one of the two proposals addresses both failure classes. A declared input schema removes the syntax class the same way prefilling does — the model is filling in fields rather than composing a document, so fences, preambles and stray punctuation have nowhere to appear — and it also removes the second class, because required fields are part of the contract the call is checked against rather than something the pipeline discovers afterwards. Required is the right marking here because these records always carry the field and the failure is the model omitting it; where a source document may genuinely not state a value, the field must instead be nullable with the absence recorded explicitly.

Repair libraries guess at intent when a document is malformed, which converts a visible failure into a silent and possibly wrong success, and they have nothing to say about a well-formed object that is missing a required field.

This is a formatting instruction with a cleanup step behind it, which is the approach already leaving 8% failing. It covers fences and not commentary or trailing commas, and every new malformation needs another defensive rule.

question:
A pipeline extracts purchase order records with a tool whose schema marks every field required. For documents that state no purchase order number and no promised delivery date, the model produces confident, plausible values that appear nowhere in the source. Two constraints complicate the fix. The downstream ERP rejects any record whose purchase order number is absent, so records without one have to be routed somewhere rather than simply passed through. And finance needs to distinguish a document that does not state a purchase order number from an extraction that failed to find one that is there, because the two are handled by different teams.

What change addresses this?
options: Make the two fields nullable, and add a status field per field — stated, not_stated, illegible — so absence is recorded as a finding and the ERP routing can key on it
Make the two fields nullable, and have the pipeline route any record with a null purchase order number to manual entry
Keep the fields required and add a per-field confidence score, routing low-confidence records to review so fabricated values are caught before the ERP sees them
Keep the fields required and instruct the model to leave them blank when the document does not state them
answer: Make the two fields nullable, and add a status field per field — stated, not_stated, illegible — so absence is recorded as a finding and the ERP routing can key on it
explanation:
This question tests schema design for absence, with a second requirement that rules out the simple fix.

Required Fields Cause the Fabrication

Marking every field required leaves the model no legal way to represent "the document does not state this," so it produces confident, plausible values. Making the two fields nullable removes that pressure — absence becomes expressible.

Why Nullable Alone Is Not Enough

Finance must distinguish the document does not state a PO number from extraction failed to find one that is there, because different teams handle each. A bare null collapses both into one value. Adding a per-field status — stated, not_stated, illegible — records absence as a positive finding with a cause, so the distinction survives into the data and the ERP routing can key on it.

Why the other options are incorrect

Nullable plus route nulls to manual entry — the strongest distractor. It stops fabrication and handles the ERP constraint correctly, then fails the finance requirement: every null looks alike, so both teams receive the same undifferentiated queue.

Required plus confidence score — keeps the fields required, so the model must still emit a value. Confidence describes how sure it is about a fabricated number; the fabrication itself continues.

Required plus "leave them blank" — an instruction that contradicts the schema it is attached to. The schema demands a value and the prompt asks for none, which is exactly the conflict that produces inconsistent output.

Key Takeaway

Make genuinely optional fields nullable, and add per-field status when downstream consumers must distinguish kinds of absence. Required-everything schemas manufacture confident fabrications.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Structured outputs → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Strict tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use
option_feedback: A required field is an instruction that a value must be supplied, and the model complies with the instruction it was given, which is where the fabrications come from — so absence has to become representable. Nullability alone is not enough here, because a null is silent about why it is null, and the second constraint is precisely that finance must tell "the document does not state one" apart from "extraction missed it". An explicit per-field status makes that distinction part of the record, and it gives the ERP routing a field to key on rather than an inference from emptiness.

This is the standard answer and it satisfies the first constraint and not the second. A null purchase order number is produced both by a document that has none and by an extraction that failed, so every routed record still has to be triaged by hand to work out which team owns it — which is the work the second constraint is trying to remove.

The fields stay required, so the model still supplies a value for documents that offer none, and fabricated values are designed to look plausible: an invented purchase order number is well-formed and an invented date is reasonable. A confidence score over a value the schema demanded is a score on a guess.

This asks the schema and the prompt for opposite things, and the schema is the stronger signal, so the conflict is usually resolved in favor of producing a value. Where the model does comply, an empty string is itself a claim that cannot be distinguished from a failed extraction.

question:
An invoice extraction pipeline uses tool calling with a strict JSON schema. No record has failed schema validation since deployment. A quarterly reconciliation surfaces three classes of defect: invoices where the extracted line items do not sum to the extracted total; a handful where the tax amount was placed in the discount field; and a smaller set where a quantity came back negative and a delivery date came back as 2019-13-04. Finance wants all three classes caught before they reach the ledger.

Which conclusion and next step are correct?
options: Schema conformance guarantees shape rather than meaning: tighten the types for the negative quantity and the impossible date, and add semantic checks for the rest
Schema conformance guarantees shape rather than meaning: no schema change helps any of these, and all three classes need semantic checks in the pipeline
The schema is too permissive: tighten numeric types, formats and permitted ranges, and re-run the quarter's invoices through the tightened schema
The findings show the schema is not actually being enforced, since an impossible date should never have validated; verify that strict validation is switched on before adding anything
answer: Schema conformance guarantees shape rather than meaning: tighten the types for the negative quantity and the impossible date, and add semantic checks for the rest
explanation:
This question tests the boundary of what schema validation guarantees — and it is deliberately a split verdict, not a clean one.

Shape Versus Meaning

A schema validates structure and types. It cannot know that line items should sum to a total, or that a tax amount was placed in the discount field — those are semantic relationships between correctly-typed values. That is why no record has failed validation while three defect classes reached reconciliation.

But two of the three defects are shape problems that a tighter schema catches: a negative quantity is excluded by a minimum constraint, and 2019-13-04 is excluded by a proper date type or format. The correct answer separates the classes rather than applying one verdict to all three: tighten types for those two, and add semantic checks in the pipeline for the sum mismatch and the field swap.

Why the other options are incorrect

No schema change helps any of these — the trap for anyone who learns "schemas check shape, not meaning" as a slogan. It is right about the principle and wrong about two of the three classes; a negative quantity and an impossible date are exactly what type constraints exclude.

Purely a permissiveness problem — the mirror error. Tightening types cannot catch a sum mismatch or a value in the wrong field, since both are perfectly well-typed.

Validation is not switched on — plausible-sounding, but an impossible date passes a permissive string-typed date field legitimately. The evidence indicates a loose schema, not a disabled one.

Key Takeaway

Schema conformance guarantees shape, not meaning. Push type-level defects into the schema and validate cross-field relationships in the pipeline — the two classes need different tools.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Structured outputs → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs

-
Anthropic — Strict tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
option_feedback: The three classes do not have one cause and the answer has to separate them. A negative quantity and a month of 13 are shape problems — a non-negative constraint and a date format catch them at validation, cheaply. Line items that fail to sum, and a tax amount sitting in the discount field, are individually well-formed numbers in fields that accept numbers, so no constraint on types or ranges can express what is wrong; they need a computed value compared against a stated one, and a cross-field check. Recognizing that the same finding list contains both kinds is the judgment being tested.

This states the principle correctly and then over-applies it. Two of the three classes are shape violations the schema layer already handles — a date format constrains the field directly, and a non-negative bound is enforced when the record is validated against the schema — so sending them to hand-written semantic checks means building and maintaining pipeline code for defects the schema itself rejects.

Tightening types is right for one class and cannot reach the other two. A tax amount in the discount field is a valid number in a numeric field, and line items that fail to sum are each within any plausible range, so no type, format or range constraint sees either of them.

Enforcement is not what is at issue for the two semantic classes, which are perfectly conformant and would have passed under any setting. The impossible date suggests the schema does not constrain date format rather than that validation is off, which is a schema change and not a configuration check.

question:
About 6% of extracted records fail validation: dates in an unexpected format, and currency given as a symbol rather than a three-letter code. The pipeline currently retries by resending the original request unchanged, three times, with near-zero success. Two retry designs are proposed. One sends a compact follow-up: the failed field names and the validator's expected formats, without the document, which keeps the retry cheap on a 40-page average document size. The other resends the original document together with the failed extraction and the validation errors.

What change makes the retry effective?
options: Retry with the failed field names and the expected formats only, leaving the document out to keep the retry cheap
Retry with the original document, the failed extraction and the validation errors, asking for a corrected record
Retry unchanged but raise the limit from three attempts to five, and treat the document as failed only after that
Retry unchanged against a larger model, leaving the request otherwise as it is
answer: Retry with the original document, the failed extraction and the validation errors, asking for a corrected record
explanation:
This question tests retry design, and the cheap-looking option is the trap.

A Retry Needs the Source and the Feedback

Resending the request unchanged retries the identical conditions and near-zero success is the expected result — nothing new is available to correct with.

An effective retry supplies both halves: the validation errors (what was wrong) and the original document (the evidence needed to produce the right value). A date in an unexpected format has to be re-read from the source to be re-rendered correctly; a currency symbol has to be mapped to the code the document's context supports. Attaching the failed extraction as well lets the model correct rather than start over.

Why the other options are incorrect

Field names and expected formats only, no document — the deliberate trap, and its cost argument is genuinely attractive on 40-page documents. But without the source, the model can only reformat what it previously produced. If the original date was misread, the retry confidently reformats the wrong value into the right shape — a well-formed wrong answer, which is worse than a rejected one.

Raise the limit to five attempts — five identical attempts instead of three. Near-zero success rate, multiplied.

Retry unchanged on a larger model — spends more per attempt while withholding the information the attempt needs. Capability does not substitute for feedback.

Key Takeaway

Retries must carry the validation errors and the source document. Feedback without evidence produces well-formatted wrong answers.
