-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use
option_feedback: This is the cost-conscious design and it assumes the corrections are string transformations. They are not: the same symbol denotes several currencies, and an ambiguous date is a real ambiguity rather than a formatting slip, so a model asked to reformat without the source guesses — which produces conforming records that are wrong, a worse outcome than the validation failure it replaced.

An identical request produces substantially the same output, which is why the current retries fail; what makes a retry a different task is the failed record and the specific errors. The document has to go back with them, because neither error class is purely a reformatting of what was returned: a currency symbol maps to different codes depending on the country stated in the document, and a date rendered ambiguously has to be resolved against context the extraction dropped. Sending all three gives the model the defect and the source of truth for correcting it.
Five identical attempts fail for the same reason three do. More attempts multiply cost without adding information.
These are not reasoning failures. A larger model may guess the expected format slightly more often, at higher cost, while the specific defect still goes uncommunicated.

question:
A contract extraction pipeline has two recurring validation failures. In the first, effective dates come back in a format the validator rejects. In the second, the contracting entity is missing — investigation shows those contracts name the entity only in a signed exhibit that is filed separately and never reaches the pipeline. Both classes are currently retried three times with the validation errors attached.

What should the team change?
options: Cap the missing-entity class at a single attempt, and keep both classes inside the retry loop
Keep retrying the format failures, and take the missing-entity failures out of the loop
Add few-shot examples showing where the contracting entity is normally stated, and retry with those in place
Make the contracting entity field optional, allowing the affected documents through validation
answer: Keep retrying the format failures, and take the missing-entity failures out of the loop
explanation:
This question tests which failures belong in a retry loop at all.

One Class Is Recoverable, One Is Not

The format failures are correctable: the effective date is present in the document, and the validation error names what the validator expects. Retrying with that feedback converges — keep them in the loop.

The missing-entity failures are structurally different. The contracting entity appears only in a signed exhibit that is filed separately and never reaches the pipeline. The information is not in the input, so no number of retries can recover it. Every attempt is guaranteed to fail, and pressuring the model to produce a value it cannot find is exactly the condition that invites fabrication. Those documents belong outside the loop — routed for the exhibit to be obtained.

Why the other options are incorrect

Cap missing-entity at one attempt — the closest wrong answer: it does cut the waste from three attempts to one. But it keeps a category with a known-zero success rate inside a loop whose purpose is recovery, and the single attempt still cannot succeed.

Few-shot examples showing where the entity is stated — teaches the model to look somewhere that is not in the document it was given. Examples cannot supply missing input.

Make the entity field optional — lets contracts through validation without a contracting entity. The pipeline stops complaining and starts emitting incomplete contract records downstream.

Key Takeaway

Retry loops are for failures the retry can fix. When the required information is absent from the input, route the case out of the loop rather than capping attempts.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Structured outputs → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls
option_feedback: One attempt on a document that cannot yield the value is still a guaranteed failure, only a cheaper one, and the record still ends up rejected with nobody in a position to supply the exhibit. Capping the cost of a dead end is not the same as giving it a route out.

Retrying is useful when the model produced the wrong form of an answer that is available to it. It cannot produce information the input does not contain: no number of attempts will extract an entity name that lives in a document the model was never given. Separating the two classes keeps retries where they work and sends the rest to a path that can actually resolve them — either by supplying the exhibit or by having a person do it.
Examples teach the model where to look. These contracts do not contain the information anywhere, so a better search of the same text still returns nothing.

Most contracts do state the entity and the pipeline extracts it correctly. Marking the field optional suppresses the failure signal across the whole corpus — including for contracts where the entity is present and was simply missed — to accommodate the subset whose exhibit was never supplied.

question:
A compliance team analyzes documents that arrive continuously throughout the day. Its contract commits to completing analysis of every document within 30 hours of arrival. The team wants to move this workload to the Message Batches API for the cost saving, and has to choose how often to submit.

Which submission strategy meets the commitment while keeping the batch discount?
options: Accumulate arrivals and submit a batch every 4 hours
Accumulate arrivals and submit one batch every 24 hours
Accumulate arrivals and submit a batch every 8 hours
Submit each document individually through the synchronous API as it arrives
answer: Accumulate arrivals and submit a batch every 4 hours
explanation:
This question tests batch cadence arithmetic against an SLA, and it is decided by a number the stem does not state outright.

Do the Arithmetic

The commitment is 30 hours from arrival. Two intervals matter:

Accumulation wait — a document arriving just after a submission waits the full interval before it is sent.

Batch processing — most batches finish within an hour, but the API's guarantee is that a batch expires at 24 hours, and the design has to survive the worst case, not the typical one.

At a 4-hour cadence: worst-case wait 4 hours + worst-case processing 24 hours = 28 hours, inside the commitment with margin. At 8 hours: 8 + 24 = 32 hours, which breaches it. At 24 hours: 24 + 24 = 48 hours, far outside.

Why the other options are incorrect

Every 24 hours — maximizes the discount and blows the SLA by 18 hours in the worst case. The cheapest cadence is not the compliant one.

Every 8 hours — the trap, because it looks comfortable against 30 hours if you only count typical processing. Sized against the 24-hour expiry it fails by two hours, and an SLA has to hold on the bad night, not the average one.

Synchronous per document — meets the deadline easily and forfeits the entire reason for the change: the 50% batch discount.

Key Takeaway

Size batch cadence as accumulation wait + worst-case processing window against the SLA. Batches typically finish within an hour but are only guaranteed within 24.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Batch processing → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing

-
Anthropic — Message Batches API → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages/batches

-
Anthropic — Create a Message Batch → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages/batches/create
option_feedback: A document's total time is the wait until the next submission plus the processing window, and a batch's window is up to 24 hours. Submitting every four hours means the oldest document in a batch waits at most four hours before submission and at most twenty-four hours in processing: a worst case of twenty-eight hours, two hours inside the commitment.

A document arriving just after a submission waits nearly twenty-four hours for the next one, then up to twenty-four hours to process: a worst case of about forty-eight hours, well outside the commitment.

Eight hours of waiting plus a twenty-four-hour window is a worst case of thirty-two hours, which breaches the commitment before any allowance for a failed or expired request. Most batches finish sooner, and a contractual commitment cannot rest on the typical case.

Synchronous processing meets the deadline comfortably and forfeits the batch discount, which is the saving the team set out to capture. It is the right choice when results are needed immediately, and this workload tolerates a day of latency.

question:
An extraction team is moving a nightly run of about five thousand documents to the Message Batches API. The current synchronous implementation uses a tool-calling loop: the model calls the team's own customer_lookup tool, receives the result, and then produces the final record. About 4% of documents fail today, most because they exceed the size the prompt can carry. The team's proposed design keeps the loop and exposes customer_lookup through an MCP server the batch workers run locally over stdio, on the argument that the tool then lives outside the request.

Which TWO statements should shape the design? (Select TWO.)
options: Moving customer_lookup behind a locally run MCP server does not restore the loop, since the client is the one that has to return the tool result and a batch request is processed with no open conversation to return it into
The 4% can be resubmitted selectively by custom_id, with the oversized documents chunked before they are sent again
The 50% saving applies only to batches that complete inside the one-hour window most batches finish in
Results are returned in submission order, so a request's position in the batch is a reliable fallback identifier if a custom_id is ever duplicated
A batch whose requests have not been processed when the window closes continues processing them at lower priority rather than failing them
answer: Moving customer_lookup behind a locally run MCP server does not restore the loop, since the client is the one that has to return the tool result and a batch request is processed with no open conversation to return it into
The 4% can be resubmitted selectively by custom_id, with the oversized documents chunked before they are sent again
explanation:
This question tests what actually changes when a tool-calling loop moves to batch — and three of the distractors are plausible-sounding batch "facts" that are simply untrue.

Where the Loop Breaks

In a tool-calling loop, the client executes the tool and returns the result into an open conversation. A batch request is processed without one: there is no client turn waiting to hand a tool_result back. Relocating customer_lookup behind a locally-run stdio MCP server changes where the tool lives, not who returns its output — so the loop still cannot complete inside a single batch request. The team's stated rationale is the misconception the question targets.

How to Handle the 4%

Each request carries a custom_id, and results are correlated by it. Failed requests can therefore be resubmitted selectively — and since most failures are oversized documents, chunking them before resubmission fixes the cause rather than retrying the same overflow.

Why the other options are incorrect

Discount only within the hour — false. The 50% saving applies to batch processing generally; the one-hour figure is typical completion time, not a discount condition.

Results in submission order — false, and dangerous as a fallback: results may return in any order, which is precisely why custom_id exists.

Unfinished requests continue at lower priority — false. The window is 24 hours and unprocessed requests expire; they do not drift on at reduced priority.

Key Takeaway

Batch requests cannot run a client-executed tool loop, wherever the tool is hosted. Correlate and resubmit by custom_id, and fix the cause before retrying.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Batch processing → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing

-
Anthropic — Message Batches API → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages/batches

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: The team's argument is the one to dispose of first: what makes the loop impossible is not where the tool implementation lives but that the client has to hand a tool result back into an open conversation, and a batch request is submitted and processed without one — so a locally run MCP server changes nothing about it. The lookup therefore moves ahead of submission, or the extraction is reshaped to complete in a single pass. The second design fact is what makes the 4% affordable: every request carries a custom_id that identifies it in the results, so only the failures are resubmitted, and the oversized documents can be chunked first rather than the whole batch re-run.

The team's argument is the one to dispose of first: what makes the loop impossible is not where the tool implementation lives but that the client has to hand a tool result back into an open conversation, and a batch request is submitted and processed without one — so a locally run MCP server changes nothing about it. The lookup therefore moves ahead of submission, or the extraction is reshaped to complete in a single pass. The second design fact is what makes the 4% affordable: every request carries a custom_id that identifies it in the results, so only the failures are resubmitted, and the oversized documents can be chunked first rather than the whole batch re-run.

The discount is a property of the batch endpoint, not of how quickly a batch finishes. Most batches complete within an hour and the window is up to 24; designing for the typical completion time confuses a latency observation with a pricing condition.
Results may be returned in any order, which is the reason custom_id exists. Position is not a fallback identifier — it is the defect that surfaces as records attributed to the wrong documents.
Requests not processed when the window closes expire rather than continuing at lower priority, so expiry is an outcome the design has to handle alongside error and cancellation.

question:
A nightly job generates tests for changed modules and then, in the same session, asks the model to review the tests it just produced. The review almost always concludes the tests are adequate, yet gaps found later in production are visible in the generated tests on inspection. The nightly window is 90 minutes and the generation phase already uses 70 of them, so a second full-cost pass over every module does not fit.

What change makes the review meaningful within the window?
options: Run the review as a separate instance on a smaller model, given only the generated tests and the code under test
Run the review as a separate instance given the generated tests, the code under test, and the generation session's transcript so the reviewer understands the intent behind each test
Keep the review in the generating session and enable extended thinking for the review step, which costs less than a second instance
Keep the review in the generating session, compact the history first, and instruct the reviewer to assume mistakes are present
answer: Run the review as a separate instance on a smaller model, given only the generated tests and the code under test
explanation:
This question tests review independence under a hard time budget.

Why the Current Review Passes Everything

The review runs in the generating session. It inherits every assumption and justification that produced the tests, so it is asked to find fault with reasoning it already holds as its own — which is why gaps visible on later inspection are approved at generation time. Self-review is structurally weak.

Fitting a Real Review in 20 Minutes

A separate instance on a smaller model, given only the generated tests and the code under test, gets independence from the fresh context and affordability from the smaller model. Reviewing existing tests against existing code is a narrower task than writing them, so a smaller model is well matched — and 20 minutes becomes sufficient.

Why the other options are incorrect

Separate instance plus the generation transcript — the sharpest distractor. It fixes the session boundary and then hands the reviewer the generator's full reasoning, re-importing the rationalizations that independence exists to escape. It also costs the most context of any option.

Extended thinking in the same session — more deliberation inside the biased context. The reviewer reasons harder toward the same conclusion.

Compact and assume mistakes — compaction summarizes the bias rather than removing it, and "assume mistakes are present" is an instruction, not an independent vantage point.

Key Takeaway

Independence comes from a fresh instance given the artifacts and the requirements — not the generator's reasoning. A smaller model is often enough for review, which is what makes independence affordable.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK overview → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview

-
Anthropic — Code Review → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: What makes self-review weak is that the reviewer holds the reasoning that produced the work and has already judged those decisions sound. Independence is a property of the context, not of the model size or the instruction, so a separate instance seeded only with the artifacts evaluates what is there rather than confirming why it was written — and because reviewing a diff-sized set of tests against their module is a narrower task than generating them, a smaller model fits the remaining twenty minutes.

This is the plausible refinement and it undoes the thing that makes the review work. Handing over the generation transcript re-imports the reasoning the reviewer is supposed to be free of, so the new instance inherits the same justifications in written form and reaches the same conclusions, at a higher token cost than the correct option.
Extended thinking deepens reasoning within the same context and the same assumptions. More thorough reasoning from a committed starting point produces a more thorough confirmation.

Compaction summarizes the history rather than removing what was concluded from it, so the judgments carry into the summary, and an instruction to assume mistakes applies skepticism to work the model has already justified to itself.

question:
In long support conversations, once the earlier history has been condensed the agent starts referring to "the refund amount discussed" rather than the figure, quotes an order number that belongs to a different order, and loses the delivery deadline the customer stated at the start.

Which change best protects this information?
options: Raise the point at which the conversation history is condensed, moving it later in the conversation
Extract the order numbers, amounts, dates and stated needs into a case-facts block included in every prompt
Instruct the step that condenses the history to preserve all of the numbers and dates exactly as stated
Re-read the full conversation transcript before composing each response, and let the model locate the figures itself
answer: Extract the order numbers, amounts, dates and stated needs into a case-facts block included in every prompt
explanation:
This question tests protecting critical facts from lossy condensation.

Condensation Loses Specifics First

Summarization compresses, and what compresses most readily is exactly what is failing: an amount becomes "the refund amount discussed," a specific order number blurs into a nearby one, a stated deadline disappears. Anything that depends on surviving condensation intact will eventually not.

Take the Facts Out of the Compressible Region

Extracting order numbers, amounts, dates and stated needs into a case-facts block included in every prompt removes them from the summarization path entirely. They are re-injected verbatim on every request, so no amount of history compression can degrade them. The conversation history can then be condensed freely — which is what it is for.

Why the other options are incorrect

Condense later — postpones the loss without preventing it. Long conversations still cross the threshold, and these are described as long conversations.

Instruct the condenser to preserve numbers exactly — the closest wrong answer, and it helps at the margin. But it makes fidelity a probabilistic property of a summarization step, on customer-facing amounts and commitments, and it silently degrades as more facts accumulate.

Re-read the full transcript each response — defeats condensation altogether, so the context problem returns in full, and it asks the model to re-locate figures in a growing transcript on every turn.

Key Takeaway

Maintain critical facts in a structured block re-injected every request. Do not rely on a summarizer to preserve the specifics that matter most.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Context windows → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows

-
Anthropic — Explore the context window → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window

-
Anthropic — Using the Messages API → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/working-with-messages
option_feedback: Delaying condensation postpones the loss rather than preventing it, and it makes the eventual summary larger and lossier because more history is compressed at once.

Precise facts are what condensation is worst at: a summarizer has no way to know that $84.50 matters more than the customer's tone, so amounts become "a refund", dates become "soon", and specific identifiers disappear. Holding those facts in a separate block that is re-injected verbatim each turn puts them outside the process that degrades them, so the agent always has the exact values regardless of how much history has been summarized.

Steering the summary is a real technique and a reasonable thing to do, but it makes the exact value of a refund depend on a summarization step getting it right every time. Facts held outside that step are not exposed to it at all, which is the difference between reducing a risk and removing it.
Re-reading the whole transcript each turn defeats the purpose of managing context and eventually exceeds it, at which point the conversation cannot continue at all.

question:
An order lookup tool returns more than forty fields per order, of which a return conversation needs about five. After three or four lookups most of the context is occupied by order records. Two facts complicate a straight projection. The five fields are not the same five for every case type: lost-package cases need three carrier-tracking fields that a return never uses, and those cases are about 4% of contacts. And a small number of contacts escalate, where the human specialist wants the full record, which the handoff pulls from the order system rather than from the agent's context.

What is the most effective change?
options: Trim each tool result to the fields the common workflows need, and expose the carrier-tracking fields through a second narrowly scoped tool
Reduce each tool result to the union of every workflow's fields before it is appended, so no case type is ever missing what it needs
Write each full result to a file, append only a reference to the conversation, and have the agent read back whichever fields it needs
Instruct the agent in its system prompt to ignore the fields it does not need, and condense the conversation history more frequently once records accumulate
answer: Trim each tool result to the fields the common workflows need, and expose the carrier-tracking fields through a second narrowly scoped tool
explanation:
This question tests tool-result trimming, with two complications that rule out the naive projection.

Trim for the Common Case, Add a Tool for the Rare One

Forty-plus fields where five are needed is straightforward waste. But the five are not the same five: lost-package cases need three carrier-tracking fields that returns never use, in about 4% of contacts.

Trimming to the common workflows' fields and exposing the carrier-tracking fields through a second narrowly scoped tool sizes each path correctly. The 96% pay for five fields; the 4% make one extra call for exactly what they need. The escalation case is already handled — the stem says the specialist's full record is pulled from the order system, not from the agent's context — so nothing is lost by trimming.

Why the other options are incorrect

Union of every workflow's fields — the tempting "safe" choice, and it makes 96% of contacts carry the tracking fields for the 4%. It also grows with every new case type, so the union drifts back toward forty fields.

Full result to a file, reference in context — solves context and adds a read step to every single lookup, converting a five-field need into a file round trip on the common path.

Instruct the agent to ignore fields, condense more often — the fields are already in context and already paid for; ignoring them saves nothing, and more frequent condensation attacks the symptom.

Key Takeaway

Trim tool results to what the common workflows use and serve rare needs through separate scoped tools. Sizing every result for the rarest case taxes every request.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Manage tool context → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Context windows → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows
option_feedback: The tokens are spent when the result enters the conversation, so the projection has to happen before it is appended — that part is not in question. What the case-type variation adds is that the projection cannot be one fixed set without either starving the 4% or carrying their fields for the other 96%. A second narrowly scoped tool resolves it at the right granularity: the common path stays small, and the rare path pays one extra call rather than every conversation paying three extra fields. The escalation case is unaffected, because the handoff can carry the full record from the backend rather than from the agent's context.

The union is the simple version of the right idea and it makes the common case pay for the rare one on every lookup, which is the cost the change is meant to remove. It also grows every time a workflow needs one more field, so the projection drifts back toward the forty-field record.

Reference-and-read-back is a sound pattern for genuinely large artifacts, and here it adds a round trip on every field the agent needs for a record that is a few hundred bytes once trimmed. The read-back also has to decide which fields to return, which is the same projection decision, now made twice.

An instruction to ignore fields does not stop them occupying the window — the agent may read past them successfully and still run out of room — and condensing more often processes the bloat after the tokens have been paid, while blurring order details in the process.

question:
A customer writes: "This is the third time I've had to contact you about this. Just get it sorted." The underlying request is a standard replacement for a damaged item, with photographs attached, which the agent's tools fully support. The account notes show the two earlier contacts were about a different order and both closed successfully — and that six days ago, on the second of them, the customer was told a specialist would call them back within 48 hours. No call is recorded. The customer has not asked to speak to anyone. Published policy covers the replacement and says nothing about missed callback commitments.

How should the agent respond?
options: Complete the replacement and confirm it, acknowledge the repeated contacts, and escalate the unfulfilled callback commitment separately with the case context
Complete the replacement and confirm it, acknowledge the repeated contacts, and note the missed callback in the account record for whoever handles the earlier case next
Escalate the whole contact to a human, on the ground that a broken commitment means the automated path has failed
Complete the replacement and confirm the new delivery date without commenting on the earlier contacts
answer: Complete the replacement and confirm it, acknowledge the repeated contacts, and escalate the unfulfilled callback commitment separately with the case context
explanation:
This question tests separating a resolvable request from a genuine policy gap in the same contact.

Two Different Things Arrived Together

The replacement is fully within the agent's tools and covered by published policy — it should simply be done, promptly, with the repeated contacts acknowledged.

The missed callback is different in kind. A commitment was made six days ago and not kept, and published policy says nothing about missed callback commitments. That is a policy gap: no rule tells the agent what remedy, if any, applies. Gaps are exactly what escalation is for, so it goes to a human separately, with the case context — while the customer's actual request is resolved now rather than being held hostage to it.

Why the other options are incorrect

Note it in the account record — the strongest distractor: it resolves the replacement and records the problem. But a note is passive. It waits for someone to open the earlier case, which may not happen, and a broken commitment with no covering policy needs a person to decide, not a breadcrumb.

Escalate the whole contact — the customer has not asked for a human and the replacement is fully automatable. Escalating everything delays a resolvable request and spends specialist time on work policy already covers.

Resolve without acknowledging — treats a third contact and a broken promise as routine. It is efficient and reads as dismissive.

Key Takeaway

Resolve what policy covers; escalate what policy does not, separately and with context. A single contact can legitimately contain both.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK overview → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview

-
Anthropic — Tool use overview → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview

-
Anthropic — Prompting best practices → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: Two separable things are in front of the agent and they have different answers. The replacement is squarely within its tools, the customer has not asked for a person, and frustration is a reason to handle someone with care rather than to queue them — so it is resolved now and acknowledged. The missed callback is not the same kind of item: a commitment the company made and did not keep is not addressed anywhere in published policy, which is exactly the gap an agent should not improvise across, so it goes to a person with the context attached rather than being decided or dropped.

This gets the replacement right and files the broken commitment where nothing acts on it. A note attached to a closed case waits for someone to open that case again, which may not happen, so the customer's third contact ends with the same unaddressed promise that helped produce it.

Escalating the whole contact makes the customer wait for the one thing the agent can complete immediately, consumes human capacity a straightforward replacement does not need, and leaves the damaged item unresolved while the escalation queues.

A purely transactional reply to a customer on their third contact reads as more of the handling that has already failed them, and it silently discards the missed callback, which is the part of this case that a person needs to see.

question:
A customer asks for a refund on "my last order" and gives a name and a city. get_customer returns two accounts: same name, same city, different order histories, and each with a recent order. Nothing else in the message separates them. The agent's remaining tools — lookup_order and process_refund — all take a customer identifier.

Which TWO actions should the agent take? (Select TWO.)
options: Continue with the account whose recent order best matches what the customer described
Ask the customer for an identifier that separates the accounts, such as the order number or the email on the account
Show the recent orders on both accounts and ask the customer to say which of the two accounts is theirs
Escalate to a human if the customer cannot supply an identifier that resolves the ambiguity, rather than picking the likelier account
Continue with the more recently active account and flag the ambiguity in the case record for someone to check afterwards
answer: Ask the customer for an identifier that separates the accounts, such as the order number or the email on the account
Escalate to a human if the customer cannot supply an identifier that resolves the ambiguity, rather than picking the likelier account
explanation:
This question tests identity ambiguity ahead of an irreversible action, and the answer is a two-step policy.

Ask, Then Escalate If Unresolved

Two accounts match on every stated detail, and the next action is a refund — irreversible, and wrong on the wrong account in two directions at once.

-
Ask for a disambiguating identifier — the order number or account email resolves it definitively, costs one turn, and asks the customer only for something they plausibly have.

-
Escalate if that fails — if no identifier resolves it, the agent has exhausted what it can do safely. Guessing on a refund is the one thing it must not do, so a human takes it.

Together they form a complete policy: resolve cheaply where possible, escalate rather than guess where not.

Why the other options are incorrect

Best-matching recent order — a guess dressed as inference. The stem says nothing in the message separates the accounts, so "best match" is reading signal into noise before an irreversible action.

Show both accounts' orders and ask — the trap, because it feels like helpful disambiguation. It discloses one customer's order history to whoever is on the line, who may not be them. Never resolve identity ambiguity by revealing the accounts.

Continue with the more active account and flag it — performs the refund first and records the doubt afterwards. The flag arrives after the money moved.

Key Takeaway

Ask for a disambiguating identifier, escalate if it cannot be supplied, and never disclose account details as a way of asking. Irreversible actions do not tolerate probabilistic identity.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Tool use overview → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Prompting best practices → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: This is identity resolution by inference. Two customers with the same name in the same city can both have a recent order, and "best matches what the customer described" is a guess presented as evidence. If it is wrong, the agent refunds one person's order against another person's account, so the cost of the error is not a mistaken answer but a mistaken transaction against a stranger.

When a lookup returns more than one match, the missing piece is something the customer has and the agent does not, so asking for one more identifier is both the cheapest move and the only reliable one: a single question, after which every remaining tool call runs against a known account. D is the other half of the same rule. An ambiguity the customer cannot resolve is the point at which the agent has stopped making meaningful progress, and everything still on its path operates on money and order records belonging to a specific person. Handing the case to someone who can verify identity by other means is the correct end of the agent's path rather than a failure of it, and it is a bounded, well-defined trigger rather than a judgment about difficulty.

It resolves the ambiguity by showing one account's order history to someone who may not own it, and the entire premise is that the agent does not yet know which of the two people it is speaking to. The disclosure cannot be taken back, and it is unnecessary: asking the customer to supply an identifier gets the same answer without revealing anything about either account.
