D is the other half of the same rule. An ambiguity the customer cannot resolve is the point at which the agent has stopped making meaningful progress, and everything still on its path operates on money and order records belonging to a specific person. Handing the case to someone who can verify identity by other means is the correct end of the agent's path rather than a failure of it, and it is a bounded, well-defined trigger rather than a judgment about difficulty.

Acting first and annotating afterwards is the same guess as the likelier-match option with a paper trail attached. The refund has already been applied to a possibly wrong account by the time anyone reads the flag, and undoing it is a second transaction experienced by a customer who did nothing wrong. A note in a case record documents a decision; it does not make the decision safe.

question:
A document-analysis subagent was given six papers. Its retries against the primary document store failed for one, and it returned five completed analyses plus structured context naming the paper it could not retrieve and what it attempted. The coordinator has eleven minutes left in the run's budget. The missing paper is the only source assigned to one of the brief's three sub-questions; the other two are well covered. An alternative retrieval path exists — a publisher gateway that takes about four minutes and succeeds roughly half the time.

What should the coordinator do?
options: Re-delegate the missing paper once through the publisher gateway, and if that fails, synthesize the five and annotate the unsupported sub-question
Synthesize the five now and annotate the third sub-question as unsupported
Re-delegate the missing paper through the publisher gateway, and if that fails, drop the third sub-question from the brief so the report contains only what the sources support
Re-delegate the missing paper to the same subagent against the primary store, treating the failure as transient
answer: Re-delegate the missing paper once through the publisher gateway, and if that fails, synthesize the five and annotate the unsupported sub-question
explanation:
This question tests what a coordinator does after receiving a well-formed structured failure — the disposition decision.

The Budget Makes the Decision

Eleven minutes remain; the alternative path takes about four and succeeds roughly half the time. So one attempt is affordable with seven minutes left for synthesis, and its expected value is high: the missing paper is the only source for one of three sub-questions.

If it succeeds, the brief is complete. If it fails, there is still time to synthesize the five and annotate the unsupported sub-question — honest reporting that tells the reader precisely what is and is not covered. One bounded attempt, then honest delivery.

Why the other options are incorrect

Synthesize now and annotate — safe and premature. It leaves seven minutes unused and forfeits a coin-flip chance at completing a third of the brief.

Attempt, then drop the sub-question — identical up to the failure, then wrong at the end. Silently dropping a sub-question the brief asked for hides scope loss; the reader cannot distinguish "not asked" from "asked and unavailable."

Retry the same store as transient — the subagent already retried against the primary store and its structured report says what it attempted. Re-running the proven-failing path spends four of eleven minutes on a known-zero option.

Key Takeaway

After a structured failure, spend one bounded attempt on a genuine alternative if the budget allows, then deliver with the gap annotated. Annotate gaps; never silently drop scope.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use
option_feedback: The structured failure tells the coordinator what is missing and what has already been tried, which is what makes one targeted alternative attempt sensible rather than a blind repeat — and the arithmetic supports it: four minutes against eleven leaves room to synthesize either way, and a 50% chance of covering a sub-question that currently has no source at all is a good return on a third of the remaining budget. If it fails, five analyses are still worth synthesizing, and annotating which sub-question rests on no source is what keeps the report honest about its own coverage.

This is the defensible conservative play and it declines a cheap option too early. The budget is not tight enough to force the choice, and the sub-question at stake has zero coverage rather than thin coverage, so the expected value of four minutes is higher here than anywhere else the time could go.

Dropping the sub-question makes the report look complete by narrowing the brief, which is the same concealment as claiming completeness — the reader cannot tell that a question was asked and went unanswered.

The subagent has already retried against that store and reported what it attempted; the structured context is evidence that the primary path is exhausted, not that it is transient. Repeating the identical request spends budget on the one route already known to be failing.

question:
An engineer has spent five days mapping a legacy billing system with an agent, a different session each day, recording findings in a scratchpad file the agent reads at the start of each session. The file is now about 4,000 lines. Day four's session spent most of its context reading it and gave noticeably vaguer answers afterwards; day five's session contradicted a day-one finding about which module owns settlement.

What addresses this?
options: Have the agent read the whole findings file at the start of each session but summarize it first, carrying the summary forward and archiving the original
Split the findings into one file per component with a short index, and have the agent read the index plus only the files relevant to the day's question
Have the agent append each day's findings to the same file and read only the most recent day's section
Switch to a model with a larger context window, and have the agent read the whole findings file at the start of each session
answer: Split the findings into one file per component with a short index, and have the agent read the index plus only the files relevant to the day's question
explanation:
This question tests external memory design, and both reported symptoms trace to the same cause.

One Monolith, Two Failures

A 4,000-line scratchpad read in full at session start consumes most of the context before work begins — day four's vagueness. And an append-only monolith accumulates contradictions in silence, because nobody re-reads day one when writing day five — hence the settlement-ownership conflict.

Index Plus Components

Splitting into one file per component with a short index fixes both. Each session reads the index — cheap — plus only the files relevant to that day's question, so context goes to the work instead of the archive. And when a finding about settlement is revised, it is revised in the settlement file, next to what it contradicts, where the conflict is visible.

Why the other options are incorrect

Summarize the whole file each session — pays the full read cost first, then compounds loss: a summary of a summary, day over day, with the original archived away.

Append and read only the latest section — cheap and amnesiac. Day five reads day four only, so day-one findings are neither honoured nor corrected — exactly the contradiction observed.

Larger context window — accommodates the monolith without improving it. Reading 4,000 undifferentiated lines still crowds attention, and contradictions still accumulate.

Key Takeaway

Structure external memory as an index plus per-topic files, and read selectively. A single growing scratchpad costs context on every session and hides its own contradictions.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Set up Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases

-
Anthropic — Explore the context window → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window

-
Anthropic — How Claude remembers your project → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: This reintroduces exactly the loss the file was created to avoid. Each day's summary compresses the previous compression, so specific class names and call paths become generalities, and archiving the original means the detail exists but is never read.

The file solved the cross-session problem and has created a within-session one: reading 4,000 lines to answer a question about one component spends the context the work needs. Splitting by component with an index restores selective reading — the agent loads the index, then the two or three files that bear on today's question — and it also addresses the contradiction, because a claim about settlement lives in one place that gets updated rather than being restated in five daily sections that can disagree.

Reading only the newest section assumes later findings supersede earlier ones, and nothing here establishes that: day five contradicted day one about settlement, and which of the two is right is exactly what the file no longer settles. Discarding the earlier sections throws away the accumulated knowledge the file exists to carry across sessions, and it leaves the contradiction standing rather than reconciled.

A larger window raises the ceiling and delays the same problem: a findings file that grows daily eventually fills any window, and reading all of it to answer a narrow question is wasteful at every size.

question:
A coordinator explores a large codebase by dispatching one subagent per question, nine in all, each writing its findings to its own output file. A run is interrupted after four have finished. On restart the coordinator dispatches all nine again. The team adds a manifest and must decide how completion is recorded, because the interruption caught a fifth subagent mid-write: its output file exists and contains about half an analysis, ending in the middle of a sentence.

Which design makes the run correctly resumable?
options: The coordinator writes a manifest entry on dispatch and marks it complete only once the returned output file has been verified
The coordinator treats the existence of a question's output file as its completion signal, and re-dispatches only the questions with no file
Each subagent writes its own manifest entry when it finishes, and the coordinator reads the manifest at startup and re-dispatches the questions with no entry
Each subagent writes its findings to a temporary file and the coordinator reads all temporary files at the end of the run, so a partial file is never mistaken for a complete one
answer: The coordinator writes a manifest entry on dispatch and marks it complete only once the returned output file has been verified
explanation:
This question tests resumability, and the partially-written file is the whole test.

Existence Is Not Completion

A fifth subagent was interrupted mid-write, leaving a file that exists and contains half an analysis ending mid-sentence. Any design that treats file present as work done accepts that truncated output as complete.

The reliable pattern separates the two states: the coordinator writes a manifest entry on dispatch (this question was started) and marks it complete only after verifying the returned output file. Restart then re-dispatches anything dispatched-but-unverified — including the half-written fifth — and skips the four genuinely finished. Completion is recorded by the component that outlives the interruption.

Why the other options are incorrect

File existence as the signal — precisely the failure the stem constructs. The truncated file counts as done and its half-analysis flows into the synthesis.

Subagents write their own manifest entries — the strongest distractor, and it is nearly right: a subagent killed mid-write leaves no entry, so it re-dispatches correctly. But the writer of the completion record is the process that can die between finishing its output and recording it, leaving a finished analysis marked incomplete — and it never verifies the file's integrity.

Temp files read at the end — helps atomicity within a run and provides no resumption at all: after an interruption there is still no record of which questions completed.

Key Takeaway

Record dispatch and verified completion separately, in the coordinator. Treating an output file's existence as a completion signal admits partial writes as finished work.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows

-
Anthropic — Run agents in parallel → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents

-
Anthropic — Work with sessions (Agent SDK) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions
option_feedback: Resumability needs durable state that outlives the process, and the half-written fifth file is the reason the state cannot be inferred from the artifacts. Recording dispatch and completion as two separate events, with completion conditional on a verification of what was written, means an interruption between them is visible as "dispatched, not confirmed" — which is exactly the fifth question's status — so the restart re-dispatches five and skips four, and no partial analysis is read as a finished one.

This is the cheapest ledger and it is the one the stem's fifth file defeats: the file exists, so the question is skipped, and half an analysis ending mid-sentence is folded into the synthesis as though it were complete. Existence is not completion.

Having each subagent record its own completion puts the write on the far side of the failure it is meant to survive — a subagent interrupted before it writes the entry looks identical to one that never started, which is recoverable, but one interrupted between writing its output and writing its entry is re-dispatched and duplicates work. It also gives the coordinator no record of what was dispatched, so an interruption before any subagent returns leaves nothing to resume from.

Deferring the read until the end guarantees that an interruption before the end leaves nine temporary files and no way to tell which are complete — the same partial-file problem, now for the whole run, with the four completed analyses no more usable than before.

question:
An extraction system reports 97% overall accuracy against a labeled validation set. On that basis the team proposes to auto-accept every extraction the model marks as high confidence, which would remove about 80% of the current human review load.

What should the team do before making this change?
options: Re-measure accuracy on a fresh random sample of the same size, confirm the 97% holds, and then automate
Hold back a random 5% sample of all extractions for human review as an ongoing check, and automate the rest
Break the figure down by document type and field, and calibrate field-level confidence against the labeled set
Have the model report one overall confidence score per document, and auto-accept every document above a threshold
answer: Break the figure down by document type and field, and calibrate field-level confidence against the labeled set
explanation:
This question tests what a single aggregate accuracy figure does not license.

97% Overall Says Nothing About the Automated Slice

Two hidden assumptions sit behind the proposal. First, that accuracy is uniform — but a 97% average can hide a document type running at 80%, and averages conceal exactly the pockets that matter. Second, that "high confidence" tracks correctness — which is a property that must be measured, not assumed.

Breaking the figure down by document type and field, and calibrating field-level confidence against the labeled set, tests both assumptions with data the team already has. The result is an evidence-based automation boundary: automate where confidence demonstrably predicts correctness, keep review where it does not.

Why the other options are incorrect

Re-measure on a fresh sample — confirms the aggregate is stable. A stable average is still an average, and it says nothing about the confidence-to-correctness relationship the proposal depends on.

Hold back a random 5% and automate the rest — the closest wrong answer, and ongoing sampling is genuinely good practice. But it ships the automation first and measures afterwards, so a miscalibrated high-confidence band runs at scale while the sample slowly accumulates evidence.

One overall confidence score per document — coarsens the signal in the wrong direction, and still auto-accepts on an uncalibrated number.

Key Takeaway

Break aggregate accuracy down by type and field, and calibrate confidence against labeled data before automating. Averages hide the pockets automation exposes.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Structured outputs → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs

-
Anthropic — Prompting best practices → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

-
Anthropic — Code Review → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review
option_feedback: A second random sample reproduces the same aggregate with the same blind spot. Confirming a figure that averages over every document type says nothing about the segment that would now pass through unreviewed.

Ongoing sampling is right in principle, but a purely random 5% is dominated by the common document types. Rare types — often the ones that extract worst — may go weeks without appearing, so a problem in them is detected late or not at all.

The proposal automates one particular subset — the extractions the model marks high confidence — so the load-bearing questions are how accurate that subset is and what the model's confidence score is actually worth. An aggregate answers neither: a document type that is 5% of volume and extracts at 60% accuracy is invisible behind a 97% headline. Breaking the figure down by document type and field exposes that, and calibrating field-level confidence against the labeled set establishes what the score means before it is allowed to decide which extractions go unseen.

A single document-level score is coarser than what already exists and shares the aggregate's blind spot, since a document can be confidently right about most fields and wrong about the one that matters — and it skips the calibration step that would establish what the number means in the first place.

question:
Two credible sources give different figures for the same industry metric: an industry association reports 18% for calendar 2025, and a market research firm reports 24% for the twelve months to June 2026. The synthesis subagent currently picks one and states it as the finding. The report's format is fixed by its readers: a one-page executive summary that must carry a single headline figure per metric, and a body of unlimited length.

How should the synthesis handle this?
options: Report both figures with their sources and periods in a contested-findings section, and have the summary carry both
Report both figures with their sources and periods in a contested-findings section, and have the summary carry the more recent one, cross-referenced
Have the executive summary carry the midpoint of the two figures with the range noted, and the body carry both figures with their sources and periods
Have the executive summary carry the more recent figure and the body note that other estimates exist, without naming the association's figure, to avoid presenting the reader with a contradiction
answer: Report both figures with their sources and periods in a contested-findings section, and have the summary carry the more recent one, cross-referenced
explanation:
This question tests provenance under a fixed output format — the summary must carry exactly one headline figure per metric.

Both Figures Are Correct

18% for calendar 2025 and 24% for the twelve months to June 2026 are not in conflict; they measure different periods. Recording that in a contested-findings section with sources and periods preserves the full picture in the body, where length is unlimited.

The summary constraint then forces a choice, and the defensible one is the more recent figure, cross-referenced to the body. The reader gets the current number plus a visible pointer to the fuller treatment — the format is honoured without concealing that a second figure exists.

Why the other options are incorrect

Summary carries both — correct on the body and breaks the stated format: readers fixed the summary at a single headline figure per metric. Right instinct, wrong container.

Midpoint with the range noted — 21% is a number no source reports and no methodology supports. Averaging across different measurement periods manufactures a figure rather than selecting one.

Recent figure, body notes estimates exist without naming the other — the subtle one: it satisfies the format and quietly strips provenance. Suppressing the association's figure to avoid an apparent contradiction leaves the reader unable to check the discrepancy — which is exactly what the body section is for.

Key Takeaway

Preserve both figures with sources and periods in the body; let the summary carry the more recent one, cross-referenced. Never average conflicting sources or omit one to look tidy.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Prompting best practices → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

-
Anthropic — Prompt engineering overview → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: This protects the evidence and ignores the format the readers have fixed. Two figures in a slot specified to hold one is either an editorial change nobody agreed to or, in practice, a summary that gets rewritten by someone else downstream — at which point the choice is made silently by a person who has not seen the sources.

Two constraints are live: the summary format admits one figure, and a disagreement between credible sources is itself a finding that has to survive into the report. Both are satisfied by making the choice explicit rather than silent — the summary carries a figure that is attributed and dated, so the reader knows which measurement they are reading, and a cross-reference sends them to the section where both figures sit with their periods. The periods also do much of the work here, since a calendar-2025 measurement and one to June 2026 are not strictly in conflict.

A midpoint of two measurements taken over different periods, by different methodologies, is a number neither source supports and no methodology produced, and putting it in the most-read part of the report gives it the most weight.

Choosing on recency is defensible; concealing what was chosen against is not. A body that mentions unnamed other estimates leaves the reader unable to weigh the disagreement or to find the association's figure, which is the part that makes the annotation useful.

question:
A fintech platform team runs an internal assistant that answers questions about service configuration by calling tools such as get_service_config and list_deployments. To reduce token spend, the developer who built the loop keeps only the latest user message and the model's latest text in the conversation, discarding tool_use and tool_result content between iterations. In a typical session the logs show get_service_config called five or six times with identical arguments, and final answers sometimes state that configuration details are unavailable even though a tool returned them earlier in the same session.

What should the developer change?
options: Set tool_choice to "auto" so the model can decide for itself when it already has the data it needs
Append each tool_use message and its tool_result to the conversation, resending the full history each request
Add a note to each tool result telling the model the data has already been retrieved and should not be requested again
Cache tool results in application code keyed by arguments, and serve repeated calls from the cache instead of re-executing them
answer: Append each tool_use message and its tool_result to the conversation, resending the full history each request
explanation:
This question tests API statelessness, and specifically that the conversation history is the model's memory.

The Model Only Knows What You Send
Every request is independent. The model's entire picture of the session is the messages array it receives — there is no server-side memory carrying earlier turns forward. Deleting the tool_use and tool_result blocks therefore erases the model's evidence that a call was ever made or answered.

That explains both symptoms exactly. The model re-requests get_service_config because, from its point of view, it has never been fetched. And it truthfully reports configuration as unavailable, because data it was never shown is data it does not have.

Appending each assistant tool_use message and its matching tool_result, then resending the full history, restores the record earlier work depends on. Token cost is managed by deliberate summarization or trimming — not by silently deleting the loop's own working memory.

Why the other options are incorrect
tool_choice: "auto" — governs whether the model may, must, or must not call tools on a request. It cannot restore absent history, so the redundant calls continue.

A note in each tool result — the note travels inside a result this loop deletes before the next request, so the model never sees it at the moment it matters.

Cache results in application code — the strongest distractor: it makes re-execution cheap. But the model's view is unchanged, so turns are still spent re-requesting, and the second symptom — answers denying the data exists — persists untouched, because it comes from the missing result, not the repeated call.

Key Takeaway
The API is stateless: send the full alternating history, including tool_use and tool_result blocks. Trim deliberately when cost demands it; never by deleting the record of work already done.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — How tool use works → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Using the Messages API → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/working-with-messages
option_feedback: tool_choice governs whether the model may, must, or must not call tools on a given request. It does not restore missing history: with "auto" the model still cannot see that a previous call already returned the answer, so the redundant requests continue.

The API is stateless: on every request the model knows only what the messages array contains. Discarding the tool_use and tool_result blocks erases the model's evidence that a call was ever made or answered, so from its point of view the configuration has never been fetched — it requests it again, and at answer time it may truthfully report that data it was never shown is unavailable. Reconstructing the full alternating history — assistant tool_use, then a user message carrying the tool_result — is what makes earlier work visible to later turns. Token cost is managed by summarizing or trimming deliberately, not by silently deleting the material the loop depends on.

The note travels inside a tool result that this loop deletes before the next request, so the model never sees the warning at the moment it matters. Even if history were kept, an instruction not to re-request is a workaround for the real defect, which is that the record of prior work is being thrown away.

A cache lowers the cost of re-execution but leaves the model's view unchanged, so turns are still spent re-requesting data and the loop still reaches its iteration limit having done less useful work. It also does nothing for the second symptom: answers that deny having data, which happens because the result is missing from context, not because the tool ran twice.

question:
An engineer at an insurance company is writing her first agentic loop for a claims-document workflow with several tools defined. She sketches four orderings of the core steps.

Which ordering is correct?
options: Send the request → execute the first tool listed in the request's tools array → append its output as plain text → repeat until the model stops responding on its own
Send the request → append a tool_result for any tool the model might need next → check stop_reason afterward and repeat until "tool_use" appears in a response
Send the request → execute all defined tools in advance → send their outputs with the request → read the final text
Send the request → check stop_reason → on "tool_use", execute the tool(s), append the assistant message plus tool_result(s) → send again → end on "end_turn"
answer: Send the request → check stop_reason → on "tool_use", execute the tool(s), append the assistant message plus tool_result(s) → send again → end on "end_turn"
explanation:
This question tests the basic agentic loop lifecycle — the sequence every tool-using agent follows.

The Correct Cycle
Send the request → inspect stop_reason → if it is "tool_use", execute the tool calls the response actually contains, append the assistant message and the matching tool_result blocks → send again → finish when stop_reason is "end_turn".

Two properties make this right. The loop reacts to what the model asked for, rather than acting on its own initiative, and it answers every request before continuing, which is what the protocol requires.

Why the other options are incorrect
Execute the first tool in the tools array — the tools array declares what is available; it is not a work queue. Running a tool the model never requested does work the conversation cannot use and ignores stop_reason entirely.

Append a tool_result for a tool the model might need — inverts the protocol twice over. A tool_result can only answer a tool_use the model has already emitted, and "tool_use" signals continue, not stop.

Execute all tools in advance — replaces the model's judgment with a fixed pre-computation. The entire point of tool use is that the model chooses which calls to make, with which arguments, given the document in front of it.

Key Takeaway
Send → check stop_reason → execute what was requested → append assistant message plus tool results → repeat → end on end_turn. React to the model's requests; never pre-run tools.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — How tool use works → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — How the agent loop works → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: The tools array in the request declares what is available; it is not an instruction to run anything. Executing a tool the model never requested does work the conversation cannot use and ignores the stop_reason signal entirely.
This inverts the protocol twice: a tool_result can only answer a tool_use the model has already emitted, and "tool_use" is the signal to continue working, not the condition for stopping.

Running every tool up front replaces the model's judgment with a fixed pre-computation. The point of tool use is that the model chooses which calls to make, with which arguments, based on the document in front of it.

The loop reacts to what the model asked for: inspect stop_reason first, and only when it is "tool_use" execute the tool calls the response actually contains, append the assistant message and the matching tool_result blocks, and go around again. "end_turn" is the signal that the model has produced its final answer and the loop should stop.

question:
A media conglomerate is building a hub-and-spoke research system: a coordinator plus four specialist subagents covering audience metrics, the advertising market, competitor programming, and broadcast regulation. During design review, the team lists candidate responsibilities and debates where each belongs.

Which TWO responsibilities belong to the coordinator rather than to the specialist subagents? (Select TWO.)
options: Running the detailed keyword searches against the audience-metrics archive
Decomposing the incoming research question into sub-questions matched to each specialist's coverage
Writing the in-depth analysis of regulatory changes from the primary sources
Reconciling the four specialists' findings into one coherent, non-contradictory answer
Deciding which individual documents inside the competitor-programming archive are worth reading
answer: Decomposing the incoming research question into sub-questions matched to each specialist's coverage
Reconciling the four specialists' findings into one coherent, non-contradictory answer
explanation:
This question tests the division of labour in hub-and-spoke architecture.

The Hub Owns Both Ends
The coordinator owns the work that requires seeing the whole problem, which is precisely the two ends of the workflow:

-
Decomposition — splitting the research question into sub-questions shaped to each specialist's coverage. No specialist can do this; none of them can see the full question or the other specialists' scopes.

-
Reconciliation — merging four sets of findings into one coherent, non-contradictory answer. Only the coordinator receives all four outputs, so only it can resolve overlaps and contradictions.

Why the other options are incorrect
Keyword searches against the audience archive — domain execution. It belongs inside the audience-metrics specialist, which holds that archive's context; pulling it into the hub rebuilds the monolithic agent the design exists to avoid.

In-depth regulatory analysis — exactly what the regulation specialist is for. The coordinator consumes its conclusions rather than redoing the reading.

Choosing which documents to read within an archive — a within-domain judgment requiring that archive's local context. It sits with the specialist working the domain.

Key Takeaway
Coordinator: decompose, route, aggregate. Subagents: execute within their domain. Work needing the cross-cutting view belongs at the hub; work needing local context belongs at the spoke.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Run agents in parallel → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents
option_feedback: Executing searches against a specific archive is domain work. It belongs inside the audience-metrics specialist, which holds the context for that archive; pulling it into the hub would recreate the monolithic agent the design is trying to avoid.

In a hub-and-spoke design the hub owns the ends of the workflow: it splits the research question into sub-questions shaped to what each spoke can answer, routes them, and then merges what comes back — resolving overlaps and contradictions into a single answer. Those two jobs require the cross-cutting view that only the coordinator has, since no specialist can see the whole question or the other specialists' outputs.
Deep analysis of regulatory sources is exactly what the regulation specialist exists to do. The coordinator consumes its conclusions; it should not redo the reading.

In a hub-and-spoke design the hub owns the ends of the workflow: it splits the research question into sub-questions shaped to what each spoke can answer, routes them, and then merges what comes back — resolving overlaps and contradictions into a single answer. Those two jobs require the cross-cutting view that only the coordinator has, since no specialist can see the whole question or the other specialists' outputs.
Judging which documents merit attention within one archive requires that archive's local context and is a within-domain decision, so it sits with the specialist working that domain.

question:
A travel-booking company's support system sends every customer inquiry through the same pipeline: a policy subagent, a booking-history subagent, a loyalty-program subagent, and a disruption-status subagent, whose outputs the coordinator then combines. A cost review finds that 68% of inquiries are single-fact questions such as "what time is my airport pickup," the median inquiry costs 4.1 times a single-subagent baseline, and median latency is nine seconds.

What is the best architectural change?
options: Have the coordinator assess each inquiry first and invoke only the subagents whose coverage that inquiry actually needs
Keep the pipeline but move all four subagents to a smaller, cheaper model to cut the per-inquiry cost
Merge the four subagents into one generalist agent that holds all the tools and eliminates coordination overhead
Cache each subagent's output keyed by the inquiry text so repeated questions skip the pipeline
answer: Have the coordinator assess each inquiry first and invoke only the subagents whose coverage that inquiry actually needs
explanation:
This question tests dynamic subagent selection, with cost evidence that names the waste precisely.

Two-Thirds of the Work Is Unnecessary
68% of inquiries are single-fact questions, yet every inquiry pays for four specialist invocations — hence a 4.1× median cost multiplier and nine-second latency. The mismatch is structural: a fixed pipeline cannot distinguish "what time is my airport pickup" from a genuine multi-facet case.

Having the coordinator assess each inquiry first and invoke only the subagents that inquiry needs puts the decision where the information is. Simple questions take one invocation; genuinely complex ones still get the full pipeline. It attacks the multiplier directly without degrading the hard cases.

Why the other options are incorrect
Cheaper model for all four — shrinks the cost of four unnecessary invocations instead of eliminating three of them, and trades quality on the complex inquiries that justify having specialists at all.

Merge into one generalist — swaps a measured cost problem for the problems specialization solved: one context holding every tool and concern, and no ability to isolate or parallelize genuinely multi-part inquiries.

Cache keyed by inquiry text — support answers depend on the specific customer's bookings and entitlements, so two identically-phrased inquiries have different correct answers. The cache either rarely hits or serves one customer's details to another.

Key Takeaway
Let the coordinator assess complexity and invoke only the subagents required. Fixed fan-out prices every request at the cost of the hardest one.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Run agents in parallel → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents
option_feedback: The evidence says the workload is mostly simple: two-thirds of inquiries need one lookup, yet every inquiry pays for four specialist invocations. Dynamic selection puts the decision where the information is — the coordinator reads the inquiry, judges its complexity, and dispatches the one subagent (or the few) it requires, while genuinely multi-facet cases still get the full pipeline. That attacks the 4.1× multiplier directly without degrading the hard cases.

A cheaper model shrinks each of four unnecessary invocations instead of eliminating three of them, so most of the waste survives. It also trades away quality on the complex inquiries, which are the ones that justify specialists in the first place.

Collapsing into one generalist trades a measured cost problem for the problems specialization solved: one context window carrying every tool and every concern, and no ability to isolate or parallelize the genuinely multi-part inquiries.

Support answers depend on the specific customer's bookings, status, and entitlements, so two identically phrased inquiries have different correct answers. A cache keyed by inquiry text would either rarely hit or, worse, serve one customer's details to another.

question:
An energy-markets research system fans a question out to two subagents. For 2025 grid-storage capacity, one returns 41 GWh citing a government statistics office; the other returns 58 GWh citing an industry association. The coordinator must produce a report a client will rely on, and the discrepancy is material to the report's conclusion.

How should the coordinator handle the conflict?
options: Adopt the figure from whichever subagent has the stronger accuracy track record, and drop the other
Report the midpoint of the two figures so neither source is privileged over the other
Report both figures with sources, flag the conflict, and dispatch a targeted follow-up on what each measures
Rerun both subagents from scratch on the same question and adopt whichever figure the second pass reproduces
answer: Report both figures with sources, flag the conflict, and dispatch a targeted follow-up on what each measures
explanation:
This question tests aggregation when two credible sources disagree materially.

A 40% Gap Usually Means Different Definitions
41 GWh from a government statistics office and 58 GWh from an industry association most likely measure different things: grid-scale only versus grid-scale plus behind-the-meter, calendar versus fiscal year, installed versus operational capacity.

The coordinator's job at aggregation is therefore to surface the conflict, preserve both claims with provenance, and spend a targeted follow-up establishing what each source actually measures. That is the only path ending in a figure the client can defend. If the follow-up cannot resolve it, the report still shows both honestly.

Why the other options are incorrect
Better track record wins — a reasonable prior, not a resolution: the historically more accurate source can still be measuring a different quantity than the report needs. Discarding the other figure also hides a disagreement the client would want to know exists.

Report the midpoint — averaging is only meaningful when two estimates target the same quantity with independent noise. Under different definitions, 49.5 GWh corresponds to nothing real and inherits both definitions' flaws.

Rerun both subagents — the same sources produce the same figures at double the cost. Reproducible is not correct; a source's definitional scope does not change on a second read.

question:
A manufacturing company's engineering assistant delegates to four subagents: a CAD-drawing checker, a tolerance analyst, a materials-property lookup, and a compliance-document writer. In about 20% of runs involving tolerance stack-up questions, the coordinator delegates to the materials-property subagent instead of the tolerance analyst. Each subagent's description states its domain accurately, but nothing more.

What is the most effective fix?
options: Rewrite each description to state when to choose it and which requests belong to its neighbors
Add few-shot routing examples to the coordinator's prompt covering each request type it might receive
Rename the subagents so that each name alone identifies the specialty and its limits unambiguously
Delegate every question to all four specialists in parallel and have the coordinator keep the best answer

What the descriptions need is selection guidance: what this specialist handles, example request shapes, and where the boundary with its neighbour lies ("stack-up questions come here even when they mention materials"). Fixing it in the descriptions repairs every consumer of these subagents, because the routing knowledge lives with the thing being selected.

Rename the subagents — the names are already accurate. A name cannot express "stack-up questions go to tolerance even though they mention materials," which is boundary information, not naming.

Broadcast to all four — quadruples cost and latency to paper over a diagnosable selection defect, and converts routing into judging four answers, which is harder.

question:
A retail platform's returns-handling subagent currently has grant_store_credit in its AgentDefinition tools list, with a prompt instruction saying credit may only be granted after a human approves. A security review demonstrates that a crafted customer message can talk the subagent into calling the tool directly. The audit requirement is that this subagent must be unable to grant credit no matter what appears in the conversation.

How should the requirement be met?
options: Strengthen the prompt instruction with explicit warnings against manipulation and repeat it at the end of the prompt
Add few-shot examples to the subagent's prompt showing it refusing credit requests embedded in customer messages
State the restriction in the parent agent's system prompt so it governs everything the subagent does
Remove grant_store_credit from the subagent's tools list and route credit issuance through the escalation path instead
answer: Remove grant_store_credit from the subagent's tools list and route credit issuance through the escalation path instead

Credit then flows through the escalation path, where human approval can actually be enforced.

Prompt-level defences reduce the probability of misuse. Removing the capability reduces it to zero, and zero is what an audit can verify.

Stronger warnings, repeated — lowers the success rate of manipulation and leaves the capability in place, so the guarantee still does not exist. The review has already demonstrated instructions of this kind can be talked around.

Few-shot refusal examples — shape behavior on inputs resembling the examples. Novel injection phrasings sit outside the demonstrated distribution, and the tool remains callable throughout.

Restriction in the parent's system prompt — rests on a false premise: a subagent runs in isolated context and does not inherit the parent's system prompt. Even passed through explicitly, it would be an instruction, not an inability.

Enforce capability limits by omitting the tool from the subagent's tools list. Prompts shape behavior; the tools list defines what is possible.

question:
A hospital network's procurement team runs a two-stage pipeline for vendor-contract research: an analysis subagent reviews the candidate contracts, then a writer subagent produces the recommendation memo. The handoff is the analysis subagent's output — currently a fluent 900-word narrative. In the last five memos, the writer misattributed clauses to the wrong vendor twice, dropped three of eleven caveats, and could not state which contract version a quoted figure came from.

What should change?
options: Have the writer re-read all the original contracts end to end to verify the narrative before drafting each memo
Make the analysis output structured findings — claim, source contract, version, caveats — consumed by the writer
Instruct the analysis subagent to write more carefully and cite the contract inline after every factual sentence
Combine both stages into a single subagent so the analysis never has to be handed off at all
answer: Make the analysis output structured findings — claim, source contract, version, caveats — consumed by the writer
explanation:
This question tests pipeline handoff design, and every listed failure points at the same cause.

Prose Loses Metadata
Misattributed clauses, three of eleven caveats dropped, and an unattributable figure are all metadata losses. Attribution, caveats and version identity all existed during analysis and dissolved when the findings were flattened into a 900-word narrative.

A handoff between pipeline stages is an interface, and it deserves a contract: structured findings — one item per claim, carrying source contract, version and caveats as fields. The writer then cannot misattribute what arrives already attributed, and a dropped caveat becomes a visible gap in a list rather than a silent omission in a paragraph.

Why the other options are incorrect
Writer re-reads the contracts — makes the writer redo the analysis stage, doubling cost and filling its context with raw documents it does not need for drafting. The defective interface also survives for the next consumer.

Inline citations after every sentence — the near-miss: it helps attribution and leaves the output as prose. Caveats live in subordinate clauses a summarizing writer compresses away, and parsing attributions back out of sentences is the lossy step already failing.

Merge both stages — removes the handoff by removing the pipeline's benefits: one context must hold full contracts and drafting, the analysis can no longer be reused, and the isolation that made each stage tractable is gone.

Key Takeaway
Define stage handoffs as structured findings carrying claim plus metadata. Fluent prose is the format in which attribution and caveats quietly disappear.

option_feedback: Re-reading the contracts makes the writer redo the analysis stage's work, doubling cost and filling the writer's context with raw documents it does not need for drafting. It also leaves the defective interface in place — the next pipeline consuming this analysis inherits the same losses.

question:
A utility company's support agent handles account closures. The regulator requires that close_account never executes before the final-bill export has completed for that account — without exception, in every conversation.

Which TWO mechanisms provide a deterministic guarantee of that ordering? (Select TWO.)
options: Application code tracks export completion in conversation state and refuses to execute close_account until the flag is set
A system-prompt rule stating that the export must always be run before closure
A few-shot transcript in the prompt demonstrating the correct order of the two operations
A sentence in the close_account tool description noting that export is a prerequisite
A PreToolUse hook that denies close_account with an explanatory reason whenever the export has not completed
answer: Application code tracks export completion in conversation state and refuses to execute close_account until the flag is set
A PreToolUse hook that denies close_account with an explanatory reason whenever the export has not completed
explanation:
This question tests which controls give deterministic guarantees — the word "without exception" is the whole test.

Only Code Can Promise "Never"

-
State-tracking gate in application code — the application records export completion for the conversation and refuses to execute close_account until the flag is set. Whatever the model emits, the invalid order cannot run.

-
PreToolUse hook that denies with a reason — intercepts the call before execution and denies it deterministically, returning an explanation the model can act on.

Both put the rule in code that executes outside the model's discretion. Either alone bounds the behavior; together they express the same guarantee at two enforcement points.

Why the other options are incorrect
System-prompt rule — raises the probability of correct ordering. Under an unusual conversation the model can still emit the calls in the wrong order, and nothing outside the model stops the execution.

Few-shot transcript — shapes typical behavior toward the demonstrated pattern. An input unlike the examples can produce an undemonstrated order, with no enforcement at execution time.

Note in the tool description — descriptions inform selection; they are read, not enforced. A description stating the prerequisite improves the odds and cannot prevent a call that arrives out of order.

Key Takeaway
Regulatory "never" requirements need code: a state gate or a PreToolUse deny hook. Prompts, examples and descriptions shift probabilities — they do not bound outcomes.

question:
A logistics company uses an agent to prepare releases. Two requirements are on the table. First, changelog entries should follow the team's phrasing style — imperative mood, reference format. Second, in the generated migration sequence, the step that drops the legacy column must never run before the data backfill has completed, because the drop is irreversible in production.

Which control design best matches the two requirements?
options: Enforce both in code: a formatting validator that rejects non-conforming changelog entries, plus a state gate on the drop step
Handle both with guidance: CLAUDE.md conventions for the changelog and a prompt rule stating the backfill must precede the drop
Guidance for the changelog phrasing; a programmatic gate that blocks the drop step until backfill completion is verified
A programmatic validator for the changelog phrasing; a prompt instruction for the migration ordering, which the model handles well
answer: Guidance for the changelog phrasing; a programmatic gate that blocks the drop step until backfill completion is verified
explanation:
This question tests proportionality — matching control strength to the cost and reversibility of failure.

Two Requirements, Two Risk Profiles
A badly-phrased changelog entry is cheap, visible in review, and trivially fixed. Guidance — CLAUDE.md conventions and prompt-level style rules — is the right-sized control.

An out-of-order column drop destroys data irreversibly in production. That needs a control whose failure rate is zero by construction: a coded gate verifying backfill completion before the drop can execute.

Matching the mechanism to the risk is the design decision. Applying the strongest control everywhere is as wrong as applying the weakest.

Why the other options are incorrect
Code for both — gating the drop is right, but a code validator for prose style is disproportionate: imperative mood is not reliably machine-checkable, so it either blocks releases on wording it misjudges or degenerates into a regex that misses the point.

Guidance for both — fine for the changelog, inadequate for the drop. A prompt rule leaves a nonzero probability of the wrong order at the one place where a single failure is unrecoverable.

Validator for style, prompt for ordering — inverts proportionality on both sides at once: deterministic machinery on the reversible requirement, probabilistic instruction on the irreversible one.

Key Takeaway
Size the control to the consequence: guidance for reversible, low-stakes conventions; programmatic gates for irreversible operations.

-

option_feedback: Gating the drop is right, but a code validator for prose style is a disproportionate control: imperative mood is not reliably machine-checkable, so the validator either blocks releases on wording it misjudges or dwindles into a regex that misses the point. The style requirement carries no risk that justifies that maintenance burden.

Guidance is fine for the changelog and inadequate for the drop: a prompt rule leaves a nonzero probability of the wrong order, and this is the one place where a single failure is unrecoverable. The design under-protects exactly where the cost concentrates.

A badly phrased changelog entry is cheap, visible in review, and trivially fixed, so prompt-level and CLAUDE.md guidance is the right-sized control. Matching the mechanism to the risk is the design decision, not applying the strongest control everywhere.

question:
An insurance support platform exposes fifteen tools. Three of them front a legacy policy system that is frozen until a 2027 migration, and they return dates as epoch milliseconds and amounts in cents; the other twelve return ISO dates and decimal amounts. The team added a PostToolUse hook to normalize results into the modern format, but it runs on every tool, and twice its transform has corrupted a modern tool's output by re-dividing an amount by 100.

What should the team do?
options: Scope the hook with a matcher so the normalization runs only on the three legacy tools
Keep the hook global and add detection logic that inspects each result to decide whether it is already normalized
Move normalization into the system prompt so the model converts legacy values when it sees them
Ask the legacy platform's owners to change the three tools to return modern formats at the source
answer: Scope the hook with a matcher so the normalization runs only on the three legacy tools
explanation:
This question tests hook matchers — scoping a transform to the tools it is meant for.

A Known Set Deserves a Matcher
Three legacy tools return epoch milliseconds and cents; twelve modern tools return ISO dates and decimals. Hooks accept matchers precisely so a transform applies where intended and nowhere else.

Scoping the hook to those three tools makes the normalization deterministic where needed and structurally incapable of touching the twelve modern ones. The two corruption incidents — an amount re-divided by 100 — disappear by construction rather than by better guessing.

Why the other options are incorrect
Global hook with detection logic — the closest wrong answer, and the incidents already show why it fails: a modern amount of 100 or a legacy-looking integer is genuinely ambiguous on inspection. When membership in the legacy set is knowable in advance, runtime sniffing is the fragile version of a matcher.

Normalization in the system prompt — moves arithmetic on customer money from deterministic code into probabilistic generation, and spends context on every response for work a hook does silently.

Ask the legacy owners to fix the source — the right long-term fix and explicitly unavailable: the stem says the system is frozen until 2027. The team needs a control that works this quarter.

Key Takeaway
Scope hooks with matchers to the specific tools they should transform. Global hooks plus format detection replace a known configuration fact with a runtime guess.

question:
A fintech company's compliance team requires a complete record — tool name, arguments, and outcome — of every tool invocation made by agent runs that touch release infrastructure, including unattended runs in CI. Today each session ends with the model summarizing its actions per a prompt template; an audit sampled the summaries and found 12% of invocations unrecorded.

Which approach satisfies the requirement?
options: Tighten the end-of-session summary template and instruct the model that the action list must be exhaustive
Increase the model's reasoning budget so it tracks and reports its own actions more reliably
Export and archive full session transcripts nightly for the auditors to consult
Log every call from a PostToolUse hook that writes name, arguments, and result to the audit store
answer: Log every call from a PostToolUse hook that writes name, arguments, and result to the audit store
explanation:
This question tests audit logging, and the 12% figure rules out the self-report family entirely.

Completeness Cannot Rest on Self-Report

A PostToolUse hook fires in code on every tool invocation, attended or headless, and writes exactly what ran, with which arguments, and what came back — at the moment it happened. Transcripts do record calls, but as session archives to be mined later: the nightly cadence leaves a window in which a session's record does not yet exist in the audit store, ephemeral CI runners can discard transcripts before export, and the per-call record must still be assembled from conversation files.

Log tool calls from a PostToolUse hook when completeness is required. Self-report and after-the-fact transcript mining both leave gaps an auditor will find.

question:
An edtech company wants an agent to raise test coverage on a 3,100-file monolith currently at 9%, within a fixed two-week agent budget. One proposal is a fixed plan: enumerate every file alphabetically and generate tests for each in order until the budget runs out.

What is the strongest counter-proposal?
options: Keep the fixed plan but start from the largest files, since more code means more untested behavior to catch
Target only files with zero coverage first, and return to the partially covered ones if budget remains
Map the codebase for risk and usage first, target the highest-impact areas, reassessing after each batch
Let each developer request tests file-by-file so the budget follows the team's immediate needs
answer: Map the codebase for risk and usage first, target the highest-impact areas, reassessing after each batch
explanation:
This question tests adaptive versus fixed decomposition on an open-ended objective.

Open-Ended Goal, Uneven Codebase, Fixed Budget
"Raise coverage meaningfully within two weeks" over 3,100 files at 9% coverage is exactly where an adaptive plan beats a predetermined sequence. Spending a small slice of budget mapping risk and usage — which modules carry traffic, change often, or guard critical paths — lets the agent put tests where failures would actually hurt. Reassessing after each batch lets it abandon low-yield areas and follow what it learns.

An alphabetical march spends identical effort on aaa_legacy.py and the payment path.

Why the other options are incorrect
Largest files first — file size is a weak proxy for risk (large files are often stable generated code), and the deeper defect remains: the order is fixed before the agent has learned anything.

Zero-coverage files first — optimizes the metric rather than the goal. A trivial zero-coverage utility gains little, while a partially-covered payment module with untested branches may be the riskiest thing in the codebase.

Developer requests file-by-file — reflects this week's local concerns rather than systemic risk, and dissipates the budget into scattered one-file tasks with no compounding map.

Key Takeaway
For open-ended goals under a budget, map first, target by impact, and reassess after each batch. Fixed enumeration orders spend effort where it happens to fall.

question:
A publishing group is reviewing four internal workloads to decide which one to implement as a fixed prompt chain — a predetermined sequence of steps executed identically on every input.

Which workload fits?
options: Incident investigation for the content platform, where the diagnostic path depends on what each probe reveals and where the evidence points

answer: The nightly press-release pipeline: every document gets fact extraction, style rewrite, then summary and metadata
explanation:
This question tests which workloads suit a fixed prompt chain — and it is a pick-the-workload reversal, so read all four shapes.

Fixed Steps, Fixed Order, Every Input
The nightly press-release pipeline applies the same three transformations — fact extraction, style rewrite, summary and metadata — uniformly, to every document, every night. That is precisely a prompt chain's shape, and its rigidity becomes a virtue: each stage can be evaluated and improved in isolation, costs are predictable, and no orchestration intelligence is spent deciding what to do next, because there is never a decision.

Why the other options are incorrect
Incident investigation — inherently branching: each probe's result determines the next. Frozen into a fixed sequence it either runs irrelevant steps every time or omits the step a specific incident needed.

Reader-support triage — interactive and data-dependent; the customer's answer changes the path. A fixed chain cannot represent "what happens next depends on what just happened."

Competitive research — the canonical adaptive workload. The set of questions is discovered during the work, so any sequence fixed in advance encodes yesterday's understanding.

Key Takeaway
Use prompt chains where the steps and their order are known in advance and identical for every input. Anything whose next step depends on the last result needs dynamic decomposition.

question:
A manufacturing-software team spent 90 minutes in a Claude Code session analyzing module boundaries in their ERP customization layer. They now want to evaluate two competing refactor strategies — strangler-fig and in-place modularization — each starting from that same analyzed baseline, and compare the resulting diffs before committing to either.

How should they proceed?
options: Continue in the same session: apply the first strategy, revert the changes, then apply the second and compare from memory
Start two fresh sessions and re-explain the module analysis to each before trying one strategy in each
Open two terminals and resume the same session in both, running one strategy in each terminal
Fork the session twice and run one strategy per fork, leaving the original session intact as the decision point
answer: Fork the session twice and run one strategy per fork, leaving the original session intact as the decision point
explanation:
This question tests session forking: one expensive baseline, two divergent continuations.

Forks Inherit the Baseline and Stay Isolated
Forking creates independent branches that each inherit the full 90 minutes of analysis at the moment of the fork. Each refactor strategy then unfolds in isolation — neither sees the other's reasoning or edits, which is what makes the comparison fair — and the original session survives untouched as the place to weigh the two diffs and decide.

This is the situation forking exists for: one costly shared baseline, multiple continuations that must not contaminate each other.

Why the other options are incorrect
Sequential in one session with a revert — the second strategy is generated with the first attempt's reasoning and diffs in context, and reverting files does not remove that influence. The comparison also depends on recalling the first diff rather than holding both.

Two fresh sessions, re-explain the analysis — pays the analysis cost twice, and re-explaining is not re-analyzing: each session's reconstructed understanding differs from the original and from the other, so the strategies no longer share a baseline.

Resume the same session in two terminals — resuming continues one session; it does not branch. Two terminals interleave into a single shared history, the opposite of an independent comparison.

Key Takeaway
Fork when several lines of work must start from the same expensive context and stay independent. Resume continues one line; forking creates branches.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Manage sessions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions

-
Anthropic — Work with sessions (Agent SDK) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions

-
Anthropic — Checkpointing → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing
option_feedback: Sequential attempts in one session contaminate the comparison: the second strategy is generated with the first attempt's reasoning, diffs, and conclusions in context, and a revert restores the files without removing that influence. The comparison also depends on recalling the first diff rather than holding both.

Fresh sessions pay the analysis cost again — and re-explaining is not re-analyzing; each session's reconstructed understanding will differ from the original and from each other, so the two strategies no longer start from the same baseline.

Resuming continues the one session; it does not create branches. Two terminals continuing the same conversation interleave into a single shared history rather than two isolated lines of work, which is the opposite of an independent comparison.

Forking creates independent branches of the session that each inherit the full 90 minutes of analysis at the moment of the fork. Each strategy then unfolds in isolation — neither sees the other's reasoning or edits — which is what makes the comparison fair, and the original session survives untouched as the place to weigh the two diffs and decide. This is the situation session forking exists for: one expensive shared baseline, multiple divergent continuations.

question:
Yesterday a logistics developer ran a named Claude Code session, "depot-routing-audit," that mapped how the routing service works. Several unrelated sessions have run in the same directory since. Today she wants to continue that investigation with its full context.

What should she run?
options: claude --resume depot-routing-audit
claude --continue in the project directory
A new claude session, which will load the previous conversation from CLAUDE.md automatically
A new claude session, asking Claude to recall yesterday's investigation

New session, ask Claude to recall — a fresh session has no memory of prior conversations. At best it reconstructs from files it can read now, which is not the session's accumulated context.

Name sessions you intend to return to, and resume them by name. --continue is positional (most recent in the directory) and unreliable once other work intervenes.

question:
A broadcaster's internal assistant has a search_assets tool. When it was built, the tool indexed only active-campaign assets, and its description reads "searches assets for active campaigns." Last quarter the backend was extended to cover archived campaigns as well, but nobody touched the description. Now, when users ask about archived material, the agent either replies that archived assets are not searchable or falls back to listing raw storage directories.

What is the right fix?
options: Add a line to the assistant's system prompt stating that archived assets are searchable through the existing tool
Register a second tool, search_archive, that points at the same backend and mentions archives in its name
Update the tool description to state its actual current coverage — active and archived campaigns — and when to use it
Tell users to include the word "archive" in their queries so the agent tries the tool anyway
answer: Update the tool description to state its actual current coverage — active and archived campaigns — and when to use it
explanation:
This question tests tool descriptions as maintained documentation.

The Model Is Obeying Incorrect Documentation
Descriptions are the tool's contract, and this one asserts a restriction — "active campaigns" — that stopped being true a quarter ago. The observed behaviour is the model correctly refusing to use a tool its documentation says cannot help, then hand-rolling a workaround.

Updating the description to state actual current coverage — active and archived campaigns, plus when to use it — fixes every agent and every session that mounts this tool, and treats descriptions as what they are: load-bearing documentation that must be maintained when the tool changes.

Why the other options are incorrect
System-prompt correction — patches one agent while the contract stays wrong for every other consumer, and forces the model to reconcile two contradictory statements about the same tool.

Register a second search_archive tool — creates a permanent selection ambiguity between two tools whose coverage overlaps entirely, to avoid a one-line documentation fix. Tool sets should shrink toward clarity.

Tell users to say "archive" — pushes the fix onto user phrasing, leaves the false description in place, and fails the moment someone asks naturally. The model trusts the description over a keyword.

Key Takeaway
Update tool descriptions when tool behavior changes. A stale description is not merely unhelpful — the model follows it, and works around capabilities it says are absent.

-

A duplicate tool over the same backend creates a permanent selection ambiguity — two tools whose coverage overlaps entirely — to avoid a one-line documentation fix. Tool sets should shrink toward clarity, not grow toward workarounds.

The model decides whether a tool applies by reading its description, so the description functions as the tool's contract — and this one now asserts a restriction that stopped being true a quarter ago. The observed behavior is the model correctly obeying incorrect documentation. Updating the description to match real behavior fixes every agent and every session that mounts this tool, and it treats descriptions as what they are: load-bearing documentation that must be maintained when the tool changes.

question:
A bank's support agent has two account tools: transaction_history, described as "returns posted transactions for an account and date range," and pending_authorizations, described as "returns card authorization holds that have not yet posted." Each description is accurate on its own. Yet for questions like "why is there a hold on my card," the agent calls transaction_history about 30% of the time, finds nothing, and tells the customer no such charge exists.

What is the most effective change?
options: Merge the two account tools into one transactions tool exposing an include_pending parameter for holds
Add boundary guidance to both descriptions, each naming the questions that belong to the other tool
Add few-shot examples of hold-related questions and correct tool choices to each agent prompt that uses these tools
Route requests containing words like "hold" or "pending" to pending_authorizations in application code before the model chooses
answer: Add boundary guidance to both descriptions, each naming the questions that belong to the other tool
explanation:
This question tests the seam between two individually-accurate descriptions.

Each Description Is Right and the Pair Is Ambiguous
A customer's "hold" question plausibly matches "transactions," and nothing tells the model where one tool's territory ends and the other's begins. That gap is what produces a 30% misroute and a customer told no such charge exists.

Descriptions carry selection knowledge, so the boundary belongs in them — each naming the adjacent case and pointing to its neighbour ("holds appear only in pending_authorizations"). That resolves the ambiguity at the point of selection, for every consumer, without changing any interface or code.

Why the other options are incorrect
Merge into one tool with include_pending — workable but heavyweight: it changes an interface every consumer depends on, and converts a visible selection decision into an easily-forgotten parameter. An agent that omits the flag reproduces today's failure with less visibility.

Few-shot examples in each agent prompt — duplicates routing knowledge into every agent that mounts the tools, to be maintained in each place. The descriptions are the shared authoritative location.

Keyword routing in code — strips the decision from the model while covering only anticipated phrasings. "Why was I charged twice for one purchase" contains no trigger word and may well be a holds question.

Key Takeaway
When two tools are individually clear but collectively ambiguous, add cross-boundary guidance to both descriptions. Fix the seam before redesigning the interface.
