-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference
option_feedback: A merge can work, but it is the heavyweight option: it changes an interface every consumer depends on, and it converts a visible selection decision into an easily forgotten parameter — an agent that omits include_pending reproduces today's failure with less visibility. A documentation seam does not by itself justify a redesign.

The failure sits in the seam between two individually accurate descriptions: a customer's "hold" question plausibly matches "transactions," and nothing tells the model where one tool's territory ends and the other's begins. Descriptions carry selection knowledge, so the boundary belongs in them — each tool naming the adjacent case and pointing to its neighbor. That resolves the ambiguity at the point of selection for every consumer, without changing any interface or code.

Prompt examples duplicate the routing knowledge into every agent that mounts the tools and must be maintained in each place separately. The descriptions are the shared, authoritative location the selector already reads.

Keyword routing in code strips the decision from the model while covering only the phrasings someone anticipated — "why was I charged twice for one purchase" contains no trigger word but may be a holds question. It adds a brittle layer to compensate for documentation that could simply say the boundary.

question:
A travel platform's cancellation policy allows refunds only within 24 hours of booking. When the support agent calls process_cancellation_refund outside that window, the tool returns {"error": "REFUSED"}. Conversation logs show the agent retrying the identical call three times, then telling the customer it is "experiencing technical difficulties."

What change to the tool's response would fix this behavior?
options: Return a structured business-rule result — refusal reason, retryable: false, and a customer-facing explanation
Add a system-prompt rule: after two consecutive tool errors, apologize and escalate the conversation to a human
Raise a protocol-level error instead of returning a result, so the agent stops calling the tool
Check the 24-hour window in application code before the model is allowed to call the tool at all
answer: Return a structured business-rule result — refusal reason, retryable: false, and a customer-facing explanation
explanation:
This question tests business-rule refusals — a successful evaluation that happens to say no.

The Agent Behaved Reasonably on Bad Information
{"error": "REFUSED"} is indistinguishable from a transient fault, and retrying transient faults is correct behaviour. Three retries and a "technical difficulties" apology is the predictable result of an opaque error.

The tool knows exactly why it refused — policy, not malfunction — and should say so in a form the agent can act on: a structured business-rule result carrying the refusal reason, retryable: false, and a customer-facing explanation with alternatives. The same agent then explains the 24-hour policy and offers what is available, instead of apologizing for a system that worked perfectly.

Why the other options are incorrect
Two-errors-then-escalate rule — caps the damage while treating every error class identically: genuine transient faults get abandoned after two tries, and policy refusals still end in escalation rather than the explanation the agent could have given.

Raise a protocol-level error — protocol errors signal that the call's mechanics failed. A policy refusal is a correct, successful evaluation; misclassifying it as malfunction denies the model the information it needs.

Pre-validate the window in code — duplicates the business rule into a second location that must stay in sync, and when code silently blocks the call, the agent never learns the reason it needs in order to explain the policy.

Key Takeaway
Return business-rule refusals as structured results with a reason, a retryability flag, and customer-safe wording. Opaque errors turn policy decisions into retry loops.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: The agent behaved reasonably given what it was told: an opaque "REFUSED" is indistinguishable from a transient fault, and retrying transient faults is right. The tool knows exactly why it refused — policy, not malfunction — and the fix is to say so in a form the agent can act on: this is a business-rule refusal, retrying cannot change it, and here is what the customer can be told and offered instead. With that response, the same agent explains the policy and presents alternatives instead of apologizing for a system that worked perfectly.

A generic two-errors-then-escalate rule caps the damage but treats every error class identically — genuine transient faults get abandoned after two tries, and policy refusals still read as "errors" that end in escalation rather than the explanation the agent already could have given.

Protocol-level errors signal that something malfunctioned in the mechanics of the call. A policy refusal is a correct, successful evaluation of a request; misclassifying it as malfunction denies the model the information it needs to respond, which is precisely today's defect.

Pre-validation duplicates the business rule in a second codebase location that must now be kept in sync with the tool, and when the code silently blocks the call, the agent never learns the refusal reason it needs in order to explain the policy to the customer.

question:
An insurance research subagent queries regulatory filings through a search_filings MCP tool. The tool sets isError: true on its result whenever a query matches zero filings. A reviewed transcript shows the subagent rephrasing one query four times, consuming about 30% of its context on the retries, and finally reporting that "the filings database appears to be unavailable."

What should the tool author change?
options: Keep the error flag but put the text "no results found" in the error content so the agent can understand
Add a rule to the subagent's prompt telling it to stop searching and report after two errored queries
Return the error flag only after a third consecutive zero-match query from the same agent
Return zero matches as a successful result with an empty list and a message like "0 filings matched"
answer: Return zero matches as a successful result with an empty list and a message like "0 filings matched"
explanation:
This question tests the boundary of the error channel: an empty result is a successful answer.

Zero Matches Is Information, Not Failure
A well-formed query that matches nothing has succeeded — it has established that nothing matches, which the agent should reason about, perhaps by broadening once deliberately or by reporting an absence finding.

Flagging it with isError teaches the agent the operation failed, and the transcript shows the consequences: four rephrasings, 30% of context burned on retries, and a false conclusion that the filings database was down. Returning zero matches as a successful result with an empty list and an explicit "0 filings matched" message puts the outcome on the right channel with a payload that says exactly what happened.

Why the other options are incorrect
"No results found" inside the error — the text improves; the signal still says failure, and error-channel semantics drive retry behavior. An agent reading that inside an error plausibly concludes the search malfunctioned before completing.

Stop after two errored queries — caps the waste without correcting the misinformation. The agent still ends believing searches failed rather than knowing they succeeded and found nothing, so its final report still misstates reality.

Flag only after a third consecutive zero-match — makes a result's meaning depend on how many times it has been asked. The same query, corpus and outcome would signal success or failure depending on history, which is harder to reason about than either consistent choice.

Key Takeaway
Reserve the error channel for operations that actually failed. Valid empty results belong on the success path with an explicit empty payload.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: The text improves, but the signal still says failure, and error-channel semantics are what drive retry behavior. An agent reading "no results found" inside an error plausibly concludes the search malfunctioned before completing — the ambiguity that caused four rephrases survives.

A stop-after-two rule caps the waste without fixing the misinformation: the agent still ends believing searches failed rather than knowing they succeeded and found nothing, so its final report still misstates reality.

Making the flag depend on how many times the agent has asked turns the result's meaning into a moving target — the same query, same corpus, same outcome now signals success or failure depending on history. That is strictly harder to reason about than either consistent choice.

An empty result set is a true, successful answer to a well-formed query — it says "nothing matches," which is information the agent should reason about, perhaps by broadening once deliberately or by reporting an absence finding. Flagging it as an error teaches the agent the operation failed, and the transcript shows the consequences: retry churn and a false conclusion that the backend was down. The error channel should be reserved for operations that actually failed; "zero matches" belongs on the success path with a payload that says so plainly.

question:
A retailer's internal operations assistant is wired to three MCP servers: inventory (9 tools), HR (7 tools), and facilities (6 tools) — 22 tools in every request. In this deployment the assistant answers only inventory questions. Measurement over two weeks shows a 14% tool-misselection rate, including HR lookups called on stock queries, plus the fixed prompt overhead of 22 tool definitions.

What should the team do?
options: Move the assistant to a larger model that can handle the bigger tool set more reliably
Mount only the inventory server, exposing just the tools this role requires
Add a system-prompt instruction restricting the assistant to using inventory tools only
Prefix every tool name by domain — inv_, hr_, fac_ — so the model can tell the domains apart
answer: Mount only the inventory server, exposing just the tools this role requires
explanation:
This question tests tool-set scoping per deployment, with measured evidence of the cost.

Sixteen Tools That Can Never Be Right
Every tool in a request is a candidate the model must weigh. This deployment answers only inventory questions, yet 22 definitions arrive on every request — so 13 of them are permanent selection noise and permanent prompt overhead, and the 14% misselection rate (HR lookups on stock queries) is the predictable result.

The deployment's job defines its tool needs, and configuration should match: mount only the inventory server. Selection accuracy improves because the wrong choices no longer exist, and the context those definitions occupied comes back on every request.

Why the other options are incorrect
A larger model — spends capability to overcome self-inflicted noise, at a higher price per request, for a problem the configuration created.

System-prompt restriction — the instruction competes with 13 live tool definitions that remain in context as selectable candidates. Prompts reduce their pull rather than eliminating it, and the token overhead is untouched. Structural problems get structural fixes.

Domain name prefixes — sharpens discrimination at the margin, but 22 definitions still occupy context and 13 remain selectable for a role that will never legitimately use them. It polishes the noise instead of removing it.

Key Takeaway
Scope each deployment's mounted servers to the role it actually performs. Unmountable-but-unused tools cost context on every request and remain selectable forever.

-

-

question:
A logistics company extracts structured data from shipping manifests. The request defines submit_manifest plus two diagnostic tools kept from development. The pipeline's contract is strict: every document must be returned through a submit_manifest call — never prose, never a diagnostic call.

Which tool_choice setting enforces this?
options: tool_choice {"type": "auto"} sent with every extraction request
tool_choice {"type": "any"} sent with every extraction request
tool_choice {"type": "tool", "name": "submit_manifest"} on each request
tool_choice {"type": "none"} sent with every extraction request
answer: tool_choice {"type": "tool", "name": "submit_manifest"} on each request
explanation:
This question tests the four tool_choice settings against a strict pipeline contract.

Name the Tool to Guarantee It
The contract is precise: every document must come back through a submit_manifest call — never prose, never a diagnostic call. {"type": "tool", "name": "submit_manifest"} forces the model to respond by calling that specific tool, which is exactly the guarantee required, regardless of what else is defined in the request.

Why the other options are incorrect
"auto" — leaves the decision to the model. It may answer in prose or select a diagnostic tool, so the guarantee does not exist.

"any" — the near-miss: it forces some tool call but not which one. With three tools defined, a diagnostic call satisfies it and breaks the contract.

"none" — forbids tool calls entirely, guaranteeing the opposite of the requirement.

Key Takeaway
"auto" = model decides; "any" = some tool, model picks; "tool" + name = that specific tool; "none" = no tools. When the pipeline requires one named tool, name it.

question:
A manufacturing-firm developer built a prototype MCP server that parses her own bench-test logs. She maintains checkouts of six plant repositories and wants the server available in all of them. It must not affect teammates, and nothing about it may be committed to any repo.

At which scope should she register it?
options: Project scope, adding it to each of the six repositories' .mcp.json files
Local scope in the repository she uses most, repeating the registration later in the others if needed
Reference it from her user-level CLAUDE.md so every session knows to load it
User scope, so the server follows her account across all her projects, outside every repo
answer: User scope, so the server follows her account across all her projects, outside every repo
explanation:
This question tests MCP scope selection against three explicit constraints.

Personal, Cross-Project, Uncommitted
The requirements are: available in all six checkouts, no effect on teammates, nothing committed. User scope satisfies all three by definition — the server is registered in her own user configuration, so it follows her account into every project she opens, lives entirely outside the repositories, and is invisible to everyone else. Personal tooling that spans projects is exactly what user scope exists for.

Why the other options are incorrect
Project scope in each repo — project scope works by committing .mcp.json so the whole team shares the server, which violates both remaining constraints: files land in the repos, and teammates get prompted to approve her personal prototype.

Local scope in one repository — private, but private to one project. She would repeat the registration six times and maintain six copies of the same config. It satisfies the constraints while ignoring the requirement that made this a question.

Reference it from user-level CLAUDE.md — CLAUDE.md carries instructions and context; it does not register MCP servers. A note there tells Claude a server exists without making one available.

Key Takeaway
User scope for personal tooling across all your projects; project scope for team-shared servers; local scope for one project, privately. Match the scope to who needs it and where.

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp

-
Anthropic — Connect to MCP servers → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart

-
Anthropic — Claude Code settings → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings
option_feedback: Project scope works by committing .mcp.json so the whole team shares the server — the opposite of both constraints: it lands in the repos and reaches teammates, who would each be prompted to approve her personal prototype.

Local scope is private, but it is private to one project — she would repeat the registration in each of the six checkouts and maintain six copies of the config. It satisfies the constraints while ignoring the requirement that made this a question.

question:
A fintech team of eight developers wants Claude Code to query each developer's own local sandbox database — a Postgres instance on each machine's localhost, seeded with that developer's test data. They are deciding how to deploy the MCP server that will expose it.

Which deployment fits?
options: One remote HTTP server, centrally hosted, that all eight developers connect to over the network
A local stdio server launched on each developer's machine, its launch command shared via project config
A central remote server, with each developer tunneling their local database to it over the network
No server — export each developer's schema and sample rows into CLAUDE.md so Claude can reason about the data

Sharing the launch command through the committed project configuration gives all eight identical setup while each instance connects to its own data.

Transport should follow the resource: local resources get local servers, shared services get remote ones.

Use local stdio servers for machine-local resources and remote servers for shared services. Share the launch command through project config so setup is uniform while data stays per-developer.

question:
An insurance company asks Claude Code how claim-intake deduplication works in their codebase. The session transcript shows the agent issuing Read on all 60 files of the intake service up front, exhausting most of the context window before analysis begins, and producing a shallow answer that misses the actual dedupe module.

What retrieval approach should the agent have used?
options: Grep for dedupe identifiers to find entry points, then Read only the files in that call chain
Read the files in six batches of ten, compacting the session between batches to keep context available
Run the session on a model with a larger context window so all 60 files fit comfortably
Read only the directory structure and file names, inferring the dedupe design from the naming conventions
answer: Grep for dedupe identifiers to find entry points, then Read only the files in that call chain
explanation:
This question tests incremental exploration versus bulk reading.

Search to Locate, Read to Understand
The question names a specific behavior — claim-intake deduplication — and specific behavior is searchable. Grep for dedupe identifiers surfaces where they appear, which files define versus call them, and therefore which handful of the 60 files actually matter. Read then follows the call chain outward only as far as the question requires.

The context window holds evidence instead of bulk, leaving room for the analysis itself — which is precisely what the failed attempt ran out of.

Why the other options are incorrect
Batch reads with compaction — still reads all 60 files and pays for them, then repeatedly summarizes detail away mid-investigation. The compacted representation of batch one is what the agent reasons from when the dedupe module turns up in batch five. Reading less beats summarizing more.

Larger context window — makes the wasteful strategy affordable without making it good: cost rises, the relevant-to-irrelevant ratio worsens, and it fails again on the next larger codebase.

Infer from names and structure — names are hypotheses, not evidence. A dedupe module called normalize.py defeats inference from labels, and the answer would be a guess dressed as analysis.

Key Takeaway
Grep entry points, then Read the call chain, expanding on evidence. Bulk-reading a service exhausts context before analysis begins.

question:
In one Claude Code session on a media company's CMS, the agent must do two things: create a brand-new scaffold file for a rendering component that does not exist yet, and change a single import line in a 2,400-line legacy module.

Which tool usage is right?
options: Edit for both — it is the file-modification tool, and creating a file is a modification of the project
Write for both — regenerate the legacy module with the corrected import line and emit the new scaffold
Write for the new scaffold; Edit for the import line, with enough surrounding context in old_str to match uniquely
Write for the new scaffold; a Bash sed one-liner for the import line, avoiding tool overhead on a trivial change
answer: Write for the new scaffold; Edit for the import line, with enough surrounding context in old_str to match uniquely
explanation:
This question tests Write versus Edit — two tasks with opposite shapes in one session.

Different Guarantees for Different Jobs
A file that does not exist has no prior content to match, so Write — which creates a file from full content — is the only fit for the scaffold.

A one-line change in 2,400 lines is the opposite: nearly everything must survive untouched. Edit guarantees that by replacing an exact matched string and failing loudly on absence or ambiguity, and including neighbouring lines in old_str is how the match is made unique.

Why the other options are incorrect
Edit for both — Edit operates on existing content by matching a string within it. With no file and nothing to match, there is nothing for it to operate on.

Write for both — regenerating 2,400 lines to change one converts a surgical edit into a full rewrite, where every untouched line becomes something the model must reproduce perfectly. Drift or truncation anywhere becomes possible from a one-line task.

sed for the import line — substitutes wherever the pattern happens to match, without Edit's uniqueness check or failure on ambiguity, and lands outside the session's normal edit-and-review flow. Trading match verification for negligible overhead on a legacy file is a poor bargain.

Key Takeaway
Write creates; Edit modifies with a uniqueness guarantee. Choose the tool for the guarantee the task needs, not for convenience.

question:
A retailer's monorepo holds eight packages, and each package's CLAUDE.md contains a pasted copy of the team's testing standards. The copies have drifted: three now name a different test runner than the others, and a recent standards change was applied to only five of the eight.

How should the standards be managed?
options: Keep the standards only in the root CLAUDE.md and delete the eight package files
Maintain one shared standards file and have each package's CLAUDE.md @import it
Symlink a single CLAUDE.md into all eight packages so the content cannot drift
Replace the pasted sections with a link to the standards page on the team wiki
answer: Maintain one shared standards file and have each package's CLAUDE.md @import it
explanation:
This question tests deduplicating shared standards across a monorepo.

One Source, Eight References
Eight pasted copies have drifted — three name a different test runner, and a recent change landed in five of eight. That is the classic cost of duplication, and the memory system has the mechanism for it: an @import pulls a shared file into a CLAUDE.md whenever that file is loaded.

The standards then live in exactly one file, every package references it, an update lands everywhere at once — and each package's CLAUDE.md remains its own file, free to carry that package's specific guidance alongside the import.

Why the other options are incorrect
Root only, delete the eight — fixes drift and deletes the vehicle for package-specific context. Packages have their own conventions, and the hierarchy exists so shared and local guidance can coexist.

Symlink one file into all eight — forces all packages to share one identical file, so no package can add local guidance without it appearing in all the others. It solves drift by abolishing local content.

Link to the team wiki — a pointer to content that never enters the session. CLAUDE.md text is loaded; Claude does not follow external links at load time, so the standards effectively vanish.

Key Takeaway
Use @import to share one standards file across many CLAUDE.md files. Copies drift; symlinks eliminate local content; external links never load.

What should the team do?
options: Duplicate the three critical rules at both the top and the bottom of the file so they cannot be missed
Reformat the whole file with ALL-CAPS emphasis and IMPORTANT markers on the rules
Split it into two 300-line files that both load at session start
Cut the file down to short, specific, verifiable rules and move the essays into docs Claude can read on demand

explanation:
This question tests why adherence falls as a memory file grows.

Three actionable rules buried in 600 lines of architecture essay compete with everything around them, and instructions that cannot be checked at a glance get missed. Trimming to short, specific, verifiable rules — each concrete enough that a violation is objectively identifiable — concentrates the file on what must shape every response, while the background moves to ordinary docs Claude reads on demand.

Duplicate the rules top and bottom — grows the file it needs to shrink and misdiagnoses placement as the problem. A rule stated twice in 620 lines competes with the same essays.

ALL-CAPS and IMPORTANT markers — emphasis inflation has a short half-life: when many things shout, nothing stands out, and the instruction-to-essay ratio is unchanged.

Split into two 300-line files loaded together — reproduces the identical 600 lines in context, same tokens, same dilution, with a file boundary in the middle. Loading is the cost, and the split does not reduce it.

Key Takeaway
Keep CLAUDE.md short, specific and verifiable; move essays to docs read on demand. Adherence tracks signal density, not emphasis or placement.

What is the right restructuring?
options: Add paths globs to the four type-specific rule files, leaving the two universal files unconditional

explanation:

Rules files support paths globs, and that field is the gate: a rule with paths loads only when files matching its globs are in play; a rule without paths loads unconditionally.

Split into smaller files — changes granularity, not gating. Without paths, every fragment still loads unconditionally, so the same total content arrives in more pieces.

Move to a subdirectory — directory placement carries no loading semantics. Rules are discovered recursively; nothing about the folder expresses "only for Terraform work."

Convert to skills — skills load their bodies when invoked. Standing constraints like "how SQL must be written here" need to be present whenever such files are edited, not when the model decides to invoke something.

option_feedback: Rules files support paths frontmatter with glob patterns, and that is the loading gate: a rule with paths loads only when files matching its globs are in play, while a rule without paths loads unconditionally. The four type-specific files get globs — SQL rules load for migrations, Terraform rules for .tf work — and sessions stop paying for standards that cannot apply to the files being touched. The two universal files correctly keep loading everywhere, which is what no frontmatter means.

Splitting changes the granularity, not the gating: without paths frontmatter every fragment still loads unconditionally in every session, so the same total content arrives in more pieces. The cost is what loads, and nothing about file size makes loading conditional.

question:
An edtech repo has two rules files. api.md, with paths ["src/api/**"], requires all handlers to return the {data, error} envelope. experimental.md, with paths ["src/api/v2/**"], says v2 handlers return bare payloads with no envelope. When the agent edits src/api/v2/sessions.ts, its output alternates between the two styles across sessions. One developer insists the fix is unnecessary because "the more specific glob wins."

What is actually true, and what is the fix?
options: Rules load in filename order and later files override earlier ones, so rename experimental.md to sort last
Both rules load when both match, with no precedence; the fix is rewriting them so they stop conflicting over v2
The developer is right: the narrower glob takes precedence automatically, so the alternating output must have another cause
Moving the v2 rule into src/api/v2/CLAUDE.md will make it override the broader rule for files in that directory
answer: Both rules load when both match, with no precedence; the fix is rewriting them so they stop conflicting over v2
explanation:
This question tests a specific misconception: that narrower globs win.

Match Semantics, Not Precedence Semantics
Path-scoped rules load when their globs match — all of them. A file under src/api/v2/ matches both patterns, so the model receives two contradictory instructions with equal standing. Alternating output across sessions is exactly what unresolved contradiction looks like.

The documentation is explicit that contradictory instructions may be resolved arbitrarily, and recommends reviewing rule files periodically to remove conflicts. So the fix is to make the rule set consistent — carve v2 out of the envelope rule's scope, or state the exception inside it — because no machinery will arbitrate what the rules themselves can simply stop disputing.

Why the other options are incorrect
Filename order overrides — load order is not authority. There is no last-writer-wins among rules; both instructions still sit in context together, so a rename reshuffles the contradiction rather than resolving it.

The narrower glob wins — the misconception the question targets, imported from CSS-style specificity. A narrower glob narrows when the rule loads; it grants no priority over other rules loaded at the same time.

Subdirectory CLAUDE.md overrides — a subdirectory memory file adds context when work happens there; it does not suppress or outrank a matching rule. Both instructions still arrive.

Key Takeaway
Every matching rule loads, with no precedence between them. Resolve conflicts by rewriting the rules, not by renaming, relocating, or relying on specificity.

question:
A manufacturing-execution-system team asks Claude Code, in plan mode, to replace a deprecated PDF library. Their stated constraint: no new native dependencies, because the plant workstations are locked down. The proposed plan is otherwise sound but includes a replacement library that requires a native binding.

What should the developer do?
options: Approve the plan and swap the library out during execution when the native build step fails
Exit plan mode and implement the replacement manually, using the plan as a reference document
Stay in plan mode, point out the violated constraint, and iterate until the plan is approvable
Start a fresh session with a longer prompt that restates the constraint more prominently
answer: Stay in plan mode, point out the violated constraint, and iterate until the plan is approvable
explanation:
This question tests what plan mode is for — the gate exists to be used.

The Gate Caught Exactly What It Should
A plan violating a stated hard constraint was surfaced while it was still words on a screen rather than changes in a repository. The response the mode invites is iteration: reject with the specific objection, let the plan be revised around a dependency-free alternative, approve when it satisfies the constraints.

The sound 90% of the plan survives, the session's accumulated understanding of the codebase survives, and execution starts from an approved design.

Why the other options are incorrect
Approve and swap during execution — spends execution effort on work that must be partially undone, and may not fail loudly: a native dependency can build fine on the developer's machine and break on the locked-down plant workstations, which is the expensive place to discover it.

Exit to manual implementation — abandons supervised execution over a fixable planning error, using as a "reference" the very plan containing the flaw.

Restart with a longer prompt — discards the session's context to re-roll the dice, when the feedback channel for exactly this situation is already open and the objection is one message away.

Key Takeaway
Iterate on the plan inside plan mode until it is approvable. Rejecting with a specific objection is cheaper than approving-and-fixing or restarting.

question:
An insurance-platform manager asks a developer for a written explanation of how claim-resubmission retries work — which conditions trigger a retry, the backoff schedule, and where retries stop. The explicit instruction: make no code changes. The developer will use Claude Code on the service's repository.

Which way of running the session fits the task?
options: Plan mode, so that any proposed modifications would be reviewed and approved before they could ever land
Normal execution mode, with a prompt instructing Claude not to modify anything in the repository
A headless claude -p invocation in CI that writes the finished explanation out to a file
A read-only investigation — search and read the retry paths, then write up findings; no edit capability
answer: A read-only investigation — search and read the retry paths, then write up findings; no edit capability
explanation:
This question tests matching session capability to the task — here, a task with no changes at all.

Comprehension Needs Reading, Not Editing
The deliverable is a written explanation: locate the retry logic, trace its conditions and backoff, write it up. Nothing in that requires edit capability, so the lightest mode that can do the work is right — search-and-read exploration producing a write-up, with no edit capability in play.

Matching the capability surface to the task is the discipline: no gate to operate, no modification risk to manage, nothing to approve.

Why the other options are incorrect
Plan mode — plan mode is itself read-only while planning, so exploring in it is safe. But its structure aims at producing a plan for approval and subsequent execution, and this task has no change to plan, nothing to approve, and no execution phase. The machinery is ceremony around a task complete when the write-up is.

Execution mode with an instruction — holds edit capability open and manages it with prose, a probabilistic control where a structural one is free.

Headless -p in CI — automation without a human in the loop, for what is an interactive comprehension task where follow-ups ("what happens after the fifth failure?") are the likely next step.

Key Takeaway
Run no-change tasks read-only. Plan mode gates changes that are coming; when none are, the gate has nothing to do.

question:
A media company's date-handling bug — subscriptions renewing a day early across DST boundaries — has survived four rounds of a developer telling Claude Code "still broken, try again" with a prose description of the symptom. Each attempt modified plausible-looking code without fixing the behavior.

What should the developer change about the iteration?
options: Write a failing test reproducing the DST boundary case, then iterate against it, sharing the failure output
Write a much more detailed prose description of the bug, including the full renewal flow and all date formats involved
Restart with a more capable model and repeat the same feedback loop from the beginning
Ask Claude to review its own fix for correctness before returning it each round
answer: Write a failing test reproducing the DST boundary case, then iterate against it, sharing the failure output
explanation:
This question tests what makes an iteration loop converge.

Four Rounds Without a Signal
"Still broken, try again" gives the next attempt nothing to aim at, and prose descriptions of date behavior are exactly the kind of specification that hides an off-by-one. That is why four rounds produced four plausible non-fixes.

A failing test converts the bug into an executable definition — this input, this expected renewal date, currently this wrong one — and each iteration gets the assertion diff as feedback. The fix is done when the test passes, not when the code looks plausible, and the test remains afterwards as a regression guard.

Why the other options are incorrect
More detailed prose — still prose: not executable, not checkable, and open to the same interpretation gaps that produced four plausible non-fixes. Detail improves the description without giving the loop a pass/fail signal.

More capable model, same loop — model capability was not the binding constraint; feedback quality was. A stronger model iterating against "still broken" is still guessing at what broken means.

Self-review each round — checks the fix against the model's own understanding of the bug, which four rounds have shown to be incomplete. Review against ground truth is what is missing.

Key Takeaway
Give the loop an executable ground truth. A failing test turns "try again" into a measurable target and leaves a regression guard behind.

question:
A fintech ledger module has three interacting defects: rounding drift on split transactions, a timezone boundary error, and a duplicate-posting guard that misfires. Two previous attempts to fix them one at a time each broke one of the others. A developer is about to engage Claude Code on the cluster.

Which TWO practices give this the best chance of success? (Select TWO.)
options: Describe all three defects and how they interact in a single message, so the fix can be designed jointly
Request the fixes strictly one at a time in three separate sequential asks, verifying each before mentioning the next
Include a concrete failing input — a transaction sequence that trips the interaction — with its expected and actual results
Start a fresh session after each fix attempt so no failed approach lingers in context
Ask Claude to fix the three issues in whatever order it judges best, without detailing how they relate
answer: Describe all three defects and how they interact in a single message, so the fix can be designed jointly
Include a concrete failing input — a transaction sequence that trips the interaction — with its expected and actual results
explanation:
This question tests how to present a cluster of interacting defects — and the defining fact rules out the intuitive approach.

Interacting Defects Are One Problem
Fixing one breaks another, twice. That means the three defects form a single design problem, and the request should present it that way:

-
All three in one message, with their interactions — so the fix is architected jointly rather than patched serially.

-
A concrete failing input — a transaction sequence that trips the interaction, with expected and actual results. It pins the coupling down precisely, gives the work a reproducible target, and becomes the verification that the joint fix holds.

Why the other options are incorrect
Strictly one at a time — re-runs the strategy that has already failed twice, for the structural reason it failed: each fix is designed blind to constraints the other two impose, and the interaction is exactly what a one-at-a-time view cannot see.

Fresh session after each attempt — discards the accumulated understanding of the module and the record of what has been tried, which is the most valuable context for not repeating a failed approach.

Let Claude choose the order without detail — ordering discretion is fine, but this withholds the interaction description, the single most important fact about the cluster. Claude would rediscover the couplings by breaking things.

Key Takeaway
Present interacting defects together with a concrete failing input. Serial one-at-a-time fixes are blind to exactly the couplings that make the cluster hard.

A repository CLAUDE.md conveying the testing conventions, loaded by the headless run as project context
A post-generation lint stage that detects and deletes any generated tests failing the convention checks
A larger, more capable model for the nightly generation job
The existing test files for each target module in context, so generation extends rather than repeats coverage
answer: A repository CLAUDE.md conveying the testing conventions, loaded by the headless run as project context

question:
A logistics company's CI review agent labels findings with a severity. Comparing runs, the team finds the same issue class — unchecked nulls on external API responses — labeled critical in one run and minor in another, and the overall severity distribution swings widely between runs on similar diffs.

What is the right fix?
options: Add "be consistent about severity levels across runs" to the review prompt's instructions
Define each severity level in the criteria, anchored by a concrete code example
Post-process the output, remapping severities with keyword rules so labels are stable
Remove severity from the output entirely and treat every finding as equal priority
answer: Define each severity level in the criteria, anchored by a concrete code example
explanation:
This question tests why unanchored labels drift between runs.

Judgment Words Resample
"Critical" and "minor" are judgment words, and unanchored judgment produces a different answer each run — hence the same issue class labelled critical then minor, and a distribution that swings on similar diffs.

A rubric anchoring each level to a concrete code example changes that: "critical: reachable crash or data corruption, e.g. this unchecked null on a payment response." The same issue class then maps to the same level because the level is defined by cases rather than adjectives, and consistency stops depending on the run.

Why the other options are incorrect
"Be consistent across runs" — asks for consistency without saying what to be consistent with. No run can see the other runs it should agree with, so the request is unactionable.

Keyword remapping in post-processing — stabilizes labels by overruling analysis. The same word accompanies trivial and severe findings, so mechanical rules misfile exactly the nuanced cases severity exists to triage. Stable and wrong is not the goal.

Drop severity entirely — abandons the feature instead of specifying it. Triage is the point of a review agent's output; a flat list pushes prioritization onto every reader.

Key Takeaway
Anchor each severity level with a concrete example in the criteria. Consistency comes from definitions, not from asking for consistency.

question:
A travel platform's PR review agent is measured over a month: 60% of its findings concern lines the PR never touched — pre-existing issues elsewhere in the modified files. Developers have begun dismissing its comments wholesale, including the valid ones on their actual changes.

What should the team change?
options: Keep the reviewer as is and post-filter its findings, dropping any whose lines fall outside the diff hunks
Shrink the context given to the reviewer so it cannot see code beyond the changed lines
Ask developers to keep dismissing irrelevant findings so the noise stays manageable
Scope the review criteria to behavior introduced or modified by the change, with pre-existing issues out of scope
answer: Scope the review criteria to behavior introduced or modified by the change, with pre-existing issues out of scope
explanation:
This question tests review-criteria scoping, and the distinction is causation versus geometry.

The Agent Was Never Told What a PR Review Is For
Given no scope, the reviewer reviews everything it can see — hence 60% of findings on untouched lines. Scoping belongs in the criteria: the object under review is the change, meaning new and modified behavior plus existing behavior the change breaks, with pre-existing conditions explicitly out of scope.

That redirects attention during analysis, so effort goes into the diff rather than being spent and discarded. It also preserves the legitimate edge case: a finding triggered by the change but manifesting in untouched code stays in scope, because the criteria are about causation.

Why the other options are incorrect
Post-filter by diff hunks — the strongest distractor. It runs after the reviewer has already spent effort on out-of-scope analysis, and it cuts on geometry rather than causation: a change that breaks an untouched caller gets filtered out precisely when the finding matters most, while in-hunk trivia survives.

Shrink the reviewer's context — reviewing a diff without surrounding code makes findings shallower, not better scoped. The reviewer needs the enclosing function and callers to judge safety.

Keep dismissing — the dismissal habit is the damage. At 60% noise, developers have stopped distinguishing signal, and valid findings die with the rest.

Key Takeaway
Scope review criteria to behavior the change introduces or breaks. Line-number filters cut by geometry and drop exactly the cross-boundary findings that matter.

question:
A utility company's support agent keeps confusing two tools on usage questions: meter_history, for raw meter readings, and consumption_report, for billed consumption summaries. Boundary cases — "how much power did I use in March?" — go to the wrong tool about a quarter of the time. The team wants to fix this with few-shot examples in the prompt.

How should the examples be designed?
options: Twenty-plus examples covering every phrasing of usage questions the team has seen in logs
Two to four examples of clear-cut requests for each tool, each showing the correct call being made
Two to four boundary-case examples, each showing the chosen tool and a one-line reason it wins
A prose rulebook enumerating the tool-selection policies and boundary conditions, in place of examples
answer: Two to four boundary-case examples, each showing the chosen tool and a one-line reason it wins
explanation:
This question tests where few-shot examples should sit when the failure is a discrimination problem.

Put the Examples on the Boundary
The agent already routes obvious requests correctly; it fails on cases like "how much power did I use in March?", which sit between raw readings and billed summaries. So the examples belong on that boundary, and each should carry the discriminating logic — a one-line reason the chosen tool wins over the plausible alternative.

That reason is what converts an example from a pattern to imitate into a principle to apply. A few contrastive, reasoned examples teach the distinction; volume and clarity elsewhere do not.

Why the other options are incorrect
Twenty-plus phrasings — invites lookup-table matching over principle, bloats every request, and still loses to the twenty-first phrasing. Coverage is the wrong axis when the model needs the distinction, not the distribution.

Clear-cut examples for each tool — demonstrates what was never failing. Examples that skip the boundary leave the boundary exactly as ambiguous as before.

A prose rulebook instead of examples — states policy in the abstract, which is what the tool descriptions already attempt. The failure is applying policy to concrete borderline requests, which worked examples demonstrate and prose does not.

Key Takeaway
Target few-shot examples at the confused boundary and include the reasoning for each choice. Examples of easy cases teach nothing about hard ones.

question:
A hospital-administration team extracts fields from patient-intake paperwork — referring clinic, insurer member ID, guarantor. Audit finds that when the referring-clinic section is blank, the model outputs a plausible clinic name anyway: 7% of extractions contain invented values. The current prompt has three examples, all of fully completed forms.

What is the most effective fix?
options: Add examples of forms with the section blank, each showing the correct output — a null referring_clinic
Add the instruction "never invent values; only extract what is present in the document"
Set temperature to 0 so extraction becomes deterministic
Mark referring_clinic as required in the output schema so the field is always handled explicitly
answer: Add examples of forms with the section blank, each showing the correct output — a null referring_clinic
explanation:
This question tests demonstrated behavior versus stated instruction, where absence is the missing case.

Every Example Says "Fill This In"
The prompt's three examples are all fully completed forms, so the model has literally never been shown what a blank section should produce. Faced with one, it does what all three demonstrations imply and supplies a plausible value.

Adding examples of blank sections with the correct output — a null referring_clinic — teaches the missing behavior directly: what absence looks like on the form, and what faithful extraction emits for it. Demonstrated behavior is the strongest lever in few-shot design, and the hole is in what has been demonstrated.

Why the other options are incorrect
"Never invent values" instruction — points the right direction while competing with three examples demonstrating the opposite pattern. Instructions generalize worse than demonstrations for output-shape behavior; it helps at the margin without filling the hole.

Temperature 0 — governs sampling variability, not grounding. A deterministic model fabricates the same plausible clinic every time: the error becomes consistent, not absent.

Mark the field required — forces the model to produce something on every form, including blank ones, which pressures toward invention. The schema change aligned with truthful absence is permitting null — and that only matters if examples show when to use it.

Key Takeaway
Demonstrate absence explicitly with examples showing null output for missing fields. Prohibitions compete with demonstrations, and demonstrations usually win.

question:
A manufacturer classifies supplier documents into a six-value category enum. A quality audit measures that 9% of real documents fit none of the six categories, and the model currently files each of those under whichever category is nearest, silently.

How should the schema be changed?
options: Expand the enum with a new value for every unmatched document type the quality audit has found
Change the category field to free text so the model can describe each document accurately
Keep the schema as is and route documents with low classification confidence to human review
Add an "other" value with a free-text detail field, capturing out-of-taxonomy documents reviewably
answer: Add an "other" value with a free-text detail field, capturing out-of-taxonomy documents reviewably
explanation:
This question tests designing an enum that can represent the truth.

Forced Choice Produces Silent Misfiles
The audit shows 9% of documents fit none of the six categories, and the schema gives the model no honest move — so it files each under the nearest wrong value, silently.

An "other" value paired with a free-text detail field makes the gap expressible, and the detail field records what the document actually is. That turns the 9% from hidden errors into reviewable data: the detail texts aggregate over time to show which genuinely recurring types deserve promotion to real enum values. The escape hatch doubles as the discovery mechanism.

Why the other options are incorrect
Enumerate every type the audit found — chases a moving tail: next quarter brings types this quarter never saw, and each addition churns a taxonomy downstream systems depend on. Without an escape value the schema is wrong again the day something new arrives.

Free text for category — repairs the 9% by destroying the 91%. Routing, aggregation and validation all depend on the closed set, and "Invoice", "invoice" and "supplier invoice" become three categories.

Confidence routing, schema unchanged — helps triage while leaving the schema unable to represent the truth. A document the model is confident fits nothing must still be filed wrong, and confidently misfiled documents never reach the queue.

Key Takeaway
Give closed enums an "other" value with a detail field. Escape hatches prevent silent misfiling and reveal which categories the taxonomy is missing.

question:
An insurer's claims-extraction schema requires ISO 8601 dates and already enforces the format with a pattern. Incoming claims carry dates in seven styles, including handwritten forms like "3rd of March 26" and ambiguous numerics like "03/04/2026" whose meaning depends on the form's country of origin. Outputs validate against the pattern but normalize the ambiguous cases inconsistently across runs.

What should the team add?
options: A stricter schema pattern on the date fields constraining the accepted ISO form and value ranges further
Normalization rules in the prompt beside the schema — day-first UK forms, century pivot, ambiguity flags
A deterministic post-processing converter that maintains one regex for each of the seven incoming formats
A validation rule rejecting documents whose dates are not already in ISO form
answer: Normalization rules in the prompt beside the schema — day-first UK forms, century pivot, ambiguity flags
explanation:
This question tests the division of labour between schema and prompt: shape versus semantics.

The Schema Is Already Doing Its Whole Job
Every output validates against the ISO pattern. The inconsistency is in which ISO date the model picks for "03/04/2026" — and that is a meaning question the schema has no vocabulary for. A pattern constrains the shape of the result; it cannot decide between March 4th and April 3rd.

Transformation policy therefore lives where interpretation happens: explicit normalization rules in the prompt, beside the schema — day-first for UK-origin forms, the century pivot for "26", and when to flag a date as ambiguous rather than guess. Schema for shape, prompt for semantics.

Why the other options are incorrect
A stricter pattern — every wrong normalization is already a well-formed ISO date. Tightening a shape constraint cannot resolve a semantic ambiguity.

One regex per incoming format — the closest wrong answer. Regexes can reformat clean, unambiguous strings, but the hard cases need context the post-processor lacks: the model sees the form's origin and layout; a regex sees ten characters. Seven formats also means a growing brittle rule pile.

Reject non-ISO documents — rejects the workload. Handwritten and legacy forms are the business; a pipeline that only accepts pre-normalized input has outsourced its job to the sender.

Key Takeaway
Schemas enforce output shape; prompts supply transformation semantics. State normalization rules explicitly when the same input string has more than one defensible reading.

question:
A fintech code-review agent posts findings on merge requests, and developers can dismiss them. The team wants dismissals to drive systematic improvement of the reviewer over time.

Which TWO design elements make that work? (Select TWO.)
options: A praise field so developers can also thumbs-up findings they liked
Automatic suppression of any check after its first dismissed finding
A machine-readable pattern identifier on every finding, recording which rule or heuristic produced it
A recurring analysis of dismissals grouped by pattern, feeding revisions to the worst-performing criteria
Automatic re-posting of dismissed findings in the next run so developers confirm each dismissal twice
answer: A machine-readable pattern identifier on every finding, recording which rule or heuristic produced it
A recurring analysis of dismissals grouped by pattern, feeding revisions to the worst-performing criteria
explanation:
This question tests building a feedback loop from dismissals — attribution plus action.

Two Halves of One Loop

-
Pattern identifier on every finding — a dismissal is only a data point if it can be traced to what produced it. Recording which rule or heuristic generated each finding lets dismissals aggregate by cause instead of piling up as anecdotes.

-
Recurring analysis grouped by pattern — periodic review of dismissal rates per pattern identifies the criteria producing noise, and those criteria get revised, scoped or retired.

Individual dismissals are opinions. Grouped by pattern over time, they become an evaluation of the reviewer.

Why the other options are incorrect
A praise field — positive signal is pleasant but does not advance the stated goal of reducing what developers reject, and it adds a second unaggregated signal while the first still drives nothing.

Suppress a check after one dismissal — one dismissal is one developer's judgment on one finding, possibly wrong or context-specific. Disabling a whole check on a single sample overfits catastrophically.

Re-post dismissed findings — doubles the noise burden on exactly the people whose trust is being spent, and teaches them the dismissal button does not work.

Key Takeaway
Attribute findings to their generating pattern, then act on aggregated dismissal rates. Capture without analysis is an archive; analysis without attribution is guesswork.

question:
A freight forwarder extracts customs invoices into its ERP. Problems surface weeks later during financial reconciliation: line items that do not sum to stated totals, invalid currency codes. Each late discovery means manual reversal of postings that other processes have already consumed. Extraction currently flows straight into the ERP.

What should the pipeline add?
options: A nightly ERP-side audit query flagging suspect postings within a day of entry rather than weeks later
An instruction in the extraction prompt telling the model to verify sums and codes before answering
Boundary validation in code — sums, code sets, ranges — feeding failures back for bounded retries
A second, independent model instance that reviews every extraction before it is allowed to post
answer: Boundary validation in code — sums, code sets, ranges — feeding failures back for bounded retries
explanation:
This question tests where to catch mechanically-checkable defects.

Fail at the Boundary, Not in Reconciliation
Sums that do not balance and invalid currency codes are deterministic properties — code verifies them with certainty. Validating at the extraction boundary, before anything posts, catches them at the one point where they are still cheap: the document is in hand and nothing downstream has consumed the record.

Feeding the specific validator errors back for a bounded retry lets the model correct with the failure in front of it, and persistent failures route to review instead of into the ERP.

Why the other options are incorrect
Nightly ERP-side audit — a day beats weeks, and the audit still runs after posting: the reversal cost, the downstream consumers and the cleanup all remain. Only the delay shrinks, and the stem's problem is where errors are caught.

Self-verification instruction — asks the pass that made the error to also catch it, with no independent signal, and guards arithmetic probabilistically when code verifies it for free.

A second model reviewing every extraction — doubles cost for a second fallible opinion on properties that are not matters of opinion. Model review earns its cost on judgment calls; these are deterministic.

Key Takeaway
Validate deterministic properties in code at the extraction boundary, with a bounded retry loop. Downstream audits shorten the delay without removing the cost.

question:
A media archive must extract structured data from 90,000 scanned articles spanning eight decades, with a three-week deadline. The extraction prompt has been tested on twelve hand-picked articles. The Batch API's 50% discount makes batch processing the obvious vehicle, and a teammate proposes submitting the full corpus tonight to maximize runway.

What should the team do instead?
options: Refine the prompt on a stratified sample — decades, layouts, scan quality — processed synchronously, then batch the corpus
Submit all 90,000 tonight as proposed, inspect the results, and fix whatever failed in a second corrected batch
Split the corpus into ten parallel batches so results arrive faster and problems surface sooner
Process the entire corpus synchronously so the team keeps full control over quality throughout the run
answer: Refine the prompt on a stratified sample — decades, layouts, scan quality — processed synchronously, then batch the corpus
explanation:
This question tests validating before scaling — twelve hand-picked articles is not validation.

The Sample Is Unrepresentative by Construction
Eight decades of layouts, typography and scan degradation, validated on twelve articles someone chose. The prompt's real failure modes live in the strata nobody picked.

A stratified sample — across decades, layouts and scan quality — processed synchronously gives fast iteration exactly where it is needed: run, inspect, fix, rerun at interactive speed until each stratum extracts acceptably. Then the corpus goes through batch, spending the 50% discount on a prompt known to work. Synchronous for iteration, batch for validated scale; three weeks comfortably accommodates a few days of sampling.

Why the other options are incorrect
Submit all 90,000 tonight — a systematic flaw hits every affected document at once, and tens of thousands of bad extractions must then be detected, diagnosed and reprocessed. A discount on the first pass does not make two passes cheaper than one validated pass.

Ten parallel batches — changes throughput, not validation. The same untested prompt reaches the same documents with the same flaws, only sooner and all at once.

Fully synchronous — forfeits the entire discount to buy control that matters during refinement, which the sample already provides at a fraction of the cost.

Key Takeaway
Refine on a stratified sample synchronously, then batch the validated corpus. Hand-picked examples validate nothing about the strata nobody picked.

question:
An edtech company's nightly batch enriches course-catalog records. This morning's results: 96% succeeded, 3% errored on a schema-validation mistake in those requests, and 1% expired unprocessed at the 24-hour boundary.

How should the pipeline handle the morning's results?
options: Rerun the entire batch tonight so the results arrive as one complete, consistent set
Log the expired 1% as failed records and fix-and-resubmit only the 3% that errored
Switch the pipeline to synchronous processing, since expiry makes batch unreliable for this workload
Merge the 96% by custom_id, resubmit the errored 3% with the validation fix, and resubmit the expired 1% unchanged
answer: Merge the 96% by custom_id, resubmit the errored 3% with the validation fix, and resubmit the expired 1% unchanged
explanation:
This question tests per-result-type handling of a completed batch.

Three Result Types, Three Actions
custom_id is what makes per-request handling possible, since results return in arbitrary order and each must be mapped back to its source record.

-
96% succeeded → merge now by custom_id.

-
3% errored on a real schema-validation defect → resubmit with the fix.

-
1% expired — never processed, and not billed → resubmit unchanged, because nothing was wrong with them.

Two small follow-up batches complete the run for a fraction of a full rerun.

Why the other options are incorrect
Rerun the entire batch — re-pays for the 96% that already succeeded to recover a 4% tail. Batch results need no single-set arrival; that is what identifier mapping is for.

Log expired as failed, fix only the errored — the trap. Expiry is not failure: nothing examined those requests and found them wanting; the window simply closed. Writing them off discards processable work and misstates the pipeline's records.

Switch to synchronous — a structural response to routine operational behavior, abandoning the 50% discount on the whole nightly workload over a 1% tail with a standard remedy.

Key Takeaway
Handle succeeded, errored and expired differently, mapping every result by custom_id. Expired requests were never processed or billed — resubmit them as they were.

question:
A manufacturing-systems team generates integration code with one Claude instance and wants a second instance to review each change with genuine independence before merge.

Which TWO inputs should the reviewing instance receive? (Select TWO.)
options: The acceptance criteria and spec the change was supposed to satisfy
The generating instance's session transcript, showing its full reasoning
A summary written by the generating instance describing the change and why it is correct
The artifacts themselves — the diff, affected files, and test results as they stand
The generating instance's own list of the parts it is least confident about
answer: The acceptance criteria and spec the change was supposed to satisfy
The artifacts themselves — the diff, affected files, and test results as they stand
explanation:
This question tests what independence actually requires as input.

Ground Truth, in Two Parts
An independent reviewer forms its own judgment from what the work was supposed to do and what the work is:

-
Acceptance criteria and spec — the requirements the change must satisfy.

-
The artifacts — the diff, affected files and test results as they stand.

From those two, the reviewer re-derives its own verdict. Everything else on offer is the generator's perspective, and importing that is how a reviewer inherits the generator's blind spots.

Why the other options are incorrect
The generating instance's transcript — a walkthrough of how the generator convinced itself. A reviewer that reads the rationalization before judging the code is led down the same path that produced any defect in it — the exact mechanism independence exists to break.

A self-summary of the change — advocacy: it frames the work in terms of why it is correct, written by the party whose work is in question.

The generator's low-confidence list — sounds efficient and anchors the review, drawing attention toward the flagged parts and away from the parts the generator was confidently wrong about — which are exactly what an independent reading would catch.

Key Takeaway
Give the reviewer the requirements and the artifacts, nothing from the generator's reasoning. Transcripts, summaries and confidence hints all import the bias being checked.

question:
A retailer's review agent attaches a confidence score to each finding, and the team plans routing on it: auto-apply high-confidence findings, send low-confidence ones to humans. Before launch, someone samples the dismissal log and finds a number of dismissed findings that carried very high confidence.

What should the team do?
options: Raise the auto-apply threshold from 0.80 to 0.95 so only near-certain findings bypass humans
First measure stated confidence against actual precision on the labeled dismissals, per band
Launch the routing now and tune the threshold from production dismissal rates as they accumulate
Ignore the model's scores and route by finding category instead, using severity as the reliability proxy
answer: First measure stated confidence against actual precision on the labeled dismissals, per band
explanation:
This question tests validating a signal before routing on it.

The Dismissal Log Already Falsified the Assumption
High stated confidence coexisting with wrongness is miscalibration, and routing on a score assumes the score means what it says. That assumption is testable before launch, using the labeled dismissal history the team already has.

Binning findings by stated confidence and computing actual precision per band, per category, shows where confidence tracks correctness and where it does not. Routing then goes live only over the demonstrated regions, with miscalibrated bands recalibrated or kept under human review. Trust in a signal is earned by measurement.

Why the other options are incorrect
Raise the threshold to 0.95 — a higher cutoff on an unvalidated score is still an unvalidated bet. The sampled log already contains very-high-confidence errors, so if the score is miscalibrated at the top, 0.95 filters volume without filtering wrongness.

question:
A travel-industry research system aggregates 30 source summaries into one synthesis call; the packed context fits comfortably within the model's window. Quality analysis across many runs shows findings that appear only in sources 12 through 19 — the middle of the packed sequence — are missing from the synthesis at four times the rate of findings from early or late sources.

What should the team change?
options: Move synthesis to a model with a much larger context window so the packed sources have far more room
Randomize the source order on every run so no single source always sits in the middle positions
Restructure the input: an up-front key-findings digest plus per-source section headers
Split synthesis into one call per source and concatenate the 30 per-source outputs
answer: Restructure the input: an up-front key-findings digest plus per-source section headers
explanation:
This question tests positional attention loss, and the key fact is that everything already fits.

Space Is Not the Failing Resource
Findings from sources 12–19 go missing at four times the rate of early and late sources. That is positional: material in the middle of a long undifferentiated sequence receives less attention than material near the start and end.

Since the packed context fits comfortably, the remedy is structure, not space — lead with a digest placing every source's key findings in the high-attention head position, and mark each source with explicit headers so the middle stops being an undifferentiated wall. Critical claims then appear at least once where attention is strongest, with detailed sections available for depth.

Why the other options are incorrect
A much larger context window — the sources already fit. A bigger window leaves the same sequence with the same middle, and the attention pattern travels with the model regardless of window size.

Randomize source order — rotates which sources suffer rather than fixing the suffering. Each run still under-attends its middle third; across runs the loss is merely distributed evenly.

One call per source, concatenated — eliminates the long context by eliminating the synthesis. Contradictions, corroborations and duplicates can only be found when sources are considered together, and thirty concatenated summaries is a stack, not an answer.

Key Takeaway
Counter middle-of-context loss with an up-front digest and explicit per-source headers. More window space does not change where attention concentrates.

question:
An energy-policy research pipeline has six upstream subagents, each returning roughly 4,000 tokens of narrative including its full reasoning. The downstream synthesis stage regularly runs out of context and has been observed silently truncating two of the six inputs.

What is the right fix?
options: Upstream returns structured key findings with citations; full reasoning stays in each subagent's logs
Have the synthesis stage process the sources in two passes of three each, merging the partial syntheses
Truncate each subagent's narrative to its first 1,500 tokens and synthesize from those
Move the synthesis stage to a model whose context window comfortably fits all six narratives
answer: Upstream returns structured key findings with citations; full reasoning stays in each subagent's logs
explanation:
This question tests designing an upstream output contract for a downstream budget.

Producers Should Shape Output for Their Consumer
Synthesis needs each subagent's findings, not the journey that produced them. Reasoning narratives are valuable for debugging a subagent — and that is where they belong: in its logs.

Defining the handoff as structured key findings with citations shrinks each input to what downstream consumption actually requires. Pressure disappears at its source, the design scales as subagents are added, and the inputs become uniform enough that nothing is silently dropped.

Why the other options are incorrect
Two passes of three, merged — loses exactly what synthesis is for: tensions and corroborations between sources landing in different halves are invisible to both passes, and the merge must reconcile two documents that each concluded without seeing all the evidence.

Truncate to the first 1,500 tokens — position-based truncation keeps whatever happens to come first, typically preamble and early reasoning, with no guarantee the findings survive. It is the current information loss, applied deliberately.

A larger context window — absorbs today's six subagents and is outgrown by the eighth, while every synthesis still pays to carry reasoning it will not use.

Key Takeaway
Define upstream outputs as structured findings sized for the consumer, keeping full reasoning in logs. Larger windows postpone an interface problem rather than fixing it.

question:
An electronics retailer's warranty support agent escalates 41% of cases against a 15% target. An audit of escalated cases finds most were fully within policy — for example, a replacement under a valid warranty that merely required three lookups to confirm. The agent's current guidance tells it to escalate cases that are "complex."

What is the right fix?
options: Replace the vague wording with a measurable trigger: escalate any case exceeding five tool calls
Remove escalation from the warranty category, since the audit shows those cases are all handleable
Keep the criteria as they are and expand the human team until the escalation queue clears
Recenter the criteria on policy boundaries — gaps, exceptions, authority limits — not effort
answer: Recenter the criteria on policy boundaries — gaps, exceptions, authority limits — not effort
explanation:
This question tests what escalation criteria should actually measure.

Complexity Is the Wrong Axis
The audit exposes a category error: "complex" measures how much work a case takes, while the real question is whether the agent has the authority to resolve it. A three-lookup warranty replacement is laborious and entirely decidable — policy covers it, so the agent should do the work.

Escalation earns its cost where the policy runs out: gaps, exceptions, and authority limits. Rewriting the criteria in those terms, and explicitly excluding effort as a trigger, sends humans only what actually needs a human.

Why the other options are incorrect
Escalate above five tool calls — complexity with a number on it. The audited failure — a fully-covered case needing several lookups — still escalates under any threshold it crosses, because the criterion still asks "how much work" instead of "whose call."

Remove escalation from warranty — the audit shows most warranty escalations were unnecessary, not all. Genuine exceptions (disputed damage, out-of-policy goodwill) exist in every category, and removing the path leaves the agent deciding cases it has no authority over.

Expand the human team — resources the defect. Humans spend their time rubber-stamping decisions policy already made.

Key Takeaway
Escalate on policy boundaries — gaps, exceptions, authority limits — and state explicitly that effort is not a trigger. Difficulty and authority are different questions.

The audit shows most warranty escalations were unnecessary, not all: genuine exceptions — disputed damage, out-of-policy goodwill decisions — exist in every category, and removing the path entirely leaves the agent resolving cases it has no authority to decide.
Staffing to a 41% rate resources the defect instead of fixing it: humans spend their time rubber-stamping decisions policy already made, which is cost without judgment being added anywhere.

A three-lookup warranty replacement is laborious and entirely decidable — policy covers it, so the agent should do the work. question:
A streaming service's support agent receives this first message: "Cancel my subscription, and I want to talk to a real person about it, not a bot."

What should the agent do?
options: Begin the cancellation flow and offer a human handoff only if the customer repeats the request
Hand off to a human right away, passing along the customer's stated intent to cancel
Ask a clarifying question first to determine whether the issue actually requires a human
Complete the cancellation itself, which resolves the request without any wait for a human
answer: Hand off to a human right away, passing along the customer's stated intent to cancel
explanation:
This question tests the clearest escalation trigger there is.

An Explicit Request for a Human Is Honored Immediately
The customer asked for a person in their first message. That is one of the least ambiguous escalation signals in support design, so the agent hands off right away — and makes the handoff good by passing along what is already known, the cancellation intent, so the customer does not restart from zero.

Why the other options are incorrect
Start the flow, offer a human if repeated — forces the customer to ask twice for what they asked for once. The request was not conditional on the bot failing first.

Ask a clarifying question — the customer has stated what the issue requires: a person. Qualifying that reads as the agent gatekeeping access to humans.

Complete the cancellation itself — executes half the request while ignoring the explicitly stated other half, and a cancellation performed by the bot the customer asked to get away from is a poor final interaction.

Key Takeaway
Honor an explicit request for a human immediately, carrying context into the handoff. Do not front-run it, gate it, or require it to be repeated.

-

-
Anthropic — Prompting best practices → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

An explicit request for a human is honored immediately — it is one of the clearest escalation triggers there is, and it is present in the very first message. The agent's remaining job is to make the handoff good: pass along what is already known, the cancellation intent, so the customer does not restart from zero. Debating the request or front-running it are both ways of overriding a customer who has said what they want.
The customer has stated what the issue requires: a person. A qualifying question second-guesses that and delays the handoff, which reads as the agent gatekeeping the humans.
