question:
A fintech research coordinator dispatches subagents against external data sources. Today every failure — rate-limit 429s, request timeouts, expired auth tokens, deleted sources — is propagated up to the coordinator along with partial results. In 40% of runs the coordinator processes more than twenty failure reports, and its context fills with retry traffic instead of research.

How should failure handling be divided?
options: Subagents retry transient failures locally with bounded backoff, propagating only non-recoverable ones with partials and the gap noted
Keep propagating everything, but collect the failure reports and deliver them to the coordinator as one batch at the end of the run
Subagents retry all failures locally, including auth and deleted-source errors, until a retry budget is exhausted
Drop failing sources silently inside each subagent so the coordinator receives only successful results
answer: Subagents retry transient failures locally with bounded backoff, propagating only non-recoverable ones with partials and the gap noted
explanation:
This question tests dividing failure handling by recoverability at the level that sees it.

Retry What Heals; Propagate What Does Not
A 429 or a timeout is self-healing — wait and retry, bounded, and most vanish without anyone above needing to know. An expired credential or a deleted source cannot be fixed by retrying at any budget: re-authentication and re-planning around a missing source are orchestration decisions.

Splitting on that line sends each failure to the lowest level that can act on it. The coordinator's context empties of retry noise while keeping visibility of every failure that genuinely affects the run — with partial results and an explicit statement of what is missing.

Why the other options are incorrect
Batch the reports at run end — changes the arrival schedule, not the division of labour. The coordinator still triages twenty reports, most of which a local retry would have dissolved, and transient failures now surface only after the run.

Retry everything locally until budget exhausted — worse than propagating: an expired token fails identically on every attempt, so the budget burns while the one actor who could fix the credential learns late.

Drop failing sources silently — converts visible failures into invisible coverage gaps. Synthesis proceeds as if missing sources agreed with the present ones, and nobody can distinguish "no evidence" from "evidence not collected."

Key Takeaway
Subagents retry transient failures with bounded backoff; propagate non-recoverable ones with partials and an explicit gap note. Never drop failures silently.

-

question:
A logistics team is running a multi-week platform-migration investigation across many Claude Code sessions, with a shared notes file as external memory. The file has grown to roughly 80,000 tokens because sessions append raw material — full config files, 400-line command outputs — and each new session begins by reading it, consuming most of its budget before any new work starts.

What should the team change about the notes practice?
options: Split the notes into ten smaller topic files and have each new session read all ten of them at startup
Have each session run /compact immediately after it finishes reading the notes file
Persist distilled findings — conclusions, decisions, open questions — with pointers to raw sources
Stop keeping notes and rely on resuming one long-lived session for the whole investigation
answer: Persist distilled findings — conclusions, decisions, open questions — with pointers to raw sources
explanation:
This question tests editorial discipline in external memory.

When the Cure Costs as Much as the Disease
External memory earns its keep only while reading it is cheaper than rediscovering the work. An 80,000-token file has crossed that line, because sessions append raw material — full configs, 400-line outputs — rather than what was learned.

The fix is discipline at write time: record conclusions, decisions and open questions, with pointers to where the raw material lives, reachable by path when a future session genuinely needs to re-examine one. With periodic condensation as understanding matures, the file stays a briefing and each session starts informed with most of its budget intact.

Why the other options are incorrect
Ten topic files, all read at startup — the same 80,000 tokens with more filenames. Topical splitting helps only when sessions read selectively, and raw-dump content gives them no basis for choosing.

/compact after reading — too late: the budget is spent ingesting the bloat before the summary happens, and compacting raw dumps is exactly the distillation that should have been done once, deliberately, at write time.

One long-lived session instead — accumulates the same bloat in conversation history with less control, puts weeks of investigation behind one session's continuity, and is unshareable with the team.

Key Takeaway
Write conclusions and pointers, not raw material, and condense periodically. External memory that costs a session's budget to read has stopped being an asset.

question:
A healthcare-administration platform session has finished phase one of a long exploration — mapping the data flows — and its conclusions are written to a findings file. Phase two, evaluating integration options, is next; it builds on phase one's conclusions and on the session's accumulated familiarity with the codebase layout. Context is at 78%.

When should the developer compact?
options: When context reaches about 95%, to get maximum use of the window first
Not at all — run /clear instead and have the new context re-read the findings file
Now, at the phase boundary, with the findings safely persisted
Let auto-compaction handle it whenever the threshold is crossed mid-phase-two

explanation:
This question tests when to compact — timing, not threshold.

A Phase Boundary Is the Cheapest Moment
Phase one's essential output is already persisted to the findings file, so what compaction's summary loses is mostly material whose conclusions are safe on disk — and no in-flight reasoning exists to damage. Compacting now hands phase two a mostly fresh window while preserving a working summary of how the session got here.

Waiting forfeits exactly this safety.

Wait until ~95% — by then the session is deep into phase two, and compaction summarizes away active reasoning — the option comparisons in progress. Squeezing the window first spends the safe moment to buy a risky one.

/clear and re-read the findings — the stem says phase two also builds on accumulated familiarity with the codebase layout, which lives in the conversation, not the findings file. Clearing wipes that; re-reading restores conclusions but not fluency.

Let auto-compaction handle it — the uncontrolled version of waiting. It fires at a threshold rather than a semantic boundary, so it lands mid-reasoning by default. Auto-compaction is the safety net, not the plan.

Compact at phase boundaries once findings are persisted. /compact continues related work; /clear is for unrelated work; auto-compaction is a backstop.

question:

Last week the team discovered a novel tariff-rider clause had been consistently misread — with high confidence — and auto-accepted for six weeks.

What monitoring should exist to catch this class of failure?
options: Lower the auto-accept confidence threshold so that more extractions get routed to the human queue
An ongoing stratified human audit of the auto-accepted pool, sized per document type
Add the tariff-rider clause to the prompt's examples and resume normal operation
A quarterly full re-run of all processed contracts against the current prompt, diffing for changes

explanation:

Confidence routing assumes confidence tracks correctness — and novel input, like a tariff-rider clause that did not exist at design time, is precisely where that assumption breaks without lowering the score. Six weeks of confident misreads flowed through the auto-accept channel unexamined.

The countermeasure is a permanent stratified human audit of the auto-accepted pool, sized per document type so each stratum gets coverage proportional to its volume and risk. A systematic misread then surfaces within a sampling cycle, from a small constant human effort. Monitoring as a standing subsystem, not a launch-time activity.

Add the clause to the examples — patches the instance and dissolves the lesson. The next novel clause type gets its own six silent weeks, because nothing was added that watches the pool. The question asks what monitoring should exist.

Quarterly full re-run against the same prompt — largely reproduces the same confident misreads; a diff against yourself cannot reveal you were wrong. Its window also allows up to three months of silent posting.

Sample the auto-accepted pool continuously, stratified by document type. Detection of confident errors requires an independent reference, not a lower threshold.

question:
An edtech strategy team's multi-stage research system produces board memos: subagents gather evidence, an aggregation stage consolidates it, and a writer produces the memo. The board has asked that every claim in a memo be checkable back to where it came from.

Which TWO practices deliver that? (Select TWO.)
options: A complete bibliography of all consulted sources appended to the end of every memo
Deduplicating the source set before synthesis so that every claim maps to exactly one source
A uniform, confident prose style applied so the finished memo reads decisively throughout
Claim-to-source mapping carried as structure through every stage, so claims arrive with sources attached
The supporting excerpt or a precise locator kept with each claim, so a reviewer can jump straight to the passage
answer: Claim-to-source mapping carried as structure through every stage, so claims arrive with sources attached
The supporting excerpt or a precise locator kept with each claim, so a reviewer can jump straight to the passage
explanation:
This question tests provenance surviving a multi-stage pipeline.

Attribution Must Travel as Structure
Checkability dies at whichever stage flattens findings into unattributed prose, so it has to survive as data:

-
Claim-to-source mapping carried through every stage — each claim paired with its sources through gathering, aggregation and writing, arriving in the memo still attached.

-
Supporting excerpt or precise locator kept with each claim — a source name alone makes verification a search problem; an excerpt or locator makes it a lookup, so the reviewer jumps to the passage and confirms.

Together they give every claim a path back to evidence at passage granularity.

Why the other options are incorrect
Terminal bibliography — proves sources were consulted, not which claim rests on which. Any claim could have come from any of them, or from none — exactly the mapping the board asked for.

Deduplicate to one source per claim — hygiene, not provenance, and it actively discards corroboration, which is part of a claim's evidentiary weight. One-to-one simplifies the truth rather than tracing it.

Uniform confident prose — works against the requirement by erasing the seams between strongly and thinly sourced claims. Style cannot substitute for attribution.

Key Takeaway

question:
A telecom developer reviews a teammate's first agentic loop. Tools sometimes fail to execute even though the model clearly asked for them: the loop decides whether to run a tool by scanning the response text for tool names. The reviewer wants the loop keyed to the correct signal.

What should the loop check?
options: Whether the response text mentions one of the defined tools by name
Whether the response contains more than one content block
Whether the response's stop_reason is "tool_use"
Whether usage.output_tokens exceeds the typical length of a plain answer
answer: Whether the response's stop_reason is "tool_use"
explanation:
This question tests the loop's control signal — which field says "execute a tool."

stop_reason Is the Protocol Signal
stop_reason is set by the API for exactly this purpose. When it is "tool_use", the model has requested tool execution, and the loop runs the calls in the response's tool_use blocks, returns results, and continues. The loop reads intent directly rather than inferring it.

Why the other options are incorrect
Text mentions a tool name — inference over prose, and the bug under review. The model may discuss a tool without calling it, or call one without naming it in the text.

More than one content block — block count is not a request signal: a plain text answer can be one block or several, and nothing about the number says "execute something."

Output token count — correlates with nothing relevant. Long answers need no tools, and short responses can carry a tool call. It is a statistic, not a signal.

Key Takeaway
Branch on stop_reason, never on response text. The API provides an explicit signal precisely so loops do not have to guess.

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference

question:
A telecom support workflow runs a fixed sequence: verify identity, look up the account, then diagnose. It is read-only — no account changes. Transcript review shows about 30% of chats stall: some customers open with their account number, others describe the outage first, others ask a question the sequence reaches only at step three. The fixed pipeline handles each opening badly.

What should the team build instead?
options: A model-driven loop given the tools, goal, and constraints, choosing its next step per conversation
The same fixed pipeline with additional branches covering each of the observed opening types
An intake form that collects identity, account, and issue in fixed order before the conversation starts
Three parallel pipelines, one per opening type, selected by a keyword classifier on the first message
answer: A model-driven loop given the tools, goal, and constraints, choosing its next step per conversation
explanation:
This question tests when a model-driven loop genuinely beats a fixed sequence — and the read-only detail matters.

The Right First Step Depends on the Customer
30% of chats stall because the correct opening varies with what the customer supplies: an account number, an outage description, or a question the sequence only reaches at step three. That is data-dependent ordering, which is exactly the condition a model-driven loop handles and a fixed pipeline cannot.

Given the tools, the goal and the constraints, the model verifies first when identity arrives first, looks up first when the account number does, and answers the question when that is what is needed. And because the workflow is read-only, the flexibility carries no irreversibility risk that would argue for rigid control — which is what makes this a safe place to adopt it.

Why the other options are incorrect
More branches — each new branch handles one anticipated opening while customers keep producing unanticipated ones. Branch growth is combinatorial and always one conversation behind.

An intake form — fixes the sequence by forcing customers into it. The friction moves from the pipeline to the customer, and the 30% who open differently are precisely who it alienates.

Keyword classifier into three pipelines — a brittle router in front of three rigid pipelines: the second message can invalidate the choice, and a misrouted conversation is back to stalling.

Key Takeaway
Use model-driven loops where the order genuinely varies with the data — especially in read-only workflows. Fixed pipelines fit fixed-shape work.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — How tool use works → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works

-
Anthropic — How the agent loop works → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop

-
Anthropic — Tutorial: build a tool-using agent → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/build-a-tool-using-agent
option_feedback: The evidence says ordering is genuinely data-dependent: the right first step depends on what the customer supplies, which is exactly the condition where a model-driven loop beats a predetermined sequence. Given the tools and the goal, the model verifies first when the customer opens with identity, looks up first when they lead with the account number, and answers the question when that is what is needed — and because the workflow is read-only, the flexibility carries no irreversibility risk that would argue for rigid control.

Each new branch handles one anticipated opening, and customers keep producing unanticipated ones — branch growth is combinatorial and always one conversation behind. It rebuilds, by hand and per case, the adaptivity the model already has.

The form fixes the sequence by forcing customers into it — the friction moves from the pipeline to the customer, which is a deflection of the problem rather than a solution, and the 30% who open differently are precisely the ones a rigid intake alienates.
A keyword classifier on the first message is a brittle router in front of three rigid pipelines: the second message can invalidate the choice, and the misrouted conversation is back to stalling.

question:
An agricultural-trading firm extracts data from grain contracts. During extraction, a price-history lookup tool occasionally times out. The loop currently catches the exception and moves on without adding anything for that call to the conversation, after which the API rejects the next request, since the model's tool_use block was never answered.

How should the loop handle a failed tool call?
options: End the run immediately and surface the timeout to the operator for manual investigation
Return a tool_result for that tool_use with is_error set and a short description for the model
Retry the tool call silently inside the loop until it eventually succeeds
Remove the assistant's tool_use block from the history and leave the protocol expecting no result for it
answer: Return a tool_result for that tool_use with is_error set and a short description for the model
explanation:
This question tests failure handling inside the protocol's contract.

Every tool_use Must Be Answered
Swallowing the exception leaves a tool_use block unanswered, which is why the API rejects the next request. Failure is itself an answer: a tool_result carrying is_error and a short description satisfies the contract and puts the failure in front of the model — the component equipped to decide what it means here. Retry once, proceed without price history and note the gap, or flag the document.

Errors are information for the model, not exceptions for the loop to absorb.

Why the other options are incorrect
End the run and escalate — a timeout on one auxiliary lookup is recoverable, and ending the run converts it into a failed document plus an operator interruption. Escalation is for failures the loop and model cannot absorb.

Silent unbounded retry — turns a slow dependency into a hung pipeline, and the decision-maker never learns the lookup is struggling, so no adaptation happens while the loop spins.

Delete the tool_use block — makes the protocol happy by making the conversation false. The model remembers asking, sees neither answer nor error, and typically re-requests the same call — the same failure with a corrupted record.

Key Takeaway
Answer failed calls with a tool_result marked is_error and a brief description. Never leave a tool_use unanswered, and never edit history to hide one.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference
option_feedback: A timeout on one auxiliary lookup is a recoverable event, and ending the run converts it into a failed document and an operator interruption. Escalation is for failures the loop and model cannot absorb, not for the first transient hiccup.

The protocol expects every tool_use to be answered, and failure is an answer: a tool_result carrying is_error and a short message satisfies the contract and puts the failure in front of the model, which is the component equipped to decide what failure means here — retry once, proceed without price history and note the gap, or flag the document. Errors are information for the model, not exceptions for the loop to swallow.
An unbounded silent retry turns a slow dependency into a hung pipeline, and the model — the decision-maker — never learns the lookup is struggling, so no adaptation can happen while the loop spins.

Editing history to erase the request makes the protocol happy by making the conversation false: the model remembers asking, sees no answer and no error, and will typically re-request the same call — the same failure, now with a corrupted record.

question:
A real-estate analytics firm runs a research system: a coordinator dispatches three subagents — rentals, sales, and permits — and the sales subagent also merges all three outputs into the final brief, a duty it acquired "because it finishes last." Design review notes two symptoms: merge quality is poor, and the sales subagent's context is bloated with the other two domains' material.

What is the right change?
options: Increase the sales subagent's context budget so it can hold the other domains comfortably
Have each of the three subagents produce a full brief independently and keep the best one
Rotate the merge duty across the three subagents so no single one carries the load
Move the merge into the coordinator, which sees all outputs and the original question
answer: Move the merge into the coordinator, which sees all outputs and the original question
explanation:
This question tests why aggregation belongs to the coordinator — for structural reasons, not stylistic ones.

The Merger Needs the Cross-Cutting View
Aggregation requires the original question plus every specialist's output, and the coordinator is the only component that naturally holds both. The sales subagent merges badly because it is a domain specialist doing a hub's job: its prompt, context and expertise are shaped for sales analysis, and the other domains arrive as foreign bulk — which also explains the context bloat.

Moving the merge up fixes both symptoms at once, and the duty stops depending on which subagent happens to finish last.

Why the other options are incorrect
More context budget — makes the misassignment fit rather than work. The subagent still lacks the coordinator's view of the overall question, and the merge is still produced by a sales specialist moonlighting as an editor.

Three independent briefs, keep the best — triples the merging problem: each specialist writes outward from its own domain, someone must still reconcile them, and "pick the best" discards two-thirds of the research.

Rotate the merge duty — shares the flaw evenly. Whichever specialist holds it has the same wrong vantage point, plus the churn of a responsibility that moves every run.

Key Takeaway
Aggregation is a coordinator responsibility because only the coordinator sees the question and all outputs. Domain specialists merge from inside one domain.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Run agents in parallel → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents
option_feedback: More context makes the misassignment fit, not work: the subagent still lacks the coordinator's view of the overall question, and its merge is still produced by a sales specialist moonlighting as an editor.

Three independent briefs triple the merging problem — each specialist writes from its own domain outward, and someone must still reconcile them. "Pick the best" discards two-thirds of the research instead of synthesizing it.
Rotation shares the flaw evenly: whichever specialist holds the duty this run has the same wrong vantage point the sales subagent has today, plus the churn of a responsibility that moves every run.

Aggregation is a coordinator responsibility for structural reasons, not stylistic ones: the merger needs the original question and every specialist's output — the cross-cutting view — and the coordinator is the only component that naturally has it. The sales subagent merges badly because it is a domain specialist doing a hub's job: its prompt, context, and expertise are shaped for sales analysis, and the other domains' material arrives as foreign bulk. Moving the merge up fixes both symptoms at once.

question:
A media-analytics company's research coordinator reviews each draft and can request refinement rounds. Logs over a quarter: every query gets at least four refinement rounds, cost per query is 3.2× the single-pass baseline, and quality reviewers judged the first draft already sufficient in 60% of runs. The refinement requests are generic — "improve depth and coverage."

How should the loop's stopping behavior be designed?
options: Cap refinement at exactly two rounds for every single query, keeping the cost per query fully predictable
Evaluate each draft against explicit sufficiency criteria and exit when met, with a hard cap as backstop
Let the drafting subagent declare its own draft final when it judges further passes unnecessary
Remove the refinement loop entirely and ship the single-pass draft for every query
answer: Evaluate each draft against explicit sufficiency criteria and exit when met, with a hard cap as backstop
explanation:
This question tests loop governance: when not to refine.

Refinement Without an Exit Condition Always Refines
A generic "improve depth and coverage" request always finds something to improve, so every query gets four-plus rounds at 3.2× baseline cost — while reviewers judged the first draft already sufficient 60% of the time.

Giving the coordinator explicit sufficiency criteria — coverage of the query's parts, sourcing thresholds, unresolved-contradiction count — turns stopping into an evaluation. The 60% exit immediately; the rest iterate until they meet the bar; a hard cap bounds the pathological case. Iteration governed by measured sufficiency, not by momentum.

Why the other options are incorrect
Cap at exactly two rounds — encodes the average instead of the answer: still wasteful on the 60% that were done at draft one, and it truncates the genuinely hard queries that needed a fourth pass. Predictable cost, wrong quality on both tails.

Drafting subagent declares itself final — the least-placed judge. It optimizes for satisfying the refinement request and inherits whatever blind spot produced the gap. Evaluation belongs with the coordinator, against stated criteria.

Remove the loop — fixes cost by abandoning the 40% of queries whose first drafts were judged insufficient. The loop is not the problem; its missing exit condition is.

Key Takeaway
Give refinement loops explicit sufficiency criteria plus a hard cap. Fixed round counts and self-declared completion both substitute a guess for an evaluation.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: A uniform cap encodes the average instead of the answer: it still wastes a round or two on the 60% that were done at draft one and cuts off the genuinely hard queries that needed a fourth pass. Predictable cost, wrong quality on both tails.

The loop refines by default because nothing tells it what "done" means — a generic "improve" request always finds something to improve. Giving the coordinator explicit sufficiency criteria — coverage of the query's parts, sourcing thresholds, unresolved-contradiction count — turns the stop decision into an evaluation: the 60% whose first draft passes exit immediately, the rest iterate until they meet the bar, and the hard cap bounds the pathological case. Iteration should be governed by measured sufficiency, not by momentum.

The drafter is the least placed judge of its own sufficiency — it optimizes for satisfying the refinement request, and self-assessment inherits whatever blind spot produced the gap. Evaluation belongs with the coordinator, against stated criteria.
This fixes the cost by abandoning the 40% of queries whose first drafts were judged insufficient. The loop is not the problem; its missing exit condition is.

question:
An HR-software team defines two review subagents: a security reviewer and a general code reviewer. When developers ask for "a security-focused review of this diff," the coordinator selects the general reviewer roughly one time in five — the two descriptions overlap around the word "review." The team needs certainty today, whenever a developer wants the security specialist.

What should the team do?
options: Rewrite both descriptions to draw a sharper boundary between the two review domains
Remove the general reviewer so the security reviewer is the only possible selection
Invoke the security subagent explicitly by name in the request when it is the one wanted
Lower the coordinator's temperature so its subagent selection is more deterministic
answer: Invoke the security subagent explicitly by name in the request when it is the one wanted
explanation:
This question tests explicit invocation versus description-based selection, under a requirement for certainty today.

Naming Removes the Judgment
Description-based selection is a relevance judgment, and every judgment has a miss rate — here one in five, because both descriptions cluster around "review." Naming the subagent explicitly in the request takes the choice out of the coordinator's discretion entirely, which is precisely what a guarantee requires.

Description work remains worthwhile for the cases where the user does not name a specialist. But a guarantee needed now calls for the mechanism that provides one.

Why the other options are incorrect
Sharper descriptions — the strongest distractor and genuinely good practice. It raises the hit rate of a probabilistic process, and the requirement is not a better rate; it is certainty when the specialist is wanted.

Remove the general reviewer — buys certainty by amputating a capability used for everything that is not security review. The problem is selection, not the existence of two specialists.

Lower the temperature — makes selection more repeatable, not more correct. A coordinator that reliably picks the same wrong reviewer is worse, not better.

Key Takeaway
Invoke a subagent by name when selection must be guaranteed; improve descriptions for the unnamed case. Determinism about a choice is not the same as removing the choice.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Run agents in parallel → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents
option_feedback: Sharper descriptions raise the hit rate of a probabilistic process, and the requirement is not a better rate — it is certainty when the specialist is named. Description work complements explicit invocation; it cannot substitute for it.
Deleting the general reviewer buys certainty by amputating a capability the team uses for everything that is not security review. The problem is selection, not the existence of two specialists.

Description-based selection is a relevance judgment, and any judgment has a miss rate. Explicit invocation bypasses the judgment: naming the subagent in the request removes the choice from the coordinator's discretion, which is precisely what certainty today requires. Description improvements are worthwhile for the cases where the user does not name a specialist — but a guarantee needed now calls for the mechanism that provides one.

Temperature makes the selection more repeatable, not more correct — a coordinator that reliably picks the same wrong reviewer is worse, not better. Determinism about the choice is not the same as removing the choice.

question:
A publishing group's coordinator invoked an analyst subagent on Monday to profile the audiobook market — part one of a two-part analysis. On Tuesday it invoked the same subagent with the prompt "continue where you left off yesterday with part two." The output ignored part one entirely and re-derived overlapping material from scratch.

Why, and what is the fix?
options: Each invocation starts fresh; the coordinator must include part one's output, or a summary, in Tuesday's prompt
The subagent was invoked under a slightly different name; using the exact registered name lets it locate its Monday session
The subagent's prompt lacks an instruction to persist its findings between invocations; adding one enables continuity
The subagent's context window was too small to retain Monday's work; a larger model fixes the continuation
answer: Each invocation starts fresh; the coordinator must include part one's output, or a summary, in Tuesday's prompt
explanation:
This question tests the absence of memory across subagent invocations.

Each Invocation Is a New Instance
A subagent invocation starts with its AgentDefinition prompt and the task it was just given — nothing else. There is no continuity between Monday's invocation and Tuesday's, so "continue where you left off yesterday" refers to a history the Tuesday instance has never seen. Re-deriving overlapping material is the correct behavior given its actual inputs.

Continuity is the coordinator's job: it holds part one's output, so it passes that material (or a distilled version) into the second invocation's prompt, making the dependency explicit in the only channel the subagent has.

Why the other options are incorrect
Wrong name prevented session lookup — the name selects which AgentDefinition to instantiate; it is not an address into stored conversations. The exact name yields the same fresh instance with the same empty history.

Add a persistence instruction — an instruction cannot create a mechanism that does not exist. The subagent has nowhere durable to remember into for this purpose, and Tuesday's instance would not read it regardless.

Context window too small — retention across invocations is not a capacity problem. No window size carries context from a conversation that ended into one that has not started; Monday's work is absent, not compressed.

Key Takeaway
Subagent invocations are independent — pass prior output forward in the next invocation's prompt. Continuity is the coordinator's responsibility, not the subagent's memory.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Work with sessions (Agent SDK) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions
option_feedback: Subagent invocations are independent: each one starts with its AgentDefinition prompt and the task it was just given, with no memory of previous invocations. "Continue where you left off" refers to a history the Tuesday instance has never seen. Continuity is the coordinator's job — it holds part one's output, so it passes that material (or a distilled version) into the second invocation's prompt, making the dependency explicit in the only channel the subagent has.
The name selects which AgentDefinition to instantiate; it is not an address into stored conversations. The exact name would have produced the same fresh instance with the same empty history.

An instruction cannot create a persistence mechanism that does not exist — the subagent has nowhere durable to "remember" into, and Tuesday's instance would not read it regardless. The instruction would be a wish, not a capability.
Retention across invocations is not a capacity problem: no window size carries context from a conversation that ended into one that has not started. Monday's work is absent, not compressed.

question:
A bank's support coordinator spawns a fraud-triage subagent mid-conversation. A new engineer wants to reason precisely about what that subagent can actually see.

Which TWO does the spawned subagent receive? (Select TWO.)
options: The parent's full conversation history with the customer
Its own system prompt, as defined in its AgentDefinition
The outputs of sibling subagents dispatched in the same phase
The task prompt composed for this specific invocation
The parent agent's system prompt, inherited automatically
answer: Its own system prompt, as defined in its AgentDefinition
The task prompt composed for this specific invocation
explanation:
This question tests exactly what crosses into a spawned subagent.

Two Inputs, and Only Two

-
Its own system prompt from the AgentDefinition — standing identity, instructions and constraints.

-
The task prompt for this invocation — what the parent composed for this specific job.

That is the whole picture. Anything else the subagent needs must be placed into that task prompt deliberately, which is why handoff design matters: the isolation is complete by default.

Why the other options are incorrect
The parent's conversation history — does not flow into subagents. That isolation is a feature, keeping the subagent's context clean and focused; if the triage needs three facts from the customer conversation, the coordinator writes those three facts into the task prompt.

Sibling subagents' outputs — siblings are equally isolated from each other, with no shared blackboard. Cross-subagent information moves only through the coordinator.

The parent's system prompt — configures the parent. The subagent has its own from its own definition; inheritance would defeat the purpose of defining specialists differently.

A subagent sees its AgentDefinition prompt plus its invocation prompt. No parent history, no parent system prompt, no sibling outputs — pass what it needs explicitly.

-

question:
A platform team's workspace-management agent maintains build environments. Business rule: delete_build_workspace may run for a workspace only after export_artifacts has completed for it — deletion first destroys the artifacts irrecoverably. Export and deletion are separate tools, and the rule must hold in every session, without exception.

Where should the ordering constraint live?
options: In the system prompt, as a rule stating that the artifact export must always precede the deletion
In the order of the tools array, listing export_artifacts ahead of delete_build_workspace
In the deletion tool's description, noting that artifacts must be exported first
In application code: a gate refusing delete_build_workspace until that workspace's state shows a completed export
answer: In application code: a gate refusing delete_build_workspace until that workspace's state shows a completed export
explanation:
This question tests where an ordering constraint must live when the wording is absolute.

"Every Session, Without Exception" Means Code
Deleting build artifacts before exporting them destroys them irrecoverably, and the rule must hold universally. That is a determinism requirement, and determinism lives in application code: the export tool's success records completion for that workspace, and a gate refuses delete_build_workspace until the state shows it.

However the model behaves, the invalid order cannot execute — and the refusal can carry a reason so the model recovers gracefully rather than stalling.

Why the other options are incorrect
System-prompt rule — followed with high probability, and the requirement has no tolerance for the remainder. One unusual session that reorders the calls destroys artifacts nothing can restore.

Order of the tools array — the array declares availability; its ordering carries no execution semantics whatsoever. The model does not read list position as sequence, so this encodes the constraint nowhere.

Note in the deletion tool's description — descriptions inform selection reasoning, which is worth having, but they are read rather than enforced. Nothing stops a deletion call that arrives first.

Key Takeaway
Encode absolute ordering rules as state gates in code. Prompts, tool ordering and descriptions all shift probabilities; only code bounds outcomes.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Hooks reference → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks

-
Anthropic — Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks

-
Anthropic — Configure permissions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions
option_feedback: A prompt rule is followed with high probability, and the requirement has no tolerance for the remainder. One unusual session that reorders the calls destroys artifacts nothing can restore.
The tools array declares what is available; its ordering carries no execution semantics whatsoever. The model does not read position in the list as sequence, so this encodes the constraint nowhere.
Descriptions inform the model's selection reasoning — good practice, worth having — but they are read, not enforced. Nothing stops a deletion call that arrives before the export ran.

"Must hold in every session, without exception" is a determinism requirement, and determinism lives in code. The application tracks per-workspace state — export_artifacts succeeding records the completion — and the gate refuses the deletion until the state shows the prerequisite ran. However the model behaves, the invalid order cannot execute, and the refusal can carry a reason so the model recovers gracefully. Prompt and description guidance shift probabilities; a state-checking gate bounds outcomes.

question:
An auto-parts platform uses an agent for an ORM migration. Mid-task it hits a wall: a circular dependency involving generated code that its two restructuring attempts could not break. Policy says hand off to a senior developer.

What should the handoff deliver?
options: The full session transcript, letting the developer see everything that happened along the way
The current diff and nothing else, since the code state is what the developer works from
A structured package: attempts and dead ends, suspected root cause, current change state, remaining risks

question:
A construction-software team requires all agent-created scratch and debug files to live under workspace/scratch/. Today a PreToolUse hook denies any write outside it; transcripts show the agent then trying several alternative paths, wasting three to five turns per incident before landing in the right place.

What is the better hook design?
options: A PreToolUse hook rewriting the write's target path into workspace/scratch/ via updatedInput
Keep the deny hook and add the path rule to CLAUDE.md so the agent's retries converge faster
Replace the pre-hook with a PostToolUse hook that moves stray files into workspace/scratch/ after they are written
Replace Write for this agent with a custom write_scratch tool that only accepts paths inside the sandbox
answer: A PreToolUse hook rewriting the write's target path into workspace/scratch/ via updatedInput
explanation:
This question tests a PreToolUse capability beyond allow/deny: modifying the pending call.

Redirect Instead of Deny
Hooks can rewrite a pending call's input. Rewriting the write's target path into workspace/scratch/ turns every off-policy write into an on-policy one in a single step: the file lands where policy wants it, the agent's intent is preserved, and the three-to-five-turn retry dance disappears because there is nothing to retry.

Denial is the right shape for calls that should not happen; redirection is the right shape for calls that should happen differently.

Why the other options are incorrect
Deny plus a CLAUDE.md path rule — improves the agent's guessing rather than removing the guesswork. Some turns are still spent failing, and the hook still rejects work it could simply have corrected.

PostToolUse move after the write — leaves a window in which the stray file exists in the wrong place, breaks the agent's own record of where it wrote things (later reads target the old path), and turns one operation into a write-then-move pair that can race with anything watching those directories.

A custom write_scratch tool — can enforce the path while swapping a transparent, general mechanism for new surface area: the agent must learn to prefer it, every other write path still needs guarding, and the team maintains a tool to solve what one hook line solves for all writes.

Key Takeaway
Use updatedInput in PreToolUse to correct a call rather than rejecting it. Deny what must not happen; redirect what should happen differently.

-

question:
A freight-rail software group has a hard rule: agents must never modify files under infrastructure/prod-config/. The rule is stated prominently in CLAUDE.md. Last month a nightly claude -p pipeline modified a prod-config file anyway; the change reached staging before being caught.

How should the rule be enforced?
options: Move the rule to the first line of CLAUDE.md and mark it as critical, non-negotiable policy
Add a PreToolUse hook that denies any edit or write targeting infrastructure/prod-config/ paths
Append the rule to the nightly job's prompt, letting headless runs receive it explicitly each night
Add a CI check that rejects any commit containing changes under infrastructure/prod-config/
answer: Add a PreToolUse hook that denies any edit or write targeting infrastructure/prod-config/ paths
explanation:
This question tests enforcement surface — and the incident happened in a headless run.

CLAUDE.md Is Context, Not Configuration
The documentation is explicit: memory files are treated as context rather than enforced configuration, and to block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook. The prod-config incident is that distinction in practice.

A hook intercepts the tool call itself and denies it in code, identically in interactive sessions and in headless -p runs — which is exactly where the failure occurred. The rule stops being a request to the model and becomes a property of the system.

Why the other options are incorrect
Move it to line one and mark it critical — placement and emphasis raise the probability of compliance; the incident shows the probability was already high and still not one. The mechanism that failed was instruction.

Append to the nightly job's prompt — duplicates guidance into a second probabilistic channel for one job, leaving every other session uncovered and enforcement still resting on the model honoring text.

CI check on commits — worthwhile defense in depth, and it fires after the modification exists. The working tree was already wrong, and anything the pipeline does with built artifacts before commit-time rejection still happens.

Key Takeaway
Enforce "never" rules with PreToolUse hooks, which apply in headless runs too. CLAUDE.md guides; hooks enforce; CI checks catch what already happened.

question:
An agricultural-technology buyer must compare five irrigation-equipment vendors — each with a large, distinct document corpus — and deliver a comparative assessment on reliability, cost, support, and integration.

Which TWO elements make the decomposition sound? (Select TWO.)
options: One subagent per vendor, run in parallel, each producing a profile from that vendor's corpus
One subagent per criterion, each reading all five corpora to compare that dimension across vendors
A single agent reading all five corpora sequentially, keeping everything in one view
One subagent per vendor pair, each directly comparing its two vendors head to head
A shared profile template — the four criteria, defined identically — that every vendor subagent fills
answer: One subagent per vendor, run in parallel, each producing a profile from that vendor's corpus
A shared profile template — the four criteria, defined identically — that every vendor subagent fills
explanation:
This question tests decomposition for a comparison task — partition plus the thing that makes the results comparable.

Partition to Match the Data, Standardize to Enable the Merge

-
One subagent per vendor, in parallel — the corpora are large and disjoint, so the natural partition is by vendor: each subagent reads one corpus once, and no subagent's context carries another vendor's bulk.

-
A shared profile template — the comparison depends on the profiles being comparable. All five subagents answer the same four criteria, defined identically, so the final comparison works from aligned inputs rather than five differently-shaped essays.

Why the other options are incorrect
One subagent per criterion — each reads all five corpora, so five large corpora get re-read four times over. The duplicated retrieval is exactly what vendor-partitioning avoids, and each criterion agent still faces the cross-corpus context problem.

A single agent reading everything — the monolith the decomposition exists to escape: capacity pressure, no parallelism, and later vendors read with less room than earlier ones.

One subagent per vendor pair — ten runs for five vendors, each re-reading two corpora, producing ten relative judgments that still need reconciling into one ranking. Quadratic cost, output that resists merging.

Key Takeaway
Partition along the data's natural boundaries and standardize the output shape so results merge. Comparison quality depends on both.

question:
A bank's migration has two sub-tasks. First: rename a logging function across roughly 300 call sites — mechanical, identical everywhere, verifiable by compile and tests. Second: split a tangled interest-calculation module whose pieces interact in ways that emerge only during the work.

How should the two sub-tasks be approached?
options: Adaptive agent-led decomposition for both — a capable agent handles mechanical work just as well
A scripted, fixed procedure for both, since migrations reward determinism end to end
Adaptive decomposition for the rename; a scripted procedure for the module split
Scripted bulk edit for the rename verified by compile and tests; adaptive decomposition for the split
answer: Scripted bulk edit for the rename verified by compile and tests; adaptive decomposition for the split
explanation:
This question tests matching method to sub-task within a single migration.

Opposite Ends of the Predictability Spectrum
The rename is uniform, identical everywhere, and mechanically verifiable — a scripted bulk edit confirmed by compile and tests is faster, cheaper and more reliable than judgment applied 300 times.

The module split is the opposite: its structure is discovered during the work, so it needs adaptive decomposition — investigate, carve off a safe seam, re-evaluate as interactions surface.

Choosing per sub-task, rather than one method for the whole migration, is the architectural decision.

Why the other options are incorrect
Adaptive for both — spends judgment on 300 identical edits: slower, costlier, and 300 opportunities for creative variation in a task whose virtue is uniformity.

Scripted for both — no fixed procedure can enumerate steps that only emerge mid-work. Scripting the split yields either a script that breaks on the first surprise or one so vague it scripts nothing.

Adaptive rename, scripted split — inverts the match on both sides at once: ceremony for the mechanical half, rigidity for the emergent half.

Key Takeaway
Script the mechanical and verifiable; use adaptive decomposition where structure emerges during the work. One migration can legitimately need both.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows

-
Anthropic — Common workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/common-workflows

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Adaptive handling of 300 identical edits spends judgment where none is needed — slower, costlier, and with 300 opportunities for creative variation in a task whose virtue is uniformity.
No fixed procedure can enumerate steps that only emerge mid-work. Scripting the module split means either a script that breaks on the first surprise or one so vague it scripts nothing.
This inverts the match on both sides at once: ceremony for the mechanical half, rigidity for the emergent half — each sub-task gets exactly the approach the other needed.

The two sub-tasks sit at opposite ends of the predictability spectrum, and the decomposition should match each. The rename is uniform and mechanically verifiable — a scripted transformation applied everywhere and confirmed by compile and tests is faster, cheaper, and more reliable than judgment applied 300 times. The module split is the opposite: its structure is discovered during the work, so it needs a plan that can reshape itself as interactions surface — investigate, carve off a safe seam, re-evaluate. Matching method to sub-task, rather than choosing one method for the whole migration, is the architectural decision.

question:
Last week, a marketplace developer's Claude Code session analyzed 90 files for a payment-flow audit — an expensive build-up of context. Git history shows exactly 6 of those files have changed since. She wants to continue the audit today.

What should she do?
options: Start a fresh session and have it re-analyze all 90 files so nothing at all is stale
Resume the session and continue the audit where it stopped
Resume the session and name the 6 changed files for re-examination before continuing
Start a fresh session and paste in a written summary of last week's audit findings
answer: Resume the session and name the 6 changed files for re-examination before continuing
explanation:
This question tests resumption economics: how much of the session is still true.

93% Current, and Git Names the Rest
84 of 90 file analyses still hold, and git identifies exactly which 6 are stale. Resuming preserves the expensive accumulated understanding; naming the 6 changed files repairs the stale part surgically — six re-reads instead of ninety.

Spend effort proportional to what actually changed: keep what is valid, refresh precisely what is not.

Why the other options are incorrect
Fresh session, re-analyze all 90 — prices the update at the cost of the original, and ignores information that is available and precise.

Resume without disclosure — the closest wrong answer: resuming is right. But the session then reasons from six silently outdated analyses, and conclusions touching those files inherit the staleness with nothing to flag it.

Fresh session with a written summary — a summary is a lossy shadow of the session's actual context; the details that make follow-up questions answerable are exactly what summaries drop. It spends more to preserve less.

Key Takeaway
Resume and name what changed. Full re-analysis wastes valid context; silent resumption carries stale context forward as if it were current.

-

-
Anthropic — CLI reference → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference
option_feedback: A full re-analysis prices the update at the cost of the original — ninety files re-read to refresh six. The information needed to be surgical exists and is ignored.

Resuming without disclosure leaves the session reasoning from six silently outdated analyses; conclusions touching those files inherit the staleness, and nothing in the session knows to doubt them. The resume is right; the missing step is telling it what moved.

The session's context is 93% current — 84 of 90 analyses still hold — and git names exactly which 6 are stale. Resuming preserves the expensive accumulated understanding, and pointing the session at the changed files repairs the stale part surgically: it re-reads six files instead of ninety. question:
A telecom developer's session holds a long dependency investigation. She wants to try a risky upgrade path — but if it goes badly, she needs the original investigation line intact to continue from.

What should she do?
options: Run /compact first, then try the upgrade in the compacted session
Fork the session and try the upgrade in the fork, leaving the original resumable
Open a second terminal and continue the same session there for the risky attempt
Copy the session's transcript file into a backup directory before proceeding
answer: Fork the session and try the upgrade in the fork, leaving the original resumable
explanation:
This question tests what forking is for.

Branch the Risky Attempt, Keep the Original
Forking gives the risky upgrade a divergent copy that inherits all the investigation context, while the original line stays untouched and resumable. If the upgrade goes badly, the fork is abandoned and nothing of value is lost.

Why the other options are incorrect
/compact first — compaction summarizes to free space; it does not create a second line of work. The risky attempt still unfolds inside the only copy of the session.

A second terminal on the same session — two terminals on one session are one conversation, not a branch. The risky turns land in the original's history, contaminating exactly the line she wanted to protect.

Copy the transcript file — a manual artifact, not the mechanism for branching work. Forking produces a real, resumable second session.

Key Takeaway
Fork to try something risky while keeping the original resumable. Compaction frees space, resuming continues one line, forking creates a branch.

-
Anthropic — Manage sessions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions

-
Anthropic — Checkpointing → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing

-
Anthropic — Work with sessions (Agent SDK) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions
option_feedback: Compaction summarizes to free space — it does not create a second line of work. The risky attempt would still unfold inside the only copy of the session.

Forking exists for exactly this: it branches the session, giving the risky attempt a divergent copy that inherits all the investigation context, while the original line stays untouched and resumable. If the upgrade goes badly, the fork is abandoned and nothing of value is lost.
Two terminals on the same session are one conversation, not a branch: the risky attempt's turns land in the original's history, contaminating the line she wanted to protect.

question:
A logistics platform team is writing the description for an internal get_shipment_status tool and has four drafts on the table.

Which draft is the well-designed description?
options: "The fastest, most powerful way to track shipments — handles everything your workflow needs with enterprise-grade reliability"
"Gets shipment info from the tracking system for a given shipment"
"Queries shp_status_v3 via cache-aside read through the Redis tier; joins carrier_events on shipment_fk; 250ms p99; retries with jitter on 5xx"
"Returns current status for one shipment. Input: tracking ID like TRK-8341-XC. Not for shipments older than 90 days — use archive search for those"
answer: "Returns current status for one shipment. Input: tracking ID like TRK-8341-XC. Not for shipments older than 90 days — use archive search for those"
explanation:
This question tests what a tool description is for — its reader is the model deciding whether and how to call.

Four Things a Good Description Carries
Draft D supplies all of them: what the tool does, the input format with a concrete example (TRK-8341-XC), an explicit boundary (not for shipments older than 90 days), and where that adjacent need goes instead (archive search). Every sentence changes the model's behavior — that is a description working as an interface contract.

Why the other options are incorrect
Marketing language — carries zero selection information: nothing about inputs, outputs or boundaries. A model reading it learns the tool is enthusiastic about itself.

"Gets shipment info" — accurate but underspecified. The model must guess input format, coverage and boundaries, and guesses are where misselection and malformed calls come from.

Implementation internals — table names, cache tiers and latency percentiles describe how the tool works, not when to use it or what to pass. It never addresses its actual audience.

Key Takeaway
Describe purpose, input format with an example, boundaries, and where out-of-scope requests should go. Internals and marketing both fail the model that has to choose.

-

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use

Accurate but underspecified — "shipment info" leaves the model to guess input format, coverage, and boundaries, and guesses are where misselection and malformed calls come from.

question:

Contracts should be explicit where the misuse happens.

question:
A document-extraction platform's tools return {"error": "..."} with a prose message for every failure. Sampled transcripts show the agent mishandling two of three failure types: it retried a malformed-input error unchanged three times, and it gave up permanently on a rate-limit error that would have cleared in seconds.

How should the tools' error responses be designed?
options: Standard HTTP-style numeric status codes, letting the agent apply well-known and long-standing semantics
Write longer, more explanatory prose messages so the agent understands each failure
A structured taxonomy — transient, validation, business — with branchable fields like retryable
A single boolean field, retryable, set true or false on every failure the tools return
answer: A structured taxonomy — transient, validation, business — with branchable fields like retryable
explanation: The two misbehaviors are one defect: the error format does not say what kind of failure occurred, so the agent cannot match response to failure type. A small taxonomy fixes the mapping — transient means retry with backoff; validation means fix the input before trying again, with the field naming what was wrong; business means stop retrying and handle the refusal. Structured, enumerable categories drive the branch reliably; the agent's recovery becomes a function of the error's declared type rather than a guess about prose.

Which TWO agent behaviors does good error design enable? (Select TWO.)
options: Switching to a different MCP server when a tool reports any error
Editing the tool's input schema at runtime so the failure cannot recur
Automatically retrying transient failures, with backoff, without human involvement
Extending the tool's execution timeout dynamically for slow operations
Explaining a business-rule refusal to the customer accurately, without pointless retries
answer: Automatically retrying transient failures, with backoff, without human involvement

Both behaviors depend entirely on the error saying what kind of failure occurred; both are impossible against an opaque error string.

Timeouts are infrastructure configuration owned by the integration, not a dial the agent turns per call. Error design shapes what the agent does next, not the transport's limits.

When a failure declares itself transient, the agent can retry with backoff on its own — the failure self-heals invisibly instead of surfacing to anyone. question:
An airline's customer-support agent handles password resets and booking status using 6 tools from the company's MCP server. Last quarter the server gained 9 admin tools — refund overrides, account merges — for the internal-operations team. Since then, the support deployment's tool-misselection rate rose from 2% to 11%. Support agents never legitimately use the admin tools.

What should the team change?
options: Serve role-scoped subsets: support mounts only its 6 tools; the ops deployment keeps the full set
Reorder the tool list so the 6 support tools come first and the admin tools sit at the end
Improve the 9 admin-tool descriptions with explicit "for internal operations only" boundary clauses
Reduce the support agent's temperature so its tool selection is more deterministic
answer: Serve role-scoped subsets: support mounts only its 6 tools; the ops deployment keeps the full set
explanation: The support role's misselection quintupled because 9 never-legitimate candidates entered its selection space — every request now weighs 15 tools where 6 are the entire real answer set. The fix is scoping by role at configuration time: each deployment exposes exactly the tools its job requires, so the admin tools are not lower-ranked candidates for support, they are not candidates at all. The 2% baseline returns because the selection problem returns to its original size — and ops loses nothing.
option_feedback: The support role's misselection quintupled because 9 never-legitimate candidates entered its selection space — every request now weighs 15 tools where 6 are the entire real answer set. The fix is scoping by role at configuration time: each deployment exposes exactly the tools its job requires, so the admin tools are not lower-ranked candidates for support, they are not candidates at all. The 2% baseline returns because the selection problem returns to its original size — and ops loses nothing.
Position in the tool list is not priority — all 15 remain live candidates occupying context, and reordering communicates nothing the model treats as scope.

This is the almost-right answer: better boundary descriptions are exactly the fix when a tool is a legitimate-but-confusable candidate. Here the admin tools should never be chosen by this role, so the correct amount of their presence is zero — a description that argues against selecting a tool is still weaker than the tool's absence, and it still spends context on tools this deployment cannot use.
Lower temperature makes selection more repeatable, including repeatably wrong. The candidate set, not sampling variance, is what changed when the misselection rate rose.

question:
A real-estate firm's lease assistant does two jobs in one conversation: it answers questions about lease documents in prose, and it performs structured extraction when asked. The team set tool_choice to {"type": "any"} to guarantee structured output — and now 40% of plain questions come back as spurious extraction calls instead of answers.

What should the team do?
options: Keep "any" and add a no_extraction tool that the model calls for conversational turns
Keep forcing tools, but route requests through a keyword classifier that picks the tool_choice per request
Keep "any" and have the model answer questions inside a notes field of the extraction tool's schema
Use "auto" so the model extracts when extraction is requested and answers in text otherwise
answer: Use "auto" so the model extracts when extraction is requested and answers in text otherwise
explanation: The workload is genuinely mixed, and "auto" is the setting that matches: the model calls the extraction tool when the request is an extraction and produces a normal text answer when the request is a question. The team forced "any" to guarantee structure and thereby forbade the text half of the assistant's job — the 40% spurious calls are the model complying with a constraint that removed its correct behavior. Where a turn must produce structure, that request can force the specific tool; the conversation default belongs on "auto".
option_feedback: A sink tool absorbs the forced call but produces no answer — the user asked a question, and the turn ends in an empty tool invocation. This pattern suits pipelines where every input must yield a disposition, not conversations where half the correct outputs are prose.

A keyword router re-implements, badly, the judgment "auto" already provides: ambiguous phrasings misroute, the classifier needs maintenance forever, and the architecture gains a component whose entire job is compensating for a misconfigured parameter.

Smuggling prose through a schema field abuses the structure the schema exists to guarantee — downstream consumers now parse answers out of extraction records, and every "extraction" from a question turn is a fake record polluting the pipeline.

question:
A payroll-software team shares an MCP server through a .mcp.json committed at the repository root. A developer who just cloned the repo reports the server's tools are missing from her Claude Code sessions, though everything works for teammates. Her config file is identical to theirs — same commit.

What does she need to do?
options: Re-add the server at user scope so it registers under her account
Approve the project server on her machine — project servers need per-user consent before activating
Delete and recreate the .mcp.json entry, forcing her client to re-read the configuration from scratch
Ask the author to convert the server to user scope instead, keeping repository configuration out of it
answer: Approve the project server on her machine — project servers need per-user consent before activating
explanation: Project-scope servers arrive with the repository — which means arriving from other people — so Claude Code treats them as untrusted until the individual user approves them: a security gate against a cloned repo silently wiring an arbitrary server into your sessions. Her config is fine and identical to everyone's; what differs is that her machine has not yet granted consent. Approving the project server when prompted (or resetting the project's approval choices so the prompt reappears) activates the tools.
option_feedback: A user-scope duplicate would work while creating a second registration of the same server that drifts from the committed one — and it misdiagnoses the situation: nothing is wrong with the project entry she already has.

Project-scope servers arrive with the repository — which means arriving from other people — so Claude Code treats them as untrusted until the individual user approves them: a security gate against a cloned repo silently wiring an arbitrary server into your sessions. The entry is not corrupted, and recreating it changes nothing about the approval state — the same consent gate greets the recreated entry, because the gate is per-user, not per-file.

Converting to user scope abandons the team's single committed source of configuration and makes every developer maintain their own copy — dismantling the sharing mechanism to avoid a one-time approval step.

question:
A manufacturing team's internal MCP server offers four capabilities: a read-only catalog of machine-configuration schemas; creating maintenance tickets; updating sensor thresholds; and triggering recalibration runs. All four shipped as tools. In practice, agents call the catalog tool in exploratory bursts — five to ten calls at the start of most sessions — just to learn what configurations exist.

How should the four capabilities be classified?
options: The schema catalog becomes a resource; the three state-changing capabilities remain tools
All four become resources, since resources are cheaper than tool calls
All four remain tools, with a caching layer to absorb the repeated catalog reads
The catalog stays a tool and is additionally exposed as a resource, letting consumers pick either
answer: The schema catalog becomes a resource; the three state-changing capabilities remain tools
explanation: The MCP primitives encode a control-model distinction: tools are model-controlled actions — the model decides during reasoning to do something — while resources are application-controlled context: reference data the client can provide to a session. The catalog is reference data by nature; agents burst-calling it to orient themselves shows it is being consumed as context through an action-shaped hole. As a resource, the catalog can be furnished to sessions directly, the exploratory call storms disappear, and what remains as tools is exactly the set that changes the world — tickets, thresholds, recalibrations — which is what should sit behind model-initiated invocation.
option_feedback: The MCP primitives encode a control-model distinction: tools are model-controlled actions — the model decides during reasoning to do something — while resources are application-controlled context: reference data the client can provide to a session. The catalog is reference data by nature; agents burst-calling it to orient themselves shows it is being consumed as context through an action-shaped hole. As a resource, the catalog can be furnished to sessions directly, the exploratory call storms disappear, and what remains as tools is exactly the set that changes the world — tickets, thresholds, recalibrations — which is what should sit behind model-initiated invocation.

The three mutations are actions with effects and arguments; a resource cannot express "create," "update," or "trigger." Classifying by cost instead of by control model breaks the state-changing capabilities entirely.

Caching cheapens the symptom and keeps the misclassification: the model still spends turns and tool calls acquiring context that the application could simply provide, and every session still starts with an orientation dance.
Dual exposure creates a permanent ambiguity — two paths to the same data, selection noise for the model, and two surfaces to maintain — to avoid deciding what the capability actually is.

question:
An energy company's operations staff run a standardized "shift handover summary" workflow several times daily: same template, one argument — the shift ID. They want it triggered explicitly by the operator from their MCP-connected client, never fired by the model on its own judgment, and standardized for everyone connecting to the server.

Which MCP primitive should the server expose for this?
options: A tool the model calls when it detects handover intent in the conversation
A resource containing the template text for the model to read and follow
A prompt — a user-invoked template that takes the shift ID as an argument
A skill installed in each operator's personal skills directory
answer: A prompt — a user-invoked template that takes the shift ID as an argument
explanation: The three MCP primitives differ by who controls invocation, and this workflow is user-controlled by requirement: the operator explicitly triggers it, with an argument, and the model should never initiate it. That is the prompt primitive precisely — a server-defined, parameterized template the user invokes deliberately from their client, standardized once on the server for every connected consumer. Requirement and primitive match exactly.
option_feedback: Tools are model-controlled — invoked when the model judges them relevant — which inverts the stated requirement. Intent detection firing the workflow on its own judgment is the behavior the operators explicitly do not want.

A resource can carry the template's text, but resources are data: nothing about them is invocable, takes a shift ID, or gives the operator a trigger. The workflow would depend on the model noticing the template and improvising the invocation the prompt primitive provides natively.

question:
A construction-software repo's convention says repository classes live in files named *Repository.ts. As part of an audit, Claude Code must produce the list of files whose names follow that pattern, across all packages, to compare against the class inventory.

Which retrieval is right for this step?
options: Grep for "class \w+Repository" across the repository's TypeScript source
Read the src directory listings package by package and collect matching names
Bash with find . -name "*Repository.ts" piped through sort
Glob with the pattern **/*Repository.ts
answer: Glob with the pattern **/*Repository.ts
explanation: The question is a filename-pattern question, and Glob is the tool whose entire job is matching file paths against patterns: one call, every package, exactly the files whose names match. The audit's comparison step needs the name-based list specifically — Glob produces precisely that set, cleanly and completely.
option_feedback: Grep matches file contents, which answers a different question: where Repository classes are declared. For this step that set is the wrong one — a misnamed file declaring a Repository class would appear in Grep's results and belongs, by definition, on the other side of the comparison.
Manual directory reading across packages spends many tool calls and context on what one pattern match returns, with omission risk at every level of nesting.

question:
A pharmaceutical distributor's internal-tools agent just used Edit to change a discount-tier boundary in the pricing module. The Edit succeeded. The task is not time-critical, and a relevant test suite exists.

What should the agent do before treating the task as done?
options: Run the pricing tests via Bash and read the output, proceeding only on green
Treat the successful Edit as completion, since the intended change was applied exactly
Re-Read the modified file to confirm the new boundary value appears in the code
Report the change to the user and ask them to confirm it looks correct
answer: Run the pricing tests via Bash and read the output, proceeding only on green
explanation: An agentic loop's iteration is not complete at the mutation — it is complete at the verification. The Edit's success means the text changed as specified; whether the change is correct is a behavioral question, and the test suite is the ground truth available for it. Running the tests and reading the actual output either confirms completion or hands the agent the failure information for its next iteration. Executing the verification is part of the work.
option_feedback: An agentic loop's iteration is not complete at the mutation — it is complete at the verification. The Edit's success means the text changed as specified; whether the change is correct is a behavioral question, and the test suite is the ground truth available for it. Running the tests and reading the actual output either confirms completion or hands the agent the failure information for its next iteration. Executing the verification is part of the work.
