Re-reading confirms what the Edit result already guaranteed — the text is present. It observes the same property, characters in a file, and still says nothing about whether pricing now behaves correctly.
Handing verification to the user outsources work the agent can do itself in seconds — and "looks correct" by eyeball is weaker evidence than the test suite the agent declined to run.

question:
A marketplace developer keeps personal working context for one repository — her sandbox URLs, test-account IDs, and a note about her local proxy setup. Teammates must never see it in the repo, and it must not follow her into the other projects she works on.

Where does this content belong?
options: Her user-level CLAUDE.md in ~/.claude, where personal working context belongs
The project's CLAUDE.md, alongside the team's shared project context
A CLAUDE.local.md in the project, left out of version control
A rules file under the project's .claude/rules directory with narrow globs
answer: A CLAUDE.local.md in the project, left out of version control
explanation: The content is personal and project-specific — the intersection the local memory file exists for. CLAUDE.local.md sits in the project so it loads for her sessions there, stays out of version control so teammates never receive it, and belongs to that one repository so her sandbox URLs do not leak into unrelated projects.
option_feedback: The user-level file follows her everywhere — its contents load in every project she opens. Sandbox URLs and test accounts for one marketplace repo become noise, or worse, misleading context, in every other codebase she touches.

question:
A payroll platform's monorepo contains a legacy/ area with unusual conventions — custom serialization, forbidden refactors. Its owning team wants three properties: the conventions cost zero tokens in sessions that never touch legacy/, they load when work happens there, and they live next to the code they govern so the owning team maintains them naturally.

What is the right mechanism?
options: A CLAUDE.md inside legacy/, loading on demand when Claude works with files in that subtree
A clearly marked legacy section in the root CLAUDE.md, prominent enough to stand out
A rules file in .claude/rules with paths ["legacy/**"] scoping it to that tree
A legacy-conventions skill that Claude invokes whenever it recognizes work on the legacy area
answer: A CLAUDE.md inside legacy/, loading on demand when Claude works with files in that subtree
explanation: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files have exactly the load semantics requested — they are pulled in on demand when Claude works with files in that part of the tree, costing nothing elsewhere — and they satisfy the third property by construction: the file sits inside legacy/, beside the code, owned and edited by the team that owns the directory. All three requirements land with one mechanism.
option_feedback: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files have exactly the load semantics requested — they are pulled in on demand when Claude works with files in that part of the tree, costing nothing elsewhere — and they satisfy the third property by construction: the file sits inside legacy/, beside the code, owned and edited by the team that owns the directory. question:
A hotel-booking platform team moved four long how-to guides out of CLAUDE.md and into skills. Baseline token usage per session dropped sharply, yet sessions still apply the guides correctly when relevant tasks come up. A developer asks how both can be true.

What is the explanation?
options: The migration truncated the guides, so there is simply less content to load
Skill bodies load only when a skill is used; by default only its name and description are present
Sessions read the guides from disk on demand without that content counting toward the context window
Skill bodies load fully at session start but are evicted after first use, and never show in baselines
answer: Skill bodies load only when a skill is used; by default only its name and description are present
explanation: This is the cost model difference between the two mechanisms. CLAUDE.md is standing memory: its entire content enters every session's context at start. A skill contributes only its lightweight metadata — name and description — until it is actually used, at which point the body loads. Four long guides therefore vanished from the per-session baseline while remaining fully available on demand: the sessions that need a guide pay for it then, and only then.
option_feedback: The guides work when invoked, which they would not if the content had been cut. Nothing was lost — its loading became conditional.

question:

Mention the skill's existence in the conversation at the start of every release discussion, manually
Rewrite the description to state what the skill does and when it applies — release prep, checklists

explanation: Autonomous invocation is driven by the description: Claude weighs the conversation against each skill's stated purpose and invokes what matches. "Helper utilities for the team" matches nothing — it names no task, no trigger, no domain, so no release conversation ever looks relevant to it. A description that says what the skill does and when it applies gives the matching process something to match, which is the entire discovery mechanism for model-initiated use.

question:
A freight company's changelog skill runs inside CI. Security requirement: while this skill is active, Bash must be unavailable — even if conversation content asks for it. The team set allowed-tools: [Read, Grep] in the skill's frontmatter, believing it restricts the skill to those tools. During a review, Bash demonstrably ran mid-skill.

What is the correct configuration?
options: disallowed-tools: [Bash] — the field that actually removes a tool during the skill
The same allowed-tools list, with Bash moved explicitly to the end as lowest priority
A sentence in the skill body: "Never use Bash while this skill is active"
Remove allowed-tools entirely so no tool is pre-approved for the skill
answer: disallowed-tools: [Bash] — the field that actually removes a tool during the skill
explanation: The two fields do different jobs, and the team used the wrong one. allowed-tools pre-approves the listed tools — they run without permission prompts — but it does not subtract anything: every other tool remains available through the normal permission flow, which is why Bash still ran. disallowed-tools is the restricting field: a tool listed there is removed while the skill is active, satisfying "unavailable even if asked" as configuration rather than hope.
option_feedback: The two fields do different jobs, and the team used the wrong one. allowed-tools pre-approves the listed tools — they run without permission prompts — but it does not subtract anything: every other tool remains available through the normal permission flow, which is why Bash still ran. disallowed-tools is the restricting field: a tool listed there is removed while the skill is active, satisfying "unavailable even if asked" as configuration rather than hope.

question:

Move the API rules into CLAUDE.md so they stop loading conditionally
Narrow the globs to the tree the rules actually govern — paths: ["src/api/**"]
Add a first line to the rule file stating it applies only to API code
answer: Narrow the globs to the tree the rules actually govern — paths: ["src/api/**"]

option_feedback: Two files with the same over-broad glob load the same content in the same sessions; the split changes the file count and nothing about scope.

question:
After an incident, a bank's platform team mandated plan mode for every agent task. One quarter in: median task completion time has doubled, and analysis shows 70% of tasks are single-file, well-scoped fixes whose approved plans were one step long. Developers have started rubber-stamping plans without reading them.

What should the team change?
options: Keep the mandate but auto-approve the plans for any task that the agent itself estimates as small
Reserve plan mode for multi-file or uncertain-blast-radius work; direct execution and review for scoped fixes
Withdraw the mandate entirely — the quarter's data, after all, shows plan mode halved the team's speed
Keep the mandate but route plan approvals to a rotating junior developer, cutting the interruption cost
answer: Reserve plan mode for multi-file or uncertain-blast-radius work; direct execution and review for scoped fixes
explanation: Plan mode adds value where a plan carries information — when the change is large, cross-cutting, or uncertain enough that reviewing intent before execution catches something. Calibrating — plan mode where blast radius is real, direct execution with normal code review where scope is tight — restores both halves: speed on small fixes, and approvals that get read because they appear when they matter.
option_feedback: An auto-approved gate is scenery: the ceremony's latency shrinks but the deeper damage — training developers that approvals are formalities — continues, now automated. It also hands the "is this small?" judgment to the agent whose work the gate was meant to check.

question:

Enter plan mode for investigation, and remain in plan mode through execution so every step stays gated

question:

How should she begin?
options: Have Claude interview her on invalidation, failure modes, and tenancy before any spec is written
Write the spec herself first, then have Claude review it for gaps and errors
Have Claude generate a full implementation immediately and refine it through repeated review rounds

question:
A streaming-media codebase has a failing integration test. Over five rounds, a developer has told Claude Code "still failing, please fix" — each round patched a different plausible spot; the test still fails. The developer summarizes the failure verbally from memory each time.

What should change in round six?
options: Re-run the test with verbose logging enabled, then continue summarizing results conversationally
Ask Claude to identify the most likely root cause from the code alone and fix that
Paste the exact test output into the round — assertion diff, expected versus actual, stack trace
Have Claude rewrite the test to match the code's current behavior, then work backward
answer: Paste the exact test output into the round — assertion diff, expected versus actual, stack trace
explanation: Five scattered patches are the signature of a fix loop running without its signal: "still failing" plus a from-memory summary gives each round almost nothing to localize with, so each round guesses somewhere plausible. The actual output — which assertion, expected value versus received value, the stack through which the failure arrives — is the discriminating evidence, and pasting it verbatim beats summarizing it, because paraphrase drops precisely the details (an offset, a null, an ordering) that distinguish the true cause from the four plausible ones already tried.
option_feedback: Verbose logging generates better evidence and then filters it through the same lossy channel — a verbal summary of rich output is the current failure mode with more input.

Which TWO flags close these gaps? (Select TWO.)

--resume, so each night continues the previous night's session
--fork-session, so each report is handled in its own branch
--max-turns, so agentic iteration is capped at a known bound

Which TWO input changes raise the job's precision? (Select TWO.)
options: A larger, more capable model for the review job
The team's review-standards document — what to flag, what to ignore — provided to each run
The merge request's diff supplied as the explicit review target, rather than the repository at large
A higher --max-turns limit so the reviewer can iterate longer on each merge request
Running the review twice per merge request and posting only the intersection of findings
answer: The team's review-standards document — what to flag, what to ignore — provided to each run

What to look at: the diff is the object under review; scoping the run to it stops the agent from surfacing observations about the surrounding repository that no merge request author can act on. Together they turn "review the changes for problems" into a bounded, criteria-driven task.

question:
A fintech team disabled their CI reviewer's concurrency-findings category after a false-positive storm eroded developer trust. The criteria for that category have since been substantially rewritten. The team wants the category back without repeating the storm.

What should gate the re-enable decision?
options: Re-enable it immediately and monitor dismissal rates closely during the first weeks of operation
Re-enable it for one sprint as a trial and switch it off again if the complaints return
Keep the category disabled for good, since trust once lost argues against a second attempt
Replay the revised criteria on the labeled past diffs; re-enable only above a precision threshold
answer: Replay the revised criteria on the labeled past diffs; re-enable only above a precision threshold
explanation: The team already possesses the perfect evaluation material: the diffs from the storm, each labeled by what developers judged, plus known-good cases. Replaying the revised criteria against that labeled set measures precisely the thing in question — would the new criteria have avoided the old failures — before any developer sees a finding. Setting a precision threshold turns re-enabling from a hope into a demonstrated property, and if the replay fails, the criteria iterate offline, costing no trust at all.
option_feedback: Monitoring after re-enabling makes developers the evaluation set again — the second storm is detected by inflicting it, and the trust being protected is the instrument being spent.
A sprint-then-decide trial is the same live experiment with a calendar attached, and complaint volume is a lagging, noisy proxy for the precision number the replay measures directly and in advance.

Permanent disablement discards a coverage area the reviewer was built to catch — concurrency defects remain the codebase's risk whether or not the reviewer looks. The evidence for safe re-enablement is obtainable offline; declining to obtain it is not caution.

question:
A grain-trading firm's extraction pipeline includes a review step whose criterion reads: "flag suspicious extractions." Comparing two months of output, reviewers find the flagging wildly inconsistent — the same discrepancy pattern flagged in one document and passed in the next.

What should replace the criterion?
options: The same criterion with "be thorough and consistent in what you flag" appended
Explicit checkable criteria — totals that fail to sum, out-of-period dates, missing required fields
A set of twenty example documents previously flagged as suspicious, provided with no other guidance
Routing every extraction to human review instead — automated flagging has proven itself unreliable
answer: Explicit checkable criteria — totals that fail to sum, out-of-period dates, missing required fields
explanation: "Suspicious" delegates the definition of the task to the model's run-by-run judgment, and unanchored judgment resamples — identical patterns flagged one day and passed the next is exactly what that looks like. Enumerating the checks turns the criterion into something with an objective answer per document: sums either reconcile or do not, dates fall inside the period or outside. Consistency follows because the criteria, not the mood of the run, decide — and the enumerated list is auditable and extensible as new discrepancy types are discovered.
option_feedback: The appended sentence asks for consistency without defining the thing to be consistent about — "suspicious" remains the operative word, and it remains undefined.

question:
An airline's support-triage prompt includes six few-shot examples — all six are billing disputes, the largest category. Measurement shows classification accuracy is fine on billing but degrades sharply on baggage claims, rebooking requests, and loyalty questions, which together make up half the volume.

How should the example set be changed?
options: Rebuild the set to span the category distribution, weighting the most-confused pairs
Add six more billing-dispute examples, deepening coverage of the single largest category
Replace the examples with concise written definitions of every category
Keep the six examples but reorder them from the most frequent category to the least frequent
answer: Rebuild the set to span the category distribution, weighting the most-confused pairs
explanation: Few-shot examples teach the shape of the whole task, and this set teaches that everything is billing — the model has never seen what a baggage claim or a rebooking request looks like as a classified example, and the errors sit exactly where the demonstrations are missing. Rebuilding for coverage — a representative example or two per major category, with extra weight on the boundaries measurement shows are confused — aligns what is demonstrated with what arrives. Diversity across the input distribution beats depth in one region of it.

question:
A customs brokerage extracts invoice totals. Some invoices carry a summary-box total that disagrees with the sum of line items. The team has settled policy: the line-item sum is authoritative, and the discrepancy must remain visible downstream. Current model output is inconsistent — sometimes the box, sometimes the sum, and the conflict is never recorded.

How should the policy be implemented in the prompt?
options: A prompt sentence stating that line-item sums take precedence over the summary boxes
Post-processing that recomputes the sum in code and overwrites the extracted total with that figure
Routing every conflicted invoice into a manual review queue for humans to resolve individually
Examples of conflicted invoices showing the full policy: line-sum total, stated value recorded, flag set
answer: Examples of conflicted invoices showing the full policy: line-sum total, stated value recorded, flag set
explanation: The policy has two halves — which value wins, and how the conflict stays visible — and the second half is an output-shape behavior: on a conflicted invoice, the correct output contains the authoritative total, the recorded stated value, and a set flag. Output shapes are what demonstrations teach best. An example of a conflicted invoice with the exactly-correct output shows the model the complete move, and the run-to-run inconsistency ends because the policy exists as demonstrated behavior, not as a preference the model must operationalize on its own.
option_feedback: The sentence covers the precedence half and is silent on the visibility half — nothing tells the model to record the losing value or set a flag, so the discrepancy keeps vanishing. Stated preference without demonstrated shape is also the weaker lever for consistency.
Overwriting in code makes the total right and silently destroys the signal the policy explicitly preserves: after the overwrite, a conflicted invoice and a clean one are indistinguishable downstream.

question:
A city permit office extracts applications into structured records. The permit_type field must be one of 8 official codes, but the model sometimes emits prose variants such as "residential remodel" instead of RES-REM.

What is the right fix?
options: List the 8 codes in the prompt and instruct the model to use them exactly
Add a post-processing table that maps known prose variants to their codes
Constrain permit_type in the output schema with an enum of the 8 codes
Lower the temperature so the model's outputs vary less
answer: Constrain permit_type in the output schema with an enum of the 8 codes
explanation: A field with a closed set of legal values is what enum constraints exist for: the schema declares the 8 codes, and output validates against them — prose variants stop being possible rather than merely discouraged. The constraint lives at the layer that enforces structure.
option_feedback: A prompt list states the expectation without enforcing it; exactness by instruction leaves a failure rate the schema removes entirely.
A mapping table chases variants after the fact — every new phrasing needs a new entry, maintaining forever a translation the enum makes unnecessary.

question:
A utility-bill extraction schema defines fields by bare names: usage, rate, period_start. Two systematic errors dominate the defect log: usage captured in the wrong unit when bills print both kWh and MWh figures, and period_start filled with the bill's posting date instead of the service-period start.

What should the team improve?
options: Rename the fields to be more specific, such as usage_kwh and service_period_start throughout
Per-field descriptions in the schema — expected unit, format, where the value appears
An extra output field in which the model reports the unit it actually used for the usage figure
Feed higher-resolution document scans so values are easier to locate
answer: Per-field descriptions in the schema — expected unit, format, where the value appears
explanation: Both defects are disambiguation failures, and the schema is where field-level meaning belongs: a description on usage stating "kilowatt-hours; when both kWh and MWh appear, use the kWh figure" and on period_start stating "start of the service period, not the posting or issue date; typically in the service-summary block" gives the model the discriminating information at exactly the decision point. Per-field descriptions are the input-schema's documentation channel, and precise ones are among the highest-leverage accuracy improvements available in structured extraction.
option_feedback: Sharper names carry a hint — usage_kwh does say the unit — but a name cannot explain which of two printed figures to choose or where the correct date lives. Names label; descriptions instruct. The rename is the shallow version of the fix.

question:
A hotel-chain accounts team extracts vendor invoices. The current schema captures only the invoice's stated grand total. Downstream reconciliation keeps discovering, weeks later, that some stated totals disagree with the invoice's own line items — and nothing in the pipeline could have noticed.

How should the extraction be redesigned so these conflicts surface at processing time?
options: Extract only the line items and compute the total from them in code, dropping the stated figure entirely
Add a prompt instruction telling the model to double-check totals before responding
Extract the stated total twice, in two separate calls, and compare the two results
Extract both the line items and the stated total, sum in code, and flag any mismatch for review
answer: Extract both the line items and the stated total, sum in code, and flag any mismatch for review
explanation: The invoice contains redundant information — a stated total and the items that should produce it — and the current schema throws the redundancy away by capturing one number. Extracting both sides gives the pipeline something it can check deterministically: code sums the items, compares against the stated figure, and a mismatch becomes a flagged, reviewable event at processing time instead of a reconciliation surprise weeks later. Designing extractions to capture verifiable redundancy is what makes self-checking possible at all.
option_feedback: Computing from the lines alone replaces one unchecked number with another — if a line item was misextracted, the computed total is wrong with nothing to disagree with it. Dropping the stated figure removes the second opinion.

question:

Which TWO rules belong in it? (Select TWO.)
options: Resend the identical request unchanged, since sampling variance often clears the failure
Escalate to a larger model automatically on the first validation failure
Skip validation on retried attempts to avoid infinite loops
Attach the specific validator errors to the retry so the model sees exactly what to fix
Cap retry attempts and route documents that keep failing to human review
answer: Attach the specific validator errors to the retry so the model sees exactly what to fix
Cap retry attempts and route documents that keep failing to human review
explanation:
These are the two load-bearing properties of a retry loop. Feedback: a retry that includes the validator's specific findings — which field, which rule, what value — turns re-prompting into correction; the model fixes what is named rather than regenerating blind. Boundedness: a cap on attempts acknowledges that some documents will not converge, and routing those to human review converts a potential infinite loop into a triaged queue. Feedback makes retries effective; the cap makes them safe.

question:
A title-insurance company processes all document-extraction requests in one nightly batch. Volume analysis: 98% are back-office bulk work with no urgency, but 2% are counter scans — a clerk is standing with a customer, waiting, and today those wait until the next morning. The batch's cost discount matters to the business case.

What should the team change?
options: Route by request class: counter scans go synchronous immediately; bulk stays in the nightly batch
Run the batch every two hours instead of nightly, sparing every request the wait until morning
Move all processing to synchronous calls so every requester gets immediate results
Keep one nightly batch and order the counter scans first, completing them earliest in the run
answer: Route by request class: counter scans go synchronous immediately; bulk stays in the nightly batch
explanation: The workload contains two request classes with irreconcilable latency needs, and the fix is a routing layer that recognizes the class at intake: the waiting-customer 2% goes through a synchronous call and returns in seconds; the indifferent 98% keeps the batch discount. Neither class subsidizes the other — the design serves each request at the latency it needs and the cost it deserves.
option_feedback: The workload contains two request classes with irreconcilable latency needs, and the fix is a routing layer that recognizes the class at intake: the waiting-customer 2% goes through a synchronous call and returns in seconds; the indifferent 98% keeps the batch discount. Neither class subsidizes the other — the design serves each request at the latency it needs and the cost it deserves.

Two-hourly batches leave a counter customer waiting up to two hours — still absurd against a seconds-scale need — while chopping the bulk work into twelve runs of overhead. It splits the difference between two requirements that should not be averaged.

Position inside a nightly run does not change the night: the batch completes when it completes, and first-in-the-run still means the clerk's customer left many hours ago.

question:

Map each result back to its source record using the custom_id assigned at submission
Move submission to 20:00 so more time has passed before the midnight read
Split the submission into five smaller batches so each one finishes sooner
Re-run the entire batch on any morning when records turn out to be missing

Map each result back to its source record using the custom_id assigned at submission

question:
A payments team uses a second Claude session to review each iteration of a generated change. The same reviewer session has now handled six successive rounds. By round four, its comments had begun restating the generator's own design rationale; in round six it approved a change containing a defect it had itself flagged in round two.

What should the team change?
options: Keep the long-lived reviewer but instruct it to remain skeptical and re-derive its analysis each round
Use a fresh reviewer instance per round, given the current artifacts, spec, and acceptance criteria
Alternate two long-lived reviewer sessions so neither accumulates more than half the rounds
Switch later rounds to generator self-review against a checklist, since reviewer value is decaying anyway
answer: Use a fresh reviewer instance per round, given the current artifacts, spec, and acceptance criteria
explanation: Review independence is a consumable: each round deposits the generator's framing, explanations, and prior approvals into the reviewer's context, and six rounds in, the reviewer is effectively reasoning inside the generator's narrative — which is what echoed rationale and a forgotten round-two flag look like. question:
A lease-abstraction pipeline uses two model instances: an extractor and an independent checker that re-derives three critical fields. On about 4% of documents they disagree. Postings from wrong values cost hours to reverse; the checker, audited alone, is also wrong sometimes. The team must define what happens on disagreement.

What is the right resolution design?
options: Adopt the checker's value automatically, since it exists precisely to catch extraction errors
Keep the extractor's value unless the checker reports higher confidence in its own
Route disagreements to human review, letting agreement auto-pass under ongoing sample audits
Add a third model instance and adopt the majority value among the three
answer: Route disagreements to human review, letting agreement auto-pass under ongoing sample audits
explanation: A disagreement between two independent derivations is the pipeline's most information-dense signal: at least one of them is wrong, nobody knows which, and the audit says it can be either. At 4% volume, sending exactly those documents to a human buys near-certain resolution on the cases proven uncertain, at a bounded, budgetable cost — while the 96% agreement pool auto-passes, with sampling audits watching for the residual case where both instances err together. Disagreement-gated review converts the checker from an arbiter into what it really is: a detector.
option_feedback: Checker-wins assumes the newer instance is right whenever they differ, and the audit has already falsified that. Automatic adoption replaces one fallible answer with another while discarding the one fact firmly established — that this document deserves scrutiny.

Comparing self-reported confidence across two differently-prompted instances treats uncalibrated numbers as commensurable evidence. The rule sounds principled and resolves nothing: it picks a winner by a signal no one has validated.

question:
A telecom support agent's request builder was changed during a cost push: it now sends only the last four messages of the conversation. Median conversations run twelve messages and fit the context window easily. Since the change, agents re-ask for account numbers customers already gave, and complaint metrics for "had to repeat myself" have tripled.

What should the team do?
options: Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent never to re-ask for information already provided
Keep the four-message window but have the model maintain a running summary appended each turn
Cache the account number in the tool layer and auto-fill it into tool calls that need it
Send the complete conversation history on every request, as the API's statelessness requires
answer: Send the complete conversation history on every request, as the API's statelessness requires
explanation: The API holds no memory between requests: the model's knowledge of the conversation is exactly the messages sent with each call. Trimming to four messages amputated everything earlier — the account number given at message two does not exist for the model at message nine, and asking again is the correct behavior given what it can see. With twelve-message conversations fitting comfortably, the optimization solved a cost problem the workload did not have and created a quality problem it now does. Sending full history restores the agent's memory at negligible cost.
option_feedback: The instruction demands the model honor information that is not in its context. It cannot avoid re-asking for what, from its perspective, was never provided — the rule is unfollowable by construction.

A model-maintained summary adds a lossy, effortful memory mechanism to compensate for discarding a history that fits in full — machinery whose failure modes (missed detail in the summary) recreate the original bug, adopted to save tokens that did not need saving.

Auto-filling one field patches the most visible symptom; everything else the customer said — the issue description, the troubleshooting already done — is still missing, and the agent still re-asks for all of it.

question:
A franchise-services firm extracts obligations from 300-page agreements in a single whole-document pass; the documents fit the context window. Field-level audits show recall for clauses located in the middle third of documents is three times worse than for early or late sections, consistently.

What should the pipeline do?
options: Process the agreement in sections aligned to its structure, extract per section, and merge
Move to a model with a much larger context window, giving the documents far more headroom
Run the whole-document pass twice and take the union of the two extraction sets
Reorder the document so its middle sections appear first, then extract from the reordered text
answer: Process the agreement in sections aligned to its structure, extract per section, and merge
explanation: The measurements show positional attention loss: with everything presented at once, material buried mid-sequence receives systematically less attention than the ends. Sectioning changes the geometry — each pass holds one structural unit, so every clause sits near the focus of its own extraction rather than in the middle of 300 pages. The merge step reassembles per-section results keyed to the document's structure. Recall stops depending on where in the binder a clause happened to live.
option_feedback: The measurements show positional attention loss: with everything presented at once, material buried mid-sequence receives systematically less attention than the ends. Sectioning changes the geometry — each pass holds one structural unit, so every clause sits near the focus of its own extraction rather than in the middle of 300 pages. The merge step reassembles per-section results keyed to the document's structure. Recall stops depending on where in the binder a clause happened to live.
The documents already fit; headroom is not the failing resource. A larger window presents the same long middle in the same single sequence, and the attention pattern that under-serves it comes along.

Both passes share the same positional bias over the same layout, so the union recovers only variance — the clauses systematically under-attended in the middle are missed by both runs alike, at double the cost.

Reordering moves which text is disadvantaged rather than eliminating the disadvantage — formerly-early sections now sit mid-sequence — and agreements are dense with cross-references ("as defined in Section 4") that scrambled ordering actively breaks.

question:
A hotel-loyalty support agent has just finished diagnosing a member's issue — a points transfer that needs one reversal, which the agent can execute immediately. Before it can say so, the member writes: "honestly, this has been a runaround and I'm about at the end of my patience." The member has not asked for a human. Transcript audits show agents in this moment plowing ahead with procedural questions, and satisfaction scores cratering.

What should the agent's designed behavior be?
options: Escalate to a human at the first sign of frustration, without mentioning the ready fix
Acknowledge the frustration, offer the ready one-step fix, and escalate if dissatisfaction continues
Execute the reversal immediately and without comment, letting the fixed result speak for itself
Ask the member to explain what has been most frustrating before taking any action
answer: Acknowledge the frustration, offer the ready one-step fix, and escalate if dissatisfaction continues
explanation: Frustration without a request for a human is a signal to change register, not necessarily to hand off: the agent acknowledges what the member is feeling, then puts the concrete, immediate resolution on the table — which is the single most de-escalating thing available, since the runaround ends right now. If dissatisfaction continues after that, escalation follows; sustained frustration is itself an escalation trigger. Had the member explicitly asked for a person, the calculus would change — an explicit request is honored immediately — but that is not what happened here, and treating every sign of impatience as a handoff wastes the resolution sitting one step away.
option_feedback: Escalating on frustration alone, with the fix in hand and unmentioned, sends the member to a queue to wait for something the agent could have completed in seconds — deepening the runaround the member is complaining about. Escalation on mere impatience also floods human capacity with cases the policy fully covers.

Acting without acknowledging skips the register change the moment calls for: the member hears silence exactly when they voiced frustration, and procedural plowing-ahead is the audited failure. The fix matters and so does saying you heard them.

An interrogative detour is more process at the moment the member is out of patience with process — and the agent already knows the answer: the diagnosis is done and the fix is ready. The question buys nothing and costs the moment.

question:
A publishing group's market-research run covers nine sub-topics; midway, the sources for two of them failed and could not be recovered before the deadline. The report is due. The current draft presents all nine sections with uniform confidence.

Which TWO practices make the delivered report honest? (Select TWO.)
options: Hold the report until the failed sources are restored and the two sections re-researched
Annotate the two affected sections as resting on partial coverage, distinguishing them from the fully-supported seven
Remove the two thin sub-topics so every published section stands on complete sourcing
Soften the language uniformly across all nine sections to avoid overclaiming anywhere
State explicitly what was not examined — which sources failed and which questions therefore remain open
answer: Annotate the two affected sections as resting on partial coverage, distinguishing them from the fully-supported seven
State explicitly what was not examined — which sources failed and which questions therefore remain open
explanation:
Honest reporting under partial failure has two components. Differentiation: the seven solid sections and the two gapped ones are different epistemic products, and the report should say which is which — section-level annotation lets readers weight conclusions by the evidence actually behind them. Disclosure: a reader also needs the shape of what is missing — which sources failed, which questions went unexamined — so the report's boundaries are visible and the gaps can be closed later. Together they deliver everything the run learned, labeled truthfully.

question:
A marketplace-platform review runs in two phases: phase-one subagents map the modules; phase-two subagents assess risk in what was mapped. Subagents are isolated by design. Output analysis shows phase-two subagents spend roughly 35% of their effort re-discovering module facts phase one had already established.

What should the coordinator do?
options: Give the phase-two subagents the complete, unabridged transcripts of every phase-one subagent
Run phase two inside the same context as phase one, spawning no subagents the second time
Distill phase-one results, injecting each phase-two subagent's relevant slice into its prompt
Accept the re-exploration as the inherent price of subagent isolation
answer: Distill phase-one results, injecting each phase-two subagent's relevant slice into its prompt
explanation: Isolation means phase-two subagents know only what their prompts contain — so the coordinator, which holds phase one's outputs, must carry the knowledge across the phase boundary deliberately. Distilling the mapping into a compact summary and injecting each phase-two subagent's relevant slice into its prompt hands over the established facts at a fraction of the cost of rediscovering them. The 35% overhead is not the price of isolation; it is the price of an empty handoff.
option_feedback: Full transcripts transfer the knowledge buried in everything else — tool calls, dead ends, verbose reasoning — consuming phase-two context on material whose useful content fits in a summary. The signal should cross the boundary, not the archaeology.

One shared context removes the isolation that motivated the design — parallelism, focused windows — and a full platform review in a single accumulating context is exactly the capacity problem subagents were solving.

question:
Mid-refactor on a construction-software codebase, a developer's Claude Code session shows context at 92%. Plenty of work remains, and the session's understanding of the refactor is still needed.

What should she run, and what will it do?
options: /clear, which resets the context entirely and lets the session start over with its full room
Nothing — continue working until the context is exhausted and see what the session does
An export of the transcript, followed by a new session pasted from it
/compact, which summarizes the conversation and frees room while keeping a working summary
answer: /compact, which summarizes the conversation and frees room while keeping a working summary
explanation: This is the situation compaction exists for: the session needs room and it needs continuity. /compact condenses the history into a summary that stays in context, so the refactor's accumulated understanding survives in working form while most of the window is reclaimed for the remaining work.
option_feedback: /clear wipes the context entirely — full room, zero continuity. The refactor knowledge the developer still needs is exactly what it deletes.
Pressing on invites the least controlled outcome: auto-compaction firing mid-thought at a moment nobody chose. Compacting deliberately now beats being compacted arbitrarily later.
Pasting an exported transcript re-feeds the bulk of the old context into the new session — reconstructing the fullness problem rather than solving it, with extra steps.

question:
A utility company is setting the auto-accept confidence cutoff for its bill-extraction pipeline: extractions above the cutoff post automatically, below it humans review. One camp advocates 0.8, another 0.9 — both by intuition. A labeled validation set of 2,000 bills with ground truth exists. Accuracy requirements differ by field: account numbers must be near-perfect; a wrong due date is recoverable.

How should the cutoff be chosen?
options: From the labeled set, per field: the lowest cutoff whose measured precision meets that field's target
Standardize on 0.9 everywhere, as the more conservative of the two proposed round numbers
Start at 0.95 and lower it gradually until the human-review queue reaches a manageable size
Adopt the extraction vendor's recommended default threshold as the professionally tested baseline
answer: From the labeled set, per field: the lowest cutoff whose measured precision meets that field's target
explanation: The labeled set makes the debate empirical: for any cutoff, the 2,000 ground-truthed bills yield the actual precision of the would-be auto-accepted pool — per field, which matters because the fields carry different stakes. Choosing the lowest cutoff that clears each field's precision target gives every field exactly the protection it requires while maximizing automation: account numbers end up gated hard, due dates flow more freely, and every number in the policy traces to a measurement instead of an intuition.
option_feedback: The labeled set makes the debate empirical: for any cutoff, the 2,000 ground-truthed bills yield the actual precision of the would-be auto-accepted pool — per field, which matters because the fields carry different stakes. Choosing the lowest cutoff that clears each field's precision target gives every field exactly the protection it requires while maximizing automation: account numbers end up gated hard, due dates flow more freely, and every number in the policy traces to a measurement instead of an intuition.
Conservative-sounding is not measured: 0.9 may still under-protect account numbers while over-gating due dates — a single unmeasured number misfits both tails of the stakes distribution at once.

Tuning until the queue is comfortable optimizes reviewer workload and lets accuracy land wherever it lands — the resulting precision is whatever staffing happened to imply, silently, with no target ever checked.
A vendor default is calibrated to nobody's field stakes in particular, and adopting it discards the one asset that answers this exact question — the team's own labeled data.

question:
An agricultural-research pipeline aggregates findings into briefings. Its conflict detector keeps flagging "contradictions" like a fertilizer price of $610 per ton against $840 per ton — where one figure comes from a 2022 report and the other from 2024 data. A review finds about 30% of flagged conflicts are actually time-separated figures, and analysts have begun ignoring the conflict flags altogether.

What should the pipeline change?
options: Suppress the conflict flags whenever the two figures differ by less than a set percentage threshold
Carry collection dates on every claim; time-separated figures then form a series, not a conflict
Prefer the most recent figure in every flagged pair and discard the older one
Have synthesis re-fetch both underlying sources every time a conflict is flagged for checking
answer: Carry collection dates on every claim; time-separated figures then form a series, not a conflict
explanation: The detector cannot distinguish disagreement from change over time because the information that distinguishes them — when each figure was collected — is stripped before synthesis sees the claims. Carrying temporal metadata on every claim fixes the classification at its root: same-period figures that differ are genuine conflicts and get flagged; different-period figures form a time series, which is not a contradiction but often a finding in itself. The 30% false-flag rate — and the alert fatigue eroding the real flags' credibility — both trace to the same missing field.
option_feedback: A magnitude threshold measures the wrong dimension: prices genuinely in conflict can differ by 5%, and a 38% move across two years can be an ordinary trend. Tuning suppression by size trades false flags for missed ones without ever learning the time distinction.

Newest-wins destroys the series — the 2022 figure is not wrong, it is history, and the price trajectory it anchors may matter more to the briefing than either endpoint alone.

Re-fetching re-reads sources whose dates were available the first time; it spends retrieval cost per flag to rediscover metadata the pipeline should have carried, and it does nothing until after the noisy flag has already fired.

question:
A fintech research system finds two different deprecation dates for a payment API: June 2027 in the provider's official changelog, and "sometime in 2026, I think they said" in a third-party blog post recalling a webinar. The migration-planning report needs a date.

How should the report handle the two sources?
options: Present both dates with equal weight and let the planning team decide between them later
Use the blog's date, since it is the more recent publication of the two
Adopt the changelog's date as the working answer, noting the blog's differing, lower-authority claim
Withhold the date from the report until a deeper investigation reconciles the two conflicting sources
answer: Adopt the changelog's date as the working answer, noting the blog's differing, lower-authority claim
explanation: The two sources are not peers: one is the provider's official record of its own API — authoritative nearly by definition — and the other is a secondhand recollection with hedging in its own phrasing. Source-quality weighting resolves this conflict directly: the report adopts the authoritative date as its working answer and still notes the discrepancy, so readers see that a differing claim exists and why it was discounted. Provenance is preserved, false balance is avoided, and the report commits where the evidence supports commitment.
option_feedback: Equal weight misrepresents the evidence — it hands the planning team a coin flip the research already knows how to call, exporting a resolved question as an open one.

Recency ranks versions of comparable sources; it cannot promote a hedged secondhand recollection over the provider's own record. The dimensions are different, and authority is the one that matters here.

question:
A wealth-management firm extracts data from account statements. On multi-account statements, the model's response often contains three tool_use blocks in one message — one lookup per account. The loop executes only the first block, appends its single tool_result, and sends the next request, which the API rejects. The developer is unsure what the protocol expects.

What should the loop do?
options: Execute only the first block, and remove the other tool_use blocks from the assistant message so the history stays consistent
Execute the first block and re-send the request so the model can re-issue the remaining calls one at a time in later turns
Execute all three requested calls and return three tool_result blocks — one per tool_use id — in the single next user message
Detect multi-block responses and re-prompt the model with an instruction to request only one tool call per response
answer: Execute all three requested calls and return three tool_result blocks — one per tool_use id — in the single next user message
explanation:
This question tests the protocol contract for parallel tool calls.

Multiple Blocks Mean Parallel Work
Three tool_use blocks in one response is the model requesting three lookups at once. The contract is per-request: every tool_use must be answered by a tool_result carrying its id, and all of them travel together in the one user message that follows.

Executing all three and returning three results satisfies the contract, preserves the parallel efficiency, and gives the model everything it asked for in a single round trip. The API rejection is simply the protocol reporting that two requests were left unanswered.

Why the other options are incorrect
Delete the other blocks from history — makes the history false rather than consistent: the model planned around three lookups, two silently vanish, and it will re-request them or reason as though they happened.

Answer one, re-send — exactly what the API rejected. Two tool_use blocks remain unanswered, and the protocol does not allow deferring results across turns.

Re-prompt for one call per response — sacrifices legitimate parallelism to avoid implementing the protocol, and as a prompt-level request it is not guaranteed: the loop must still handle a multi-block response the day one arrives.

Key Takeaway
Execute every tool_use in a response and return one tool_result per id in the single next user message. Results cannot be deferred across turns.

-

-

-
Anthropic — How tool use works → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works

Re-sending after answering only one block is exactly what the API rejected: two tool_use blocks remain unanswered. The protocol does not allow deferring results across turns; the next message must settle all outstanding calls.

Multiple tool_use blocks in one response are the model requesting parallel work, and the protocol's contract is per-request: every tool_use must be answered by a tool_result carrying its id, and all of them travel together in the one user message that follows. Executing all three and returning three results satisfies the contract, keeps the parallel lookups' efficiency, and gives the model everything it asked for in a single round trip.

question:
A food-delivery support agent's loop iterates until stop_reason is "end_turn" — and nothing else bounds it. Last night one conversation looped for 400 turns before an engineer noticed the cost spike, and the log shows the model cycling between two lookups that kept returning inconsistent data.

Which TWO guards belong in the loop? (Select TWO.)
options: An explicit iteration cap enforced by the loop's own counter
A system-prompt instruction telling the model to stop after a reasonable number of steps
Removing one of the two inconsistent lookup tools so the cycle cannot form
On hitting the cap, surfacing the partial progress and the reason for stopping instead of ending silently
A lower max_tokens value so runaway conversations become too expensive to continue
answer: An explicit iteration cap enforced by the loop's own counter
On hitting the cap, surfacing the partial progress and the reason for stopping instead of ending silently
explanation:
This question tests bounding a loop — and what happens when the bound fires.

The Bound and Its Landing

-
An iteration cap in the loop's own counter — a loop that can only end when the model decides it is finished has no defense against the model never deciding. A counter-based cap enforced in code is the structural guarantee that 400-turn nights cannot happen.

-
Surfacing partial progress and the reason on cap — a silent stop turns a bounded failure into a vanished conversation. The cap bounds the loop; the on-cap behavior makes the bound survivable, routing what was accomplished to the customer path or an operator queue.

Why the other options are incorrect
A prompt instruction to stop — asks the component that failed to terminate to please terminate: probabilistic advice layered on the exact judgment that is misfiring. The bound must exist outside the model.

Remove one inconsistent tool — patches one observed cycle. The next inconsistent pair, or a single flaky tool, re-creates the loop; the guard must hold for cycles nobody has seen.

Lower max_tokens — bounds one response's length, not the number of responses. 400 short turns pass under any per-turn limit — wrong axis entirely.

Key Takeaway
Cap iterations in code and design what happens at the cap. Prompt-level stopping instructions and token limits do not bound turn count.

-
Anthropic — How the agent loop works → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop

-
Anthropic — How tool use works → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices

And the cap needs a designed landing: when it fires, the loop should surface what was accomplished and why it stopped — to the customer path or an operator queue — because a silent stop turns a bounded failure into a vanished conversation. The cap bounds the loop; the on-cap behavior makes the bound survivable.

question:
A warehouse-robotics developer reviews a teammate's first agent. The teammate defined four tools in the request's tools parameter and is confused that the model answered a question in plain text "without running any of my tools."

What does the tools parameter actually do?
options: It declares the available tools and schemas; nothing runs unless the model calls one
It queues the listed tools for execution, and the API performs them in order before generating the response
It guarantees the model will call at least one of the listed tools on every request
It uploads the tool implementations so the API can run them server-side when needed
answer: It declares the available tools and schemas; nothing runs unless the model calls one
explanation:
This question tests what the tools parameter is.

A Declaration, Not a Queue
tools declares what is available: names, descriptions and input schemas telling the model what it could call and how. Whether any call happens is the model's decision based on the request — a question answerable directly gets a direct answer. Execution, when requested, is the application's job.

Why the other options are incorrect
A queue the API executes — the API executes no tools, in any order, ever. The model requests; the caller executes.

A guarantee of at least one call — that is what tool_choice settings like "any" or a named tool provide. The default with tools present leaves the choice to the model.

Uploads implementations for server-side execution — only the schemas travel to the API. Implementations stay in the application.

Key Takeaway
tools declares availability and schemas; tool_choice governs whether a call is required. Nothing executes unless the model requests it and your code runs it.

question:
A sports-analytics firm built a research system with twelve subagents — one per source file type: one for CSVs, one for PDFs, one for box-score HTML, and so on. Telemetry over a month: about 70% of tokens go to coordination — dispatch prompts, handoffs, aggregation — rather than analysis, and most runs invoke eight or more subagents for a single question.

What should the team change?
options: Keep the twelve subagents but cut the coordination cost with much shorter dispatch prompts and considerably terser handoffs
Consolidate into about three specialists split by analysis domain, each handling all file types its domain needs
Add a thirteenth routing subagent that decides which of the twelve to invoke for each question
Move all twelve subagents to a cheaper model so the coordination overhead costs less
answer: Consolidate into about three specialists split by analysis domain, each handling all file types its domain needs
explanation:
This question tests subagent granularity — the partition axis is wrong.

File Format Is Not a Unit of Expertise
Specialization pays when each specialist owns a meaningful body of expertise. Splitting by file type forces nearly every real question — which spans formats — through many subagents, so the system's work becomes mostly handoffs. That is what the 70%-coordination figure measures.

Consolidating into about three specialists split by analysis domain, each handling all the file types its domain needs, gives each subagent a coherent scope and collapses eight-subagent relay chains into one or two invocations. Granularity should follow the shape of the questions, not the shape of the files.

Why the other options are incorrect
Shorter prompts and terser handoffs — shaves percentage points off a structural cost. The number of hops is the problem, and twelve format specialists guarantee many hops per question however efficiently each is phrased.

A thirteenth routing subagent — does not reduce the hops: questions still span formats, so the router still fans out widely, and the system gains another coordination layer on top of the overhead it was meant to cut.

A cheaper model — makes the waste cheaper, not smaller. 70% of spend on coordination is an architecture measurement that survives any per-token price.

Key Takeaway
Partition subagents by domain of expertise, not by input format. Over-fine granularity converts analysis budget into coordination budget.

question:
A municipal-utilities research platform fans one large question out to about forty subagents across four domains — rates, infrastructure, regulation, demographics. The single coordinator now fails at aggregation: forty returns overflow its context, and quality reviewers trace missing cross-references to the coordinator summarizing away detail while triaging the pile.

What is the right structural change?
options: Move the coordinator to the largest available context window so all forty returns fit
Have the coordinator process the returns in four sequential batches of ten, compacting between the batches
Cap the system at fifteen subagents and accept shallower coverage per domain
A sub-coordinator per domain aggregates its ten; the top merges four summaries
answer: A sub-coordinator per domain aggregates its ten; the top merges four summaries
explanation:
This question tests hierarchical coordination when a flat fan-out outgrows one hub.

Re-Partition the Aggregation Burden
One coordinator over forty spokes concentrates the entire merge at a single point, and the failure follows: the merge needs everything at once, and everything no longer fits.

A sub-coordinator per domain aggregates its own ten returns with domain context and full detail; the top coordinator then merges four coherent domain summaries — a task that fits comfortably. Cross-references within a domain are preserved where they occur, and the design scales by adding domains rather than by inflating one context.

Why the other options are incorrect
The largest context window — makes forty returns fit today and defers the failure to subagent fifty, while one context performing a forty-way synthesis still dilutes attention across all of it — which is where the summarized-away details went.

Four sequential batches with compaction — loses cross-batch connections by construction: a rates finding cannot be linked to an infrastructure finding compacted two batches ago. The missing cross-references get worse.

Cap at fifteen subagents — trades coverage, the system's purpose, for coordinator comfort. The workload legitimately needs the breadth.

Key Takeaway
Introduce sub-coordinators when a flat fan-out overwhelms one aggregator. Hierarchy re-partitions the merge along the work's natural structure.

question:
An event-ticketing company is designing its support automation. The workflow: identify the order, answer questions about it — delivery status, seat details, transfer rules — using three read-only tools. An architect has proposed a five-agent system: intake, routing, lookup, policy, and response-drafting agents. Traffic analysis shows conversations average four turns with one or two tool calls.

What should the reviewer recommend?
options: A single agent holding the three tools — this workflow has nothing for multiple agents to do
The five-agent design — separation of concerns keeps each agent simple and testable
A compromise: two agents, one for lookups and one for drafting responses
The five-agent design, but with all five agents running on a small, cheap model
answer: A single agent holding the three tools — this workflow has nothing for multiple agents to do
explanation:
This question tests when not to build a multi-agent system.

Multi-Agent Buys Parallelism and Isolation — Neither Applies Here
The workflow is a short sequential chain with three read-only tools, averaging four turns and one or two calls. There is no independent work to run in parallel, and no distinct bodies of specialist context needing isolation — the whole domain fits comfortably in one agent's prompt.

A single agent holding the three tools does everything the five would, minus four handoffs of overhead, latency and failure surface per conversation. Simplicity is the correct architecture whenever the added structure has no work to do.

Why the other options are incorrect
The five-agent design for separation of concerns — separation is a virtue when concerns are separable and substantial. Here it manufactures five trivial agents and four inter-agent boundaries for a two-call conversation: each piece is simple, and the complexity has moved into the seams.

Two agents as a compromise — halving an overbuild is still overbuilding. Lookup and drafting are consecutive steps in one short flow.

Five agents on a cheap model — model price does not address the objection. The overhead is architectural — extra hops, latency and failure points — whatever each hop costs.

Key Takeaway
Use multiple agents when you need parallelism or context isolation. Short sequential workflows with a handful of tools belong in one agent.

question:
A publishing group's research coordinator dispatches a subagent to analyze one imprint's backlist performance. The team is drafting the invocation prompt and debating what it must contain, given that the subagent starts with no context beyond its own definition.

Which TWO belong in the invocation prompt? (Select TWO.)
options: The coordinator's full conversation so far, giving the subagent complete background
The specific data slice for this task — the imprint, the catalog extract, the period under analysis
The other subagents' interim findings, keeping the analysis consistent with theirs
The AgentDefinition's system prompt repeated verbatim, in case it did not load
The output contract — what fields and structure the returned findings must have
answer: The specific data slice for this task — the imprint, the catalog extract, the period under analysis
The output contract — what fields and structure the returned findings must have
explanation:
This question tests what an invocation prompt must carry, given complete isolation.

Scoped Input, Explicit Output Shape

-
The specific data slice — the subagent sees only what this prompt carries, so the imprint, the catalog extract and the period must be in it, scoped to the task rather than everything the coordinator holds.

-
The output contract — the return will be consumed programmatically at aggregation, so the prompt states the fields, structure and what counts as a finding.

Scoped input plus explicit output shape is what makes the handoff clean in both directions.

Why the other options are incorrect
The coordinator's full conversation — buries the task in irrelevant history and spends the subagent's context on material it does not need, the opposite of the scoped slice that makes isolation an advantage.

Sibling interim findings — couples work that was decomposed to be independent, anchoring the analysis and importing errors the siblings have not had reviewed. Consistency is the coordinator's job at aggregation.

The AgentDefinition prompt repeated — loads as the subagent's system prompt by the machinery itself. Repeating it wastes tokens and creates a second copy that can drift.

Key Takeaway
Invocation prompts carry the task's specific data and its output contract. Not parent history, not sibling outputs, not a copy of the definition.

question:
A solar-operations platform runs a nightly pipeline with four subagent types: three do mechanical work — normalizing inverter logs, matching serial numbers, formatting tickets — and one synthesizes a maintenance-priority briefing from everything the others produced. All four currently run on the same premium model; the mechanical three account for 85% of calls. Output review shows the mechanical tasks are never the quality problem.

How should the team use the AgentDefinition model field?
options: Keep one premium model everywhere, and the pipeline's behavior stays completely uniform
A small model for the three mechanical subagents; the capable one for synthesis
Assign the small model everywhere — 85% of the work is mechanical anyway
Let each night's run pick its models dynamically, based on the previous night's measured error rates
answer: A small model for the three mechanical subagents; the capable one for synthesis
explanation:
This question tests per-subagent model assignment.

Match Capability to Task
The model field exists so capability can be assigned per subagent, and this workload splits cleanly. Normalization, serial matching and ticket formatting are high-volume mechanical tasks a small model does indistinguishably well — the review explicitly says they are never the quality problem. The synthesis step is where judgment concentrates.

Small model for the three mechanical subagents, capable model for synthesis cuts the bill on 85% of calls at no quality cost, and keeps premium capability exactly where the briefing is written.

Why the other options are incorrect
Premium everywhere — uniform overpayment: the premium model's advantage is unused on mechanical work, and the review found no quality there to preserve.

Small model everywhere — downgrades the pipeline's one judgment-heavy step, the briefing the whole night exists to produce, to save on 15% of calls. The asymmetry runs the other way.

Dynamic per-night selection — makes each night's behavior depend on the previous night's noise, and mechanical error rates would rarely justify changes anyway. Assignment should follow the task's nature, which does not change nightly.

Key Takeaway
Assign models per subagent: cheap models for high-volume mechanical work, capable models where judgment concentrates.

-

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Model configuration → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config
option_feedback: Uniformity here is uniform overpayment: the premium model's advantage is unused on mechanical work — the review found no quality problem there to preserve.

The model field exists so capability can be assigned per subagent, and this workload splits cleanly: normalization, matching, and formatting are high-volume tasks a small model does indistinguishably well — the review says so — while the synthesis step is where judgment concentrates and quality is actually earned. Matching model to task cuts the bill on 85% of calls with no quality cost, and keeps premium capability exactly where the briefing is written.
Downgrading the synthesis subagent trades the pipeline's one judgment-heavy step — the briefing the whole night exists to produce — for savings on 15% of calls. The asymmetry runs the other way.

question:
A credit union's support coordinator delegates to a dispute-investigation subagent. That subagent's tools list currently includes the spawning tool, and traces show it spawning its own ad-hoc helpers — sometimes three levels deep. Nobody designed those helpers; runs have become slow, expensive, and hard to audit, with fan-out varying wildly between similar cases.

What should the team change?
options: Add a prompt rule to the subagent: spawn at most one helper, and only when strictly necessary
Keep the capability but log every spawn so the audit trail captures the full tree
Remove the spawning tool from its tools list; delegation stays at the coordinator
Cap the run's total token budget so deep spawning trees exhaust it early and stop
answer: Remove the spawning tool from its tools list; delegation stays at the coordinator
explanation:
This question tests where fan-out is controlled.

Delegation Is Architecture, and the Tools List Enforces It
A subagent holding the spawning tool can create sub-trees, and three-level ad-hoc trees are what the traces show: slow, expensive, hard to audit, with fan-out varying per run.

Removing the spawning tool from its list makes deep trees structurally impossible and concentrates delegation at the coordinator, restoring the designed shape — one level of deliberate, observable delegation. If investigation genuinely needs a helper, that helper gets designed and dispatched where cost and observability live.

Why the other options are incorrect
A prompt rule limiting spawns — leaves the capability in place and negotiates with it. "Strictly necessary" is the subagent's own judgment, which is exactly what produced three-level trees.

Log every spawn — makes the chaos visible without making it smaller. The audit trail faithfully records slow, expensive, wildly varying runs; observability answers a different question.

A total token cap — converts runaway spawning into truncated runs. The tree still forms and spends the budget; the actual investigation is what gets cut off.

Key Takeaway
Control fan-out by withholding the spawning tool from leaf subagents. Prompt limits and budget caps constrain the symptoms, not the structure.

-

-
Anthropic — Create custom subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Configure permissions (Agent SDK) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions
option_feedback: A prompt rule leaves the capability in place and negotiates with it — "strictly necessary" is the subagent's own judgment, which is precisely what produced three-level trees. Structure, not phrasing, is what bounds structure.
Logging makes the chaos visible without making it smaller: the audit trail faithfully records slow, expensive, wildly varying runs. Observability is worth having and answers a different question.

Delegation is an architectural decision, and the tools list is where the architecture is enforced: a subagent that does not hold the spawning tool cannot create sub-trees, full stop. Concentrating spawning at the coordinator restores the designed shape — one level of deliberate, observable delegation — and makes fan-out a property of the design again rather than of each run's improvisation.
