question:
A parcel-network's document agent posts extracted customs entries into the ERP via a submit_entry tool. Twice this month, a submit call timed out on the network after the ERP had actually committed the entry; the loop retried, and the entry posted twice. Reversals take finance an hour each.

What is the right fix?
options: A prompt rule instructing the agent never to retry submit_entry after timeouts and network failures
Increase the tool's network timeout substantially so slow ERP commits stop being reported as spurious failures
Have the agent query the ERP for a duplicate before every submit call
Give each submission an idempotency key so the ERP ignores the retried duplicate
answer: Give each submission an idempotency key so the ERP ignores the retried duplicate
explanation:
This question tests the classic timeout-retry ambiguity on a mutation.

Make the Retry Harmless
A timeout after commit leaves the caller unable to know whether the operation landed. Safety therefore comes from making the retry safe, not from guessing: an idempotency key, derived from the entry's identity and attached by the tool layer, lets the ERP recognize the second submission as the same operation and ignore it.

Retries become safe by construction — for the agent, the loop, and any future caller, no matter why or how often they happen.

Why the other options are incorrect
Never retry after a timeout — converts double-posting risk into lost-entry risk: a timeout where the commit genuinely failed now leaves a missing customs entry. The ambiguity is unresolved; only the guess changed. It also rests on the model honoring prose.

A longer timeout — shrinks the window without closing it. Some commit eventually outlasts any limit, and tuning constants is not a correctness mechanism.

Check for a duplicate before submitting — a race: state can change between the check and the submit, and it doubles traffic on every entry to guard against a rare event. Dedupe belongs inside the operation, where it is atomic.

Key Takeaway
Give mutations idempotency keys so retries are safe. Retry policies and timeout tuning manage the ambiguity; idempotency removes it.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use
option_feedback: Never-retry converts double-posting risk into lost-entry risk: a timeout where the commit genuinely failed now results in a missing customs entry, and the rule rests on the model honoring prose in every conversation. The ambiguity is still unresolved; only the guess changed.
A longer timeout shrinks the window without closing it — some commit will eventually outlast any limit, and the ambiguity returns. Tuning constants is not a correctness mechanism.

Check-then-submit is a race: between the agent's duplicate query and its submit, the state can change, and the check itself doubles traffic on every entry to guard against a rare event. The dedupe belongs inside the operation, where it is atomic.

Timeout-then-retry against a mutation is a classic ambiguity: the caller cannot know whether the first attempt landed, so safety has to come from making the retry harmless. An idempotency key — derived from the entry's identity, attached by the tool layer — lets the ERP recognize the second submission as the same operation and ignore it. Retries then become safe by construction, for the agent, for the loop, and for any future caller, no matter why or how often they happen.

question:
A marketing agency's outreach agent researches contacts, drafts personalized vendor emails, and sends them. Policy requires human approval "in the workflow," and the current design gates the research plan: a human approves the plan, then the agent researches, drafts, and sends unattended. Last week an approved plan still produced a factually wrong sent email.

Where should the approval gate sit?
options: Gate the send: review the actual drafted email; earlier steps flow freely
Where it is now, but with a far more detailed plan template so approvals catch more of the problems
At both ends — approve the plan first and the send as well — doubling the protection
After sending, as a sampled audit of delivered emails feeding weekly corrections
answer: Gate the send: review the actual drafted email; earlier steps flow freely
explanation:
This question tests gate placement: at the irreversible step, on the reviewable artifact.

Approve What Can Be Judged, Before What Cannot Be Undone
Sending is the workflow's only irreversible act, and the draft is the artifact an approver can actually evaluate. The plan approval happened before the risky content existed, which is precisely why an approved plan still produced a wrong sent email.
Gating the send means every email is reviewed as itself, and everything upstream — research, drafting — runs unattended because all of it remains reversible until the gate.

Why the other options are incorrect
A more detailed plan template — a richer plan still cannot contain the email's eventual facts, which are introduced during research and drafting. The gate inspects the wrong artifact however detailed the template.

Gate both ends — the send gate does all the protective work; the plan gate catches nothing the send gate will not see better and later. Doubling ceremony without doubling protection trains approvers to rubber-stamp.

Post-send sampled audit — improves next week's emails while this week's wrong email reaches a vendor. Audit complements a gate; it cannot replace one on an irreversible act.

Key Takeaway
Place approval gates immediately before the irreversible step, reviewing the actual artifact. Everything reversible upstream can flow freely.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Automate actions with hooks → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide

-
Anthropic — Choose a permission mode → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes

-
Anthropic — Configure permissions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions
option_feedback: A gate protects by standing between what can be inspected and what cannot be undone. Sending is the workflow's only irreversible act, and the draft is the artifact the approver can actually judge — the plan approval happened before the risky content existed, which is why a bad email sailed through an approved plan. Moving the gate to the send means every email is reviewed as itself, and everything upstream — research, drafting — can run unattended because all of it remains reversible until the gate.

A richer plan cannot contain the email's eventual facts — the errors are introduced during research and drafting, after the plan is approved. The gate inspects the wrong artifact no matter how detailed the template.

The send gate does all the protective work; the plan gate adds an approval that catches nothing the send gate will not see better and later. Doubling ceremony without doubling protection trains approvers to rubber-stamp.

Post-hoc sampling improves next week's emails; the requirement is that this week's wrong email not reach a vendor. Audit complements a gate — it cannot substitute for one when the act is irreversible.

question:
A point-of-sale software company runs agents in its release pipeline. The security team wants graded control over tool calls: read-only operations should proceed untouched, a defined set of forbidden operations must never run, and the middle band — schema migrations, dependency changes — should pause for a human decision each time.

How should this be implemented?
options: Two PreToolUse hooks: one allowing reads, one denying everything else, with the middle band moved out of the pipeline
A PreToolUse hook returning a permission decision per call: allow for read-only, ask for the middle band, deny for the forbidden set
A system-prompt policy section describing the three bands and instructing the model to request explicit human approval for every middle-band call
A PostToolUse hook that reverses any middle-band operation a human retroactively declines
answer: A PreToolUse hook returning a permission decision per call: allow for read-only, ask for the middle band, deny for the forbidden set
explanation:
This question tests the three-valued PreToolUse permission decision.

Allow, Ask, Deny — One Hook, Three Bands
The hook's permission decision is three-valued for exactly this shape of policy: allow passes read-only calls untouched, deny blocks the forbidden set, and ask suspends middle-band calls pending a human answer.
One hook inspecting each pending call and mapping it to its band delivers the security team's graded behavior — friction-free reads, hard-stopped forbidden operations, and a human in the loop for exactly the calls judged to deserve one — all enforced in code at the call boundary.

Why the other options are incorrect
Two hooks, middle band removed from the pipeline — a binary allow/deny architecture cannot express "pause and ask," so it exiles the middle band rather than governing it. The requirement was human judgment on those calls, not their absence.

System-prompt policy — makes the model the enforcer of restrictions on itself; the bands become suggestions with a failure rate. "Must never run" needs enforcement outside the model.

PostToolUse reversal — fires after execution: a migration has already run before the human declines it, and schema changes are exactly what does not reliably reverse.

Key Takeaway
Return allow / ask / deny per call from a PreToolUse hook to express graded policy. Approval must precede execution, which is what ask provides.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Hooks reference → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks

-
Anthropic — Intercept and control agent behavior with hooks → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks

-
Anthropic — Configure permissions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions
option_feedback: A binary allow/deny architecture has no way to express "pause and ask," so it amputates the middle band from the pipeline rather than governing it — the requirement was human judgment on those calls, not their exile.

The hook's permission decision is three-valued for exactly this shape of policy: allow passes the call, deny blocks it, and ask suspends it pending a human answer. One hook inspecting each pending call and mapping it to its band gives the security team the graded behavior they specified — friction-free reads, hard-stopped forbidden calls, and a human in the loop for precisely the operations judged to deserve one — all enforced in code at the call boundary.

Prompt policy makes the model the enforcer of restrictions on itself; the bands become suggestions with a failure rate. The requirement's "must never run" needs an enforcement point outside the model.

PostToolUse fires after execution — a migration has already run before the human declines it, and "reversing" a schema change is exactly the kind of operation that does not reliably reverse. Approval must precede execution, which is what ask provides.

question:
A veterinary-practice-management vendor enforces a business rule — expense claims above a threshold require a cost-center code — via a PreToolUse hook in the Claude Code setup the operations agents use. An audit finds violations in the database anyway: a nightly ingestion service calls the same MCP submission tool directly and never passes through anyone's session hooks.

Where should the rule live?
options: In a second copy of the same hook, installed separately inside the nightly ingestion service's own configuration
In the shared CLAUDE.md, where every Claude-based consumer of the tool learns the rule
Validate in the tool itself, server-side; hooks stay for session-scoped policy
In the database — a constraint, rejecting rows that lack a cost-center code
answer: Validate in the tool itself, server-side; hooks stay for session-scoped policy
explanation:
This question tests choosing the enforcement layer by who passes through it.

An Operation-Level Invariant Belongs in the Operation
The rule is a property of the submission itself — no high-value claim without a cost-center code — so it belongs in the tool's own server-side validation, which every caller passes through by definition: sessions, the nightly ingestion service, scripts, and whatever integrates next.
Hooks then do what only hooks can: session-scoped policy for a particular deployment — extra approval friction, logging, environment rules — layered on a tool that is already safe by itself.

Why the other options are incorrect
A second copy of the hook in the nightly service — covers the one bypass the audit happened to find. The rule now lives in N configurations that drift, and consumer N+1 starts unprotected.

The shared CLAUDE.md — reaches only Claude sessions that load it, and the nightly service is not one. It is guidance rather than enforcement even where it does reach.

A database constraint — real enforcement at the wrong primary layer: it fires after the tool accepted the submission, rejecting work late with a datastore error the agent cannot interpret, and a threshold rule is richer than a NOT NULL. Good defense in depth; wrong home.

Key Takeaway
Enforce operation-level business rules server-side in the tool, where every caller passes. Reserve hooks for session-scoped policy.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp

-
Anthropic — Automate actions with hooks → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide

-
Anthropic — Connect to external tools with MCP (Agent SDK) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/mcp
option_feedback: Copying the hook covers the one bypass the audit happened to find; the rule now lives in N configurations that drift, and consumer N+1 starts unprotected. Per-caller enforcement of an operation-level invariant is a treadmill.
CLAUDE.md reaches only Claude sessions that load it — the nightly service is not one — and it is guidance rather than enforcement even where it does reach. The audit's violation path stays open.

The rule is a property of the operation — no high-value claim without a cost center — so it belongs where the operation lives: in the tool's own server-side validation, which every caller passes through by definition. Sessions, services, scripts, and whatever integrates next are all covered automatically. Hooks then do what only hooks can: session-scoped policy for a particular deployment — extra approval friction, logging, environment rules — layered on top of a tool that is already safe by itself.

A database constraint is real enforcement but at the wrong layer to be the answer: it fires after the tool accepted the submission, rejecting work late with a datastore error the agent cannot interpret well, and the business rule as stated — threshold logic — is richer than a NOT NULL. Defense in depth, yes; the primary home is the tool.

question:
A K-12 curriculum publisher is decomposing a standards-alignment analysis across its content library. The current design dispatches one subagent invocation per lesson activity — about 800 invocations — and per-invocation overhead (dispatch, context setup, result handling) now exceeds the analysis work itself. Each activity's analysis is small; a full unit's material fits comfortably in one context.

How should the work be repartitioned?
options: Keep per-activity invocations but batch the dispatches so overhead is paid in parallel
Give one subagent the whole library in a single giant invocation to eliminate the overhead entirely
Keep per-activity invocations and shorten the per-invocation prompts to cut setup cost
Chunk at the unit level: one invocation per unit's activities, sized so each fits context comfortably
answer: Chunk at the unit level: one invocation per unit's activities, sized so each fits context comfortably
explanation:
This question tests work-unit sizing between two competing costs.

Below the Useful Floor
Per-invocation overhead argues for bigger units; context limits argue for smaller ones. Per-activity units sit far below the floor — 800 overhead payments for 800 small tasks, with overhead exceeding the analysis itself.
The stem says a full unit's material fits comfortably in one context, so unit-level chunks collapse ~800 invocations into a few dozen, each doing enough work to dwarf its own setup. Related activities also land in the same context, which alignment analysis benefits from. Size the unit to the largest coherent chunk that fits comfortably; both costs stay small.

Why the other options are incorrect
Batch the dispatches — pays the same 800 overheads at the same total cost. Concurrency compresses wall-clock time, not the overhead-to-work ratio the team measured.

The whole library in one invocation — swings past the ceiling: the material no longer fits, attention dilutes, and a single failure loses everything.

Shorten per-invocation prompts — shaves a constant off each of 800 payments. The count is the problem; no per-invocation economy makes 800 tiny tasks the right partition.

Key Takeaway
Size work units so per-invocation overhead is small relative to the work, while still fitting context comfortably. Both extremes fail, in opposite ways.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Run agents in parallel → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows
option_feedback: Parallel dispatch pays the same 800 overheads at the same total cost — concurrency compresses wall-clock time, not the overhead-to-work ratio the team measured.

One invocation for the entire library swings to the other failure: the material no longer fits, attention dilutes across it, and a single failure loses everything. The floor was too low; this is through the ceiling.
Trimming prompts shaves a constant off each of 800 payments; the count is the problem. No per-invocation economy makes 800 tiny tasks the right partition.

Work-unit sizing is a balance between two costs: per-invocation overhead argues for bigger units, context limits argue for smaller ones. Per-activity units sit far below the useful floor — 800 overhead payments for 800 small tasks — while the stem says a unit's material fits comfortably, so unit-level chunks collapse ~800 invocations into a few dozen, each doing enough work to dwarf its own setup. Related activities also land in the same context, which alignment analysis benefits from. Size the unit to the largest coherent chunk that fits comfortably; both costs stay small.

question:
A telecom-software team split an API-inventory task across five subagents, one per repository group. The subagents finished, and then the merge failed: one output grouped endpoints by service, another by team, two used different field names for the same attributes, and one returned prose. Reconciling them manually took longer than the analysis.

What should the team do differently next time?
options: Define the merge contract first: shared schema, field names, grouping keys
Add a sixth subagent that runs after the five and converts all their outputs into one common format
Run the five sequentially so each can see the previous outputs and match their format
Have one subagent do the entire inventory alone — decomposition caused the mismatch
answer: Define the merge contract first: shared schema, field names, grouping keys
explanation:
This question tests the half of decomposition teams forget: the join.

Design the Merge Before the Split
The team decided how to split and never decided how the results recombine — so five subagents each chose their own grouping, field names and format, and reconciliation cost more than the analysis.
Defining the merge contract first — shared output schema, agreed field names, grouping keys, stated in every invocation — makes five conforming outputs merge mechanically. The failure was not splitting the work; it was splitting without designing the join.

Why the other options are incorrect
A normalization subagent afterwards — reverse-engineers five ad-hoc formats: inferring that two field names mean the same thing, restructuring prose into records. That is the lossy manual reconciliation just performed, automated but no more reliable.

Run the five sequentially — forfeits the parallelism that motivated the split, and format-by-imitation is a fragile contract: each subagent matches its predecessor approximately, and drift compounds.

One subagent alone — the task partitioned cleanly along repository groups; the merge failed for want of a contract. Retreating gives up real speedup to avoid writing a schema.

Key Takeaway
Decomposition has two decisions: how to split and how to merge. Specify the shared output contract before dispatch.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Run agents in parallel → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents

-
Anthropic — Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/workflows
option_feedback: Decomposition is two decisions, and the team made only one: how to split. How the results recombine is the other half, and it must be settled before dispatch — a shared schema with agreed field names and grouping keys, stated in every invocation as the output contract. Five conforming outputs then merge mechanically. The failure was not splitting the work; it was splitting without designing the join.

A normalization subagent reverse-engineers five ad-hoc formats after the fact — inferring that two field names mean the same thing, restructuring prose into records — which is exactly the lossy reconciliation the team just did manually, automated but no more reliable.

Serializing five independent analyses to propagate format by imitation forfeits the parallelism that motivated the split, and imitation is a fragile contract — each subagent formats like its predecessor approximately, and drift compounds down the chain.

The task partitioned cleanly along repository groups; the merge failed for want of a contract, not because parallel work is inherently unmergeable. Retreating to one agent gives up real speedup to avoid writing a schema.

question:
A hotel-technology developer has kept one Claude Code session running for three weeks, mixing unrelated work: a booking-widget bug, a database migration, invoice formatting, and now a caching investigation. Suggestions have started referencing decisions from the migration while she works on caching.

What is the better working habit?
options: Run /compact regularly in the long session to keep it manageable
Start a fresh session per distinct task, resuming a session only to continue that same piece of work
Keep the long session, but begin every new task with a message clearly announcing the topic change first
Raise the context limit so old topics fit alongside new ones in the long session
answer: Start a fresh session per distinct task, resuming a session only to continue that same piece of work
explanation:
This question tests session hygiene across unrelated tasks.

Context Is Memory, and Old Topics Are Noise
Three weeks of mixed work means migration decisions sit in context while she works on caching — and cross-contamination in the suggestions is the symptom. One session per distinct task keeps each context coherent: the session holds what its task needs and nothing else, with resuming reserved for continuing that same piece of work.

Why the other options are incorrect
Regular /compact — shrinks the mixture without unmixing it. The summary still carries migration decisions into caching work; size was not the problem, relevance was.

Announce the topic change — asks the model to disregard context it still holds. Earlier material keeps its influence, and the announcement adds a wish on top.

Raise the context limit — preserves more of the irrelevant past, deepening the problem. The goal is not fitting old topics in; it is their absence.

Key Takeaway
Start a fresh session per task and resume only to continue the same work. Compaction and larger windows manage volume, not relevance.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Manage sessions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions

-
Anthropic — Explore the context window → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window

-
Anthropic — Best practices for Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Compaction shrinks the mixture without unmixing it — the summary still carries migration decisions into caching work. Size was not the problem; relevance was.

A session's context is its memory, and memory of the migration is noise — or worse, false premises — while working on caching. One session per task keeps each context coherent: the session holds what its task needs and nothing else, and resuming remains the right move when it is genuinely the same work continuing. The observed cross-contamination is the symptom this habit prevents.
A topic-change announcement asks the model to disregard context it still holds. Earlier material keeps its influence; the announcement adds a wish on top.
More room preserves more of the irrelevant past — it deepens the problem. The goal is not fitting old topics in; it is their absence.

question:
A legal-operations team's matter-search tool returns every matching record in full — often 400 rows of complete JSON, including internal audit fields. Transcripts show the agent misquoting totals from mid-payload, latching onto the first few records, and occasionally running out of context in long sessions.

How should the tool's output be redesigned?
options: Return the same rows but strip all of the internal audit fields, reducing each record's size
Compress the payload so more rows fit in the same number of tokens
Keep the full output and instruct the agent to read only the first fifty records
Return a concise set: the fields tasks use, a total count, and a pagination handle when needed
answer: Return a concise set: the fields tasks use, a total count, and a pagination handle when needed
explanation:
This question tests designing tool output for its actual consumer.

Tool Output Is Model Input
400 rows of complete JSON produces exactly the observed symptoms: misquoted mid-payload totals, first-record bias, and context exhaustion. Output should be designed for consumption — enough to act on, little enough to attend to.
A concise result set — the fields the agent's tasks use, a total count for the aggregate questions it was garbling, and a pagination handle for deeper dives — matches what consumption requires. All three symptoms end because they all trace to the dump.

Why the other options are incorrect
Strip audit fields — slims each record while keeping 400 of them. Attention and context problems are about volume, which survives the trim mostly intact.

Compress the payload — tokens are the model's units; no compression makes 400 rows attend like 20. Denser packing of the same content is the same burden.

Instruct the agent to read fifty — leaves the whole payload in context, paid for and competing for attention, and makes correctness depend on the model consistently ignoring what it was handed. Selection belongs tool-side.

Key Takeaway
Return the fields consumers use, a count, and a pagination handle. Filtering after the tokens are spent does not recover the attention they cost.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Manage tool context → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/manage-tool-context

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference
option_feedback: Dropping audit fields slims each record while keeping 400 of them — the attention and context problems are about volume, and volume survives the trim mostly intact.
Tokens are the model's units; there is no compression that makes 400 rows attend like 20. Denser packing of the same content is the same burden.

The instruction leaves the whole payload in context — paid for and still competing for attention — and makes correctness depend on the model consistently ignoring what it was handed. Selection belongs on the tool side, before tokens are spent.

A tool's output is model input, and it should be designed for that consumer: enough to act on, little enough to attend to. The agent's tasks use a handful of fields — so return those; the total count answers the aggregate questions the agent was garbling; and a pagination handle keeps deep dives possible without shipping everything every time. Misreads, first-record bias, and context exhaustion all trace to the 400-row dump, and all three end when the output matches what consumption actually requires.

question:
A freight-forwarding data team reviews its rate-lookup tool, whose responses look like {"amount": 1200, "distance": 480}. Agents have quoted the amount as dollars when the backend stores cents, and mixed kilometers with miles in one report.

What is the fix?
options: Document the units carefully in the team wiki so agent authors configure their prompts correctly
Standardize all backends on one unit system so the numbers cannot be misread
Self-describing output: amount_cents, currency, distance_km
Add a system-prompt note to each agent stating the units this tool uses
answer: Self-describing output: amount_cents, currency, distance_km
explanation:
This question tests self-describing tool output.

Units Should Travel With Values
{"amount": 1200} invites the model to guess dollars or cents. Field names and companion fields that state the unit and currency — amount_cents, currency, distance_km — resolve the ambiguity in the payload itself, unambiguously, for every consumer, with no external knowledge required.

Why the other options are incorrect
Document in the wiki — documentation at a distance: the model never reads it, and every agent author must transcribe it into every prompt forever.

Standardize all backends — a large migration that still ships bare numbers at the end, so future consumers must still learn the convention from somewhere else.

System-prompt notes per agent — patches each consumer separately and drifts as tools evolve. The tool's own response reaches every consumer automatically.

Key Takeaway
Name and structure tool output so units and currency travel with the values. Bare numbers push interpretation onto every consumer.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference

-
Anthropic — Structured outputs → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: A wiki is documentation at a distance — the model never reads it, and every agent author must remember to transcribe it into every prompt, forever.
Backend standardization is a large migration that still ships bare numbers at the end — future consumers must still know, from somewhere else, what the convention is.

The ambiguity lives in the payload, so the payload should resolve it: field names and companion fields that state the unit and currency make every reading unambiguous at the point of use, for every consumer, with no external knowledge required. A bare number invites the model to guess; a self-describing one leaves nothing to guess about.
Per-agent prompt notes patch each consumer separately and drift as tools evolve; the tool's own response is the one place the information reaches every consumer automatically.

question:
A biotech lab-operations platform has a validate_batch tool that checks ten submitted sample manifests at a time. When two manifests fail validation, the tool currently returns one error for the whole call. Agents respond by resubmitting all ten — including the eight that were fine — and some retry loops have resubmitted the same valid manifests four times.

How should the tool report this outcome?
options: Per-item statuses in a success envelope, failures carrying their issues
An error, as today, but listing exactly which two manifests failed inside the error message text
A success when the majority passed, and an error only when six or more of the ten fail
As ten separate tool results, one per manifest, each carrying its own status
answer: Per-item statuses in a success envelope, failures carrying their issues
explanation:
This question tests reporting partial success.

Eight Passed — That Is a Result
The operation did its job: it validated ten manifests and learned eight are fine and two are not. That is a successful run with mixed findings, so the envelope should say so — per-item statuses, with the two failures carrying their specific issues.
The agent then resubmits two corrected manifests instead of ten, and the retry churn on valid items ends because the result no longer condemns the whole batch for its worst members.

Why the other options are incorrect
An error naming the two failures — helps, but the envelope still signals that the call failed, and error-channel semantics drive wholesale retries. The eight passes remain unreported as results.

Majority-threshold success — makes the same two failures read as success or error depending on their neighbours. A result's meaning should not depend on arithmetic over unrelated items.

Ten separate tool results — one tool_use produces one tool_result; the protocol has no way to answer a single call with ten. The per-item structure belongs inside the one result.

Key Takeaway
Report partial success as a success envelope with per-item statuses. Whole-call errors force wholesale retries of work that already succeeded.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: The operation did its job: it validated ten manifests and learned eight are fine and two are not. That is a successful validation run with mixed findings, and the envelope should say so — per-item statuses, with the two failures carrying their specific issues so the follow-up fixes exactly what is wrong. The agent then resubmits two corrected manifests, not ten, and the retry churn on valid items ends because the result no longer condemns the whole batch for its worst members.

Naming the failures inside an error helps, but the envelope still signals that the call failed — and error-channel semantics are what drive wholesale retries. The eight passes remain unreported as what they are: results.
A majority threshold makes the same two failures read as success one day and error another depending on their neighbors — the envelope's meaning should not depend on arithmetic over unrelated items.

One tool_use produces one tool_result; the protocol has no way to answer a single call with ten results. The per-item structure belongs inside the one result, which is exactly what the success envelope provides.

question:
A food-delivery company's support agent calls an order-adjustment tool. When the backend rejects a request, the tool passes through the raw exception — a 40-line Java stack trace. Transcripts show the agent quoting stack frames to customers, and in several cases retrying calls that failed for reasons the trace stated only in an internal class name.

What should the tool return instead?
options: The same stack trace, but with an instruction in the agent's prompt to summarize it politely
A model-actionable error: what failed, how to change the request, and what to tell the customer
Only a generic "adjustment failed" message, keeping anything internal out of conversations
The stack trace plus a numeric error code, giving the agent both the detail and some structure
answer: A model-actionable error: what failed, how to change the request, and what to tell the customer
explanation:
This question tests writing errors for the right audience.

The Audience Is the Model
An error message's audience is whoever must act on it, and here that is the model: it needs to know what failed, whether and how to change the request, and what is appropriate to tell the customer.
A response built around those three questions produces the right behavior directly — corrected retries where correction is possible, honest customer-facing explanations where it is not. Stack traces answer none of them; they are the implementation talking to its own developers.

Why the other options are incorrect
Trace plus a "summarize politely" instruction — asks the model to translate an artifact that lacks the needed information. A stack frame does not say whether the request was fixable or what may be relayed; politeness cannot recover what was never there.

A generic "adjustment failed" — nothing leaks and nothing informs. The agent can neither correct the request nor explain anything, so every failure ends in a generic apology.

Trace plus an error code — the code adds a label while the trace remains the bulk, still in the conversation and still quotable to customers. Structure around unusable content does not make it usable.

Key Takeaway
Write tool errors for the model: what failed, how to fix the request, what the customer may be told. Stack traces and bare failure notices both leave the agent unable to act.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: The prompt instruction asks the model to translate an artifact that lacks the needed information — a stack frame does not say whether the request was fixable or what the customer may be told. Politeness cannot recover what the message never contained.

An error message's audience is whoever must act on it, and here that is the model: it needs to know what failed, whether a changed request could succeed and how to change it, and what is appropriate to relay to the customer. A response designed around those three questions produces the right behavior directly — corrected retries where correction is possible, honest customer-facing explanations where it is not. Stack traces answer none of those questions; they are the implementation talking to its own developers.

A bare failure notice swings to the opposite extreme: nothing leaks and nothing informs. The agent can neither correct the request nor explain anything, so every failure ends in a generic apology — the current problem with less noise.

The code adds a label; the trace remains the bulk, still in the conversation and still quotable to customers. Structure around unusable content does not make it usable — the content itself must be written for the model.

question:
A sports-media research pipeline ends each run with a synthesis request: the model composes the final report from findings already gathered. The request reuses the same configuration as earlier turns, tools included, and the model keeps issuing lookup calls mid-synthesis — the report arrives late and fragmented.

Which tool_choice setting fits the synthesis request?
options: {"type": "auto"}
{"type": "any"}
{"type": "none"}
{"type": "tool", "name": "compose_report"}
answer: {"type": "none"}
explanation:
This question tests tool_choice on a turn whose correct output is prose.

Synthesis Needs No Tools
The evidence is already in context and the desired output is a report. Setting {"type": "none"} on the synthesis request forbids tool calls, so the model composes in one uninterrupted pass. tool_choice is per-request: earlier turns keep their tools; this turn declares that its job needs none.

Why the other options are incorrect
"auto" — leaves the door open, and the observed behavior is the model walking through it. Optional tools on a turn that should not use any.

"any" — forces a tool call on the one turn whose correct output is text, the exact opposite of the requirement.

{"type": "tool", "name": "compose_report"} — no such tool exists in this pipeline; the report is the text response. Forcing a named tool would mean inventing structure the workflow does not need.

Key Takeaway
Use "none" for composition turns where the answer is prose. tool_choice is set per request, so different turns in one pipeline can carry different settings.

-
Anthropic — Tool reference (tool_choice) → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference

-
Anthropic — How tool use works → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works

-
Anthropic — Structured outputs → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: Auto leaves the door open, and the observed behavior is the model walking through it — optional tools on a turn that should not use any.
Any forces a tool call on the one turn whose correct output is prose — the opposite of the requirement.

The synthesis turn is pure composition: the evidence is already in context, and the desired output is text. Setting tool_choice to none for that request forbids tool calls, so the model writes the report in one uninterrupted pass. tool_choice is per-request — earlier turns keep their tools; the synthesis turn declares that its job needs none.
No compose_report tool exists in this pipeline; the report is the text response itself. Forcing a named tool would require inventing structure the workflow does not need.

question:
A wealth-management support agent can trigger portfolio-statement regeneration, which takes three to five minutes in the document system. The tool currently blocks on completion with a 60-second timeout, so nearly every invocation "fails," the agent apologizes or retries — and duplicate regeneration jobs pile up behind the scenes.

How should the tool be redesigned?
options: Raise the timeout to six minutes so the tool can block until the regeneration finishes
Make the tool fire-and-forget: start the job, return nothing, and let the customer check back later
Keep the 60-second tool but instruct the agent to treat its timeouts as probable successes
Return a job handle immediately, plus a status tool the agent polls, so progress can be reported
answer: Return a job handle immediately, plus a status tool the agent polls, so progress can be reported
explanation:
This question tests interface design for a long-running operation.

A Three-to-Five-Minute Operation Is a Job, Not a Call
The interface should say so: the trigger tool returns a job handle immediately, confirming the job started, and a status tool lets the agent check progress when the conversation needs it.
The agent can then tell the customer the statement is being generated, answer other questions meanwhile, and confirm completion — and duplicates disappear because starting a job becomes distinguishable from failing to.

Why the other options are incorrect
Raise the timeout to six minutes — holds the turn hostage to the slowest regeneration: the conversation freezes, transport layers strain against long-held connections, and the day a job takes seven minutes the ambiguity returns. Blocking scales with the operation; handles do not.

Fire-and-forget — discards the second half of the contract. The agent can never confirm completion, report failure, or answer "is it ready yet" — the conversation's whole reason for triggering the job.

Treat timeouts as probable successes — converts an interface defect into a policy of optimism. Genuine failures now read as probable successes, and the customer is told a statement exists that may not.

Key Takeaway
Return a handle plus a status tool for operations that outlast a turn. Blocking calls and fire-and-forget each drop half of what the conversation needs.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Tool reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference

-
Anthropic — Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: A six-minute blocking call holds the turn hostage to the slowest regeneration — the conversation is frozen, transport layers strain against long-held connections, and the day a job takes seven minutes, the ambiguity returns. Blocking scales with the operation; handles do not.
Fire-and-forget discards the second half of the contract: the agent can never confirm completion, report failure, or answer "is it ready yet" — the conversation's whole reason for triggering the job.
Treat-timeouts-as-success converts an interface defect into a policy of optimism — genuine failures now read as probable successes, and the customer is told a statement exists that may not.

A three-to-five-minute operation is a job, not a call, and the interface should say so: the trigger tool returns immediately with a handle confirming the job started, and a companion status tool lets the agent check progress when the conversation needs it. The agent can tell the customer the statement is being generated, answer other questions meanwhile, and confirm completion — and duplicates disappear because starting a job is now distinguishable from failing to. question:

question:
A hotel-tech developer asks Claude Code why last night's integration run failed. The only evidence is a 40,000-line CI log. The agent's first attempt was Read on the whole file, which consumed most of the context window before analysis began.

What is the right retrieval approach?
options: Read the file in ten sequential chunks, compacting the session between each of the chunks
Have Bash split the log into forty files and Read each one in turn
Read only the final 200 lines, where CI failures normally appear
Grep the failure signature to locate the region, then Read that slice with offset and limit
answer: Grep the failure signature to locate the region, then Read that slice with offset and limit
explanation:
This question tests targeted retrieval in a very large log.

Search the Space, Then Read the Slice
A 40,000-line log is a search space, not reading material. Grep finds the failure markers — error strings, exit codes, the failing job's name — and returns locations; Read with offset and limit then pulls the few hundred surrounding lines that actually explain the failure.
Context holds evidence instead of bulk, leaving room for the analysis the developer asked for.

Ten chunks with compaction — still ingests all 40,000 lines and pays for them, with compaction repeatedly summarizing material that was mostly irrelevant. The relevant slice ends up compressed alongside the noise.

Split into forty files and Read each — changes the packaging, not the strategy: forty Reads of forty files is the same full ingestion with more steps.

Read the final 200 lines — a guess about log structure. Terminal lines are often teardown noise while the causal error fired thousands of lines earlier in a parallel job. Search finds the failure wherever it is.

Key Takeaway
Grep to locate, then Read with offset and limit. Position heuristics and chunked full reads both mis-handle large logs.

question:
A municipal-software developer receives a plan-mode proposal for a permit-fee recalculation change. The plan reads: "1. Review the fee module. 2. Update the calculation logic appropriately. 3. Make sure related code is consistent. 4. Test thoroughly." The tone is confident, and the developer is tempted to approve and move on.

What should the developer do, and why?
options: Approve it — plan mode has already done its job by forcing a pause, and the details will emerge during execution
Approve it but watch execution closely, intervening the moment a step goes somewhere unexpected
Send it back: an approvable plan names files, changes, per-phase verification, risks
Reject the plan and switch to direct execution, since planning is adding delay without value here
answer: Send it back: an approvable plan names files, changes, per-phase verification, risks
explanation:
This question tests what makes a plan approvable.

A Plan You Cannot Evaluate Is Not a Gate
"Update the calculation logic appropriately" and "test thoroughly" could describe any change to any module, so approving this plan approves nothing in particular. Confident tone is not information.
The developer's leverage is at the gate: require the plan to name the files it will touch, the nature of each change, what verification each phase runs, and where the risks sit. That plan can be genuinely evaluated, and its approval genuinely authorizes something.

Why the other options are incorrect
Approve; details emerge in execution — the pause is not the value, the evaluation is. Details emerging after the gate is exactly where surprises were supposed to be caught before.

Approve and watch closely — moves review from the cheap moment to the expensive one, judging changes as they land with no baseline for what "unexpected" even means.

Reject planning entirely — recalculating fees a municipality charges is precisely where a reviewable plan earns its delay. The failure is this plan's vagueness, not planning.

Key Takeaway
Send back plans that name no files, changes, verifications or risks. Vague plans turn the approval gate into a formality.

question:
A consultant is handed an event-ticketing company's inherited codebase — unfamiliar, poorly documented, of unknown quality — and will spend the first days purely building understanding before any change is agreed. She is setting up her Claude Code sessions for this orientation phase.

How should she run them?
options: Normal execution mode, relying on her own review of anything the agent proposes
Normal execution mode, with a CLAUDE.md note stating that this engagement is analysis-only for now
Headless -p invocations that write analysis reports, leaving no interactive session able to modify anything
Plan/read-only mode for the orientation phase, switching to execution modes when change work is agreed
answer: Plan/read-only mode for the orientation phase, switching to execution modes when change work is agreed
explanation:
This question tests matching session capability to engagement phase.

Orientation Is Reading
No change has been agreed, so nothing legitimate in this phase is an edit. Running the orientation read-only makes that structural: the consultant explores an unfamiliar system with zero risk of altering what she does not yet understand — which also matters contractually in someone else's codebase. When change work is agreed, the modes change with the work.

Why the other options are incorrect
Execution mode plus her own review — holds capability open that the phase cannot legitimately use, managed only by attention, in exactly the setting where an unintended modification is hardest to spot.

Execution mode with a CLAUDE.md note — context, not constraint: helpful framing, but the sessions still hold edit capability and the note is advice the model weighs.

Headless report generation — headless runs are not inherently non-modifying (a -p run holds whatever its configuration grants), so the safety claim still rests on configuration — and it forfeits the interactive follow-up that understanding a strange codebase depends on.

Key Takeaway
Run investigation phases in read-only/plan mode and switch modes when change work begins. Capability should track the phase, not the intention.

question:
A wealth-tech developer ran a three-hour Claude Code refactoring session against a reporting module: seven improvement rounds, no commits along the way. Round seven introduced a subtle breakage; with no intermediate state to return to, she reverted the branch and lost all seven rounds.

What working practice prevents this?
options: Commit at each green milestone, so a later breakage reverts one round instead of the whole session
Run the whole refactor in one round instead of seven, leaving nothing intermediate to lose
Keep a parallel copy of the module's directory before each round as a manual backup
Have the agent describe each round's changes in detail so they can be reapplied by hand after a revert
answer: Commit at each green milestone, so a later breakage reverts one round instead of the whole session
explanation:
This question tests recovery points during iterative work.

Checkpoint at Each Green Milestone
Iterative work needs recovery points at the granularity of the iterations. A commit after every round that passes tests turns the session into a ladder: round seven's breakage costs one rung — reset to round six and re-attempt — instead of the whole climb.
The tests define "green," the commit records it, and the habit costs seconds per round against the three hours it just saved.

Why the other options are incorrect
One giant round — trades away iteration's advantages (reviewable diffs, testable increments) and concentrates all risk in a single all-or-nothing change, which is more likely to hide a subtle breakage.

Directory copies before each round — version control minus everything: no history, no diffs, no test-state association, manual bookkeeping that fails the round someone forgets.

Prose descriptions for manual reapplication — not a recovery mechanism. Reapplying six rounds by hand from notes is slower and less faithful than the code commits would have preserved exactly.

Key Takeaway
Commit at each green milestone so a later breakage costs one round. Version control is the checkpoint mechanism agent iteration should lean on.

question:
A point-of-sale team's agent just fixed a failing checkout test on round three of an iterative session. The team is codifying what the loop should do at the end of every fix round, before moving to the next issue.

Which TWO practices belong in the loop? (Select TWO.)
options: Ask the agent to confirm in prose that its fix is correct and complete
Re-run only the test that was failing, since that is the fix's target
Re-run the full relevant suite, so a fix that breaks something adjacent is caught in the round that broke it
Delete the reproduction test now that the underlying bug is fixed
Keep the failing case as a permanent regression test in the suite
answer: Re-run the full relevant suite, so a fix that breaks something adjacent is caught in the round that broke it
Keep the failing case as a permanent regression test in the suite
explanation:
This question tests how to close a fix round.

Verify Wide, Remember Permanently

-
Re-run the full relevant suite — a change that fixes one test can break a neighbour, and checkout code is shared code. Running the suite in the same round pins collateral damage to the change that caused it, while the context to fix it is still loaded.

-
Keep the failing case as a regression test — the reproduction becomes a permanent guard, so this bug's return is caught automatically by every future round and pipeline run.

Why the other options are incorrect
Prose self-confirmation — adds words where the suite adds evidence. The agent asserting completeness is exactly the signal tests exist to replace.

Re-run only the failing test — how adjacent breakage escapes the round: green on one test says nothing about the neighbours the change touched, and the collateral surfaces later, unattributed.

Delete the reproduction test — discards the round's most durable output, the executable statement of the bug — precisely the artifact preventing silent reintroduction.

Key Takeaway
End each fix round with the full relevant suite and keep the reproduction as a regression test. Narrow verification and deleted reproductions both let the bug return unnoticed.

question:
A marketing-tech company wired its Claude review job as a required status check: any run that posts findings fails the build and blocks the merge. One month in, 22% of blocked merges were released by developers marking findings not applicable, two incident hotfixes waited on re-runs, and the deterministic checks the pipeline already ran — tests, lint, type-check — were passing throughout. The team still wants the review to carry weight.

How should the job be wired?
options: Keep it blocking, but allow any developer to override the failed check with a comment on the PR
Advisory PR comments that don't block; hard-fail only deterministic checks; track resolution rates
Keep it blocking and raise the reviewer's confidence threshold until far fewer findings ever appear
Keep it blocking for pull requests above a size threshold and make it advisory below that line
answer: Advisory PR comments that don't block; hard-fail only deterministic checks; track resolution rates
explanation:
This question tests what a probabilistic signal should be wired to.

Merge Gates Belong on Unambiguous Checks
A test fails or it does not; a model's review findings are judgments with a false-positive rate. That is why 22% of blocked merges were dismissed and why hotfixes queued behind re-runs — while the deterministic checks passed throughout.
Advisory PR comments that do not block, with hard failure reserved for tests, lint and type-check, puts findings where developers act on them without giving a probabilistic signal veto power over the merge button. Weight then comes from measurement: tracking resolution rates shows whether the reviewer is earning attention.

Why the other options are incorrect
Blocking with a comment override — a gate everyone can wave through is a gate in name only: it preserves the ceremony and latency while removing the enforcement, and trains developers to treat overriding as routine.

Raise the confidence threshold — reduces volume without changing what the gate is wired to. Whatever findings survive still block merges on a judgment call, so one confident false positive still stops a hotfix.

Blocking above a size threshold — PR size proxies neither correctness nor risk; a one-line payment-path change outranks a large mechanical rename. Arbitrary blocking, and large PRs still stall on dismissible findings.

Key Takeaway
Wire probabilistic review findings to advisory comments and hard-fail only deterministic checks. Measure resolution rates to give the reviewer weight.

-
Anthropic — Code Review → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review

-

question:
A telecom-software team's CI runs a Claude review job on every push to every branch. The monthly bill has tripled: work-in-progress branches trigger reviews nobody reads, and rapid push sequences leave several reviews of already-obsolete commits running in parallel.

Which TWO changes control the cost? (Select TWO.)
options: Move the review job to a smaller model to cut the price of each run
Trigger reviews on pull-request readiness — opened or marked ready — rather than on every push
Cache review results so identical diffs are never reviewed twice
Configure concurrency so a new push cancels the still-running review of the branch's superseded commit
Limit reviews to files under 500 lines to shrink each run
answer: Trigger reviews on pull-request readiness — opened or marked ready — rather than on every push
Configure concurrency so a new push cancels the still-running review of the branch's superseded commit
explanation:
This question tests CI cost control through trigger discipline.

Two Trigger Problems, Two Fixes

-
Trigger on PR readiness — aligns spend with intent: a review runs when the author declares the work ready for eyes, not on every WIP save. The unread reviews stop.

-
Concurrency cancellation on new pushes — when a new commit supersedes the one under review, the obsolete run stops instead of billing to completion.

Together they make each dollar buy a review someone will read, of a commit that still exists.

Why the other options are incorrect
A smaller model — discounts the waste without reducing it. Unread reviews of obsolete commits still run, at a lower rate; the volume, not the unit price, is the finding.

Cache identical diffs — almost never hits in practice, since pushes change the diff by definition. It adds infrastructure for a case the workload barely produces.

Skip files over 500 lines — shrinks runs by excluding exactly the files most likely to need review, trading cost for blind spots rather than for discipline.

Key Takeaway
Control CI cost with trigger discipline: run on PR readiness and cancel superseded runs. Model size and file-size cutoffs trade quality for price.

question:
A K-12 software team's CI reviewer was configured under the philosophy "flag everything, humans filter." Six months of data: 96 findings per week on average, a 92% dismissal rate, and two incidents that post-mortems traced to real findings developers scrolled past inside the noise. The team lead insists recall matters most because "a missed bug is worse than a wasted click."

How should the criteria be redesigned?
options: Keep flag-everything but add a severity field so developers can sort before filtering
Keep flag-everything and rotate the filtering duty weekly so no one developer fatigues
A precision floor that keeps findings credible, with recall concentrated on high-impact defect classes
Invert the philosophy entirely, flagging only the findings that the model is nearly certain about
answer: A precision floor that keeps findings credible, with recall concentrated on high-impact defect classes
explanation:
This question tests the recall-versus-precision trade when the evidence refutes the intuition.

The Post-Mortems Refute the Team Lead
Two real bugs were flagged and still missed, because a 92% dismissal rate had trained developers to scroll. Recall on paper is not recall in effect — a finding only counts if someone acts on it, so credibility is a precondition, not a luxury.
The redesign prices both sides: hold precision above the floor where developers demonstrably keep reading, and spend the recall budget where defects are most expensive — the impact-weighted classes. That maximizes caught-and-acted-on bugs, which was always the goal.

Why the other options are incorrect
Severity sorting — reorganizes the noise: 96 weekly findings at 92% dismissal still bury the real two, now under a sort order. Fatigue is about volume.

Rotate the filtering duty — shares the fatigue rather than fixing it. Each week's filterer faces the same noise stream, and the incident mechanism operates on whoever is on duty.

Flag only near-certain findings — overcorrects to the opposite failure: precision soars while recall collapses everywhere, including the high-impact classes the system exists to guard. The asymmetry deserves a tuned floor, not a flipped extreme.

Key Takeaway
Set a precision floor that keeps findings credible, then concentrate recall on high-impact classes. Findings nobody reads have zero effective recall.

question:

When the weekly flagged-invoice rate jumped from 6% to 11%, nobody could say which criteria change caused it, when it landed, or what the criteria even were on any given past date.

What practice fixes this?
options: Restrict criteria edits to one owner, giving every change at least a single accountable author
Freeze the criteria permanently, and the metric becomes comparable week over week
Keep an informal changelog document where engineers note their edits when they remember
Version the criteria like code, and stamp every output with the criteria version that produced it

Freeze permanently — buys comparability by forbidding improvement. Real drift in invoice formats will eventually demand changes, leaving the system wrong-but-stable.

An informal changelog — the current state with a document attached. The gaps in a when-they-remember log are precisely the changes that turn out to matter.

Version criteria like code and stamp outputs with the version that produced them. Ownership and informal logs record intent; version stamps make metrics attributable.

What is the correct fix?
options: Update the examples to the current schema, coupling future schema and example revisions
Add a prompt instruction stating that the schema takes precedence, and the examples yield wherever they disagree
Remove the examples entirely — the schema alone now defines the output correctly
Keep the examples but append a note to each one marking it as illustrative rather than exact

Two Instruction Attempts, Two Points of Improvement
The failure is situational — a refund raised mid-complaint — and the example set has never shown that shape handled correctly. Instructions have hit their ceiling because prohibitions describe what not to do while the model needs the positive pattern.
Worked examples of exactly this situation — acknowledge the request, run the eligibility lookup, then state the amount — demonstrate the correct sequence through the tempting moment. Demonstrations of the exact failure case are the highest-leverage addition when a specific behavior resists instruction.

Why the other options are incorrect
Two more instructions — mines a vein that has yielded two points from two attempts. The gap is demonstrative, not declarative.

Replace all eight with refund conversations — overcorrects: the generic examples anchor the agent's ordinary competence, and an all-refund set teaches an agent that mostly handles other things that everything is refunds.

Remove the refund capability — makes the failure impossible by making the feature absent, so customers with legitimate refund questions get an agent that cannot answer. A product regression, not a fix.

Key Takeaway
When instructions plateau on a situational failure, demonstrate the correct handling of that exact situation. Add targeted examples; do not restate prohibitions or amputate the capability.

question:
A legal-operations team extracts filing records with a schema nested five levels deep — matter → filings[] → parties[] → representatives[] → contacts[] — mirroring their database's foreign-key structure exactly. Field-level accuracy at the deepest two levels runs three times worse than at the top, with values landing under the wrong parent as often as being wrong themselves.

What should the team change?
options: Keep the schema as is, adding a prompt instruction that walks through the nesting level by level
Split every extraction into five separate calls, one per nesting level
Keep the depth but shorten the field names so the structure is less verbose
Flatten to a shallow shape with linking keys, so code can rebuild the hierarchy afterward
answer: Flatten to a shallow shape with linking keys, so code can rebuild the hierarchy afterward
explanation:
This question tests schema shape against the model's reliability profile.

Misplacement Is a Structural Error
Values landing under the wrong parent is what five-level nesting produces: at level five, every value must be placed correctly relative to four enclosing contexts at once, and misplacement multiplies.
Flattening to a shallow shape with linking keys — records carrying matter_id and filing_id — changes the task's geometry: "which filing does this contact belong to" becomes a stated field rather than a bracket-depth position. Deterministic code then reassembles the tree, which is the part machines do perfectly. The schema should fit the model's reliability profile; the database's shape is code's problem to restore.

Why the other options are incorrect
A level-by-level walkthrough instruction — documents the difficulty without reducing it. The model still performs five-deep structural placement, now with prose describing the cliff.

Five separate calls, one per level — quintuples cost and creates a worse correlation problem: each call must reproduce parent context to attach correctly, so misattachment moves between calls rather than away.

Shorter field names — cosmetic. The three-times error gradient tracks depth, not verbosity.

Key Takeaway
Flatten deep schemas and rebuild hierarchy in code from linking keys. Nesting depth, not field length, drives structural misplacement.

question:
A biotech lab-operations pipeline extracts equipment-maintenance records, validates each extraction against the schema and re-prompts on failure, then hands the passing records to a downstream parser. Outputs satisfy every declared field, yet they frequently carry extra invented keys — technician_notes, follow_up_flag — that the schema never defined. The parser is strict and rejects any record containing an undeclared key, so batches keep failing on records that cleared validation.

What is the right fix?
options: Loosen the downstream parser to silently ignore any keys it does not recognize
Add the recurring invented keys to the schema so the outputs become legal
Constrain the schema to reject undeclared keys, so validation enforces the exact expected contract
Add a post-processing step that strips any unknown keys from each record before it reaches the parser
answer: Constrain the schema to reject undeclared keys, so validation enforces the exact expected contract
explanation:
This question tests closing a schema against undeclared keys.

The Schema Says What Must Be Present, Not What May Be
That silence is where invented keys come from. Constraining the schema to reject undeclared properties makes the contract exact — declared keys only, enforced at validation, which is the same boundary the parser already demands.
Because the pipeline validates and re-prompts before the parser, extra-key outputs now fail fast at extraction where the retry loop can correct them, instead of downstream where batches die.

Why the other options are incorrect
Loosen the parser — makes every consumer tolerant of undefined content: the invented keys flow through unvalidated, and anything downstream reading them consumes fabrication. Contracts should tighten at the source.

Add the invented keys to the schema — legitimizes fields nobody designed. technician_notes becomes official, populated by imagination, and the schema grows by whatever the model dreams up next.

Strip unknown keys in post-processing — papers over the signal. A model emitting undeclared fields is drifting from the contract, and silent removal hides the drift the closed schema would surface and correct.

Key Takeaway
Close schemas against undeclared keys so validation enforces the exact contract. Downstream stripping and parser loosening both hide contract drift.

question:
An event-ticketing support pipeline extracts callback details from conversations. The schema's phone field is a single string, and when customers give two numbers, outputs like "555-0142 and 555-0177 after 6pm" land in it, breaking the auto-dialer.

What is the schema fix?
options: An array of phone entries — number plus an optional note
Keep one string but instruct the model to pick the customer's first-mentioned number
Add a second field, phone_2, for conversations that mention two numbers
Keep the string field and split it on the word "and" in post-processing
answer: An array of phone entries — number plus an optional note
explanation:
This question tests modelling multi-valued data.

The Data Is a List
Customers give one number or several, sometimes with conditions like "after 6pm." An array of structured phone entries, each with the number and an optional note, says exactly that: every real conversation maps cleanly, the dialer iterates entries, and nothing gets crammed into prose inside a string.

Why the other options are incorrect
First-mentioned only — discards information the customer deliberately provided; the second number and the timing condition exist because they matter to the callback.

A phone_2 field — hardcodes the count at two. The third number breaks it again, and consumers must forever check a pair of fields that are really one list.

Split on "and" — parses prose with string surgery. "After 6pm" is not a phone number, and the next phrasing — "or", commas, "either" — defeats the splitter.

Key Takeaway
Model multi-valued data as arrays of structured entries. Single strings, numbered duplicate fields and string-splitting all fail on the second value.

question:
A freight-audit pipeline validates extracted invoices and currently treats every check the same way: any failure rejects the extraction into the retry loop. Result: a 30% rejection rate, much of it from checks like "amount unusually high for this lane" firing on genuinely expensive shipments, and the retry loop burning attempts on extractions that were correct.

Which TWO changes fix the validation design? (Select TWO.)
options: Deterministic violations — schema breaks, failed sums, invalid codes — stay hard failures that reject to retry
Lower every check's sensitivity across the board so that total rejections drop below ten percent
Run the validation suite only on a random sample of extractions in order to cut rejection volume
Remove the plausibility checks from the pipeline entirely, since they caused the false rejections
Plausibility checks — unusual-but-possible values — become soft warnings: accept, flag for sampled review
answer: Deterministic violations — schema breaks, failed sums, invalid codes — stay hard failures that reject to retry
Plausibility checks — unusual-but-possible values — become soft warnings: accept, flag for sampled review
explanation:
This question tests tiering validation by what each check can actually establish.

Two Questions, Two Consequences

-
Deterministic violations stay hard failures — a broken sum or an invalid code is wrong by definition, and rejection into the retry loop is exactly right.

-
Plausibility checks become soft warnings — "amount unusually high for this lane" cannot distinguish a misread from a genuinely expensive shipment, so rejecting it punishes correct work. Accept, flag, and let sampled human review adjudicate.

Hard checks gate correctness; soft checks route attention. That split is what dissolves the 30% rejection rate without losing coverage.

Why the other options are incorrect
Lower every check's sensitivity — weakens the deterministic checks too, so sums that almost balance start passing. It trades false rejections for false acceptances across the board.

Validate a random sample — lets the unchecked majority through unvalidated, including the deterministic failures that were being caught correctly. The volume problem is in the consequences, not the coverage.

Remove plausibility checks — they carry real signal: flagged-and-reviewed is how systematic misreads on expensive lanes would surface. Their failure was being wired to rejection, not their existence.

Key Takeaway
Reject on deterministic violations; flag plausibility concerns for sampled review. Matching consequence to check type beats desensitizing everything.

-

question:
A solar-industry document pipeline quietly degraded: a prompt edit in June dropped first-pass validation yield from 91% to 72%, tripling retry volume — and the team learned this in August, from a cost complaint, by manually correlating invoices with deploy dates.

What should exist so this cannot happen silently again?
options: A rule that prompt edits are allowed only in the first week of each quarter, and frozen otherwise
Standing loop metrics: first-pass yield and retries per document, per prompt version, with alerts
A monthly manual audit where an engineer samples recent extractions for quality
A larger retry budget so that degraded first-pass yield still converges without ever failing visibly
answer: Standing loop metrics: first-pass yield and retries per document, per prompt version, with alerts
explanation:
This question tests instrumenting a feedback loop so regressions announce themselves.

The Numbers Existed; Nobody Was Watching Them
Every validation pass and retry was an event. First-pass yield and retries per document, tracked per prompt version, with alerts on regression are the loop's vital signs: cheap to record, directly tied to cost and quality, and diagnostic when partitioned by version.
With the June edit stamped on its outputs, a 91→72 drop alerts within a day and names its own cause — rollback in June, not forensic accounting in August.

Why the other options are incorrect
Restrict edits to quarterly windows — scheduling does not detect bad edits. A quarterly-window regression is identical, just calendar-aligned, and the freeze slows every improvement for no visibility.

A monthly manual audit — might catch a 19-point yield drop weeks late and might not. Sampling variance versus continuous measurement of an already-recorded signal is not a close call.

A larger retry budget — the silent-degradation enabler: it absorbs the symptom, ships the cost, and guarantees the next regression is also discovered by complaint.

Key Takeaway
Track first-pass yield and retry rates per prompt version, with alerts. Feedback loops without instrumentation have their regressions discovered by finance.

question:
A book publisher is extracting metadata from 80,000 digitized out-of-print titles. The prompt was validated on a stratified sample last month and performs well. An engineer is about to submit the entire corpus as one batch and asks for a review of that plan.

What should the reviewer recommend?
options: Submit the single batch as planned — the prompt validation already de-risked the run
Split the corpus by decade and submit all the decade-batches simultaneously
Submit in staged chunks — verify the first chunk's results, then release the rest in waves
Run the corpus synchronously instead, so problems surface one document at a time
answer: Submit in staged chunks — verify the first chunk's results, then release the rest in waves
explanation:
This question tests operational risk at corpus scale — distinct from prompt risk.

Prompt Validation Is Not Operational Validation
The stratified sample de-risked the prompt. The remaining risks live in the run itself: a data defect in one source segment, a bug in the submission mapping, an infrastructure surprise — and a single 80,000-request batch gives them maximum blast radius with zero visibility until everything lands.
Staged chunks convert the run into a controlled rollout: the first chunk verifies the pipeline end to end on real results, and the waves that follow give checkpoints, partial results early, and a small worst-case cost for any defect found mid-run.

Why the other options are incorrect
Submit as planned — the sample validated extraction quality, not the submission pipeline, corpus uniformity or result handling. All-at-once bets the whole spend on zero operational surprises.

Simultaneous decade-batches — one big batch with partitions: every request is committed before any result is seen, forfeiting exactly the verification value staging provides.

Fully synchronous — surrenders the discount and throughput for a granularity of feedback the staged first chunk already delivers at full savings.

Key Takeaway
Stage large batch runs and verify the first chunk before releasing the rest. Prompt validation and operational validation are different risks.
