question:
A municipal-services pipeline enriches permit records in nightly batches. The pipeline reads results, merges them into the database, and moves on — the raw batch outputs are never stored. Five weeks after one run, an auditor asks for the exact model outputs behind a disputed permit decision; the batch results are no longer retrievable from the API, and the team has nothing to show.

What should the pipeline do differently?
options: Keep each batch's results retrievable by scheduling a monthly re-download from the API
Re-run the disputed records through the same prompt and reconstruct what the outputs would have been
Rely on the merged database records, since they contain everything that was extracted
Download and persist each batch's raw results into the team's own storage as soon as the run completes
answer: Download and persist each batch's raw results into the team's own storage as soon as the run completes
explanation:
This question tests custody of batch outputs against the API's retention window.

Retention Is Bounded; Obligations Are Not
Batch results are retrievable from the API for a bounded window — around 29 days — so any obligation that can outlive it means the pipeline must take custody of the raw outputs itself: fetch on completion, store durably, retain per the team's own policy.
The marginal cost is a copy step at the end of each run; the payoff is that "show me exactly what the model produced" has an answer at week five, week fifty, or whenever the auditor arrives.

Why the other options are incorrect
Monthly re-download — a race against a ~29-day window that loses for any batch completing early in the month, and it leaves custody with the API's schedule instead of the team's.

Re-run the disputed records — produces today's outputs from today's model and configuration: evidence of what the system would say now, not what it said then. For an audit, a reconstruction is precisely what it is not.

Rely on merged database records — the post-merge state is transformed, possibly corrected, possibly overwritten. The auditor asked about raw model outputs, which the merge consumed.

Key Takeaway
Persist raw batch results to your own storage on completion. API retention is a convenience window, not an archive.

question:
A warehouse-automation team runs full independent model review on every generated change — including one-line config tweaks — and the review budget now rivals the generation budget, while genuinely risky changes wait in the same queue as trivial ones.

Which TWO changes make the review architecture proportionate? (Select TWO.)
options: Drop review for changes generated by the most capable model, whose quality is already high
Review a random 20% sample of all changes regardless of what they touch
Classify each change by risk — paths touched, size, blast radius — at generation time
Route by tier: full independent review for high-risk changes, lightweight automated checks for low-risk ones
Let the generating instance decide which of its changes deserve independent review
answer: Classify each change by risk — paths touched, size, blast radius — at generation time
Route by tier: full independent review for high-risk changes, lightweight automated checks for low-risk ones
explanation:
This question tests proportionate review through classification plus routing.

Signal, Then Spend

-
Risk classification at generation time — paths touched, size, blast radius: observable properties, computed cheaply and deterministically.

-
Tiered routing — full independent review for high-risk changes, lightweight automated checks for low-risk ones.

The queue unclogs, the expensive reviewer concentrates on payment paths instead of config tweaks, and total protection rises even as cost falls.

Why the other options are incorrect
Exempt the most capable model's output — generator capability is not change risk. Capable models produce risky changes too, and exempting them removes review precisely where confidence most needs checking.

Random 20% sample — risk-blind by construction: 80% of high-risk changes ship unreviewed while the sample spends budget on trivia. The whole point is that changes are distinguishable.

Generator self-selection — puts the conflict of interest inside the routing decision. The changes a generator is most wrong about are the ones it least suspects need a second opinion.

Key Takeaway
Classify changes by risk at generation time and route review by tier. Uniform review, random sampling and self-selection all misallocate the expensive pass.

question:

Where does this content belong?

In the first user message only, with later turns referring back to it
In a tool result injected at the start of each conversation

answer: In the system prompt, stated once, since it applies to the whole conversation
explanation:
This question tests where standing instructions belong.

System Prompt: Once, for the Whole Conversation
Policy, tone rules and escalation contacts are standing instructions. Stated once in the system prompt, they are present for every turn, cleanly separated from what the customer actually said. Twelve duplicated blocks collapse to one, the history stops bloating, and user messages go back to containing user content.

Why the other options are incorrect
First user message only — works until the conversation grows, and it entangles standing policy with customer content in the same message role — the separation the system prompt exists to provide.

A fabricated tool result — a tool result is the record of a tool call. Smuggling policy through that channel misuses it and confuses any later audit of what actually ran.

Keep repeating it — repetition buys no attention worth its cost. The model sees the conversation whole, and eleven redundant copies are pure token spend plus noise around the customer's messages.

Key Takeaway
Put standing instructions in the system prompt, once. Repeating them per turn inflates history without improving adherence.

question:
A K-12 research assistant answers questions about a 30-page standards document across a long conversation. The integration appends the full document to each new user question "so the model has it fresh" — by turn ten, the conversation history contains five complete copies, and cost per turn keeps climbing.

What is the correct handling?
options: Keep appending, but alternate between full text and a summary on alternating turns
Include it once, early; the history carries it forward, and later turns simply ask their questions
Replace the document with a summary everywhere, accepting some loss of detail
Re-send the full document only on those turns whose questions look detailed enough to truly need it
answer: Include it once, early; the history carries it forward, and later turns simply ask their questions
explanation:
This question tests understanding that history is the persistence mechanism.

One Copy Is Permanently "Fresh"
Each request re-sends the accumulated messages, so a document included once, early, is present for every subsequent turn. Re-appending it creates copies, not presence — five complete copies by turn ten, with cost climbing accordingly.
Include it once, then let later turns simply ask their questions.

Why the other options are incorrect
Alternate full text and summary — still accumulates redundant copies into a history that already carries the original. It halves the waste without understanding why it is waste.

Summarize everywhere — gives up detail to solve a problem that was never about size. One full copy was affordable; five were not. The fix is copy count, not fidelity.

Re-send on detailed-looking turns — still misdiagnoses: no turn needs a re-send, because the turn-one copy is already in every request. The heuristic just adds copies on an unpredictable schedule.

Key Takeaway
Include long reference material once; the conversation history carries it forward. Re-appending duplicates rather than refreshes.

question:
A credit union's support agent operates around the clock; its human escalation team works business hours. At 2 a.m., a member reports something the agent correctly determines needs a human — a suspected unauthorized transfer beyond the agent's authority. Current behavior: "Please contact us during business hours," and the conversation ends there. Members have described restarting from scratch the next day.

What should the 2 a.m. escalation do instead?
options: Attempt to resolve the transfer issue anyway, since no human is available to take it
Promise the member a callback within an hour to keep them reassured overnight
Create the ticket now with context, state pickup time, capture a callback channel
Provide the fraud team's direct email address so that the member can write up all the details themselves
answer: Create the ticket now with context, state pickup time, capture a callback channel
explanation:
This question tests separating "escalate to a human" from "a human is available."

The Escalation Can Complete at 2 a.m. Even If Its Human Half Starts at 9
The agent creates the ticket immediately with the whole conversation's context attached, tells the member honestly when a person will pick it up, and records their preferred callback channel. The member's 2 a.m. effort is preserved, morning staff start with everything, and nobody re-explains anything.
The dead end was never the hour; it was the agent treating unavailability as case closure.

Attempt resolution anyway — the agent already judged this beyond its authority (suspected fraud on a member account), and out-of-hours pressure does not expand authority. This is exactly when serious mistakes happen.

Hand over an email address — outsources the escalation to the member: retype everything and hope it lands. That is the restart-from-scratch experience with an extra step.

Create the escalation with full context immediately, set an honest expectation, and capture a callback channel. Human unavailability delays the handoff, not the escalation.

question:
A food-delivery support team analyzes churn and finds a pattern: customers who contacted support three or more times about the same unresolved issue cancel at four times the baseline rate. The agent currently treats every contact as fresh — same priority, same script — regardless of history.

What should change?
options: After a second contact, have the agent apologize far more prominently for the still-unresolved issue
Cap the number of contacts per issue at two, after which the case closes automatically
Have the agent recap prior contacts and their outcomes to the customer at the start of each new one
Detect repeats on the same issue and raise priority, escalating by the third with the full thread
answer: Detect repeats on the same issue and raise priority, escalating by the third with the full thread

A Third Contact Is a Signal, Not a New Conversation

Auto-close after two contacts — converts "we haven't fixed it" into "we've stopped listening" — the churn mechanism, accelerated by policy.

Recap prior contacts — proves the system remembers while still treating the contact as routine. Memory without escalation is recognition without consequence.

Detect repeat contacts on the same issue and escalate with the full thread. Repeat contacts are failure telemetry the routing layer should consume.

question:
A municipal-data research run queries nine external registries through subagents. One registry began failing mid-run; run telemetry shows 31% of total runtime spent on retries against that single source — subagents kept trying it for every query, backing off, and trying again, while the other eight registries answered normally.

What failure-handling mechanism is missing?
options: A longer backoff interval, retrying the failing registry less often per query and per subagent
A rule that any registry failure immediately ends the run, delivering whatever partial report exists
Per-query retry caps, so that each individual query gives up on the failing registry after two attempts
A circuit breaker: after consecutive failures, mark the registry degraded and stop dispatching this run
answer: A circuit breaker: after consecutive failures, mark the registry degraded and stop dispatching this run
explanation:
This question tests shared, stateful failure knowledge.

Every Query Independently Rediscovering a Dead Source
One registry failing consistently while each query re-probes it is what burns 31% of runtime. A circuit breaker makes the failure knowledge shared and stateful: after N consecutive failures, the registry is marked degraded run-wide, dispatching stops, and the run proceeds on eight healthy sources with the gap recorded for the report's coverage notes.
Per-query retries handle transient blips; a breaker handles a source that is down.

Why the other options are incorrect
Longer backoff — shrinks each query's waste while preserving the architecture of the waste: every query still individually probes a registry the run collectively knows is dead.

End the run on any registry failure — inverts the proportionality. Eight sources are fine, and the correct output is their results plus an honest gap note.

Per-query retry caps — bounds each query's spend, but the knowledge still does not travel: a hundred queries make two hundred doomed attempts. The missing piece is shared state, not tighter per-query limits.

Key Takeaway
Add a circuit breaker so a failing dependency is marked degraded run-wide. Per-query retry policy cannot share what one query has learned.

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Subagents in the SDK → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use
option_feedback: Longer backoff shrinks each query's waste while preserving the architecture of the waste — every query still individually probes a registry the run collectively knows is dead.
Ending the run over one registry inverts the proportionality: eight sources are fine, and the correct output is their results plus an honest gap note — not a run abort that discards them.
Per-query caps bound each query's spend but the knowledge still does not travel — a hundred queries make two hundred doomed attempts. The missing piece is shared state, not tighter per-query limits.

The pattern — one source failing consistently while every query independently rediscovers that fact — is what circuit breakers exist for. Failure knowledge should be shared and stateful: after N consecutive failures, the registry is marked degraded run-wide, dispatching to it stops, and the run proceeds on eight healthy sources with the gap recorded for the final report's coverage notes. question:
A telecom developer finished a payment-gateway integration in her Claude Code session an hour ago and is about to start an unrelated task in the same session: refactoring the notification templates. Context sits at 60%. She asks whether to /compact before starting.

What is the right move, and why?
options: /compact — it frees space while keeping the gateway work summarized in case it becomes relevant
/clear — the task is unrelated, and a summary of gateway decisions invites stale assumptions into it
Neither — 60% leaves plenty of room, and she should simply begin the refactor
/compact now and again at 80%, keeping one continuous session for the whole day
answer: /clear — the task is unrelated, and a summary of gateway decisions invites stale assumptions into it
explanation:
This question tests /compact versus /clear by task relationship, not by space.

Unrelated Work Deserves an Empty Context
Compaction preserves a summary because the next work builds on the prior work. Here the next work shares nothing with the gateway integration, so what a summary preserves is precisely the hazard: gateway-era decisions and assumptions bleeding into template judgments.
/clear gives the refactor what an unrelated task deserves — a context containing only itself.

Why the other options are incorrect

Neither; 60% is plenty — room is not the issue, relevance is. Sixty percent of capacity holding another task's history means the refactor starts inside someone else's context.

One long session with periodic compaction — accumulates summaries of summaries across unrelated tasks, exactly the sediment task-boundary clearing prevents.

Key Takeaway
/compact to continue related work; /clear at unrelated task boundaries. The choice is about relevance, not remaining space.

Read all twelve up front but instruct the model to memorize all the key points and then disregard the rest

question:
A veterinary-billing extraction pipeline routes flagged records to human review. The queue is worked first-in-first-out; the backlog averages four days. An analysis finds high-dollar invoices with likely extraction errors waiting behind hundreds of low-value records flagged for cosmetic issues — one $40,000 misread posted while it sat in the queue.

How should the review queue be redesigned?
options: Order it by expected cost of being wrong — error likelihood times impact — riskiest records first
Keep FIFO but add reviewer headcount until the backlog clears within one day
Split it into two FIFO queues by dollar amount, with reviewers alternating between them
Keep FIFO for fairness, but let reviewers manually pull urgent records whenever they notice them waiting
answer: Order it by expected cost of being wrong — error likelihood times impact — riskiest records first
explanation:
This question tests queue ordering as triage.

FIFO Is Triage by Arrival Time
Arrival time has no relationship to what review is for. Each record already carries the two triage inputs: how likely the flag is to be a real error, and what a mistake costs downstream.
Ordering by their product means the $40,000 likely-misread is reviewed within minutes while cosmetic trivia waits — the same reviewer effort, allocated where the risk is. A backlog can even persist harmlessly, so long as it is the harmless records waiting.

Why the other options are incorrect
Add headcount — attacks the average wait while preserving the allocation flaw: until the backlog is literally zero, high-stakes records still queue behind trivia, at higher payroll.

Two FIFO lanes by dollar amount — priority half-done: a likely-correct high-dollar record still outranks a likely-wrong mid-dollar one, and alternation caps how much attention the risky lane can get.

Manual pulling — makes triage depend on reviewers noticing: unsystematic, invisible in metrics, and absent whenever the queue is worked heads-down, which is exactly when backlogs happen.

Key Takeaway
Order review queues by expected cost of being wrong — error likelihood times impact. FIFO allocates the scarce resource by an irrelevant variable.

question:
A municipal-policy research team reviews a draft briefing and finds every claim stated with identical confidence — "the program reduced commute times by 12%" reads the same whether it rests on three corroborating studies or one advocacy-group blog post. The board has been burned before by acting on thin claims that sounded solid.

Which TWO practices fix the briefing's design? (Select TWO.)
options: A uniform disclaimer on the cover noting that confidence varies across the report
Excluding every claim that rests on a single source, so only corroborated findings remain
Rewriting all claims in hedged language so nothing sounds more certain than anything else
Calibrating each claim's assertion strength to its evidence — corroborated findings stated plainly, thin ones marked as preliminary or single-source
Surfacing the evidential basis per major claim — how many independent sources, and of what quality
answer: Calibrating each claim's assertion strength to its evidence — corroborated findings stated plainly, thin ones marked as preliminary or single-source

explanation:

Uniform hedging — the mirror image of uniform confidence: still zero information in the language, now with well-supported findings undersold alongside weak ones.

Tie each claim's assertion strength to its evidence and surface the basis per claim. Blanket disclaimers, exclusion and uniform hedging all destroy the distinction readers need.

question:
A podcast network's transcript-extraction loop branches on stop_reason: if it equals "tool_use", execute tools; otherwise, record the output as complete. Last week a response arrived with a stop_reason value the code had never seen, and a half-empty record was filed as complete.

How should the loop handle stop_reason values?
options: Keep the current else-branch but log every unrecognized stop_reason value for later review
Handle known values explicitly; treat anything unrecognized as incomplete and flag it
Retry the identical request repeatedly until a recognized and expected stop_reason comes back
Map unrecognized values to "end_turn", since new values are rare in practice
answer: Handle known values explicitly; treat anything unrecognized as incomplete and flag it
explanation:
This question tests loop termination logic, and specifically that a control flow branching on stop_reason must treat unrecognized values as failures rather than as success.

What stop_reason actually communicates
Every response carries a stop_reason describing why generation ended: end_turn (Claude finished naturally), tool_use (Claude is requesting a tool), max_tokens (the output limit was reached mid-thought), stop_sequence, pause_turn, refusal, and others added over time. These are not interchangeable outcomes. Only end_turn means "this output is complete." max_tokens means the opposite — the record was cut off mid-sentence, which is precisely the half-empty transcript the team filed.

The bug is the shape of the branch, not the missing value
The code says: if tool_use, run tools; otherwise, complete. That otherwise silently maps every present and future value onto "success," so the system's correctness depends on the API never introducing a value the code has not seen. That is not a property any client can guarantee. The fix inverts the default: enumerate the values you handle, give each its specific behavior, and route everything else to a conservative branch — not confirmed complete, flag for inspection. Unknown values then become visible operational events rather than corrupt records that look clean.

Why the other options are incorrect
Logging makes the failure discoverable after the fact but does not stop it. The half-empty record is still stamped complete and still enters the downstream pipeline; the team now has a log line describing data corruption it also permitted.

Blind retries assume the unknown value signals a transient glitch. If it is a real terminal state — a refusal, a stop sequence — the loop spins indefinitely, and each discarded response may have contained usable partial output.

Mapping unknown values to end_turn is the existing defect promoted to a deliberate policy. It hard-codes the exact assumption — "unknown means done" — that filed the bad record.

Key Takeaway
Enumerate the stop_reason values you handle and default the rest to incomplete. A safe default fails loudly; an unsafe default fails silently, and silent failures reach production data.

-
Anthropic — Handling stop reasons → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons

-
Anthropic — How tool use works → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works

-

question:
A 3D-printing service's internal agent shows odd transcripts: apology messages about "tool problems" on turns where no tool was ever called. The cause is in the loop's error handling — when the API request itself fails with an overloaded/529-class error, the code fabricates a tool_result saying "API overloaded" and appends it to the conversation before retrying.

What is the correct architecture for these failures?
options: Keep the fabricated tool_result but reword it so the model understands it is not about a tool
Surface transport errors to the end user immediately and end the conversation cleanly
Retry transport failures at the request layer with backoff; only tool outcomes enter history
Retry at the request layer, but append a note to the conversation after recovery describing the outage
answer: Retry transport failures at the request layer with backoff; only tool outcomes enter history
explanation:
This question tests error-plane separation in an agent loop, and specifically that transport failures and tool failures are different categories of event that must be handled at different layers.

Two planes, two remedies
A tool failure is a conversational fact. The model asked for something, the world answered, and the answer was "no" — the record is out of stock, the ID does not exist, the permission was refused. The model should see it, reason about it, and adapt. The protocol carries these as a tool_result block with is_error set.
A transport failure is infrastructure. A 529 or a connection reset means one HTTP request did not complete. Nothing happened in the conversation at all — the model never generated a turn, no tool was ever called. The remedy is mechanical: retry the request with exponential backoff until it lands. The conversation should be entirely unaware this occurred.

Why fabricating a tool_result is a category error
The tool_result channel exists to answer a specific tool_use block by ID. Manufacturing one for an event with no corresponding tool call injects a fictional occurrence into the conversation's record. The model, reading a conversation in which tools apparently failed, does the reasonable thing with the evidence it has: it apologizes for tool problems. The odd transcripts are not a prompt-tuning issue — they are the accurate downstream consequence of a corrupted history.

Why the other options are incorrect
Rewording preserves the structural violation. Whatever the text says, the conversation still contains a result block answering a call that was never made, and infrastructure events still consume conversational space reserved for tool outcomes.

Overload errors are transient by construction. Ending the conversation converts a condition that a two-second retry absorbs invisibly into a user-facing failure, degrading availability for no gain.

A post-recovery note still spends context on an event with no bearing on the task. The model gains nothing it can act on, and every network blip permanently enlarges the transcript.

Key Takeaway
Retry transport errors at the request layer with backoff; let only real tool outcomes enter the conversation. If it did not happen in the conversation, it does not belong in the conversation.

-
Anthropic — API errors → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors

-

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use
option_feedback: Rewording keeps the category error: the conversation still records an event that belongs to the transport layer, inside a channel (tool results) reserved for answering tool calls the model actually made — a protocol violation dressed in better prose.
Overload errors are transient by nature; ending conversations over them converts routine infrastructure weather into user-facing failures that a two-second retry would have absorbed invisibly.

There are two error planes, and they must not mix. A 529 means one HTTP request didn't get through — the conversation itself is untouched, and the remedy is mechanical: retry that request with backoff until it lands. Tool errors are conversation-level facts the model should reason about; transport errors are infrastructure noise the model should never see. The fabricated tool_result smuggles plane one into plane two, corrupting the conversation with events that never happened in it — hence apologies about tools nobody called.
A post-recovery note still spends conversation content on infrastructure events with no bearing on the task — the model gains nothing actionable, and the transcript accumulates noise for every blip.

question:
A museum consortium's research coordinator has an 1,800-line system prompt: routing logic plus the complete working procedures of all six subagents, pasted in "so the coordinator understands its team." Last month a subagent's own prompt was revised; the coordinator's embedded copy was not, and it began dispatching tasks based on capabilities the subagent no longer has.

How should knowledge be placed in this system?
options: Keep the copies but add a sync script that mirrors subagent prompt changes into the coordinator
Move all six procedures into every subagent, and each one then understands the whole team
Slim the coordinator down to almost nothing, removing routing knowledge along with the procedures
Coordinator holds routing and aggregation knowledge; each procedure lives only in its own subagent
answer: Coordinator holds routing and aggregation knowledge; each procedure lives only in its own subagent
explanation:
This question tests knowledge placement in a hub-and-spoke multi-agent system, and specifically that duplicated knowledge is a defect waiting for its first revision.

What the coordinator needs versus what it was given
A coordinator's job is selection and aggregation: decide which specialist a task belongs to, dispatch it, and merge what comes back. That job requires knowing what each subagent is for — its purpose, its boundaries, the shape of what it returns. It does not require knowing how each subagent works internally. Those are different knowledge classes, and the 1,800-line prompt confuses them by embedding six complete working procedures the coordinator will never execute.

Duplication has a predictable failure mode
Subagents run in isolated contexts; each carries its own system prompt. When a procedure lives in two places, every revision must find both. It will not, and the moment it does not, the two copies disagree — with no error, no alert, and no way for either component to detect the drift. The consortium's incident is the generic outcome: the coordinator dispatched against capabilities that had already been removed. Single-sourcing each procedure inside its own subagent eliminates the class of bug entirely rather than managing it.

The secondary benefit
A coordinator prompt containing only routing and aggregation knowledge is small, which means its routing instructions receive the model's attention undiluted by thousands of tokens of irrelevant procedure.

Why the other options are incorrect
A sync script builds machinery to keep two copies of something that needs one copy. It preserves the duplication, adds a component that can itself break or lag, and leaves the stale-copy failure available whenever the sync misfires.

This multiplies the problem sixfold. Each subagent would carry five procedures it never runs, every revision would need to reach six destinations instead of two, and every subagent's context would be padded with irrelevant instruction.

Removing routing knowledge along with the procedures over-corrects past the useful boundary. Without knowing what each subagent is for, the coordinator cannot route at all. The line sits between selection knowledge and execution knowledge, not at zero.

Key Takeaway
Knowledge lives where it is used: routing and aggregation in the coordinator, execution procedures in the subagent that executes them, each in exactly one place.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Subagents in Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Modifying system prompts → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/modifying-system-prompts
option_feedback: A sync script maintains duplication instead of removing it — tooling to keep two copies equal of something that needs one copy, and a new failure mode when the sync itself breaks.
This multiplies the duplication six-fold: every subagent now carries five procedures it never executes, and every revision must propagate to six places instead of two.

Over-trimming removes the knowledge the coordinator genuinely needs — without knowing what each subagent is for, it cannot route at all. The line sits between selection knowledge and execution knowledge, not at zero.

Knowledge should live where it is used. The coordinator's job needs selection-level knowledge — what each specialist is for, when to dispatch it, how to merge returns — not the internals of how each specialist works. Procedures belong to the subagents that execute them, in exactly one place each. The drift incident is the tax duplication always charges: two copies of a fact eventually disagree, and the stale copy misleads. Sharp knowledge boundaries also keep the coordinator's prompt small enough to do its actual job well.

question:
A property-management support coordinator assembles tenant-billing answers from three subagents. Last week a subagent returned an empty utilities section — its lookup had silently failed — and the coordinator forwarded the assembled answer anyway; the tenant was told their account had no utility charges. It was not the first such incident.

What is missing from the coordinator's design?
options: Validate returns against the task contract before aggregation; re-dispatch or flag failures
A disclaimer appended to answers noting that some information may be incomplete or delayed
A self-certification step where each subagent confirms its own return is complete and correct before sending
A human review of every outgoing answer before it reaches the tenant
answer: Validate returns against the task contract before aggregation; re-dispatch or flag failures
explanation:
This question tests the coordinator's role as a quality boundary, and specifically that aggregation must validate subagent returns against the task contract before assembling an answer.

Aggregation is the last defensible checkpoint
In a hub-and-spoke design, the coordinator sits at a structurally privileged position: it is the first component that can compare what a subagent returned against what that subagent was asked for, and the last component before the assembled answer becomes customer-facing. A coordinator that forwards returns unexamined is not orchestrating — it is relaying, and it relays defects as faithfully as results.

Silent failure versus explicit failure
The dangerous property of the utilities lookup is not that it failed but that it failed quietly: an empty section is structurally indistinguishable from a genuine "no charges on this account." Only the coordinator, holding the original task contract, can tell the two apart — it asked for utility charges and can check whether the query was actually executed and whether required fields are present. That check is cheap and mechanical, and it converts a silent failure into a handled one: re-dispatch the subagent, or state honestly that utilities could not be retrieved. The distinction between an access failure and a valid empty result is the entire substance of the incident.

Why the other options are incorrect
A blanket disclaimer distributes doubt evenly across correct and incorrect answers. The tenant with a wrong balance is no better protected, and every accurate answer is undermined. Detectable defects deserve detection, not hedging.

Self-certification asks the failing component to catch its own failure. The lookup failed without the subagent noticing — that is the definition of a silent failure, and it is exactly the case a self-check cannot cover.

Routing every answer through a human prices the fix at the value of the whole automation, in order to catch a defect class — missing required sections — that a contract check catches for free. Human review is the right tool for judgment calls, not for structural completeness checks.

Key Takeaway
Validate every subagent return against its task contract at the aggregation boundary. An empty result and a failed query look identical until something compares them to what was requested.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: the agent loop → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop

-
Anthropic — Reduce hallucinations → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations
option_feedback: Aggregation is the coordinator's quality boundary: it is the first point where a return can be judged against what was asked for, and the last point before defects become customer-facing answers. Checking each return against its task contract — the utilities section exists, the account was actually queried, required fields are present — costs little and converts silent failures into handled ones: re-dispatch the subagent, or flag the gap honestly. Forwarding unvalidated returns makes the coordinator a conduit for whatever went wrong below it.
A blanket disclaimer converts a detectable defect into ambient doubt on every answer — the tenant with a wrong answer gets no protection, and every correct answer gets undermined.
The subagent that silently failed is the component least positioned to certify itself — its lookup failed without its noticing, which is exactly the case self-certification cannot catch.
Human review of every answer prices the fix at the whole automation's value, to catch a class of defect — missing required sections — that a mechanical contract check detects for free.

question:
An internal-tools team is writing its first AgentDefinitions and asks for a review of what content belongs in the description field versus the prompt field.

Which TWO placements are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Selection criteria go in the prompt, so the subagent knows the boundaries of its own scope
The description carries what the coordinator needs for selection — what this subagent is for and when to choose it
Both fields should carry the same content, so nothing is lost whichever one is read
The prompt carries execution instructions — how the subagent does its work once invoked
Neither field matters much for selection, since the model field determines which subagent is chosen
answer: The description carries what the coordinator needs for selection — what this subagent is for and when to choose it
The prompt carries execution instructions — how the subagent does its work once invoked
explanation:
This question tests the AgentDefinition contract, and specifically that description and prompt serve two different readers at two different moments.

The two readers

-
description is read before invocation, by the coordinator that is choosing among subagents. It is the only thing the selecting model sees when it decides where a task goes. It should therefore answer selection questions: what is this subagent for, when should it be chosen, what falls outside its scope.

-
prompt becomes the subagent's system prompt after selection has already occurred. It is read by the subagent itself, in its own isolated context, and should answer execution questions: what procedure to follow, what output to produce, what constraints to respect.

Why the placement matters so much here
Subagent contexts are isolated — the subagent does not inherit the parent's history or system prompt, and the coordinator never reads the subagent's prompt. So a fact placed in the wrong field is not merely inelegant; it is invisible to the party that needed it. Selection criteria buried in the prompt reach the subagent after the routing decision they were meant to inform has already been made.

Why the other options are incorrect
Selection criteria in the prompt arrive too late to affect selection. The coordinator has already chosen by the time the prompt is read, so boundaries stated there cannot prevent the misrouting they exist to prevent.

Identical content in both fields doubles the tokens each reader must process, dilutes the selection signal with execution detail, and creates two copies that drift apart on the first revision.

The model field selects which model runs the subagent — a capability and cost decision, not a routing one. Selection is driven by description.

Key Takeaway
description is selection-facing (what and when); prompt is execution-facing (how). Match the content to the reader, and never duplicate across the two.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: subagents (AgentDefinition) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Subagents in Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Modifying system prompts → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/modifying-system-prompts
option_feedback: Selection criteria in the prompt arrive after selection has already happened — the coordinator never sees the prompt when choosing, so boundaries placed there cannot influence the choice they exist to guide.

The two fields address two different readers at two different moments. The description is read by the selecting coordinator before invocation: it should say what this subagent is for, when to choose it, and where its boundaries lie — selection-facing content. The prompt becomes the subagent's system prompt after selection: it should say how to execute — procedures, output expectations, constraints. Right content in the right field means the coordinator selects on clean signal and the subagent executes on full instructions.
Duplication bloats both readers' inputs and creates two copies that drift; each field has a distinct reader, and content should follow the reader.

The two fields address two different readers at two different moments. The description is read by the selecting coordinator before invocation: it should say what this subagent is for, when to choose it, and where its boundaries lie — selection-facing content. The prompt becomes the subagent's system prompt after selection: it should say how to execute — procedures, output expectations, constraints. Right content in the right field means the coordinator selects on clean signal and the subagent executes on full instructions.
The model field sets which model runs the subagent — capability, not selection. Selection is driven by descriptions.

question:
A wind-energy siting study runs six research subagents whose full analyses run 8,000 to 10,000 tokens each. All of it returns inline to the coordinator, whose context fills before aggregation finishes; the final synthesis has been observed dropping two subagents' material entirely.

How should subagent output be handled?
options: Move the coordinator onto the very largest available context window so all six full analyses fit inline
Have each subagent compress its analysis to a single paragraph before returning
Process subagents sequentially and compact the coordinator's context after each return
Subagents write full analyses to files, returning a compact summary plus the path for selective reading
answer: Subagents write full analyses to files, returning a compact summary plus the path for selective reading
explanation:
This question tests context management across a fan-out, and specifically that filesystem handoff decouples full-fidelity output from the coordinator's context budget.

The arithmetic that forces the design
Six subagents at 8,000–10,000 tokens each is 48,000–60,000 tokens of inline return, before the coordinator's own system prompt, the original brief, and the synthesis it still has to write. The dropped material is not a bug in the synthesis step; it is the predictable result of asking a fixed-size context to hold more than fits and then reason over all of it at once.

Separating conclusions from evidence
The coordinator's actual need is asymmetric. It needs every subagent's conclusions to synthesize, but only occasionally needs any single subagent's full reasoning — when a conclusion looks wrong, conflicts with a sibling's, or needs its supporting detail quoted. So the return should split along that line: the subagent writes its complete analysis to a file and returns a compact summary plus the path. Aggregation runs over six short summaries that fit comfortably; when the synthesis needs depth on one topic, the coordinator reads that one file on demand. Nothing is lost, and the files remain as durable artifacts for human readers after the run.

Why the other options are incorrect
A larger window defers the arithmetic rather than fixing it — a seventh subagent or a larger study re-creates the squeeze. And even when six full analyses fit, packing them all in dilutes the model's attention across 60,000 tokens during the step that most needs focus.

A mandatory one-paragraph compression is lossy in a way that cannot be reversed: the subagent compresses before knowing which details the cross-cutting synthesis will need, and the discarded material is simply gone. The file-plus-summary pattern gets the same context relief while keeping the full text recoverable.

Sequential processing with compaction gives up parallelism and still summarizes away early returns. By the sixth subagent, the first exists only as a compacted trace — which is another route to the same dropped material.

Key Takeaway
Have subagents persist full output to files and return summaries plus paths. Fidelity lives on disk; the context holds only what the current step needs.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Context windows → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: manage the context window → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window

-
Anthropic — Working with large codebases → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases
option_feedback: A larger window postpones the arithmetic — the seventh subagent or the next study size re-creates the squeeze — and six full analyses packed inline still dilute the synthesis attention across everything at once.

A single mandatory paragraph is compression chosen blind: the subagent cannot know which details the cross-cutting synthesis will need, and what it drops is unrecoverable. The file keeps everything; the summary just indexes it.

Sequential-plus-compaction serializes the work and then summarizes away earlier returns anyway — by subagent six, subagent one exists as a compacted shadow of itself, which is how material gets dropped.

The coordinator needs every subagent's conclusions but only occasionally needs any subagent's full reasoning — so the design should separate the two. Files hold the complete analyses durably; the inline return carries a compact summary and the path. Aggregation works from six summaries that fit comfortably, and when a conclusion needs interrogating, the coordinator reads that one file on demand. Full fidelity is preserved, context pressure disappears, and the artifacts remain for humans afterward.

question:
A records-digitization bureau runs a three-day workflow per batch: scan intake, extraction, verification, notary approval, archival. The workflow's state — which batch sits at which stage, who approved what — currently lives only in a long-running Claude session's conversation. Last Tuesday the session was lost, and with it the knowledge of where forty batches stood.

Where should workflow state live?
options: Keep state in the conversation as it is now, with the transcript exported to disk every night as backup
In longer-lived sessions with automatic resume, so loss becomes less likely
An application datastore holds the state machine; sessions reference it
In CLAUDE.md, which persists across sessions and loads into each new one
answer: An application datastore holds the state machine; sessions reference it
explanation:
This question tests durable state design for long-running workflows, and specifically that a conversation is a working context, never a system of record.

What a conversation is and is not
A session context is optimized for one thing: giving a model the material it needs for the turn in front of it. It is not queryable, not shareable across consumers, not transactional, bounded in size, and — as Tuesday demonstrated — exactly as durable as the process holding it. None of those properties is acceptable for the operational truth of forty in-flight batches spanning three days each.

What this state actually is
"Which batch sits at which stage, who approved what" is a state machine with structured records: batch ID, current stage, approver, timestamp. That belongs in an application datastore, with tools that update it as each stage completes. The inversion is the point: instead of sessions owning state, sessions become disposable workers that read and write durable state. Any session can pick up any batch; a dashboard can render the queue; an auditor can query approvals; a crashed process costs nothing but its current turn. This is the same reasoning behind capturing results as application state rather than relying on session resume — the store, not the conversation, is the thing you can depend on.

Why the other options are incorrect
Nightly transcript exports back up the wrong representation. State stays embedded in prose, recoverable only by re-reading a transcript, up to twenty-four hours stale, and still owned by a conversation. A backup of a bad design is a bad design with a copy.

Longer-lived sessions with resume reduce how often the catastrophe occurs without reducing its size. Forty batches' operational truth still lives inside a single context's lifetime, and process restarts, host failures and context limits all remain.

CLAUDE.md is standing project guidance loaded into sessions — context, not a transactional store. Rapidly changing per-batch stage data would make every session load a churning ledger as "memory," misusing the mechanism and consuming context for data that should be queried on demand.

Key Takeaway
Multi-day workflow state belongs in an application datastore modeled as an explicit state machine. Sessions reference it; they never own it.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: sessions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: sessions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: memory (CLAUDE.md) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: Nightly exports back up the wrong representation: state embedded in prose, recoverable only by re-reading a transcript, up to a day stale, and still owned by a conversation.
Longer-lived sessions lower the frequency of the catastrophe without changing its size — the design still puts forty batches' operational truth inside one context's lifetime.

A conversation is a working context, not a system of record — it is unqueryable, unshareable, size-limited, and exactly as durable as Tuesday proved. Multi-day workflow state is structured operational data: batch, stage, approver, timestamp. It belongs in an application store as an explicit state machine that tools update as stages complete. Any session — or dashboard, or auditor — then reads current state from the store; sessions become disposable workers over durable state instead of fragile owners of it.

CLAUDE.md is standing guidance loaded into sessions, not a transactional store — forty batches' rapidly-changing stage data would make every session load a churning ledger as "memory," misusing both mechanisms.

question:
A fashion-retail codegen pipeline chains two tools: create_draft_page returns a page id, and attach_imagery takes a page_id parameter. In about 2% of runs, the model passes attach_imagery an id that looks right but was never returned — imagery lands on the wrong page or errors surface far downstream.

What is the right defense?
options: Add a prompt instruction telling the model to double-check the id before calling attach_imagery
Have attach_imagery validate ids server-side, rejecting unknown ones with a recoverable error
Switch to short sequential integer ids, which are easier for the model to copy correctly
Let attach_imagery accept the page's human-readable name instead of an id
answer: Have attach_imagery validate ids server-side, rejecting unknown ones with a recoverable error
explanation:
This question tests tool-boundary validation for chained calls, and specifically that a cross-step reference is an untrusted input the receiving tool must verify.

Where the check has to live
create_draft_page produces an ID; attach_imagery consumes one. From attach_imagery's perspective, the page_id it receives is a claim — the model asserts this page exists and is the right one. Sometimes that claim is a faithful copy of a real return value, and roughly 2% of the time it is a plausible-looking fabrication. The tool cannot tell by inspection, which is why it must ask the system of record: does this page exist, and does it belong to this run? A tool that acts on unverified references delegates its correctness to the caller's fidelity.

Why the failure mode is worse than it looks
An unvalidated bad ID does not fail cleanly. If the ID happens to match a real page, imagery is attached to the wrong customer's page and nothing errors at all. If it matches nothing, the error surfaces at some later stage, far from its cause. Server-side validation converts both into an immediate, explicit, recoverable error — one the model can react to by re-checking the earlier return, re-calling, or surfacing the problem. Errors that arrive at the point of the mistake are worth far more than errors that arrive downstream.

Why the other options are incorrect
"Double-check the ID" asks the generator to detect its own fabrication. A plausible hallucinated ID looks correct to the model by construction — that is what makes it plausible. Reliability at the 2% level requires a check outside the component producing the errors, and prompt instructions carry a non-zero failure rate by nature.

Short sequential integers are marginally easier to copy and dramatically easier to fabricate convincingly, since every small integer is a valid-looking candidate. Worse, an off-by-one now lands on a real neighboring page — turning loud failures into silent wrong-object mutations.

Human-readable names replace an exact reference with an ambiguous one. Duplicate and near-duplicate page names convert the reference problem into a matching problem, adding a resolution step that can itself select the wrong page.

Key Takeaway
When one tool's output feeds another tool's input, the receiving tool validates the reference server-side and returns a recoverable error on failure. Cross-step references are inputs, and tools validate inputs.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Define tools (input schemas and validation) → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls (is_error results) → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — Tool use overview → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use
option_feedback: "Double-check" asks the component that fabricated the id to detect its own fabrication — the model's plausible-but-wrong ids look correct to the model by construction. The 2% needs a check that lives outside the generator.

When one step's output feeds another step's input, the receiving tool is the enforcement point: it should treat the id as an untrusted claim and verify — does this page exist, does it belong to this run — before acting. A fabricated id then produces an immediate, explicit error the model can react to (re-check, re-call, or surface the problem), instead of a mutation applied to the wrong object and discovered downstream. Cross-step references are inputs like any other; tools validate inputs.

Sequential integers are easier to copy and vastly easier to fabricate convincingly — every small integer is plausible, and off-by-one now lands on a real neighboring page, converting loud failures into silent wrong-object mutations.
Names are ambiguous where ids are exact — duplicate and near-duplicate page names turn the reference problem into a matching problem, adding a resolution step that can itself pick the wrong page.

question:
A port-logistics CI pipeline guards infrastructure paths with a PreToolUse deny-hook. During one run, the hook script itself crashed on a malformed input — and every guarded call proceeded unblocked for the rest of the run. The team is deciding what a hook error should mean.

What is the right policy?
options: Enforcement hooks fail closed: error = deny + alert; observability hooks may fail open
Fail open with a try/catch wrapped around hooks — a hook bug then never blocks legitimate pipeline work
Run each enforcement hook twice per call and require both executions to agree
Back the hook with a CLAUDE.md rule so guidance still applies when the hook is down
answer: Enforcement hooks fail closed: error = deny + alert; observability hooks may fail open
explanation:
This question tests hook failure semantics, and specifically that an enforcement control's behavior when it breaks is part of the guarantee it offers.

Fail-closed versus fail-open
PreToolUse hooks exist to make decisions deterministically, before a tool runs, in a way that does not depend on the model's cooperation — a hook returning a deny decision blocks the call outright. That deterministic property is exactly what makes fail-open so damaging: if a crashed hook silently admits everything, then the guarantee "infrastructure paths are protected" quietly becomes "infrastructure paths are protected whenever the guard happens to be running." An attacker needs only to crash the guard; an accident needs only a malformed input, which is what happened.

Fail-closed makes the failure visible and safe
Under a fail-closed policy, a hook error denies the call and alerts. The system degrades toward safety rather than toward permissiveness, and the bug gets fixed under the pressure of blocked work rather than discovered during an incident review. The exception is principled, not arbitrary: observability hooks — logging, metrics, notifications — should fail open, because losing a log line is a smaller harm than halting the pipeline. The rule is that the failure mode should follow the hook's purpose.

Why the other options are incorrect
A try/catch that swallows hook errors is the incident the team just experienced, adopted deliberately as policy. It makes the guard's uptime the ceiling on the guarantee and converts "never" into "usually" without anyone noticing.

Running the hook twice defends against nondeterminism, not crashes. The malformed input that killed the first execution kills the second identically, and the policy still owes an answer to "what does a double failure mean?" — which is the original question, unanswered.

CLAUDE.md is context supplied to the model, not enforced configuration; the documentation is explicit that blocking an action regardless of what Claude decides requires a PreToolUse hook. Guidance as the fallback for a broken gate is a sign on an open door.

Key Takeaway
Enforcement hooks fail closed — an error means deny plus alert. Observability hooks may fail open. Match the failure mode to the hook's purpose.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: hooks reference → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: get started with hooks → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: hooks → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: memory (context, not enforced configuration) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: A security control's failure mode is part of the control. If a broken enforcement hook admits everything, then the guarantee is only as strong as the hook's own uptime — an attacker or an accident needs only to crash the guard. Fail-closed inverts that: a hook error blocks the call and pages someone, so the system degrades toward safety and the bug gets fixed under pressure of blocked work rather than after an incident. Observability hooks are the legitimate exception — losing a log line should not stop the pipeline.
Fail-open is the incident the team just had, adopted as policy: the guard's availability becomes the ceiling on the guarantee, and a crashing hook silently converts "never" into "usually."

Double execution defends against nondeterminism, not crashes — the malformed input that killed one execution kills both, and the agreement rule still needs a policy for what a double-crash means, which is the original question.
CLAUDE.md is advice to the model; the hook exists precisely because advice is not enforcement. A guidance fallback for a broken gate is a sign on an open door.

question:
A telehealth scheduling-and-billing support agent's lookup tools return payment records that include full card numbers. Compliance requires that card numbers never enter the model's context at all — masking in the final reply is not sufficient.

How is the requirement met?
options: A system-prompt rule directing the agent to ignore card numbers and never repeat them
A nightly job that scrubs card numbers from stored transcripts and logs
A request to the payments team to change the API's response format next quarter
A PostToolUse hook that masks card numbers in tool results before the model receives them
answer: A PostToolUse hook that masks card numbers in tool results before the model receives them
explanation:
This question tests where a data-exclusion control must sit, and specifically that a PostToolUse hook can transform tool output before the model ever receives it.

Reading the requirement precisely
The compliance rule is not "do not display card numbers" — it is "card numbers must never enter the model's context at all." That phrasing places the boundary at the model's input, which means any control operating on the model's behavior or on stored artifacts is already too late by definition. The only place a control can satisfy this requirement is between the tool's raw response and the model's next turn.

The mechanism that fits
That is exactly where PostToolUse operates. The hook receives the tool result, rewrites the card number to a masked form, and the masked version is what reaches the model. The transformation is deterministic — it happens on every call, in every conversation, without depending on the model noticing or complying — and it is auditable, since the hook is a single reviewable piece of code rather than a behavior distributed across prompt adherence. Prompt rules and log scrubbing govern what happens after exposure; the hook prevents the exposure.

Why the other options are incorrect
An instruction to ignore the card number is necessarily read alongside the card number — the data has already entered context, which is precisely what the requirement forbids. Behavior rules cannot un-receive data, and they carry a non-zero failure rate besides.

Transcript scrubbing cleans the archive after the model has already processed raw values in live conversation. It addresses storage hygiene, not the input boundary the requirement names.

Changing the payments API is the correct long-term source fix and does nothing for the intervening quarter. The hook closes the gap immediately and remains valuable as defense in depth even after the API changes.

Key Takeaway
To keep data out of the model's context, transform it in a PostToolUse hook before the model sees it. Instructions govern behavior after exposure; hooks prevent exposure.

Transcript scrubbing cleans the archive after the model processed the raw values in live conversation; the boundary being enforced is the model's input, not the storage.
The API change is the right long-term source fix and does nothing for the intervening quarter — the hook closes the gap now and remains as defense in depth after.

The requirement is about what reaches the model, so the control must sit between the tool's raw output and the model's input — which is exactly where a PostToolUse transform operates. The hook masks the card number in every result, deterministically, before the model sees it: the data never enters context, satisfying the compliance boundary as stated. question:
A staffing agency's three-week market study collapsed in week three: the plan spent weeks one and two on straightforward market-sizing sections, and the final week's centerpiece — regional wage benchmarking — turned out to depend on a dataset that was discontinued. The post-mortem asks how the plan should have been sequenced.

What is the right principle?
options: Keep the same order but add a buffer week at the end for surprises
Run every section in parallel from day one so nothing waits on anything
Probe the highest-uncertainty dependency first — a cheap week-one check would have reshaped the plan
Avoid designing studies around external datasets whose availability the team does not itself control
answer: Probe the highest-uncertainty dependency first — a cheap week-one check would have reshaped the plan
explanation:
This question tests sequencing within task decomposition, and specifically that plan order should be driven by uncertainty rather than by convenience.

Decomposition includes ordering
Breaking work into sections is only half of decomposition; the other half is deciding what runs when. The staffing agency's plan ordered by ease — comfortable market-sizing first, the hard centerpiece last — which is the natural order and the wrong one. Ordering by uncertainty asks a different question: which assumption, if false, invalidates the most downstream work? Here that was unmistakably the regional wage dataset, on which the entire deliverable rested.

The asymmetry that makes this cheap
Verifying the dataset's availability cost roughly an hour. Discovering its discontinuation in week three cost the study. That asymmetry — trivial to check, catastrophic to assume — is the signature of a risk that belongs at the front of the plan. Had the check run on day one, the team had two full weeks to substitute sources, renegotiate scope, or reshape the deliverable. Probing critical unknowns early converts late catastrophes into early course corrections; it is a cheap purchase of optionality.

Why the other options are incorrect
A terminal buffer week assumes surprises arrive on schedule and are buffer-sized. A discontinued primary dataset is not a one-week problem, and the discovery still lands with no room left to change direction.

Full parallelism commits the whole team's capacity before the risky assumption has been tested. The wage section fails identically, now alongside sunk parallel work — a worse outcome than the sequential plan, which at least completed its other sections.

Refusing to depend on external data amputates the study's substance; wage benchmarking is the deliverable, and external sources are unavoidable in genuine research. The lesson is to verify dependencies early, not to have none.

Key Takeaway
Sequence plans by uncertainty, not by ease. Probe the assumption whose failure would be most expensive while the schedule still has room to absorb the answer.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: common workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/common-workflows

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: best practices → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: A terminal buffer assumes surprises arrive politely at the end and are buffer-sized; a discontinued dataset is not a one-week problem, and the discovery still lands with no room to maneuver.

Full parallelism spends the whole team's capacity before the risky assumption is checked — the wage section still fails, now alongside sunk parallel work rather than after sequential work that at least completed.

Decomposition includes sequencing, and sequencing should be governed by uncertainty: the wage dataset was the plan's riskiest assumption, and its verification cost was an hour of checking — not a week of work. Probing critical unknowns first converts late catastrophes into early course corrections: had the discontinuation surfaced in week one, the team could have substituted sources or renegotiated scope with two weeks in hand. Easy sections keep; risky assumptions don't.
Renouncing external data amputates the study's substance — wage benchmarking is the deliverable. The lesson is to verify dependencies early, not to have none.

question:
A coffee-chain platform team split a 300-file refactor between two parallel subagent runs by file count: files 1–150 and 151–300, alphabetically. Both runs edited the same shared interfaces from opposite sides, and the merge produced dozens of conflicts plus two incompatible signature changes.

How should the split have been made?
options: The same alphabetical halves, plus a third pass dedicated to resolving the overlap afterward
Along module and dependency seams, each run owning whole modules and their interfaces
Sequentially rather than in parallel, letting the second run see the first run's interface decisions
Into six alphabetical chunks of fifty files instead of two chunks of one hundred fifty
answer: Along module and dependency seams, each run owning whole modules and their interfaces
explanation:
This question tests parallel work partitioning, and specifically that a partition's quality is measured at its boundaries, not by the evenness of its chunk sizes.

Why alphabetical halves failed
Alphabetical order is orthogonal to code structure. Splitting 300 files at the alphabetical midpoint slices through modules arbitrarily, which means shared interfaces end up with pieces on both sides — and therefore two simultaneous owners, each free to change a signature without seeing the other's decision. The conflicts and the two incompatible signature changes were not bad luck during the merge; they were determined by the partition before either run began. Both halves had exactly 150 files, which is why the split looked reasonable.

What a seam-aligned split buys
Partitioning along module and dependency boundaries gives each run whole modules including their interfaces. Every interface then has exactly one owner, the boundary between runs coincides with a boundary the code already respects, and the merge is mechanical because the two runs touched disjoint surfaces. Independent subtasks parallelize cleanly; coupled ones do not, so the partition's job is to find where the coupling actually is.

Why the other options are incorrect
A third reconciliation pass budgets for the damage instead of preventing it. Reconciling two incompatible signature changes after the fact is redesign work — the most expensive kind, done with the least context.

Going sequential removes the collisions by removing the parallelism. It costs half the throughput to compensate for a partition problem that a seam-aligned split solves while keeping the parallelism.

Six chunks of fifty files subdivide the same arbitrary axis, producing more boundaries that cut through modules and more shared interfaces with split ownership. Finer slices of a bad partition make the problem worse, not better.

Key Takeaway
Partition parallel work along module and dependency seams so each unit owns its interfaces. Split where the code already separates, not where the file list happens to divide evenly.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Working with large codebases → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: common workflows → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/common-workflows
option_feedback: A conflict-resolution pass budgets for the damage instead of preventing it — reconciling two incompatible signature changes after the fact is redesign work, the most expensive kind.

A partition's quality is measured at its boundaries. Alphabetical order is orthogonal to the code's structure, so it slices through modules and gives shared interfaces two simultaneous owners — the conflicts were built into the split before either run started. Partitioning along dependency seams gives each run whole modules, interfaces included: every interface has exactly one owner, the boundary between runs is the module boundary, and parallel work composes because the units were divided where the code actually separates.
Sequencing removes the collision by removing the parallelism — half the throughput to compensate for a bad partition, when a seam-aligned partition delivers parallelism without collisions.
Finer slices of the same arbitrary axis multiply the boundaries that cut through modules — six chunks means more shared-interface seams with split ownership, not fewer.

question:
An airline-cargo team's nightly claude -p triage job misbehaved last night — it labeled every report critical. The job's captured stdout shows the wrong outputs but nothing about why. The engineer wants to understand what actually happened in that run.

What should she do?
options: Resume the recorded session and interrogate it — context, calls, where labels went wrong
Re-run the job with maximum verbosity tonight and diff the two nights' outputs
Add more logging to the job and wait for the failure to recur with better instrumentation
Replay last night's input in a fresh interactive session and simply watch how the labeling behaves
answer: Resume the recorded session and interrogate it — context, calls, where labels went wrong
explanation:
This question tests debugging of non-interactive runs, and specifically that headless sessions are recorded and resumable, so the failed run itself is the evidence.

The evidence already exists
A claude -p run creates a session on disk exactly as an interactive run does. That session holds what the captured stdout does not: the prompt as it was actually received, the project context that loaded, every tool call and its result, and the reasoning that produced all-critical labels. Stdout is the output of a process whose state was persisted alongside it. Resuming that session by ID turns debugging from reproduction into interrogation — the engineer can inspect what was in context and ask follow-up questions inside the run that failed.

Why reproduction is the weaker instrument
Model behavior is not deterministic, and a re-run has different inputs besides. Any strategy that begins "make it happen again" is betting on a recurrence that may not come, and even a successful recurrence only produces a second failing run to examine — when the first is already on disk and available now.

Why the other options are incorrect
Tonight's verbose run is a different run over different reports. A diff explains last night only if the failure recurs identically, which is exactly what cannot be assumed, and the wait costs a day for evidence already available.

Adding logging and waiting treats the record as lost. It postpones diagnosis to the failure's next appearance while a complete record of its first appearance sits resumable on disk.

A fresh interactive session replaying the input reproduces the conditions approximately at best. If it labels everything correctly, the engineer has learned nothing about the run that did not.

Key Takeaway
Headless runs are sessions. Resume the failed session by ID and interrogate the actual context and tool calls rather than trying to reproduce the failure.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: headless mode → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless

-

-
