-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: sessions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions
option_feedback: Headless runs record sessions just as interactive ones do — the failed run's session still exists, holding the actual conversation: the prompt as received, the context that loaded, the tool calls, the reasoning that led to all-critical labels. Resuming it turns debugging into interrogation of the real artifact: she can examine the run's state and ask follow-up questions inside it. No reproduction, no waiting — the evidence is already on disk.

Tonight's verbose run is a different run — different inputs, possibly different behavior — and a diff against it explains last night only if the failure kindly recurs identically. The actual failed run is available without re-rolling the dice.
Instrument-and-wait treats the evidence as lost; it postpones diagnosis to the failure's next appearance when the full record of its first appearance is resumable now.
A fresh session replaying the input reproduces the conditions approximately at best — nondeterminism means it may label everything correctly, proving nothing about the run that didn't.

question:
Four turns ago in a car-rental codebase session, the agent began an ill-advised refactor of the booking module's adapter layer; the developer let it run before recognizing the mistake. Everything it changed, it changed through its own file edits — no installs, no scripts. The conversation and those files now carry the refactor's effects, while the earlier part of the session — a careful audit of the booking engine — is valuable and worth keeping.

What is the right recovery?
options: Run /clear and rebuild the audit context from scratch in a clean session
Revert the changed files with git and carry on in the session as it stands
Abandon the session and start fresh, re-running the audit first
Use /rewind to return the session to the checkpoint before the swap began
answer: Use /rewind to return the session to the checkpoint before the swap began
explanation:
This question tests session recovery, and specifically that checkpoints let you discard a bad recent segment while keeping the valuable earlier one.

The shape of the problem
The session has two parts with opposite value: a careful booking-engine audit worth keeping, and four turns of ill-advised refactor worth erasing — and the damage exists in two places at once, in the conversation and in the files. Any recovery that treats the session as a single unit must sacrifice one part to fix the other. /rewind is the mechanism that does not: it returns the session to a checkpoint from before the refactor began, restoring both the conversation state and the file edits Claude itself made since then.

Why the stem's constraint matters
The question is explicit that everything the agent changed, it changed through its own file edits — no installs, no scripts, no external side effects. That matters because checkpointing covers Claude's own edits, not arbitrary system state. Within that boundary — which this scenario deliberately establishes — the rewind is complete: the audit context survives, the refactor is gone from the transcript and the working tree alike, and recovery is a single command.

Why the other options are incorrect
/clear resets the entire context, discarding the audit along with the refactor. It is the maximal response to a problem four turns wide, and it forces the expensive rebuild that checkpoints exist to avoid.

A git revert restores the files but leaves the conversation carrying the refactor's reasoning, intent and justification. A model steered by that history is liable to steer back toward the approach it still remembers choosing — and the developer must then fight the context for the rest of the session.

Abandoning the session pays for the full audit a second time in order to escape four bad turns. Same cost as clearing the context, with extra steps.

Key Takeaway
/rewind restores a session to a checkpoint, undoing both the conversation and Claude's own file edits since then. Use it when a session has a good past and a bad recent stretch.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: checkpointing → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: sessions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: interactive mode → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/interactive-mode

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: slash commands → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands
option_feedback: /clear wipes everything — the refactor and the audit alike. It is the maximal response to a problem that is four turns wide.

Git cleans the files but not the conversation: the session still carries the refactor's reasoning and intent in context, and a model steered by that history may well steer back toward the approach it still remembers choosing.
A fresh session pays the full audit again to escape four bad turns — the expensive rebuild that the rewind mechanism makes unnecessary.

This is the situation checkpoints exist for: the session has a good past and a bad recent segment, and /rewind returns it to the checkpoint before the wrong turn — restoring the conversation and the file edits Claude itself made since then. Because the stem confines the damage to exactly those edits, the audit context survives intact and the refactor's pollution is gone, in the transcript and on disk alike. Recovery is one command instead of a rebuild.

question:
A museum-research team is reviewing a hand-rolled agentic loop for protocol correctness and lists candidate invariants about tool_result blocks.

Which TWO must be true of every tool_result? (Select TWO.)
options: It references the id of a tool_use block from the immediately preceding assistant message
It appears inside an assistant-role message, since the assistant requested the tool
It is delivered in a user-role message
It arrives before the tool actually executes, reserving its place in the conversation
It echoes the tool's input arguments so the pairing is unambiguous
answer: It references the id of a tool_use block from the immediately preceding assistant message
It is delivered in a user-role message
explanation:
This question tests the tool_result protocol contract, and specifically the two pairing invariants a hand-rolled loop must honor.

The two pairing invariants

-
Identity and adjacency — Every tool_result carries the tool_use_id of the specific tool_use block it answers, and that block lives in the assistant message immediately preceding. This is what makes results unambiguous when several tools are called in one turn, and what makes the conversation well-formed: results cannot be deferred across intervening turns and delivered later. If the assistant message requested three tools, the very next message must carry results for all three.

-
Role placement — Results travel back in a user-role message. This follows from what a result is: input to the model's next turn. The assistant role carries what the model produced; the user role carries what is supplied to it. Tool results are supplied, so they are user content — a structural rule, not a stylistic convention, and the one hand-rolled loops most often get wrong.

Why the other options are incorrect
A tool_result inside an assistant message would have the model answering its own request. The role split exists precisely to separate the request (assistant) from the response (application), and collapsing it violates the conversation's structure.

A result reports an outcome, so it necessarily follows execution. Nothing in the protocol reserves a conversational slot in advance, and a placeholder result would assert an outcome that does not yet exist.

The tool_use_id alone establishes the pairing unambiguously. Echoing the input arguments adds redundant bulk to every turn that the protocol neither requires nor consults.

Key Takeaway
A tool_result references the tool_use id from the immediately preceding assistant message and is delivered in a user-role message. Identity plus placement — those are the two invariants.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Handle tool calls (tool_result, tool_use_id) → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

-
Anthropic — How tool use works → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works

-
Anthropic — Working with messages → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/working-with-messages

-
Anthropic — Parallel tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use
option_feedback: These are the two pairing rules the protocol enforces. Identity: every tool_result answers a specific tool_use by carrying its id, and the tool_use it answers lives in the assistant message immediately before — results cannot be deferred past intervening turns. Placement: results travel back to the model as user-role content, because they are input to the model's next turn; the user message following a tool-using assistant message carries the tool_result blocks for all of that message's calls.
The assistant requests; the application answers. A result inside an assistant message would be the model answering itself — the role structure exists precisely to separate request from response.

These are the two pairing rules the protocol enforces. Identity: every tool_result answers a specific tool_use by carrying its id, and the tool_use it answers lives in the assistant message immediately before — results cannot be deferred past intervening turns. Placement: results travel back to the model as user-role content, because they are input to the model's next turn; the user message following a tool-using assistant message carries the tool_result blocks for all of that message's calls.
Results report outcomes, so they follow execution by definition; nothing about the protocol reserves conversational slots in advance.
The id alone carries the pairing; echoing arguments is redundant bulk the protocol neither requires nor uses.

question:
During a wind-farm siting study, the turbine-supplier subagent noticed that grid-interconnection queues — a sibling's assigned territory — seemed outdated in the sources it was reading. It quietly expanded its own scope to re-research the topic. The run overspent its budget, and the two subagents' interconnection findings then disagreed in the final synthesis.

What should the subagent have done, and why?
options: Exactly what it did — initiative on discovered gaps is why subagents get autonomy
Nothing — the topic sat outside its assignment, and scope discipline means leaving it alone entirely
Report it to the coordinator and continue its assignment; the whole-run view decides
Spawn a small helper subagent of its own to verify the interconnection data in parallel
answer: Report it to the coordinator and continue its assignment; the whole-run view decides
explanation:
This question tests scope discipline in a hub-and-spoke system, and specifically that a subagent should escalate discovered gaps rather than absorb them.

The observation was good; the decision was not
Noticing that a sibling's territory looks stale is genuinely valuable information — it is exactly the kind of signal a distributed research run should surface. The failure lies in what followed: the subagent made a run-level decision from a lane-level view. Scope changes ripple outward into budget, sibling assignments, and synthesis consistency, and only the coordinator holds all three. The two costs the run actually paid — the budget overrun and the contradictory findings — are the structural consequences of two uncoordinated researchers covering the same ground, not accidents of this particular run.

What signal-up looks like
Report the suspected staleness to the coordinator as a finding, and continue the assigned work. The coordinator can then do what only it can: re-task the interconnection subagent, extend the budget deliberately, drop a lower-priority section to fund the recheck, or note the uncertainty in the synthesis. The discovery is preserved and the decision is made where the information to make it exists. This is the same reason a coordinator, not a subagent, owns routing and aggregation — one lane cannot see the run.

Why the other options are incorrect
Autonomy is granted for executing an assignment, not for redrawing it. The overrun and the contradiction are what unilateral scope expansion structurally produces, however sound the underlying instinct was.

Staying silent discards genuinely useful information. If the interconnection data really is stale, the whole run is better for knowing. The discipline concerns who decides, not whether the observation is voiced.

Spawning a helper delegates the same unilateral decision one level down. The scope still expands, the budget is still spent, the sibling's work is still duplicated — with an extra layer of fan-out and less visibility.

Key Takeaway
Subagents report discovered gaps upward and continue their assignment. Scope decisions belong to the component with the whole-run view.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Subagents in Claude Code → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: the agent loop → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: Autonomy is for executing the assignment, not redrawing it — the incident's costs (overrun, contradiction) are what unilateral scope changes structurally produce, however good the underlying instinct.
Silence discards the observation entirely — the interconnection data may genuinely be stale, and the run is better for knowing. The discipline is in who decides, not in pretending nothing was seen.

The observation was valuable; the unilateral expansion was the failure. A subagent sees one lane, and scope changes ripple across the run — budget, sibling assignments, synthesis consistency — which only the coordinator can see. The designed move is signal-up: report the suspected staleness as a finding, keep working the assigned scope, and let the coordinator decide with full information. That preserves the discovery and prevents both costs the run actually paid: duplicated work and contradictory findings from two uncoordinated researchers.
Spawning delegates the same unilateral decision to a helper — the scope expanded, the budget spent, the sibling still duplicated, with an extra layer of fan-out on top.

question:
A staffing-platform team is standardizing the names of its internal MCP tools and compares four candidate naming sets for the same three operations.

Which set is best designed, and why?
options: doQuery, handleStuff2, procX — short names that are quick to emit
get_invoice, search_orders, create_ticket — consistent verb_noun names stating action and object
invoice, orders, ticket — minimal noun names free of clutter
GetInvoiceForCustomerAccountingV2, searchOrdersByDateRangeInternal, create_ticket_new_final — maximally explicit names
answer: get_invoice, search_orders, create_ticket — consistent verb_noun names stating action and object
explanation:
This question tests tool naming, and specifically that names are primary selection signal and consistency is itself information.

Names do work at selection time
When the model chooses among tools, it works from names and descriptions. A name in the form verb_noun — get_invoice, search_orders, create_ticket — states the action and the object it acts on, which is the whole content of a selection decision. Beyond any individual name, the pattern carries signal: once a toolset establishes a convention, the model generalizes it, and a new cancel_shipment is correctly understood before its description is even read. Consistent names produce predictable selection; inconsistent ones make every choice an independent guess.

Why the other options are incorrect
doQuery, handleStuff2, procX carry no information about either action or object. handleStuff2 does not even indicate a domain, and the numeric suffix implies an unexplained sibling. Every selection collapses onto the description alone, with the name actively contributing noise.

Bare nouns — invoice, orders, ticket — name the object but omit the action. Does invoice fetch, create, or void one? The ambiguity sits exactly where mis-selection happens, and it worsens as the toolset grows to include several operations per object.

GetInvoiceForCustomerAccountingV2 buries the operation under qualifiers, and the set mixes three casing styles across three names, destroying the pattern the model would otherwise generalize. Suffixes like V2 and new_final are repository churn markers, not semantics; they tell the model nothing about when to choose the tool.

Key Takeaway
Use consistent verb_noun names that state action and object. The convention is as valuable as any individual name, because the model generalizes it across the toolset.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Define tools (names and descriptions) → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Tool use overview → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: Opaque abbreviations and numbered variants carry no information about action or object — every selection becomes a guess anchored on the description alone.

The model selects tools largely by name and description, so names should carry selection information: a consistent verb_noun pattern states what the tool does and to what — and consistency itself is signal, letting the model generalize the convention across the whole toolset. Predictable names produce predictable selection.
Bare nouns name the object but not the action — does invoice fetch, create, or void? The ambiguity lands exactly where misselection happens.
Kitchen-sink names bury the operation in qualifiers, drift into inconsistency (three styles in one set), and version suffixes like V2 and new_final are churn markers, not meaning.

question:
A regional bank's support agent uses get_customer_profile, which — unknown to most consumers — also writes a "contact event" into the CRM on every call. The agent naturally calls it several times per conversation while orienting. The outreach team now sees customers logged with a dozen phantom contacts a week and is drawing wrong conclusions about engagement.

What is the right fix?
options: Make the read pure; expose the contact write as its own explicitly named tool
Keep the behavior but document the side effect prominently in the tool's description text
Add a prompt rule limiting profile calls to one per conversation, and audit compliance weekly
Have the outreach team filter agent-generated contact events out of their reports
answer: Make the read pure; expose the contact write as its own explicitly named tool
explanation:
This question tests the read/write contract of a tool interface, and specifically that a get_* tool must be free of side effects because agents call reads liberally.

The broken promise
A name beginning get_ tells every caller — human or model — that invoking it is consequence-free, which licenses exactly the behavior the agent exhibits: calling it several times per conversation while orienting, re-checking after an update, confirming before an action. That usage pattern is correct given the interface's promise. Hiding a CRM write behind it means the promise is false, and normal, well-behaved usage silently corrupts engagement data that another team is making decisions from.

The design fix
Separate the two operations along the line that already exists in the domain. get_customer_profile becomes a genuinely pure read that can be called freely. Recording a contact becomes its own explicitly named tool — invoked deliberately when a contact has actually occurred, not incurred as a byproduct of looking something up. Side effects should be visible in the interface and chosen, never bundled into an operation whose name disclaims them.

Why the other options are incorrect
Documenting the side effect makes the trap legible without removing it. Every caller must now remember to ration a tool whose name invites the opposite, and phantom events continue at whatever rate that memory fails — which for a model reading a long tool list is a meaningful rate.

A prompt rule capping profile calls at one per conversation degrades legitimate behavior to suppress an accidental write: the agent loses re-checks it genuinely needs, weekly auditing is pure overhead, and one permitted call still logs one phantom contact. It also relies on instruction adherence to enforce a data-integrity constraint.

Filtering downstream concedes the data is wrong and patches a single consumer's view of it. Every other CRM consumer — reports, segmentation, other teams, future integrations — continues reading phantom engagement.

Key Takeaway

question:
A port authority's manifest-extraction service returns "validation failed" — nothing more — whenever a submission is rejected. Agents respond by resubmitting near-identical payloads, guessing at what to change. The team is redesigning the error response.

Which TWO fields make the error actionable? (Select TWO.)
options: The hostname of the server that performed the validation
A retry_after value indicating when to resubmit
Which field failed validation
The full submitted document echoed back for reference
The constraint that was violated and the expected form
answer: Which field failed validation
The constraint that was violated and the expected form
explanation:
This question tests error-response design for validation failures, and specifically that an actionable error must answer where and what.

The two questions a corrector has to answer

-
Which field failed — To fix a rejected payload, the model needs to know which part to change. Naming the field localizes the problem to one element of the submission instead of the whole document.

-
The violated constraint and expected form — The model also needs to know what the change must accomplish. "arrival_date must be ISO 8601; got 14/03/2026" converts the fix from a search into a single deterministic edit.

Why the current response produces the observed behavior
With both pieces present, the resubmission is targeted. With either missing, the model is searching blind along one axis — which is precisely the near-identical-resubmission behavior in the transcripts. "Validation failed" is a bare rejection with no gradient to follow. The rational response, given zero information about what was wrong, is to change something plausible and try again — which is what the agents are doing. The guessing is not a model defect; it is the correct behavior under an uninformative error.

Why the other options are incorrect
The validating hostname is operations metadata. Nothing about the payload changes because of which server rejected it, and it adds a field the model must read and discard on every failure.

retry_after belongs to transient failures, where waiting is the cure. A validation failure is deterministic — the same payload fails at every hour of the day — so a retry hint actively misdirects, suggesting the fix is patience rather than correction.

Echoing the full submitted document returns information the agent already holds, doubling the payload in context while adding zero bits about what was wrong.

Key Takeaway
Actionable validation errors name the failing field and state the violated constraint with the expected form. Location plus requirement turns a guess into a fix.

question:
A streaming-radio support agent queries a catalog API that rate-limits aggressively at peak hours. The tool currently surfaces a bare "too many requests" error; transcripts show the agent immediately retrying several times in a row, deepening the throttle, then giving up mid-conversation.

How should the tool's rate-limit error be designed?
options: Ask the catalog team to raise the rate limit for the support agent's credentials
On rate limits, have the tool silently switch to a secondary catalog mirror
Return it as transient with an explicit retry_after the agent honors before one spaced retry
Classify rate limits as permanent failures so the agent apologizes rather than hammering the API
answer: Return it as transient with an explicit retry_after the agent honors before one spaced retry
explanation:
This question tests transient-error design, and specifically that a rate limit should be returned as a classified transient failure carrying an explicit retry_after.

The error must contain the recovery
A rate limit is the best-behaved failure a system can produce: it is temporary, and the cure is known exactly — wait, then retry. But the agent can only act on what the error tells it. A bare "too many requests" conveys that something went wrong and nothing about what to do, so the model does the only thing available: it retries immediately, several times, which deepens the throttle and burns the conversation's remaining patience before it gives up. Returning the failure as transient plus a retry_after value converts that spiral into disciplined behavior — hold briefly, tell the customer it needs a moment, retry once after the stated interval, succeed.

Classification is what makes branching possible
This is the general principle behind structured error taxonomies: the agent's recovery strategy differs completely for transient, validation, and business failures, and it can only select the right one if the error says which it is. retry_after is the transient class's actionable payload, exactly as the failing field is the validation class's.

Why the other options are incorrect
Raising the limit moves the ceiling without teaching anything to respect ceilings. Peak traffic finds the new threshold, and the identical burst-retry behavior returns — now against a limit that is more expensive to raise again.

Silently failing over to a secondary mirror assumes a synchronized secondary exists, which the scenario never establishes, and trades an honest few-second delay for consistency risk the customer is never told about.

Classifying rate limits as permanent is simply false, and the falsehood costs resolutions: conversations end in an apology for a condition that clears in seconds. It stops the hammering by giving up.

Key Takeaway
Return rate limits as transient with an explicit retry_after, and have the agent honor it before a single spaced retry. Errors should carry the information their recovery requires.

-
Anthropic — Rate limits → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits

-
Anthropic — API errors → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors

-

-
Anthropic — Troubleshooting tool use → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/troubleshooting-tool-use
option_feedback: Raised limits move the ceiling without teaching anyone to respect ceilings — peak traffic finds the new limit, and the burst-retry behavior returns at a higher threshold.
A silent mirror assumes a synchronized secondary exists — the stem gives none — and silent source-switching trades an honest delay for consistency risk the customer never learns about.

A rate limit is a transient failure with a known cure — wait, then retry — and the error response should carry exactly the information that enables it: the failure's transient classification plus a retry_after value. The agent's behavior then follows from the message: hold the turn briefly or tell the customer it needs a moment, retry once after the stated interval, and succeed. The observed burst-retry spiral is what an uninformative error produces; a structured backoff hint is what disciplined recovery consumes.
Permanent classification is false, and the falsehood costs resolutions: conversations end in apology for a condition that clears in seconds.

question:
A telehealth billing-document pipeline sets tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "submit_claim_record"} globally — every request, every turn. About one turn in ten is actually a clarification exchange with the operator, and those turns now produce garbage claim records, since the model must call the tool with something.

What is the right configuration?
options: Keep the global forced tool and filter the garbage claim records out downstream instead
Switch the global setting to auto so every turn can choose freely
Add a no_op tool for the model to call on clarification turns
Set tool_choice per request: force on extraction turns, auto or none on clarification turns
answer: Set tool_choice per request: force on extraction turns, auto or none on clarification turns
explanation:
This question tests tool_choice configuration, and specifically that it is a per-request parameter that should track what each request is actually for.

The three settings and what they guarantee
{"type": "auto"} lets Claude decide — it may answer in text or call a tool. {"type": "any"} requires that some tool be called, with the model choosing which. {"type": "tool", "name": "..."} forces one specific tool. The forcing settings work by prefilling the assistant turn, which is why a forced turn cannot produce a natural-language reply first: the structure is guaranteed because the alternative has been removed.

Why a global setting is the bug
That guarantee is exactly right for extraction turns and exactly wrong for clarification turns. When the pipeline forces submit_claim_record on a turn whose purpose is to ask the operator a question, the model has no path to a text reply — so it does the only thing the configuration permits and emits a claim record built from nothing. The garbage records are not a model failure; they are the configuration's specified behavior applied to a turn it was never meant for. Since tool_choice is set per request, the fix is to set it per request: force on extraction turns, auto or none on clarification turns.

Why the other options are incorrect
Downstream filtering admits fabricated claim records into the pipeline and then spends detection effort separating them from real ones — solving by inspection a problem the configuration manufactures on every tenth turn.

Global auto repairs the clarification turns by surrendering the extraction guarantee on all the others. The structured-output assurance that motivated forcing in the first place is quietly given up wholesale.

A no_op tool satisfies the forced call but produces nothing the operator can read. A clarification turn's entire deliverable is prose to a human, and a tool invocation is not prose.

Key Takeaway
tool_choice is per request. Force it where structured output is required; use auto or none where a text reply is the deliverable.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — How tool use works (tool_choice) → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works

-
Anthropic — Tool use reference → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-reference

-
Anthropic — Tool use overview → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview

-
Anthropic — Structured outputs → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: Downstream filtering accepts fabricated claim records into the pipeline and then tries to distinguish them from real ones — spending detection effort on garbage the configuration itself manufactures.
Global auto fixes the clarification turns by un-guaranteeing the extraction turns — the structured-output assurance that motivated forcing is quietly given up for all the turns that need it.
A no_op tool satisfies the forced call while producing nothing the operator can read — the clarification turn's entire purpose is a text reply, which a tool invocation is not.

tool_choice is a per-request parameter, and this pipeline has two kinds of request. Extraction turns want the guarantee — force submit_claim_record, structured output assured. Clarification turns want prose to the operator — auto or none, no tool pressure at all. Setting the parameter per turn type gives each request the behavior its job requires; the garbage records disappear because no turn is ever forced to fabricate one.

question:
A property-management document platform has two MCP servers mounted, and both expose a tool that searches documents: one indexes current leases, the other indexes the archive — a distinction stated nowhere. The agent alternates between them unpredictably, and identical questions get different answers on different runs.

What should the team do for this deployment?
options: Add a prompt instruction telling the agent to always prefer the current-lease server's search
Pick the authoritative server per domain; mount only the one this deployment needs
Merge the two indexes into a single backend so any search tool returns everything
Rename one of the two tools — the near-identical names, at least, stop colliding
answer: Pick the authoritative server per domain; mount only the one this deployment needs
explanation:
This question tests deployment-level tool curation, and specifically that ambiguous selection is fixed by removing the ambiguity, not by weighting it.

Where the nondeterminism comes from
The model selects tools from names and descriptions. Two tools that search documents, with nothing in either description distinguishing current leases from archive, present the model with two indistinguishable candidates for one job. Faced with a genuine tie, selection is effectively arbitrary — which is precisely why identical questions return different answers on different runs. The run-to-run variance is not a reliability defect in the model; it is the honest consequence of an underdetermined choice.

The configuration answer
MCP servers are mounted per deployment, and each deployment has a data domain. If this deployment's job is current leases, mount the current-lease server and leave the archive server for deployments that do archival work. The tie disappears because there is no longer anything to break. This also restores a healthy property: the toolset a deployment exposes mirrors the work that deployment does, which keeps selection reliable as the tool count grows.

Why the other options are incorrect
A prompt preference leaves both candidates mounted and tilts the choice. Alternation is reduced rather than eliminated, and this deployment's context still carries a tool it has no legitimate use for — adding a candidate the model must consider on every selection.

Merging the indexes is a cross-team backend migration standing in for a configuration change, and it may be wrong on the merits: consumers that depend on the current-versus-archive distinction lose it permanently to fix one deployment's mounting mistake.

Renaming makes the two tools easier for a human to tell apart without telling the model which is correct for this deployment. The guess remains a guess; only the labels changed.

Key Takeaway
Mount the authoritative server for the deployment's domain and leave the rest out. Curate the toolset so the right choice is the only choice.

-

-

-

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/mcp
option_feedback: A preference instruction leaves both candidates live and weighs one — reduced alternation, not eliminated, and the context still carries a duplicate tool this deployment never legitimately needs.

The nondeterminism comes from offering two candidates for one job with nothing to distinguish them. The deployment-level fix is configuration: decide which server is authoritative for this deployment's data domain — current leases — and mount only it; the archive server stays available to deployments whose job is archival. Selection becomes deterministic because the selection problem is gone, and each deployment's toolset again mirrors its actual task.

A merged index may be the right platform project eventually, but it is a cross-team backend migration standing in for a config change — and merging current with archive can be wrong for consumers that need the distinction the merge erases.

question:
A staffing-software team maintains an MCP server used by several internal teams. Version 2 renames search_docs to docs_search for consistency. When v2 deployed, every consuming agent broke overnight — calls to the old name simply failed.

How should the rename have been rolled out?
options: Expose both names through a migration window, then remove the deprecated one
Deploy the rename and hotfix every consuming agent's configuration the same night
Adopt a policy of never renaming tools once they have consumers
Have consumers discover tools dynamically at session start so tool names stop mattering to them
answer: Expose both names through a migration window, then remove the deprecated one
explanation:
This question tests tool interface versioning, and specifically that a tool name is a public contract that changes through a migration window.

Why the flag day failed
Tool names are how agents invoke functionality — they appear in prompts, in configurations, in code. Renaming search_docs to docs_search and shipping it is a breaking change to a published interface with no compatibility period, so every consumer that still says search_docs breaks at the moment of deploy. This is the standard API-versioning failure, and it has the standard remedy.

What a migration window provides
Serve both names simultaneously: docs_search as canonical, search_docs retained as an alias whose description carries a deprecation notice and a removal date. Three things follow. Consumers keep working through the deploy, so the rename is a non-event operationally. Maintainers get told what to change and by when, in the place they will actually see it. And the server can measure calls to the deprecated name, so removal happens when usage reaches zero rather than on a hopeful schedule. The rename still ships — it just ships without the outage.

Why the other options are incorrect
Same-night hotfixes assume the full set of consumers is known and reachable, which the overnight breakage disproves — a server used by "several internal teams" surprised its own maintainers. A plan whose success condition is perfect knowledge of your dependents is not a plan.

Never renaming buys compatibility by accumulating inconsistency permanently. Renames have real value; the cost of doing them is what migration windows are for, and prohibition is an overcorrection.

Dynamic discovery enumerates what exists, but consumers still invoke tools by name in prompts and code. When the old name disappears from the listing, those invocations fail exactly as before — discovery changes how names are learned, not whether they matter.

Key Takeaway
Ship renames behind a deprecation window: serve both names, mark the old one deprecated, and remove it once usage has fallen to zero.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Define tools → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: MCP → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp

-
Anthropic — Tool use overview → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview
option_feedback: A tool name is a public interface, and interface changes get migration paths, not flag days. Serving both names — the new one canonical, the old one aliased with a deprecation note in its description — keeps every consumer working the moment v2 lands, tells maintainers where to move and by when, and lets usage of the old name be watched down to zero before removal. The rename ships, nothing breaks, and the window closes on evidence.

Same-night heroics assume every consumer is known and reachable — the overnight breakage shows the server's consumers were not fully enumerated, and a scramble is a plan whose success condition is perfect knowledge.
A permanent freeze preserves compatibility by accumulating inconsistency forever — the cost of renames is real, which is why they get migration windows rather than prohibition.
Dynamic discovery lists what exists; consumers still invoke tools by name in their prompts and code, so the old name's disappearance breaks them regardless of how they learned it.

question:
A coffee-chain developer reports that "the inventory MCP server doesn't work" in her Claude Code sessions — tools missing, no obvious error. A teammate is walking her through diagnosis.

What is the right first step?
options: Reinstall Claude Code to rule out a corrupted installation
Delete and re-add the server's configuration entry from scratch
Move the server to user scope, where she has heard connections behave more reliably
Run /mcp and read the server's actual state: connection, tool list, authentication
answer: Run /mcp and read the server's actual state: connection, tool list, authentication
explanation:
This question tests MCP troubleshooting method, and specifically that /mcp converts a vague symptom into a specific diagnosis before any fix is attempted.

"Doesn't work" is a symptom class, not a problem
Missing tools with no visible error is consistent with several unrelated causes: the server is configured in a scope that does not apply here; the server process fails to start; the connection dropped; authentication expired; or — very commonly for project-scoped servers — the server is configured correctly but this user has not approved it yet, because project servers from .mcp.json prompt each developer for approval on first use. Each of these has a different remedy, and choosing a remedy before identifying the cause is guessing.

What /mcp shows
/mcp lists the configured servers, their live connection status, the tools each exposes, and their authentication state. Reading it takes seconds and answers the only question that matters first: which failure is this? The fix then follows from the finding — approve the server, re-authenticate, fix the launch command, or add it to the right scope.

Why the other options are incorrect
Reinstalling the client is maximal intervention chosen with zero diagnostic information. Nearly every cause of a missing server lives in configuration, approval, or connection state, none of which a reinstall touches.

Deleting and recreating the entry assumes the entry is wrong. If the real cause is authentication or a failing server process, the recreated entry fails identically — and the churn has destroyed the evidence that would have identified it.

Scope controls where a server is available, not how reliably it connects. Moving scopes reshuffles configuration while carrying the actual fault along unchanged, and it may also make a team-shared server personal.

Key Takeaway
Diagnose before fixing: /mcp reports connection, tools, and auth state, which tells you which of several unrelated failures you actually have.

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: connect to an MCP server → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: slash commands → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: debug your configuration → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/debug-your-config
option_feedback: Reinstalling the client is maximal surgery chosen before any diagnosis — almost every cause of a missing server lives in configuration or connection state that reinstalling does not touch.
Recreating the config guesses that the entry is wrong; if the failure is auth or server startup, the fresh entry fails identically and the churn has erased the evidence.
Scope determines where a server is available, not how reliably it connects — moving scopes reshuffles configuration while the actual fault rides along.

"Doesn't work" spans many distinct failures — server not configured in this scope, process failing to start, connection dropped, auth expired, tools present but unapproved — and each has a different fix. /mcp shows which one this is: the configured servers, their live status, the tools they expose, and their auth state. Thirty seconds of reading turns a vague symptom into a specific problem, and the fix follows from the finding instead of preceding it.

question:
A new hire on a fashion-commerce team asks where the project's shared MCP server configuration lives — the one every teammate automatically gets when they clone the repo.

What is the answer?
options: In each developer's ~/.claude.json, synchronized by a setup script
In .claude/settings.local.json at the repository root
In .mcp.json at the repository root, committed to version control
In the project's CLAUDE.md, in a servers section
answer: In .mcp.json at the repository root, committed to version control
explanation:
This question tests MCP configuration scopes, and specifically that project scope is the mechanism for team-shared server configuration.

The three scopes
Local scope stores servers in the user's own configuration for the current project only — private and unshared. User scope stores them for all of that user's projects — also private. Project scope stores them in a .mcp.json file at the repository root, which is checked into version control and therefore travels with the repo. That last property is exactly what the new hire is asking about: clone the repository, receive the server definitions.

One practical detail worth knowing
Project-scoped servers still prompt each developer for approval the first time an interactive session encounters them — a security boundary, since a repository can otherwise cause code to run on a teammate's machine. So the flow is "clone, approve once, done," and .mcp.json commonly uses environment-variable expansion so each developer supplies their own credentials against a shared definition. Non-interactive contexts such as claude -p, the Agent SDK, and cloud sessions load project servers without prompting.

Why the other options are incorrect
~/.claude.json is per-user configuration. A setup script pushing team servers into every developer's personal file is a hand-rolled, drift-prone imitation of the sharing that project scope provides natively — and nothing keeps the copies in sync after the first run.

settings.local.json is deliberately personal and unshared local configuration, conventionally gitignored. It is the opposite of a file teammates receive on clone.

CLAUDE.md supplies guidance and context to sessions; nothing in it registers a server. A "servers section" there would be prose about configuration rather than configuration.

Key Takeaway
Team-shared MCP servers live in .mcp.json at the repository root, committed to version control. Each developer approves them once on first use.

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: connect to an MCP server → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart

option_feedback: ~/.claude.json is per-user configuration — a sync script pushing team servers into personal files is a hand-rolled, drift-prone imitation of what project scope does natively.
settings.local.json is personal, unshared local configuration — the opposite of a file teammates receive.

Project-scope MCP configuration lives in .mcp.json at the repo root, and committing it is the sharing mechanism: clone the repo, get the server definitions, approve them once, and the team runs identical configuration from a single source of truth.

question:
A fashion-commerce team is upgrading to a new major version of its payments SDK, released well after the model's knowledge cutoff. The agent's first attempt generated integration code using patterns the new version has removed — compiling against memories of the old API.

What should the agent do differently?
options: Keep generating from training knowledge and fix each deprecation as the tests catch it
Fetch the current migration guide and API docs; work from those
Downgrade the project to the SDK version the model knows best
Paste the entire new SDK source tree into the session as context
answer: Fetch the current migration guide and API docs; work from those
explanation:
This question tests retrieval versus recall, and specifically that a knowledge-cutoff gap is closed by fetching current documentation into context.

Diagnosing the failure correctly
The agent did not reason badly; it reasoned correctly from stale premises. The SDK's new major version was released after the model's training cutoff, so the patterns in its memory describe an interface that no longer exists. That is an information deficit, and information deficits are fixed by supplying information — not by trying harder, not by iterating, and not by changing the model's disposition.

What fetching actually buys
The migration guide is written for this exact situation: it enumerates removed patterns, their replacements, and the intended upgrade path, all curated by the people who made the change. Together with the current API reference, it puts authoritative, current signatures into context, and generation then proceeds from documents rather than recollection. This is also a general working habit worth internalizing: for any fast-moving dependency, check the current docs before generating against it, because the model's knowledge is dated by construction and its confidence is not a signal about currency.

Why the other options are incorrect
Fixing deprecations as tests catch them discovers the new API one failure at a time, and the discovery is bounded by coverage — any changed pattern the tests do not exercise ships wrong and silent. It is also far slower than reading the guide once.

Downgrading to the version the model knows inverts the dependency: the codebase now tracks a model's training date, forfeiting the security patches and features that motivated the upgrade. Tooling should serve the code, not the reverse.

Pasting the entire SDK source floods the context with implementation internals when the task needs interface knowledge. The docs contain that knowledge at a small fraction of the tokens, already organized for exactly this purpose.

Key Takeaway
When a library moved past the model's training cutoff, fetch the migration guide and current API docs into context. Retrieval fixes staleness; iteration does not.

-

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: best practices → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices

-

-

option_feedback: Test-driven whack-a-mole discovers the API one deprecation at a time — slow, and bounded by test coverage: patterns the tests never exercise ship wrong.

Training knowledge has a cutoff and this library moved past it — the failure is informational, so the fix is retrieval. Fetching the current migration guide and API reference puts the actual new interface in context, and generation proceeds from documents rather than memories: current signatures, renamed patterns, the upgrade path the vendor wrote. Working knowledge should be as fresh as the thing being worked on, and the web tools exist precisely to close that gap.
Pinning the dependency to the model's memory inverts the relationship — the codebase now tracks the model's training date, forfeiting the security and feature reasons the upgrade existed.

question:
A museum's digitization team asks Claude Code to deduplicate and normalize a 200 MB CSV of catalog records. The agent's first move was Read on the file, which failed against the context window before any work began.

What is the right approach?
options: Sample a few rows, then write and run a script that processes the whole file
Split the CSV into a hundred 2 MB chunks and Read each chunk in sequence
Move the session to the largest available context window and retry the Read
Paste the file into the conversation in sections and have the model transform each section by hand
answer: Sample a few rows, then write and run a script that processes the whole file
explanation:
This question tests the division of labor between the model and the machine, and specifically that bulk data belongs in a script, not in the context window.

Why Read was the wrong first move
Read exists to put file contents in front of the model so it can understand them. A 200 MB CSV is not something to understand; it is something to process. The model needs to learn the file's structure — column layout, delimiters, how duplicates present, what normalization the records need — and a few dozen sampled rows convey all of that. The remaining 199.9 MB contains no additional information about the shape of the problem, only more instances of it.

The correct shape of the work
Sample rows to learn the format, write a transformation script from that understanding, and run it with Bash. The 200 MB flows through the interpreter, never through the context window; the transformation is applied identically to every record because it is code rather than repeated judgment; and the work is fast, deterministic, and re-runnable when a rule needs adjusting. Read informs the code; the code touches the data.

Why the other options are incorrect
A hundred chunked reads route the same 200 MB through context on an installment plan. It is slow, expensive, and worse than a single pass in one respect: a hundred separate judgment calls invite inconsistent handling across chunks.

No context window holds 200 MB, and the premise is mistaken even where the arithmetic might work — bulk transformation gains nothing from the model perceiving every row individually.

Hand-transforming pasted sections makes the model perform mechanical work token by token. It is the slowest, costliest, and least reliable route to a result one script produces deterministically.

Key Takeaway
Sample to understand the format; script to process the volume. Read informs the code — the data itself never needs to enter context.

question:
A wind-energy monorepo's root CLAUDE.md has absorbed everything: shared engineering standards, but also the SCADA package's database layout, its test-fixture conventions, and its deployment quirks. Sessions in the web-dashboard package load all of it; developers there report irrelevant SCADA guidance surfacing in suggestions, and baseline tokens climbing.

How should the content be organized?
options: Trim the root file down to nearly nothing so that no package ever pays for another's context
Copy the full content into every package's CLAUDE.md — each one, then, is fully self-sufficient
Keep one root file but reorder it so shared standards come before package specifics
Shared standards stay in the root file; each package's specifics move into that package's CLAUDE.md
answer: Shared standards stay in the root file; each package's specifics move into that package's CLAUDE.md
explanation:
This question tests the CLAUDE.md hierarchy in a monorepo, and specifically that content scope should match loading scope.

What the hierarchy is for
Memory files load by position: the root CLAUDE.md loads for every session in the repository, while a subdirectory CLAUDE.md loads on demand when Claude works with files in that part of the tree. That structure is a scoping tool, and the monorepo's root file has defeated it by hoisting package-specific content — SCADA's database layout, its fixtures, its deployment quirks — to a position that loads everywhere.

The two costs of misplaced content
Both symptoms in the scenario follow directly. Rising baseline tokens: every web-dashboard session pays for SCADA's internals before doing any work. Irrelevant suggestions: the model is faithfully applying context it was given, and it was given SCADA conventions in a dashboard session. Moving each package's specifics into that package's own CLAUDE.md fixes both simultaneously — SCADA sessions retain everything they had, dashboard sessions stop carrying it — while genuinely shared standards stay at the root where their scope actually is. Keeping the root file lean is also the documented aim; a memory file is meant to be read, and files that grow past a couple of hundred lines lose their edge.

Why the other options are incorrect
Emptying the root discards the content whose entire purpose is to load everywhere. Shared engineering standards are correctly placed; only the package specifics are misplaced.

Copying everything into every package maximizes both problems at once: every session loads every package's internals, and each duplicate drifts from the others on the first edit.

Reordering changes where content sits in the file, not whether it loads. All the SCADA sections still enter every dashboard session in full — the token cost and the distraction are unchanged, merely relocated.

Key Takeaway
Shared standards go in the root CLAUDE.md; package specifics go in that package's CLAUDE.md. Match the content's scope to the scope at which it loads.

question:
Mid-session, a car-rental platform developer tells Claude Code: "we always run migrations with make db-migrate — remember that." She means permanently, for every future session in this project.

What actually makes that stick?
options: Nothing extra is required — statements like this one are remembered automatically across all future sessions
Putting the command in a comment at the top of the main migration file
Adding it to the project's CLAUDE.md — via the # shortcut or /memory — so every future session loads it
Repeating the instruction at the start of each new session
answer: Adding it to the project's CLAUDE.md — via the # shortcut or /memory — so every future session loads it
explanation:
This question tests persistence of project knowledge, and specifically that durable instructions must be written to a memory file rather than stated in conversation.

Sessions do not inherit conversations
Everything said in a session lives in that session's context and ends with it. A new session starts from its configured memory files and the project state — not from what someone told a previous session, however emphatically. So "remember that" spoken mid-conversation reliably lasts exactly until the conversation closes.

Where it should go, and how
CLAUDE.md is the project's memory file: loaded at the start of every session in the project, committed to version control, and therefore shared with the whole team. Claude Code provides two conveniences for exactly this moment — the # shortcut, which adds a line to a memory file without leaving the conversation, and /memory, which opens the memory files for editing. Either turns a passing remark into standing project knowledge with a single action. /context afterwards confirms which memory files actually loaded, if she wants to verify.

Why the other options are incorrect
Conversational statements are not automatically retained across sessions. Believing they are produces exactly the surprise where a "remembered" rule quietly stops applying, which is worse than knowing it was never persisted.

A comment at the top of a migration file reaches a human who opens that file. Sessions load memory files, not arbitrary source comments, so the instruction remains invisible at session start.

Re-stating the rule every session makes the developer the memory system — a manual ritual that fails whenever she forgets or a teammate does not know to perform it. That is precisely the job the memory file exists to do.

Key Takeaway
Durable project instructions belong in CLAUDE.md — add them with # or /memory. Conversations end; memory files load every session and travel with the repo.

Which TWO statements are true? (Select TWO.)
options: A user-level CLAUDE.md in ~/.claude applies across all of that user's projects
A project's CLAUDE.md is committed to the repository and shared with the team
CLAUDE.local.md is committed to the repository by default
Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files all load in full at session start
The user-level file overrides the project file, suppressing its contents

A project's CLAUDE.md is committed to the repository and shared with the team

This question tests the memory hierarchy's scope semantics, and specifically which file reaches whom.

User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is personal and global. — It follows the developer into every project they open, which makes it the correct home for individual working preferences that have nothing to do with any particular repository. It is not shared through version control.

Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load on demand, when Claude works with files in that directory. Conditional loading is their entire purpose; loading them all at start would eliminate the benefit.

The levels combine rather than override. User-level and project-level content both apply to a session, which is what allows personal preferences and team standards to coexist without one silently suppressing the other.

User-level memory is personal and applies to all projects; project memory is committed and shared with the team. The levels combine — they do not override one another.

question:
A ports-operations team built a /handover slash command for shift handovers, meant to be used as "/handover 42A" with the shift id. In practice the command runs but ignores whatever id the operator types — the generated summary never mentions the shift, and the command's body text never references the typed value anywhere.

What is missing?
options: A separate command per shift, such as /handover-42A, so the id is part of the name
A $ARGUMENTS (or $1) reference in the body where the shift id should flow in
An argument-hint entry in the command's frontmatter so the id is captured
An instruction telling operators to send the shift id as a second message after the command
answer: A $ARGUMENTS (or $1) reference in the body where the shift id should flow in
explanation:
This question tests slash-command argument passing, and specifically that typed arguments reach the prompt only through an explicit placeholder.

How a slash command expands
A command file's body is a prompt template. When the operator types /handover 42A, the text after the command name is made available to that template as $ARGUMENTS (all of it) or positionally as $1, $2, and so on. Expansion is a substitution: wherever a placeholder appears in the body, the typed value is inserted. Where no placeholder appears, nothing is inserted — the body expands to the identical static text on every invocation, which is exactly the reported behavior.

The fix
Reference the placeholder where the value belongs: "Generate the handover summary for shift $ARGUMENTS…". The mechanism is deterministic — the value lands in the prompt every time, in the right position, with no reliance on the model inferring a connection.

Why the other options are incorrect
A command per shift replaces one placeholder with an unbounded set of static commands. It breaks the day a new shift is added, clutters the command list, and still provides no general way to pass any value.

argument-hint is a discoverability field — it shows users what to type after the command name during autocomplete. It does not pipe the typed value into the body, so a hint without a placeholder produces a well-documented ignored argument.

Sending the id in a follow-up message abandons the argument mechanism and relies on conversational context to associate the value with the earlier command. That is unreliable and unnecessary when the placeholder does it deterministically.

Key Takeaway
Slash-command arguments arrive via $ARGUMENTS or $1. If the body never references a placeholder, the typed value is silently discarded.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: slash commands → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: skills (frontmatter, argument-hint) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: interactive mode → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/interactive-mode
option_feedback: A command per shift multiplies static commands to avoid one placeholder — unworkable the day shifts change, and still no general way to pass a value.

Slash-command arguments reach the prompt through placeholders: the text typed after the command is available as $ARGUMENTS (or positionally as $1), and the body must reference it where the value belongs — "Generate the handover summary for shift $ARGUMENTS…". Without a placeholder, the typed id has nowhere to land and the command's expanded prompt is the same static text every time, which is exactly the observed behavior.
argument-hint is discoverability — it shows users what to type after the command. It does not pipe the value into the body; a hint plus no placeholder is a well-documented ignored argument.
A second message abandons the argument mechanism and hopes conversational context connects the id to the earlier command — unreliable, and unnecessary when the placeholder does it deterministically.

question:
A records-bureau developer is building a new filing-checklist skill and iterating rapidly — a dozen revisions a day, most of them broken mid-thought. She has been committing each tweak to the repo's .claude/skills directory, and teammates keep invoking half-finished versions and reporting bugs that are just work in progress.

What is the right development flow?
options: Develop in personal ~/.claude/skills until stable, then move into the project's committed skills
Keep committing to the project but announce in chat that the skill is not ready for use
Keep it in the project but add "EXPERIMENTAL — DO NOT USE" to the skill's description
Develop on a long-lived git branch, merging the skill's directory once it finally stabilizes
answer: Develop in personal ~/.claude/skills until stable, then move into the project's committed skills
explanation:
This question tests skill scopes as a development lifecycle, and specifically that personal scope is the isolation boundary for work in progress.

What each scope actually means
A skill in ~/.claude/skills/ is personal: it is live in that developer's own sessions and invisible to everyone else. A skill in the project's .claude/skills/ directory is committed and shared: every teammate who pulls receives it, and — importantly — Claude may auto-invoke it based on its description, without anyone typing its name. That second property is what makes committing broken drafts so disruptive: teammates do not have to choose to run the half-finished skill for it to affect their sessions.

The lifecycle the scopes describe
Develop in personal scope, where a dozen broken revisions a day cost nothing and iteration is immediate — the skill is genuinely live in her sessions the whole time, so she is testing the real thing. When it stabilizes, promote it: copy into the project's skills directory and make one clean commit. Teammates encounter the skill exactly once, in a working state. The scopes were designed to support this progression.

Why the other options are incorrect
A chat announcement does not change what is installed. The skill remains present and invocable for everyone, and auto-invocation by description proceeds regardless of what was said in a channel.

An "EXPERIMENTAL" warning in the description rides on a skill that still loads, still matches, and still runs. Worse, the description is the selection signal — filling it with a warning instead of an accurate account of the skill's purpose degrades selection for everyone.

A long-lived branch does hide the work in progress, but it forces the iteration loop through branch switches and prevents her own everyday sessions from using the skill naturally. Personal scope gives the same isolation with none of that ceremony.

Key Takeaway
Iterate on skills in ~/.claude/skills/, then promote to the project's .claude/skills/ when stable. Committed skills are live for everyone and can be auto-invoked.

-

-

option_feedback: Skill scopes give development a natural lifecycle: personal scope is invisible to everyone else, so a dozen broken revisions a day bother no one — she iterates at full speed with the skill live in her own sessions. When it stabilizes, promotion is a copy into the project's skills directory and one clean commit. Teammates meet the skill exactly once: finished.

question:
A coffee-chain platform's .claude/rules directory contains one 500-line file with no paths frontmatter, mixing SQL standards, React conventions, API-handler rules, and infrastructure policies. Every session loads all 500 lines; the file is also a merge-conflict hotspot, since every team edits the same file.

What is the right structure?
options: Keep the single 500-line file but add a detailed table of contents so the model navigates it better
Move the whole file's content into CLAUDE.md, where shared standards belong
Keep one file but add a paths list combining all four teams' globs at the top of it
Per-concern rule files, each with paths scoped to its file types
answer: Per-concern rule files, each with paths scoped to its file types
explanation:
This question tests .claude/rules/ organization, and specifically that path scoping only pays off once rules are split by concern.

Two properties, both defeated by one file
Rules files support a paths frontmatter field listing globs; a rule so scoped loads only when Claude reads or edits files matching those patterns. Rules without paths load unconditionally, with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md. The 500-line file has no paths, so every session in the repository loads SQL standards, React conventions, API-handler rules and infrastructure policy regardless of what it is doing. Separately, one file with four owners is a structural merge-conflict generator — the file's boundaries do not match the teams' boundaries.

Why splitting is the enabling move
Per-concern files — sql.md scoped to SQL globs, react.md scoped to component globs, and so on — fix both problems with the same change. Loading becomes conditional and precise: a React session loads React conventions and nothing else. Ownership becomes clean: each team edits its own file, and edits to unrelated concerns cannot collide. The paths field is the scoping mechanism; the split is what makes the mechanism expressible at all, because a single file can only have one scope.

Why the other options are incorrect
A table of contents helps navigate content that has already loaded. All 500 lines still enter every session's context, and four teams still edit one file — neither symptom is touched.

CLAUDE.md loads unconditionally by design. Moving the content there makes the everything-everywhere behavior permanent and official, and relocates the merge hotspot rather than removing it.

A combined glob list scopes the file to the union of all four teams' file types, so nearly every session matches something and the full 500 lines keep loading almost everywhere. The four teams also still collide in one file.

Key Takeaway
Split rules by concern, one file per topic, each with paths scoped to its file types. Scoping needs separate files; a single mega-file can only have one scope and one owner.

-

-

CLAUDE.md is unconditionally loaded — the move makes the everything-everywhere problem permanent and official, and the merge hotspot moves with it.

A combined glob list scopes the file to the union of all four teams' file types — nearly every session still matches something in it, so the whole 500 lines keep loading almost everywhere, and the four teams still collide in one file.

question:
A museum consortium's compliance office requires that the upcoming vendor-codebase assessment be demonstrably non-modifying: the report must be able to state that the analysis sessions could not have changed the code.

Which setup supports that claim?
options: Instruct the agent that the engagement is read-only and keep transcripts as the evidence
Run normally, then attach a git diff showing the tree unchanged after the assessment
Plan/read-only permission mode, making modification capability absent by configuration
Run the assessment against a disposable copy of the repository
answer: Plan/read-only permission mode, making modification capability absent by configuration
explanation:
This question tests permission modes as a compliance control, and specifically the difference between a capability guarantee and a behavioral observation.

Read the compliance wording carefully
The report must state that the sessions could not have changed the code. That is a claim about capability — what was possible — not about conduct, what happened to occur. Evidence of good behavior, however complete, never establishes impossibility; it establishes that nothing bad was observed. Only configuration that removes the capability supports the stronger claim.

Why plan/read-only mode satisfies it
Plan mode is a read-only operating mode: the session can read files and run read-only commands, while edits and source-changing execution are blocked until a plan is approved. Running the assessment in that mode makes modification structurally unavailable, so the report can cite the mode itself as the control. No reliance on instruction adherence, no reliance on the agent's discipline, and the claim survives the auditor's obvious follow-up — what if it had tried?

Why the other options are incorrect
Instructions plus transcripts document that modification was discouraged and appears not to have occurred. Prompt instructions carry a non-zero failure rate, and "was told not to, and seems not to have" is exactly the weaker claim the compliance wording rules out.

A clean git diff shows the tree ended unchanged. It cannot demonstrate that change was impossible, and it misses anything modified and reverted during the assessment. That is detection evidence, not capability evidence.

A disposable copy protects the production repository while conceding the capability question entirely — on the copy, the sessions could modify freely. The required sentence still cannot be written, and the assessment now runs against a clone that may drift from the real thing.

Key Takeaway
"Could not have" is a claim about capability, so it needs a configuration control. Read-only permission mode removes the ability; instructions and after-the-fact diffs only describe behavior.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: permission modes → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: permissions → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: settings → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: hooks reference → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks
option_feedback: Instructions plus transcripts document that modification was discouraged and apparently avoided — "was told not to and seems not to have" is precisely the weaker claim the compliance wording rules out.
A clean diff shows the tree ended unchanged — it cannot show changes were impossible, and it misses anything modified and reverted mid-assessment. Detection evidence, not capability evidence.

The claim to be defended is "could not have," which is a statement about capability, not behavior — and only configuration speaks to capability. Sessions run in plan/read-only permission mode lack the ability to modify, so the report cites the mode as a structural property: no discipline, memory, or good behavior involved. That is the difference between an assurance and an observation.
A disposable copy protects the real repository while conceding the capability question entirely — on the copy, the sessions could modify freely, so the required sentence still cannot be written.

question:
A developer new to Claude Code is about to try plan mode on a rental-fleet codebase and asks a teammate: "If I enter plan mode, is it going to start changing my files while it plans?"

What is the accurate answer?
options: It may make some small changes while it plans, but everything it does is fully reversible afterward
No — it investigates and proposes; edits happen only after the plan is approved
It changes only test files and scratch files during planning, never source files
It depends on which model the session is running
answer: No — it investigates and proposes; edits happen only after the plan is approved
explanation:
This question tests the plan-mode contract, and specifically that the planning phase is non-modifying and approval is the gate.

How the two phases divide
Plan mode splits work into investigate-then-execute. During planning, the session reads files and runs read-only commands to understand the problem, and produces a proposed plan. Edits stay blocked throughout. Execution — and therefore any file change — begins only after a human approves the plan. The value of the mode is precisely that separation: the developer gets to see and shape the approach before anything is touched, which is why it earns its overhead on multi-file or uncertain-blast-radius work.

Why the newcomer's worry is well-founded but unnecessary
It is a reasonable thing to ask, because "let it explore my codebase" sounds like exposure. The accurate reassurance is unqualified: no changes during planning, approval required before any occur.

Why the other options are incorrect
"Small changes, all reversible" understates the guarantee and misstates it. The planning phase makes no modifications at all, which is stronger, simpler, and easier to rely on than a promise about reversibility.

No file class is exempt. Test files and scratch files are files, and the read-only phase does not carve out categories — a carve-out would make the guarantee conditional on classification the developer would have to verify.

The mode's semantics belong to the mode, not to the model. Planning is non-modifying regardless of which model the session runs; permission behavior is configuration, not a model capability.

Key Takeaway
Plan mode investigates and proposes without modifying anything. Edits begin only after the plan is approved.

-

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: best practices → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: interactive mode → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/interactive-mode
option_feedback: "Small but reversible" misstates the contract — the planning phase makes no changes at all, which is a stronger and simpler guarantee than reversibility.

Plan mode is the read-only half of a two-phase workflow: the session explores and reads, then presents a plan; nothing is modified while planning, and edits begin only once the human approves the plan for execution. The gate between proposal and change is the mode's entire point.
