question:
A streaming-radio support agent's prompt is patched reactively: each notable complaint triggers a same-day wording tweak by whoever is on rotation. Two of the last five hotfixes regressed other behaviors, and nobody can say which of the 30 accumulated tweaks still matter.

What should replace this process?
options: Periodic refinement: cluster failures weekly, target changes per cluster, validate before deploying
The same reactive hotfixes, but applied within the hour instead of the same day
A quarterly ground-up prompt rewrite incorporating everything learned since the previous rewrite
A freeze on prompt changes, since the recent regressions show change itself is the risk
answer: Periodic refinement: cluster failures weekly, target changes per cluster, validate before deploying
explanation:
This question tests prompt-refinement process, and specifically that iteration needs evidence, batching, and a regression check.

Why reactive patching degrades over time
Each hotfix is fitted to a single anecdote, applied under time pressure, by a different person each rotation, with no record of intent and no validation. Three failures compound. Signal: a single complaint cannot distinguish a systematic weakness from noise, so the prompt accumulates fixes for problems that may not exist. Regression: an untested wording change can break behaviors nobody thought to check, which is how two of five fixes caused new failures. Legibility: thirty undocumented tweaks become a prompt nobody can reason about, so every subsequent change is made blind.

What the disciplined loop replaces it with
Cluster the week's failures and you can see which problems are patterns worth an intervention. Target changes at clusters rather than instances, so each edit addresses a real weakness with a stated purpose. Validate against a set of known-good behaviors before deploying, which is the step that catches cross-regressions while they are still cheap. The cadence also removes the pressure that makes reactive edits careless.

Why the other options are incorrect
Hourly hotfixes intensify every pathology — less consideration per change, the same anecdote-driven targeting, the same absent regression check, at a higher rate. Speed is not the missing ingredient.

Quarterly ground-up rewrites let failures accumulate for months and then stake the agent's entire behavior on one enormous change that is nearly impossible to validate. Maximum batch size is maximum risk.

A freeze indicts change in general when the evidence indicts unvalidated change. It locks in every current failure permanently to avoid a risk that a test set manages directly.

Key Takeaway
Refine on a cadence: cluster failures to find patterns, target changes at clusters, and validate against known-good behaviors before deploying.

question:
A car-rental platform developer has drifted into a habit: when the agent proposes a diff, he accepts without reading — "it usually works." This week a quietly wrong rate-rounding change shipped to production inside an otherwise good refactor.

What is the discipline that prevents this?
options: Rely on CI to catch bad changes — automated checks, after all, are more thorough than tired human eyes
Have the agent re-examine its own diff and confirm correctness before he accepts
Accept as now, but tag agent-authored commits so problems can be traced during audits later
Read the diff before accepting — and keep iterations small enough that reading them stays practical
answer: Read the diff before accepting — and keep iterations small enough that reading them stays practical
explanation:
This question tests the human review gate in agent-assisted development, and specifically that reviewing diffs and keeping iterations small are one discipline, not two.

What the accept step is
In an agent iteration loop, the moment a developer accepts a diff is the single point where human judgment enters before the change becomes part of the codebase. The loop is designed around that gate — it is what makes the arrangement supervised. Accepting without reading does not weaken the gate; it removes it, leaving an agent with effective unreviewed commit access to production code.

Why the two halves depend on each other
"Read every diff" fails on its own if diffs are large, because reading a 600-line change carefully is an afternoon's work and nobody sustains it — the habit of skimming grows out of iterations that are too big to review. Keeping each iteration small is what makes the review affordable, and affordable review is what makes it habitual. The rate-rounding change is the characteristic failure: subtly wrong, embedded in a larger correct refactor, invisible to a skim and obvious to a reader.

Why the other options are incorrect
CI verifies what the tests encode. This defect shipped because no test covered that rounding path — which is typical of subtle logic errors, since untested behavior is exactly where they hide. Human review is the layer that catches what the suite does not yet know to check.

Asking the agent to re-examine its own diff re-runs the reasoning that produced the error, with the same premises. Self-review by the author is the weakest form of review, and it leaves the human gate exactly as unattended as before.

Tagging agent-authored commits improves the archaeology after damage has shipped. The question is about the discipline that prevents shipping, and traceability is not prevention.

Key Takeaway
Read every diff before accepting, and keep iterations small enough that reading stays practical. Small steps exist so the human gate remains affordable.

Skipping it converts supervised iteration into unsupervised commit access. question:
A port-logistics nightly review job prints its findings to the CI console and exits. Result: developers never see the findings unless they open old job logs — none do — and the team cannot answer whether finding volume is trending up or down across months.

Which TWO output changes fix this? (Select TWO.)
options: Post each run's findings as comments on the relevant pull request, where developers already work
Email the complete session transcript to the engineering mailing list nightly
Print a summary block at the top of the console log instead of the bottom
Persist each run's findings as a structured artifact, enabling trend analysis across runs
Capture the console output as a screenshot and post it to the team wiki
answer: Post each run's findings as comments on the relevant pull request, where developers already work
Persist each run's findings as a structured artifact, enabling trend analysis across runs
explanation:
This question tests CI output design, and specifically that the two named failures require two different delivery channels.

The two failures, two channels

-
Findings nobody reads — Console output in a completed CI job is technically available and practically invisible; it requires a developer to know a finding exists, navigate to the job, and open the log, which is why none do. The fix is delivery to where the work already happens: comments on the pull request. The finding appears in front of the person who wrote the code, on the change it concerns, at the moment fixing it is cheapest.

-
No trend visibility — "Is finding volume trending up or down across months?" is a question about data, and log text is not data. Persisting each run's findings as a structured artifact — one record per run, with categories, counts, and file references — turns months of runs into an analyzable series: volume by category, recurring offenders, and whether a criteria change actually reduced noise.

One channel serves the developer today; the other serves the team's understanding over time. Neither substitutes for the other.

A nightly full-transcript email is the console log relocated into inboxes: unstructured, unread, untrended, and now generating delete-on-sight fatigue that will spread to messages that matter.

Moving the summary to the top of a log nobody opens optimizes the interior of an unvisited room. Placement cannot fix a channel problem.

Screenshots are the least structured persistence available — unsearchable, unparseable, and useless for precisely the trend questions the team wants answered.

Deliver findings where developers work (PR comments) and persist them as structured artifacts for trend analysis. Visibility and analyzability are separate problems with separate solutions.

question:
A staffing-agency CI review job specifies no versions: the workflow tracks the action's latest release, and the job inherits whatever default model that ships. One morning the job's output format had shifted overnight; the result parser broke, and merges were blocked until someone diagnosed it.

What is the right configuration practice?
options: Wrap the result parsing in retries, with fallbacks covering several possible output formats
Loosen the parser to accept any output shape the job might produce
Pin action and model versions; upgrade deliberately with a validation run
Run the job twice nightly and alert when the two outputs disagree
answer: Pin action and model versions; upgrade deliberately with a validation run
explanation:
This question tests CI configuration hygiene, and specifically that pinned versions make pipeline behavior a function of your own repository.

What floating versions actually delegate
A workflow tracking "latest" hands a third party the ability to change your pipeline's behavior at a time of their choosing, with no notice and no review. The overnight output-format shift was not an unusual event; it is the ordinary consequence of that arrangement, and the same exposure covers every other change a release might contain — new defaults, changed flags, different model behavior. Merges being blocked while someone diagnoses it is the cost of learning about a dependency change by outage.

What pinning changes
Pin the action version and the model, and every run's behavior becomes reproducible from your repository's own contents. Upgrades still happen — nobody is arguing for staleness — but they happen as a deliberate change: bump the pin in a branch, run a validation job, confirm the output still parses and the findings still look right, then merge. Format shifts are caught in that validation run rather than in the morning's blocked merges. Overnight surprises become scheduled migrations.

Why the other options are incorrect
Multi-format fallback parsing hardens one symptom of the exposure while leaving the exposure itself intact. Any change that is not a parse-shape change — a behavioral difference, a new default — still arrives unannounced, and the parser grows a maintenance burden of its own.

A parser that accepts any shape validates nothing. Malformed or truncated results now flow through as readily as changed ones, converting a loud, diagnosable failure into silent wrong data downstream.

Running twice nightly doubles the cost to detect some drift after it has already landed. Two runs on the same floated versions will usually agree with each other while both differ from yesterday — so the comparison misses exactly the change it was meant to catch.

Key Takeaway
Pin action and model versions in CI, and upgrade deliberately behind a validation run. Unpinned dependencies let someone else's release schedule deploy into your pipeline.

-

-

option_feedback: Multi-format fallback parsing hardens one symptom while the root exposure — unpinned dependencies changing under the job — remains for every failure mode that isn't a parse shift.
A parser loose enough to accept anything validates nothing — malformed results flow through as easily as changed ones, trading a loud failure for silent wrong data.

A CI job is production automation, and production automation runs on pinned dependencies for exactly the reason the outage demonstrated: floating versions let third-party release schedules deploy changes into your pipeline at random times. Pinning makes every run's behavior a function of your own repository; upgrades still happen — deliberately, on the team's schedule, with a validation run to catch format shifts before they block merges. Overnight surprises become scheduled migrations.

question:
A fashion-commerce CI reviewer flags the team's registry pattern — a deliberate architectural choice — as a "global state risk" nearly every week. Developers dismiss it every time; the dismissals now number forty, and trust in the reviewer's other findings is eroding.

What should the team do?
options: Codify the pattern as a documented exception — approved where intentional, rationale stated
Add a dismissal hotkey so recurring findings cost developers less time to wave away
Remove the global-state category from the criteria, and the finding cannot recur
Expect the reviewer to learn from the accumulating dismissals without any criteria change
answer: Codify the pattern as a documented exception — approved where intentional, rationale stated
explanation:
This question tests review-criteria maintenance, and specifically that repeated justified dismissals are the signal to amend the criteria.

What forty dismissals mean
The reviewer is not malfunctioning; it is applying a sound general rule — global state is a risk — to a codebase where one specific instance of that pattern is a deliberate architectural decision. The rule is right in general and wrong about this one case, and the place where that distinction belongs is the criteria. Forty dismissals are forty pieces of evidence that the criteria are incomplete, and nothing in the loop acts on that evidence unless the team writes it down.

Why the trust erosion is the real damage
A reviewer with a reliably wrong weekly finding trains its readers to dismiss quickly, and quick dismissal generalizes to findings that deserve attention. That is why "it costs us thirty seconds a week" understates the cost: the reviewer's credibility is the asset being spent. Documenting the registry pattern as an approved exception — with the rationale, which gives the exception boundaries — removes the false positive at its source while preserving detection of accidental global state that falls outside the documented pattern.

Why the other options are incorrect
A dismissal hotkey optimizes the cost of noise rather than removing the noise. Forty dismissals become forty faster dismissals, and the erosion of trust continues on exactly the same schedule.

Deleting the global-state category trades a weekly false positive for blindness to real defects of that kind. The category is valuable; only its application to one documented pattern is wrong, and the fix should be equally precise.

Dismissals are not a feedback channel into the reviewer. Each run applies the criteria as written, so no volume of dismissals changes future behavior until the team amends the criteria themselves.

Key Takeaway
Encode deliberate architectural exceptions in the review criteria, with rationale. Recurring justified dismissals mean the criteria need amending — and unamended false positives spend the reviewer's credibility.

question:
A port authority's manifest-review agent flagged 40 manifests last week; humans confirmed 4 as real problems. A manager asks which quality metric this describes and what the tuning direction should be.

What is the answer?
options: Recall is failing — the criteria should be loosened so more real cases get caught
Precision — 10% of flags are real; tighten and specify the criteria
Throughput is failing — the pipeline needs more compute for review
Calibration is failing — the confidence scores, not the criteria, need rescaling
answer: Precision — 10% of flags are real; tighten and specify the criteria
explanation:
This question tests evaluation vocabulary, and specifically that a flagged-versus-confirmed ratio measures precision and points to a specific tuning direction.

Reading the numbers
Precision is the share of positive predictions that turn out to be real: 4 confirmed out of 40 flagged is 10%. Nine of every ten flags consume reviewer attention for nothing, which is a precision failure — the criteria match cases they should not. The tuning direction follows from the definition: tighten and specify the criteria so fewer non-problems qualify.

What this measurement cannot tell you
Recall — the share of real problems that got flagged — asks a different question, one about the manifests that were not flagged. Answering it requires ground truth on unflagged items, which nobody in this scenario has collected. That distinction matters practically: precision and recall usually trade against each other, so a team that tightens criteria should expect to check whether real cases are now being missed. But nothing in "40 flagged, 4 confirmed" speaks to that yet.

Why the other options are incorrect
Loosening criteria is the exact opposite of the indicated direction. It would multiply the noise being measured, and the 4-of-40 figure contains no evidence of missed problems in the first place.

Throughput is a capacity concept. The pipeline produced its 40 flags without difficulty — the flags were mostly wrong, which no amount of compute repairs.

Calibration concerns whether stated confidence tracks actual correctness. No confidence scores appear in this measurement at all; the finding is about the flags themselves.

Key Takeaway
Flags confirmed ÷ flags raised = precision. Low precision means tighten and specify the criteria; recall is a separate question needing ground truth on what was not flagged.

question:
A wind-farm document pipeline's few-shot examples were drafted by an engineer who left "NOTE: verify this" comments trailing two of the example outputs. In production, 12% of extractions now end with a fabricated NOTE line, which breaks the downstream parser.

What is the fix?
options: Add a prompt instruction forbidding notes and commentary in outputs
Add a post-processing step that strips trailing NOTE lines from outputs
Add several more clean examples while leaving the two annotated ones in place for coverage
Clean the examples — models imitate everything shown, quirks included
answer: Clean the examples — models imitate everything shown, quirks included
explanation:
This question tests few-shot example hygiene, and specifically that a model imitates everything an example output contains, including artifacts nobody meant to teach.

Why the NOTE lines reproduce
A few-shot example is a demonstration of a complete desired output. The model has no channel for distinguishing "this part is the answer" from "this part is an editorial comment the author left behind" — both are simply present in the shown output. Two of five examples ending in NOTE: verify this therefore assert that outputs sometimes end that way, and roughly 12% reproduction is the model faithfully honoring a pattern it was shown 40% of the time, moderated by everything else in the prompt pulling the other direction.

Why cleaning is the structural fix
The rule that follows is simple and general: an example output must be exactly what a correct production output should look like — no annotations, no placeholders, no editorial residue. Everything in a demonstration is being taught, whether or not the author intended it. Cleaning the two examples removes the source of the behavior rather than suppressing its consequences.

Why the other options are incorrect
A prohibition in the prompt contradicts what the demonstrations show. Instruction-versus-example conflict is resolved inconsistently by the model, which produces exactly the kind of intermittent rate the team is seeing — and leaves the misleading examples in place for every future reader.

A downstream stripper launders the symptom while the examples continue teaching the quirk. It also generalizes badly: the next imitation artifact — a different tag, a sign-off, a stray blank line — needs its own stripper, and each one is discovered by a production break.

Adding clean examples dilutes the imitation rate without removing its source. Two annotated demonstrations still assert that notes belong, and the model now has contradictory evidence to be inconsistent about.

Key Takeaway
Clean your examples. Whatever appears in a demonstration output is being taught — comments, placeholders, and formatting quirks included.

question:
A telehealth admin team's intake-form extraction runs on OCR text. Its five examples were written by hand: tidy field-and-value pairs in a consistent order. Real OCR output is messier — transcription noise, fields split across lines, values from margin annotations landing mid-record. Accuracy on the tidy minority is fine; the error rate concentrates entirely on the messy majority.

What should change about the examples?
options: Keep the invented examples but describe the expected transcription messiness thoroughly in the prompt
Preprocess all incoming OCR text until it resembles the tidy examples
Replace them with redacted real OCR output, so examples carry the noise the model must handle
Lower the confidence threshold so messy forms route to human review
answer: Replace them with redacted real OCR output, so examples carry the noise the model must handle
explanation:
This question tests example–input distribution alignment, and specifically that examples must be drawn from the data the pipeline actually receives.

The mismatch that explains the error pattern
Hand-written examples showed tidy field-and-value pairs in consistent order. Real traffic is noisy OCR text with transcription errors, fields split across lines, and margin annotations landing mid-record. The examples therefore demonstrate a task the pipeline almost never faces, and the model has never once been shown what correct extraction through noise looks like. The error rate concentrating entirely on the messy majority is not a coincidence — it is the exact input class the examples do not cover.

Why real (redacted) examples are the fix
Replacing the invented examples with redacted real OCR output aligns the demonstrated distribution with the production distribution. The examples now carry the noise — the split fields, the stray margin values — and their outputs demonstrate the resolution: which fragment belongs to which field, what to do with a value that landed out of place. That is teaching by demonstration on the cases that matter, which is what few-shot examples are for.

Why the other options are incorrect
Describing messiness in prose is secondhand relative to showing it. The examples still demonstrate tidy extraction, so the model still lacks a worked instance of handling a split field — and prose about noise does not teach the handling of noise.

Preprocessing helps at the margin but cannot reconstruct field boundaries the OCR pass destroyed. It also inverts the effort: building a text-repair pipeline to protect unrepresentative examples, when fixing the examples is the smaller and more direct change.

Routing messy forms to humans concedes the majority of the workload rather than teaching the model to handle it — a staffing policy substituting for an example fix.

Key Takeaway
Draw few-shot examples from real production inputs, including their noise. Examples define the task by demonstration, so they must demonstrate the task you actually have.

question:
A museum's catalog-extraction pipeline states field rules twice: once in prompt prose ("acquisition_date is the accession date, not the display date") and once in the schema's field descriptions. A recent edit updated the schema descriptions only; the prompt prose now contradicts them, and outputs have split between the two interpretations.

What is the right structure?
options: Keep both locations but update them together in the same commit from now on
Schema descriptions own field semantics; the prompt defers to them
Move all of the field semantics into the prompt prose and strip the schema down to bare types only
Add a line to the prompt stating that the schema wins wherever the two disagree
answer: Schema descriptions own field semantics; the prompt defers to them
explanation:
This question tests where field semantics belong, and specifically that duplicated authority produces divergence and split behavior.

One fact, two homes, two answers
acquisition_date had its meaning stated in prompt prose and in the schema's field description. That is fine only while the copies agree — and copies of a fact do not stay equal through edits. When the schema was updated alone, the model received two contradictory definitions in one request and resolved the conflict differently on different documents, which is what "outputs split between the two interpretations" describes. The defect is structural: nothing prevented the divergence, and nothing detected it.

Why the schema is the right single source
Per-field descriptions sit exactly where the model reads each field's definition at generation time, adjacent to the field's type and constraints. That proximity is why schema descriptions are the documented place to explain what a field means, what unit or format it takes, and where the value comes from. The prompt keeps task-level guidance — what document this is, what the overall job is — and defers on field semantics. With one home, there is nothing to fall out of sync.

Why the other options are incorrect
Same-commit discipline preserves the duplication and stakes correctness on a process holding forever. The current incident is precisely what the week that bet loses looks like, and it will recur.

This picks the wrong single source. Stripping the schema to bare types removes semantics from the artifact that carries field definitions to the model most directly, weakening extraction accuracy in order to strengthen prose.

A precedence rule ships the contradiction and asks the model to adjudicate at runtime. The prompt now contains statements known to be wrong plus a note about which wrong statements to disregard — extra tokens, extra ambiguity, same underlying defect.

Key Takeaway
Field semantics belong in schema field descriptions, and only there. Duplicated definitions diverge, and divergence produces split behavior.

question:
A regional bank's conversation summarizer emits one overall confidence score per summary. Policy routes any summary under 0.8 to full human re-review — currently 30% of volume — even when the doubt concerns a single field, such as the callback number, in an otherwise solid summary.

What schema change makes review effort proportionate?
options: Per-field confidence, each with a brief basis, so review can target the specific doubtful fields
Two overall scores instead of one — content confidence and format confidence
A tuned global threshold, lowered gradually until the re-review queue reaches a comfortably manageable size
No confidence fields at all, with every summary routed through full human review
answer: Per-field confidence, each with a brief basis, so review can target the specific doubtful fields
explanation:
This question tests confidence granularity, and specifically that review effort should be proportionate to where the doubt actually sits.

The mismatch between doubt and routing
A single overall score forces a single decision about a whole summary. When the model is unsure about one callback number in an otherwise sound document, that one uncertainty drags the entire summary below threshold and into full re-review — a reviewer re-reads everything to check one field. At 30% of volume, that is a large, structurally avoidable cost, and it is the direct consequence of a schema whose confidence granularity is coarser than its uncertainty.

What per-field confidence changes
Emit confidence per field, each with a brief basis — "callback number transcribed from voicemail audio," "balance read from the account API." Routing then operates at the same granularity as the doubt: the reviewer checks the one flagged field in seconds instead of re-reading the summary. The basis matters too, because it tells the reviewer what to look at rather than merely that something is uncertain. Field-level confidence, validated against labeled data per field, is also what makes selective automation defensible — some fields can be trusted at a given threshold while others cannot.

Why the other options are incorrect
Two coarse scores split the same bluntness in half. A low content score still cannot indicate which content, so the re-review remains wholesale.

Tuning a global threshold to queue size optimizes workload while abandoning the accuracy target. Summaries between the old and new thresholds ship unreviewed because the queue was long, not because they earned trust.

Reviewing everything is the maximally disproportionate response — it prices a doubtful-field problem at the cost of the entire automation, and discards the confidence signal that was working.

Key Takeaway
Emit confidence per field with a stated basis, so review targets the specific doubtful values instead of re-reading whole documents.

question:
A coffee-chain invoice pipeline extracts amounts into a schema where total is typed as a string. Outputs arrive as "1,240.50" — and the analytics job that sums totals keeps failing on the commas.

What is the right fix?
options: Keep the string type and parse the formatting downstream with carefully maintained per-locale rules
Instruct the model to write amounts without thousands separators
Add a second field holding the numeric form alongside the display string
Type the field as a number in the schema, so outputs are numeric values without formatting
answer: Type the field as a number in the schema, so outputs are numeric values without formatting
explanation:
This question tests schema type selection, and specifically that types are the cheapest and most reliable formatting constraint available.

The type is the rule
total holds a quantity, and quantities have a type. Declaring the field as a number means the output is a numeric value — no thousands separators, no currency symbol, no locale convention to interpret — and that constraint is enforced by the schema rather than requested in prose. Every downstream consumer receives arithmetic-ready data by construction, which is why the analytics job stops failing. Declared once, enforced automatically, and impossible to drift.

Why string typing created the bug
A string field invites string-shaped output, and "1,240.50" is a perfectly reasonable rendering of a total as text. The pipeline asked for text and got text; the mistake was upstream of the model, in the schema that described a number as prose.

Why the other options are incorrect
Downstream locale parsing re-derives numberhood from formatting, permanently. "1.240,50" and "1,240.50" are the same quantity under different conventions and different quantities under one — precisely the ambiguity a numeric type never permits to exist, and per-locale rules are a maintenance burden that grows with every new supplier.

An instruction is a soft constraint applied to something the type system settles hard. Some fraction of outputs will keep separators anyway, and the parser fails at exactly that rate — a probabilistic fix for a deterministic requirement.

A dual field stores the same value twice and invites the copies to disagree. It also leaves a string field in the schema for a future consumer to read by mistake, which is the original bug preserved as an option.

Key Takeaway
Type numeric fields as numbers in the schema. Types enforce format deterministically where instructions only request it.

question:
A records bureau's deed-extraction pipeline validates schema and plausibility, and both pass — yet a title-company audit found about 3% of critical values are not present anywhere in the source document: plausible, well-formed, invented. Confidence on these was high.

What check does the pipeline lack?
options: A stricter schema whose tighter types and patterns exclude the invented values
A second independent extraction of every document, adopting only those values where the two independent runs agree
A grounding pass confirming each critical value appears in — or derives from — the source, flagging the rest
A higher confidence threshold so uncertain extractions route to human review
answer: A grounding pass confirming each critical value appears in — or derives from — the source, flagging the rest
explanation:
This question tests validation layers, and specifically that intrinsic checks cannot detect fabrication — only grounding against the source can.

Why every existing check passed
Schema validation asks: is this value well-formed? Plausibility validation asks: is this value reasonable? Confidence asks: how sure is the model? All three examine the output in isolation, and a fabricated value can satisfy all three simultaneously — that is what makes fabrication dangerous rather than merely wrong. A hallucinated parcel number has a valid format, a believable range, and high confidence. The one property it lacks is presence in the document.

What a grounding pass adds
Grounding is the extrinsic check: for each critical value, confirm it appears in the source or derives from it. Names, parcel identifiers and dates should match the document text exactly or after normalization; derived figures should be recomputed from the values they came from. Anything that cannot be anchored gets flagged for review. This test is aimed precisely at the failure mode the audit found, because it checks the only attribute fabrications reliably fail.

Why the other options are incorrect
The audit explicitly says the invented values are well-formed and plausible. Tightening types and patterns constrains shape, and shape is not where these errors live — no pattern can detect that a correctly-shaped value has no origin.

Two runs of the same model on the same document produce correlated errors: the same ambiguous scan invites the same plausible invention twice. Agreement is therefore weak evidence, and the check doubles cost while still never consulting the source as ground truth.

The stem forecloses this directly — confidence on the fabricated values was high. Raising a threshold filters on a signal these particular errors do not carry, while pushing genuinely uncertain but correct extractions into review.

Key Takeaway
Add a grounding pass that anchors each critical value to the source document. Schema, plausibility and confidence checks all inspect the output alone, and fabrications pass all three.

question:
A telehealth billing pipeline routes doubtful extractions to human reviewers, who fix errors directly in the billing system and move on. The pipeline never changes: the same error class has recurred for five months, corrected by hand each time, invisible to the team that owns the prompt.

Which TWO changes close the loop? (Select TWO.)
options: A weekly all-hands meeting where the reviewers describe the errors they can remember fixing
Capture each correction as labeled data — document, model output, corrected value — as the reviewer fixes it
Require reviewers to write a short free-text note explaining every fix they make in the billing system
Switch the extraction to a different model, since this one has apparently stopped improving
Periodically mine corrections for patterns, driving prompt/example updates and growing the eval set
answer: Capture each correction as labeled data — document, model output, corrected value — as the reviewer fixes it
Periodically mine corrections for patterns, driving prompt/example updates and growing the eval set
explanation:
This question tests the human-in-the-loop feedback cycle, and specifically that it requires both capture and consumption.

The two halves of the loop

-
Capture: the correction is the label — Every fix a reviewer makes is a complete labeled example — the source document, the model's wrong output, and the correct value. That is the most valuable training and evaluation data the pipeline will ever produce, and it is being generated free, five months running, then discarded into the billing system where no one who owns the prompt can see it. Recording it structurally at the moment of correction costs the reviewer a click and preserves the whole signal.

-
Consumption: labels only matter if something reads them — Captured data sitting unexamined is an archive, not a loop. Mining corrections periodically turns individual fixes into visible patterns — the recurring error class becomes obvious in week two rather than month five — and those patterns drive two distinct outputs: targeted prompt and example updates that fix the problem, and a growing evaluation set built from real failures that proves the fix worked and catches its regression later.

Capture without consumption is storage; consumption without capture is guesswork.

Why the other options are incorrect
Verbal reports from memory lose exactly what labels preserve — the specific documents and values — and recalled anecdote frequency is a poor proxy for the real error distribution. The loudest error is not necessarily the most common.

Free-text notes are capture in its least usable form: unstructured prose about corrections, with no machine-readable before/after pair. It cannot be aggregated, cannot become an eval set, and adds friction to the reviewer's work for little return.

The model did not stop improving; nothing was ever feeding it. Switching models discards five months of latent signal and leaves the new model in the same closed-loop-less pipeline, where it will plateau identically.

Key Takeaway
Capture each human correction as structured labeled data, then mine it periodically to drive prompt updates and grow the eval set. A feedback loop needs both halves.

question:
A museum improved its catalog-extraction prompt substantially last month; current intake now runs through it. But two years of earlier records — about 400,000 documents — were extracted with the weak old prompt, and curators keep hitting their known defects. Nothing about the re-processing is urgent.

How should the backlog be handled?
options: Leave the old records as they are and fix defects individually as curators report them
Re-process the archive with the improved prompt as batch jobs — non-urgent bulk at the discount
Re-process the archive synchronously at a trickle, spreading the cost over several months
Re-process only the records that curators have explicitly flagged so far
answer: Re-process the archive with the improved prompt as batch jobs — non-urgent bulk at the discount
explanation:
This question tests batch-workload selection, and specifically that large, uniform, latency-tolerant work is exactly what the Message Batches API exists for.

Why this backlog is the textbook case
Three properties decide it. Volume: 400,000 documents is far too much to process interactively. Uniformity: every record runs the same improved prompt, so the work is homogeneous. Latency tolerance: the stem states nothing is urgent — no curator is blocked waiting on any individual record. Batch processing serves exactly that profile at roughly half the cost of standard requests, with most batches completing well inside their 24-hour window.

Practical shape of the job
Submit the archive as batch jobs chunked for operational control — batches are bounded (on the order of 100,000 requests or 256 MB each), so 400,000 documents becomes several submissions rather than one. Use a unique custom_id per request to correlate results back to records, since results are not guaranteed to return in input order, and retrieve results within the retention window. Current intake continues on the improved prompt undisturbed, and the archive converges to a single quality standard.

Why the other options are incorrect
Fixing defects as curators report them leaves 400,000 known-defective records in place indefinitely. Every future search, study and export inherits the old prompt's errors, paid down one discovery at a time, forever.

A synchronous trickle does identical work at full price, stretched over months. It pays a premium for latency the workload does not want and delays the quality convergence.

Re-processing only flagged records bounds the work by what curators happened to notice. The unflagged majority carries the same systematic defects — undiscovered is not the same as absent.

Key Takeaway
Large, uniform, non-urgent workloads belong in the Batch API: roughly 50% cheaper, chunked with custom_id correlation, with no impact on live traffic.

question:
A port-logistics nightly batch enriches shipping documents. A reliable upstream classifier already splits the load: about 90% are simple lookup-and-format records, 10% are multi-page reconciliations needing real reasoning. Today every request runs on the premium model, and the nightly cost is dominated by the simple 90%.

How should the batch be configured?
options: Route by class in one batch: simple records to a small model, hard ones to the capable model
Run everything on the small model, retrying on the premium model whatever visibly fails validation
Keep everything on the premium model, since batch discounts already control the cost
Split into two separately maintained pipelines, one per document class
answer: Route by class in one batch: simple records to a small model, hard ones to the capable model
explanation:
This question tests per-request model routing, and specifically that model choice is a property of the request, not of the pipeline.

The cost structure the stem hands you
A reliable upstream classifier has already done the hard part: it separates 90% simple lookup-and-format records from 10% multi-page reconciliations. The premium model's capability is genuinely needed for the reconciliations and adds nothing detectable on the simple ones — yet the simple ones dominate the bill precisely because they dominate the volume. That is overpayment concentrated exactly where the classifier already gives you a free routing signal.

Why one batch can carry both
Each request in a batch specifies its own model, so a single pipeline can run a mixed fleet. The classifier's label becomes a routing field: simple records ride the small model, reconciliations ride the capable one. Submission, monitoring, and result collection stay unified; only the model field varies per request. The dominant cost term disappears while quality is preserved where quality was actually being purchased.

Why the other options are incorrect
Small-model-with-retry assumes failures announce themselves. A hard reconciliation done badly but confidently produces no validation signal, so the 10% that needs capability receives it only when the error happens to be mechanically detectable — which is the least reliable subset of errors.

The batch discount applies to whatever you spend; 50% off premium pricing for trivial work is still substantial overpayment at 90% of volume. The stem locates the cost precisely there, and a discount does not change which model each record needs.

Two separate pipelines duplicate submission, polling, error handling and monitoring code to express what a per-request model field expresses in one line — twice the operational surface for the same routing outcome.

Key Takeaway
Route model choice per request inside one batch: cheap model for easy work, capable model for hard work. Match the model to the request, not to the pipeline.

question:
A staffing agency generates branded landing-page copy with an agent. Quality is high-variance: some drafts are excellent, others miss the brand voice entirely, and the current fix-it-in-rounds loop spends many iterations dragging weak drafts upward.

Which TWO practices exploit the variance instead of fighting it? (Select TWO.)
options: Iterate harder on the single draft, with more specific feedback each round
Generate ten variants per page by re-prompting each draft with the previous one as a seed
Generate two or three independent candidates per page, since high variance means independent draws differ meaningfully
Have an independent selector judge the candidates against the stated brand criteria and pick the strongest
Have the generator review its own candidates and submit the one it prefers
answer: Generate two or three independent candidates per page, since high variance means independent draws differ meaningfully
Have an independent selector judge the candidates against the stated brand criteria and pick the strongest
explanation:
This question tests best-of-N generation, and specifically that high output variance is a resource to sample from rather than a defect to iterate away.

The two working parts of best-of-N

-
Sampling: take another draw instead of repairing this one — When drafts vary from excellent to off-brand, the distribution has good outputs in it — the current process just happens to land on a weak one and then spends several corrective rounds dragging it upward. Generating two or three independent candidates usually surfaces a draft near the top of that distribution in a single parallel step. Independence is what makes this work: each draw explores the space fresh.

-
Selection: judge against criteria, independently — Sampling alone produces three drafts and no decision. The gain is realized by an independent selection pass that scores candidates against the stated brand-voice criteria and picks the strongest. Separating generation from judgment is the point — the selector evaluates against an explicit standard rather than against the generator's own taste.

Sample the distribution, then select against criteria: neither delivers without the other.

Why the other options are incorrect
Iterating a weak draft upward is the expensive path the variance makes unnecessary. Each round fights the particular draw that was landed on, when another draw costs one generation.

Seeding each variant from the previous draft makes the draws dependent. Every variant inherits the first one's framing and blind spots, so ten seeded variants explore far less of the distribution than three independent generations — it converts the property that makes best-of-N valuable into its opposite.

Self-selection reuses the taste that produced the misses. The generator's preference correlates with its own biases, which is exactly what an independent selector judging against stated criteria exists to break.

Key Takeaway
Generate a few independent candidates and have a separate selector judge them against explicit criteria. Independence in generation, independence in selection.

question:
A regional bank's support conversations often run past forty turns, and the history carries every tool result in full — including early account lookups long since superseded by later ones. Per-turn cost climbs steadily, and the model has twice cited stale balance figures from old results instead of the current ones.

How should the application manage the history?
options: Ask the model each turn to disregard any outdated tool results it notices
Drop the oldest half of the conversation whenever the cost and latency cross a threshold
Keep tool results out of the history entirely, storing them in application logs instead
Curate: prune superseded tool results, keep decisions, commitments, and the current facts
answer: Curate: prune superseded tool results, keep decisions, commitments, and the current facts
explanation:
This question tests conversation-history curation, and specifically that superseded tool results are both a cost and a correctness hazard.

Two problems from one cause
The full history carries every account lookup ever performed, including balances that later lookups replaced. Because every request re-sends the whole conversation, those obsolete results are re-billed on every turn — the steady cost climb. And because they are present, well-formed and plausible, they compete with the current figure for the model's attention — the twice-observed stale citations. One accumulation, two failure modes.

Curation, not truncation
The application controls exactly what it sends, so it can prune deliberately: drop or summarize tool results that a later call has superseded, while keeping what the conversation still depends on — the customer's verified identity, decisions made, commitments given, and the current state of every fact. That is a semantic operation, informed by knowing which lookups replaced which. It shrinks the request and removes the stale-data hazard in the same pass. Where progressive summarization is used instead, precise values like balances and dates should be re-injected as a persistent facts block, because summaries lose exactly those details.

Why the other options are incorrect
Asking the model to disregard outdated results sets an instruction against present, plausible data — the same contest it has already lost twice. The remedy is the data's absence, not advice about its presence.

Dropping the oldest half cuts by position rather than relevance. Early turns commonly hold identity verification and the original request — the material a support conversation can least afford to lose — while recent superseded lookups survive.

Removing tool results entirely goes too far: the model cannot cite a current balance it never received. The correct distinction is superseded versus current, not tool results versus everything else.

Key Takeaway
Curate long histories: prune superseded tool results, keep decisions, commitments and current facts. Stale context costs tokens and competes with the truth.

Wholesale truncation cuts by position, not by relevance — early turns often hold identity verification and the original request, precisely what the conversation cannot lose.
Results the model never sees cannot inform any answer — the current balance has to be in context to be cited; the distinction is superseded versus current, not tool results versus everything else.

The application owns the request it sends, and long conversations deserve curation: a superseded balance lookup is noise wearing the uniform of data — it costs tokens and, as the stale citations show, actively competes with the current figure. Pruning or summarizing superseded results while keeping what the conversation still depends on — decisions made, commitments given, the latest state — shrinks cost and removes the stale-fact hazard at once. The discipline is deliberate: curate what is superseded, never truncate blindly.

question:
A podcast-industry research request packs source material to about 195,000 tokens of a 200,000-token window, then asks for a comprehensive comparison table. The response cuts off mid-table every time, whatever max_tokens is set to.

What is the actual problem?
options: max_tokens is set too low and simply needs raising
The model writes tables inefficiently and should be asked for the same comparison in prose
The window is shared by input and output — 195k of input leaves ~5k for the answer; trim the inputs
Switch to streaming the output, since streamed tokens arrive incrementally rather than at the end
answer: The window is shared by input and output — 195k of input leaves ~5k for the answer; trim the inputs
explanation:
This question tests context-window accounting, and specifically that input and output share one budget.

The arithmetic
A 200,000-token context window covers the entire request: system prompt, conversation history, source material, and the response being generated. Packing 195,000 tokens of sources leaves roughly 5,000 tokens of headroom. A comprehensive comparison table across that much material needs far more, so generation stops when the window is exhausted — which is why raising max_tokens changes nothing. The truncation point is set by the arithmetic, not by the setting.

What max_tokens actually does
max_tokens is a ceiling on the response, applied within whatever room remains. It can lower the limit; it cannot raise the window. When the binding constraint is the window remainder, the parameter is not the lever.

The fix is input budgeting
Plan the window as a budget with two line items. Decide how much room the answer needs — a large comparison table might want 15,000–20,000 tokens — and fit the inputs into what is left, by selecting the most relevant sources, summarizing the rest, or processing in sections and combining. Deciding output space first is the habit that prevents this failure.

Why the other options are incorrect
No value of max_tokens conjures space the input already consumed. Raising it is the natural first guess and is inert here, which is precisely why the symptom persists "whatever max_tokens is set to."

Prose describing the same comparison consumes tokens on the same scale — sometimes more. Output format changes the shape of the answer, not the accounting that truncates it.

Streaming changes when tokens arrive, not how they are counted. Streamed output tokens occupy the window exactly like buffered ones.

Key Takeaway
The context window is one budget shared by input and output. Reserve room for the answer before filling the window with sources.

-

option_feedback: max_tokens caps the response within available space; no value of it conjures room past what the input left. Raising it changes nothing when the window remainder is the binding limit.
Prose describing the same comparison spends tokens on the same scale — format tweaks the shape of the output, not the arithmetic that truncates it.

The window is one budget covering both directions: input tokens and output tokens share the same 200k. Packing 195k of sources leaves roughly 5k of ceiling for the answer — a comprehensive comparison table cannot fit, so it truncates at the arithmetic, not at any setting. The fix is planning the budget like a budget: trim, summarize, or select the inputs so the window holds the sources and the room the answer needs.
Streaming changes delivery timing, not accounting — streamed tokens are output tokens, counted like any others.

question:
An airline-cargo support agent receives: "please cancel my booking." The customer has two active bookings — a shipment departing tomorrow and one next month. Last quarter, an agent guessed in this exact situation and cancelled the wrong shipment; the cargo missed its flight and the claim was expensive.

What should the agent do?
options: Cancel the more recent booking, since customers usually mean the one they made last
Ask one question naming both bookings; cancel only after the customer specifies
Cancel both bookings to be safe, since the customer can rebook whichever they still need
Escalate every cancellation request involving multiple bookings to a human agent, and let them decide
answer: Ask one question naming both bookings; cancel only after the customer specifies
explanation:
This question tests when to clarify versus when to act, and specifically that ambiguity plus irreversibility calls for one question.

Two conditions, both present
The request has two possible referents — a shipment departing tomorrow and one next month — and cancellation is irreversible with real consequences, as last quarter's missed flight and expensive claim demonstrate. When a request is ambiguous and the action cannot be undone, asking is unambiguously correct. One question, naming both bookings so the customer can answer in a word, costs ten seconds and eliminates the failure entirely.

Where the boundary sits
The reasoning generalizes in both directions. If the customer had only one booking, there is nothing to ask and asking would be friction for its own sake. If the action were trivially reversible — updating a display preference, say — acting on the likelier reading and offering to change it is reasonable. It is the conjunction that makes the question mandatory here, and multiple matching records is the standard trigger: ask for an identifier rather than guessing which record was meant.

Why the other options are incorrect
"Customers usually mean the most recent" is a guess with better branding, and the last guess in this exact situation caused the claim. Heuristics are for when asking is impossible, not merely slightly inconvenient.

Cancelling both converts a possible wrong cancellation into a certain one. The tomorrow shipment misses its flight by policy rather than by accident, and "they can rebook" is not true of a shipment that has already departed.

Escalation buys queue time to obtain the same clarification the agent is fully able to request. The agent lacks nothing a human has here except an answer it can ask for directly — and the customer waits longer for the identical outcome.

Key Takeaway
Ask one clarifying question when a request is ambiguous and the action is irreversible. Multiple matching records means request an identifier — never guess.

Anthropic — Claude prompting best practices → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

-

-
Anthropic — Build a tool-using agent → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/build-a-tool-using-agent
option_feedback: Recency is a guess with better branding — the last guess in this situation cost a missed flight and a claim. Heuristics are for when asking is impossible, not merely mildly inconvenient.

The request is genuinely ambiguous — two referents, one instruction — and the action is irreversible with a documented expensive failure. That combination is exactly when one clarifying question earns its turn: name the two bookings, let the customer pick, then act with certainty. Ten seconds of friction against a repeat of last quarter's claim is not a close call. Clarify when ambiguity meets irreversibility; act directly when either is absent.
Cancel-both converts one possible wrong cancellation into one certain wrong cancellation — the tomorrow shipment misses its flight by policy rather than by accident.
The agent lacks nothing a human has here except the answer to one question it is fully able to ask — escalation buys queue time to obtain the same clarification.

question:
A property-management support agent's policy reads "escalate when unsure." An audit finds the agent almost never reports being unsure — and 15% of its confident resolutions were wrong, including tenants told their leases permitted things they did not. The team concludes "unsure" is doing no work.

What should replace it?
options: Structural triggers — unseen request types, empty or conflicting lookups, contradictory data
The same policy with a lowered bar — escalating, from now on, at even mild uncertainty
A self-check step where the agent asks itself whether it is sure before finalizing
Escalating a random fifteen percent of resolutions, so wrong answers get sampled at their observed rate
answer: Structural triggers — unseen request types, empty or conflicting lookups, contradictory data
explanation:
This question tests escalation-trigger design, and specifically that self-reported uncertainty is an unreliable basis for routing.

Why "escalate when unsure" produced nothing
The policy asks the model to detect its own failures using its own confidence. The audit measures exactly how well that works: 15% of resolutions were wrong, and they arrived confidently — tenants were told their leases permitted things the leases did not. Confident errors are the dominant error mode, not a rare edge case, and no threshold on a signal these errors do not emit can catch them. The policy is not merely weak; it is orthogonal to the failure it is meant to intercept.

What structural triggers do differently
Replace self-assessment with observable conditions that correlate with being wrong, regardless of how the model feels: the request type matches nothing in the policy set; the policy lookup returned empty; two retrieved clauses conflict; the account data contradicts itself. These are checkable facts about the situation rather than introspective reports, which makes them robust against overconfidence by construction. They also map onto the canonical escalation triggers — a policy gap or silence, an inability to make meaningful progress, and an explicit request for a human, which is honored immediately.

Why the other options are incorrect
Lowering the bar on a signal that never fires still produces no escalations. The 15% were not mildly-unsure cases filed just above a line; they were confident, and confident is confident at any threshold.

A self-check asks the same judge the same question a second time. It inherits the exact bias it is meant to detect, and adds latency and cost for a second opinion from the same source.

Random 15% sampling is a measurement instrument, not a routing policy. It escalates by chance rather than by risk, so roughly 85% of wrong resolutions still ship — and correct ones consume review capacity.

Key Takeaway
Base escalation on structural triggers — unseen request types, empty or conflicting lookups, contradictory data — not on the model's self-reported uncertainty. Confidence is a poorly calibrated proxy for correctness.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Reduce hallucinations → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations

-
Anthropic — Increase output consistency → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency

-
Anthropic — Claude prompting best practices → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: hooks reference (deterministic gates) → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks
option_feedback: "Unsure" delegates the trigger to self-assessment, and the audit shows the failure precisely there: the wrong answers came with confidence, so no confidence-based rule at any threshold would have fired. Structural triggers move the decision onto observable conditions that correlate with being wrong — this request type matches nothing in policy, the policy lookup returned nothing or two conflicting clauses, the account's data contradicts itself. Those conditions are checkable regardless of how sure the model feels, which is what makes them robust against exactly the confident-error mode the audit measured.
Lowering the bar on a signal that never fires still yields no escalations — the 15% were not mildly-unsure cases misfiled; they were confident.
Asking the same judge the same question twice re-samples its bias — the self-check inherits the very overconfidence it is supposed to catch.
Random sampling is a measurement instrument, not a routing policy — 85% of wrong resolutions still ship, selected by chance rather than by risk.

question:
A museum consortium's research run covers nine collections; mid-run, source failures wiped out six of them, leaving usable material for three. The deadline is tonight. The team debates what the system should be designed to do in this situation.

What is the right designed behavior?
options: Deliver all nine sections, annotating the six thin ones as based on partial coverage
Keep retrying the failed sources until the deadline and deliver whatever exists at that moment
Enforce a pre-set coverage floor: below it, stop, report, escalate the decision
Deliver the three well-covered sections and omit the other six without comment
answer: Enforce a pre-set coverage floor: below it, stop, report, escalate the decision
explanation:
This question tests graceful degradation, and specifically that the response to partial failure must be proportionate to how much was lost.

Annotation has a range, and this is outside it
Annotating gaps is the right answer when a run loses a little: the deliverable still answers its question, and the annotation tells the reader which parts rest on thinner evidence. Six of nine collections lost is a different situation. The report no longer answers what it was commissioned to answer, and shipping it — however carefully annotated — invites decisions built on a document that is mostly absence. Disclosure does not repair a deliverable whose scope has collapsed.

Why a pre-set coverage floor is the design
Defining the floor before the run is what makes the stopping rule principled rather than improvised under deadline pressure. Below the floor, the correct output is not a report but a failure report: what was lost, why, what partial material exists — plus an escalation, so a human decides whether to extend the deadline, descope to the three viable collections, or accept the partial work knowingly. That is the difference between a system that degrades gracefully and one that quietly ships whatever it managed to assemble. The general principle: annotate small gaps, halt and escalate on collapse.

Why the other options are incorrect
Six annotated husks around three real sections is disclosure in form and a hollow report in substance. The annotation pattern serves runs that lost a little, and applying it here dresses a failed run as a completed one.

Retrying until deadline spends the remaining hours on sources already proven unavailable, and guarantees that whatever is chosen at the end is chosen at the worst possible moment — with no time left for any alternative.

Silent omission is the worst outcome available: the reader sees three sections and no indication that six others were ever in scope. Scope loss is concealed rather than reported, which is how a reader concludes the field was covered.

Key Takeaway
Set a coverage floor in advance. Above it, annotate gaps; below it, stop, report what was lost, and escalate the decision to a human.

Official Documentation References

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: subagents → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents

-
Anthropic — Agent SDK: the agent loop → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop

-
Anthropic — Reduce hallucinations → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations
option_feedback: Six annotated husks around three real sections is disclosure in form and a hollow report in substance — the honest annotation pattern serves runs that lost a little, not most, of their scope.
Retry-until-deadline burns the remaining hours on sources already proven down, guaranteeing the worst version of every other option at exactly deadline time.

Annotation is the honest dress for small gaps; it cannot dress a report missing two-thirds of its scope — at that point the deliverable no longer answers the question it was commissioned to answer, and shipping it invites decisions built on a hollow document. A coverage floor, defined before any run, gives the system a principled stopping rule: below the floor, the correct output is a failure report — what was lost, why, what partial material exists — and an escalation, so a human decides whether to extend, descope, or accept the three sections knowingly. Proportionality is the design: annotate small gaps, halt on collapse.
Silent omission is the worst of all: the reader sees three sections and no evidence that six others were ever in scope — scope loss concealed rather than reported.

question:
A car-rental platform team keeps an architecture-map.md that Claude Code sessions read for orientation. It was written four months ago; since then, two modules were merged and a new payments service appeared. This week a session confidently modified code based on the map's obsolete module list.

What is the right practice for such maps?
options: Delete the map and have every session explore the codebase fresh
Regenerate the map from scratch at the start of every session
Keep the map but label it as possibly outdated so sessions treat its claims skeptically
Living-document discipline: sessions fix drift; sections carry dates
answer: Living-document discipline: sessions fix drift; sections carry dates
explanation:
This question tests external-memory maintenance, and specifically that a durable reference document is only valuable while it remains true.

Stale documentation is worse than none
The architecture map's whole purpose is to let sessions skip exploration and trust a summary. That trade is sound only while the summary is accurate — and when it is not, the session does not fall back to exploring; it acts confidently on wrong information, which is exactly what happened. A stale map converts a time-saving device into a confident-error generator, and the error is harder to catch than the ignorance it replaced.

The living-document discipline
Two habits keep it honest at near-zero cost. First, any session that discovers reality diverging from the map fixes the map as part of that work — drift is repaired continuously, by whoever encounters it, in the same pass. Second, sections carry dates, so a reader can see that the module list was last confirmed four months ago and weigh it accordingly. Maintenance rides along with normal usage instead of being a separate project nobody schedules, and this is the same discipline that keeps CLAUDE.md and other project memory useful over time.

Why the other options are incorrect
Deleting the map prices four months of drift at the value of the whole artifact. Every session then re-pays full exploration forever — a large recurring cost to avoid an update habit that costs minutes.

Regenerating each session makes every session's first act an expensive full survey, which is precisely the cost the map exists to amortize across sessions. It also discards the human-curated judgment a good map accumulates.

A "possibly outdated" label turns documentation into rumor. Sessions must now re-verify everything the map claims — exploration cost plus reading cost — and the wrong module list remains wrong for the next reader.

Key Takeaway
Treat reference maps as living documents: sessions repair drift as they find it, and sections carry dates. Stale orientation produces confident errors.

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: memory → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory

-
Anthropic — Working with large codebases → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases

-
Anthropic — Claude Code: best practices → https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Deletion prices four months of drift at the whole artifact — every session re-pays full exploration forever to avoid the update habit that would have cost minutes.
Per-session regeneration turns every session's first act into an expensive full survey — the map exists precisely to amortize that cost across sessions.
A skepticism label converts documentation into a rumor: sessions must re-verify everything the map says, which is the exploration cost plus the reading cost, while the wrong module list stays wrong.

External memory pays for itself only while it tells the truth, and codebases move — so the map needs the discipline living documents get: any session that discovers reality diverging from the map fixes the map as part of its work, and dated sections make each claim's age inspectable. Maintenance rides along with normal usage at near-zero marginal cost, and the map stays what it was meant to be: orientation that can be trusted.

question:
A junior developer starts every Claude Code session by pasting the full contents of three configuration files into the first message — "so it has the context." The files total several thousand lines; most sessions touch none of them.

What is the better habit?
options: Keep pasting, but compress the files by stripping comments and blank lines first
Mention the paths; the agent reads what a task needs, when it needs it
Paste one file per message across the first three messages so no single message is huge
Move the three files' contents into CLAUDE.md so they load into every session automatically
answer: Mention the paths; the agent reads what a task needs, when it needs it
explanation:
This question tests context economy, and specifically that a path is a cheaper reference than a file body.

Pointers convert a prepaid cost into a free option
The three configuration files live on disk, and the agent has file-reading tools. Mentioning the paths — "the service config is at config/service.yaml" — tells it exactly where to look, and it reads whichever file a task actually needs, at the moment it needs it. Sessions that never touch those files pay nothing at all, which the stem says is most sessions. Pasting the bodies pays the full cost up front, every session, against a possibility that usually does not materialize.

Why "so it has the context" misidentifies the goal
Context should hold what the work is using, not everything the work might use. Several thousand lines of unused configuration is not neutral: it consumes budget the task's real material needs, it dilutes attention across content irrelevant to the request, and it grows the cost of every turn in the session, since the whole conversation is re-sent each time.

Why the other options are incorrect
Stripping comments and blank lines shrinks the paste marginally while keeping the fundamental mistake: thousands of lines still enter context for tasks that mostly never consult them. It also removes the comments a human — or the model — might have wanted.

Splitting the paste across three messages changes its packaging, not its accounting. The identical content lands in context before the work begins.

Moving the contents into CLAUDE.md promotes a bad per-session habit into a permanent automatic one, taxing every future session in the project with three files' bulk — the opposite of what memory files are meant to hold.

Key Takeaway
Reference files by path and let the agent read them on demand. Context should carry what the task is using, not everything it might use.

A session that needs database settings reads that file then; sessions that need nothing pay nothing. question:
A coffee-chain invoice pipeline set its auto-accept confidence thresholds correctly at launch, from a labeled validation set. Eight months later, new suppliers and new invoice layouts dominate the traffic — and a quarterly audit has just found that auto-accepted precision quietly sank well below target months ago.

Which TWO practices keep threshold-based automation honest over time? (Select TWO.)
options: Re-running the original launch validation once a year as a scheduled ritual
Trusting launch thresholds, since they were derived from labeled data
Raising all thresholds whenever traffic volume grows significantly
Tracking measured precision per confidence band continuously, from an ongoing sample of labeled cases
Alerting and investigating when any band's measured precision drifts below its target
answer: Tracking measured precision per confidence band continuously, from an ongoing sample of labeled cases
Alerting and investigating when any band's measured precision drifts below its target
explanation:
This question tests calibration maintenance, and specifically that thresholds are only valid for the distribution they were measured on.

Why correct thresholds went wrong without anyone changing them
A confidence threshold is not a property of the model alone — it is a measured mapping from confidence score to observed precision, established on a particular input distribution. The launch thresholds were derived properly. Then eight months of new suppliers and new invoice layouts replaced the distribution underneath them, and the mapping silently stopped holding. Nothing broke, nothing errored, and the automation kept accepting at the old cutoffs while precision drifted below target. Calibration is perishable, and its decay is invisible without measurement.

The two practices that keep it honest

-
Continuous measurement — Maintain an ongoing labeled sample and score measured precision per confidence band, so the actual confidence-to-precision mapping is a live number rather than a historical one. Per-band matters — drift often hits one band first.

-
A tripwire on that measurement — Alert when any band falls below its target and investigate, so the problem is caught weeks in rather than at the next quarterly audit. The instrument detects; the alarm converts detection into action.

Why the other options are incorrect
Annual re-validation institutionalizes the very gap that caused this incident, allowing up to a year of undetected drift on a calendar instead of by accident.

The launch derivation was sound and is not in question — its validity expired with the distribution it measured. Trusting it indefinitely is exactly the assumption the audit falsified.

Traffic volume is not miscalibration. Raising thresholds because volume grew changes the automation rate while measuring nothing about correctness — it could equally hide drift behind a smaller auto-accept pool.

Key Takeaway
Measure precision per confidence band continuously against labeled samples, and alert on drift below target. Thresholds are valid only for the distribution they were calibrated on.

-
Anthropic — Increase output consistency → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency

-
Anthropic — Reduce hallucinations → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations

-
Anthropic — Structured outputs → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: An annual re-validation leaves up to a year of undetected drift — this incident's silent months, institutionalized on a calendar.
The launch derivation was sound and is not the question; its validity expired with the distribution it measured. Trust without re-measurement is how the audit shock happened.
Volume is not miscalibration — thresholds moved by traffic size shift the automation rate while measuring nothing about correctness.

Calibration is a perishable property: thresholds map confidence to precision for the input distribution they were measured on, and eight months of new suppliers is a new distribution. Keeping the map honest requires a continuous instrument — an ongoing labeled sample scoring measured precision per confidence band — and a tripwire attached to it: when a band drifts below target, an alert fires and someone investigates while the drift is weeks old, not quarters. Measure continuously, alarm on drift; the quarterly-audit shock is what their absence looks like.
