question:
A podcast-industry brief cites a listener-conversion statistic to "an industry blog." Checking the chain, the researcher finds the blog was quoting a research firm's annual report — the figure's actual origin, which also carries the methodology and the collection year.

How should the brief cite the statistic?
options: Cite the research firm's report — the origin — with its date, having followed the chain
Cite the blog, since that is where the researcher actually found the figure
Cite both the blog and the report with equal standing, since both of them published it
Drop the statistic, since it was not found in a primary source directly
answer: Cite the research firm's report — the origin — with its date, having followed the chain
explanation:
This question tests provenance, and specifically that a citation records where a figure originated, not where the researcher happened to find it.

Discovery path versus provenance
The researcher encountered the statistic on an industry blog and then followed the chain to the research firm's annual report, which is where the figure was actually produced. Those are two different facts, and only the second belongs in a citation. Provenance answers "what document supports this claim and can be checked?" — and the answer is the report, which carries the methodology and the collection year that give the number meaning.

What citing the origin buys
Three things follow from citing the report with its date. The claim is anchored to a document that can actually substantiate it, rather than to one that merely repeated it. The reader receives the methodology and collection year, which is what allows them to judge whether the figure applies to their situation — a conversion statistic from a three-year-old survey means something different than a current one. And the citation survives the blog post's eventual deletion or rewrite. Carrying collection dates on claims is also what lets figures from different periods read as a series rather than as a contradiction.

Why the other options are incorrect
Where the researcher found the figure is biography, not evidence. The blog adds no authority, may have transcribed the number imperfectly or stripped a qualifier, and cannot answer any question about how the figure was produced.

Equal standing misrepresents the chain. One document produced the figure; the other repeated it. Flat dual citation conceals exactly the hierarchy that provenance exists to record, and leaves the reader unsure which to check.

The primary source was found — by following the chain, which is the intended research method. Discarding a traceable, well-sourced statistic because its discovery was indirect confuses the route with the destination.

Key Takeaway
Follow the chain and cite the origin, with its date and methodology. Where you found a figure is not where it came from.

-
Anthropic — Reduce hallucinations → https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations

-

-

Citing the origin anchors the claim to the document that can actually support it, survives the blog post's eventual disappearance, and hands readers the context they need to weigh the number. Discovery path and provenance are different things; citations record the second.

question: Maya maintains the Brightwater Press website with Claude Code. She wrote .claude/rules/images.md with the image optimization conventions (use the OptimizedImage component, generate webp variants, never embed raw img tags), but the file has no frontmatter, so it loads in every session even when the task has nothing to do with images. The affected files are scattered: the src/components/media/ folder, the src/lib/images.ts helper and the scripts/optimize-images.mjs script, and the last two folders also contain a lot of unrelated code. What is the most precise way to make the rule load only when Claude is working with those files?
options: Create a nested CLAUDE.md with the same rules in src/components/media/, in src/lib/ and in scripts/, and delete the file from .claude/rules/.
Leave the file without frontmatter and open it with the sentence: these rules apply only when you are working with the site images.
Add the frontmatter --- paths: ["src/components/media/**", "src/lib/images.ts", "scripts/optimize-images.mjs"] --- and keep the file in .claude/rules/.
Turn the file into a skill at .claude/skills/images/SKILL.md with user-invocable: false so that Claude invokes it whenever it detects image work.
answer: Add the frontmatter --- paths: ["src/components/media/**", "src/lib/images.ts", "scripts/optimize-images.mjs"] --- and keep the file in .claude/rules/.
explanation:
The general rule is that a convention which only matters for part of the codebase belongs in .claude/rules/ with paths frontmatter, and that field is a list: you can enumerate several globs and specific files in a single rule. That way the image rule activates whenever Claude reads any of those paths, even though they live in different folders, and stops consuming context in the sessions that never touch them. The key distinction against nested CLAUDE.md files is granularity: the nested file triggers on an entire directory, while paths triggers on a pattern and can point at a single file inside a folder full of unrelated code.

RULE: A rule in .claude/rules/ can carry several globs in paths; the list is the mechanism for covering scattered files without duplicating the rule.

TRAP: Assuming the only way to scope a convention to certain files is to nest CLAUDE.md per folder, when paths accepts a list of patterns and specific files.

TRY IT: Create .claude/rules/test.md with paths: ["src/lib/images.ts", "scripts/*.mjs"], ask Claude to read a file in src/lib/ that is not images.ts and then images.ts, and use /context to check in which of the two cases the rule shows up.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: Nested CLAUDE.md files are pulled in when Claude reads files from that folder, but src/lib/ and scripts/ hold plenty of code unrelated to images, so the rule would load far more often than needed and would be triplicated across three files you then have to keep in sync.

Without the paths field, a rule loads at the start of every session exactly like .claude/CLAUDE.md; the sentence is an instruction Claude interprets, but the context cost in every session does not go away.
Correct: the paths field accepts a list of globs, so a single rule can cover scattered locations and it only activates when Claude reads files matching one of the patterns.

A skill is loaded on demand when Claude decides to invoke it based on its description; that fits procedures, but a convention tied to specific files should be triggered by path matching instead of depending on the model recognizing it in every task.

question: The post-purchase agent at Northlane Outfitters, built with the Agent SDK, has the tools lookup_order, generate_return_label and escalate_to_human. A customer wants to return a coat she bought 52 days ago: the published policy allows returns for up to 30 days, but she states the garment arrived with a manufacturing defect, a case the policy says nothing about. Dana, who owns the agent, wants it to resolve on its own everything it can without making decisions nobody authorized. What should the agent do with this request?
options: Generate the return label right away, because a manufacturing defect justifies the exception and it meets the first-contact resolution goal.
Refuse the return citing the 30-day window, because the agent must apply the published policy exactly as written.
Ask the customer for photos and further details until it has gathered enough evidence to decide for itself whether there was a manufacturing defect.
Look up the order, summarize the case (dates, reason, what the policy does not cover) and call escalate_to_human, telling the customer that a person will take it from there.
answer: Look up the order, summarize the case (dates, reason, what the policy does not cover) and call escalate_to_human, telling the customer that a person will take it from there.
explanation:
The general rule is that an agent resolves autonomously whatever the policy covers and whatever is local and reversible, and escalates when it hits a policy gap, when it cannot make progress, or when the action is hard to reverse or touches shared systems. Issuing a return label outside the window creates an exception no rule authorized, so the right move is to gather the context and hand the case to a person with an actionable summary. The key distinction against approving the return is that a first-contact resolution goal does not entitle the agent to invent policy: escalating well prepared is also resolving.

RULE: Faced with a policy gap or an action that is hard to reverse, the agent prepares the case and escalates; it does not invent the missing rule.

TRAP: Mistaking the first-contact resolution goal for authorization to decide exceptions the policy never contemplated.

TRY IT: Add to the system prompt of a test agent the instruction to escalate when the policy does not cover the case, give it an escalate_to_human tool and send it an out-of-window request with an unforeseen justification; check that it calls the tool with a summary instead of deciding.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: First-contact resolution is desirable, but here the agent would be creating a policy exception nobody defined; an action that affects shared systems and is hard to reverse needs a person to authorize it.
Applying the policy is right when the case is covered, but the policy says nothing about manufacturing defects: denying the request autonomously is also deciding a case the policy does not resolve.

Gathering context is useful as a preliminary step, but no matter how much evidence it collects, the agent still has no rule that lets it decide; turning it into the judge of the case drags out the conversation without closing the policy gap.

Correct: the agent does what it actually can (verify the order and assemble the summary) and delegates the decision the policy does not cover to a human, with the context ready so the resolution is fast.

question: The team at Cascade Power implements the agentic loop of its operations agent directly against the Messages API, without using the Agent SDK. In the first response Claude returns stop_reason "tool_use" with two tool_use blocks: one checks the status of a substation and the other lists the open work orders. Nora has already run both functions and has the two results in hand. What is the correct way to continue the loop?
options: Send a single user message whose content starts with the two tool_result blocks, one per tool_use_id → keep the same tools array in the request → repeat while stop_reason is still tool_use.
Send a user message with a sentence summarizing both results and then the two tool_result blocks → keep the full history → repeat until Claude stops asking for tools.
Send one message per tool_result, in the same order Claude requested them → wait for the response between one and the next → repeat while there are pending tool_use blocks.
Add the two tool_result blocks inside the assistant message that requested them → resend that corrected message → repeat while stop_reason is tool_use.
answer: Send a single user message whose content starts with the two tool_result blocks, one per tool_use_id → keep the same tools array in the request → repeat while stop_reason is still tool_use.
explanation:
The general rule is that the tool use loop continues with a user message containing only the tool_result blocks, one for each tool_use returned, and that the new request repeats the same tools array. When Claude asks for several tools in the same response, the results of all of them come back together in that single message and the tool_result blocks are placed first in the content array; the continuation message must not carry any other block: adding text after the results can produce empty end_turn responses. The key distinction against the most tempting option is that adding an explanatory sentence before the results breaks the pairing and the API returns a 400 error.

RULE: The tool_result blocks of a turn travel together and first in the content of a single user message that carries nothing else, and the request keeps the same tools array.

TRAP: Assuming the loop allows text interleaved between tool_result blocks, or that the results can be split across several successive messages.

TRY IT: Build a request with two tools, run both tool_use blocks and try sending the tool_result blocks in two separate messages: watch which error the API returns.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons
option_feedback: Correct: every tool_result from a turn comes back in a single user message, they go first in the content array and the request must repeat the same tools array; the loop continues while stop_reason is tool_use.
Putting text ahead of the tool_result blocks leaves the tool_use blocks without their result immediately afterwards and the API responds with a 400 error; the result blocks have to come first.
Splitting them across several messages leaves tool_use blocks unanswered within the same turn: the documentation requires all tool_result blocks to come back in one single user message.
tool_result blocks are content of the user role; the assistant message holding the tool_use blocks is resent unchanged as part of the history.

question: At the City of Fairview, Marcus classifies citizen requests into four categories with this example block in the prompt: Request repair of the streetlight on Maple Street → street_lighting Request trimming of the tree in front of 45 Cedar Avenue → parks Complaint about a pothole on Jefferson Avenue → roads Complaint about an overflowing dumpster next to the farmers market → waste . The tool that receives the label declares input_schema {"type": "object", "properties": {"category": {"type": "string", "enum": ["street_lighting", "parks", "roads", "waste"]}}}. Since launch, requests starting with "Complaint" almost never get street_lighting or parks even when they are about streetlights or trees, and those starting with "Request" rarely get roads or waste. What change should be made?
options: Add the instruction "ignore the first word of the request when classifying" right before the example block and leave the examples as they are.
Turn the classification into a tool with strict: true and an enum with the four categories so the output is always valid.
Duplicate the example block to have two per category, keeping in each one the same phrasing they already use.
Rewrite the examples so that every category appears with different phrasings and edge cases, keeping between 3 and 5 relevant examples.
answer: Rewrite the examples so that every category appears with different phrasings and edge cases, keeping between 3 and 5 relevant examples.
explanation:
The general rule is that few-shot examples must be relevant, diverse and well delimited: they should cover edge cases and vary enough that Claude does not pick up unintended patterns. Here the four examples share an accidental correlation between the first word and the category, and the model learned it as if it were the rule. Rewriting the set with varied phrasing per category removes the correlation at its source. The key distinction against the tool with a strict enum is that structured outputs guarantee the format of the label, not the criterion used to choose it.

RULE: A set of examples teaches everything they have in common, including the accidental: vary the form so that the only thing they share is the criterion.

TRAP: Assuming a strict enum or a one-off instruction fixes a bias that the examples themselves keep teaching on every request.

TRY IT: Build a classifier with 4 examples in which the first word matches the category, try 10 requests that cut across that correlation, and repeat with examples of varied phrasing to compare the hit rate.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: An explicit instruction may mitigate this particular symptom, but the example set keeps teaching a spurious correlation and probably others you have not spotted yet; patching symptoms one by one is fragile.
The strict enum guarantees the label is one of the four valid ones, but it does not change which one the model picks: the first-word bias would still be there, only with perfect formatting.
More examples help only if they add variety; duplicating the current ones reinforces exactly the unwanted pattern the model learned.
Correct: the documentation asks for diverse examples that cover edge cases and vary enough that Claude does not pick up unintended patterns; here the spurious pattern is the first word.

question: Nora organized the instructions for the Brightwater Press site with imports. The root CLAUDE.md contains these two lines: "Code conventions: @docs/conventions.md" and "Content policy: @docs/legal/policy.md". In turn, docs/conventions.md ends with the line "Editorial glossary: @glossary.md", and the file docs/glossary.md exists. When a session starts at the root of the repository, what happens with these files?
options: conventions.md and policy.md are expanded only when Claude reads files inside docs/, just like a nested CLAUDE.md, so the initial context does not grow.
All three files are expanded at the start of the session; glossary.md resolves to docs/glossary.md because the path is relative to the file containing the import.
conventions.md and policy.md are expanded at the start, but @glossary.md is looked for at the root of the repository, does not exist there and the line stays as literal text.
Only the imports written in the root CLAUDE.md are expanded; the import that appears inside conventions.md is ignored because expansion is not recursive.
answer: All three files are expanded at the start of the session; glossary.md resolves to docs/glossary.md because the path is relative to the file containing the import.
explanation:
The general rule is that @ imports in a CLAUDE.md are expanded and loaded when the session starts, recursively up to four hops, and that relative paths resolve against the file containing the import. That is why the three files enter the context from the very first turn and the glossary is found at docs/glossary.md. The key distinction against the most tempting option is the moment of loading: a nested CLAUDE.md is pulled in when Claude reads files from that folder, whereas an import is resolved when the session launches and therefore saves no context; if you want conditional loading, the mechanism is .claude/rules/ with paths.

RULE: @ imports are expanded at the start and resolve against the file that contains them; they organize, but they do not reduce context.

TRAP: Extrapolating the on-demand loading of nested CLAUDE.md files to @ imports, which are resolved when the session launches.

TRY IT: Create docs/a.md with the line @b.md, docs/b.md with a recognizable text, import @docs/a.md from CLAUDE.md, start a session and confirm with /context that both show up among the loaded memory files.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: Nested CLAUDE.md files are indeed loaded on demand, but @ imports are different: they are expanded and loaded at the start, which is why the documentation clarifies that they help organize but do not reduce context.

Correct: imports are expanded when the session launches, they support recursive imports up to four hops, and relative paths resolve against the file containing the import, not against the working directory.

Resolving against the working directory is the usual intuition, but the documentation specifies that a relative path resolves against the file doing the import, so @glossary.md points to docs/glossary.md.
Imports are recursive: the documentation allows nested imports with a maximum depth of four hops, and here there are only two levels.

question: An administrative agent at Cedar Ridge Health, built with the Agent SDK, processes insurer authorizations in sessions that last several hours. The read_authorization tool returns the full text of each PDF, around 6,000 words. In the first message of the session, the intake coordinator wrote: "For the insurer Northstar Mutual, do not record any authorization without the contract code". For the first two hours the rule held; after that, records without a code started slipping through, with increasingly erratic accuracy in other fields, and after a system message with subtype compact_boundary the rule stopped being applied altogether. What are the two most likely causes? (Select TWO)
options: The context filled up with very long tool outputs and, as it grew, the model's ability to retrieve details from early instructions degraded (context rot).
When the window filled up, the API silently dropped the oldest messages, including the coordinator's instruction, and kept answering with the rest of the history.

Automatic compaction summarized the conversation and the detailed instruction from the first turn did not survive the summary; rules that must govern the whole session belong in CLAUDE.md or in the system prompt.
The prompt cache for the instructions expired after 5 minutes of inactivity and, without the cache, the model stopped receiving that part of the context.
The agent's max_tokens value also limits how much history the model reads, so with a low value the oldest turns are ignored.
answer: The context filled up with very long tool outputs and, as it grew, the model's ability to retrieve details from early instructions degraded (context rot).

Automatic compaction summarized the conversation and the detailed instruction from the first turn did not survive the summary; rules that must govern the whole session belong in CLAUDE.md or in the system prompt.
explanation:
The general rule is that context is a finite resource with diminishing returns: the more it grows, the worse the model retrieves details, and when automatic compaction kicks in, whatever is not in the system prompt or in CLAUDE.md can disappear from the summary. The two symptoms match two different mechanisms: the gradual decay comes from a context inflated with entire PDFs, and the total loss after the compact_boundary comes from an instruction that lived only in the history. Neither cause implies that the API drops messages: if the input exceeds the window, the API responds with an error instead of trimming silently, which is the distinction that rules option B out.

RULE: Whatever must hold for the whole session goes in the system prompt or in CLAUDE.md, not in a history message that compaction can summarize away.

TRAP: Assuming the API silently trims the oldest messages when the window fills up, instead of returning an error or compacting.

TRY IT: In an Agent SDK session, give a rule only in the first message, force several compactions by sending /compact as a prompt and watch whether the rule still applies; repeat with the same rule in the system prompt and compare.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/how-claude-code-works https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation describes how, as the number of tokens in the window grows, the precision with which the model retrieves information from context goes down; returning entire PDFs for every authorization accelerates that decay.

The API does not trim the history on its own: if the input exceeds the window it returns a 400 error (prompt is too long) and, in Claude Code and the Agent SDK, what happens before that is automatic compaction, not a silent drop.

Correct: the documentation warns that compaction preserves your requests and key fragments, but detailed instructions from early stages of the conversation can be lost; persistent rules belong in CLAUDE.md or in the system prompt.
Prompt caching changes what you pay for tokens, not what the model sees: an uncached prefix is processed in full anyway, so expiration does not hide instructions.
max_tokens only caps the output the model generates in each turn; it neither trims nor weights the input, so it does not explain the lost instruction.

question: Falcon Labs built an MCP server on top of its internal ticket system for the agents that review PRs. It exposes tickets_list, tickets_search, tickets_find_by_text and tickets_get, each with a single-line description such as "Searches tickets" or "Lists tickets". In evaluations, Claude picks the wrong tool in one out of every three ambiguous requests and sometimes calls tickets_list only to filter the list by hand afterwards. Marcus wants to improve selection without changing models. Which two measures are the most effective? (Select TWO)
options: Add one tool per endpoint of the ticket API (open, closed, by author, by label) so that every request has an exact tool.
Rewrite each description with three or four sentences stating what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, and what information it does not return.
Force tool_choice with type any on every agent call so that Claude always invokes one of the server's tools.
Annotate the read tools with readOnlyHint set to true so the model tells query tools apart from the ones that modify tickets.
Merge tickets_search and tickets_find_by_text into a single search tool with filter parameters, and retire tickets_list in favour of that search.
answer: Rewrite each description with three or four sentences stating what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, and what information it does not return.
Merge tickets_search and tickets_find_by_text into a single search tool with filter parameters, and retire tickets_list in favour of that search.
explanation:
The general rule is that selection reliability depends on each tool having a distinct purpose and a detailed description: what it does, when to use it and when not to, what it returns and what it does not. Rewriting the descriptions attacks the direct cause of the confusion, and consolidating the overlapping tools (one search with filters instead of two searches and a listing) removes the ambiguous decision point that not even a human engineer would know how to resolve. The key distinction against adding one tool per endpoint is that more tools do not improve results: they increase ambiguity and context consumption.

RULE: Fewer tools, with distinct purposes and three-to-four-sentence descriptions that say when to use them and when not to.

TRAP: Assuming more tools, one per endpoint, give more precision, when overlap is exactly what confuses the model.

TRY IT: Take two similar tools from a server of your own, rewrite their descriptions stating when to use each and what they do not return, and repeat ten ambiguous requests before and after to compare how often Claude picks the right one.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents
option_feedback: Wrapping every endpoint in a tool is a frequent mistake: more overlapping tools increase selection ambiguity and distract the agent; the guidance recommends fewer tools, more capable and with distinct purposes.
Correct: the description is the single most important factor in a tool's performance; explaining when to use it and when not to, and what it does not return, is exactly what separates similar tools.
tool_choice any forces a tool call, but it does not help choose which one among several similar tools; the problem here is selection, not Claude answering without tools.
Annotations are behavioural hints for the client or host (safety, parallelism) and do not describe each tool's purpose; they do not resolve the confusion between two search tools.

Correct: consolidating overlapping operations into a single search tool with filters removes the ambiguous decision point and prevents the agent from listing everything and filtering by hand, which burns context.

question: The Cedar Ridge Health pipeline extracts administrative fields from authorizations (date, provider, contract number, no clinical data) through an extraction tool and a validation loop with retries. Nora reviews the design with her team and writes down several statements about how validation and retries work. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?
options: When the extraction breaks a business rule, returning a tool_result with is_error: true and a message explaining what failed and what to fix lets Claude adjust the next call.
With strict: true on the tool, retries caused by schema violations disappear, but business rules such as ranges or coherent dates are still validated in your code.
If the response ends with stop_reason max_tokens and the tool_use block was left incomplete, the request has to be retried with a larger max_tokens.
With temperature at 0 the extraction is completely deterministic, so a single attempt is enough and the validation loop becomes unnecessary.
answer: With temperature at 0 the extraction is completely deterministic, so a single attempt is enough and the validation loop becomes unnecessary.
explanation:
The general rule is that the quality of an extraction is secured with structural guarantees (strict tool use for the schema) plus programmatic validation of the business rules and retries with instructive feedback, never with the hope that sampling will be deterministic. Options A, B and C describe documented mechanisms: instructive errors in tool_result, strict to eliminate schema violations, and retrying with a larger max_tokens after truncation. The key distinction is that temperature reduces sampling variability but does not eliminate it: the documentation says explicitly that at 0.0 results are not fully deterministic, so the validation loop is still necessary.

RULE: The consistency of an extraction is guaranteed with a strict schema and validation in code, not with temperature.

TRAP: Reading temperature 0 as total determinism and using it as a substitute for the validation loop.

TRY IT: Send the same extraction request ten times with the same prompt to a model that accepts temperature 0 and compare the outputs field by field; you will find variations, however small.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/messages/create https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls
option_feedback: It is correct: the documentation recommends instructive error messages in the tool_result instead of a generic "failed", because Claude incorporates that context to recover without guessing.
It is correct: strict tool use guarantees the input complies with the input_schema through constrained sampling, and unsupported numeric or length restrictions are checked on the client side.
It is correct: a truncated tool_use cannot be repaired; the documentation says to retry with a higher output limit to obtain the complete call.

This is the false statement: the documentation clarifies that not even with temperature 0.0 are results fully deterministic, and models after Opus 4.6 only accept the default value; validation is still needed.

question: The support agent at Kestrel Pay runs with the Agent SDK inside containers that autoscaling creates and destroys throughout the day, and it handles several simultaneous conversations in the same process. When a customer writes back hours later, Maya needs to resume exactly that conversation even though the container that served it no longer exists. Today the code calls query() with no session options and every response starts from scratch. Which two changes solve the problem? (Select TWO)
options: Pass continue_conversation on every request so the SDK picks up the most recent conversation in the working directory.
Store the session_id that comes in the ResultMessage of each conversation and resume it later by passing resume with that identifier.
Enable fork_session on every new message so each turn starts as an independent branch of the previous conversation.
Configure a session_store that replicates the transcripts to shared storage so another container can resume the session.
Raise cleanupPeriodDays so session transcripts are kept considerably longer before being deleted.
answer: Store the session_id that comes in the ResultMessage of each conversation and resume it later by passing resume with that identifier.
Configure a session_store that replicates the transcripts to shared storage so another container can resume the session.
explanation:
The general rule is that resuming a specific conversation requires two different things: knowing which session to resume, and the transcript still being reachable from wherever the process runs. The session_id in the ResultMessage identifies the conversation and resume picks it back up, while a session_store adapter replicates transcripts off the local disk, which is ephemeral in an autoscaled environment. The key distinction against continue is that continue looks for the most recent session in the directory, something that only works when there is one conversation at a time.

RULE: With several conversations or several nodes, store the session_id and use resume; continue only works for one conversation per directory.

TRAP: Confusing continue, which takes the most recent one in this directory, with resume, which takes a specific session by identifier, and assuming the local transcript outlives the container.

TRY IT: Launch two conversations in the same process, note the session_id of each ResultMessage and check which one continue returns to compared with resume using a specific identifier.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hosting
option_feedback: Continue looks for the most recent session in the current directory: it works when the application carries one conversation at a time, but here there are several in parallel and it would return another customer's.
Correct: the session_id comes in the ResultMessage of every result, successful or failed, and resume takes that specific identifier, which is exactly what a multi-user scenario demands.
Forking creates a new session with a copy of the history to explore an alternative path; using it on every turn multiplies sessions without solving how to find the customer's.
Correct: local transcripts do not survive a container restart or a node change, and the session_store adapter replicates them off the local disk so they can be resumed from another machine.
Retention decides when old transcripts are deleted, not where they live: if the container that wrote them is gone, the file is no longer available.

question: The compliance team at Riverbank Financial built a multi-agent system for its regulatory reviews. Owen notices that even a single-fact query, such as identifying which regulatory bulletin governs a type of fee, launches eight subagents searching in parallel, takes minutes to converge and costs far above forecast. The genuinely complex queries, on the other hand, work well. What should you do?
options: Scale effort to complexity: resolve a single fact with one agent and a handful of tool calls, and reserve the fan-out of subagents for complex research.
Keep the eight subagents and switch them to a cheaper model, so the cost per query drops without touching the system architecture.
Raise the lead agent's turn limit so it closes the synthesis sooner and returns the answer without waiting for every subagent.
Add a vote among the eight subagents and keep the majority answer, to gain confidence in the result of each query.
answer: Scale effort to complexity: resolve a single fact with one agent and a handful of tool calls, and reserve the fan-out of subagents for complex research.
explanation:
The general rule is to scale effort to the complexity of the query: Anthropic's engineering documentation sets out a heuristic of one agent with three to ten tool calls for a simple search, two to four subagents with ten to fifteen calls for direct comparisons, and more than ten subagents only for complex research. Owen's system applies the most expensive pattern to everything, and multi-agent systems consume around fifteen times more tokens than a conversation. The key distinction against switching models is that the real saving comes from not launching subagents the task does not need.

RULE: Size the number of agents and calls by the complexity of the query, not by the complexity of the system you built.

TRAP: Assuming an over-decomposition problem is fixed by making the model cheaper instead of reducing how many subagents are launched.

TRY IT: Take five real queries from your system, classify them as simple, comparison and complex, and record how many subagents and how many tool calls each one uses today.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Correct: Anthropic's engineering guidance recommends scaling effort to complexity, with one agent and between three and ten tool calls for a simple fact-finding task, so you do not overinvest in easy questions.
A cheaper model reduces the price of each call, but you still pay on the order of fifteen times more tokens than a simple conversation for a query that needs no parallelism.
Cutting the wait short can leave the synthesis incomplete and does not attack the cause: the problem is how many subagents are launched, not how long the lead takes to close.
Voting helps when several perspectives increase confidence in a result, but it multiplies cost precisely in the case that is already too expensive.

question: The records digitization agent at the City of Fairview classifies case files with the Messages API in a long conversation. At the start of each session it calls the permit_catalog tool, which returns the table of permit codes currently in force, and then processes hundreds of case files. Maya enabled context editing with the clear_tool_uses_20250919 strategy using the default values. Since then, when the conversation goes past roughly 100,000 input tokens, the agent starts inventing permit codes or asking for the catalog again, and the responses include context_management with cleared_tool_uses greater than zero. What is the most likely cause?
options: The prompt cache covering the catalog expired after 5 minutes without use and, no longer cached, that table stopped being part of the context the model receives.
The permit_catalog output exceeded the 25,000-token-per-tool-response limit and was truncated from the very first turn, so the model never saw the complete table.

The strategy deleted the oldest tool_result blocks, starting with the catalog, and replaced it with a placeholder text; that tool should be preserved with exclude_tools or the table moved into the system prompt.
The conversation exceeded the model's context window and the API started returning stop_reason model_context_window_exceeded with responses cut off halfway.
answer: The strategy deleted the oldest tool_result blocks, starting with the catalog, and replaced it with a placeholder text; that tool should be preserved with exclude_tools or the table moved into the system prompt.
explanation:
The general rule is that context editing with clear_tool_uses_20250919 frees space by clearing the oldest tool results server-side in chronological order, replacing them with a placeholder text, and that any reference data living only in an early tool_result will be the first to disappear. The symptom appears exactly when crossing the default 100,000-token threshold and comes with cleared_tool_uses, which is the strategy's signature. The fix is to move that data out of the clearing scope: list permit_catalog in exclude_tools or include the table in the system prompt. The key distinction against the cache is that caching changes the cost of tokens, never what the model has in front of it.

RULE: Whatever the agent needs for the whole session cannot live only in an old tool_result: protect it with exclude_tools or move it to the system prompt.

TRAP: Assuming prompt cache expiration or tool size limits explain a loss that coincides exactly with the context editing threshold.

TRY IT: Enable clear_tool_uses_20250919 with a tool_uses trigger at 3 and keep at 1, make 4 tool calls in a conversation and check context_management.applied_edits in the response to see which results were cleared.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing
option_feedback: The cache only affects the price of tokens, not what the model sees; an uncached prefix is processed in full, so expiration does not erase the catalog.
That limit is a Claude Code practice for tool responses, not a rule of the Messages API, and it would not explain why the agent worked fine for the first 100,000 tokens.

Correct: with clear_tool_uses_20250919, once the threshold is crossed (100,000 tokens by default) the API clears the oldest tool results in chronological order and replaces them with a text stating they were removed; the catalog, being first, is the first to go.
That stop_reason appears when generation hits the window limit, which is precisely what context editing avoids; at 100,000 input tokens the window is far from full.

question: A team has the skill .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md, which deploys to production. They want only a person to be able to launch it by typing /deploy, and Claude never to invoke it on its own. Which frontmatter field achieves that?
options: user-invocable: false
allowed-tools: Bash(git push *)
disallowed-tools: Skill
disable-model-invocation: true
answer: disable-model-invocation: true
explanation:
The general rule is that a skill's frontmatter controls who can invoke it: by default both the user and Claude can, disable-model-invocation: true reserves it for the user, and user-invocable: false reserves it for Claude. For a production deploy, which has side effects, the documentation recommends disable-model-invocation: true, so Claude cannot decide to launch it and its description does not take up context. The key distinction is not to confuse it with user-invocable: false, which does exactly the opposite, nor with allowed-tools, which manages tool permissions and not the invocation of the skill.

RULE: disable-model-invocation: true reserves the skill for the user; user-invocable: false reserves it for Claude. Flows with side effects use the first one.

TRAP: Reading user-invocable: false as if it restricted a user, when it actually removes the user and leaves the skill to the model alone.

TRY IT: Add disable-model-invocation: true to a test skill, ask Claude in natural language to use it and watch it not invoke it, while typing /name does run it.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
option_feedback: user-invocable: false does exactly the opposite: it hides the skill from the / menu and lets only Claude invoke it, which is what the team wants to avoid.
allowed-tools grants tool permissions during the turn that invokes the skill, without asking for confirmation; it says nothing about who can launch the skill.
disallowed-tools removes tools from the available set while the skill is active; it is not a control over invoking the skill itself.

Correct: with disable-model-invocation: true the skill can only be invoked by the user with /deploy, and its description does not even enter the model's context; it is the recommended setting for flows with side effects.

question: Your team downloads the results of a Message Batch from results_url in .jsonl format to load them into a database. Which field should you use to match each result with the request that produced it?
options: The custom_id you defined on each request, because results can come back in any order.
The position of each line in the file, which preserves the order in which you sent the requests.
The id of the message object inside result, which is generated from the request index.
The request_id in the HTTP header of the download, which identifies each request in the batch.
answer: The custom_id you defined on each request, because results can come back in any order.
explanation:
The general rule is that a Message Batch is processed asynchronously and concurrently, so results can be returned in any order and not necessarily in the order of creation. That is why each request carries a unique custom_id (1 to 64 alphanumeric characters, hyphens and underscores) and the documentation says to always use it to match results with requests. The key distinction against the position in the file is that the .jsonl reflects the order of completion, not the order of submission.

RULE: In batches there is no order: always match by custom_id.

TRAP: Assuming a line-by-line results file respects the order in which the requests were sent.

TRY IT: Create a batch of 5 requests with custom_id values like doc-1 to doc-5 and different max_tokens values, download the results and check whether the order of the lines matches the order of submission.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation warns that the order of results may not match the order of submission and that you should always use custom_id to do the matching.
It is a frequent assumption but a false one: results are written as they complete and their order is not guaranteed.
The message id identifies the response that was created, not the original request, and it encodes no position within the batch.
The request-id header identifies the HTTP download call, not each individual request inside the batch.

question: At Southline Logistics, the tracking MCP server exposes the track_shipment tool. Today, when the agent passes a tracking number with an invalid format, the server raises an exception that reaches the client as a JSON-RPC error with code -32603, and the agent usually gives up on the first attempt. Tyler will change the server so that this case returns a normal tools/call result with isError set to true and the text "Invalid tracking number: use the format SL-1234567; received: SL1234567". Which two effects will the change have? (Select TWO)
options: The host will interrupt the agent's turn as soon as it receives isError set to true and will show the message to the human operator instead of handing it to the model to retry.
The model will receive the message as a tool result and will be able to retry with the corrected code, because execution errors are designed for self-correction.
The tools/call response will carry a result field and not an error field, so the client will treat it as a valid call rather than a protocol failure.
Claude will treat the call as successful, because isError only affects the server's logging and does not change the content the model sees.
Claude Code will mark the server as disconnected after several results with isError set to true and it will have to be reconnected from /mcp.
answer: The model will receive the message as a tool result and will be able to retry with the corrected code, because execution errors are designed for self-correction.
The tools/call response will carry a result field and not an error field, so the client will treat it as a valid call rather than a protocol failure.
explanation:
The general rule is that MCP distinguishes two mechanisms: protocol errors (JSON-RPC responses with error) for structural problems such as an unknown tool or a malformed request, and execution errors, which travel inside the result with isError set to true and actionable content. By moving format validation to the second mechanism, the call stops looking like a protocol failure and the model receives a message telling it exactly what to fix, which enables the retry. The key distinction is that a protocol error signals something the model can hardly fix, while an execution error is designed for self-correction.

RULE: What the model can correct goes in the result with isError set to true; what breaks the structure of the request goes as a JSON-RPC error.

TRAP: Assuming isError set to true stops the agent or is just logging, when it is precisely the channel through which the model sees the error and retries.

TRY IT: In a test MCP server, make a tool return isError set to true with a message stating the correct format, pass it an invalid argument from Claude Code and watch the model retry with the corrected format.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools
option_feedback: isError does not interrupt the loop: the result goes back to the model within the turn, and the documentation asks precisely that clients hand execution errors to the model so it can correct itself.

Correct: the specification defines execution errors (input validation, business rules, API failures) as results with isError set to true that contain actionable feedback so the model can retry with adjusted parameters.
Correct: an execution error is reported inside the result of tools/call, not as a JSON-RPC error; the protocol error is reserved for unknown tools, malformed requests or server failures.
isError is the signal that tells the model the call failed; together with the content text, it is what lets it see there was an error and self-correct, not a mere logging detail.
The server's connection state does not depend on the results of individual calls; an isError set to true is per-call information and does not affect the MCP session.

question: At Northlane Outfitters, Dana wants to delegate the analysis of one specific return to a subagent: review the ticket, look up the customer history in the catalog API, check the attached photos and return a recommendation. The main agent has already read the ticket and agreed with the ops lead on which exchange policy applies in this case. What is the correct sequence for the subagent to be able to do its job?
options: Define the subagent with its description and its prompt → ask it to review the recent history of the main conversation → wait for its final recommendation.
Define the subagent with its description and its prompt → put the order number, the photo paths and the agreed policy in the prompt of the Agent tool → receive its final message.
Resume the main session in fork mode → let the subagent inherit the entire conversation → ask it to summarize only the returns part.
Write the agreed policy in the main agent's system prompt → launch the subagent with no specific instructions → ask it to look up whatever it is missing.
answer: Define the subagent with its description and its prompt → put the order number, the photo paths and the agreed policy in the prompt of the Agent tool → receive its final message.
explanation:
The general rule is that a subagent starts with a clean context window: it receives its own system prompt, the project CLAUDE.md and the definitions of its tools, but not the parent conversation or its tool results. The only content passed from parent to subagent is the prompt string of the Agent tool, and that is why the documentation asks you to include file paths, error messages and decisions the subagent needs there. The key distinction against the most tempting option is that it is not enough for the data to exist in the main conversation: if it is not in that prompt, the subagent does not see it.

RULE: Everything the subagent needs to know goes in the prompt of the Agent tool, because it inherits neither the conversation nor the parent's system prompt.

TRAP: Assuming the subagent can consult the parent's history simply because it was launched from that conversation.

TRY IT: Launch a subagent with a prompt that omits a path the parent had already read and check in its transcript whether it searches for it from scratch or asks for it.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: The subagent does not see the parent conversation or its tool results: its context window starts clean, so asking it to review that history gives it nothing.
Correct: the only thing that travels from parent to subagent is the prompt string of the Agent tool, so that is where the paths, identifiers and decisions it needs must go.
Forking exists and does inherit the whole conversation, but it is a different mechanism from a normal subagent and here it shares back exactly the context you wanted to isolate.
The subagent does not receive the parent's system prompt either, and launching it without specific instructions is what produces duplicated work or gaps in the result.

question: Northlane Outfitters receives around 40,000 supplier invoices in PDF every night to extract their data with the same extraction tool and the same 3,000-token system prompt. Accounting processes the results the following morning, but purchasing also flags around 200 invoices a day as urgent, which must be extracted within minutes, the moment they arrive. Ethan wants the lowest possible cost without breaking either requirement. Which design is right?
options: Send everything in a single batch at 11 p.m., since most batches finish in under an hour and that covers both the nightly close and the urgent ones.
Process every invoice through the synchronous Messages API with prompt caching on the system prompt and the tool, which is cheaper than the batch.
Send everything in one batch and consume results_url as a stream to process each urgent invoice as soon as its request completes.
Process the urgent ones through the synchronous Messages API and the rest in one or more nightly batches, sharing the same prefix with cache_control across all requests.
answer: Process the urgent ones through the synchronous Messages API and the rest in one or more nightly batches, sharing the same prefix with cache_control across all requests.
explanation:
The general rule is that the Message Batches API is for work that does not need an immediate response: it takes 50 % off all tokens, but results can only be read when the whole batch ends or when it expires at 24 hours, and order is not guaranteed. That is why the flow with a minutes-level requirement goes through the synchronous Messages API and the nightly volume goes through a batch, preferably several batches with monitoring and retries. Since prompt caching and batch discounts stack, putting the same cached prefix (system prompt and tool) on every request of both flows makes it cheaper still. The key distinction against consuming results_url as a stream is that streaming is only a way of downloading the final file, not a request-by-request delivery.

RULE: Batch for what can wait, synchronous API for what cannot; and the same cached prefix in both flows.

TRAP: Reading the recommendation to download results as a stream as if a batch delivered each result the moment it completes.

TRY IT: Create a batch with 3 requests of different lengths and poll GET /v1/messages/batches/{id} every 30 seconds: notice that results cannot be downloaded until processing_status turns to ended.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
option_feedback: The 50 % discount applies, but the documentation only guarantees access to the results when the whole batch finishes or at 24 hours, whichever comes first: the urgent ones cannot depend on that.
The cache only discounts the shared prefix; the content of each invoice and the output are paid at full price, whereas the batch discounts 50 % of everything and also combines with the cache.
The recommendation to download results as a stream refers to the final file; the results of a batch are only available once every request has finished or at 24 hours, not request by request.
Correct: it separates the latency-bound flow from the bulk flow, applies the batch discount to the volume and takes advantage of cache and batch discounts stacking on the shared prefix.

question: Chloe integrates the Kestrel Pay payments MCP server, which exposes get_customer and lookup_transaction over HTTP, into Claude Code. She added this entry to the repository .mcp.json: {"mcpServers": {"payments": {"url": "${PAYMENTS_MCP_URL}", "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${PAYMENTS_TOKEN}"}}}}. Both environment variables are defined, but Claude Code does not connect to the server and reports the entry as a configuration error. What is wrong?
options: ${VAR} expansion only works inside the env block of stdio servers; in url and headers you have to write literal values.
The "type": "http" field is missing; without it Claude Code reads the entry as a stdio server, and an entry with url but no type is a configuration error.
Authentication headers are not supported in .mcp.json; they must be passed with the --header flag when running claude mcp add on each machine.
The correct field is "transport": "http", just like the --transport flag on the command line; "type" is not a valid key inside .mcp.json entries.
answer: The "type": "http" field is missing; without it Claude Code reads the entry as a stdio server, and an entry with url but no type is a configuration error.
explanation:
The general rule is that every .mcp.json entry declares its transport with the type field (stdio, http, sse, or the streamable-http alias for http), and that Claude Code treats an entry without type as stdio. That is why an entry with url but no type is a configuration error: there is no command to launch and the url goes unused. The key distinction is between the command line interface, where the transport is given with --transport, and the JSON file, where the key is type; variable expansion in url and headers is supported and is not the cause of the failure.

RULE: In .mcp.json every remote server carries "type": "http" and its url; an entry with url and no type is read as stdio and fails.

TRAP: Carrying the name of the --transport flag over to the JSON, or assuming the url is enough to infer the transport, when the required field is type.

TRY IT: Create a .mcp.json with an entry that has url and no type, run claude mcp list to see the error, add "type": "http" and list again to confirm the server shows up with its connection status.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: The documentation explicitly lists url and headers among the places where ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} are expanded, along with command, args and env; expansion is not the problem.

Correct: in .mcp.json an entry without type is read as a stdio server, so an entry with url and no type is a configuration error; with "type": "http" (or its streamable-http alias) the entry is valid.
headers is a valid field of HTTP entries in .mcp.json, variable expansion included; --header is just the equivalent way of stating them from claude mcp add.
--transport is the flag of the claude mcp add command, but in the JSON the field is called type; there is no transport key in .mcp.json entries.

question: The research system at Lakeside Online University calls an MCP tool that returns the full text of each paper, between twenty thousand and forty thousand tokens per call. After three or four queries the agent's context window is saturated and the cost per session soars, but the audit team requires the full text to be kept exactly as it arrived. Which design best resolves both constraints?
options: Wrap the call in a PreToolUse hook that rewrites the parameters to ask for fewer pages, so the tool returns a shorter text from the start.
Register a PostToolUse hook that archives the full text and replaces the tool output with an excerpt before Claude sees it, using updatedToolOutput.
Instruct the system prompt to ignore the irrelevant sections of the paper and keep only methods and results when reading each response.
Let the context fill up and rely on automatic compaction to summarize the history as it approaches the window limit.
answer: Register a PostToolUse hook that archives the full text and replaces the tool output with an excerpt before Claude sees it, using updatedToolOutput.
explanation:
The general rule is that the size of a tool output is controlled by intercepting it, not by asking the model to ignore it. A PostToolUse hook runs in the application process, outside the context window, and its updatedToolOutput field replaces the output before Claude sees it, which lets you keep the full text for the audit and hand the agent only what it needs. The key distinction against PreToolUse is the moment each hook acts: PreToolUse reaches the input parameters, and here the problem is in what the tool returns.

RULE: To trim what enters the context, transform the output with a PostToolUse hook; PreToolUse only reaches the input parameters.

TRAP: Confusing normalizing the input with normalizing the output: asking for less is not the same as replacing what the tool already returned.

TRY IT: Register a PostToolUse hook on a noisy tool that returns updatedToolOutput with the first few lines and check in the transcript which version ended up in the context.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: Modifying the input with updatedInput is a valid technique for normalizing or redirecting parameters, but it depends on the tool having that parameter and does not guarantee what comes back will fit in the window.

Correct: hooks run in your process and consume no context, and updatedToolOutput replaces the output before the model reads it, so the full text stays archived and the window receives only the excerpt.
An instruction changes what the model attends to, but the full text already entered the window and has already been paid for: the spend happens when the response is received, not when it is read.
Compaction mitigates overflow by summarizing the history, but it arrives late and lossy: every full response is still paid for before being summarized.

question: Heartland Agronomics builds a nightly yield-by-zone report with a lead agent that splits the work among four subagents: weather, soils, prices and historical yields. In the first runs two subagents bring back the same block of prices, nobody covers the soil data and the lead receives four different formats it cannot combine. Priya is going to redesign the delegation. What is the correct sequence?
options: Launch one subagent per source with a general instruction → let each one decide its own scope → ask the lead to unify whatever comes back.
Ask the lead to write the full report first → split the sections among the subagents so they verify them → rewrite the final result.
Write for each subtask its objective, its boundaries and its output format → launch the subagents with those descriptions → synthesize in the lead and leave citations for the end.
Give the same prompt to all four subagents to compare their outputs → keep the most complete one → ask the lead to fill in whatever is missing afterwards.
answer: Write for each subtask its objective, its boundaries and its output format → launch the subagents with those descriptions → synthesize in the lead and leave citations for the end.
explanation:
The general rule is that in a coordinator-subagent pattern quality depends on how the lead describes the delegation: each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on which tools and sources to use and clear task boundaries. Anthropic's documentation points out that without detailed descriptions agents duplicate work, leave gaps or fail to find the information they need, which are the three symptoms of the nightly report. The key distinction against launching subagents with general instructions is that the division of labour is defined before delegating, not negotiated afterwards.

RULE: Before delegating, write for each subagent its objective, its boundaries, its sources and its output format: whatever you do not delimit gets duplicated or lost.

TRAP: Assuming it is enough to name each subagent's area and that they will split the scope between themselves without overlapping.

TRY IT: Take the current prompt of one of your subagents, check whether it contains those four things, add the ones that are missing and run the report again.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system
option_feedback: Delegating without clear boundaries for each subtask is exactly what makes agents duplicate work or leave gaps, which is what Priya is seeing.
Writing first and verifying afterwards is a valid review pattern, but it does not split the research: the lead would have to gather all the data itself.

Correct: the documentation states that each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources and clear task boundaries, and that citation is best resolved in a dedicated final step.
Repeating the same prompt four times is a vote, useful for gaining confidence in one answer, not for covering four different areas of the report.

question: A CI job runs Claude Code in non-interactive mode and needs to read the final response and the session_id from a single JSON object when it finishes, to pass it to jq in the next step. Which claude -p invocation produces that output?
options: claude -p "..." --output-format json
claude -p "..." --json-schema '{...}'
claude -p "..." --output-format stream-json
claude -p "..." --verbose
answer: claude -p "..." --output-format json
explanation:
The general rule is that non-interactive mode (claude -p) has three output formats: text (the default), json (a structured object with result, session_id and metadata) and stream-json (line-by-line JSON events for streaming). For a pipeline that needs a single object at the end and extracts fields with jq, the format is json. The key distinction against stream-json is that stream-json emits many intermediate newline-delimited messages, designed for real-time consumption, while json delivers a single wrapper with the final result.

RULE: In CI, claude -p with --output-format json returns a single object with result and session_id; stream-json is for line-by-line streaming.

TRAP: Confusing --json-schema, which validates the shape of the response, with --output-format json, which defines the command's output wrapper.

TRY IT: Run claude -p "Say hello" --output-format json | jq -r ".session_id" and check that you get the session identifier.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference
option_feedback: Correct: --output-format json returns structured JSON with the result, the session_id and metadata such as cost, number of turns and duration, ideal for chaining with jq.

--json-schema is used to validate the response against a schema and receive it in the structured_output field; it complements the output format, but it is not what defines the wrapper with session_id and metadata.
stream-json emits newline-delimited JSON messages for real-time consumption (and requires --verbose); for a single object at the end the option is json.
--verbose turns on detailed session logging; it does not change the output format, which by default remains plain text.

question: The operations agent at Cascade Power runs a scheduled outage in four steps: validate the work order, notify the affected customers, execute the cut in the SCADA system and record the closure. The third step is irreversible and can only happen if the first two finished cleanly. Marcus wants the ordering and the checkpoint to stop depending on the model obeying instructions. Which two measures apply? (Select TWO)
options: Split the flow into separate calls and put a programmatic check between them that verifies the previous step's output before enabling the next one.
Spell out the mandatory sequence in the agent's system prompt and repeat it in the description of each of the four tools involved.
Move the agent to a more capable model and raise the effort level so it reasons better about the correct order of the steps.
Put a human review pause before the irreversible step, so the agent stops and waits for approval to continue.
Log every step with a PostToolUse hook into an audit trail, so you can reconstruct afterwards what happened in each scheduled outage.
answer: Split the flow into separate calls and put a programmatic check between them that verifies the previous step's output before enabling the next one.
Put a human review pause before the irreversible step, so the agent stops and waits for approval to continue.
explanation:
The general rule is that whatever must always hold is enforced outside the model. Decomposing the flow into chained calls with a programmatic check between steps turns the ordering into a property of the code, and stopping the flow at a checkpoint so a person approves the irreversible action is the handoff pattern Anthropic's documentation describes for autonomous agents. The key distinction against strengthening the prompt or upgrading the model is that those measures change the probability of the error, not the possibility of committing it.

RULE: Mandatory ordering is enforced with code gates between steps, and irreversible actions are handed to a person at a checkpoint.

TRAP: Assuming that describing the sequence in the prompt and in the tool descriptions is equivalent to preventing it from running out of order.

TRY IT: Split the irreversible step into a separate call whose trigger depends on a verification in your code and try asking the agent to run it first.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Correct: prompt chaining decomposes the task into successive calls and allows intermediate programmatic checks that act as a gate and always hold, because they live in the code.
Writing the sequence improves the odds the model follows it, but it is still an instruction: it reduces the error without eliminating it, which is exactly what Marcus wants to avoid.
A more capable model or more reasoning effort help on hard tasks, but they do not turn a preference into a mandatory rule of the system.
Correct: the documentation describes agents that pause for human feedback at checkpoints or when blocked, which is the handoff pattern called for before an irreversible action.
Auditing is essential for reconstructing what happened, but it records after the fact: an outage executed out of order is not undone by a log.

question: Kestrel Pay wants to cut first-contact resolution time. Today a single agent handles the conversation calling get_customer, lookup_transaction and, where applicable, issue_refund in order; each step depends on the previous result and all of them need the same customer context. Grant proposes turning it into a coordinator with five subagents in parallel. The budget per conversation is tight and the team measures token consumption. What should be done?
options: Keep a single agent with its tool loop, because the subtasks are sequential, they share context and a multi-agent system burns around fifteen times more tokens.
Build the coordinator with five parallel subagents and assign them a cheaper model, so latency drops without cost exploding.
Run the same analysis three times in parallel and keep the answer the majority agrees on, to resolve sooner and with more confidence.
Split the conversation into three sequential subagents that pass the result along in the prompt of the Agent tool, one per step of the current flow.
answer: Keep a single agent with its tool loop, because the subtasks are sequential, they share context and a multi-agent system burns around fifteen times more tokens.
explanation:
The general rule is to start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it is needed, because agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance. Here the steps are strictly sequential and share the same customer context, which is the case the documentation advises against for multi-agent: agents use on the order of four times more tokens than a conversation and multi-agent systems around fifteen times more. The key distinction against making the model cheaper is that parallelism buys nothing when each step needs the previous one's result.

RULE: Parallelize independent subtasks; if the steps depend on each other and share context, a single agent is faster and cheaper.

TRAP: Assuming that opening subagents always reduces latency, even when the subtasks are sequential and share the same context.

TRY IT: Measure the token consumption of ten conversations with the single agent and compare it with ten from the multi-agent prototype before deciding.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Correct: the engineering documentation points out that the multi-agent approach pays off when there are genuinely parallelizable subtasks and does not fit domains that demand shared context and real-time coordination.
A cheaper model reduces the price per token, but a parallel fan-out does not speed up steps that depend on each other and it multiplies total consumption.
Voting is useful when several perspectives increase confidence in a result, not when the flow is a fixed sequence of lookups about the same customer.
Each subagent starts with its own context and only receives the prompt of the Agent tool, so the customer context would have to be rebuilt three times and latency gets worse.

question: Ben uses Claude Code on the Brightwater Press site and runs this command: claude -p "Fix the bug in the homepage paginator". Claude replies that it has already fixed the problem, but the bug persists; Ben repeats the command twice more with small variations and gets the same pattern: different changes each time and the claim that it is resolved. Which change to the prompt is most likely to make the iteration converge?
options: Add the word ultrathink to the prompt so Claude devotes more reasoning to the cause before touching the paginator code.
Describe the symptom and the expected result, and ask it to run the paginator tests and show their output before calling it resolved.
Add --max-turns 40 to the command so Claude has many more internal iterations to find the real cause of the bug.
Switch to --model opus so a more capable model finds the root cause of the paginator without needing more detail in the prompt.
answer: Describe the symptom and the expected result, and ask it to run the paginator tests and show their output before calling it resolved.
explanation:
The general rule of iterating with Claude Code is that every task needs a verifiable objective: describe the symptom and what the solution looks like, and give Claude a way to check its work, such as running the tests and showing the output. That turns the cycle into something that converges, because Claude can see when it fails and when it passes instead of asserting success. The key distinction against the other changes is that more reasoning, more turns or a bigger model improve the execution of a well-defined task, but they do not replace evidence; trusting without verifying is one of the documented failure patterns.

RULE: Give Claude a verifiable success criterion and ask for evidence; without that, the iteration will not converge no matter how many turns or how big a model you add.

TRAP: Assuming that a lack of verification is fixed with more compute (reasoning, turns or model) instead of with a test or an explicit check.

TRY IT: Ask Claude to fix a real bug describing the symptom, the expected result and the test command that must pass, and check that the final answer includes the test output as evidence.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: ultrathink does increase the reasoning of that turn, but it gives Claude no way to check that the bug is resolved; without verification, it will keep claiming success with no evidence.

Correct: the best-practice guidance asks you to describe the symptom and what fixed means, and to give Claude a way to verify its work (tests, a build, a screenshot) so it shows evidence instead of claiming it is done.
More turns do not fix a prompt with no success criterion: Claude will keep making changes without a test telling it when to stop; --max-turns is a safety cap, not a convergence mechanism.
Upgrading the model does not replace the missing information: with no symptom, expected behaviour or verification, even a more capable model guesses and declares success without checking.

question: Summit Mutual Insurance gets the structured output of its claims classifier from a tool called classify_claim and the tool_choice parameter. Before going to production, Erin goes over with her team what each setting of that parameter guarantees and what it does not. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?
options: With tool_choice of type tool and the name of the tool, the model always uses that tool; with any it uses one of the provided tools, but you do not choose which one.
If you also mark the tool definition with strict: true, the inputs comply with the input_schema and you stop needing retries for schema violations.
With tool_choice any the model can first write a sentence explaining what it is going to do and then emit the tool_use block in the same response.
To get natural language text as well as a specific tool, leave tool_choice on auto and state in the user message that it should use that tool in its response.
answer: With tool_choice any the model can first write a sentence explaining what it is going to do and then emit the tool_use block in the same response.
explanation:
The general rule is that forcing a tool with tool_choice any or tool is not merely an order to the model: the API prefills the assistant turn, and that is why the response starts directly in the tool_use blocks, with no preamble. That is the reason forcing produces JSON with a guaranteed shape and why the documentation clarifies that the model will not emit an explanation beforehand even if you ask for one. The key distinction against auto is that auto does allow text before the call, and it is what you should use when you want both things.

RULE: Forcing a tool removes the preceding text; if you need an explanation and a call, use auto and ask for the tool in the user message.

TRAP: Reading tool_choice any as "mandatory but conversational": forcing suppresses any text before the tool_use block.

TRY IT: Send the same request twice, once with tool_choice auto and once with any, asking in both to explain its reasoning before calling the tool, and compare whether any text block appears before the tool_use.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
option_feedback: It is correct: the documentation defines any as "must use one of the provided tools, without forcing a particular one" and tool as always forcing a specific tool.
It is correct: strict tool use constrains sampling to outputs that are valid according to the schema, so missing fields and incompatible types disappear.
This is the false statement: with any or tool the API prefills the assistant turn to force tool use, so the model emits no text or explanation before the tool_use blocks, even if you ask for it.
