options: Mark all six pipeline tools with strict: true, so no call in the report can fall outside its schema at any step.
Leave the schemas as they are and raise the number of retries in the loop, which already fixes most cases in two or three attempts.
Mark only extract_series with strict: true and keep validating in your code the business rules the schema cannot express.
Replace the validation loop with a second review pass in which another instance of the model fixes the malformed JSON.
answer: Mark only extract_series with strict: true and keep validating in your code the business rules the schema cannot express.
explanation:
The general rule is that structural guarantees are applied where it hurts: strict tool use completely removes schema violation retries through constrained sampling, and the documentation itself advises marking only critical tools as strict instead of all of them, because every strict schema adds complexity. What strict does not cover are business rules, which are not part of the supported JSON Schema subset and are validated in your code after the call. The key distinction against marking all six tools is that the other five are not causing retries: paying complexity for them buys nothing.

RULE: Mark strict only on the tool that fails and leave the business rules the schema cannot express to your code.

TRAP: Believing strict also validates ranges and coherence between fields, when it only guarantees the shape of the input.

TRY IT: Run a hundred extractions with the tool without strict, count how many trigger a schema retry, enable strict: true on that single tool and repeat the measurement.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: It is the exhaustive option, but the guidance recommends marking only critical tools as strict and relying on natural adherence for the simple ones; every strict schema adds complexity and compilation.
It is true that on an invalid call the model retries with corrections, but every retry costs tokens and minutes: exactly what the nightly window constraint does not allow.

Correct: strict eliminates schema violation retries on the tool that causes them, and the rules the schema does not accept, such as ranges or coherence between dates, are still checked on the client side.
A second pass is useful for quality judgements, but for a shape problem it doubles the cost and latency of every report when the schema can already guarantee it.

question: At Riverbank Financial, every contract the model analyses then passes through a human analyst, with no exceptions, and the queue is already three weeks behind. Evan needs to cut the review load without losing control over the cases that genuinely need it, which are the ones with the greatest regulatory exposure. What should you do?
options: Ask for a structured output with the classification and a confidence level per field, and route the low-confidence fields to human review.
Review a fixed random sample of 10 % of the contracts and accept the rest automatically until the queue is caught up.
Replace the analysts with a second instance of the model that approves or rejects each contract against a written rubric.
Ask the model at the end of each contract whether it is sure of its analysis and automatically accept every case where it answers yes.
answer: Ask for a structured output with the classification and a confidence level per field, and route the low-confidence fields to human review.
explanation:
The general rule is that human review is expensive and slow, so it is reserved for where it adds value: uncertain cases and high-impact ones. Asking the model for a structured output that carries a confidence level per field alongside the classification turns that uncertainty into data you can route on, and leaves the analysts the volume they can actually absorb. The key distinction against random sampling is that a sample measures overall quality but does not protect the doubtful contract, which is exactly what Evan cannot let through.

RULE: Human review is routed by uncertainty and impact, not by blind sampling or by a yes from the model.

TRAP: Confusing a random quality-control sample with confidence-based routing: the sample measures, it does not protect the doubtful case.

TRY IT: Add a per-field confidence value to the output schema, process a hundred already-reviewed contracts and check what proportion of the real errors would fall inside the low-confidence band.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests
option_feedback: Correct: classification with structured categories and confidence scores is a documented use of structured outputs, and it lets you concentrate human time on the uncertain and the high-impact.
Random sampling measures the quality of the system, but it is blind to the individual case: a doubtful, highly exposed contract has the same chance of passing unreviewed as a trivial one.

An evaluator with a rubric scales well and is a documented technique, but human reviewers catch edge cases, hallucinations and source biases that automated evaluation misses, and here the decision is high risk.
Giving permission to admit uncertainty helps, but a free-form answer at the end is not data you can route on: it does not distinguish fields and cannot be thresholded consistently.

question: To consolidate the history of a property, the City of Fairview sends eight case files in PDF in a single request, with citations enabled on all the document blocks, and asks for a summary stating which case file each fact comes from. Three of the eight are old typewriter scans. The statements coming from those three come back with no citation at all and, on top of that, attributed to the adjacent case file. What is the most likely cause?
options: Citations must be enabled on all documents in a request or on none, and by mixing both cases the API stopped citing the documents that arrived at the end of the batch.
The document_index field is numbered from 0 and the team read it as starting at 1, which is why every citation points at the neighbouring case file.
Those three case files are scans with no extractable text and a PDF like that is not citable, so the summary has no anchor and the attribution drifts.
The title and context of each document block do not count as cited content, so the model has no way of telling one case file from another.
answer: Those three case files are scans with no extractable text and a PDF like that is not citable, so the summary has no anchor and the attribution drifts.
explanation:
The general rule is that the citations feature anchors every statement in a real fragment of the document, and for that the document has to have text: scanned PDFs containing no extractable text are not citable. The pattern of the failure confirms it, because only the three scans lose the citation while the rest of the batch responds correctly. With no anchor, the model describes what it interprets from the image and the attribution is left to its judgement, which is where the reference to the neighbouring case file comes from. The fix is to run those case files through OCR and send the resulting text, not to change the citations configuration.

RULE: A scanned PDF with no extractable text is not citable: run OCR before demanding provenance from it.

TRAP: Looking for a configuration or indexing error when the failure pattern points precisely at the documents that have no text.

TRY IT: Send the same case file twice with citations enabled, first as a scan with no text layer and then after OCR, and compare whether the response carries citation blocks in each case.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/pdf-support
option_feedback: The rule exists, but here citations is enabled on all eight document blocks, so the condition is met and it cannot explain why only three fail.
That off-by-one on the index is a classic error, but it would produce a shift in every citation; here the five case files with text return correct citations.

Correct: the documentation states that scanned PDFs with no extractable text are not citable; the model still sees the page image, but without text it cannot return a citation and provenance stops being verifiable.

It is true that title and context are passed to the model but are not used for cited content; even so the case files with text did return correctly attributed citations, so telling documents apart works.

question: Riverbank Financial reviews every contract against nine regulatory criteria in a single call that returns a verdict per criterion. In testing, the first criteria receive solid analysis and the last ones are dispatched with generic phrases, and which criterion falls short changes from one run to the next. Caleb needs coverage of all nine to be stable before taking it to audit. Which architecture is right?
options: Run the same nine-criteria call three times and keep the verdict that repeats in the majority of the runs.
Add at the end of the prompt the instruction to verify the report against the nine criteria before considering the response finished.
Split the review into one call per criterion and combine the nine verdicts afterwards in your code before passing them to audit.
Chain an evaluator that scores the whole report and an optimizer that rewrites it until it clears the rubric threshold.
answer: Split the review into one call per criterion and combine the nine verdicts afterwards in your code before passing them to audit.
explanation:
The general rule is that when a task gathers several considerations, the model performs better if each one is handled in its own call: decomposing into small, consistent subtasks gives every criterion full attention and reduces consistency errors. The described symptom, final criteria dispatched without analysis and a blind spot that moves between runs, is that of a single call with too many considerations. The key distinction against voting is that repeating the same prompt does not spread the load: it multiplies the cost while the model still attends to nine criteria at once.

RULE: When a prompt has to handle many criteria, spread the work across calls, one per criterion, and combine the results in your code.

TRAP: Confusing repeating the same prompt (voting) with splitting the work (sectioning): repeating frees no attention, it only multiplies the spend.

TRY IT: Run ten contracts with the nine-criteria prompt and another ten with one call per criterion, and count in each case how many verdicts come back with no concrete grounding.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/increase-consistency
option_feedback: Voting is useful when you want several perspectives on the same question, but repeating an overloaded prompt triples the cost and preserves the blind spot causing it.
Self-verification is a documented and cheap technique, but it runs in the same call and with the same attention split across nine criteria.
Correct: by decomposing into subtasks each criterion receives the model's full attention, which is the recommendation for reducing consistency errors in flows at scale.
The evaluator-optimizer pattern shines when there are clear criteria and iterative improvement adds value, but here the problem is coverage and the evaluator would inherit the same saturated prompt.

question: Caleb is migrating the Southline Logistics rate system and needs Claude Code to give him the list of files in the repository that still contain the identifier RATE_LEGACY_V1, regardless of the name or extension of the files. Which built-in tool is the right one for that search?
options: Glob, with a pattern such as **/*RATE_LEGACY_V1*, which locates files by name match across the whole tree.
Bash, running a recursive grep -r command, because it is the only way to search for text inside the content.
Grep, with the pattern RATE_LEGACY_V1 and the files_with_matches mode, which returns the paths that contain the text.
Read, going through the files of the rates module one by one to check which contain the identifier.
answer: Grep, with the pattern RATE_LEGACY_V1 and the files_with_matches mode, which returns the paths that contain the text.
explanation:
The general rule is that Glob and Grep answer different questions: Glob locates files by their name or path with patterns such as **/*.ts, while Grep, built on ripgrep, searches for patterns inside content and can return only the matching paths (files_with_matches, its default mode), the lines (content) or the count. Searching for an identifier inside files is a content problem, so the tool is Grep. The key distinction against a grep through Bash is that the dedicated tool is the one designed for this task and it respects .gitignore, with no need for a shell command.

RULE: Glob searches by file name; Grep searches inside content. To find which files contain a text, Grep with files_with_matches.

TRAP: Confusing Glob (names) with Grep (content), or reaching for Bash when a dedicated search tool exists.

TRY IT: Ask Claude Code to list the files containing a constant from your project and watch in the trace that it uses Grep with files_with_matches instead of Bash or Glob.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
option_feedback: Glob finds files by name pattern, not by their content; an identifier inside a file does not appear in its path.
A grep through Bash works, but it is neither the only way nor the indicated one: the built-in Grep tool is designed to search content, respects .gitignore and returns the file list directly.
Correct: Grep searches for patterns inside file content, and its default files_with_matches mode returns exactly the list of files containing the text.
Read is for viewing the content of a specific file; walking the repository file by file is slow, burns context and may miss files outside the module.

question: The Cedar Ridge Health assistant reviews administrative authorizations and flags the ones that need human intervention. Its prompt says, in capitals, that it MUST flag any authorization with the slightest hint of inconsistency and that when in doubt it should flag it anyway. Today it flags 40 % of cases and, on review, most of them were correct. Nora wants to cut the false positives without missing the real cases. Which two changes attack the cause? (Select TWO)
options: Lower the temperature to 0 so the criterion for deciding to flag stops varying from one authorization to the next.
Add twenty few-shot examples of flagged authorizations so the assistant better recognizes the pattern of problem cases.
Raise the model effort to xhigh so it reasons more deeply before deciding whether the authorization needs human review.
Replace the imperative language and the "when in doubt, flag it" with a normal instruction enumerating which inconsistencies count as a flag.
Require every flag to cite the fragment of the authorization that supports it, and allow it to state that no relevant fragments were found.
answer: Replace the imperative language and the "when in doubt, flag it" with a normal instruction enumerating which inconsistencies count as a flag.
Require every flag to cite the fragment of the authorization that supports it, and allow it to state that no relevant fragments were found.
explanation:
The general rule is that an excess of flags almost always comes from the prompt: aggressive language and formulas of the when-in-doubt-do-it kind cause overtriggering, and a criterion that is never enumerated leaves the model to decide what an inconsistency is. The two correct measures act through independent routes: one rewrites the instruction so the criterion is explicit and the tone stops pushing towards flagging, and the other forces every flag to rest on a citation from the document, with permission to say there is no relevant evidence. The key distinction against raising effort or adding examples is that neither of those defines the criterion: one reasons better over it and the other reinforces the bias that already exists.

RULE: Faced with too many false positives, enumerate what counts as a flag and require the citation that supports it, instead of asking the model for more effort.

TRAP: Assuming "when in doubt, flag it" increases coverage for free, when it is the instruction that triggers overtriggering.

TRY IT: Run the same fifty authorizations through the current prompt and through one with the criterion enumerated and the citation required, and compare how many flags come back with no supporting fragment.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations
option_feedback: Temperature reduces sampling variability, it does not define what counts as an inconsistency; besides, models after Opus 4.6 reject any value other than the default.
More examples help when they are diverse and cover edge cases; twenty examples that only show flags teach precisely how to flag, and would worsen the current bias.
More reasoning over an undefined criterion produces better-argued flags, not fewer flags, and it makes each review more expensive without touching the cause.

Correct: the documentation warns that instructions of the "when in doubt, use the tool" kind cause overtriggering and recommends toning down the imperative language; the enumerated criterion is what separates a flag from a suspicion.
Correct: anchoring each flag in a verbatim citation from the document and giving explicit permission to say there is no evidence are two documented techniques for reducing unsupported claims.

question: Ethan starts a session in the Falcon Labs monorepo with claude --permission-mode plan and writes: "Migrate session-based authentication to JWT; it affects apps/api, apps/web and packages/auth". He has not approved any plan yet. Which two statements correctly describe what happens in that session? (Select TWO)
options: Claude reads files and can run exploration commands, but it does not edit the source code while the plan is not approved.
To leave plan mode, Ethan can approve the proposed plan or press Shift+Tab, which abandons planning without approving anything.
Claude starts editing the files in packages/auth, but asks for confirmation before each edit until Ethan approves the whole plan.
Plan mode is unnecessary here because the task is described in one sentence, and the guidance recommends executing directly.
The written plan is lost if the context is compacted, so Ethan must approve it before the session grows too large.
answer: Claude reads files and can run exploration commands, but it does not edit the source code while the plan is not approved.
To leave plan mode, Ethan can approve the proposed plan or press Shift+Tab, which abandons planning without approving anything.
explanation:
The general rule is that plan mode separates investigation from execution: Claude reads files, runs exploration commands and drafts a plan, but does not edit the code until the plan is approved, at which point the session leaves plan mode; you can also leave with Shift+Tab without approving. A change that spans several packages is exactly the kind of task where the guidance recommends planning. The key distinction against Manual mode is that there Claude does edit, asking permission for each change, whereas in plan mode there are no edits to approve but a plan to review.

RULE: In plan mode Claude explores and proposes; it only edits after you approve the plan, and Shift+Tab gets you out without approving.

TRAP: Confusing plan mode with Manual mode: in the former there are no edits to confirm, there is a plan to approve or reject.

TRY IT: Start claude --permission-mode plan, ask for a small change, check that Claude proposes a plan without touching files (git status clean) and exit with Shift+Tab without approving it.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Correct: in plan mode Claude investigates and proposes changes without making them: it reads files, runs commands to explore and writes a plan, but it does not modify the code.
Correct: the documentation states that you leave plan mode by approving the plan or by pressing Shift+Tab again, which abandons it without approving.
Editing with per-file confirmation is the behaviour of Manual mode (the default), not of plan mode, which does not edit source code at all.
The criterion is not the length of the request but the clarity of the diff: a change spanning three packages is exactly the case where the guidance recommends planning.
The written plan is reinjected from disk after compaction; there is no need to approve it out of fear of losing it.

question: Summit Mutual Insurance wants the claim summaries the model writes to go through an automatic review against its internal rubric before reaching the analysts. Erin reviews which multi-pass review architectures are documented in order to decide which to build first. Which two designs correspond to those patterns? (Select TWO)
options: Ask in the same call for it to write the summary, critique it against the rubric and deliver the corrected final version directly.
Run the same prompt three times on each claim and keep the longest of the three summaries as the definitive version.
Have one instance write the summary and a separate, independent instance review it against the rubric and approve it or send it back.
Chain draft, review against explicit criteria and rewrite, with each step in a separate call you can log.
Send the summaries in a nightly batch to take advantage of the 50 % discount before the analysts receive them.
answer: Have one instance write the summary and a separate, independent instance review it against the rubric and approve it or send it back.
Chain draft, review against explicit criteria and rewrite, with each step in a separate call you can log.
explanation:
The general rule is that a multi-pass review needs separate steps: the documentation describes sectioning, in which one instance produces and another examines the output, and the self-correction chain, in which a draft is generated, reviewed against criteria and refined, with each step in a distinct call so you can log, evaluate or branch. The two measures are independent of each other: one separates who reviews, the other separates when the review happens. The key distinction against asking for everything in a single call is that there no intermediate inspection point is left, and against the batch it is that the batch changes the cost, not the architecture.

RULE: Real review requires a separate pass: another instance that examines, or a review and refinement step in its own call.

TRAP: Confusing repeating the generation with reviewing it: without a pass that evaluates against criteria, there is no review.

TRY IT: Build both versions over ten claims, one with writing and review in the same call and one with a separate reviewing instance, and compare how many rubric breaches each one detects.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: Self-verification inside the call is a real and cheap technique, but merging writing and review loses the inspection point and both tasks share the same attention.
Voting exists as a pattern, but it consists of comparing diverse outputs or setting vote thresholds; length is not a documented quality criterion.
Correct: this is the sectioning pattern applied as a guardrail, with one instance producing and another examining the output, each with focused attention.
Correct: this is the documented self-correction chain, generate, review against criteria and refine, with separate steps so you can log, evaluate or branch at any point.
The batch makes the volume cheaper and is compatible with the above, but it is not a review architecture: it adds no pass that evaluates the summary.

question: The Cascade Power operations agent, built with the Agent SDK, connects the cascade MCP server, which exposes check_grid_status (read-only) and schedule_outage (high impact). The current options are: {"permissionMode": "acceptEdits", "allowedTools": ["Read"], "mcpServers": {"cascade": {"type": "http", "url": "${CASCADE_MCP_URL}"}}}. Julia wants status queries to run without intervention and schedule_outage to keep requiring approval, but in the traces the queries are blocked for lack of permission. What has to change?
options: Add "mcp__cascade__check_grid_status" to allowedTools: acceptEdits does not approve MCP tools and the list grants only that tool.
Change permissionMode to bypassPermissions, which does approve MCP tools, and trust that the model will not invoke schedule_outage unnecessarily.
Set tools: ["mcp__cascade__*"] in the options, so the server's tools enter the agent's available set.
Mark check_grid_status with readOnlyHint set to true on the server, so Claude Code treats it as a read-only tool with no permission needed.
answer: Add "mcp__cascade__check_grid_status" to allowedTools: acceptEdits does not approve MCP tools and the list grants only that tool.
explanation:
The general rule of the Agent SDK is that MCP tools require explicit permission and that it is best granted with allowedTools rather than with permission modes, because acceptEdits does not automatically approve MCP tools and bypassPermissions approves too much. An mcp__cascade__check_grid_status entry in allowedTools authorizes exactly that tool and leaves schedule_outage under approval, which is the split of trust Julia needs. The key distinction is between the two layers: tools decides which built-in tools exist in the session, while allowedTools decides which ones run without asking; and server annotations take part in neither.

RULE: For MCP in the SDK, grant permissions with allowedTools by full name (mcp__server__tool); acceptEdits does not cover MCP and bypass covers too much.

TRAP: Assuming acceptEdits approves any safe tool, when it only covers file edits and not MCP tools.

TRY IT: In an SDK script with an MCP server, run a query with permissionMode acceptEdits and no allowedTools, observe the block, add the mcp__server__tool name to allowedTools and confirm the call runs without asking.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/mcp https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions
option_feedback: Correct: the SDK documentation recommends allowedTools over permission modes for MCP, because acceptEdits does not approve MCP tools; listing only check_grid_status leaves schedule_outage subject to approval.
bypassPermissions does approve MCP tools, but it also disables almost every other safeguard and would approve schedule_outage; for a high-impact tool that is exactly the opposite of what is wanted.
tools controls which built-in tools are available and does not affect MCP ones; besides, it is an availability layer, not a permission one, so the queries would still be blocked.
Annotations are metadata, not enforcement: a readOnlyHint grants no permission in the host; approval is decided by permission rules, not by hints from the server.

question: The support agent at Kestrel Pay runs with the Agent SDK and exposes the lookup_transaction tool from an in-process MCP server. When the banking core responds 503, the handler of that tool raises an exception nobody catches. Dana assumes the customer's query ends there and that the session has to be restarted. What actually happens to the agent loop?
options: The SDK catches the exception and hands it to Claude as an error result with the raw message; the loop continues and Claude can retry.
The exception propagates up to the query call, which ends with an error, and the conversation is cut off until your application reopens it.
The failure travels as a JSON-RPC protocol error, so Claude does not see it and answers as if the tool did not exist in the session.
The SDK retries the same call three times with the same arguments and only then hands the error to the model to decide.
answer: The SDK catches the exception and hands it to Claude as an error result with the raw message; the loop continues and Claude can retry.
explanation:
The general rule is that a tool error does not break the agentic loop: the SDK's in-process MCP server captures handler exceptions and returns them as error results. So what you really choose when writing the handler is not whether the query survives, but which message Claude reads: the raw exception or a text you compose by returning isError with context about what failed and what is worth trying. The key distinction against the intuition behind B is that the failure is contained inside the tool, not in your application.

RULE: An exception in the handler does not stop the agent: it only decides whether Claude reads the raw traceback or the actionable message you write.

TRAP: Assuming an uncaught exception aborts execution, when the only thing that changes is the quality of the text the model receives to recover.

TRY IT: Make a handler raise an exception on purpose, observe that the agent keeps answering, and then return the same failure with isError and a message of your own to compare what Claude does in each case.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/custom-tools
option_feedback: Correct: the SDK's in-process MCP server catches handler exceptions and turns them into error results, so the query does not fail and Claude sees what happened.
That is what would happen with an ordinary function in your application, but the handler runs inside the SDK's MCP server, which isolates the failure and returns it as a result.
Protocol errors are reserved for problems with the request, such as an unknown tool; an execution exception comes back in the result so the model can react.
There is no automatic retry of the handler: the one who decides to retry is Claude when it reads the error result, and that is why the text should say what to do.

question: Falcon Labs migrated its automated PR review from the beta of the GitHub action to version 1. The step ended up like this: uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 / with: prompt: "Review the diff and comment on the risks", max_turns: 5, model: claude-sonnet-5. The workflow runs and comments, but it ignores the turn cap and uses the default model. What explains that behaviour?
options: The with block in version 1 does not accept prompt: the instruction is passed with direct_prompt and that is why the rest of the parameters are discarded.
The anthropic_api_key entry is missing from the step, and without explicit credentials the action falls back to its defaults instead of failing.
max_turns and model are no longer their own inputs: in version 1 they go inside claude_args, for example claude_args: "--max-turns 5 --model claude-sonnet-5".
max_turns only applies in interactive mode; in automation mode the limit of the run is defined with trigger_phrase and the job timeout.
answer: max_turns and model are no longer their own inputs: in version 1 they go inside claude_args, for example claude_args: "--max-turns 5 --model claude-sonnet-5".
explanation:
The general rule is that version 1 of the action unifies the configuration: the action itself only defines integration inputs (prompt, credentials, GitHub token, settings) and everything that is Claude Code behaviour travels in claude_args as CLI arguments. An input that no longer exists does not break the workflow, it simply does nothing, and that is what produces a job that runs but with no turn cap and no chosen model. Migrating from the beta consists of exactly that: direct_prompt becomes prompt, and max_turns and model move into claude_args.

RULE: In the v1 action, whatever is Claude Code configuration goes in claude_args as CLI flags; the standalone beta inputs are silently ignored.

TRAP: Assuming an unknown input in the with block fails visibly, when it simply does not apply and the job looks correct.

TRY IT: Change the step to pass claude_args with --max-turns 1, run the workflow on a PR and confirm in the log that execution stops when it reaches the limit.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/github-actions
option_feedback: It is the other way round: direct_prompt was the beta name and in version 1 it is called prompt, which is exactly the only thing the step is passing correctly.
Without credentials the action would not run; here the job does execute and comment, so authentication is resolved by the secret or by the app token.
Correct: version 1 accepts any CLI argument through claude_args, and the standalone beta inputs are ignored without breaking the workflow.
trigger_phrase decides when the action fires in interactive mode, not how many turns Claude uses; the turn cap is a CLI argument in any mode.

question: Cascade Power redesigns its operations agent so it delegates the analysis of work orders by zone to subagents, and at peak hours the main agent has dozens of them working at once on different substations. Before setting the system caps, Nora wants to write down in the internal documentation what the runtime does when a concurrency or budget limit is reached. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?
options: If a subagent reaches its maxTurns, its output comes back marked as partial so the agent receiving it knows the run was left unfinished, and that session can be resumed.
When the max_budget_usd cap is reached the query keeps running until the task finishes and only a warning is recorded in the final ResultMessage.
When the concurrency limit is reached, the attempt to launch another subagent returns "Concurrent subagent limit reached" as the result of the Agent tool (formerly Task).
Claude decides on its own when to launch a subagent and how many, and each subagent makes its own requests, which count towards the query's total_cost_usd.
answer: When the max_budget_usd cap is reached the query keeps running until the task finishes and only a warning is recorded in the final ResultMessage.
explanation:
The general rule is that not every orchestration cap manifests the same way: some degrade the run and one terminates it. A subagent's turn cap degrades, because the output comes back marked as partial and the session remains available to resume with a higher limit. The concurrency cap also degrades, because it arrives as a tool result and the model can reorganize the work or wait its turn. The budget cap is the only terminal one: new launches are rejected, background subagents are stopped and the query closes with an error subtype. The key distinction is not to confuse an informational warning with a real spending cut-off.

RULE: maxTurns and concurrency degrade the run; max_budget_usd cuts it: it rejects launches with "Budget limit reached" and closes the query with subtype error_max_budget_usd.

TRAP: Assuming every runtime cap warns without cutting anything, when the budget one is the only one that rejects launches and ends the running query.

TRY IT: Run an SDK query with max_budget_usd set very low, ask it for a task that delegates to several subagents and confirm in the final ResultMessage that the subtype is error_max_budget_usd and not success.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: It is correct: on hitting its turn cap the subagent does not disappear, its output arrives marked as partial so whoever receives it knows it was left unfinished and the session can be resumed.

Correct as the answer to a negative item, because the statement is false: on reaching the budget cap the runtime rejects new launches with "Budget limit reached", stops the subagents running in the background and closes the query with subtype error_max_budget_usd.
It is correct: the simultaneous subagent cap does not interrupt the run, it is reported to the model as a tool result and the model can reorganize the work.
It is correct: the documentation warns that the model chooses how many subagents to launch and that their spend adds to the query's, which is why limits are advisable.

question: At Riverbank Financial, Nora launched an agent that prepares compliance reports: it reads case files, drafts findings into a working file, updates the case status in the internal system and sends the final report to the regulator. Today the agent asks for human confirmation before every action, even to write a draft, and the analysts end up approving automatically without reading. Nora wants to cut the number of confirmations without losing control over what really matters. Which escalation criterion should you implement?
options: Ask for human confirmation only when the model declares a confidence below the threshold you set in the prompt and let it execute the rest without intervention.
Group all the confirmations at the end of the flow so the analyst approves in a single screen the whole batch of actions the agent has already executed.
Ask for confirmation on actions that are hard to reverse or visible to third parties, such as sending the report to the regulator, and execute the local and reversible ones without asking.
Block the agent's execution with a hook until an analyst approves the full plan before the first tool call of the flow.
answer: Ask for confirmation on actions that are hard to reverse or visible to third parties, such as sending the report to the regulator, and execute the local and reversible ones without asking.
explanation:
The general rule is that escalation is designed by reversibility and impact, not by uniform frequency. The documentation encourages the agent to take local and reversible actions, such as editing files or running tests, and to ask before those that are hard to reverse, affect shared systems or are visible to other people. That leaves the confirmations where they add value: the submission to the regulator and the change of case status. The key distinction against asking permission for everything is that a gate which fires every time gets approved automatically and stops protecting precisely at the critical action.

RULE: Escalate by reversibility and impact: the local and reversible is executed, the irreversible or third-party-visible is confirmed.

TRAP: Confusing asking permission every time with having control: automatic approval cancels the review exactly where it matters most.

TRY IT: Classify your agent's four actions into reversible and irreversible, drop the confirmation on the former and measure how many approvals a day are left.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: Confidence declared by the model itself is not a criterion the documentation supports for routing to review, and the documented criterion looks at the impact of the action, not the model's certainty.
Reviewing in a batch reduces interruptions, but approving after execution is not control: the submission to the regulator already happened by the time the analyst looks at it.

Correct: the documentation asks you to consider reversibility and impact, letting the agent take local and reversible actions and confirming what is destructive, irreversible or affects shared systems.
Approving a plan up front is useful when the approach is uncertain, but it puts back a single indiscriminate gate and does not tell the draft apart from the submission to the regulator.

question: The monthly reconciliation at Kestrel Pay always walks through the same four steps in the same order: download the processor file, validate its format, classify the discrepancies and write the summary for finance. No case departs from that sequence and every step has an exit criterion that can be checked in code. Marcus proposes building an autonomous agent with the four tools and letting it decide the path on each run. Which design does the documentation recommend for this case?
options: Hand the agent the four tools and a system prompt with the exact order of the reconciliation, and let it decide on each run when to call each one.
Launch the four steps in parallel with subagents and ask a coordinator to combine the results at each month's close.
Apply an evaluator-optimizer pattern: one agent runs the whole process and another evaluates the final output and requests corrections.
Chain the four steps in code (prompt chaining), with a programmatic check between steps that stops the flow if one does not meet the format.
answer: Chain the four steps in code (prompt chaining), with a programmatic check between steps that stops the flow if one does not meet the format.
explanation:
The general rule of the effective agents guidance is to look for the simplest solution that solves the problem and raise complexity only when needed. A workflow with steps predefined in code is preferable to an autonomous agent whenever the sequence is known and fixed, and prompt chaining is described precisely for tasks that decompose cleanly into fixed subtasks, with programmatic checks between steps. The key distinction against the autonomous agent is that agents exist for open-ended problems where you cannot predict the number of steps, and in exchange they pay more latency, more cost and the risk of compounding errors.

RULE: If you know the steps in advance, write a workflow; save the autonomous agent for when you cannot predict how many steps are needed.

TRAP: Confusing autonomy with capability: giving decision freedom to a flow that already has a fixed path adds risk without adding value.

TRY IT: Take a fixed flow from your team, implement it as three chained calls with a code validation between them and compare cost and variability against the agent version with all the tools.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: This is the design Marcus proposes: it grants freedom nobody needs here and adds latency, cost and the possibility of the model skipping a step that must always happen.
Parallelization is for independent subtasks, but here each step consumes the previous one's output, so running them at once breaks the dependency.
That pattern pays off when there are clear criteria and iterative improvement adds measurable value, not to impose a fixed sequence that is already defined in advance.
Correct: when the task decomposes cleanly into fixed subtasks, a prompt chain with gates between steps is the indicated pattern and the simplest thing that works.

question: Falcon Labs connected six MCP servers to the same session and already has more than sixty tools loaded at once. What effect does Anthropic document for that number of tools?
options: Precision in choosing the right tool degrades above 30 to 50 tools loaded at once, on top of the context cost.
The effective limit is 128 tools per session and, until it is reached, selection behaves the same as with a handful of available tools.
The only cost is context: selection precision stays stable as long as each description is clear and specific.
Past twenty tools the model starts calling them in parallel to compensate, which raises token consumption and latency.
answer: Precision in choosing the right tool degrades above 30 to 50 tools loaded at once, on top of the context cost.
explanation:
The general rule is that more tools do not mean more capability: the definitions consume context and, above all, the precision with which the model picks the right tool falls when more than 30 to 50 are loaded at once. That is why the documentation recommends deferring definitions with tool search, splitting large catalogs across subagents and consolidating overlapping tools. The tempting option reduces the problem to context: it describes half the phenomenon correctly and omits the drop in precision.

RULE: Past 30 to 50 tools loaded at once, selection degrades: defer definitions, split across subagents or consolidate similar tools.

TRAP: Reading an excess of tools as a purely token problem and not as a decision problem for the model.

TRY IT: Connect several MCP servers to the same session until you pass fifty tools, look with /context at how much their definitions occupy and ask for an ambiguous task to compare which tool Claude picks against the same session with a single server connected.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/tool-search https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents
option_feedback: Correct: that is why tool search, splitting across subagents and consolidating similar tools all exist.
128 is the maximum length of a tool name, not a number of tools; and the degradation appears well before any hard cap.
Good descriptions help and are the first lever, but the documentation also points to a drop in precision tied to the number of loaded tools.
Parallelism depends on tool_choice and disable_parallel_tool_use, not on the size of the catalog, and it is not an automatic compensation.

question: The digitization pipeline at the City of Fairview extracts data from case files with a tool called record_case_file. Around 8 % of the calls come back with a required field missing or with the file number as text instead of an integer, and the code retries the whole call. Grant has a fixed token budget for the quarter and needs to cut those retries without losing the validations specific to the process, such as the intake date not being later than the resolution date. What should you do?
options: Raise the client's maximum number of retries and lengthen the exponential backoff between attempts to give the model more chances to get it right.
Enable strict: true on record_case_file to eliminate schema retries and leave in your code the process validations the schema does not express.
Add a second call in which Claude reviews the extracted JSON, fixes the mistyped fields and completes the missing ones before saving it to the municipal case file.
Lower the temperature to 0 and add three examples of valid JSON in the system prompt so the output format is stable across documents.
answer: Enable strict: true on record_case_file to eliminate schema retries and leave in your code the process validations the schema does not express.
explanation:
The general rule is that what the schema can guarantee is guaranteed at sampling time and what the schema cannot express is validated in your code. With strict: true the API constrains generation to inputs valid for the input_schema, so retries for missing fields or incompatible types disappear, which is exactly the 8 % Grant is paying for. Coherence checks between dates are not expressible in the supported schema, so they remain the application's responsibility. The key distinction against retrying or self-correcting is that those options spend tokens to repair a problem constrained sampling prevents before it occurs.

RULE: What the schema can guarantee is enforced with strict; what the schema does not express is validated in your own code.

TRAP: Assuming strict also checks business rules: it guarantees types and required fields, not that two dates are coherent with each other.

TRY IT: Take twenty case files that fail today, resend them with strict: true on the tool and count how many schema retries are left.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: Backoff with retries is designed for transient network or rate limit failures; a JSON that does not meet the schema will fail to meet it again and every extra attempt burns budget.
Correct: strict constrains sampling to outputs valid according to the input_schema, so no schema violation retries are needed, and business rules are still validated in your application.
The self-correction chain is useful when the problem is one of judgement or wording, but here it doubles the cost to fix something constrained sampling prevents at the root.
Examples improve consistency and a low temperature reduces variability, but not even at 0.0 is the result deterministic, and newer models reject values other than the default.

question: The compliance agent at Riverbank Financial reviews contracts with the Agent SDK and has to deliver its verdict to the audit system, which expects three fields: rule, compliant and evidence. Today the pipeline takes the agent's final text and parses it with regular expressions, and every time the agent adds a courtesy sentence or changes the order of the fields, the load fails. Dana needs the handoff to the audit system to arrive validated and without fragile parsing. What should you do?
options: Add to the system prompt the instruction to reply only with JSON, include an example of the expected format and keep parsing the agent's final text with the same script.
Pass output_format with a json_schema in the query options and read structured_output from the result message, which the SDK validates against that schema.
Register a Stop hook that takes the agent's final response and rewrites it into the three-field format the audit system expects.
Define an internal tool only the agent uses and ask it in the prompt to call it at the end of every review with the three fields as arguments.
answer: Pass output_format with a json_schema in the query options and read structured_output from the result message, which the SDK validates against that schema.
explanation:
The general rule is that a handoff between an agent and another system is defined with a contract validated by the platform, not with an implicit agreement about how the text looks. In the Agent SDK that contract is output_format with a json_schema: the SDK validates the output and asks again if it does not comply, and the result is available in structured_output, so the pipeline stops depending on the format of the final text. It is also worth treating a success result that arrives without structured_output as a failure, and allowing for the error_max_structured_output_retries subtype. The key distinction against forcing a tool is that the latter neither validates against the schema nor delivers the data in a result field.

RULE: When the agent's output feeds another system, ask for structured output with a json_schema and read structured_output; do not parse the final text.

TRAP: Confusing asking for a format in the prompt with guaranteeing it: the instruction validates nothing and the first extra sentence breaks the consumer.

TRY IT: Run a query with output_format json_schema and a three-field schema, print structured_output from the result message and test which subtype appears when the schema asks for a field the agent cannot fill.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/structured-outputs https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: It improves the hit rate, but it leaves the handoff contract in the model's hands: any extra text breaks the parsing again, which is exactly the problem to remove.
Correct: the SDK validates the output against the schema and retries if it does not fit, and the result arrives in its own field instead of having to be extracted from the final text.
A Stop hook can validate the closing or prevent the agent from finishing, but continuing to rewrite free text reproduces the fragile parsing inside the hook.

Forcing the structure with tool use is a valid technique on the raw API, but in the Agent SDK it duplicates a mechanism that already exists and neither validates the result nor exposes it in the result message.

question: The claims triage at Summit Mutual Insurance does two things in the same turn: it looks up the policy with the lookup_policy tool, which requires a properly typed policy number and date, and then it returns to the internal queue a fixed object with category, estimated_amount and needs_analyst. Maya needs both parts to always be valid, without writing repair code and without adding a second call to the model. Which configuration should you use?
options: Define a return_triage tool whose input_schema is the final object and force it with tool_choice of type tool on every triage request.
Mark lookup_policy with strict: true and ask for the final response with output_config.format of type json_schema in the same request.
Prefill the assistant turn with the opening brace of the object and cut the output with a stop sequence as soon as the JSON closes.
Describe the final object in the system prompt with an example and retry the call when the response does not parse as valid JSON.
answer: Mark lookup_policy with strict: true and ask for the final response with output_config.format of type json_schema in the same request.
explanation:
The general rule is that strict: true controls how Claude calls your tools and output_config.format controls what Claude answers, and the documentation states explicitly that they can be used independently or together in the same request. In an agentic flow like this one that provides exactly the two guarantees needed in a single turn: valid arguments for lookup_policy and a final object conforming to the schema. The key distinction against forcing an output tool is that tool_choice of type tool obliges the use of that tool and excludes any other call in the turn, so the policy lookup would disappear.

RULE: strict: true validates how Claude calls your tools; output_config.format fixes what Claude answers. You can use both in the same request.

TRAP: Reading forcing a tool as if it guaranteed the final output: tool_choice of type tool excludes the other tools from the turn.

TRY IT: Send a request with strict: true on the tool and output_config.format at the same time, and check in the response that both the tool_use block and the final object conforming to the schema appear.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
option_feedback: It is the classic pattern for getting JSON with a guaranteed shape, but forcing a specific tool obliges the model to use that one and only that one in the turn, so lookup_policy never gets called.
Correct: they are two independent features that can be combined, and together they guarantee valid tool arguments and a final response with the exact shape the queue expects.
Prefilling was the usual technique before structured outputs, but current models no longer accept a prefilled assistant turn and return a 400.
Asking for the format often works, but Maya's constraint is to write no repair code and no extra calls, and this option makes the retry part of the design.

question: Brightwater Press keeps its publishing routine in .claude/skills/publish/SKILL.md, whose frontmatter is: --- description: Publishes the day's draft to the site / allowed-tools: Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *) ---. What exactly does that allowed-tools line do?
options: During the turn in which you invoke the skill, Claude runs those commands without asking permission; the grant ends with your next message.
It restricts the skill to those two tools: while it is active, any other tool is out of Claude's reach in that session.
It adds the two rules to the project's permissions.allow permanently, exactly as if you had saved them yourself from the permissions menu.
It only documents which tools the skill expects to use; the actual permission is still decided by the permission mode active in the session.
answer: During the turn in which you invoke the skill, Claude runs those commands without asking permission; the grant ends with your next message.
explanation:
The general rule is that allowed-tools in a skill's frontmatter grants permission, not availability: the listed tools run without a prompt during the turn that invokes the skill and the grant switches off as soon as you send the next message. Anything not on the list is still governed by your permission rules and by the active mode. The key distinction against the most common reading is that the field does not restrict: to remove tools while the skill is active there is disallowed-tools.

RULE: allowed-tools auto-approves for the turn that invokes the skill; disallowed-tools is the one that removes tools from scope.

TRAP: Reading allowed-tools as a whitelist that restricts, when it only skips the prompt for what it names and leaves the rest available.

TRY IT: Create a skill with allowed-tools: Bash(git status *), invoke it and confirm the command runs without a prompt; ask for the same thing in your next message and watch it ask for permission again.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
option_feedback: Correct: allowed-tools is a permission scoped to the turn of the invocation, designed precisely so a repeated routine does not fill up with prompts.
That is what disallowed-tools does, which does remove tools from the available set; allowed-tools limits nothing, it only skips the prompt for the ones it names.
Nothing is written to your configuration: the permission lives for the duration of the turn and does not appear in .claude/settings.json or in the local file.
The field is not documentation: it grants real permission in that turn, although for anything not listed your rules and the active mode do still apply.

question: Riverbank Financial runs a contract review overnight with the Agent SDK. The reviewer subagent is defined with permissionMode dontAsk in its AgentDefinition, precisely so it never interrupts the run, and the main session starts in acceptEdits because it also applies patches to the policy repository. Even so, the run sits waiting for approvals of tools launched by the subagent and by morning it has not finished. What is the most likely cause?
options: The dontAsk mode only covers file tools; MCP tools always go through the can_use_tool callback before running, regardless of the mode.
The subagent runs in the parent's mode: its permissionMode only applies if the parent session is in default, dontAsk or plan, and acceptEdits is not on that list.
The subagent inherits allowed_tools from the parent and any tool not on that list is blocked until somebody approves it by hand from the console.
The subagent's permissions are evaluated twice, once in its own session and once in the parent's, which is why extra prompts appear in long runs.
answer: The subagent runs in the parent's mode: its permissionMode only applies if the parent session is in default, dontAsk or plan, and acceptEdits is not on that list.
explanation:
The general rule is that a subagent runs in the parent session's permission mode, and the permissionMode of its AgentDefinition only replaces it when the parent is in default, dontAsk or plan. The nightly session starts in acceptEdits, which is not on that list, so the subagent's dontAsk never applies and tools that are not pre-approved end up asking for approval. The key distinction against the other explanations is that what fails here is neither the tool list nor the callback, but the condition under which the mode declared in the definition takes effect. As a related point, Claude Code also never applies a bypassPermissions value declared in an AgentDefinition.

RULE: An AgentDefinition's permissionMode only rules if the parent session is in default, dontAsk or plan; in any other mode the subagent inherits the parent's.

TRAP: Assuming what is declared in the subagent definition always beats the state of the session that launches it.

TRY IT: Define a subagent with permissionMode dontAsk, launch the same task with the parent session in default and then in acceptEdits, and compare in which of the two permission prompts appear.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: It mixes two things: dontAsk does not distinguish by tool type and, in fact, in that mode the callback is not even called, because anything not pre-approved is denied.
Correct: with the parent in acceptEdits, the AgentDefinition's permissionMode is ignored and the subagent inherits the main session's mode, which does ask for approvals.
allowed_tools auto-approves, it does not restrict, and anything not listed falls into the normal permission evaluation; besides, it is not what decides the subagent's behaviour here.
It is true that subagent prompts multiply and that auto-approving with hooks or rules is advisable, but there is no double per-session evaluation that explains the block.

question: Southline Logistics exposes its legacy tracking system through an MCP server. The mcp__tracking__get_shipment tool only accepts the tracking number in upper case and with the SL prefix, but the agent calls it with the number exactly as the customer typed it and the lookup fails in one out of every five conversations. Maya wants the correction to always happen, without depending on the model remembering the format and without spending a turn on the retry. What should you do?
options: Expand the tool description with three or four sentences explaining the exact format of the tracking number, with one valid and one invalid example so the model tells them apart.
Register a PostToolUse hook that detects the format failure and rewrites the output with updatedToolOutput so the model understands what happened and retries.
Register a PreToolUse hook with matcher mcp__tracking__get_shipment that normalizes the number and returns it in updatedInput inside hookSpecificOutput.
Return from the tool a tool_result with is_error set to true and a message stating the correct format, so the agent retries with the number written properly.
answer: Register a PreToolUse hook with matcher mcp__tracking__get_shipment that normalizes the number and returns it in updatedInput inside hookSpecificOutput.
explanation:
The general rule is that data normalization that must always happen is done in a PreToolUse hook, which runs before each tool call and can replace the arguments through updatedInput inside hookSpecificOutput. That way the agent never emits a malformed call and no turn is spent discovering the error. The key distinction against the tool_result with is_error is one of timing: the instructive error is for failures you cannot anticipate, while a known, deterministic format is corrected before executing. It is also best to return a new object in updatedInput instead of mutating the original tool_input.

RULE: What can be normalized deterministically is fixed in PreToolUse with updatedInput; what is only discovered at execution time is reported with an error tool_result.

TRAP: Reading PostToolUse as if it could fix the input: by the time that hook runs, the call with the bad arguments has already executed.

TRY IT: Register a PreToolUse hook with a matcher for one of your tools that upper-cases the argument in updatedInput, ask the agent to call it in lower case and check in the log which value the tool received.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks
option_feedback: A good description greatly reduces format errors and is worth having, but it remains a hint to the model: it lowers the frequency of the problem without eliminating it.
PostToolUse runs after the tool executes, when the call with the malformed number has already failed: it can improve the message, but it does not avoid the wasted call.
Correct: the hook runs before the tool executes and hands over the already normalized input, so the call always goes out well formed and with no wasted turns.
An instructive error is the right way to communicate a real failure and helps the agent recover, but it accepts that one in five lookups spends an extra turn.

question: Cascade Power keeps its switching manuals in the repository as PDFs, some of them over a hundred pages long. How does the Read tool work with a file like that?
options: It does not open it: Read only accepts text files, so the PDF has to be converted first with a Bash command and the result read instead.
It returns it in full in a single call, with line numbers, just as it would with a project source file.
It returns only the metadata and a page index so you can choose which page to extract later with another project tool.
It reads it by ranges with the pages parameter, up to twenty pages per call, because the PDF is longer than ten pages.
answer: It reads it by ranges with the pages parameter, up to twenty pages per call, because the PDF is longer than ten pages.
explanation:
The general rule is that Read is not only for code: it returns images as visual content, reads notebooks with their outputs and opens PDFs. For long documents the reading is paginated: PDFs of more than ten pages are read by ranges with the pages parameter, up to twenty pages per call, which keeps the context bounded. The alternative of converting the file through Bash duplicates the work and adds a permission prompt the dedicated tool does not need.

RULE: Read opens text, images, notebooks and PDFs; if the PDF is longer than ten pages, it is read by ranges with pages, up to twenty per call.

TRAP: Assuming Read is a cat with line numbers and setting up a Bash conversion for something the tool already does.

TRY IT: Put a PDF of more than a hundred pages in the project, ask Claude to summarize a section near the end and watch the Read call include the pages parameter with a bounded range instead of reading the whole file.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
option_feedback: Read is not limited to plain text: it also returns images as visual content and reads PDFs and notebooks with no prior conversion.
Short PDFs are indeed read whole, but a hundred-page one does not fit at once: past ten pages reading switches to ranges.
There is no index step: Read delivers the content of the pages you ask for, and it is Claude that decides which range to read next.
Correct: short PDFs are read whole and long ones by bounded ranges, which also avoids filling the context with an entire manual.

question: Marcus has spent two hours in the same Claude Code session on the Lakeside Online University monorepo. He opened dozens of files to understand the enrollment module, corrected the same misunderstanding about where the validation lives three times, and now Claude is again proposing changes they had already ruled out and mentioning paths that do not exist. Neither the model nor the project rules changed during the session. What is the most likely cause?
options: The context accumulated exploration dumps and contradictory corrections, and as tokens grow the retrieval of what is relevant degrades.
The project CLAUDE.md is no longer in context because memory files are discarded once the conversation passes a certain size.
The model exhausted its context window and the API returned a prompt-too-long error the client never managed to display.
The read tools returned relative paths and the model cannot resolve them without an absolute path to the repository.
answer: The context accumulated exploration dumps and contradictory corrections, and as tokens grow the retrieval of what is relevant degrades.
explanation:
The general rule is that more context is not better context: as the number of tokens grows, precision and recall degrade, a phenomenon described as context rot, and irrelevant content competes for the model's attention. A two-hour session with massive exploration and three corrections on the same point is exactly that scenario, and the best practices guidance recommends clearing the session and starting again with a more specific prompt when you have corrected the same thing more than twice. The key distinction against the other causes is that there is no error and no lost configuration here: the material is still in context, but it stops guiding the answer.

RULE: If you correct the same thing more than twice, the problem is no longer the next prompt: clear the context and start with a more specific one.

TRAP: Assuming a long session is an informed session: what has accumulated competes with what is relevant and degrades recall.

TRY IT: In a long session ask for a summary of the state, run /clear and repeat the same task with a specific prompt; compare the quality of the two responses.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation describes how, as tokens in the window increase, the ability to recall precisely what is in it falls, and it recommends starting clean after two failed corrections.
The root CLAUDE.md survives compaction and Claude reads it again from disk, so it is not what gets lost in a long session.
That overflow shows up as an explicit error or as a context-exceeded stop reason, not as fluent responses that contradict what was already decided.
Requiring absolute paths is good interface design advice for agents, but it does not explain reopening a decision that was ruled out three times.

question: Southline Logistics exposes its tracking system with an MCP server. When asking for the week's shipments, the session shows: the result of mcp__tracking__list_shipments exceeded the maximum allowed tokens, it was saved to the session's tool-results directory and replaced by the file path. The agent is left with no data to continue and Erin needs a solution that holds up under daily use. What should be done?
options: Export MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS with a high value so the full response fits into the conversation instead of going to a file.
Redesign the tool with filters and pagination, and return only the fields the agent needs to decide the next step.
Ask Claude to open the file saved in tool-results with Read and continue the analysis from that content.
Declare in the tool the metadata field that raises the result character cap to its maximum allowed per server.
answer: Redesign the tool with filters and pagination, and return only the fields the agent needs to decide the next step.
explanation:
The general rule is that the output limit of MCP tools is not an obstacle to be lifted but a signal that the tool returns more than the agent can use. The tool design documentation asks you to return high-signal information and to control size with pagination, filters and field selection, with sensible defaults. Raising the maximum or rereading the saved file solve today's symptom and move the same volume into the context, which is the scarce resource; redesigning the response solves it at the source and durably.

RULE: When an MCP tool hits the output limit, shrink the response with filters, pagination and useful fields before enlarging the limit.

TRAP: Mistaking a configuration cap for the problem: raising MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS moves the dump into the context instead of removing it.

TRY IT: Add a status filter and a default limit of twenty results to the tool, repeat the same request and compare with /context how much the response now occupies.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents
option_feedback: The limit is configurable and useful for one-off cases, but raising it pushes thousands of irrelevant rows into the context and worsens the agent's attention on every call.
Correct: the response stops being a dump of the legacy system and becomes high-signal information, with a stable size call after call.
It is a valid one-off way out, but it loads the same volume into the context through another door and does not stop the problem from repeating tomorrow.
That per-tool setting exists and raises the ceiling, but it is the same strategy as A: enlarging the container instead of reducing what the tool returns.

question: Brightwater Press has a root CLAUDE.md with the site's general conventions and a file .claude/rules/editorial-style.md whose frontmatter limits the rule to the articles in content with the mdx extension. During the first hour of the session Claude respects the editorial guide. After a long compaction, it still applies the general conventions but goes back to writing headlines in the old style. What explains the change?
options: Compaction discards all instruction context, so neither the CLAUDE.md nor the rules come back until you restart the session.
The root CLAUDE.md is reread from disk after compacting, whereas a rule with paths only returns once Claude reads a matching file again.
Rules with paths have lower priority than the CLAUDE.md, and as context shrinks compaction preserves the higher priority material first.
The glob stopped matching because after compacting Claude resolves relative paths against the rule file and not against the project root.
answer: The root CLAUDE.md is reread from disk after compacting, whereas a rule with paths only returns once Claude reads a matching file again.
explanation:
The general rule is that each piece of instruction comes back after a compaction through its own trigger. The root CLAUDE.md and rules without paths are reread from disk immediately; a rule with paths, by contrast, is conditional loading and reappears when Claude reads a file matching the pattern again. That is why the symptom is asymmetric: the general conventions are still present and the editorial guide is not. The key distinction against the priority option is that there is no conflict between rules here: there is one that has not been triggered yet.

RULE: After compacting, the root CLAUDE.md and rules without paths come back on their own; a rule with paths waits for a matching file to be read again.

TRAP: Assuming everything that was in context reappears the same after compacting, when conditional material reloads through its trigger.

TRY IT: Create a rule in .claude/rules/ with paths limited to one extension, work until you force a compaction with /compact and confirm with /context that the root CLAUDE.md came back on its own while the rule only reappears when you open a file matching the glob again.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: The root CLAUDE.md and rules without paths survive compaction because Claude reads them from disk again; the forgetting is selective, not general.
Correct: conditional loading is triggered by reading files that match the glob, and compaction is not one of those triggers.
Priority decides which instruction wins when two contradict each other, not what survives a compaction: what decides here is the load trigger.
paths patterns are always interpreted the same way, against the project root, and compaction does not change how they resolve.

question: Northlane Outfitters split its returns agent into three subagents the main agent launches in every conversation: one verifies the purchase, another applies the exchange policy and another issues the label. Since the change, responses take considerably longer, the customer has to repeat the order number and the main agent explains the whole case again on every delegation. None of the three produces voluminous output. What is the most likely cause?
options: The subagent model is slower than the main agent's, so model inherit has to be set in every AgentDefinition to match them.
Subagents run in the background by default, and the main agent answers the customer without waiting for the result of the phase it just delegated.
The three phases share context and require back and forth with the customer: that work belongs in the main conversation, because a subagent starts with no history.
The parallel subagent limit is queueing Northlane's launches, and each phase waits its turn before it can run against the order system.
answer: The three phases share context and require back and forth with the customer: that work belongs in the main conversation, because a subagent starts with no history.
explanation:
The general rule is that a subagent is worthwhile when the task is autonomous, produces voluminous output you do not want in the main context and can be returned as a summary. The documentation says the opposite for this case: work with frequent back and forth, phases that share a lot of context and situations where latency matters, because the subagent starts with an empty context and needs time to gather what the main agent already knew. That explains all three symptoms at once: more delay, context asked for again and the case repeated on every delegation. The key distinction against the infrastructure explanations is that no runtime limit is failing here, but the decision to decompose.

RULE: Delegate what is autonomous and voluminous; leave in the main conversation what needs iteration and shared context.

TRAP: Assuming decomposing always improves things: if each phase needs the previous one's context, delegation adds latency and information loss instead of isolating noise.

TRY IT: Take a conversational flow you split into subagents, merge two phases back into the main conversation and compare time to first response and how often a piece of data is asked for twice.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: Pinning the model affects latency per response, but it explains neither the repeated question to the customer nor the need to retell the case at every step.
It is true that background is the default behaviour, but Claude asks for foreground execution when it needs the result to continue, so it does not produce this picture.
Correct: the documentation reserves subagents for autonomous work that returns a summary and recommends the main conversation when there is iteration and shared context.
The concurrency cap returns an explicit notice as the result of the Agent tool (formerly Task) and here they are launched one at a time per conversation, so there is no queue to justify the delay.

question: The nightly pipeline at Heartland Agronomics launches, for each farm, a subagent that reads thousands of lines of sensor logs and returns a three-paragraph summary to the coordinator. The summary is exactly what the report needs and the team does not want to change the decomposition, but that mechanical reading consumes most of the process tokens and the monthly bill has doubled. Ben has to cut the cost of that stage without losing the summary or the parallelization. What should be done?
options: Set max_budget_usd on the query so the run stops as soon as the estimated cost of the whole tree reaches the monthly cap finance set.
Lower the subagent's maxTurns to two so it reads fewer lines per run and finishes before accumulating so much consumption in its context window.
Remove the subagent and have the coordinator read each farm's logs in its own context window, which is already open for the whole run.
Set model haiku in that subagent's AgentDefinition and route the voluminous work to a faster, cheaper model.
answer: Set model haiku in that subagent's AgentDefinition and route the voluminous work to a faster, cheaper model.
explanation:
The general rule is that each subagent can run with its own model, and that is precisely the documented lever for controlling cost: routing bounded, mechanical tasks to faster and cheaper models while the coordinator keeps the strong model for synthesis.
