Here the expensive stage is a massive read with short output, the typical case for Haiku, and the change touches neither the decomposition nor the parallelism. The key distinction against max_budget_usd is that a budget does not reduce the spend of each task, it only stops the run when the cap is reached and returns a result with subtype error_max_budget_usd.

RULE: To cut the cost of a stage, change that stage's model; the query budget is a brake, not a saving.

TRAP: Confusing limiting spend with reducing it: max_budget_usd and maxTurns cut work, they do not make it cheaper.

TRY IT: Run the same summarization task with model sonnet and with model haiku in the AgentDefinition and compare total_cost_usd and the quality of the summary over the same batch of logs.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents
option_feedback: A budget is good production practice, but it is an emergency brake: it cuts the run with error_max_budget_usd instead of making the work that has to be done cheaper.
Trimming turns does not make the reading cheaper, it truncates it: the subagent hits the limit and returns output marked as partial, so the summary stops being reliable.
That moves thousands of lines into the coordinator's context, which is what the decomposition was avoiding, and it also loses the parallelism across farms.
Correct: the model field in the definition lets you route mechanical tasks to a cheaper model, which is the cost control the documentation associates with subagents.

question: Brightwater Press is reorganizing its conventions in the project's .claude/rules/ directory: some apply to the whole repository and others only to the site templates. Before splitting the content, Hannah wants to be sure how those files are loaded. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?
options: Files without paths frontmatter are loaded at the start of the session, with the same priority as a project .claude/CLAUDE.md.
All .md files are discovered recursively, so you can group rules into subfolders inside .claude/rules/.
Rules with paths are also loaded at startup and the glob only decides which files the already-loaded instructions apply to.
Rules in ~/.claude/rules/ are loaded before the project ones, so the project ones end up with higher priority.
answer: Rules with paths are also loaded at startup and the glob only decides which files the already-loaded instructions apply to.
explanation:
The general rule is that paths frontmatter turns a file in .claude/rules/ into conditional loading: the rule enters context when Claude works with files matching the glob, and not before. That is precisely the advantage over putting everything in the root CLAUDE.md, because the startup context does not grow with instructions that are not needed today. The other three statements describe the mechanism correctly: without paths the rule is permanent, discovery is recursive, and user rules load before project ones.

RULE: The paths glob decides when the rule is loaded, not only which files it applies to once loaded.

TRAP: Reading paths as an application filter over instructions already present, instead of as the condition that triggers their loading.

TRY IT: Put two files in .claude/rules/, one without frontmatter and one with paths limited to a folder, open a new session and compare in /context which of the two appears loaded before you touch any project file.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: It is correct: a rule without paths is permanent context, which is why it should be reserved for what applies to the whole repository.
It is correct: discovery walks subdirectories, which lets you separate by area without losing automatic loading.
This is the false statement: the glob decides when the rule is loaded, not only what it applies to; until Claude reads a matching file, that rule is not in context.
It is correct: user rules apply across all your projects and the project can adjust them because it loads afterwards.

question: Summit Mutual Insurance automated the quality gate of its triage. Three Claude calls evaluate each case: one writes a prose verdict on the classification, another comments on the cited evidence and the third gives an opinion on the tone of the summary. A script sends the case to human review when any of the three texts looks negative to it. The notes change from one run to the next on the same case and the analysts keep finding errors in cases the gate let through. What is the most likely cause of the inconsistency?
options: The judge needs a lower temperature, because with the default value two evaluations of the same case diverge between runs.
The threshold the script uses to flag a case was set too high, which is why doubtful cases never reach the claims analysts' queue.
The evaluation has no explicit rubric and no comparable output, so three prose verdicts do not produce a stable score across runs.
Three parallel calls are too few to vote and more instances evaluating the case are needed for the verdict to stabilize.
answer: The evaluation has no explicit rubric and no comparable output, so three prose verdicts do not produce a stable score across runs.
explanation:
The general rule is that an automated evaluator needs detailed criteria and a comparable output in order to be calibrated. The published lessons on evaluation with models indicate that the most consistent setup was a single call with one prompt returning a score from 0.0 to 1.0 and a pass or fail verdict, against a clear rubric of dimensions such as factual accuracy, citation precision and completeness. Three prose verdicts are comparable neither with each other nor across runs, so the gate cannot be calibrated against the cases the analysts have already reviewed. The key distinction against adding more votes is that the problem is not the number of opinions but the absence of criteria and of a scale.

RULE: An automated judge needs a detailed rubric and comparable output: a single call with a score and a verdict, not three prose opinions.

TRAP: Confusing more instances evaluating with better evaluation: without explicit criteria, each vote measures something different.

TRY IT: Take ten cases already reviewed by analysts, run them through a single judge with a rubric and an output of 0.0 to 1.0 plus pass or fail, and measure the agreement with the current gate.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests
option_feedback: Temperature affects sampling variability, but not even at 0.0 is the result fully deterministic and newer models reject values other than the default; the problem lies in the design of the evaluation.
There is no threshold to tune here: the script interprets free text, so there is no number to raise or lower while the output is not comparable.
Correct: the most consistent documented configuration is a single call with a detailed rubric that returns a score from 0.0 to 1.0 plus a pass or fail.
Voting helps gain confidence through multiple perspectives, but without explicit criteria each vote measures something different and adding instances only adds noise.

question: To redesign the publishing pipeline, Brightwater Press starts the session with: claude --permission-mode plan "Propose how to migrate the site to the new template". The work will take several hours and there will probably be at least one compaction along the way. Which two statements correctly describe that session? (Select TWO)
options: Claude will not be able to run any shell command until you approve the plan, because the mode blocks all execution.
Claude investigates by reading files and running exploration commands, but it does not edit your sources until you approve the plan.
The approved plan is saved and reinjected after a compaction, so it survives the long session.
Leaving the mode with the mode-switch shortcut is equivalent to approving the plan and enables the edits it proposed.
The Plan subagent that investigates during the mode shares the context window of the main conversation.
answer: Claude investigates by reading files and running exploration commands, but it does not edit your sources until you approve the plan.
The approved plan is saved and reinjected after a compaction, so it survives the long session.
explanation:
The general rule is that plan mode separates investigating from executing: Claude can read and explore with commands, but it does not touch your sources until you approve the plan, and approval is an explicit act of the dialogue, not an effect of leaving the mode. The second property is what makes it useful in long sessions: the plan is written down and reinjected after compaction, just like the root CLAUDE.md, so the agreement on scope is not lost halfway through the work. The exploration, moreover, runs in the Plan subagent's context and comes back summarized.

RULE: In plan mode Claude investigates and proposes without editing; approving the plan is an explicit act and the approved plan survives compaction.

TRAP: Confusing leaving the mode with approving the plan, and assuming the mode also forbids reading and exploring.

TRY IT: Start with --permission-mode plan, ask for a specific change, leave the mode with the shortcut without approving and check with git status that no file was modified.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window
option_feedback: The mode prevents modifying your sources, not exploring: Claude reads files and runs exploration commands to understand the project before proposing.
Correct: that is the definition of the mode, investigate and propose changes without applying them, which is why it is the entry mode for work of uncertain scope.
Correct: along with the root CLAUDE.md, the written plan is one of the pieces Claude recovers from disk when the context is compacted.
Leaving with the shortcut abandons the mode without approving anything; approval is given in the plan dialog, where you also choose how the edits will be applied.
That subagent works in its own context and returns a summary, which is precisely what avoids filling the conversation with the exploration.

question: Southline Logistics implements its own loop against the Messages API for a rates agent. On some runs the loop stops without any tool being executed: the response arrives with HTTP 200, there is no 4xx or 5xx error in the logs, and its last block is a tool_use whose input JSON is cut off halfway. Derek checks the stop_reason field to decide how to continue. What is the cause and the right correction?
options: The server's sampling loop reached its iteration limit running server tools and the API marked it with pause_turn, so the response should be resent as is to continue the turn.
A safety classifier declined the generation and the API marked it with refusal, so stop_details has to be read to see the category and the request retried on a fallback model.
The conversation exceeded the context window and the API marked it with model_context_window_exceeded, so the history has to be compacted and the request resent with fewer messages.
Generation was cut off on reaching the output cap and the API marked it with max_tokens, leaving an incomplete tool_use: it has to be retried with a larger max_tokens.
answer: Generation was cut off on reaching the output cap and the API marked it with max_tokens, leaving an incomplete tool_use: it has to be retried with a larger max_tokens.
explanation:
The general rule is that stop_reason does not signal a system failure but the reason Claude stopped generating, and each value has its own handling. A tool_use block cut off halfway is produced only by the turn's output cap: the response is truncated, there is no tool to execute and no tool_result to return, and the only documented way out is to repeat the request with a higher token limit. The key distinction against pause_turn is that this value appears when the server pauses a long server tool turn and the continuation is to resend the response as is, with no client tool left half written.

RULE: Always read stop_reason before deciding the recovery: max_tokens is retried with more tokens and pause_turn is continued by resending the response as is.

TRAP: Treating a truncated response as a network or server error: it arrives with HTTP 200 and no identical retry completes it.

TRY IT: Call the Messages API with tools and a deliberately low max_tokens, check the stop_reason and the last block of the response, and repeat the same request with a larger max_tokens.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons
option_feedback: pause_turn appears when the server's own server tool loop reaches its iteration limit and the continuation is to resend the response unchanged; a response leaving a client tool half written never arrives with that value.
refusal also comes as HTTP 200 and is therefore tempting, but it corresponds to a generation declined for safety, not to a block cut off halfway; stop_details is null for any other stop reason.

model_context_window_exceeded also leaves the response truncated, but it is triggered by the size of the history and not by the turn's output cap, so it is fixed by trimming the input and not by raising the limit.

Correct: a tool_use cut off in the middle of the input JSON is the signature of max_tokens, and with that truncated block there is nothing to execute and no tool_result to return, so the documentation says to retry with a higher token limit.

question: The root CLAUDE.md at Brightwater Press includes these three lines: "Format the code properly", "IMPORTANT: never edit .env or the deployment files" and "Run npm test before every commit". Even so, code style keeps varying between sessions and at some point Claude edited the .env. Which two changes does the documentation recommend? (Select TWO)
options: Mark the three lines with IMPORTANT so none of them falls below the model's attention threshold.
Move the three lines into .claude/rules/ files with paths so they load only when appropriate.
Import the content with a reference to another file so the startup context is lighter.
Replace "Format the code properly" with a concrete, verifiable instruction stating the exact formatter and indentation.
Move the ban on touching the .env into a PreToolUse hook, because CLAUDE.md is context and not enforced configuration.
answer: Replace "Format the code properly" with a concrete, verifiable instruction stating the exact formatter and indentation.
Move the ban on touching the .env into a PreToolUse hook, because CLAUDE.md is context and not enforced configuration.
explanation:
The general rule is that CLAUDE.md holds facts and conventions the model must keep in mind, written concretely and verifiably, and that anything which must hold without exception is enforced in code. Hence the two fixes: turning a vague instruction into a checkable one, and moving the ban into a PreToolUse hook, which runs before every tool call and does not depend on the model remembering it. The key distinction against emphasis is that underlining many lines dilutes attention instead of concentrating it.

RULE: In CLAUDE.md write rules you can verify; whatever must always hold is enforced with a hook, not with capitals.

TRAP: Confusing emphasis with guarantee: repeating IMPORTANT on several lines weakens all of them and still blocks nothing.

TRY IT: Register a PreToolUse hook with matcher Edit|Write that exits with code 2 when the path is .env, and ask Claude to edit that file to see the block.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory https://code.claude.com/docs/en/features-overview
option_feedback: Emphasis works when it flags a single rule that keeps being skipped; if you emphasize many lines, none stands out and the effect is lost.
Rules with paths are the answer when a convention applies to part of the code; these three apply to the whole repository.
Imports organize the material, but they do not reduce context: the imported file is expanded and loaded all the same when the session starts.
Correct: an instruction you cannot check does not change behaviour; the documentation asks for concrete rules such as the indentation or the exact command.
Correct: to block an action without exceptions you need a hook, which always runs; the line in capitals remains a piece of advice.

question: The research system at Lakeside Online University produces syntheses with citations for the tutors. The quality rubric is already written and explicit: factual accuracy, citation accuracy, topic coverage and source quality. In internal testing, when a human reviewer points out what a draft is missing, the second version improves clearly and measurably. Erin wants to automate that cycle without losing that gain. Which multi-agent design applies?
options: Apply voting: run the same synthesis three times in parallel with different prompts and keep the version that agrees with the other two on the most points.
Expand the writer agent's prompt with the full rubric and three examples of approved syntheses so it aims at the standard from the first draft.
Set up an evaluator-optimizer loop: one agent writes the synthesis and another evaluates it against the rubric and returns concrete corrections until it passes.
Add at the end of the flow a citations subagent that walks the already written text and adds the references corresponding to each statement in the draft.
answer: Set up an evaluator-optimizer loop: one agent writes the synthesis and another evaluates it against the rubric and returns concrete corrections until it passes.
explanation:
The general rule is that the pattern is chosen by the shape of the problem, not by the number of agents. The evaluator-optimizer is indicated when there are clear evaluation criteria and when iterative improvement adds measurable value, and its two fit signals are exactly the ones the team observed: responses improve when someone articulates the feedback, and that judgement can be expressed in a rubric another model can apply. The key distinction against voting is what happens to the attempts: voting generates several independent outputs and chooses, whereas here you want to refine the same output until it meets the standard.

RULE: With clear criteria and demonstrable improvement on receiving feedback, use evaluator-optimizer; voting is for gaining confidence through independent attempts.

TRAP: Confusing parallelizing with iterating: running the same task several times does not replace a cycle of critique and correction against a rubric.

TRY IT: Write the rubric as the prompt of an evaluator that returns a list of gaps and a pass or reject, and measure across twenty cases how many iterations the writer needs to pass.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system
option_feedback: Voting helps gain confidence through several attempts or perspectives, but it chooses among independent drafts instead of improving one against a known rubric.
It is a reasonable improvement to the first attempt, but it does not capture what the team measured: the gain appears when somebody points out the concrete gaps in that draft.
Correct: there are clear evaluation criteria and evidence that articulated feedback improves the result, which are the two documented signals for this pattern.
A citations agent at the close is part of the documented research system, but it covers only one of the four rubric dimensions and generates no iteration.

question: To debug its pipeline traces, Falcon Labs changes the Messages API call and leaves the tools configuration like this: "tool_choice": {"type": "auto", "disable_parallel_tool_use": true}. The available tools are still the same. Which two behaviours should you expect in the model's responses? (Select TWO)
options: There will be exactly one tool call in every response, with no possibility of the model answering with text only.
There will be at most one tool call per response, so chaining several requires several turns.
The model will no longer be able to write text before the tool_use block, because the configuration prefills the assistant message.
The model can answer without calling any tool when it considers it unnecessary, because auto leaves that decision to it.
The tool_result blocks may be sent in separate user messages, one per call, since there is no parallelism.
answer: There will be at most one tool call per response, so chaining several requires several turns.
The model can answer without calling any tool when it considers it unnecessary, because auto leaves that decision to it.
explanation:
The general rule is that tool_choice and disable_parallel_tool_use control different things: the first decides whether the model is obliged to use a tool and the second how many calls it can emit in a single response. With auto the model keeps the decision not to call anything, and disabling parallelism makes the cap one call per response. That is why the combination is at most one, not exactly one: that change to exactly one is what any or tool would produce, and they also prefill the response and suppress preceding text.

RULE: auto decides whether a tool is used and disable_parallel_tool_use how many fit per response: with auto, at most one; with any or tool, exactly one.

TRAP: Reading the disabling of parallelism as an obligation to call a tool, mixing the count with the requirement.

TRY IT: Send the same request with and without disable_parallel_tool_use and count the tool_use blocks in each response; repeat swapping auto for any to see the difference.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/parallel-tool-use https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
option_feedback: That happens with any or with tool, which force tool use; with auto there is no obligation and the minimum can be zero calls.
Correct: the parameter disables parallelism, and with auto the result is a cap of one call per response instead of a fixed number.
The prefill happens with any and with tool, not with auto: here the model can explain what it is going to do before calling the tool.
Correct: auto is the default value when tools are present and it keeps the decision to use them with the model.
The format does not change: every tool_result comes back in a single user message and before any text block.

question: Cascade Power connected an MCP server called ops to Claude Code, with high-impact tools such as schedule_outage and close_work_order. To audit every call, Marcus adds a PreToolUse hook whose matcher is mcp__ops and tests it by asking for a switching operation. The hook log stays empty even though the tool did run. What is going on?
options: The matcher is compared as exact text and no tool is called that; to reach the whole server you have to write mcp__ops__.* as the matcher.
The matcher is correct and reaches every tool on the server, but PreToolUse hooks do not fire with MCP tools, only with built-in tools.
The hook fires only with the first tool from the server Claude uses in the session, and later calls no longer trigger it.
The matcher is invalid and Claude Code discards the hook at session start, showing a configuration error on startup.
answer: The matcher is compared as exact text and no tool is called that; to reach the whole server you have to write mcp__ops__.* as the matcher.
explanation:
The general rule is that in hook matchers the tool name is written in full, in the format mcp__server__tool, and to cover a whole server you use a regular expression with the server prefix. A matcher that only names the server is compared as exact text and matches no tool, so the hook stays installed but never runs. The key distinction against permission rules is that there the server name alone does reach all its tools: the syntax of one place does not carry over to the other.

RULE: In hook matchers MCP names go in full: mcp__server__tool, and for a whole server you write it as a regular expression with that prefix.

TRAP: Carrying over the syntax of permission rules, where the server name reaches all its tools, to hook matchers, which do not accept it.

TRY IT: Add a PreToolUse hook with the bare mcp__server matcher, request a tool from that MCP server and check that the log stays empty; then change the matcher to mcp__server__.* and repeat the same request to see it fire.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions
option_feedback: Correct: the real name is mcp__ops__schedule_outage, and the matcher only reaches the whole server when written as a regular expression.
Hooks do fire with MCP tools: the documentation's example uses exactly that kind of matcher to audit an entire server.
There is no one-time rule for hooks; what does exist is the once field, which has to be declared explicitly.
The matcher is syntactically valid, it simply matches nothing; that is why there is no visible error and the hook looks installed but never runs.

question: Erin is about to enable structured outputs on the City of Fairview case file extraction. Her schema declares fourteen properties and leaves twelve out of required, because many case files do not carry every field, and it allows additional properties so no unexpected fields are lost. She wants the object reaching the permits system to always be valid and as cheap as possible to compile. What should you do with the schema?
options: Leave additionalProperties as true to keep the unexpected fields and filter out the ones you do not recognize afterwards in your own code.
Keep the twelve fields optional and add a free-text field where the model explains which data did not appear in the case file.
Nest the infrequent fields in a secondary object so the main schema stays short and the model fills it only if it applies.
Declare additionalProperties as false in every object and move the fields into required, with an explicit value such as not stated when the data does not appear.
answer: Declare additionalProperties as false in every object and move the fields into required, with an explicit value such as not stated when the data does not appear.
explanation:
The general rule is that a schema for structured outputs is designed closed and with few optionals. The documentation requires additionalProperties to be false for objects and warns that every parameter not in required duplicates part of the grammar's state space, so it recommends making them required and asking the model itself to supply the default value. That way the object always reaches the permits system complete and the grammar compiles faster. The key distinction against keeping the fields optional is that the absence of a value is represented as an explicit value, not as a property that is sometimes there and sometimes not.

RULE: In structured outputs additionalProperties is false and optionality is expensive: make fields required and ask for an explicit value for what is missing.

TRAP: Assuming leaving fields optional is being more flexible: it makes the grammar costlier and additionalProperties other than false returns a 400.

TRY IT: Send your current schema with output_config.format and observe the 400 pointing at additionalProperties, fix it to false and compare the latency of the first compilation.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: That flexibility is valid in open extraction without structured outputs, but here additionalProperties other than false is unsupported and the request returns a 400.
It looks natural, but every optional parameter multiplies part of the grammar's state space, and the text field provides no validity guarantee.
Nesting objects with optional fields is exactly what the documentation asks you to avoid, because complexity compounds; the recommendation is to flatten the structure.
Correct: additionalProperties must be false in the objects and the guidance recommends reducing optional parameters by having Claude return an explicit default value.

question: Brightwater Press created .claude/skills/style-review/SKILL.md with this frontmatter: --- description: Reviews the style of the article / context: fork --- and a body that starts with the sentence "review the article we just edited and adjust the tone". When invoked with the slash command after half an hour working on a post, the result talks about some unrelated article. Why?
options: Because context: fork also requires declaring the subagent type in the frontmatter, and without that line the skill runs with a read-only agent.
Because the skill runs in the background and what appears on invoking it is a provisional result that completes on the next turn.
Because context: fork runs the body as the prompt of a subagent that does not see the history; the file has to be named in the skill or passed as an argument.
Because invoking the skill with no arguments leaves the argument placeholder empty and the subagent reads the request as a generic review.
answer: Because context: fork runs the body as the prompt of a subagent that does not see the history; the file has to be named in the skill or passed as an argument.
explanation:
The general rule is that context: fork turns the skill into a subagent's task: the body of the SKILL.md becomes its prompt and that subagent starts in its own context, without your conversation history. That is what makes it cheap in context and also what forces you to write it self-sufficiently, with explicit paths or arguments instead of references to what was just done. The most tempting alternative, background execution, describes a real property of the fork, but it affects when the result arrives, not its content.

RULE: A skill with context: fork has to be self-sufficient: the subagent only reads the body and its arguments, never your conversation.

TRAP: Assuming a fork inherits the conversation because you launch it from there: the body of the skill is all the context it receives.

TRY IT: Add argument-hint to the skill, invoke it passing the file path and compare the result with the version that only says the article we just edited.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
option_feedback: The agent type is optional and has a general-purpose default; the problem is not which agent runs but which context it receives.
It is true that a skill with fork runs in the background by default and that you can wait for it, but that changes when the result arrives, not which article it talks about.
Correct: the fork isolates the context, so a reference such as the article we just edited means nothing to the subagent.
An empty placeholder would be a problem if the skill expected an argument, but here it does not even use one: the emptiness that matters is the history's.

question: At Falcon Labs, Rachel asked for a symbol to be renamed across the whole monorepo. Claude edited three files with its editing tools and also ran a codemod script through Bash that rewrote another twelve. The result breaks the build and Rachel opens the rewind menu to restore code and conversation from the previous prompt. What should she expect of the working tree?
options: The three files Claude edited with its tools come back, and the twelve the script rewrote stay modified on disk.
The whole tree returns to the checkpoint state, including the twelve files the script touched, because the script ran inside the session.
No file comes back: restoring code and conversation rewinds the messages and leaves the disk exactly as it is at that moment.
All fifteen files come back, provided the script ran in the foreground and inside the project directory.
answer: The three files Claude edited with its tools come back, and the twelve the script rewrote stay modified on disk.
explanation:
The general rule is that Claude Code checkpoints are a safety net for fast iteration, not a version control system: every prompt creates a restore point for the edits made with the agent's tools, but the changes produced by shell commands are not recorded. That is why the rewind leaves the repository halfway, which is the worst possible state for continuing to iterate. The key reading is that the scope depends on who made the change, not where or when it ran: hence the advice to commit with git before launching a codemod.

RULE: Checkpoints revert what Claude edits with its tools, not what shell commands rewrite: that is what git is for.

TRAP: Reading the checkpoint as a commit of the whole tree and trusting the rollback of a shell script to a feature that does not observe it.

TRY IT: Ask Claude to edit a file with its tools and also modify another with a Bash command, use /rewind to restore code and conversation from the previous prompt and check with git status that only the one edited with Edit was rolled back.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Correct: the checkpoint covers what Claude does with its editing tools and does not track what shell commands change.
Running inside the session is not enough: the checkpoint records the tools' edits, not the effects of an external process.
That is the option that restores only the conversation; the one Rachel chose does revert the edits Claude made with its tools.
Neither the foreground nor the directory changes the scope: what decides is which tool made the change, and a shell script falls outside.

question: Cedar Ridge Health processes 12,000 authorizations a night with the Message Batches API. Ben builds each request like this: {"custom_id": "req-1", "params": {"model": "claude-sonnet-5", "max_tokens": 1024, "messages": []}} and numbers them req-1, req-2, req-3 following the order of the authorization list, planning to walk the results .jsonl file and assign each line to the authorization in the same position. What should you correct before sending the batch?
options: Add the authorization number inside the prompt of each request and ask the model to repeat it in its response so they can be matched.
Sort the results file by each message's timestamp before walking it line by line and assigning them to the list.
Split the submission into twelve batches of a thousand requests so each results file preserves the order in which its lines were sent.
Use the authorization number as custom_id and match each result line by that field, because results can come back in any order.
answer: Use the authorization number as custom_id and match each result line by that field, because results can come back in any order.
explanation:
The general rule of batch processing is that matching is done by identifier, never by position. The documentation says explicitly that results may be returned in any order and may not match the order of creation, and it recommends using meaningful and unique custom_id values precisely because order is not guaranteed. With the authorization number as custom_id, each line of the results file is assigned unambiguously. The key distinction against repeating the number in the prompt is that custom_id is a field of the request itself and does not depend on what the model writes.

RULE: Batch results can come back in any order: always match by custom_id, never by position in the file.

TRAP: Assuming a batch returns results in the same order the requests were sent.

TRY IT: Send a test batch with five requests and different custom_id values, download the .jsonl and check whether the order of the lines matches the order of submission.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing
option_feedback: It would burn tokens and leave traceability dependent on the model copying the number correctly, when the API already offers an identifier for that.
There is no documented guarantee that temporal order reconstructs submission order, because each request in the batch is processed independently.
Splitting very large sets is good practice, but order is still not guaranteed within each batch, however small.
Correct: the documentation warns that results can come back in any order and asks you to always use custom_id, with unique and meaningful values, to match them.

question: The automated tutor at Lakeside Online University answers student questions using only the course notes, which arrive complete in the prompt. Its instruction says it must always answer with a developed explanation and an example. In the audit, Dana found confident, well-written answers about topics the notes do not cover, with examples that appear in no material; answers about covered topics, by contrast, cite correctly. What is the most likely cause?
options: The retriever delivers irrelevant fragments and the model fills them in with its general knowledge of the course subject.
The instruction forces it to always answer and gives it no explicit permission to admit that the course material does not cover that question.
The notes fill the context window and the model loses the final stretch of the material, which is where those topics were.
The default temperature pushes the model to invent creative examples when the available material on the course topic is thin.
answer: The instruction forces it to always answer and gives it no explicit permission to admit that the course material does not cover that question.
explanation:
The general rule is that a prompt demanding an answer every time and offering no honest way out pushes the model to fill the gaps. The documentation on reducing hallucinations recommends giving explicit permission to admit uncertainty, with a concrete phrase the model can use when the material falls short, and restricting the answer to the information provided. The pattern fits here: what is covered is cited well and what is not covered is invented, which is the symptom of an instruction with no escape valve. The key distinction against a retrieval failure is that such a failure would degrade the correct answers too, which the audit rules out.

RULE: Give it explicit permission to say it does not know: without an honest way out, demanding an answer every time pushes it to invent one.

TRAP: Reading an invention as a retrieval failure when it is the prompt itself that forbids answering that the material does not cover it.

TRY IT: Add to the prompt the explicit out that there is not enough information in the material and run the same off-syllabus questions again to count how many inventions remain.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations
option_feedback: If retrieval were failing, answers about covered topics would degrade too, and the audit shows those cite correctly.
Correct: the documentation recommends giving explicit permission to acknowledge uncertainty and offering an out such as saying there is not enough information, which greatly reduces invention.
An overflow produces truncation or an error, and besides the problem is not missing answers but answers about topics the material does not address.
Sampling changes the wording, not the obligation to answer: as long as the prompt demands an explanation and an example every time, the model will fill the gap.

question: Maya reviews a Claude Code session in the Falcon Labs monorepo. Claude first ran "cd packages/api" and then "export DB_URL=postgres://local/test && npm run seed". On the next call, "echo $DB_URL" prints an empty line, but "pwd" still returns the packages/api folder. Which two statements about the Bash tool explain what she sees? (Select TWO)
options: Each command runs in a separate process, so an export does not survive until the next call.
Bash preserves the full environment within the session, and what failed was the order in which Claude chained the calls.
Commands joined with two ampersands run in different processes, which is why the export never reached the seed command.
The change of directory is preserved between calls as long as it points to the project or to an added directory.
The variables are lost because the active permission mode cleans the environment before running each command.
answer: Each command runs in a separate process, so an export does not survive until the next call.
The change of directory is preserved between calls as long as it points to the project or to an added directory.
explanation:
The general rule is that each Bash call opens its own process, so whatever lives in that process's environment dies with it: an export does not reach the next call. The working directory is the documented exception, because the session remembers it as long as it points to the project or an added directory, and hence the asymmetry in the example. The practical consequence is to write the export in the same command that needs it or leave the variable in the session configuration, instead of relying on state that does not persist.

RULE: In Bash every call is a new process: the working directory persists, exported variables do not.

TRAP: Assuming the session is a continuous shell and carrying an export between calls that do not share a process.

TRY IT: Ask for two commands in a row, first an export and then an echo of that variable, and check that the second prints empty; repeat the experiment with cd and pwd.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
option_feedback: Correct: that is why environment variables have to be set in the same command that uses them or left in the session configuration.
If the environment were preserved, the variable would be available; what persists between calls is the working directory, not exported variables.
Within a single call the chain shares a process and the seed did see the variable; the loss happens when moving to the next call.
Correct: the working directory persists within those bounds, which is exactly the asymmetry Maya observes with pwd.
Permission modes decide what is approved and what is blocked, not the process environment; here the reason is that each call opens a new process.

question: The system prompt that classifies requests at the City of Fairview starts like this: "Do not use Markdown. Do not invent data. Do not answer with a preamble. Do not go on at length. Classify the request in {{CASE_FILE}}." Derek observes that the responses still come with introductory sentences and bulleted lists, and that when a piece of data is missing the model fills it in on its own. How should you rewrite those instructions?
options: Raise the emphasis by writing CRITICAL and YOU MUST in capitals in front of each of the prohibitions in the prompt.
Add five examples of badly formed responses, labelled as incorrect, so the model learns which formats to avoid.
State each instruction positively describing the desired format and ask for the classification inside its own XML tag.
Move the prohibitions to the end of the prompt, after the case file text, so they are the last thing the model reads before answering.
answer: State each instruction positively describing the desired format and ask for the classification inside its own XML tag.
explanation:
The general rule is that the model needs to see the result you want described, not the list of errors you do not want. The best practices guidance proposes replacing instructions such as do not use Markdown with a positive description of the format, and reinforcing it with format indicators in XML tags, which also make extracting the classification from the text trivial. For the missing data, the positive formulation amounts to stating what to write when it is not recorded. The key distinction against raising the emphasis is that the documentation advises against aggressive language of the CRITICAL or YOU MUST kind, which tends to produce excessive behaviours instead of precision.

RULE: Say what you want it to do, not what you do not want: describe the desired format and delimit it with XML tags.

TRAP: Assuming a repeated prohibition amounts to a specification: the model imitates what you describe, not what you forbid.

TRY IT: Rewrite a single line positively, for example asking for the label inside an XML tag, and compare twenty outputs before and after counting how many carry a preamble.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: The current guidance asks for exactly the opposite, toning down aggressive language, because extreme emphasis does not improve compliance and causes excessive behaviours.
Examples are very effective, but they teach the pattern they show: filling the prompt with defective outputs invites reproducing them.
Correct: the documentation recommends saying what to do instead of what not to do and using format indicators with XML tags to delimit the output.
Putting the long document at the top and the query at the end is good advice for large inputs, but reordering prohibitions does not fix them being phrased negatively.

question: To extract data from authorizations, Cedar Ridge Health added four examples to the extraction prompt. All four come from the same insurer, with the same one-page form and every field filled in. Since then, with documents from other insurers the model returns the fields in the positions of the familiar form and invents a value when that field does not exist in the document it is reading. What should you do with the examples?
options: Replace them with examples covering the forms of several insurers and edge cases, such as missing fields or two-page documents.
Add twenty more examples from the same insurer and cache them, because with prompt caching it is worth including many high-quality examples in the prompt.
Remove the examples and describe in prose the list of fields to extract from each type of authorization form.
Move the examples above the document to be extracted so the model reads them before the text of the scanned case file.
answer: Replace them with examples covering the forms of several insurers and edge cases, such as missing fields or two-page documents.
explanation:
The general rule is that examples teach the pattern they show. The documentation asks for them to be relevant, to closely reflect the real use case, and above all diverse, covering edge cases and varying enough that the model does not pick up unwanted patterns. Four identical examples from a single insurer with every field present teach the layout and teach that a value is never missing, which is exactly what the model is reproducing. The key distinction against adding more examples is that number does not correct the bias: variety does.

RULE: Examples teach what they show: if they all look alike, the model learns the likeness instead of the task.

TRAP: Confusing more examples with better examples: the documentation asks for diversity and edge cases, not volume from the same mould.

TRY IT: Replace two of the four examples with documents from another insurer with missing fields and measure how many inventions remain over the same test batch.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation asks for examples that are relevant and diverse, that cover edge cases and vary enough that the model does not learn unwanted patterns.
The caching advice talks about twenty or more diverse examples; repeating the same mould reinforces exactly the pattern causing the problem.
Abstract instructions are less effective than showing the desired output; the documentation recommends constraining with examples, not replacing them with descriptions.
The recommended placement is the opposite, with long documents at the top and the query at the end, and in any case the problem is the content of the examples, not their position.

question: The nightly process at Summit Mutual Insurance dispatches 80 subagents in a single batch to review claims in parallel. Within a few minutes, a good share of them finish with no result and the coordinator receives rate limit errors; the subagents that do get to run work fine and return complete reviews. Tyler needs the run to finish in full without touching the review logic of each subagent. What should you do?
options: Immediately retry every subagent that fails, as many times as needed, until its request is eventually accepted.
Raise max_tokens in each subagent so they finish in fewer turns and free the run's shared quota sooner.
Nest the delegation so each subagent launches its own in turn and the dispatch spreads itself out over time.
Split the dispatch into smaller batches and launch them in a staggered way, instead of issuing a single wide fan-out of subagents.
answer: Split the dispatch into smaller batches and launch them in a staggered way, instead of issuing a single wide fan-out of subagents.
explanation:
The general rule is that agent parallelism is bounded by the API quota, not only by the agent's logic. The documentation points out that wide subagent fan-outs can hit rate limits and advises dividing the work into smaller batches instead of issuing a single wide dispatch. Since the subagents that do run work fine, there is nothing to fix in their logic: the failure is in the shape of the dispatch. The key distinction against retrying is that an immediate retry competes for the same quota again, whereas staggering reduces instantaneous demand.

RULE: A wide subagent fan-out hits rate limits: spread the work across smaller, staggered batches.

TRAP: Assuming parallelism is free: the bottleneck is not the agent's logic but the API quota.

TRY IT: Launch the same load in four batches of twenty with a pause between them and compare how many subagents finish against the single fan-out.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hosting https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits
option_feedback: Retrying with no wait makes the problem worse: the official guidance describes retries with exponential backoff and respect for the retry-after header, not in bursts.
max_tokens sets the generation ceiling and does not reduce the number of requests per minute, which is what is hitting the limit.
Nesting staggers nothing: it multiplies the number of concurrent agents and worsens the pressure on rate limits.
Correct: the hosting documentation warns that wide subagent fan-outs hit rate limits and recommends splitting the work into smaller batches.

question: Falcon Labs connected two MCP servers to the same agent: one for the ticket system and one for the code repository. Each exposes a tool called search, with brief and very similar descriptions. The agent searches the repository when asked for a ticket's history and vice versa. What should you do first?
options: Leave only one of the two tools available and ask in every prompt that the user clarify which system they want to search before calling it.
Rename them with the service first, tickets_search and repo_search, and describe in each one what it returns and when not to use it.
Move the agent to a more capable model so it tells the two tools apart from the context of the conversation.
Add to the system prompt a few-shot example with one correct call to each of the two similar tools.
answer: Rename them with the service first, tickets_search and repo_search, and describe in each one what it returns and when not to use it.
explanation:
The general rule is that the model picks a tool from its name and its description, so two identically named tools from different services are an interface design problem, not a model capability one. Namespacing by service and by resource is the documented technique for catalogs that mix sources, and it is completed with descriptions stating what each tool returns, when to use it and when not to. The key distinction against examples or a bigger model is that those reduce the error rate without removing the ambiguity at its source.

RULE: Name tools with the service first and describe their boundaries: selection is played out in the name and the description.

TRAP: Treating a naming ambiguity as a model capability problem and answering with more prompt instead of a better interface.

TRY IT: Stand up two MCP servers of your own each exposing a tool called search, measure across ten requests how often Claude picks the wrong one, rename them tickets_search and repo_search with descriptions stating when not to use them, and repeat the measurement.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
option_feedback: It resolves the confusion by removing capability and shifting the work to the user, when the problem is in how the two tools are presented.
Correct: selection is decided by name and description, so namespacing by service and explicit boundaries attack the cause.
A better model can help, but if an engineer cannot say which of the two applies, the agent cannot be expected to get it right either.
Examples improve consistency, but every new situation still depends on two ambiguous names that do not distinguish themselves.

question: Northlane Outfitters handles post-purchase support by chat with Claude and, separately, extracts data from supplier invoices in PDF overnight. To cut the monthly bill, Caleb proposes moving everything, including the chat responses, to the Message Batches API and keeping the 50 % discount. The product constraint does not change: the customer waits for the answer while still in the conversation. What should be done?
options: Send one batch per chat message and poll that batch's status in a loop until it finishes so the answer can be returned.
Use the Batches API for the chat with stream enabled, to show the answer token by token while the batch is processed.
Group the chat messages into batches of ten to shorten the processing time of each submission and still keep the discount.
Leave the chat on the Messages API, with prompt caching over the stable part of the prompt, and use batches only for the nightly invoice extraction.
answer: Leave the chat on the Messages API, with prompt caching over the stable part of the prompt, and use batches only for the nightly invoice extraction.
explanation:
The general rule is that the Message Batches API is chosen when responses are not needed immediately: you process large volumes, accept asynchrony and optimize cost. Access to results happens when every request in the batch has finished or when 24 hours pass, whichever comes first, and a batch does not support streaming, so it cannot sustain a live conversation. The nightly invoice extraction fits perfectly and the chat does not. The key distinction against slicing the batch is that no size turns an asynchronous process into an interactive one: to make the chat cheaper the documented lever is prompt caching.

RULE: Batches is for work that can wait: results arrive when the whole batch finishes or at 24 hours, and there is no streaming.

TRAP: Chasing the 50 % discount in an interactive flow: the saving is paid for with a latency the chat cannot tolerate.

TRY IT: Send a single request as a batch and measure how long the result takes to become available against the same call through the Messages API.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
option_feedback: A batch of a single request is still asynchronous: results are accessed when the whole batch finishes or at 24 hours, so the chat would be left waiting.
It is not possible: batches do not support stream set to true because results arrive as a single file, not as a stream of events.
No batch size guarantees latency: the documentation only says most finish in under an hour, far from conversation time.
Correct: batches are designed for work that does not need an immediate response, and savings in the interactive flow are sought with caching, whose discount also stacks with the batch one.

question: A Riverbank Financial contract review finished with a ResultMessage of subtype error_max_turns, after the agent had already edited two working files of the case. Rachel wants to pick that same run back up with a higher limit instead of starting from scratch, and before doing so she needs to know what resuming gives back and what it leaves out. Which two statements are correct? (Select TWO)
options: The session stores the conversation and not the file system: on resuming, the history of the review comes back, but the files stay on disk as the agent left them.
On resuming, the SDK re-executes the tool calls in the transcript to rebuild the state of the files before continuing work.
A run that ended with error_max_turns can no longer be resumed, so a new session has to be opened and the original review prompt sent again.
Resuming always creates a new session with a copy of the history and leaves the original intact, so Rachel will end up with two separate transcripts.
Recovering from a limit is one of the documented reasons to resume: the same session can be picked up with a higher max_turns and continue from where it stopped.
answer: The session stores the conversation and not the file system: on resuming, the history of the review comes back, but the files stay on disk as the agent left them.
Recovering from a limit is one of the documented reasons to resume: the same session can be picked up with a higher max_turns and continue from where it stopped.
explanation:
The general rule is that a session is the accumulated conversation, not the state of the world. On resuming, the whole history comes back, including the files read, the analysis done and the actions recorded, but the effects those actions had on disk stay as they were, and reverting them requires file checkpointing. At the same time, ending with error_max_turns does not invalidate the session: recovering from a limit is one of the documented reasons to resume, raising the limit in the new query. The key distinction against a fork is that a fork creates a new session with a copy of the history, while resumption continues the same one.

RULE: Resuming returns the conversation, not the file system; and an error result, such as error_max_turns, is still a resumable session.

TRAP: Assuming the transcript is a state of the world you can rewind: what comes back is the history, not the effects of the tools.

TRY IT: Run a query with a low max_turns until you get error_max_turns, note the session_id in the result, resume with a higher limit and check that the modified files are still in the state they were left in.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation clarifies that sessions persist the conversation; to revert file changes you need file checkpointing, not resumption.
Resuming restores the history of what was read, analysed and done, but it re-executes nothing: a tool that was running when the session was cut is not relaunched either.
It is precisely the opposite: recovering from a limit is among the documented reasons to resume, and the error result also carries the session identifier.
That is the description of a fork, which is requested explicitly; a normal resumption continues the same session and keeps its identifier.
Correct: the documentation lists a cut-off by turn or budget limit as a typical case for resuming with a higher limit.

question: The catalog team at Northlane Outfitters answers internal queries by combining product records it retrieves from its own internal index. Rachel needs every statement in the answer to say which record it came from, with the title and the identifier of the source, and that reference to be verifiable without depending on the model remembering to cite or on reviewing the text by hand. What should you implement?
options: Ask in the prompt for every sentence to end with the record identifier and check with a regular expression that no sentence is left unmarked.
Insert the retrieved records as plain text in the system prompt and number them so the model refers to them by that number.
Pass each retrieved record as a search_result block with citations enabled and read the citations that come back with their source and title.
Return the answer with output_config.format and an array of sources per statement, so the schema forces provenance to be included.
answer: Pass each retrieved record as a search_result block with citations enabled and read the citations that come back with their source and title.
explanation:
The general rule is that verifiable provenance is solved with the citations feature, not by asking for it in the prompt. search_result blocks allow Claude to cite your own content retrieved by your search engine in the same way it cites web search results, and the citations come back with source, title and indices of the cited block, so they are valid pointers by construction. Moreover, the quoted text does not count as output tokens and the official evaluations show better fragment selection than prompt-only approaches. The key distinction against forcing an array of sources with structured outputs is that the combination is not allowed: enabling citations together with output_config.format returns a 400.

RULE: For verifiable provenance use citations over document or search_result blocks: the prompt asks for citations, the feature guarantees them.

TRAP: Combining citations with structured outputs: the API returns 400 because citations are interleaved with the text and a strict schema does not allow it.

TRY IT: Send two records as search_result blocks with citations enabled and check the source, title and index fields of each returned citation in the response.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/search-results https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations
option_feedback: Citing through the prompt works, but the pointers are not guaranteed and the quoted text is paid for as output tokens; the dedicated feature cites better and cheaper.
Numbering by hand creates no verifiable citation structure: the model can refer to the wrong number and nothing catches it.
Correct: search_result blocks let Claude cite your own content just as it cites web search results, returning citations with source, title and indices of the fragment.
A schema can require the field, but not that its content be real; besides, enabling citations together with output_config.format returns a 400.

question: Heartland Agronomics hardened the agent that builds its reports: it registered a PreToolUse hook, added deny rules in settings.json, listed three tools in allowed_tools and left the can_use_tool callback implemented. Now a single tool call can be reached by several of those mechanisms and Tyler needs to document which one overrides which. In what order does the SDK evaluate these steps on a tool call?
options: deny rules → hooks → permission mode → allow rules → can_use_tool callback → ask rules
Permission mode → hooks → deny rules → allow rules → ask rules → can_use_tool callback
Hooks → deny rules → ask rules → permission mode → allow rules → can_use_tool callback
can_use_tool callback → hooks → deny rules → ask rules → allow rules → permission mode
answer: Hooks → deny rules → ask rules → permission mode → allow rules → can_use_tool callback
explanation:
The general rule is that hooks are evaluated before any other permission mechanism, which is why they are the right place for checks that must run on every tool call: a denial from a hook applies even in bypassPermissions, and an allow returned by a hook does not skip the deny or ask rules. Then come the deny rules, the ask rules, the permission mode, the allow rules and, finally, the can_use_tool callback. The key distinction that usually trips people up is that an auto-approved tool never reaches the callback, so the logic you put there does not run for anything listed in allowed_tools.

RULE: If something must be checked on every tool call, put it in a PreToolUse hook: it runs before everything and its deny holds even in bypassPermissions.

TRAP: Trusting validation to the can_use_tool callback: auto-approved tools never reach it and the check is silently skipped.

TRY IT: List a tool in allowed_tools, put a print inside can_use_tool and another inside a PreToolUse hook, and watch which of the two runs when the agent calls that tool.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions
option_feedback: It puts deny rules ahead of hooks and leaves ask rules at the end; in reality hooks run first and ask rules are evaluated before the permission mode.
It places the permission mode at the start, but the mode is evaluated only after the hooks and the deny and ask rules, which apply even in bypassPermissions.
Correct: this is the documented permission evaluation order, with hooks at the front and the callback as a last resort only if nothing resolved it earlier.
It inverts the extremes: the callback is the last step and is only invoked when evaluation gets as far as requesting a decision, not the first.

question: The post-purchase agent at Northlane Outfitters has to meet two conditions without exception: leave a note in the CRM before closing any case, and wait for a human analyst's approval before issuing refunds above a certain amount. Evan is looking for mechanisms that do not depend on the model remembering the rule in every conversation. Which two sequences implement those guarantees as documented? (Select TWO)
options: The agent tries to finish → a Stop hook returns decision block with a stopReason → the agent continues and writes the CRM note before closing the case
The agent closes the case → a PostToolUse hook detects the note is missing → the hook reopens the session and asks the agent to write it before answering
The agent calls the refund tool → a PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision defer → the query ends and is resumed when the analyst approves
A line in capitals is added to the project CLAUDE.md → the agent reads it at the start of the session → it never closes a case without leaving the CRM note
The agent calls the refund tool → a PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision ask → the model itself decides whether it is worth continuing with the call
answer: The agent tries to finish → a Stop hook returns decision block with a stopReason → the agent continues and writes the CRM note before closing the case
The agent calls the refund tool → a PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision defer → the query ends and is resumed when the analyst approves
explanation:
The general rule is that what must always happen is enforced with deterministic runtime mechanisms and not with instructions. For the closing, a Stop hook returning decision block with a stopReason prevents the agent from finishing and tells it what is missing, so the note is written before closing. For the refund, a PreToolUse returning permissionDecision defer ends the query at that point and allows it to be resumed once the analyst has approved, which is the documented way of inserting an external decision into the middle of the flow. The key distinction against ask is who decides: ask routes the call to the application's or a person's permission evaluation, never to the model's judgement.

RULE: To stop a final step from being skipped, block the closing with a Stop hook; to wait for a person, cut the query with defer and resume it.

TRAP: Reading defer and ask as synonyms: defer ends the query to be picked up later, while ask only routes the call to the permission decision.

TRY IT: Register a Stop hook that returns decision block when a mandatory step is missing, verify the agent continues instead of finishing and check stop_hook_active to break the loop.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks
option_feedback: Correct: a Stop hook can prevent the agent from finishing and return the reason to it; it is worth checking stop_hook_active so as not to enter a loop of blocks.
PostToolUse runs after each tool and can audit or complete the result, but it does not reopen sessions or revive a case the agent has already closed.
Correct: defer cuts the query at that point precisely so an external decision happens outside the loop and the work is picked up afterwards.
CLAUDE.md is injected as project context and improves behaviour, but it is advice: it does not stop the model from closing a case without the note.
The ask value routes the call to the application's or the person's permission decision, not to a choice by the model, which is what the option describes incorrectly.

question: Derek has to migrate the billing module at Falcon Labs, which touches four packages of the monorepo and a library he does not know. He wants Claude to investigate, write a proposal he can review and edit, and only then execute. Today he starts with: claude --permission-mode acceptEdits "Migrate the billing module", and Claude starts modifying files on the first turn. What should you do?
options: Start with --permission-mode plan: Claude investigates and proposes without editing, and on approving the plan execution continues in the same session.
Keep acceptEdits and add to the prompt that it should not modify anything until it confirms the approach with the user who opened the session.
Restrict the session with --tools to the read tools and remove that restriction by hand once the proposal is ready.
Delegate the investigation to an exploration subagent and ask Claude to write the proposal with the summary it returns.
answer: Start with --permission-mode plan: Claude investigates and proposes without editing, and on approving the plan execution continues in the same session.
explanation:
The general rule is that planning is worthwhile when the scope is unclear, the change touches several files or the code is unfamiliar, and that the way to get it is not to ask for it in the prompt but to use the mode that enforces it. In plan mode Claude reads and explores, delivers a proposal you can open and edit, and only on approval does it enable execution within the same session. The key distinction against acceptEdits plus an instruction is that this mode auto-approves edits: the restriction lives in the configuration, not in the text of the request.

RULE: If the change spans several files or the code is unfamiliar, plan first: plan mode investigates without editing and approval releases execution.

TRAP: Confusing asking it not to edit with a mode that prevents it: acceptEdits auto-approves edits even if the prompt says otherwise.

TRY IT: Repeat the same request with --permission-mode plan and check with git status that there are no changes in the tree until you approve the plan.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Correct: plan mode separates investigating from executing and leaves the plan visible and editable before a single line is touched.
The prompt is advice and acceptEdits auto-approves edits: the first time Claude reads that you have confirmed, it starts writing.
It prevents editing, but it loses exploration with commands and forces a restart with another configuration right when the plan has to be executed.
Isolated exploration helps avoid filling the context, but nothing stops the main conversation from editing in the meantime.

question: A team asks Claude to review, in the same session, the code it has just written, and the reviews always come back clean. What does the documentation recommend so that review adds something?
options: Lower the temperature of the responses during the review so the model is stricter with the code it already wrote.
Ask for the review in the same turn but listing inside the prompt the criteria it must apply when reviewing.
Run a compaction before reviewing, so the model loses sight of the implementation details.
Review in a separate session, because a fresh context avoids the bias towards the code the model itself has just written.
answer: Review in a separate session, because a fresh context avoids the bias towards the code the model itself has just written.
explanation:
The general rule is that review improves when the reviewer is not the author, and in Claude Code that translates into separating sessions: one implements and another, with a clean context, reviews the file or the diff and reports gaps. The documentation describes it as the writer and reviewer pattern, and points out that a fresh context avoids the bias towards freshly produced code. The alternatives improve the prompt or reduce the context, but the session is still the one that wrote the code and still defends it.

RULE: Whoever writes does not review: open a new session or a subagent to review, because a fresh context does not defend the code it just produced.

TRAP: Confusing reducing the context with changing the reviewer: compacting summarizes the same conversation and keeps the authorship bias.

TRY IT: Ask Claude to write a function with a badly handled edge condition and to review it in the same turn, then open a new session, paste only the code and ask for the same review, and compare how many problems each one finds.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: It is not a parameter you govern from Claude Code, and the problem is not sampling variability but the context the session carries.
Explicit criteria always help and are worth using, but they do not correct the bias of reviewing code you have just produced.
Compaction summarizes the conversation and keeps the essentials; it is not equivalent to a fresh context and it does not undo authorship of the code.
Correct: this is the writer-session and reviewer-session pattern, with the result of the review returned to the first one to fix.

question: The claims agent at Summit Mutual Insurance queries a registry service that sometimes fails. Today your code returns this to the model: {"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01F", "content": "failed", "is_error": true}, inside a user message that starts with a sentence explaining what happened and places the block after that text. The agent retries the same call over and over without changing strategy. Which two changes improve its recovery? (Select TWO)
options: Remove is_error and send the failure as a normal user text message so the model reads it inside the conversation.
Include the full exception trace from the registry service so the model has every technical detail of the failure.
Replace failed with a message stating what failed and what to try, for example that the registry is not responding and to retry in 60 seconds.
Place the tool_result block first in the message content, right after the tool_use, and leave any text after the results.
Retry the call on the client up to five times without returning anything to the model and continue the turn only if a response arrives.
answer: Replace failed with a message stating what failed and what to try, for example that the registry is not responding and to retry in 60 seconds.
Place the tool_result block first in the message content, right after the tool_use, and leave any text after the results.
explanation:
The general rule is that the model can only recover from what it sees and understands. A tool_result with is_error set to true is the right channel, but its content must explain what failed and what to try next, as the guidance shows when contrasting a generic failed with a message such as rate limit exceeded, retry in 60 seconds. The shape of the message matters too: tool_result blocks must immediately follow the tool_use and appear first in the content, with any text afterwards. The key distinction against the other options is that neither hiding the failure nor dumping the full trace gives the agent a different action to try.

RULE: A tool error comes back as a tool_result with is_error and an actionable message, and that block goes first in the message content.

TRAP: Confusing reporting the error with reporting it well: failed does not tell the model what to do differently on the next attempt.

TRY IT: Trigger a service failure, return failed first and then a message with cause and next step, and compare whether the agent repeats the call or changes strategy.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls
option_feedback: It breaks the tool use loop: a tool's result must come back as a tool_result associated with its tool_use_id, and is_error is what marks that there was a failure.
Opaque traces burn context without telling it what to do differently; the guidance asks for specific, actionable errors, not technical dumps.
Correct: the documentation asks you to write instructive errors stating what happened and what Claude should try next, so it can recover without guessing.
Correct: tool_result blocks must come immediately after their tool_use and first in the content array, with text always afterwards.
Retrying transient failures is reasonable, but hiding the failure entirely stops the agent from adapting its plan when the service is still down.

question: The list_builds tool of the Falcon Labs MCP server returns, for each build, this object: {"id": "b3f9c1d2-7a44-4e58-9f01-2c6d0b", "artifact_mime_type": "application/zip", "log_url_256": "..."}. The agent confuses builds with one another and sometimes invents identifiers when asking for the detail. Which change to the response helps most?
options: Return every field available in the CI system so the agent never needs a second call to the tool.
Wrap the same response in XML instead of JSON, because that format is always interpreted better than objects.
Replace the opaque identifier with a semantic, stable one such as the build name, and keep only the fields that guide the next step.
Add the full commit hash and the timestamp in epoch format so the agent can sort and disambiguate.
answer: Replace the opaque identifier with a semantic, stable one such as the build name, and keep only the fields that guide the next step.
explanation:
The general rule is that a tool's response is designed for the decision the agent has to make, not to mirror the schema of the source system. The documentation asks you to return high-signal information and to avoid low-level technical identifiers: resolving those opaque codes into semantic, stable names measurably improves accuracy when referencing them, because the model no longer has to copy meaningless strings. Adding fields or changing the format does not touch that cause and, in the case of the fields, worsens context consumption.

RULE: Return names before opaque codes and only the fields that guide the next step: the response is designed for the decision, not for the schema.

TRAP: Assuming returning everything the system knows is safer, when the noise buries the signal and does not fix the invented references.

TRY IT: Duplicate the tool: one version returns the opaque identifier and the MIME type, the other the build name and the file type; give the same task to each and compare the reference errors.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
option_feedback: More fields is not more signal: the context fills with data that guides no decision and the confusion between builds does not go away.
