Format matters and is worth testing, but there is no format that always wins; here the problem is the chosen fields, not the wrapper.
Correct: human-readable identifiers reduce hallucinations when referencing them and high-signal fields guide the next action.
It adds two more technical strings to copy without error; sorting is solved by returning the results already sorted, not by demanding more precision from the model.

question: A team let the project CLAUDE.md grow to six hundred lines and notices that Claude overlooks conventions written in it. What size does the documentation recommend and on what grounds?
options: Under five hundred lines: past that point Claude Code stops loading the file and warns about it at the start of every session.
Under two hundred lines per file, because long files consume context and reduce adherence.
Under one hundred lines, because the content is injected inside the system prompt and competes with the product instructions.
There is no size target: what matters is that each section carries a clear heading so Claude can locate it.
answer: Under two hundred lines per file, because long files consume context and reduce adherence.
explanation:
The general rule is that CLAUDE.md competes for the model's attention in every session, so the documentation sets a target of under two hundred lines per file and warns that long files consume more context and reduce adherence. When the file grows, the way out is not to compress the text but to distribute it: conventions for part of the code go to .claude/rules/ with paths, multi-step procedures go to a skill. The frequent confusion is mixing that target with the five-hundred-line limit of SKILL.md, which follows a different logic.

RULE: Aim for under two hundred lines per CLAUDE.md: what does not fit goes to .claude/rules/ with paths or into a skill.

TRAP: Assuming more instructions equal more obedience, when a long file dilutes attention across every line.

TRY IT: Measure with /context how much your CLAUDE.md occupies today, trim it to under two hundred lines by moving the specific parts to .claude/rules/ with paths, and check in a new session whether Claude respects a convention it used to overlook.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory https://code.claude.com/docs/en/features-overview
option_feedback: A size cut-off does exist but it is far higher, on the order of megabytes; five hundred lines is the guidance for a different artifact, the SKILL.md.
Correct: that is why what does not fit is spread into .claude/rules/ files or turned into a skill loaded on demand.
The content arrives as a user message after the system prompt, not inside it, and the documented guidance is not one hundred lines.
Headings help you read the file, but the documentation does set a size target because length affects adherence.

question: The nightly runs at Heartland Agronomics are launched headless with the -p flag from the pipeline orchestrator and leave their report in the data lake. The following morning, Megan wants to pick up one specific run from the terminal to ask for an additional analysis of what it already reviewed, but claude --continue opens another conversation from the directory and the nightly run does not appear when she lists sessions with claude --resume either. What should you do?
options: Run each nightly task in an interactive session from the same directory so it is registered in the picker and can be picked up the next morning.
Raise cleanupPeriodDays in the configuration so the night's transcripts are not deleted before somebody can open them in the morning.
Pick it up with claude --continue from the same directory and add --fork-session to recover the most recent run without overwriting the original transcript.
Store the session_id that comes in the ResultMessage of each run and resume that session by identifier with claude --resume followed by that value.
answer: Store the session_id that comes in the ResultMessage of each run and resume that session by identifier with claude --resume followed by that value.
explanation:
The general rule is that continuing works when your application handles one conversation at a time and you do not want to track anything, while resuming by identifier is what applies when there are many sessions or when the one you want is not the most recent. Here a documented detail is added: sessions created by the SDK or with the -p flag do not appear in the interactive picker or in claude --continue, although they remain resumable by identifier. That is why the fix is for the pipeline to store the session_id that comes in each run's ResultMessage. The key distinction against the fork is that here a copy of the history is not what is missing, the reference to the right session is.

RULE: If your pipeline will return to a specific run, store its session_id: -p and SDK sessions are invisible in the picker but resume by identifier.

TRAP: Assuming that continuing the most recent conversation in the directory is enough to return to an automated run that was never interactive.

TRY IT: Launch a task with claude -p, note the session_id in the result, check that it does not appear in the claude --resume picker and then resume it by passing that identifier.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions
option_feedback: It turns an automated process into a manual one to solve a visibility problem in the picker, when those sessions are already resumable by identifier.
Retention defines how long transcripts live, but the problem is not that they expired: the default value covers a single night many times over.
Forking copies the history of the session being continued, but --continue still does not see sessions launched with -p, so it would open the wrong conversation.
Correct: SDK and -p sessions stay out of the picker and of --continue, but they resume without trouble if the pipeline kept their identifier.

question: The research coordinator at Lakeside Online University holds conversations lasting several hours: it commissions searches, receives summaries and decides which lines to follow. When the conversation grows, the system loses decisions taken at the start, such as which sources were discarded and why, and commissions searches that were already done. Hannah needs the work to keep moving in the same thread without losing those decisions. Which two measures solve it? (Select TWO)
options: Raise max_tokens on each request so more conversation fits before the context runs out entirely.
Delete every tool result with clear_tool_uses keeping zero calls, to free as much space as possible.
Enable server-side compaction and return the compaction block in every subsequent request of the conversation.
Restart the conversation whenever the context reaches 80 % and paste the original research brief again.
Give it the memory tool and have it write the decisions and the discards into files, outside the context window.
answer: Enable server-side compaction and return the compaction block in every subsequent request of the conversation.
Give it the memory tool and have it write the decisions and the discards into files, outside the context window.
explanation:
The general rule is that compaction and memory solve different problems and combine. For long agentic conversations the documentation points to server-side compaction as the main strategy: the API returns a compaction block you must resend, and everything before it is ignored. But a summary, by definition, leaves things out, and that is why the memory tool guidance explains that compaction keeps the active context small while memory preserves the information that must survive the summary. The key distinction against clearing tool results or restarting is that those options free space but do not guarantee the discarded decisions remain available.

RULE: Compaction keeps the thread alive; external memory preserves what cannot be lost in the summary.

TRAP: Assuming compaction preserves everything: it summarizes, and whatever must survive has to be written outside the context.

TRY IT: Enable compaction in a long conversation and check that, on resending the compaction block, the agent still cites the decisions it saved into memory files.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool
option_feedback: max_tokens limits what the model generates in one response; it neither widens the context window nor preserves anything already said.
Clearing tool results is the gentlest form of compacting, but emptying everything removes evidence the agent still needs and invalidates the cached prefix.
Correct: server-side compaction is the main strategy for long conversations and agentic flows, and the returned block must be resent in subsequent requests.
Starting clean is useful in other scenarios, but here it loses exactly what has to be preserved: the intermediate decisions and the discards.
Correct: memory lives in your application and preserves the information that must survive the summary, complementing compaction.

question: Brightwater Press wants every pull request on the site to receive an automatic review as soon as it is opened, without anybody writing anything. They installed the GitHub action with the minimal step, without the prompt input, and triggered it on the pull request opened event. The job runs, ends green and leaves no comment. What should you do?
options: Change the trigger phrase to text that appears in any comment, so the action fires on every pull request.
Pass a prompt in the with block: with a prompt the action runs in automation mode on the configured event, without waiting for the trigger phrase.
Add the id-token permission to the workflow, because without that permission the action never gets to run the pull request review.
Replace the action with a custom step that runs the CLI in non-interactive mode and posts the comment with the GitHub tool.
answer: Pass a prompt in the with block: with a prompt the action runs in automation mode on the configured event, without waiting for the trigger phrase.
explanation:
The general rule is that the GitHub action has two modes and which one activates depends on a single fact: if you do not pass it a prompt, it stays in interactive mode and waits for the trigger phrase in an issue or pull request comment; if you pass it a prompt, it runs in automation mode on the event the workflow defines. That is why the job ends green doing nothing: it fired, found no phrase and exited. The key distinction against loosening the trigger phrase is that this route still depends on somebody writing a comment.

RULE: Without a prompt the action waits for the trigger phrase; with a prompt it runs on its own on the workflow event.

TRAP: Forcing interactive mode with a generic trigger phrase instead of declaring the prompt that enables automation mode.

TRY IT: Duplicate the Claude Code action workflow on a branch, add the prompt input inside the with block, open a test pull request and compare whether the job now leaves a comment since it no longer waits for the trigger phrase.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/github-actions
option_feedback: It is a trick on interactive mode that depends on somebody commenting something; the mode designed to run on its own is a different one and needs no phrases.
Correct: the presence of the prompt is what distinguishes the two modes, and in automation execution is triggered by the workflow event.
That permission is needed for the action's default authentication, but here the job already runs and ends fine: what is missing is what it should do.
It is a real and sometimes useful alternative, but it rewrites by hand what the action already does and adds maintenance without solving the cause.

question: Cedar Ridge Health splits authorization review among several subagents, each with a turn limit. In the last run, two subagents reached that limit and their output came back marked as partial. The coordinator merged it with the rest and the final report went out with two unreviewed areas, with nobody noticing until the audit. What should you do?
options: Remove the subagents' turn limit so no review can be left incomplete halfway through.
Treat any output marked as partial as unfinished work and resume that subagent before merging the results.
Relaunch the whole run from scratch whenever a subagent is left incomplete, to guarantee a coherent report.
Upgrade the coordinator's model so it detects from reading the summaries which reviews came up short on content.
answer: Treat any output marked as partial as unfinished work and resume that subagent before merging the results.
explanation:
The general rule is that in a multi-agent system errors propagate and have to be handled where they are signalled. When a subagent reaches its turn limit, its output is marked as partial precisely so the agent receiving it knows the run did not finish, and that work can be resumed instead of repeated. Merging a partial output as if it were final turns a local failure into a wrong report. The key distinction against relaunching the whole run is that resuming preserves what is already done, which is what the production lessons recommend: continue from where the agent was when the error occurred.

RULE: Output marked as partial is unfinished work: resume from where it stopped instead of merging it or restarting everything.

TRAP: Merging partial results as final because the summary they return reads complete and well formed.

TRY IT: Set a low turn limit on a subagent, observe the partial mark in its result and check that your coordinator blocks it before merging.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system
option_feedback: Stop conditions exist to bound cost and loops; removing them trades an incomplete report for runs with no ceiling.
Correct: the output is marked as partial precisely so whoever receives it knows the run was left unfinished, and that subagent can be resumed.
Restarting discards valid work and multiplies the cost; the documented lesson is to resume from where the agent was when the failure occurred.
There is no need to infer what is already signalled: the partial mark is an explicit signal the coordinator's code should respect.

question: Kestrel Pay defines a reconciliation subagent to cross settlements against wallet movements and wants it to run on an economical model. Four possible sources for that value coexist in the team: the model given at invocation, the model field of the subagent definition, the CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL environment variable and the main conversation's model. In what order does Claude Code resolve the model the subagent runs on?
options: Model given at invocation → model field of the definition → CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL → main conversation's model
Model field of the subagent definition → model given at invocation → main conversation's model → CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL
CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL → model field of the definition → model given at invocation → main conversation's model
Main conversation's model → model field of the definition → CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL → model given at invocation
answer: Model given at invocation → model field of the definition → CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL → main conversation's model
explanation:
The general rule is that a subagent's configuration is resolved from the most specific to the most general. First comes the model passed at invocation, then the model field of the subagent definition, then the CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL environment variable and, if none of that is present, the main conversation's model is used. For Kestrel Pay's case it is enough to set model in the reconciler's definition, because nothing overrides it except an invocation naming another model. The key distinction against the alternatives is the position of the environment: it is a global fallback, not an override of what you declared in the definition.

RULE: A subagent's model is resolved from the most specific to the most general: invocation, definition, environment variable and, finally, the main conversation.

TRAP: Assuming a global environment variable overrides what is declared in the AgentDefinition; the environment only acts when nobody set the model earlier.

TRY IT: Define a subagent with model haiku, export CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL with another value, launch it and check in the per-model usage record which of the two actually ran the task.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: Correct: this is the documented order, from the most specific to the most general, with the main conversation acting as a last resort.
It swaps the first two and leaves the environment variable last: what is given at invocation is the most specific and beats the definition.
It puts the environment variable above everything, but the environment only acts when neither the invocation nor the definition set a model.
It starts with the most general fallback and ends with the most specific, which is exactly the opposite of the documented order.

question: The first-contact classifier at Summit Mutual Insurance assigns one of nine categories to each claim notice. The categories were defined with one sentence each and several overlap; 20 % of notices get a category the analyst later corrects. Evan has a firm constraint: he cannot change models or add new calls to the pipeline. Which two changes improve precision within that constraint? (Select TWO)
options: Raise effort to xhigh on every classification so the model reasons more before choosing the notice category.
Redefine each category with its boundaries and its edge cases and establish that only one can apply to each notice.
State in the prompt that, when in doubt, it should flag the notice for a human analyst on the team to review.
Allow several categories ordered by probability and keep the first of that list in the code.
Ask it to write its analysis first inside a reasoning tag and then the category in an intent tag.
answer: Redefine each category with its boundaries and its edge cases and establish that only one can apply to each notice.
Ask it to write its analysis first inside a reasoning tag and then the category in an intent tag.
explanation:
The general rule is that classification precision depends above all on how well defined the categories are and on only one being applicable to each case. With nine one-sentence definitions that overlap, the model has nothing to decide with, and no compute lever fixes that. The second documented change is asking for the reasoning inside a tag and then the classification label in another, which improves the decision and leaves the output easy to extract, all within the same call. The key distinction against raising effort or escalating when in doubt is that those options spend budget or shift work to the analysts without touching the cause.

RULE: Classification precision is proportional to how well defined the categories are: explicit boundaries and a single applicable label.

TRAP: Trying to buy precision with more reasoning or more human review when the problem is overlapping categories.

TRY IT: Rewrite two overlapping categories with their boundaries and one edge case each, and reclassify the same hundred notices to compare the corrections.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/ticket-routing https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: More effort consumes more tokens and latency, and it does not resolve two categories describing the same case: the model would still be choosing between ambiguous definitions.
Correct: the ability to classify well is proportional to how well defined the categories are, and the single-applicable-category rule removes the ambiguity.
Instructions of the when-in-doubt kind cause overtriggering, so the analyst queue would grow without the classification improving.
Moving the decision into the code does not improve it: the documentation asks the model to return only the single most applicable category.
Correct: reasoning before labelling, with the output separated into tags, is the documented pattern for classification and adds no calls to the pipeline.

question: Lakeside Online University split its research flow into three subagents, and the analyst is defined with tools Read, Grep and Glob to work on the papers the searcher passes it. In production two behaviours appear: when the student's query is ambiguous, the analyst never asks for clarification and answers anyway, and it does not download the PDFs it is pointed to either, with no error and no permission request recorded. Which two documented facts explain those behaviours? (Select TWO)
options: The download tool is not in the subagent's tools list, and a tool that is not listed does not exist in its session: it works without it, with no warning and no error.
AskUserQuestion is not available inside a subagent: it is one of the tools the runtime removes, so it has no way to ask the student.
The subagent inherits the parent's conversation and treats as clarified a question that was in fact still ambiguous for the student.
Subagents launched in the background lose their MCP tools, which is why the analyst cannot download any of the cited files.
The parent's PreToolUse hook silently denies tools it does not recognize and the subagent receives no reason explaining the block.
answer: The download tool is not in the subagent's tools list, and a tool that is not listed does not exist in its session: it works without it, with no warning and no error.
AskUserQuestion is not available inside a subagent: it is one of the tools the runtime removes, so it has no way to ask the student.
explanation:
The general rule is that decomposing a flow is not only splitting tasks: it also defines what each part can do, and whatever is left out disappears silently. When the AgentDefinition lists a subset in tools, the absent tools are not in the subagent's session, which carries on without them and without raising an error or a permission request. On top of that, the runtime removes from every subagent the tools that interact with the person, among them AskUserQuestion, so a subagent cannot resolve an ambiguity by asking. The key distinction against the other explanations is that there is no block and no denial: there is absence, which is why nothing shows up in the logs.

RULE: What you leave out of tools is not blocked, it stops existing for the subagent; and no subagent can ask the person.

TRAP: Expecting an error or a permission request when a tool is missing: the subagent simply resolves without it and the symptom shows up in quality, not in the logs.

TRY IT: Define a subagent with tools Read and Grep, ask it for a task that needs to write a file and watch it finish without using Write and without recording any permission error.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents
option_feedback: Correct: restricting tools does not block calls, it removes the tool from the subagent's context outright, and it carries on as if it did not exist.
Correct: that tool is removed from every subagent's set, which is why the analyst answers with what it has instead of asking for clarification.
A subagent that is not a fork starts with an empty context: it does not see the parent's conversation, so it cannot treat anything there as clarified.
Background subagents run with a reduced set of built-in tools, but they keep all their MCP tools, so that is not what is missing here.
A denial from a hook returns a permissionDecisionReason to the model precisely so it knows why it failed and does not retry blindly.

question: The content team at Northlane Outfitters generates product descriptions with a flow configured like this: {"flow": "generate, evaluate, refine", "evaluator": {"prompt": "Evaluate whether the description is good", "output": "free text"}, "max_iterations": 3}. After the three rounds, the descriptions change style on each iteration but do not improve measurably, and sometimes the third version is worse than the first. What is the main defect of this configuration?
options: A stop condition is missing, which is why the loop keeps refining until it exhausts the run's budget.
The evaluator should run in the same instance that generates, so as not to lose the context of the original draft.
Three iterations are insufficient and the pattern needs at least ten rounds for the text to converge.
The evaluator has no explicit criteria and no comparable output, so the refine step receives opinions and not corrections.
answer: The evaluator has no explicit criteria and no comparable output, so the refine step receives opinions and not corrections.
explanation:
The general rule is that the evaluator-optimizer pattern is especially effective when clear evaluation criteria exist and when iterative refinement adds measurable value, just as happens when a person articulates their critique and the text improves with it. Asking it to evaluate whether the description is good and returning free text gives the refine step no concrete dimension to correct, so each round optimizes a different criterion and the result oscillates. The evaluation guidance adds that the judge needs a detailed rubric and an empirical output, such as a scale or a binary verdict. The key distinction against adding iterations is that without criteria each round is a change of style, not an improvement.

RULE: The evaluator-optimizer loop only works with clear criteria and actionable feedback: without a rubric, iterating only changes style.

TRAP: Assuming iterating improves things by itself: without explicit criteria, each round optimizes something different and the result oscillates.

TRY IT: Change the evaluator to return a score per criterion and a list of concrete corrections, run the same descriptions again and compare the scores of the first and third rounds.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests
option_feedback: Stop conditions are necessary, but this configuration already has one: it stops at the third iteration.
Quite the opposite: separating the evaluation into its own call is what allows focused attention on that specific aspect.
No such number exists in the documentation; the pattern depends on the quality of the criteria, not on a minimum number of rounds.
Correct: the evaluator-optimizer pattern is effective when there are clear evaluation criteria and the feedback is articulable and actionable for the next round.

question: Nora, at Kestrel Pay, asks Claude to raise the HTTP client timeout that calls the banking core from thirty to forty-five seconds. The file is six hundred lines long and the rest must stay untouched, because there is retry logic nobody wants to disturb. What is the correct approach?
options: Use Write with the full content of the already modified file, to have exact control over how the final result looks.
Use Bash with an in-place substitution on the file, because it avoids the prior read step and resolves the change in one command.
Use Read with offset and limit over the timeout area and ask Claude to describe the change to apply in its response.
Use Edit with an old_string that includes enough context around the value, so the match is unique.
answer: Use Edit with an old_string that includes enough context around the value, so the match is unique.
explanation:
The general rule is that Write is for creating a file or replacing it entirely, while a partial change to an existing file is made with Edit, which substitutes an exact string and touches nothing else. In a six-hundred-line file the difference is one of risk: rewriting it whole puts code nobody asked to modify in play, and a single line reproduced differently is enough to lose the retry logic. The key distinction against a shell substitution is that Edit requires a unique match and its changes stay within the scope of the checkpoint.

RULE: Write creates or overwrites the whole file; for a partial change to an existing file, Edit with a unique match.

TRAP: Confusing wanting control over the result with rewriting the whole file: Write does not merge, it replaces everything that was there.

TRY IT: Ask Claude for a one-line change in a long file and watch which tool it uses and how much context it puts in old_string; then ask for the same change on a value that appears twice and observe the ambiguous match error.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
option_feedback: Write creates or overwrites the whole file, so everything else depends on the content being reproduced without a single difference.
It works, but it asks for permission, does not apply the unique match check and leaves the change outside what the checkpoint can revert.
Reading a fragment is a reasonable first step, but describing the change does not apply it: the tool that actually edits the file is missing.
Correct: Edit replaces an exact string and leaves the rest of the file intact, which is exactly Nora's requirement.

question: The list_shipments tool of the Southline Logistics MCP server responds like this when the query spans too many shipments: {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Error: result too large"}], "isError": true}. The agent repeats the same call twice more and then abandons the task. How should that response be redesigned?
options: Report it as a JSON-RPC protocol error so the client cuts the call before the agent spends turns retrying.
Keep the error and add the legacy system trace, so the agent understands where the volume problem comes from.
Raise the server's internal limit so the eight thousand shipments fit in a single response and the agent does not have to retry.
Return the first page of results with a note stating how many were left out and which filters to use to narrow it down.
answer: Return the first page of results with a note stating how many were left out and which filters to use to narrow it down.
explanation:
The general rule is that a tool response, even when it truncates, must leave the agent able to take the next step: partial results plus an indication of what was omitted and with which parameters to narrow it down. An error with no way out only invites repeating the same call, which is exactly what the trace shows. The key distinction against raising the limit is that truncation with instructions steers the agent towards more token-efficient strategies, such as filtering and paginating, while enlarging the container moves the problem into the context.

RULE: If you truncate, tell the agent what is missing and how to ask for it: partial results with instructions are worth more than an error with no way out.

TRAP: Assuming marking isError is enough for the model to correct itself, when without parameters or a next step all it can do is retry the same way.

TRY IT: Make your tool return twenty of five hundred rows with a note about the available filter and cursor, repeat the same request and count how many calls the agent needs against the version that only returned the error.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools
option_feedback: Protocol errors are for problems with the request and the model rarely recovers from them; here the call was valid, it simply returned too much.
A trace describes the inside of the server and does not say what to do differently; the agent still does not know which parameters would narrow the query.
It avoids the error at the cost of dumping everything into the context, which is exactly what the tool design guidance asks you to avoid with filters and pagination.
Correct: the agent receives usable data and a concrete instruction for the next call, instead of a wall to retry against.

question: The operations agent at Cascade Power opens each incident with a diagnostic pass that queries four read-only tools defined in an in-process MCP server with the SDK: grid status, outage history, weather and open work orders. Grant sees in the logs that the four calls run one after another and add up to eight seconds before the first response to the operator, even though none depends on the others' result. What should you do to make them run in parallel?
options: Ask in the system prompt for the agent to call the four tools in parallel when opening each diagnosis, before answering the operator.
Remove disable_parallel_tool_use from the query's tool_choice to enable the agent's simultaneous calls.
Mark those four tools with readOnlyHint in their annotations, because custom tools run sequentially by default.
Launch each query in a background subagent and wait for the four results before answering the operator.
answer: Mark those four tools with readOnlyHint in their annotations, because custom tools run sequentially by default.
explanation:
The general rule of the SDK loop is that read-only tools can execute concurrently while those that modify state run serially, and that a custom tool is considered a write tool unless its annotation says otherwise. That is why the fix is to declare readOnlyHint in the annotations of the four query tools: from then on the runtime can run them at once and the diagnostic pass stops being a queue. The key distinction against asking for it in the prompt is one of layer: the prompt influences how many calls the model emits, not how the runtime executes them, and annotations are definition metadata, not a permission rule.

RULE: Read-only tools run in parallel, but a custom tool is sequential until its readOnlyHint annotation says otherwise.

TRAP: Confusing the model layer with the runtime layer: asking for parallelism in the prompt does not change how custom tools are executed.

TRY IT: Instrument two custom tools with start and end timestamps, ask the agent to call both, and compare the intervals before and after adding readOnlyHint.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/custom-tools https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: The prompt can encourage the model to emit several calls together, but the execution of custom tools remains sequential until you enable it in the definition.
That field exists in the Messages API to force one tool at a time, it is not what governs the execution of custom tools inside the Agent SDK.
Correct: readOnlyHint is the annotation that enables concurrent execution, and without it every custom tool stays in the sequential lane.
It parallelizes, but it pays the cold start of four subagents for four simple reads, when latency is precisely what you want to reduce.

question: To speed up a migration, Erin works with Claude Code on the City of Fairview permits repository. After half an hour of investigation she knows the failure lives in two specific files and delegates the review to a subagent with the message: review what we just found and propose the fix. The subagent returns a generic analysis about another module, without mentioning those files. There were no API errors, no output marked as partial and no turn limit reached. What is the most likely cause?
options: The subagent started with a fresh context and only received the text of the delegation message, which names neither the files nor the finding.
The subagent reached its turn limit and returned what it had done up to that point of the module review.
Compaction summarized the main session's investigation and the subagent inherited that summary instead of the full detail.
The subagent could not open the files because its tool configuration does not include the necessary write permission.
answer: The subagent started with a fresh context and only received the text of the delegation message, which names neither the files nor the finding.
explanation:
The general rule is that a subagent does not see the conversation of whoever invokes it. Except in the case of a fork, its context window starts clean and the only content travelling from parent to subagent is the prompt string of the Agent tool, so file paths, error messages and decisions already taken have to be written there explicitly. A brief such as review what we just found means nothing to somebody who was not in that conversation, and the subagent does the only thing it can: explore on its own and choose badly. The key distinction against compaction is that this is not a degraded summary, it is that there is no context inheritance at all.

RULE: A subagent does not see your conversation: paths, errors and decisions go written into the delegation message.

TRAP: Assuming what we just found means something to the subagent: its context window starts clean.

TRY IT: Repeat the delegation with the same objective but including the paths of the two files and the exact symptom, and compare the result with the vague message.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents
option_feedback: Correct: unless it is a fork, the subagent starts with a clean window and the only thing arriving from the parent is the delegation prompt string.
The stem rules that case out, and besides that situation is signalled by marking the output as partial so the parent knows.
The subagent inherits neither the detail nor the summary of the parent's conversation: it does not see its turns at all.
Reading only needs read permissions, and a denial would come back as a tool result explaining the block, not as an analysis of another module.

question: Cascade Power audits every tool call by sending it to a corporate webhook that takes around 1.2 seconds to answer. The team solved it with a PostToolUse hook that publishes the event and returns, and since then the operators notice the agent is noticeably slower on shift. The audit must keep recording every call, but that hook does not need to block anything or modify what the model sees. Which change is right?
options: Return an asynchronous output from that audit hook so the agent continues without waiting for the webhook, accepting that it can no longer block or inject context.
Move the audit to a PreToolUse hook so the logging happens before the tool runs and does not add to the latency of the result the operator is waiting for.
Lower that hook's timeout to two seconds to bound the impact of each call in the worst case of the shift.
Record the audit from the tool's own code instead of a hook, and return the result only once the webhook has confirmed receipt.
answer: Return an asynchronous output from that audit hook so the agent continues without waiting for the webhook, accepting that it can no longer block or inject context.
explanation:
The general rule is that a hook producing only side effects does not have to be on the critical path. Asynchronous output lets the agent continue immediately while the hook finishes its work, and it is documented precisely for logging, metrics and notifications. The explicit price is that an asynchronous hook cannot block the operation, modify it or inject context, which is acceptable here because the audit only observes. The key distinction against lowering the timeout is that a timeout bounds the worst case without removing the usual wait, while asynchronous output eliminates it for every call.

RULE: A hook that only observes is returned asynchronously; only what needs to decide or modify deserves to be on the critical path.

TRAP: Assuming moving the hook event or trimming its timeout removes the wait: as long as the hook is synchronous, the agent waits.

TRY IT: Measure the time between two tool calls with a PostToolUse hook that sleeps for a second, and repeat the measurement returning asynchronous output from that same hook.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks
option_feedback: Correct: asynchronous output is designed for side effects such as logging, metrics and notifications, and giving up the ability to block costs nothing in this case.
It changes the moment, not the wait: PreToolUse also blocks the call while it runs, and on top of that it delays the tool's execution instead of its result.
The timeout limits the damage of a hung webhook, but in normal operation the agent still waits the 1.2 seconds of every publication.
It moves the logic out of the hook but keeps the wait inside the tool's execution, so the operator perceives exactly the same delay.

question: The record_authorization tool at Cedar Ridge Health receives a free-text rejection_reason field. Claude fills it sometimes with a long sentence in the third person, sometimes with two loose words and sometimes by copying the whole paragraph from the document verbatim, so the weekly report is unreadable. The schema cannot express that style and Ben does not want to add a second rewriting call. What should you do?
options: Add input_examples to the tool definition with two or three valid calls showing the expected style of the field.
Enable strict: true on the tool so the content of the field matches exactly what the schema declares.
Add minLength and maxLength to the field to bound its length and thereby force more uniform wording.
Lower the temperature of the model call so the wording of the field does not vary from one authorization document to another.
answer: Add input_examples to the tool definition with two or three valid calls showing the expected style of the field.
explanation:
The general rule is that format, tone and structure are taught by showing examples, because that is more effective than describing them in the abstract. When what has to be fixed is how a tool argument is filled in, those examples have their own place: the input_examples field of the definition, whose examples must be valid according to the input_schema and show the model exactly what a correct call looks like. That solves the style without adding a second call. The key distinction against strict: true is that the schema guarantees the shape of the data, not the writing convention of a free-text field.

RULE: Format and tone are taught with examples; for tool calls that example lives in input_examples.

TRAP: Expecting the schema to impose style: it guarantees types and fields, not how a free-text field is written.

TRY IT: Add two valid input_examples to the tool, pass ten documents and count how many rejection_reason values respect the style compared with the previous run.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: Correct: examples are the most reliable way to set format, tone and structure, and for tool calls those examples travel in input_examples, validated against the input_schema.
strict guarantees types, required fields and valid names, but free text is still a string: the schema has no way of demanding a writing style.
String restrictions are not supported by structured outputs and using them returns a 400; besides, length does not define style.
Temperature adjusts sampling variability, it does not set a writing convention, and the most recent models reject values other than the default.

question: The Kestrel Pay agent calls the Messages API directly and combines a client tool of its own, lookup_transaction, with the web_search server tool to check the status of the acquiring network. In some responses Maya sees stop_reason equal to pause_turn arrive, with no client tool block waiting to be executed. What is the correct sequence for continuing the conversation?
options: Treat pause_turn as a transient API error → retry the same request from scratch with exponential backoff → continue the loop when a clean response arrives.
Build a tool_result for the pending server_tool_use → send it in a user message → follow the loop until stop_reason is end_turn.
Return the received response as is as the assistant turn → send a new request with that conversation → repeat until stop_reason stops being pause_turn.
Raise max_tokens and resend the last user message → let Claude redo the search from the beginning → break the loop on reaching end_turn.
answer: Return the received response as is as the assistant turn → send a new request with that conversation → repeat until stop_reason stops being pause_turn.
explanation:
The general rule is that stop_reason describes why Claude stopped generating and not an error: pause_turn appears when the server's sampling loop reaches its iteration limit running server tools such as web_search. The documented continuation is to return the response as is and issue a new request, so the server picks the pending work back up. The key distinction against client tools is who executes: for lookup_transaction you return a tool_result, whereas for web_search you build nothing and simply continue the conversation.

RULE: On pause_turn do not retry and do not build a tool_result: return the response as is and send a new request.

TRAP: Reading pause_turn as a network error or a token limit, when it is a normal pause of the server tool loop arriving with HTTP 200.

TRY IT: Fire a request with the web_search server tool and a question requiring several searches, see whether stop_reason pause_turn arrives, resend the response as is and check that the next one continues the work.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works
option_feedback: pause_turn arrives with HTTP 200 and does not indicate a failure: it is a normal pause in a long response, so retrying from scratch repeats work and discards what the server tool already resolved.
Server tools are executed by Anthropic and you never build a tool_result for them. That step applies only to client tools such as lookup_transaction.
Correct: the documentation says to continue by sending the response as is; the server's sampling loop picks up where it left off and closes with another stop_reason when it has no work left.
max_tokens governs the length of the output, not the iteration limit of the server tool loop, so raising it does not change the reason pause_turn arrived.

question: Summit Mutual Insurance classifies 40,000 claims every night and each request repeats the same coverage manual of around 30,000 tokens before the text of the case. The results are only needed the following morning and Nora's team has an aggressive cost-per-classification target. Which strategy cuts the total cost of the nightly job the most?
options: Send the 40,000 requests through the Messages API with high concurrency, marking the manual with cache_control so they all read the same cache entry.
Send the work with the Message Batches API including identical cache_control blocks in every request and sustaining a steady flow so the cache does not expire.
Send the work by batch placing the claim text first and the coverage manual at the end of each request, with cache_control on the manual.
Drop the batch because its requests do not benefit from prompt caching and use only the 1-hour cache in synchronous calls to the manual.
answer: Send the work with the Message Batches API including identical cache_control blocks in every request and sustaining a steady flow so the cache does not expire.
explanation:
The general rule is that the Message Batches API and prompt caching discounts stack, because they are independent mechanisms: one cuts the price of all tokens by 50 % and the other charges cache reads at 0.1 times the input price. For the second to work inside a batch you have to include identical cache_control blocks in every request and keep a flow of submissions that stops the entry expiring after five minutes. The key distinction against the synchronous option is that the work does not need an immediate response, and against putting the manual at the end is that the cache only reuses prefixes: everything that changes per request must come after the marked block.

RULE: Stable content goes at the start and with the same cache_control in every request; the batch and the cache add up, they do not exclude each other.

TRAP: Assuming a batch and prompt caching compete with each other, or placing the cache_control after content that changes on every request.

TRY IT: Send the same long prefix twice with cache_control and check in usage whether cache_read_input_tokens stops being zero; then move the marked block behind the variable text and check that it returns to zero.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
option_feedback: Prompt caching helps, but you give up the batch's 50 % discount and a cache entry only becomes available after the first response starts, so a parallel burst produces repeated writes instead of reads.
Correct: the batch's 50 % discount and the reduced price of cache reads stack, and the documentation asks for exactly identical cache_control in every request and a sustained flow to maximize hits.
The cache covers the prompt prefix up to the marked block; if each request starts with different text, the prefix always changes and you pay for a new write without ever getting to read.
Batch and caching discounts do stack according to the documentation, with typical hit rates of 30 % to 98 %; giving up the batch over that belief leaves half the saving on the table.

question: Brightwater Press keeps the site in one repository and the design system in another. Marcus opens Claude Code in the site repository and adds the other with --add-dir ../design-system, which has its own CLAUDE.md with the component conventions. Claude edits the design system files without trouble, but it keeps applying the site's conventions and none from the other repository. What explains this behaviour?
options: Claude Code concatenates the additional directory's CLAUDE.md after the project's CLAUDE.md, but the project rules take priority and end up overriding it.
Directories added with --add-dir give access to the files, but their CLAUDE.md is not loaded unless you import it from the project CLAUDE.md or enable the environment variable provided for that.
The additional directory's CLAUDE.md is loaded only when Claude reads a file from that directory, so it arrives too late for the first edit.

The path is missing from permissions.additionalDirectories, which is the key that loads an additional directory's configuration, while --add-dir grants access to the files but reads nothing from its .claude folder.
answer: Directories added with --add-dir give access to the files, but their CLAUDE.md is not loaded unless you import it from the project CLAUDE.md or enable the environment variable provided for that.
explanation:
The general rule is that Claude Code builds the CLAUDE.md hierarchy from the working directory up to the root of the file system and, downwards, loads subdirectory files when it reads files in them. A directory added with --add-dir is in neither of those two positions: it provides file access, not memory. That is why the design system CLAUDE.md only enters context if you import it from the project CLAUDE.md or if you enable the environment variable that loads the configuration of additional directories. The key distinction against on-demand loading is geometric: that loading only happens below the working directory.

RULE: Granting access to a path and loading its memory are different things: --add-dir does the first, not the second.

TRAP: Assuming working with files from another repository is the same as working inside it: the CLAUDE.md hierarchy is computed from the launch directory.

TRY IT: Open a session with --add-dir pointing at another repository, run /context and check that its CLAUDE.md does not appear among the loaded memory files.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions
option_feedback: Discovered CLAUDE.md files are concatenated without overriding each other, so the priority premise is false; besides, the additional directory's file never got loaded at all.
Correct: the memory hierarchy is computed from the launch directory upwards, and additional directories fall outside that hierarchy unless you import them or enable them explicitly.
That is the on-demand loading of CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories of the working directory; a directory added with --add-dir is not a subdirectory of the project.

The settings key exists and is the persistent way of adding a directory, but the split works the other way round: that key grants file access and nothing more, while the flag does load skills, commands and subagents from that path. What neither loads by default is the CLAUDE.md.

question: At Cascade Power the scheduled outage procedure lives in a project skill, at .claude/skills/scheduled-outages/SKILL.md, and the main agent follows it step by step. Marcus delegates the planning to a subagent defined in the agents field, without restricting tools, and its plans always omit the critical customer verification the skill requires. That same subagent does apply the conventions from the repository CLAUDE.md. What is the most likely cause?
options: The subagent starts with the parent's system prompt but without its history, so the skill instructions are lost on switching execution context.
Skill content is not preloaded into a subagent: the skill has to be listed in the skills field of its AgentDefinition for it to arrive in full.
Skills are only loaded when settingSources includes project, and that source does not reach the subagent even though the parent already has it active.
By not declaring tools in the AgentDefinition, the subagent is left without Read and cannot open the repository SKILL.md file.
answer: Skill content is not preloaded into a subagent: the skill has to be listed in the skills field of its AgentDefinition for it to arrive in full.
explanation:
The general rule is that a subagent starts with a fresh context window and only receives what you pass it explicitly: its own system prompt, the Agent tool prompt and the project CLAUDE.md hierarchy. Skill content does not travel with it; the documentation states that the skills field of the AgentDefinition preloads in full the material the subagent needs. The key distinction against the lost-context hypothesis is that nothing was truncated here: that procedure never entered the subagent's session.

RULE: What the subagent needs is declared: skills in the skills field and context in the Agent tool prompt; it inherits nothing from the parent.

TRAP: Assuming that whatever the main agent already has loaded, skills included, automatically travels to the subagent it launches.

TRY IT: Define a subagent that depends on a project skill, invoke it first without declaring skills and then declaring it, and compare whether the plan it returns includes the SKILL.md steps.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/claude-code-features
option_feedback: A subagent receives neither the parent's system prompt nor its history: it starts with its own. Context isolation is real, but this option's premise is not.
Correct: the subagent receives its own prompt, the Agent tool prompt and the project CLAUDE.md, but skill content is only preloaded if you declare it in the skills field.
Skills do depend on the setting sources, but the subagent inherits that configuration from the session, and the fact that it applies the project CLAUDE.md proves the project source is active.
Omitting tools does the opposite: the subagent inherits every available tool. Restricting the set is a deliberate decision, not the default state.

question: Kestrel Pay keeps one session per customer and resumes it every time the person writes back. On Tuesday Nora changed the refund policy in the system prompt append and deployed. Since then new conversations apply the new policy, but resumed ones keep reasoning with the old one, even though the process was restarted and the deployment is the same for all of them. What is the most likely cause?
options: Prompt caching is serving a cached prefix from the previous version and will keep doing so until that entry expires, because the resume reuses the same cache_control from the first turn.
The system prompt is built once in the session's first request and stored; the new append only applies in a new session or after a compaction.
On resuming, the SDK rereads the project CLAUDE.md and its content overrides the system prompt append in those sessions.
resume restores the transcript but discards the query options, so those sessions run with the minimal default system prompt.
answer: The system prompt is built once in the session's first request and stored; the new append only applies in a new session or after a compaction.
explanation:
The general rule is that a session stores the conversation and also the system prompt it was born with: it is built in the first request and recorded alongside the transcript. That is why a change to the append is only noticed in new sessions or when an existing session compacts and the prompt is rebuilt. The key distinction against the caching hypothesis is that the cache never alters the content sent and invalidates itself when the prefix changes, so it does not explain a stable difference between new and resumed conversations.

RULE: The system prompt is frozen in the session's first request: for a change to apply in live conversations, open a new session or wait for compaction.

TRAP: Assuming resuming a session rebuilds the system prompt from scratch with the current deployment configuration.

TRY IT: Create a session with an append setting a rule, resume it with a different append and check which of the two rules applies; then open a new session and compare the result.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/modifying-system-prompts https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions
option_feedback: A resumed session does reuse a stable prefix and each cache entry has its own expiry, but prompt caching only changes cost and latency: it does not decide which text is sent and the entry invalidates itself as soon as the prefix changes.
Correct: a session's prompt is built at the start and saved with it, so a different append on a later resume does not apply until the session compacts or until a new one is opened.
The CLAUDE.md is injected as project context into the conversation and does not replace the system prompt; besides, it behaves the same in new sessions, which do apply the new policy.
resume does take the options you pass in the query; if it discarded the configuration, those sessions would also lose their tools and the symptom would be far more visible.

question: Dana opens the session with claude --permission-mode plan to prepare the article template change at Brightwater Press: it touches 12 files and three contain legal text a lawyer reviews line by line. Claude finishes the plan and the approval prompt appears with the options "Yes, and use auto mode", "Yes, manually approve edits" and "No, keep planning". Which option matches what Dana needs?
options: Yes, and use auto mode, so the classifier reviews every command and every edit and the session moves forward without interruptions.
Yes, manually approve edits, to leave the approved plan and have each edit shown and approved one at a time.
No, keep planning, so Claude splits the plan into two phases and only then is the legal part approved.
Press Shift+Tab to leave plan mode, since the written plan applies anyway and each edit will ask for permission.
answer: Yes, manually approve edits, to leave the approved plan and have each edit shown and approved one at a time.
explanation:
The general rule is that a plan's approval prompt decides not only whether the plan is executed, but with how much supervision: each option sets the permission mode of the next phase. With files a person has to review one by one, the right option is manual approval of edits, which keeps the prompt on every change. The key distinction against auto mode is who reviews: there a classifier reviews and the session moves on by itself, reasonable for routine work but not for text with legal implications.

RULE: Approving a plan is also choosing the execution mode: auto delegates the review to the classifier, manual approval leaves it in your hands.

TRAP: Reading the three options as if they only differed in whether the plan runs, when what they change is the permission level afterwards.

TRY IT: Enter plan mode with Shift+Tab, ask for a change touching two files and approve with the manual approval option: check that each edit asks for permission separately.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Auto mode reduces the prompts because a classifier reviews the actions, but it removes precisely the edit-by-edit human review that is mandatory here.
Correct: it approves the plan and executes with manual approval, so every file touched, the legal ones included, goes through the permission prompt.
That option returns the session to plan mode to keep refining; there is no automatic splitting of the plan into separately approvable phases.
Shift+Tab leaves the mode without approving the plan: there is no handoff to execution and nothing in the plan applies on its own.

question: The internal MCP server at Falcon Labs exposes deploy_preview, which needs a personal token from the hosting provider. Today, when the token is missing, the tool returns an error asking the person to paste the token into the chat. Derek wants to redesign that point so the credential is not recorded in the conversation history and does not have to pass through the agent's hands. What should you do?
options: Ask for the token with an elicitation in form mode, marking the field as sensitive inside the requestedSchema so the client displays it hidden.
Declare the token as a required parameter of the tool's inputSchema, with a description explaining where to get it and a note asking not to reuse it across environments.
Use an elicitation in URL mode, which takes the person to the provider's authorization page so the sensitive interaction does not pass through the MCP client.
Return a JSON-RPC protocol error with code -32602 so the client opens its own credentials dialog.
answer: Use an elicitation in URL mode, which takes the person to the provider's authorization page so the sensitive interaction does not pass through the MCP client.
explanation:
The general rule is that when a tool is missing information there are two routes: return an actionable error in the result, or pause and ask for the value with elicitation. But elicitation has two modes and the specification is categorical: form mode must not be used for passwords, API keys, tokens or payment data, while URL mode exists precisely for sensitive interactions that must not pass through the MCP client. The key distinction against the form option is that hiding the field in the interface does not change the fact that the secret would travel through the client's channel.

RULE: Data the person can type without risk, form mode; credentials and authorizations, URL mode outside the MCP client.

TRAP: Assuming marking a field as sensitive in a form makes it suitable for credentials: the specification explicitly forbids it.

TRY IT: Walk through your server and mark every point where you ask the user for data: the ones that are credentials must be resolved with URL mode, not with a form.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/client/elicitation https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: Form mode is for requesting structured data, but the specification forbids using it for passwords, API keys, access tokens or payment data, no matter how the client hides them.

Documenting where the token comes from and warning against reusing it is good practice in a tool description, but declaring it as a parameter turns it into an argument the model composes and which ends up written into the conversation history, which is exactly what Derek wants to avoid.
Correct: URL mode exists for sensitive interactions that must not cross the client, and it lets the provider deliver the authorization through its own channel.
Protocol errors describe problems with the request and trigger no credentials dialog; besides, the model can hardly recover from them.

question: In the Go repository of the Cascade Power work order system, Maya asks to find every use of interface{}. Claude calls Grep with pattern "interface{}" and the result comes back empty, even though she knows there are dozens of matches in the code. What should you do?
options: Switch to Glob with the pattern **/*.go and review by hand every file the search returns.
Escape the metacharacters in the pattern, interface\{\}, because Grep uses ripgrep syntax.
Repeat the search with multiline true so the pattern can cross line breaks between the braces.
Run grep -F with the Bash tool, because Grep does not accept braces inside the pattern.
answer: Escape the metacharacters in the pattern, interface\{\}, because Grep uses ripgrep syntax.
explanation:
The general rule is that Grep is not POSIX grep: it is built on ripgrep and uses its regular expression syntax, so metacharacters have to be escaped. The braces of interface{} are read as a quantifier and the pattern matches nothing; written as interface\{\} they become literal text again. The key distinction against jumping to Bash is that the dedicated tool is still the right one: the problem was not the tool but the pattern.

RULE: Grep speaks ripgrep: if the pattern carries braces, parentheses or literal dots, escape them before doubting the tool.

TRAP: Reading an empty result as an absence of matches in the code, when the emptiness was produced by the interpretation of the pattern itself.

TRY IT: Search for interface{} in a Go repository first unescaped and then as interface\{\}, and compare the number of matches.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
option_feedback: Glob finds files by name, not lines inside them; opening dozens of files by hand is exactly the work Grep avoids.
Correct: Grep is built on ripgrep and applies its regular expression syntax, so braces are interpreted as metacharacters until you escape them.
Multiline allows patterns spanning several lines, but it does not change how braces are interpreted inside the pattern.
Bash would work, but the premise is false: Grep accepts the pattern once escaped and, besides, it does not ask for permission inside the working directory.

question: Falcon Labs has to migrate 60 test files from Jest to Vitest. Grant prepares this loop: for file in $(cat files.txt); do claude -p "Migrate $file from Jest to Vitest. Answer OK or FAIL." --allowedTools "Edit,Bash(git commit *)"; done. The run will be unsupervised overnight. Which two practices does the documentation recommend before letting it loose on the full list? (Select TWO)
options: Add --dangerously-skip-permissions so no run stops at a permission prompt.
Launch the 60 runs in parallel with & so the whole migration finishes in a single pass.
Test first with two or three files and review the diffs before launching the loop over the entire list.
Pass --permission-prompts none, so anything that would ask for permission is denied instead of leaving the run waiting for somebody.
Switch to --output-format stream-json to follow the progress of each file in real time.
answer: Test first with two or three files and review the diffs before launching the loop over the entire list.
Pass --permission-prompts none, so anything that would ask for permission is denied instead of leaving the run waiting for somebody.
explanation:
The general rule of batch work is to validate the instruction on a small scale and decide in advance what happens to anything that would require a person. Testing with two or three files reveals whether the prompt and the allowed tool list are sufficient, and denying pending prompts stops a run from being blocked indefinitely waiting for an answer nobody will give. The key distinction against skipping permissions is that denying and approving everything are not the same: the first fails visibly and in a controlled way, the second hands over the machine.

RULE: Before automating over dozens of files, test with two or three and define what happens when something asks for permission.

TRAP: Confusing not asking with approving everything: --permission-prompts none denies what is not allowed, bypassPermissions authorizes it.

TRY IT: Run the loop with two files and --permission-prompts none, and check in the output which actions were denied before widening the list.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless
option_feedback: It removes the prompts, but the documentation reserves that mode for isolated containers or virtual machines and as a non-root user, not for the team's working machine.
It speeds up the clock, but several sessions writing over the same working tree step on each other and you lose the intermediate review.
Correct: the automation guidance recommends validating the instruction on a few files, because a badly calibrated prompt multiplied by 60 costs far more than the test.
Correct: in runs where nobody can answer, the documentation recommends denying up front anything not pre-approved instead of waiting.
It gives visibility, and it also needs --verbose, but it does not reduce the risk of the migration or replace testing on a few files.

question: The nightly sweep at Southline Logistics uses a lead agent that delegates to subagents across the tracking, fleet and rates MCP servers. Grant observes two things: adding subagents barely reduces the total run time, and when one fails after forty minutes because of a transient error in the fleet MCP, the sweep is redone from scratch and the cost doubles. What are the two most likely causes of that behaviour? (Select TWO)
options: The lead executes the groups of subagents synchronously: it waits for the slowest to finish before launching the next, so real parallelism stays bounded.
The lead's model is too small to plan a sweep of this size and that is why it distributes the work badly among the subagents.
There are no checkpoints: agents are stateful and errors compound, so without resume points a late failure forces all the previous work to be repeated.
The subagents share the lead's context window and compete for it, so adding more only leaves less space available for each one.
total_cost_usd does not account for the subagents' requests, so the budget cap does not cut the run when the cost spikes.
answer: The lead executes the groups of subagents synchronously: it waits for the slowest to finish before launching the next, so real parallelism stays bounded.
There are no checkpoints: agents are stateful and errors compound, so without resume points a late failure forces all the previous work to be repeated.
explanation:
The general rule is that in a multi-agent system time is set by coordination and reliability is set by resume points. Synchronous execution makes the lead wait for each set of subagents before continuing, so parallelism does not scale with the number of agents; and since agents are stateful and errors compound, a late failure without checkpoints brings down everything achieved so far. The key distinction against the other hypotheses is that none explains both symptoms at once, and two of them start from false premises about context and about cost accounting.

RULE: In multi-agent, attack latency with asynchronous execution and reliability with checkpoints that allow resuming from the point of failure.

TRAP: Assuming adding subagents speeds things up by itself, when the lead waits synchronously for each set before continuing.

TRY IT: Instrument a run with two groups of subagents and record when each one starts and finishes, to see whether the second group starts before the first closes.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: Correct: the lead's synchronous execution is a documented bottleneck, because while it waits for the full set of subagents it can neither advance nor dispatch the next group.
A more capable model may plan better, but that explains neither why the time does not drop when adding subagents nor why a late failure destroys all the work already done.
Correct: the production guidance recommends combining the agent's adaptability with deterministic safeguards, such as retries and regular checkpoints that allow resuming from the point of failure.
Each subagent runs with its own context window, and that isolation is precisely one of the reasons to delegate, so they do not compete for the lead's context.
It is the other way round: total_cost_usd includes the subagents' requests and the max_budget_usd cap is compared against exactly that total.

question: The policy assistant at Summit Mutual Insurance answers coverage questions from five documents the team sends as document blocks in every request. Today the prompt asks for each statement to close with a reference of the form document 2, page 4, and the analysts found references to pages that do not exist. Marcus needs every statement tied to a real fragment of the document. What should you do?
options: Keep the prompt-requested references and add a second step where the model verifies each citation against the document and withdraws the statement if it finds no support.
Enable the citations feature on the document blocks so the response carries citation blocks with cited_text and the corresponding document_index.
Enable citations only on the two most consulted documents to bound the cost and leave the other three with prompt-requested references.
Force a schema with output_config.format that includes a mandatory source field next to every statement in the response.
answer: Enable the citations feature on the document blocks so the response carries citation blocks with cited_text and the corresponding document_index.
explanation:
The general rule is that provenance is obtained with the mechanism that returns verified pointers, not by asking the model to write the reference into the text. The citations feature guarantees every citation points to an existing fragment of the document, returns the quoted text and the document index, and its cited_text is not billed as output. The key distinction against the extra verification step is that the step reduces the rate of invented references but does not eliminate it and adds a call, while the feature attacks the cause: the pointer stops being generated text.

RULE: If you need verifiable provenance, enable citations on the documents instead of asking for references inside the generated text.

TRAP: Confusing a reference written by the model with a pointer to the document: the first is text and can be invented, the second is built by the API.

TRY IT: Send a plain text document with citations enabled and a question whose answer is in a specific paragraph; check the cited_text and the character indices returned in the response.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations
option_feedback: Verifying each statement and withdrawing what has no citation is a documented technique, but it still depends on the model copying the pointer correctly and costs an extra call the feature resolves at the source.

Correct: the feature's citations always point to a real fragment of the document, cited_text does not count as output tokens and, in Anthropic's evaluations, it cites the most relevant passages better than the prompt-based approach.
You cannot mix: the documentation states citations must be enabled on all the documents in the request or on none.
Structured outputs guarantees the shape of the JSON, not that the value of the source field exists; besides, combining citations with output_config.format in the same request returns a 400 error.

question: The automated tutor at Lakeside Online University runs with the Agent SDK. On some queries it enters a long cycle: it repeats searches, rephrases and keeps calling tools without closing the answer, and a single one of those sessions consumed a whole day's budget. Hannah wants hard cuts on the loop, imposed by the application and not by the prompt. Which two SDK options give her that? (Select TWO)
options: Reduce max_tokens on each request so responses are shorter and the agent reaches the end of the tool loop sooner.
Set max_turns, which counts only turns with tool use and ends the query with a ResultMessage of subtype error_max_turns.
Define stop_sequences with a closing marker so generation stops as soon as the agent writes it in its response.
Set max_budget_usd, which stops the query when the client's cost estimate reaches that value and includes the subagents' spend.
Lower effort to low so the agent reasons less and needs fewer steps before closing the answer.
answer: Set max_turns, which counts only turns with tool use and ends the query with a ResultMessage of subtype error_max_turns.
Set max_budget_usd, which stops the query when the client's cost estimate reaches that value and includes the subagents' spend.
explanation:
The general rule is that cuts to the agentic loop are enforced with application parameters and not by asking the model. The SDK offers two independent caps: max_turns counts turns with tool use and max_budget_usd cuts by estimated cost, including the subagents' spend; both end the query with a ResultMessage of an error subtype you can handle and, where appropriate, resume with a higher limit. The key distinction against max_tokens, stop_sequences or effort is that those three act within one response and do not bound how many iterations the agent takes.

RULE: Every production agent carries a turn cap and a spend cap: max_turns and max_budget_usd, not instructions in the prompt.

TRAP: Confusing the limits of one response, such as max_tokens or stop_sequences, with the limits of the agentic loop.

TRY IT: Run a query with max_turns equal to 2 on a task that needs more steps and check that the ResultMessage arrives with subtype error_max_turns.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons
option_feedback: max_tokens limits the length of a response, not the number of loop iterations; besides, if it cuts a tool_use block in half, it forces the request to be repeated with a higher limit.
Correct: max_turns is a hard cap on the SDK loop; on reaching it the query ends with that subtype and you can resume the session with a higher limit if the task deserves it.
Stop sequences cut the generation of one response and are reported in stop_reason as stop_sequence, but they do not stop the loop from taking another turn of tools.
Correct: max_budget_usd bounds the spend of the whole query, covers the subagents' requests and ends with the error_max_budget_usd subtype.
effort regulates how much reasoning effort the model applies and may reduce steps on average, but it is not a cap: the number of iterations still depends on the model.
