question: Dana asks to bring up the local Kestrel Pay API and then run the integration tests. Claude runs Bash("npm run dev"), the server stays in the foreground and the session is blocked until the command hits its time limit and is moved to the background. Only then do the tests arrive. How should that call have been made?
options: Call Bash with run_in_background true for the server and make a second call with the tests, which is what is intended for long-running processes.
Raise BASH_MAX_TIMEOUT_MS so the server keeps running inside the same call without being cut off.
Chain the two things in one command, npm run dev && npm run test, so the tests start as soon as the server is up and listening.
Run the server from another call with a prior cd into the API directory, because each command runs in its own process.
answer: Call Bash with run_in_background true for the server and make a second call with the tests, which is what is intended for long-running processes.
explanation:
The general rule is that the Bash tool is designed for commands that finish, and for those that do not there is the parameter that sends them to the background. A development server falls into the second category: launched in the foreground it occupies the session until the time limit runs out, at which point Claude Code moves it to the background anyway, but with several minutes lost. The key distinction against raising the time limit is that the problem is not duration but the nature of the process: it is never going to finish on its own.

RULE: What does not finish on its own goes to the background from the start: servers, watchers and long processes are not solved by extending the timeout.

TRAP: Treating a permanent process as a slow command and looking for the solution in time limits.

TRY IT: Ask to bring up a development server and watch in /tasks that the background call leaves the session free while the process stays alive.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
option_feedback: Correct: servers and watchers are launched in the background and the session stays free for the next call, without waiting for the time limit to expire.
It moves the ceiling of the time limit, but a server never finishes: the call would keep occupying the session until the new limit and the problem simply lasts longer.
With && the second command waits for the first to finish successfully, and a server in the foreground does not finish: the tests would never run.
It is true that each Bash command runs in a separate process and that cd persists in the session, but changing directory does not stop the server from blocking the call.

question: Your team wants the GitHub Actions workflow to consume the subscription instead of an API key, storing a long-lived token as a repository secret. Which command issues that token?
options: claude setup-token, which issues a long-lived OAuth token designed for CI.
claude auth login, which opens the CLI's interactive session on the machine where it runs.
claude mcp login, which completes the OAuth flow of a remote MCP server.
claude doctor, which checks the installation and the configuration sources.
answer: claude setup-token, which issues a long-lived OAuth token designed for CI.
explanation:
The general rule is that a runner cannot complete an interactive login, so it needs a credential issued in advance and stored as a secret. The command that issues the long-lived OAuth token for that use is claude setup-token, and the GitHub action receives it as an alternative to the API key. The key distinction against the CLI login is the recipient: one authenticates your terminal, the other produces a portable secret for automation.

RULE: In CI the credential is issued beforehand with claude setup-token and stored as a secret; it is never written into the workflow file.

TRAP: Confusing logging in on your own terminal with issuing a reusable credential for a non-interactive environment.

TRY IT: Run claude setup-token, store the token it prints as a secret of a test repository and check in the workflow YAML that only the secret name appears there and never the credential.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/github-actions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference
option_feedback: Correct: that token is stored as a secret and the action receives it in claude_code_oauth_token, so usage goes against the subscription.
It authenticates your terminal, but it does not produce a reusable credential you can store as a repository secret.
That flow authorizes a specific MCP server; it has nothing to do with authenticating Claude Code on a runner.
It is a diagnostic tool: it reports on the environment and the configuration, and it issues no credentials.

question: Heartland Agronomics extracts soil lab values (pH, organic matter, nitrogen) from PDF reports and loads them into its data warehouse. The schema is strict, so the JSON is always valid, but an audit found that in 4 % of the reports the loaded value is not the one in the PDF and nobody notices until the customer complains. Maya wants to detect those cases before the load. Which two measures attack that problem directly? (Select TWO)
options: Ask it to return, alongside each value, the verbatim quote from the report it was taken from, and check in your code that the text appears in the document.
Set temperature to 0 so extraction is deterministic and the same report always produces the same numeric value.
Add to the prompt an instruction in capitals forbidding it to invent values under any circumstance before answering.
Make every numeric field in the schema optional so extraction never fails the load validation.
Run the same report twice with the same prompt and send to review only the cases where the two extractions disagree.
answer: Ask it to return, alongside each value, the verbatim quote from the report it was taken from, and check in your code that the text appears in the document.
Run the same report twice with the same prompt and send to review only the cases where the two extractions disagree.
explanation:
The general rule is that a strict schema guarantees the shape of the JSON, not the truth of the values: extraction quality is controlled with evidence and with comparison. Asking for the verbatim quote supporting each field lets you validate in code that the value comes from the document, and repeating the extraction to compare outputs exposes the inconsistencies that usually indicate invention. The two measures are independent: one creates verifiable per-field evidence and the other measures stability across runs. The key distinction against lowering the temperature or strengthening prohibitions is that those options try to avoid the error without producing any signal that would let you detect it.

RULE: A valid JSON is not a correct JSON: demand a verbatim quote per field and compare runs to detect what the schema cannot see.

TRAP: Assuming strict removes extraction errors: it guarantees types and structure, not that the number corresponds to the document.

TRY IT: Take 30 already-audited reports, run the extraction twice asking for the quote of each field and measure how many of the known errors fall into the group of disagreements or of quotes not found.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation recommends anchoring every claim in a verbatim quote and discarding what has no support; here the quote turns a silent error into a programmatic check.
Even at temperature 0 results are not fully deterministic, and newer models reject values other than the default; repeating the same error does not detect it either.
The guidance asks you to say what to do instead of what not to do and to tone down imperative language; a prohibition generates no signal that would let you detect the 4 % of errors.
Every optional parameter adds complexity to the schema and, above all, hides the problem: a wrong value would still come through with nothing flagging it.
Correct: this is the best-of-N verification Anthropic documents; inconsistencies between runs point precisely at the fields where the model is not anchored in the text.

question: The nightly pipeline at Heartland Agronomics validates every call to the write tools against an external service through a PreToolUse hook. The processing window is three hours and that service sometimes takes several minutes to respond. Ben needs no write to go out unvalidated and, at the same time, a delay from the service not to eat the entire window. Which hook configuration best fits that constraint?
options: Leave the event's default timeout, around ten minutes, and trust the external service to answer before the pipeline falls behind.
Set a short timeout in the HookMatcher and accept the failure mode: if it expires, the tool does not run and Claude receives a tool result stating the hook did not answer.
Return an asynchronous output from the hook so the agent continues immediately and the validation finishes in the background.
Move the validation to a command hook in settings.json so it runs outside the application process and does not block the agent loop.
answer: Set a short timeout in the HookMatcher and accept the failure mode: if it expires, the tool does not run and Claude receives a tool result stating the hook did not answer.
explanation:
The general rule is that a PreToolUse hook is the point where a condition is enforced before the tool runs, and that its timeout failure mode is closed: on expiry the call is not executed and the model receives a tool result explaining the hook did not answer. That is why bounding the timeout in the HookMatcher preserves the guarantee while limiting how much a slow service can cost the pipeline. The key distinction against asynchronous output is that it gives up precisely the ability to block, which is the one thing that cannot be negotiated here.

RULE: If the hook must block, do not make it asynchronous: bound its timeout and accept that on expiry the tool does not run.

TRAP: Confusing an asynchronous output, designed for side effects, with a prior validation that has to be able to deny the call.

TRY IT: Register a PreToolUse hook with a two-second timeout and a validation that sleeps for five, request a write and observe that the tool does not run and which tool result the model receives.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks
option_feedback: The default value exists so as not to cut off legitimate validations, but ten minutes per blocked call is incompatible with a three-hour window and several writes per run.
Correct: the timeout is a HookMatcher field and PreToolUse fails closed, so shortening it bounds the wait without giving up the guarantee that nothing is written unvalidated.
Asynchronous outputs are for side effects such as logging or metrics: they cannot block, modify the input or inject context, so the write would go out unvalidated.
A command hook runs in another process, but it is still synchronous with respect to the loop: the agent waits all the same and the total run time does not improve.

question: The reconciliation MCP server at Kestrel Pay exposes around 40 tools and Ethan notices the initial context grows considerably when he enables it. He tries this entry in .mcp.json: {"mcpServers": {"reconciliation": {"type": "http", "url": "${RECON_MCP_URL}", "alwaysLoad": true}}}. What effect does alwaysLoad have in that entry?
options: It keeps the connection open for the whole session so the server does not disconnect through inactivity.
It automatically approves that server's tools, with no need for permission rules to use them.
It forces the server to connect before the first question and blocks the session from starting until it has the list.
It exempts the server from tool search: its tool definitions are loaded in full at the start instead of being deferred.
answer: It exempts the server from tool search: its tool definitions are loaded in full at the start instead of being deferred.
explanation:
The general rule is that tool search defers MCP tool definitions: at the start only the names and the server instructions enter, and the full schema is loaded when Claude needs it. Marking a server with alwaysLoad takes it out of that mechanism and goes back to paying the context of the 40 definitions from startup, which is exactly the opposite of what Ethan wants. The key distinction against the permission and connection options is the layer: alwaysLoad decides what enters context, not what is authorized or when the server connects.

RULE: With tool search only the names enter; alwaysLoad is the exception that loads that server's full schemas from the start.

TRAP: Reading alwaysLoad as always available or always allowed when it means always loaded in context.

TRY IT: Run /context with the server marked with alwaysLoad and again without marking it, and compare how much the tool definitions occupy.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: Inactivity cut-offs are tuned with timeout environment variables; this field plays no part in the life of the connection.
Approval is configured with permission rules such as mcp__reconciliation__*; alwaysLoad does not touch permissions at all.
MCP server startup is not blocking by default and this field does not change that behaviour.
Correct: with tool search active only the names and the server instructions enter, and alwaysLoad is the exception that loads the full schemas again.

question: The compliance team at Riverbank Financial reviews one regulatory bulletin at a time with a specialized subagent they defined in the agents field. Dana wants that same subagent to pick the analysis back up with everything it read before when an erratum to an already reviewed bulletin arrives, instead of starting from scratch. The main session is preserved on disk. What should you do?
options: Invoke the subagent again with the same subagent_type and paste a summary of what was reviewed into the prompt, so it rebuilds the previous state from that text.
Use the Explore subagent for the second pass, which keeps its transcript between invocations and picks the analysis up where it left off.
Store the agentId the Agent tool result returns and resume the session with the same definition in agents, giving that agent id in the prompt.
Resume the main session with fork_session enabled, so the subagents of the original session resume along with it.
answer: Store the agentId the Agent tool result returns and resume the session with the same definition in agents, giving that agent id in the prompt.
explanation:
The general rule is that subagents save their transcript in their own files, which persist independently of the main conversation, and that is why they can be resumed. The documented route is to capture the agentId that appears in the Agent tool result and return to the session passing that id in the prompt, with the same agent definition in agents: the resumed subagent retains its whole history. The key distinction against the fork is what gets branched: the fork copies the main session to explore another path, it does not resume a specific subagent.

RULE: To pick a subagent back up, store its agentId and resume the session with the same definition in agents; the fork branches the conversation, not the subagent.

TRAP: Assuming that resuming or forking the main session drags along the state of the subagents that ran inside it.

TRY IT: Invoke a subagent, note the agentId in its result, resume the session asking it to continue with that id and check whether it remembers the files it had already read.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions
option_feedback: It works as an approximation, but a summary loses detail and spends tokens rebuilding something that is already saved: subagent transcripts persist in their own files.
Explore is a read-only subagent designed to discover files and is single use: it returns no agentId, so there is nothing to resume.
Correct: the Agent tool result includes the agentId, and resuming the session with the same definition and that id in the prompt keeps the subagent's full history.
fork_session creates a copy of the main session with a new id to try another direction: it branches the conversation history, it does not return a subagent to its previous point.

question: At Cedar Ridge Health, Grant improves authorization extraction with few-shot: with five examples precision goes up, and in tests with twenty-five diverse examples it goes up considerably more. The problem is that block adds around 18,000 input tokens to each of the 12,000 daily requests and the cost spikes. How do you keep the quality of the twenty-five examples without paying for them in full on every request?
options: Trim the set to the five most representative examples, because the documentation sets that maximum and more examples degrade the result.
Move the example block to the end of the prompt, after the document to be extracted, so it falls outside the billed prefix.
Turn the twenty-five examples into input_examples inside the extraction tool definition, which are not part of the prompt and are not billed.
Leave the twenty-five examples at the start of the prompt and mark the end of that block with cache_control to reuse them as a cache read.
answer: Leave the twenty-five examples at the start of the prompt and mark the end of that block with cache_control to reuse them as a cache read.
explanation:
The general rule is that the 3 to 5 example recommendation is a starting point for prompts without caching, and that with prompt caching the documentation itself invites you to go above 20 diverse, high-quality examples because the block is written once and then read cheaply. Placing the examples at the start and marking the end of that block with cache_control turns that stable content into a reusable prefix, with reads at 0.1 times the input price that also do not consume the ITPM limit. The key distinction against trimming the set is that the cost here is a problem of repeated billing, not of too many examples.

RULE: With prompt caching, a large block of diverse examples at the start of the prompt is paid for once and read many times.

TRAP: Reading the 3 to 5 example recommendation as an upper limit instead of as the starting point without caching.

TRY IT: Build a prompt with twenty examples, mark the end of the block with cache_control and compare input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens between the first and second calls.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: The guidance recommends 3 to 5 examples as a starting point, not as a ceiling: with prompt caching the documentation suggests including more than 20 diverse, high-quality examples.
Position does not change what is billed: the whole prompt counts as input, and leaving stable content at the end is precisely what prevents caching a reusable prefix.
input_examples is for showing valid calls, but it also consumes tokens, on the order of 100 to 200 per complex example, and it travels inside the tool definitions.
Correct: this is the pattern prompt caching documents for large example sets; cache reads cost 0.1 times the input price and also do not count towards the ITPM limit.

question: At Brightwater Press, Nora redesigns the homepage and Ben fixes the search, both at the same time on the same site repository. Since the two sessions edit the same working tree, they overwrite each other's files and one person's tests fail because of the other's changes. Ben proposes launching his session with claude --worktree search. What resolves the situation best?
options: Have each person launch their session in their own worktree, with claude --worktree or with git worktree add, so each has its own checkout and branch.
Use /batch to split both tasks among subagents, since each works in its own worktree and opens its own pull request.
Have Ben pick up Nora's session with claude --continue so both see the same changes and there is no conflict.
Split the work between two subagents within a single session, each with its isolated context and its own set of tools, so both tasks progress in parallel.
answer: Have each person launch their session in their own worktree, with claude --worktree or with git worktree add, so each has its own checkout and branch.
explanation:
The general rule is that Claude Code has two different and non-interchangeable isolations: context isolation, provided by subagents and forks, and file isolation, provided by worktrees. The described symptom is about files, not context, so the solution is one checkout per session. The key distinction against /batch is purpose: /batch also creates worktrees, but to fan one instruction across many items and open pull requests, not to sustain two interactive lines of work in parallel.

RULE: Context is isolated with subagents; files are isolated with worktrees.

TRAP: Extrapolating the context isolation of subagents to the file system, which they still share with the main session.

TRY IT: Run claude --worktree test, confirm that its own checkout appears in .claude/worktrees and edit a file without your main copy changing.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees
option_feedback: Correct: each worktree is an independent checkout on its own branch, so the two sessions stop sharing files and each test suite only sees its own changes.
It is true that /batch spreads subagents across worktrees, but it is designed to apply one instruction to many items, not for two people with different, iterative tasks.
Continuing the most recent conversation shares context, it does not isolate files: both people would still be writing over the same checkout.

Subagents genuinely isolate context and can each receive a different subset of tools, but that isolation does not reach the file system: both still edit the same working tree and the conflict remains.

question: The research system at Lakeside Online University moved from sweeps of five subagents to literature reviews coordinating dozens of agents per run. Now the coordination work itself fills the lead agent's window: the conversation is crowded with invocations and results, and the final synthesis degrades. Erin confirms that each subtask on its own still works fine. What should you do?
options: Raise CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS above its default of twenty and lower each subagent's maxTurns, so the run dispatches more agents at once and each finishes sooner.
Chain levels of subagents, with intermediate coordinators distributing the work up to the nesting depth limit.
Move the orchestration into a Workflow tool script, which the runtime executes outside the conversation, and leave subagents for the few delegations per turn.
Compact the lead's conversation more often and archive the full transcript with a PreCompact hook before each summary.
answer: Move the orchestration into a Workflow tool script, which the runtime executes outside the conversation, and leave subagents for the few delegations per turn.
explanation:
The general rule is to choose the orchestration mechanism by scale: delegating to subagents is designed for a few tasks per turn, because each invocation and each result occupies the coordinating agent's window. When a run needs dozens or hundreds of agents, orchestration stops being a conversation and becomes a program: the Workflow tool executes that script in the runtime, outside the context. The key distinction against raising concurrency or nesting more layers is that those measures change how many agents run, not where the coordination lives.

RULE: A few delegations per turn, subagents; dozens or hundreds of agents, orchestration goes into a Workflow tool script, outside the conversation.

TRAP: Treating a coordination context problem as a concurrency problem and raising the parallel agent limits.

TRY IT: Launch a run with ten subagents and review the lead's transcript counting how many messages are Agent tool invocations and results against those of the analysis itself.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: Both controls are real: the concurrency limit bounds how many subagents run in parallel and maxTurns cuts each one's conversation. But neither changes how much context the coordination leaves in the lead's window, and dispatching more agents at once fills that window even faster.
Nesting distributes the coordination, but each layer still spends context, there is a default depth limit and you add summarization hops where information is lost.

Correct: the documentation states that subagents perform well with a few delegated tasks per turn and that, for runs coordinating dozens or hundreds of agents, Workflow takes the orchestration out of the context.
Compacting and archiving relieves the symptom and preserves evidence, but every summary loses detail: if the coordination stays inside the conversation, the context fills up again.

question: Southline Logistics records in its audit log every approval that passes through the canUseTool callback, which also asks for human confirmation on write tools. The session runs in default mode. Derek notices that calls to mcp__fleet__update_route execute normally but never appear in the log, while those to mcp__rates__set_rate are always recorded. What is the most likely cause?
options: That tool is listed in allowed_tools and auto-approved tools never reach the callback: canUseTool runs only when evaluation ends in a prompt.
The session is in dontAsk mode and in that mode the callback is never invoked, not even for tools that are not pre-approved.
The callback only receives built-in tools; MCP tools are resolved by their own permission scheme and do not pass through canUseTool.
The callback only sees calls from the main thread, and those writes are made by subagents, which evaluate their permissions independently of the parent.
answer: That tool is listed in allowed_tools and auto-approved tools never reach the callback: canUseTool runs only when evaluation ends in a prompt.
explanation:
The general rule is that canUseTool is invoked only when permission evaluation determines that a prompt is needed: if an allow rule has already approved the call, the tool runs without passing through the callback. That is why a tool listed in allowed_tools falls outside any log built on that callback, while unlisted ones do pass through it. The key distinction against dontAsk mode is the observable result: that mode also skips the callback, but it denies anything not pre-approved, and here the calls execute. For checks that must run on every call, the documentation says to use a PreToolUse hook.

RULE: Auditing from canUseTool leaves out everything auto-approved; what must run on every call goes in a PreToolUse hook.

TRAP: Reading allowed_tools as the list of tools permitted to the model, when it is an auto-approval list that skips the permission callback.

TRY IT: Add one tool to allowed_tools, leave another out and log every invocation from canUseTool: check which of the two appears in the record.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/python
option_feedback: Correct: a tool listed in allowed_tools is approved at the allow rules step and the flow never reaches the callback; to audit every call without exception you need a PreToolUse hook.
In dontAsk the callback is indeed not called, but anything not pre-approved is denied: those writes would not run, and the symptom says they do execute.
MCP tools go through the same permission evaluation as the rest, and in fact the rates ones do reach the callback, which rules out their MCP origin as the reason.
Subagents have their own permissions, but the symptom separates two tools of the same kind within the same run, not two different execution scopes.

question: The post-purchase agent at Northlane Outfitters answers 9,000 queries a day about exchanges and shipping. Today a team of three people reviews a sample of 60 responses per day by hand and cannot keep up with the prompt changes shipped every week. Dana wants an evaluation scheme that scales with the volume without losing the ability to detect rare cases. What should you propose?
options: Automate with code checks whatever is exactly verifiable, use an LLM judge with a rubric where judgement is needed, and sample edge cases by hand.
Expand the human review team until it covers 100 % of responses, since it is the most flexible and highest quality method the documentation describes.
Ask the model for a confidence score alongside each response and review by hand only those below a fixed threshold agreed with the team.
Ask the same model to judge its response with a yes or no question about whether it is correct and flag for review only those it answers no to.
answer: Automate with code checks whatever is exactly verifiable, use an LLM judge with a rubric where judgement is needed, and sample edge cases by hand.
explanation:
The general rule is to choose the cheapest evaluation method that gives enough signal for each kind of question: code checks are the fastest and most scalable but miss nuance, LLM judging is flexible and scalable if it has a detailed rubric, and human review is the most expensive and is reserved for what automation cannot see. The documentation also prefers more questions with slightly weaker signal and automatic grading over a few reviewed by hand. The key distinction against reviewing everything by hand is that this route does not scale to 9,000 daily queries, and against binary self-judging is that without a rubric the verdict is inconsistent.

RULE: Automate in code what is verifiable, use an LLM judge with a rubric for what requires judgement and spend the human hours on a sample of edge cases.

TRAP: Confusing maximum quality with the right method: full human review is the most precise and the one the documentation recommends avoiding as slow and expensive.

TRY IT: Take 50 responses already reviewed by people, write a four-criterion rubric for an LLM judge and compare its verdicts with the human ones before scaling the method.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation orders the methods by cost and scale, code first, then LLM and finally people, and it reminds you that human review is what detects edge cases, hallucinations and source biases.
It is true that it is the most flexible and highest quality method, but the same documentation describes it as slow and expensive and recommends avoiding it when an automatable alternative exists.
A confidence score is a valid field in a structured output, but there is no official guidance setting a threshold and the number does not say which part of the response fails or cover rare cases.
An LLM grader without a detailed rubric and with a binary output and no criteria is inconsistent; the documentation asks for clear rubrics and empirical, specific criteria.

question: You want Claude to investigate the code and propose a plan without touching any file yet, within a session that is already open. Which two documented ways activate plan mode? (Select TWO)
options: Press Shift+Tab until the status bar shows the plan mode indicator.
Prefix the prompt with /plan followed by the description of what you want planned.
Write a line in capitals in CLAUDE.md forbidding it to edit files before having a plan.
Start the session with --permission-mode acceptEdits and approve the plan when the investigation finishes.
Run /compact before asking for the plan to free context in the conversation.
answer: Press Shift+Tab until the status bar shows the plan mode indicator.
Prefix the prompt with /plan followed by the description of what you want planned.
explanation:
The general rule is that plan mode is a client permission mode and is activated through client routes: the Shift+Tab cycle, the /plan prefix in the prompt or the --permission-mode plan flag at startup. In an already open session the first two are the applicable ones. The key distinction against the CLAUDE.md option is that memory instructions are context the model almost always respects, whereas the mode is a restriction Claude Code enforces by itself.

RULE: Plan mode is activated from the client: Shift+Tab, the /plan prefix or --permission-mode plan when starting the session.

TRAP: Assuming an instruction written in CLAUDE.md can put the session into a permission mode.

TRY IT: Open a session, press Shift+Tab until the status bar shows plan mode, leave the mode and write a line in CLAUDE.md forbidding edits without a plan: you will see the indicator stays off no matter how you ask.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands
option_feedback: Correct: the permission mode cycle is walked with Shift+Tab and the status bar confirms which one you are in.
Correct: that prefix asks for the plan without switching mode by hand and is the most direct route within an already open session.
CLAUDE.md is loaded as context, not as enforced configuration: it influences behaviour but does not change the session's permission mode.
acceptEdits approves file edits automatically, which is the opposite of investigating without touching the code.
It summarizes the conversation to free context, which is useful, but it has nothing to do with the permission mode.

question: Cedar Ridge Health chains three calls to process each authorization: {"pipeline": ["extract_authorization", "summarize_for_audit", "record_in_system"]}. Each step receives the previous one's output with no intermediate check. When the extraction returns an incomplete policy number, the summary repeats it verbatim and the record enters the system with that value. What change should be made to this pipeline?
options: Merge the three steps into a single call so the model sees the whole document and does not carry errors between steps.
Insert a programmatic check between steps that validates the extraction output and breaks the chain when the value does not meet the expected format.
Add to the second step's prompt the instruction to verify that the policy number is complete and to return a status field with the reason when it is not.
Add a fourth step where another call reviews the final record and reports the inconsistencies to the audit team.
answer: Insert a programmatic check between steps that validates the extraction output and breaks the chain when the value does not meet the expected format.
explanation:
The general rule of prompt chaining is that programmatic checks, the gates, can be inserted between calls to stop the flow when an intermediate output does not meet expectations. Here the error is born in the extraction and propagates because nobody looks at it before passing it to the next step, so the gate goes right after that call. The key distinction against merging the steps is that the chain exists precisely to allow inspecting and cutting in the middle, and against reviewing at the end is that by that point the wrong value is already written into the system.

RULE: Between two steps of a chain goes a code check: the next step should only receive already validated inputs.

TRAP: Trusting format validation to the next step's prompt, when it is a deterministic check that belongs in the code.

TRY IT: Build a chain of two calls where the first returns JSON, add between them a function that validates the format and breaks the flow, and test with an incomplete document to confirm the second step never runs.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: Merging everything returns the task to a single harder call and removes the ability to inspect intermediate outputs, which is precisely the advantage of prompt chaining.
Correct: the documentation describes prompt chaining with programmatic gates between steps, so each step receives an already validated input and the error never reaches the end.

Asking for a status field makes the problem visible and helps within a step, but it is still the model checking itself: a format check is deterministic, belongs in the code and has to be able to break the chain, not merely note the reason.
Reviewing at the end detects the problem late and after writing to the system; the cheap gate goes immediately after the step that can fail.

question: The automated tutor at Lakeside Online University holds long conversations with students and uses context editing with the clear_tool_uses_20250919 strategy in its default configuration. Evan observes a pattern: when the conversation passes 100,000 input tokens, the next response arrives with cache_read_input_tokens at zero and the tutor looks up the course syllabus it had already read twice. What is the most likely cause?
options: The tool result clearing fired at its default threshold and, by replacing the old results, invalidated the cached prefix from that point on.
The prompt caching entry expired through its five-minute lifetime between two student messages and the whole prefix had to be written again.
Server-side compaction summarized the conversation, discarded the tool results and restarted the window with the summary.
The conversation exceeded the model's context window and the API started discarding the oldest messages on its own.
answer: The tool result clearing fired at its default threshold and, by replacing the old results, invalidated the cached prefix from that point on.
explanation:
The general rule is that context editing acts server-side on the history: on reaching the configured threshold it clears the oldest tool results and replaces them with a placeholder text, and that clearing invalidates the cached prefix from the point where it happens. Both symptoms match the same event and appear exactly on crossing the default value of 100,000 input tokens. The key distinction against cache expiry is the trigger: an expired TTL is not tied to a token threshold and does not erase information from the context. The clear_at_least parameter avoids clearing in dribs and drabs and paying the invalidation every time.

RULE: Every tool result clearing erases context and breaks the cache from that point: use clear_at_least and keep outside the conversation whatever must survive.

TRAP: Attributing to TTL expiry a cache loss that always appears at the same token threshold, which is the signature of a context clearing.

TRY IT: Configure clear_tool_uses with a low trigger, run a conversation with several tools and watch the context_management.applied_edits field in the response alongside the drop in cache_read_input_tokens.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
option_feedback: Correct: the default clear_tool_uses trigger is 100,000 input tokens, the cleared results are replaced by a placeholder and the clearing invalidates the cache where it happens; clear_at_least exists so each clearing is worth it.

A TTL expiry is possible in slow conversations, but it would explain cache misses at any moment and not precisely on crossing the threshold, and it does not explain the information disappearing from context either.
Compaction returns a compaction block at the start of the response that has to be resent, and its default trigger is 150,000 input tokens, not 100,000.
The API does not discard messages on its own: if the input exceeds the window it returns a 400 error, or generation ends with stop_reason model_context_window_exceeded.

question: Three months ago Summit Mutual Insurance completely replaced the human sampling of its claims triage with an automated evaluation using an LLM judge. The rubric covers data accuracy, policy application and fraud signals, and the judge still scores above 0.9 on the test set it was validated against the analysts' verdicts with. Even so, a new kind of fraudulent claim has been passing triage unflagged. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model acting as judge changed version and its criterion drifted from the moment it was validated against the analysts.
The judge's rubric does not cover fraud signals and that is why that kind of claim is never flagged in review.
The judge returns a continuous score instead of a pass or fail verdict and the cut-off threshold was set too high.
The test set does not include that modality and, by removing the human sample, they lost the control that detects unforeseen edge cases.
answer: The test set does not include that modality and, by removing the human sample, they lost the control that detects unforeseen edge cases.
explanation:
The general rule is that an automated evaluation measures very well what its test set represents and is blind to what is not there: a high, stable score over the same set says nothing about new cases. Anthropic recommends combining LLM evaluation, which scales, with a small human sample, because it is people who detect edge cases, hallucinations and selection biases automation misses. The key distinction against the incomplete rubric hypothesis is that the rubric does include fraud and performance did not fall: what changed is the population of cases, not the criterion.

RULE: Automate evaluation to scale, but always keep a human sample: it is the only control that sees what the test set does not contain.

TRAP: Reading a high, stable judge score as coverage: it only proves it keeps getting right the cases that were already in the test set.

TRY IT: Add ten never-evaluated cases to your test set and rerun the judge: compare its score on the old set and on the new cases.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests
option_feedback: A model change can move the scores, but then performance on the test set would also fall, and the stem says it stays above 0.9.
It would be a reasonable cause, but the stem clarifies that the rubric does include fraud signals; the problem is not what it measures but which cases it measures over.
The documentation in fact recommends a score from 0.0 to 1.0 alongside a pass or fail verdict; moving the threshold does not help when the new case does not even appear in what is being evaluated.
Correct: automated evaluation only measures what is already in the test set, and Anthropic points out that human review is what detects edge cases, hallucinations and biases automation cannot see.

question: The post-purchase agent at Northlane Outfitters resolves catalog questions with a search tool over the internal API. Tyler sees that, faced with vague requests such as "the black jacket I bought in March", the agent fires very long, highly specific queries, finds nothing and repeats variants until it exhausts the conversation budget. The goal is to resolve on first contact and with few calls. Which search strategy should you instruct it to use?
options: Expand the set of search tools so the agent can choose the most suitable one for each ambiguous request from the customer.
Raise the agent's effort to a high level so it reasons more before writing each query to the internal catalog.
Tell it to start with short, broad queries, assess what is available and only then narrow the focus progressively.
Launch several subagents in parallel, each with a different specific query, and keep the first one that returns results.
answer: Tell it to start with short, broad queries, assess what is available and only then narrow the focus progressively.
explanation:
The general rule when searching with an agent is to start with short, broad queries, assess what turns up and narrow progressively, instead of betting from the outset on a long, hyper-specific query that returns zero results. That heuristic is what turns a vague request into a bounded set of candidates with few calls, which is exactly what the first-contact resolution goal demands. The key distinction against parallelism is cost: firing several specific queries at once multiplies tokens without correcting the starting error.

RULE: Start broad and narrow afterwards: a short query tells you what exists, a hyper-specific one only tells you it found nothing.

TRAP: Assuming a more precise query from the first attempt saves steps, when what it does is fail leaving no information for the next one.

TRY IT: Take three real vague requests and compare how many calls the agent needs starting from a two-word query against starting with the customer's full sentence.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system
option_feedback: More tools do not fix a wrong query strategy and add another decision; the guidance asks for each tool to have a distinct purpose, not for multiplying similar options.
More reasoning effort produces better-thought-out queries, but just as narrow: the problem is not the quality of the reasoning but starting too specific.
Correct: this is the documented heuristic of starting broad and narrowing afterwards; a short query reveals what exists in the catalog and guides the next step instead of failing silently.
Parallelism is for independent subtasks that are worth their cost; here it multiplies the tokens of a conversation that has to be resolved on first contact.

question: Falcon Labs versions a .claude/settings.json in the repository whose permissions.allow includes "Bash(npm test *)" and "Edit(/src/**)". In Chloe's terminal everything runs without prompts. In the CI job, which runs claude -p "Run the tests and fix what fails" --permission-mode dontAsk, the run ends with no changes and the log shows permission denials. What is the most likely cause?
options: Project allow rules only apply after accepting the workspace trust dialog, and claude -p never shows it.
dontAsk denies everything not pre-approved, so the correct mode for the edits to go through is acceptEdits.
--setting-sources project is missing so Claude Code reads .claude/settings.json instead of only the user file.
Rules with parentheses are not valid in settings.json and Claude Code discards them when loading the file.
answer: Project allow rules only apply after accepting the workspace trust dialog, and claude -p never shows it.
explanation:
The general rule is that project allow rules and additionalDirectories are conditioned on workspace trust, an interactive step that only exists in the terminal. In a run with claude -p that dialog cannot be shown, so Claude Code warns the workspace is untrusted and does not apply those rules, although it still honours the deny rules, the hooks and the environment variables in the file. With dontAsk, which denies everything not pre-approved, the result is a run with no changes. The key distinction against the setting sources hypothesis is that the file is read all the same: what changes is which part of it is applied.

RULE: In headless there is no trust dialog: project allow rules do not apply and CI permissions go on the command line.

TRAP: Assuming a versioned permissions file is worth the same in the terminal and in CI, when workspace trust is an interactive step.

TRY IT: Run claude -p in a freshly cloned repository and observe the untrusted workspace warning; repeat passing --allowedTools "Bash(npm test *)" and compare the result.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless
option_feedback: Correct: in non-interactive mode there is no trust dialog, so the project allow rules have no effect and CI permissions have to be passed on the command line or through --settings.
dontAsk does deny what is not pre-approved, but the problem comes earlier: the project rules never got applied, and acceptEdits would not approve the Bash commands either.
The project source is loaded by default and the file is read; what is not applied without workspace trust is its list of allow rules.
The ones discarded on loading are mcp__ rules written with parentheses; Bash(npm test *) and Edit(/src/**) have exactly the documented form.

question: Brightwater Press stores its articles as markdown in content/2026/ and its editorial style conventions in .claude/rules/style.md, whose frontmatter is --- paths: ["*.md"] ---. Nobody sees the convention applied when Claude edits an article, even though the rules file is where it should be. What does the documentation predict about this configuration?
options: The pattern matches only the markdown files at the project root; for the nested articles you need content/**/*.md.
The rule loads in every session anyway because .claude/rules/ is read in full at startup; what fails is its priority against CLAUDE.md.
Rules with paths are activated on every tool call, so the problem is that Claude has not used any tool yet.
The frontmatter field should be called files and not paths, which is why Claude Code ignores the rules file entirely.
answer: The pattern matches only the markdown files at the project root; for the nested articles you need content/**/*.md.
explanation:
The general rule is that paths frontmatter decides when the convention enters: the rule is loaded on reading a file matching one of its globs. Globs follow the usual semantics, where one asterisk covers a level and two asterisks cross directories, so a root pattern never reaches nested articles. The key distinction against the priority hypothesis is that here the rule does not even compete: it never gets loaded.

RULE: In path rules the glob is the switch: one asterisk covers a level, two asterisks cross the tree.

TRAP: Reading a single-asterisk glob as if it were recursive and looking for the fault in the priority between memory files.

TRY IT: Change the pattern to content/**/*.md, open an article in content/2026/ and confirm with /context that the rule now appears among the loaded material.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: Correct: a single asterisk does not cross directories, so the rule never activates when opening a file inside content/2026/.
Rules without paths frontmatter do load at startup, but as soon as you declare paths the loading becomes conditional and depends on the pattern.
They are activated when Claude reads files matching the pattern, not on every tool use: the trigger is the read, not the activity.
The documented field is paths; with an invented name the rule would have no patterns and would always load, which is not what is observed either.

question: Cascade Power registers three independent PreToolUse hooks with the same matcher for the work order tool: one verifies the operator's authorization and stores it in a shared dictionary, another validates the parameters by reading that dictionary, and the third writes the audit entry. In testing everything passes, but in production the validator fails intermittently because it cannot find the operator. What is the most likely cause?
options: The hook returning allow beats the one returning deny, so the result depends on which of the three managed to write its decision first.
With several hooks under the same matcher the SDK runs only the first that matches, and the other two never run on each call.
Hooks run inside the agent's context window, so the model decides in which order to interleave them on each turn.
Every matching hook runs in parallel and their completion order is not deterministic, so one cannot depend on another having finished.
answer: Every matching hook runs in parallel and their completion order is not deterministic, so one cannot depend on another having finished.
explanation:
The general rule is that hooks matching an event execute in parallel, in your application's process, and that the order in which they finish is not guaranteed: that is why the documentation asks you to write each hook so it works on its own. Chaining state between hooks of the same event, such as writing into a shared dictionary for another to read, works when the timing cooperates and fails intermittently when it does not. If a sequence is needed, the order is enforced inside a single hook or in the logic that runs the tool. The key distinction against decision precedence is that deny over defer over ask over allow resolves which decision wins, not when each hook finishes.

RULE: Hooks of the same event run in parallel with no guaranteed order: each must work alone, and if you need a sequence put it inside one hook.

TRAP: Assuming the order in which you register the hooks defines the order in which they run and finish.

TRY IT: Register two PreToolUse hooks with the same matcher, one that sleeps a second before writing into a dictionary and another that reads it immediately, and repeat the call several times.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks
option_feedback: The precedence is documented and is the opposite: deny takes priority over defer, defer over ask and ask over allow, regardless of which hook answered first.
Every hook matching the matcher runs, not only the first: registering several independent hooks under the same matcher is the documented pattern.
Hooks run in your application's process and not in the agent's context window, which is why they consume no context and are not ordered by the model.
Correct: the documentation states that matching hooks run in parallel and that the order in which they finish is not guaranteed, so each must act independently.

question: Ben uses Claude Code to migrate the permits module at the City of Fairview. At the start of the session he told it by chat that every new endpoint must record its latency with the internal logger. After several hours and an automatic compaction, the following endpoints come out without that logger call, even though the commit style and the conventions from the root CLAUDE.md are still respected. What is the most likely cause?
options: Compaction erased the root CLAUDE.md from the context and with it all the project conventions.
The rule was in a .claude/rules/ file whose paths pattern stopped matching the module's new files.
The model lost the instruction because the conversation exceeded the context window and the API returned a prompt-too-long error.
Compaction preserves the requests and the key code, but detailed instructions given at the start can be lost.
answer: Compaction preserves the requests and the key code, but detailed instructions given at the start can be lost.
explanation:
The general rule is that automatic compaction summarizes the conversation to free space: it preserves the requests and the relevant code fragments, but detailed instructions given at the start can disappear from the summary. What does survive is whatever is reinjected from disk, starting with the root CLAUDE.md, and that explains why the project conventions are still honoured while the chat instruction is lost. The key distinction against the path rules hypothesis is where the instruction lived: a rule given by chat is conversation history, not configuration loaded from a file.

RULE: Whatever must survive a compaction goes in CLAUDE.md or in a rules file, not in a message from the start of the conversation.

TRAP: Assuming everything said at the start of the session is still in force after compacting: only what is reloaded from disk comes back into context.

TRY IT: Give it a rule by chat at the start, work until it compacts and check with /context what stayed loaded; then move the same rule to CLAUDE.md and repeat the test.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/how-claude-code-works https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window
option_feedback: The root directory CLAUDE.md is reinjected after compacting, and in fact the conventions coming from it are still being applied in the session.
Path rules are reloaded on reading a file matching their glob, but here the instruction was given by chat and does not live in any rules file.
If the input exceeded the window, the request would fail with a 400 error instead of continuing to work with incomplete instructions.
Correct: that is how the Claude Code documentation describes it, which is why it recommends putting persistent rules in CLAUDE.md instead of trusting the conversation history.

question: The nightly report at Heartland Agronomics has two process conditions: the current metrics glossary must enter the conversation along with the request, before the model starts working, and no report file may be written until the metrics validation has run. Rachel wants both conditions enforced with hooks, each at its point in the flow. Which two measures achieve that? (Select TWO)
options: When the request arrives → return the glossary in systemMessage from the hook, which is the route for the model to read it before reasoning.
When the request arrives → a UserPromptSubmit hook that returns additionalContext with the current version of the glossary, which enters alongside the prompt.
Before each write → a PreToolUse hook with matcher Write that returns permissionDecision deny, with its reason, if the validation has not run yet.
When building the session → add the glossary to the system prompt with append and ask there that nothing be written without validating first.
After each write → a PostToolUse hook that reviews the already written report and reverts it if the validation had not run before.
answer: When the request arrives → a UserPromptSubmit hook that returns additionalContext with the current version of the glossary, which enters alongside the prompt.
Before each write → a PreToolUse hook with matcher Write that returns permissionDecision deny, with its reason, if the validation has not run yet.
explanation:
The general rule is to choose the event by the moment in the flow where you have to act and the field by who receives the information. UserPromptSubmit runs when the request enters the conversation, and additionalContext injects the glossary there so the model sees it from the first turn; PreToolUse runs before executing the tool, and permissionDecision deny prevents the write while the condition is unmet. The key distinction against systemMessage is who reads: that field shows a message to the person, not to the model.

RULE: additionalContext writes for the model and systemMessage for the person; PreToolUse prevents and PostToolUse only corrects afterwards.

TRAP: Confusing systemMessage, which is visible to whoever uses the agent, with additionalContext, which is the only thing that reaches the model.

TRY IT: Register a UserPromptSubmit hook that returns additionalContext with a keyword and another that puts it in systemMessage, and ask the agent which of the two it saw.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: systemMessage shows a message to the person using the agent, not to the model: the glossary would not enter the conversation and the report would be written without it.
Correct: UserPromptSubmit runs when the request is sent and additionalContext is the field that injects information into the conversation before the model answers.
Correct: PreToolUse runs before the tool executes, and a deny decision with a reason prevents the write and explains to the model what is missing, without depending on it obeying an instruction.
The append adds instructions to the system prompt and is useful for stable conventions, but it is advice the model can overlook, and besides the glossary changes between runs.
PostToolUse runs once the tool has executed: it can audit or replace the output the model sees, but the file already exists, so it arrives too late to prevent it.

question: At Brightwater Press, Hannah creates .claude/skills/publish-draft/SKILL.md with the frontmatter --- name: publish description: Publishes the current draft to the staging environment --- and restarts the session. Typing /publish brings nothing up in the menu, although /skills does list the skill. What explains what is happening?
options: The frontmatter needs user-invocable true for the skill to be offered in the command menu.
In personal and project skills the command comes from the directory name: here it is /publish-draft.
The skill has to be registered in .claude/settings.json for the command menu to recognize it.
The frontmatter is malformed because name and description were written on the same line, so it is ignored.
answer: In personal and project skills the command comes from the directory name: here it is /publish-draft.
explanation:
The general rule is that the command name of a personal or project skill is set by the directory containing it, while the name field in the frontmatter is only the label displayed. That is why the skill exists, appears listed and responds, but to the command matching its folder. The key distinction against the invocation hypothesis is that user-invocable is already true: were it false the skill would not appear in the menu under any name.

RULE: A skill's command comes from its directory name; name is the visible label, not the command.

TRAP: Assuming name defines the command because in plugin skills it does determine the last segment of the name.

TRY IT: Rename a skill's directory without touching its name field and check in the menu that the command changed along with the folder.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
option_feedback: That field is already true by default; what hides a skill from the menu is setting it to false, and then only Claude could invoke it.
Correct: the directory defines the command and the name field works only as a visible label, except in plugin skills, where it does set the last segment.
Skills are discovered by their location in the file system; settings.json only adjusts their visibility with keys such as skillOverrides.
If the frontmatter were malformed the skill would not be listed, and /skills shows it without trouble.

question: Northlane Outfitters filters product reviews with three parallel calls answering the same question, whether the review is inappropriate, with three different prompts. The aggregation rule is {"reject_if": "at least 1 of 3 flags the review"}. With that scheme 11 % of reviews are rejected and the moderators confirm that almost all those rejections are legitimate customer comments. Which adjustment should you make first?
options: Raise the threshold and reject only when at least two of the three calls agree, which is the lever between false positives and false negatives.
Replace the three calls with a single one that evaluates the review and returns a single verdict with its justification.
Keep the current rule and send every rejection to human review before hiding the review from the site.
Run the same prompt three times instead of three different prompts, so the three calls measure exactly the same moderation criterion.
answer: Raise the threshold and reject only when at least two of the three calls agree, which is the lever between false positives and false negatives.
explanation:
The general rule of the voting pattern is that several calls evaluate the same content and the vote threshold defines the balance point between false positives and false negatives: requiring a single vote is the most sensitive setting and the one producing the most undue rejections. With moderators confirming the rejections are legitimate, the problem is not in the prompts but in the aggregation rule, and raising it to two of three is the cheapest and most direct change. The key distinction against adding human review is that this option absorbs the error instead of correcting it, and against merging into one call is that you lose the contribution of multiple perspectives.

RULE: In voting, the vote threshold is the dial between false positives and false negatives: tune it before touching the architecture.

TRAP: Treating an excess of false positives as a prompt problem when it is produced by an aggregation rule that rejects on a single vote.

TRY IT: Take 50 already-moderated reviews, run the three calls and compare the false positive and false negative rates with thresholds of one, two and three votes before fixing the rule.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation describes the voting variant with different vote thresholds precisely to balance false positives and false negatives without changing the architecture.
Going back to a single call removes the advantage of voting, which is obtaining several perspectives for a higher-confidence result, and it does not fix the aggregation rule.
Adding people at the end is slow and expensive for 11 % of the volume; the aggregation rule generating the false positives should be fixed first.
Repeating an identical prompt reduces the diversity of perspectives that makes voting useful and leaves the aggregation rule, which is the cause of the extra rejections, untouched.

question: Erin's team at the City of Fairview extracts amounts from case files with structured outputs from the Python SDK, with this schema: {"type": "object", "properties": {"approved_amount": {"type": "number", "minimum": 0, "maximum": 500000}}, "required": ["approved_amount"], "additionalProperties": false}. The requests are processed without error, but every so often the application raises a validation exception with a seven-figure amount. What explains that behaviour?
options: The SDK strips minimum and maximum before sending the schema and validates the response against your original schema, so that limit is applied by the client and not by sampling.
The API rejects schemas using minimum or maximum with a 400 error, so the SDK retries the request without those restrictions and returns the retry's result unvalidated.
The grammar applies minimum and maximum during sampling, so a seven-figure amount can only come from a response truncated by max_tokens.
The field falls outside the schema because additionalProperties is false and its value is returned unvalidated as an extra property.
answer: The SDK strips minimum and maximum before sending the schema and validates the response against your original schema, so that limit is applied by the client and not by sampling.
explanation:
The general rule is that structured outputs supports types, enum, required and additionalProperties, but not numeric restrictions such as minimum or maximum. The official SDKs transform the schema before sending it: they strip what is unsupported, describe it in text inside the descriptions and validate the response against the original schema with all its restrictions. That is why the API responds 200 with an out-of-range number and the exception appears on the client side. The key distinction against the 400 error is who sends the schema: without the SDK transformation an unsupported keyword does return 400, and with it the limit becomes a later validation, not a sampling guarantee.

RULE: The grammar guarantees shape and types; ranges and lengths are business rules your code validates after receiving the response.

TRAP: Reading minimum and maximum inside a strict schema as if sampling enforced them, when the SDK strips them and only checks them when validating the response.

TRY IT: Repeat the extraction with a case file whose amount exceeds the maximum and observe that the API responds 200 with the out-of-range value and that the exception is raised by the SDK validation.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use
option_feedback: Correct: the SDK transformation removes unsupported restrictions, moves them into the descriptions and validates afterwards against the original schema; the grammar only guarantees types and structure.

It is true that an unsupported keyword returns 400 when you send the schema as is over HTTP, but the SDK does not retry blindly: it transforms the schema before sending and afterwards validates the response against your original schema, which is exactly where the exception comes from.
Numeric restrictions are not supported by the grammar, and a truncated response arrives with stop_reason max_tokens and incomplete JSON, not with an out-of-range number.
additionalProperties false forbids undeclared properties; approved_amount is declared and required, so it always travels inside the schema.

question: For two weeks the Kestrel Pay support agent has been failing on one specific kind of conversation: when the customer mentions two transactions in the same message, it resolves one and considers the query closed. Caleb has already rewritten the system prompt three times and tried wording variants, without understanding where the agent loses the thread. What is the most useful next step?
options: Simulate the task step by step with the agent's own prompts and tools, watching each turn of the loop to see where it goes off track.
Move the agent to a larger model, which follows complex instructions in conversations with several requests more faithfully.
Add to the system prompt three few-shot examples of conversations with two transactions resolved correctly from start to finish.
Put an agent to work testing the support tools and rewriting their descriptions so they are clearer and more distinct from each other.
answer: Simulate the task step by step with the agent's own prompts and tools, watching each turn of the loop to see where it goes off track.
explanation:
The general rule before changing the prompt again is to reproduce the failure from the agent's position: simulate the task with the exact prompts and tools and watch the process step by step, which is what the engineering guidance calls thinking like your agents. That turns a diffuse symptom into a concrete point in the loop, and only then do you choose the remedy. The key distinction against the other options is that they are all valid interventions, but applied without a diagnosis: they change the model, the prompt or the tools without knowing which of the three is failing.

RULE: Before rewriting the prompt a fourth time, put yourself in the agent's position: simulate the task with its prompts and tools and watch the process step by step.

TRAP: Treating an undiagnosed failure with generic remedies, such as upgrading the model or adding examples, instead of reproducing the agent's process.

TRY IT: Take a conversation that failed, reproduce it with the same system prompt and the same tools and note at which turn of the loop the agent stops considering the second transaction.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Correct: the guidance recommends thinking like your agents and simulating the process with the exact prompts and tools, because that is where you see the specific point at which the reasoning breaks.
A more capable model may mask the symptom, but without knowing where the agent loses the thread you will not know whether the problem was task decomposition, a tool or the prompt.
Few-shot examples improve consistency when you already know which behaviour you want to fix; here they would be another blind attempt at the same prompt.
Letting an agent test and rewrite tool descriptions is a documented and very effective technique, but it targets the tool interface, not a failure you have not located yet.

question: The scheduling agent at Cedar Ridge Health, built with the Agent SDK, asks the operator for confirmation before almost every step, even before reading the day's schedule or listing available slots. The operators already approve without reading. When they confirm, the agent executes the action correctly and never responds with recommendations instead of acting. Its system prompt includes a line asking it to confirm before any action that affects the system. What is the most likely cause of the excess confirmations?
options: The prompt follows the conservative pattern asking it to inform and recommend instead of acting when the user's intent is ambiguous.

The environment's permission mode requires approval for every tool call, without distinguishing schedule reads from the writes that create, move or cancel appointments, so everything goes through the operator.
The system prompt rule does not distinguish between local, reversible actions and destructive, hard-to-reverse or externally visible ones, so it fires on everything.
The model tends by default to confirm in clinical tasks because of its safety training and that behaviour cannot be adjusted from the prompt.
answer: The system prompt rule does not distinguish between local, reversible actions and destructive, hard-to-reverse or externally visible ones, so it fires on everything.
explanation:
The general rule is that escalation is defined by the type of action, not by action in the abstract: the guidance recommends encouraging the agent to do local and reversible things on its own, and to ask for confirmation for what is destructive, hard to reverse or visible to other people. A rule saying to confirm before any action that affects the system does not draw that line and ends up catching even reads, with the known effect that operators approve without looking. The key distinction against the conservative ambiguity pattern is the symptom: that pattern would make the agent recommend instead of act, and here it acts as soon as it is confirmed.

RULE: Write the confirmation rule by class of action: free for the local and reversible, confirmation for the destructive, irreversible or externally visible.

TRAP: Writing the escalation with a broad category such as any action that affects the system, which includes reads and turns approval into a rubber stamp.

TRY IT: Rewrite the system prompt line naming the actions that do require confirmation, rerun ten test cases and count how many approval requests are left.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: That pattern produces a different symptom: the agent would answer with recommendations instead of executing, and here it executes without trouble as soon as it receives the confirmation.

Such a permission mode exists and would produce a similar symptom, but it lives on the environment side and not in the prompt: the stem places the confirmation rule in the system prompt, and a permissions approval would be requested by the client for every tool, even those the prompt does not mention.
Correct: the guidance suggests explicitly authorizing local and reversible actions and asking for confirmation only for destructive, hard-to-reverse or third-party-visible ones.
Behaviour in the face of ambiguity and of risky actions is steerable from the prompt: the documentation provides concrete snippets for both the conservative and the proactive extremes.

question: The research system at Lakeside Online University synthesizes answers from papers and lecture notes the coordinator passes as documents. Hannah detects statements that appear in no source and others where the model fills in with its own general knowledge. She wants every statement in the synthesis to be traceable to a document. Which two prompt instructions attack that problem? (Select TWO)
options: Ask for a confidence score per paragraph and automatically discard anything below 0.7.
Increase the number of search subagents so each statement has more sources available.
Lower temperature to zero so the model does not add content that is not in the documents.
State explicitly that it should use only the information in the provided documents and not its general knowledge.
Ask it to first extract the relevant verbatim quotes, base the analysis only on those quotes and say so if it finds none.
answer: State explicitly that it should use only the information in the provided documents and not its general knowledge.
Ask it to first extract the relevant verbatim quotes, base the analysis only on those quotes and say so if it finds none.
explanation:
The general rule for synthesizing several sources is twofold: limit where the information can come from and force the evidence to be shown. The external knowledge restriction stops the model filling gaps with what it knows, and extracting verbatim quotes first, with permission to declare that it found none, leaves every statement anchored in a concrete fragment. They are independent measures: one bounds the source and the other produces the evidence. The key distinction against the confidence score is that a number summarizes an impression of the model and does not point at the document supporting each statement, which is what the reviewer needs to audit the synthesis.

RULE: For a synthesis to be auditable, limit the permitted sources and require the verbatim quote before the analysis, with permission to say there are no quotes.

TRAP: Confusing confidence with provenance: a high score does not indicate which document supports the statement or allow it to be verified.

TRY IT: Ask for a synthesis of three documents with and without the instruction to extract quotes first, and count in each case how many statements you can locate verbatim in the sources.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: A structured output can carry confidence scores, but a number is not provenance: it does not tell the reviewer which document supports the statement.
More sources do not create the link between statement and document, and a multi-agent system consumes on the order of fifteen times more tokens than a conversation.
Temperature controls sampling variability, not grounding in the sources; besides, newer models reject values other than the default.
Correct: the external knowledge restriction is one of the documented techniques for reducing unsupported claims in document tasks.
Correct: anchoring the answer in quotes extracted first, with explicit permission to say there are no relevant quotes, is what the documentation recommends for long documents.

question: Northlane Outfitters analyses its supplier invoices every month with a lead agent and several subagents reviewing different categories in parallel. Evan wants to order the flow so the lead does not lose its plan when the analysis runs long and so its context does not fill up with the material the subagents read. Which sequence best follows the documented orchestrator-workers pattern?
options: Launch the subagents → dump each one's full transcript into the lead's context → filter what is relevant there → write the report.
Ask each subagent to report every finding as it works → adjust the plan on the fly → close when all have finished → write the report.
Write the report with what the lead already knows → launch one subagent per paragraph to verify it → fix what does not hold → publish the result.
Save the lead's plan in external memory → launch the subagents in parallel with bounded tasks → receive only each one's final message → synthesize and cite.
