answer: Save the lead's plan in external memory → launch the subagents in parallel with bounded tasks → receive only each one's final message → synthesize and cite.
explanation:
The general rule of the orchestrator-workers pattern is that the lead plans, delegates bounded tasks and synthesizes, while each worker works in its own context window and returns a compact result. Saving the plan in external memory protects it from a context that can truncate in long analyses, and receiving only each subagent's final message is what stops the lead's context growing with everything they read. The key distinction against the sequence that dumps transcripts is compression: the value of delegating is that the lead receives a summary and not the complete material.

RULE: The lead saves its plan, delegates in parallel and receives only each subagent's final message: the full material stays in the context of whoever read it.

TRAP: Assuming the lead needs to see everything the subagents read in order to trust the result they return.

TRY IT: Run an analysis with two subagents and review the lead's transcript to confirm that only their final message appears from each one as the Agent tool result.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: Dumping full transcripts cancels the benefit of delegating: only the subagent's final message comes back as the Agent tool result, and that is what keeps the context bounded.
Constant updates between agents are one of the documented early failures: they distract each other and the lead spends context coordinating instead of synthesizing.
Verifying at the end is part of a review, not of distributing work: the lead would write without evidence and the subagents would work over conclusions already written.

Correct: the lead persists its plan so as not to lose it if the context truncates, the subagents work in parallel with their own contexts, only their final message comes back and the citations are added at the close.

question: Falcon Labs maintains an MCP server with the refresh_cache tool, which deletes and rebuilds a customer's search index. Since the agent uses it too cautiously and asks before every call, Erin sets readOnlyHint to true inside the annotations and leaves the handler exactly as it is. What will happen?
options: The client will reject the call as soon as the handler tries to write, because it compares the declared annotation against the real operation, and it will also revert the index to its previous state.
Claude Code will stop asking permission for that tool in every mode, because read-only tools do not need it.
The handler will keep deleting the index, because annotations are hints, and on top of that the tool will now be enabled to run in parallel with other read-only ones.
The server will stop exposing the tool until you also declare destructiveHint as false, because the two annotations turn out to be incompatible.
answer: The handler will keep deleting the index, because annotations are hints, and on top of that the tool will now be enabled to run in parallel with other read-only ones.
explanation:
The general rule is that annotations describe a tool's intent to help whoever displays it and whoever decides when to use it, but they enforce nothing: the handler is the only truth about what the tool does. Declaring readOnlyHint on a destructive tool does not prevent the write and, on top of that, has a real unwanted consequence, because that mark enables parallel execution with other read-only tools. The key distinction against the idea that the client will block the call is that the specification warns the opposite: annotations must be treated as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server.

RULE: Annotations are hints, not restrictions: what the tool does is decided by the handler, and a false hint only misleads the client.

TRAP: Reading readOnlyHint as a lock the client will enforce, when it is metadata that also enables parallelism.

TRY IT: Set readOnlyHint to true on a tool that writes a file, run it and check that the file changes all the same.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/custom-tools https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools
option_feedback: Stopping a write before it happens is possible, but with permission rules or a PreToolUse hook, not with annotations: nobody compares at run time what is declared against what the handler does, and nothing undoes the effects of a tool that has already run.
MCP tool permissions are decided with rules of the mcp__server__tool kind, not with annotations: marking it does not make it pre-approved.
Correct: they are declarative metadata, not an executable contract, and readOnlyHint does have a real effect: it enables parallel execution with other tools marked read-only.
destructiveHint only makes sense when readOnlyHint is false, but no combination stops the server exposing the tool.

question: Riverbank Financial has a monorepo of 40,000 files with compliance rules scattered across the code. Megan's agent starts every task by loading the twelve files of the regulatory module into context just in case, and by mid-session it answers less precisely about the files that actually mattered. How should you handle context in this exploration?
options: Preload the entire regulatory module at the start of the session so the agent has any file it might need available.
Let the agent keep lightweight identifiers, such as paths and searches, and load the content at the moment with grep and targeted reads.
Switch to a model with a one-million-token window so the twelve files fit without competing with the rest of the conversation.
Ask the agent for a summary of each file in the module and paste the twelve summaries into the system prompt of every session.
answer: Let the agent keep lightweight identifiers, such as paths and searches, and load the content at the moment with grep and targeted reads.
explanation:
The general rule of context engineering is to look for the smallest set of high-signal tokens: context is a finite resource with diminishing returns and retrieval degrades as it grows, an effect known as context rot. Just-in-time retrieval keeps lightweight identifiers in context, such as paths and queries, and loads the content with search tools and targeted reads only when needed. The key distinction against widening the window is that the problem is not capacity but attention: everything fitting does not mean the model retrieves well.

RULE: In a large repository, keep references and load the content when you need it: preloading just in case spends attention without adding signal.

TRAP: Assuming a bigger context window fixes the loss of precision, when retrieval degrades all the same as context grows.

TRY IT: Run the same query twice, once with the twelve files preloaded and once letting the agent find them with grep, and compare the accuracy of the answers and the tokens used.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows
option_feedback: Preloading is precisely what produces the problem: more context is not better context and retrieval precision falls as the number of tokens grows.
Correct: this is the just-in-time retrieval Anthropic describes, with lightweight identifiers and progressive loading at run time instead of preloading data.
A larger window delays the limit but does not avoid context rot: retrieval degrades as context grows, even if everything fits.
Summarizing everything in advance still spends attention budget on material the day's task may not need, and it adds the risk of losing the exact detail.

question: The City of Fairview classifies citizen requests into fourteen categories. To patch specific errors, the system prompt grew to 90 rules of the kind if the text mentions a water meter and also construction work, then the category is public works. New requests that fit no rule are classified worse than before, and the team cannot keep adding rules without making each call more expensive. Which prompt redesign is right?
options: Replace the list of cases with a clear definition of each category and the reason for the classification, so the model generalizes to unforeseen cases.
Turn each of the 90 rules into a few-shot example with its input and its expected category, wrapped in example tags.
Raise the effort level of the classification calls so the model reasons more about the existing rule set.
Add at the end of the prompt a section with the most frequent prohibitions in capitals so the model does not repeat the known errors.
answer: Replace the list of cases with a clear definition of each category and the reason for the classification, so the model generalizes to unforeseen cases.
explanation:
The general rule is that a system prompt should sit at the right altitude: specific enough to guide behaviour and flexible enough to give good heuristics, instead of a list of edge cases hard-coded one by one. The documentation recommends explaining the context and the reason behind an instruction because the model generalizes from the explanation, and the quality of a classification is proportional to how well defined the categories are. The key distinction against turning the rules into examples is that examples show the desired pattern, but ninety exceptions are still exceptions: they neither define the category nor cover what is new, and they multiply the cost per call.

RULE: Define the categories well and explain the why of the instruction: the model generalizes from a good definition, not from a list of exceptions.

TRAP: Answering every error with a new rule until the prompt becomes a catalog of cases that never says what each category means.

TRY IT: Write a two-sentence definition per category, replace the specific rules with them and compare the accuracy over twenty new requests that no rule covered.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation recommends giving context and motivation behind instructions because the model generalizes from the explanation, and it warns against piling up a list of edge cases.
Examples help when they show the desired pattern, but ninety examples encoding the same exceptions make every call more expensive and increase the risk of learning unwanted patterns.
More effort adds reasoning over the same ambiguous material and makes each call more expensive; it does not fix a category definition that fails to cover new cases.
The guidance asks you to say what to do instead of what not to do and to tone down imperative language; besides, a list of prohibitions does not define the categories any better.

question: Grant adds .claude/rules/terraform.md with the frontmatter --- paths: ["infra/**/*.tf"] --- so the Falcon Labs infrastructure conventions only enter context when somebody touches those files. Since the team already lost an afternoon to a rule they thought was active and was not, he wants to check it without guessing, repeatably and for any session on the team. What should you do?
options: Review the output of claude doctor, which diagnoses the installation and the project's configuration sources.
Open /hooks, which shows the loaded memory and rules files in a read-only browser.
Register a PostToolUse hook with matcher Read to note every file Claude reads in the session.
Register an InstructionsLoaded hook, whose path_glob_match matcher fires when a rule with paths enters context.
answer: Register an InstructionsLoaded hook, whose path_glob_match matcher fires when a rule with paths enters context.
explanation:
The general rule is that a rule with paths loads conditionally, on reading files matching the pattern, so its presence on disk proves nothing about a specific session. To observe it there are two documented routes: look at /context after opening a matching file, or hook the InstructionsLoaded event, whose matchers identify the load reason, among them glob matching. The key distinction against the read hook is what is measured: one records file accesses, the other records the effective loading of instructions.

RULE: To know which instructions entered context, look at /context or hook the InstructionsLoaded event.

TRAP: Assuming a rule that exists on disk is already in context: with paths the loading is conditional and has to be observed.

TRY IT: Register an InstructionsLoaded hook that writes the load reason to a file, open a .tf file and check that path_glob_match appears.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: It is useful for verifying the environment and which configuration files are read, but it does not report which instructions entered context in a session.
/hooks lists the configured hooks; loaded memory is inspected with /context, not there.
It tells you which files were read, which is an indirect clue, but it does not confirm that the associated rule entered context.
Correct: that event exists precisely to debug the loading of CLAUDE.md and rules, and the load reason distinguishes conditional activation by glob.

question: The audit team at Riverbank Financial works with Claude Code and resumes long regulatory review sessions after closing the terminal. Before writing the internal guide, Hannah reviews exactly what a resumed session recovers and what has to be provided again. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?
options: On resuming, the conversation history, the model and the permission mode are restored, except bypassPermissions and plan, which are not.
Resuming the same session in two terminals without forking it interleaves the messages of both into a single transcript.
Startup flags such as --mcp-config and --add-dir are saved in the session and are reapplied automatically when it is resumed.
A tool that was running when the process died is not re-executed when the session is resumed.
answer: Startup flags such as --mcp-config and --add-dir are saved in the session and are reapplied automatically when it is resumed.
explanation:
The general rule is that a session stores the conversation and part of the working state, but not the invocation the process was launched with. That is why the documentation clarifies that flags such as --mcp-config or --add-dir have to be passed again every time, while the history, the model, the active agent and the permission mode are restored, with the exceptions of bypassPermissions and plan. The key distinction is between what lives in the transcript and what lives on the command line.

RULE: The session recovers the conversation, not the invocation: startup flags are always passed again.

TRAP: Assuming resuming rebuilds the whole environment, including the MCP servers and the extra directories passed by flag.

TRY IT: Open a session with --add-dir pointing at another folder, close it, resume it without that flag and ask to read a file from that folder to see whether it is still available.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions
option_feedback: It is a correct statement: the resumed session recovers the history, the model, the active agent and the permission mode, with those two documented exceptions.
It is a correct statement: without forking, both terminals write to the same session and their messages end up interleaved in the same transcript.
Correct as the answer, because it is the false statement: those flags belong to the invocation and have to be passed again on each startup, they do not travel with the session.
It is a correct statement: resuming restores the conversation, but an interrupted tool is not relaunched on its own.

question: You are preparing a Messages API call in which Claude must answer with text only, even though the request still carries several tools that other turns do use. Which tool_choice value applies?
options: auto, which lets Claude decide whether to call any tool and is the default value when you define tools.
any, which forces the use of one of the available tools without fixing which one.
tool, giving in the same object the name of the tool you want to force.
none, which prevents Claude from using any tool and is the default value when there are no tools.
answer: none, which prevents Claude from using any tool and is the default value when there are no tools.
explanation:
The general rule is that tool_choice has four values and each answers a different question: auto lets it decide, any forces the use of one, tool forces a specific one and none forbids them all. Since here the definitions must stay in the request but this turn must call nothing, the value is none, which is also the default when no tools are sent. The key distinction against auto is who decides: with auto the decision still belongs to the model.

RULE: tool_choice none switches tools off without removing them from the request; auto is the default when tools are present and none when they are not.

TRAP: Believing the only way to prevent a tool call is not to send the definitions, losing the cache and the coherence of the request.

TRY IT: Repeat the same request with the tools defined, once with tool_choice auto and once with none, and compare the stop_reason of each response: with none no tool_use block appears even though the definitions are still sent.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
option_feedback: It is the default value when tools are present, but it still lets Claude decide to call one, which is what this turn must avoid.
It forces exactly the opposite and, besides, suppresses the natural language text before the tool_use blocks.
It forces a specific tool: useful for structured output, not for preventing tool use.
Correct: it switches off tool use in that turn without removing them from the request, so the rest of the conversation can keep using them.

question: To audit administrative case files, Cedar Ridge Health sends in every request a 45,000-token agreement, four few-shot examples of well-done audits and the auditor's question. Today the message is assembled in this order: first the instructions, then the four examples, then the question and the agreement at the end. The quality of the responses is uneven. How should you order the prompt?
options: Put the agreement at the very top and below it the instructions, the examples and the auditor's question at the end.
Leave the auditor's question at the very start so the model knows what to look for while reading the agreement.
Keep the current order and split the agreement into 5,000-token fragments distributed among the four examples.
Move the four examples to the end, after the agreement and the question, so they are the last thing the model reads before answering.
answer: Put the agreement at the very top and below it the instructions, the examples and the auditor's question at the end.
explanation:
The general rule for inputs over 20,000 tokens is to put the long data at the start, above the query, the instructions and the examples, and leave the question at the end: the documentation reports improvements of up to 30 % in quality with queries at the end, especially with complex or multi-document inputs. Here the agreement is at the end and the question in the middle, which is the opposite of the recommended order. The key distinction against moving the question up is that the intuition of giving the objective first does not hold with long documents: what improves the result is the query closing the prompt.

RULE: Long document at the top, instructions and examples after, question at the end: that order improves quality with inputs over 20,000 tokens.

TRAP: Ordering the prompt by narrative intuition, putting the question first and the document last, exactly the reverse of what the documentation recommends.

TRY IT: Run the same ten questions with the document at the end and with the document at the start and the query at the close, and compare the answers against the reference audits.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: Correct: the guidance says to place long documents near the start, above the query, the instructions and the examples, and to leave the question at the end.
It sounds reasonable, but the guidance documents the opposite for long inputs: queries at the end improve quality by up to 30 % in their tests.
Interleaving fragments breaks the structure of the document and mixes data with instructions, which is exactly what the ordering and the tags aim to avoid.
What the documentation says to move to the start is the long document; the examples go with the instructions and the question stays at the end, not before the examples.

question: Riverbank Financial offers its compliance reviewer as a service to several institutions and stands up one Agent SDK agent per client, all on the same fleet of containers. Audit requires that no local customization, accumulated memory or configuration of one institution be able to influence another's agent. Which configuration should you apply when starting each agent?
options: Open a new session on every query, since each session starts with a fresh context window independent of the others.
Put each institution's rules in a CLAUDE.md inside its folder and work with the cwd pointing at that folder.
Restrict the tools with disallowed_tools and run in dontAsk mode so no agent reaches another institution's files.
Pass an empty list of settingSources and give each institution its own cwd and its own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when starting the agent.
answer: Pass an empty list of settingSources and give each institution its own cwd and its own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR when starting the agent.
explanation:
The general rule is that isolation in multi-tenant systems is configured when the session starts and not with permissions. Passing an empty list of setting sources stops the agent loading user, project and local settings, CLAUDE.md and the .claude artifacts; and separating the working directory and the configuration directory per institution stops the state the agent writes in one reaching another, because that state lives under the configuration directory. The key distinction against restricting tools is which layer is protected: permissions govern actions, setting sources govern what context enters.

RULE: To isolate tenants, empty the setting sources and give each client its own cwd and its own CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR.

TRAP: Assuming a new session is enough to isolate, when every startup rereads settings, CLAUDE.md and the state left in the file system.

TRY IT: Stand up two agents with different cwds, one with an empty settingSources and one without that option, and ask both about the project conventions to see which one knows them.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/migration-guide https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hosting
option_feedback: It is true that each session starts with fresh context, but that does not stop the agent reloading settings, CLAUDE.md and the state saved in the file system on every startup.

A CLAUDE.md per folder organizes the conventions, but it is still loaded along with the rest of the settings sources, and the state each agent accumulates still goes to the same shared configuration folder.
Restricting tools and permissions limits what the agent can do, not what it loads as context at startup: configuration isolation is a different layer.

Correct: this is the documented multi-tenant pattern, because with an empty settingSources the agent loads no user, project or local settings, no CLAUDE.md and no .claude artifacts, and its own cwd and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR keep each institution's state in its own place.

question: The research coordinator at Lakeside Online University launches search subagents in parallel and sometimes one ends badly: through a turn limit, a denied tool or an API error. Derek reviews how those failures reach the coordinator and the model. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?
options: A tool_result with is_error set to true is incorporated into the model's reasoning, so it should state what failed and what to try next.
When a subagent exhausts its turn limit, its output is marked as partial so the model knows it was left incomplete and can be resumed.
When a tool call is denied, the reason for the refusal comes back as the tool result and the agent usually tries another route.
If an API error cuts the subagent short before it finishes, that error reaches the coordinator as the subagent's result so it can decide on the retry.
answer: If an API error cuts the subagent short before it finishes, that error reaches the coordinator as the subagent's result so it can decide on the retry.
explanation:
The general rule is to distinguish between the errors the model sees and those only your system sees. Failures that come back as a tool_result, with is_error or with the reason for a denial, enter the agent's reasoning and let it adapt, and an output truncated by a turn limit is marked partial so it can be resumed. By contrast, an API error that ends the subagent early, such as a rate limit, is not delivered as the subagent's result: it is the system that has to detect it, retry and pick up from the last checkpoint. The key distinction is exactly that boundary: what the model can correct by itself versus what needs deterministic safeguards.

RULE: Tool errors are returned to the model so it can adapt; API errors that cut an execution are handled by your system with retries and checkpoints.

TRAP: Assuming any failure ends up as a result visible to the model, and leaving unhandled the API errors that cut the subagent short returning nothing.

TRY IT: Force a tool failure by returning a tool_result with is_error and an instructive message, and compare the agent's reaction with that of an execution cut short by an API error.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls
option_feedback: It is correct: the documentation asks for instructive error messages, of the rate limit exceeded, retry in 60 seconds kind, instead of a generic error.
It is correct: partial results from a turn limit are marked as such and the work can be picked back up instead of starting from scratch.
It is correct: the reason for the denial is sent to Claude as a tool result and the agent normally tries another route or reports it cannot continue.

Correct as the answer to this item: the documentation says the opposite, an API error that ends the subagent early is never delivered as its result, which is why system-side retries and checkpoints are needed.

question: The Southline Logistics rates MCP server currently returns the text "failed" when the legacy system does not respond, and the agent keeps repeating the same call. Tyler wants the agent to know whether it is worth retrying and when, and proposes adding errorCategory and isRetryable fields to the result. What should you do?
options: Add those two fields to the result, since the protocol defines them precisely so the client can decide the retry policy.
Return the error in the result with isError true and actionable text: the rates system did not respond, it is worth retrying in 60 seconds.
Return a JSON-RPC protocol error with code -32603 so the client applies its own retry logic with incremental backoff before reporting.
Declare an outputSchema with a status field and return in structuredContent the detail of each legacy system failure.
answer: Return the error in the result with isError true and actionable text: the rates system did not respond, it is worth retrying in 60 seconds.
explanation:
The general rule is that errors the model can correct or work around are returned inside the result, with isError set to true and text explaining what failed and what to try next. MCP has no fields for the error category or for marking whether it is retryable: that information travels in the text, which is precisely what the model reads. The key distinction against the idea of adding fields is that the recipient of the message is the model, not a client that would interpret a custom schema.

RULE: A good tool error needs no new fields: isError set to true and text saying what happened and what to do next.

TRAP: Inventing protocol fields, such as errorCategory or isRetryable, for information the model gets from the result text.

TRY IT: Make that tool on your MCP server return isError set to true with text saying what failed and when to retry, repeat the request from Claude Code and observe the agent stop repeating the call blindly.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls
option_feedback: MCP defines neither errorCategory nor isRetryable: the only error field in the result is isError, and everything else travels as text the model reads.
Correct: the error travels in the result, the model reads it and the message tells it what happened and what to do next, which is what lets it recover without guessing.
Failures of an upstream system are tool execution errors; as a protocol error the model can almost never recover because it does not even see them as a result.
The outputSchema describes the shape of a successful result; failures are signalled with isError and an actionable message, not by inventing a status inside the result.

question: A team uses structured outputs with an enum field whose declared values are APPROVED, REJECTED and PENDING. What does the documentation guarantee about the value arriving in that field?
options: That the value comes from the declared list and respects exactly the capitalization written in the schema.
That if the model cannot pick a value from the declared list, the entire request fails with a 400 schema validation error.
That the value arrives accompanied by stop_reason refusal when the model hesitates between two options in the list.
That the value comes from the declared list, but not its capitalization, so it should be compared case-insensitively.
answer: That the value comes from the declared list, but not its capitalization, so it should be compared case-insensitively.
explanation:
The general rule is that structured outputs constrains sampling to the declared set of values, but it does not guarantee the capitalization of enum or const values: the response completes normally, with no error and no special stop_reason, and may arrive with a different combination of upper and lower case. That is why the documentation recommends comparing case-insensitively and avoiding lists where two values differ only in capitalization. The key distinction against the usual reading is that the guarantee is about the set of values, not about their exact written form in the schema.

RULE: An enum guarantees which value, not how it is written: always compare case-insensitively.

TRAP: Assuming the grammar copies the enum character by character and comparing with strict equality against the schema string.

TRY IT: Define an enum with values in capitals, run several extractions over different texts and check the exact capitalization arriving in each response.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: This is the assumption that breaks parsing: the documentation clarifies that the capitalization of enum and const values is not guaranteed.
A 400 is returned for using unsupported schema keywords, not for the content of an enum; a response with an enum completes normally.
The refusal stop_reason corresponds to a policy refusal by the model, not to uncertainty between options in an enum.
Correct: the documentation asks you to compare enum values case-insensitively and to avoid values differing only in capitalization.

question: The claims classifier at Summit Mutual Insurance returns summaries with bullet points and internal jargon the customer portal cannot display. The system prompt has accumulated eight prohibitions of the do not use markdown, do not use internal abbreviations, do not include estimated amounts kind, and they still appear in one out of every six responses. The budget does not allow adding a second cleanup call per claim. Which change is right?
options: Rewrite the eight prohibitions in capitals and head them with the word CRITICAL so the model gives them more weight.
Add a second call that receives the classifier's response and rewrites the bullets and internal jargon into continuous prose before publishing it on the customer portal.
Set a role in the system prompt, for example customer communications writer, and leave the eight prohibitions as they are.
Replace the prohibitions with a description of what it should produce: paragraphs in continuous prose, with no internal acronyms and with confirmed amounts.
answer: Replace the prohibitions with a description of what it should produce: paragraphs in continuous prose, with no internal acronyms and with confirmed amounts.
explanation:
The general rule is to tell the model what it should do instead of what it should not: the documentation contrasts a prohibition such as do not use markdown with a positive instruction such as write paragraphs in continuous prose, and it also recommends toning down imperative language rather than raising it. A positive description of the format gives a target to aim at, whereas a list of prohibitions leaves open what to produce. The key distinction against the role is one of scope: a role sentence focuses the tone and helps, but it does not describe the output format; and against the second step, that the cost constraint rules it out and the problem is solved by rewriting the prompt.

RULE: Describe the result you want, not the list of what is forbidden: a positive instruction gives a target, a prohibition only closes doors.

TRAP: Answering an instruction that is not followed by raising the emphasis and the capitals, instead of rewriting it as a description of what is expected.

TRY IT: Run fifty claims with the prohibition prompt and another fifty with the positive format description, and count in how many responses bullets or internal acronyms appear.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: The guidance recommends toning down imperative language and that emphasis does not fix the underlying problem, which is describing the result by what it must not contain.

A two-step chain would give the desired format and is a valid technique when the cleanup cannot be requested up front, but the stem rules out the cost of a second call per claim and the same result is achieved by describing the format in a single one.
A role focuses the tone and helps even in one sentence, but on its own it does not replace a positive description of the expected output format.
Correct: the documentation asks you to say what to do instead of what not to do, and that rewording is what steers the model towards the desired format.

question: A tool on the internal Falcon Labs MCP server returns from its handler: {content: [{type: "text", text: "3 open PRs, the oldest is 9 days old"}], structuredContent: {open_prs: 3, oldest_days: 9}}. Erin added the text block because she finds it more readable for the model than the JSON. What will Claude receive when using that tool from Claude Code?
options: Both blocks, first the text and then the structured JSON, because the result reaches the model exactly as the tool handler composes it.
Only the text block, because structuredContent exists to validate against the outputSchema and is not sent to the model.
Neither of the two until you declare an outputSchema: without a schema, the structured result is discarded entirely.
Only the structured JSON, plus any images or resources in content: text blocks are not forwarded because they are assumed to be duplicates.
answer: Only the structured JSON, plus any images or resources in content: text blocks are not forwarded because they are assumed to be duplicates.
explanation:
The general rule is that structuredContent and content do not add up: if the handler returns structured data, Claude receives that JSON along with any images or resources in content, and the text blocks are omitted because they are assumed to be a serialization of the same data. The practical consequence is that the readable nuance Erin wrote by hand never reaches the model, so if that reading adds anything it has to be inside the JSON, for example as a field with the summary. The key distinction against receiving both is that the specification asks for precisely that duplication for compatibility, and the client resolves it by keeping the structured version.

RULE: If you return structuredContent, the text in content does not reach the model: whatever you want it to read has to be inside the JSON.

TRAP: Assuming content and structuredContent accumulate, when the text is discarded as a copy of the structured data.

TRY IT: Return from an SDK tool a text content and a structuredContent with different data, and look in the transcript to see which of the two reached the model.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/custom-tools https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools
option_feedback: The result is not forwarded as is: when there is structured data, Claude Code decides which parts of the duplicated untrusted content it passes to the model.
The outputSchema is for validating, but the structured content does reach the model: it is the part that is kept.
Declaring an outputSchema is advisable and enables validation, but its absence does not cause the result to be discarded.
Correct: when structuredContent is present, the text in content is considered a copy of the structured data and is not delivered to the model.

question: Maya is preparing the overnight processing of 150,000 digitized case files from the City of Fairview with the Message Batches API. It is the first run with a new request format and the results are needed the following morning. How should you assemble the submission?
options: Send a single batch with the 150,000 case files and let the API queue the excess as it processes the first ones.
Send a single batch and rely on the 200,000 requests in the processing queue the account allows, which more than covers that volume.
Split the work into two batches below the 100,000 request limit and test a single request through the Messages API first.
Send a single batch and, if it has not finished at 24 hours, cancel it and resend it split into smaller parts.
answer: Split the work into two batches below the 100,000 request limit and test a single request through the Messages API first.
explanation:
The general rule is to size the batch within the documented limits and validate the format before sending: a batch accepts at most 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever comes first, and the documentation advises splitting very large data sets into several batches. Besides, validation of each request's params is asynchronous and its errors are only reported when the whole batch finishes, so testing a single request through the Messages API avoids discovering an invalid format the next morning. The key distinction against the 200,000 limit is that this number is the account's processing queue, not the size of a batch.

RULE: Split into batches of under 100,000 requests or 256 MB and test a single request first: validation errors only appear at the end of the batch.

TRAP: Reading the 200,000 queued request limit as if it were the maximum of one batch, which is 100,000.

TRY IT: Send a single request with the new format through the Messages API, confirm it responds 200 and only then assemble the batch with unique, meaningful custom_id values.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits
option_feedback: A batch accepts at most 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever is reached first; above that the request is rejected with a 413, it is not queued.
That limit is the organization's total of queued batch requests, not the size of one batch: the maximum per batch is still 100,000 requests.
Correct: it respects the per-batch limit and, since params validation errors are only reported when the whole batch finishes, the documentation recommends testing a single request first.
If a batch expires, the unprocessed requests come back with an expired result and are not billed, but the whole night is lost; the submission should be sized properly from the start.

question: Cascade Power added the remote work orders MCP server with claude mcp add --transport http orders and the gateway URL. When listing the servers, that one appears with the status "Needs authentication" and none of its tools can be used. What should you do?
options: Add the server again with --transport sse, because that status means it does not accept the chosen HTTP transport.
Raise MCP_TIMEOUT, since that status appears when the server takes more than 30 seconds to start.
Open /mcp in the session and complete the server's OAuth 2.0 flow, or do it with claude mcp login.
Store a personal token in the entry with --header Authorization and share it with the team through the repository.
answer: Open /mcp in the session and complete the server's OAuth 2.0 flow, or do it with claude mcp login.
explanation:
The general rule is that remote MCP servers authenticate with OAuth 2.0 and that Claude Code marks them as pending authentication when the server responds 401 or 403. The documented route is to complete that flow from /mcp inside the session or with the login subcommand, and the tokens are stored and refreshed automatically. The key distinction against changing the transport is what the status reports: it does not say the connection fails, it says authorization is missing.

RULE: A remote server responding 401 or 403 is pending authentication: it is resolved with OAuth from /mcp, not by changing the transport.

TRAP: Reading an authorization state as a connection problem and starting to change transports or timeouts.

TRY IT: Add a remote server requiring OAuth with claude mcp add --transport http, run /mcp and check that its status stops being Needs authentication only after completing the authentication flow in the browser.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: SSE is deprecated in favour of HTTP and, above all, that status is not about transport but about pending authorization.
A slow start is reported as a connection failure; pending authentication is a different state with its own signal.
Correct: Claude Code marks the server this way when it responds 401 or 403, and the OAuth flow is completed from /mcp or from the login subcommand.
Remote servers support OAuth, which avoids handing out credentials; besides, a versioned personal token exposes a credential to the whole team.

question: Southline Logistics is going to version .mcp.json in the repository so the whole team has the same tracking and rates MCP servers. The gateway URL changes between environments, the token is personal to each person and part of the team runs Claude Code inside automated pipelines. Which two things should you keep in mind? (Select TWO)
options: That variable values are not written into the file: url, headers, command, args and env accept ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default value}.
That each person must import the servers with claude mcp add-from-claude-desktop so they are registered on their machine.
That a server from .mcp.json wins over the same name in local scope, because the project file is the team's shared source.
That the interactive approval of .mcp.json servers does not happen in automated runs, where they are loaded without asking.
That MCP_TIMEOUT should be set inside each entry of the file so remote servers do not fail to start.
answer: That variable values are not written into the file: url, headers, command, args and env accept ${VAR} and ${VAR:-default value}.
That the interactive approval of .mcp.json servers does not happen in automated runs, where they are loaded without asking.
explanation:
The general rule is that .mcp.json is designed to be shared through version control, and that demands two precautions. The first is that nothing specific to a person or an environment is written literally: the URL and the headers accept environment variable expansion, with an optional default value. The second is that approval of project servers is an interactive step, so in automated runs they are loaded without asking and have to be explicitly disabled if they should not be used. The key distinction against the precedence option is that the shared source does not win: a server defined in local scope overrides the one in the project file.

RULE: The .mcp.json is shared: what varies goes in ${VAR} and, in automated runs, nobody approves the project servers for you.

TRAP: Assuming the interactive approval of project servers also protects runs with no person present.

TRY IT: Write an entry in .mcp.json whose url is ${GATEWAY_URL:-http://localhost:8080}, open the session with that variable exported and then without it, and check in /mcp which address it connects to in each case.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: Correct: environment variable expansion lets you share the file with no secrets and with a different URL per environment, with a fallback value when the variable is absent.
That command imports servers configured in Claude Desktop and only works on macOS and WSL; the project file ones are already read from the repository.
Precedence by name is the reverse: local first, then project and then user, and the winning source's entire entry is used.
Correct: the approval prompt only exists in interactive sessions, so in pipelines they have to be excluded with disabledMcpjsonServers or with --strict-mcp-config.
MCP_TIMEOUT is an environment variable, not a field of the file; what does exist per server is a timeout field in milliseconds.

question: The nightly pipeline at Summit Mutual Insurance classifies claims with structured outputs and with strict on the extraction tool. Tyler observes that in a small percentage of requests the JSON reaching the database is incomplete or does not match the schema, even though the request returned a 200 code. Which two documented behaviours must his code handle? (Select TWO)
options: That the API can return valid JSON with additional properties when the schema does not declare additionalProperties.
That a response with stop_reason max_tokens can come back incomplete and fail to meet the schema, and it has to be retried with a larger max_tokens.
That the grammar also applies to thinking blocks, so long reasoning can break the final JSON.
That the first use of a schema can return a 400 while the grammar compiles, so an immediate retry is needed.
That a refusal by the model arrives with stop_reason refusal and code 200, and its text may not respect the declared schema.
answer: That a response with stop_reason max_tokens can come back incomplete and fail to meet the schema, and it has to be retried with a larger max_tokens.
That a refusal by the model arrives with stop_reason refusal and code 200, and its text may not respect the declared schema.
explanation:
The general rule is that structured outputs guarantees the shape of the output while generation proceeds normally, and it documents two exceptions that still arrive with a 200 code. If the response is cut off by the token limit, the stop_reason is max_tokens and the output can be incomplete and fail the schema, and the fix is to retry with a larger max_tokens. If the model refuses, the stop_reason is refusal and the rejection message takes priority over the schema restrictions, so that output must not be parsed. They are independent cases: one is truncation and the other a refusal, and both require checking the stop_reason before parsing.

RULE: Before parsing a structured output, check the stop_reason: with max_tokens the output is truncated and with refusal it does not follow the schema.

TRAP: Treating a 200 code as a synonym for valid JSON and parsing the response without checking the stop_reason.

TRY IT: Run the same extraction with a deliberately low max_tokens and check the stop_reason and the JSON that arrives, to confirm your code does not try to parse a truncated output.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/handling-stop-reasons
option_feedback: The structured outputs schema requires additionalProperties to be false for objects, so that case does not arise: a schema without that key is rejected with a 400.
Correct: the documentation describes exactly that case for structured outputs and recommends retrying with a higher max_tokens to obtain the complete output.
The grammar applies only to the model's direct output, not to thinking or to tool calls and results, and its state resets between sections.
The first time a schema is used there is extra latency from compilation, and the compiled grammar is cached for 24 hours from last use, but that does not produce a 400.
Correct: on a refusal the rejection message takes priority over the schema restrictions, so the code must not parse that response as if it were valid.

question: The editorial review skill at Brightwater Press lives in .claude/skills/review/SKILL.md and is 900 lines long: the review procedure takes up 60 and the rest is the full style guide, which is only needed in rare cases. Every time somebody invokes the skill, all that text enters the conversation and stays there. What should you do?
options: Move the style guide into the project CLAUDE.md so it is available in every session without having to invoke the skill.
Split the skill into four smaller skills, one per section of the guide, and invoke whichever applies in each case.
Keep only the procedure in SKILL.md and move the style guide into a supporting file Claude reads when needed.
Add context: fork to the frontmatter so the skill runs in its own subagent and does not occupy the main conversation's context.
answer: Keep only the procedure in SKILL.md and move the style guide into a supporting file Claude reads when needed.
explanation:
The general rule is progressive disclosure: SKILL.md holds the procedure, short and under 500 lines, and extensive reference material lives in supporting files in the same directory that Claude reads only when it needs them. That way the usual invocation costs little context and the full guide remains available for the rare cases. The key distinction against the fork is what is saved: the fork moves the cost into another context but does not reduce the size of what is loaded, and it also cuts off access to the ongoing conversation.

RULE: A short SKILL.md with the procedure; the long reference in supporting files read only when needed.

TRAP: Confusing something being in a skill with it loading only when needed: invoking it brings it into the conversation in full.

TRY IT: Move half the text of a skill into a supporting file, invoke it and compare with /context how much it occupied before and how much it occupies now.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
option_feedback: It makes the problem worse: CLAUDE.md is loaded in full in every session and the recommendation is to keep it under 200 lines.
It multiplies the commands you have to remember and does not address the point: each invoked skill still enters the conversation in full.
Correct: progressive disclosure keeps SKILL.md short with the instructions and reserves the reference material in files read on demand.
The fork isolates the context, but the subagent still receives the skill content as its prompt, loses the conversation history and returns only a summary.

question: The GitHub MCP server Falcon Labs uses exposes around 40 tools, but only the subagent that reviews pull requests needs them. Chloe wants those tools at hand when that subagent works and absent from the main session, where the rest of the team writes code and context is already tight. What should you do?
options: Add mcp__github__* to permissions.allow in .claude/settings.json so those tools are only approved when the subagent uses them.
Write in the project CLAUDE.md that the GitHub tools should only be used from the review subagent.
Declare the server in the subagent's mcpServers frontmatter, so its tools live only in that subagent's context.
Set ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH to false so the definitions are loaded only when somebody asks for them.
answer: Declare the server in the subagent's mcpServers frontmatter, so its tools live only in that subagent's context.
explanation:
The general rule is to distinguish three layers: which tools exist in a context, which are permitted and which are deferred to save space. Chloe's request belongs to the first layer, and the documented mechanism is to declare the server in the subagent's frontmatter, so its tools travel with that role and the main session does not carry them. The key distinction against the permission rule is that permitting is not making available: an allow rule merely avoids the prompt for tools that are already there.

RULE: If some tools only serve one role, declare them in its subagent: what is not in its frontmatter does not weigh on the main session.

TRAP: Confusing permitting, which is what allow rules do, with making available, which is which tools exist in that context.

TRY IT: Declare the MCP server in a subagent's mcpServers frontmatter, run /context in the main session to see those tools are not there, and invoke the subagent to confirm it does use them.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: An allow rule decides what runs without asking, not in which session the tools exist: they would still be present in the main session.
CLAUDE.md influences behaviour, but it is context and not availability: the tools would still be loaded and Claude could use them anyway.
Correct: a server declared in the subagent is available while that subagent works, and the main session does not pay for its definitions.
With that value the opposite happens: every MCP tool is loaded up front, because deferral is precisely the default behaviour.

question: The custom MCP client at Cascade Power stores the nextCursor returned by tools/list and reuses it in the next session to resume pagination; it also assumes pages of 50 tools to calculate how many are left. Which two consequences does the specification predict about errors and pagination? (Select TWO)
options: The server will respond with isError set to true, because an expired cursor is an execution error the model can correct on its own.
Pagination will keep working as long as the server is not restarted, because cursors encode the offset within the list.
Reusing a cursor stored from another session can return an invalid params error, code -32602, because cursors are not persisted.
The server will reject the whole listing with -32601, method not found, as soon as it does not recognize the cursor it receives.
The calculation of remaining pages is not reliable: page size is decided by the server and the only end signal is nextCursor not arriving.
answer: Reusing a cursor stored from another session can return an invalid params error, code -32602, because cursors are not persisted.
The calculation of remaining pages is not reliable: page size is decided by the server and the only end signal is nextCursor not arriving.
explanation:
The general rule of pagination in MCP is that the cursor is an opaque token: it is not parsed, not modified and not stored between sessions, and page size is decided by the server on each response. Hence the two consequences: reusing an old cursor can return an invalid params error with code -32602, and any count based on an assumed page size is unreliable, because the only end signal is the response not carrying a nextCursor. The key distinction against the isError option is which category the failure belongs to: an invalid cursor describes a malformed request and therefore travels as a protocol error, not as a tool execution error.

RULE: The cursor is opaque and session-scoped: do not parse it, do not store it and do not infer from it how many results are left.

TRAP: Treating the cursor as a numeric offset in disguise and expecting an invalid cursor to come back as a tool execution error.

TRY IT: Request tools/list from a server with more than one page of tools, save the nextCursor, restart the server and send that cursor again: you will see the -32602 error and, in valid responses, that the end of the list is marked by the absence of nextCursor.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/utilities/pagination https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools
option_feedback: An invalid cursor is a problem with the request, not with a tool's execution: the specification treats it as a protocol error and not as a result with isError.
The cursor is an opaque token: you must not assume it encodes an offset or that it stays valid outside the session that issued it.
Correct: the specification asks you to treat cursors as opaque and not persist them between sessions, and it names -32602 as the code for an invalid cursor.
That code indicates the method is not supported; a cursor the server does not recognize falls under invalid params, not a non-existent method.
Correct: clients must not assume a fixed page size, and the absence of nextCursor is the only thing indicating there are no more results.

question: At Brightwater Press, Dana has on her machine the file ~/.claude/rules/style.md with the frontmatter paths: ["**/*.mdx"] and the line "Headlines go in lower case except the first word". The site repository brings its own .claude/rules/style.md, with the same glob and the line "Headlines go in Title Case". Dana opens content/blog/post.mdx and asks Claude for a headline. What happens with the two rules?
options: Both are loaded, the user one first and the project one after; faced with the contradiction the project one prevails, as it has higher priority.
Only the project one is loaded: when two rules files share a name, the one closest to the code replaces the other and the user one is discarded.
Only the user one is loaded, because rules in ~/.claude/rules/ apply to every project and win over the repository's.
Neither is loaded: the conflict between two rules with the same glob leaves the convention undefined until it is resolved by hand.
answer: Both are loaded, the user one first and the project one after; faced with the contradiction the project one prevails, as it has higher priority.
explanation:
The general rule is that every instruction found, whether CLAUDE.md or .claude/rules/ files, is concatenated into context instead of overriding. User rules, in ~/.claude/rules/, are loaded before the project ones, and that order is precisely what gives the repository's rules higher priority. The key distinction against the idea of substitution by name is that this behaviour exists for skills and subagents, not for memory or for path rules.

RULE: Rules add up: user rules load first and project rules after, which is why the project has the last word.

TRAP: Assuming two rules files with the same name are resolved by name, like skills, instead of being concatenated.

TRY IT: Create the same rule file in ~/.claude/rules/ and in .claude/rules/ with opposite instructions, open a file matching the glob and check with /context that both appear among the memory files.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: Correct: rules files add to the context instead of replacing each other by name, and the load order leaves the project rule with the last word.
Skills and subagents are indeed resolved by name, but rules and CLAUDE.md files are concatenated: the user file also enters context.
It is true that user rules apply across all your projects, but that does not put them above: they load first precisely so the project can adjust them.
Claude Code does not cancel contradictory rules; it loads them all and, if they genuinely contradict each other, it may keep one arbitrarily, which is why priority matters.

question: The City of Fairview reviews permit case files with a single instruction: "Review case file {{CASE_FILE}} and decide whether it is complete, check the signature, the seal and the attachments, and note observations." Maya finds that in a third of cases the response does not mention the attachments and that sometimes the verdict arrives before the seal has been checked. For this process both the order of the checks and their completeness matter. What should you change first in the prompt?
options: Raise the call's effort to xhigh so the model devotes more reasoning to each case file before issuing the verdict.
Rewrite the instruction as numbered steps, one per check, in the order they must be done and with the verdict at the end.
Add three examples of already-reviewed case files with their verdict, so the model learns the expected response format.
Add at the end of the instruction the sentence CRITICAL: you must ALWAYS review all four points before answering, written in capitals.
answer: Rewrite the instruction as numbered steps, one per check, in the order they must be done and with the verdict at the end.
explanation:
The general rule is that instructions are written as numbered sequential steps when the order or the completeness of the checks matters. A single sentence listing four verifications leaves the model to decide how many it does and in what order, and that is what the results show. Numbering the steps turns the implicit list into an explicit structure and leaves the verdict as the last step. The difference against adding examples is that an example teaches the output format, not the sequence of checks that precedes it.

RULE: When the order and completeness of the checks matter, write numbered steps, not one sentence with everything together.

TRAP: Confusing emphasis with structure: raising the tone or the effort does not tell the model how many checks there are or in what order.

TRY IT: Split the instruction into four numbered steps, run ten case files with each version and count in how many responses the result of the attachment check appears explicitly.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: More effort produces deeper reasoning, but it does not tell the model how many checks there are or in what order to do them: the omission is an instruction problem, not a thinking budget one.
Correct: the documentation asks you to give instructions as numbered sequential steps when order or completeness matter, which is exactly what fails here.
Examples are excellent at fixing the format and tone of the output, but an input-output pair does not show the sequence of checks to walk through before producing it.
The documentation recommends precisely the opposite, toning down that imperative register; and emphasis in capitals does not turn a running sentence into a list of four verifiable steps.

question: The claims classifier at Summit Mutual Insurance relies on a single example inside the prompt: a collision claim with photos, a police report and a clear amount. With that example the output format is stable, but cases with no photos, with a late report or with several damages come out with invented labels or empty fields. Marcus is free to rewrite the example block. Which two measures does the documentation recommend for improving consistency in those cases? (Select TWO)
options: Expand the block to between three and five examples covering the real edge cases: no photos, late report and a claim with several damages.
Replace the examples with a more detailed abstract description of each category, with its boundaries and exceptions written out in prose.
Ask Claude to evaluate the current examples for relevance and diversity, or to generate additional examples from that initial set.
Add twenty examples taken from the most frequent claim types of the last quarter, so the block covers the bulk of the real volume.
Define in the system prompt a role of claims adjuster with twenty years of experience at the insurer, to set the classification criterion that way.
answer: Expand the block to between three and five examples covering the real edge cases: no photos, late report and a claim with several damages.
Ask Claude to evaluate the current examples for relevance and diversity, or to generate additional examples from that initial set.
explanation:
The general rule is that examples teach what they show: if they all resemble each other, the model learns that resemblance instead of the task. The documentation asks for three to five relevant and diverse examples covering the edges, and it adds a second, less well-known lever: asking Claude to evaluate your set for relevance and diversity or to generate more from it. The two measures are independent: one changes the content of the block, the other uses the model to audit it. Against adding twenty frequent cases, the key distinction is that the documented criterion is diversity, not volume.

RULE: Three to five examples covering the edges; and if you doubt your set, ask Claude to evaluate it for relevance and diversity.

TRAP: Confusing quantity with diversity: twenty examples of the frequent case teach the frequent case better, not the edge case.

TRY IT: Build a test set with ten claims with no photos or with several damages, classify them with your single example and then with three to five examples covering those edges, and compare how many invented labels remain in each run.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation sets three to five examples and asks for them to be diverse, so they cover edge cases and the model does not learn an accidental pattern.
Defining the categories well helps, but the documentation is explicit that giving examples of the desired output is more effective than abstract instructions; removing them goes the other way.
Correct: the documentation suggests exactly that, using the model itself to audit the example set for relevance and diversity or to expand it.
With prompt caching you can include twenty examples or more, but the documented criterion is diversity: twenty frequent, similar cases reinforce the very pattern that is already failing.
Setting a role focuses the tone and behaviour, and even a single sentence helps, but it does not teach the model how to handle a claim with no photos.

question: The Brightwater Press pipeline runs a style review with Claude Code and Maya wants to follow progress live in the job log, not receive a single block at the end. She wrote the step as claude -p "Review this week's drafts" --output-format stream-json --max-turns 8, and the job ends immediately with a usage error, before doing anything. What is missing from the command?
options: Swap stream-json for --output-format json, which is the only format the CLI accepts together with --max-turns in non-interactive mode.
Add --verbose, because in -p mode the stream-json format requires that flag to emit the events line by line.
Add --include-partial-messages, which is the flag that enables streaming of the messages while the agent works.
Add --input-format stream-json, since the input and output formats have to match when streaming.
answer: Add --verbose, because in -p mode the stream-json format requires that flag to emit the events line by line.
explanation:
The general rule is that -p mode offers three output formats with different contracts: text for reading, json for a single object with result and session_id, and stream-json for newline-delimited JSON in real time. stream-json is only enabled together with --verbose, so without that flag the invocation is rejected before it starts. The key distinction against --include-partial-messages is that this flag enriches an existing stream with token deltas, while --verbose is what switches it on.

RULE: In -p mode, stream-json always goes with --verbose; json returns a single object at the end and is no use for following progress.

TRAP: Confusing the flag that switches streaming on with the one that enriches it: --include-partial-messages does not replace --verbose.

TRY IT: Run claude -p "Summarize this repository" --output-format stream-json, observe the error, repeat adding --verbose and compare the output with that of --output-format json.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference
option_feedback: json is indeed valid, but it returns a single object at the end, exactly the opposite of what Maya wants; besides, the error does not come from the combination with --max-turns.
Correct: with both flags the job receives newline-delimited JSON while the agent works, and the last line is the result message.
That flag exists and adds the token deltas, but it is an extra on a stream that already works: it does not replace the --verbose requirement.
--input-format controls what comes in through stdin, for multi-turn conversations; it has nothing to do with the output format or with this error.

question: At Riverbank Financial, Nora built a regulatory review agent with the Agent SDK. So that read-only queries to the internal MCP stop asking for permission, she registered a PreToolUse hook with matcher "^mcp__core__" returning permissionDecision allow with its reason. Weeks earlier, during an incident, the security team had added "mcp__core__*" to disallowed_tools and nobody removed it. Since then every call to mcp__core__list_policies comes back blocked, even though the hook log shows it ran and returned allow. What is the most likely cause?
options: A PreToolUse hook matcher only accepts exact tool names, so a pattern like "^mcp__core__" never matches that server's tools.
The hook runs after the permission evaluation, so its allow arrives too late for a tool the previous step had already rejected.
A deny rule in disallowed_tools blocks the call even if the hook returns allow, because a hook's allow does not skip the deny or ask rules.
The session is in permission_mode dontAsk, and in that mode the callback step is skipped and the tool is denied without consulting the hook.
answer: A deny rule in disallowed_tools blocks the call even if the hook returns allow, because a hook's allow does not skip the deny or ask rules.
explanation:
The general rule is that permission is evaluated in ordered steps: first the hooks, then the deny rules, then the ask rules, the permission_mode, the allow rules and finally the callback. Hooks running first means they can deny definitively, not that their allow has the last word: the documentation clarifies that a hook returning allow does not skip the deny or ask rules, and that a deny rule blocks even in bypassPermissions. That is why the right pattern for reopening those tools is to remove or narrow the disallowed_tools entry, not to insist with the hook. The key distinction against the ordering distractor is that the problem is not when the hook runs, but how far its decision reaches.

RULE: A hook returning allow auto-approves, but it does not override a deny rule: deny rules win even in bypassPermissions.

TRAP: Reading "hooks run first" as if it meant "hooks have the last word": they run first and the evaluation continues all the same.

TRY IT: Register a PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision allow for Bash, add "Bash(rm *)" to disallowed_tools and check that an rm is still blocked.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks
option_feedback: Matchers do accept regular expressions, and besides the log itself shows the hook ran: if it did not match, there would be no record of its decision.
It is the other way round: hooks are the first step of the evaluation, and that is precisely why the documentation recommends them for checks that must run on every call.
Correct: hooks run first, but an allow only auto-approves; evaluation continues and a matching deny rule blocks the tool even in bypassPermissions.
In dontAsk what is skipped is can_use_tool, not the hooks: those run in any mode. And here the hook did run, so the mode does not explain the block.

question: Your team splits skills between the personal directory and the project one, and also carries old files in .claude/commands/. Which TWO statements about where skills live and how their names are resolved are correct? (Select TWO)
options: When a personal skill and a project one share a name, Claude Code loads both and concatenates their bodies into a single instruction.
A personal skill in ~/.claude/skills/ is only available if you also declare it in an enabled-skills block of the configuration.
Files in .claude/commands/ stopped working when commands were merged with skills and have to be migrated before upgrading.
If the same name exists at several levels, enterprise wins over personal, and personal over project.
A file at .claude/commands/frontend/component.md creates the command /frontend:component, with the slash turned into a colon.
answer: If the same name exists at several levels, enterprise wins over personal, and personal over project.
A file at .claude/commands/frontend/component.md creates the command /frontend:component, with the slash turned into a colon.
explanation:
The general rule is that skills are discovered by their location and resolved by name: they are not merged. When the same name appears at several levels the order is enterprise over personal and personal over project, so a file in your personal folder can mask the repository's. The command name, by contrast, comes from the path: in .claude/commands/ each subdirectory is translated with a colon. The key distinction against CLAUDE.md files is that those do add up across levels.

RULE: Skills are resolved by name, in the order enterprise, personal and project; the file path decides the command, with a colon per subdirectory.

TRAP: Extrapolating the additive behaviour of CLAUDE.md files to skills: a repeated name is not concatenated, it is resolved by priority.

TRY IT: Create ~/.claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md and .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md with different texts, type /deploy and check which of the two was loaded.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
option_feedback: CLAUDE.md files and rules are concatenated, but skills and subagents are resolved by name: only one of the two stays active.
No such declaration exists: skills are discovered by their location on disk, and what the configuration adjusts is their visibility with skillOverrides.
The documentation says the opposite: those files still work, although for new work the skill format is recommended, since it supports supporting files.
Correct: that is the resolution order, and it explains why a personal skill can mask the repository's with no warning.
Correct: the path relative to commands/ is translated into the command name by replacing each slash with a colon.

question: The Kestrel Pay platform team distributes this policy through managed settings: {"deniedMcpServers": [{"serverName": "payments-sandbox"}], "allowedMcpServers": [{"serverUrl": "https://mcp.kestrelpay.com/*"}]}. Grant still uses the remote server at that URL without trouble, but his personal stdio server, called local-notes and launched with npx, has stopped loading since the rollout. Why is that server left out?
options: Because the name local-notes is not in allowedMcpServers and serverName is the only way to authorize a server.
Because local scope servers do not coexist with managed settings: to keep using it he has to move it into the project .mcp.json.
Because an mcp__local-notes rule is missing from permissions.allow; without it the server connects but its tools stay blocked.
Because once allowedMcpServers is defined every server must match some entry, and a stdio server only matches a serverCommand entry, which is missing here.
answer: Because once allowedMcpServers is defined every server must match some entry, and a stdio server only matches a serverCommand entry, which is missing here.
explanation:
The general rule of managed MCP policy is that the two lists are evaluated in order: first the denylist, which nothing can override, and then the allowlist, which only acts if it is defined at some level. Within the allowlist each transport has its own entry form: remote servers must match a serverUrl entry and stdio ones a serverCommand entry, which compares the command and all its arguments in order. Since the allowlist is now defined, every server must match one of its entries: the remote one matches the serverUrl entry and this stdio server matches none. The key distinction against a block by name is that this server was not denied: it was never authorized.

RULE: In managed MCP the denylist rules first; if there is an allowlist, remote servers need a serverUrl entry and stdio ones a serverCommand.

TRAP: Reading an allowlist with only serverUrl entries as if it did not affect stdio servers, when anything not matching the allowlist is left out.

TRY IT: Define allowedMcpServers with a single serverUrl entry, then add a stdio server with claude mcp add and confirm with claude mcp list that it does not connect.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp
option_feedback: serverName exists in both lists, but the documentation warns it is not a security control, and above all it is not what decides here: stdio servers are authorized by command.
Local scope servers coexist with the policy without trouble; what changed is that an allowlist now exists and this server matches none of its entries.
Permission rules decide whether Claude can call a tool, not whether the server gets loaded; here the server does not even appear in the list.
Correct: evaluation first discards what falls in the denylist and then requires each server to match the allowlist, with serverUrl for remote ones and serverCommand for stdio ones.

question: The Falcon Labs CI job classifies each PR with claude -p "Classify the risk of the change" --output-format json --json-schema '{"type": "object", "properties": {"risk": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["risk"]}' and the next step reads the output with jq. In which field of the returned object does the response already validated against that schema arrive?
options: In result, as a text string with the JSON inside that has to be parsed again.
In structured_output, the field added to the object when --json-schema is used.
In a separate file, whose path is printed at the end of the non-interactive run.
In the last assistant message of the transcript, which has to be located and walked.
answer: In structured_output, the field added to the object when --json-schema is used.
explanation:
The general rule is that --output-format json returns a single object with fixed fields, such as result, session_id, num_turns and usage.
