When you also pass --json-schema, Claude Code validates the response against that schema and leaves it in structured_output, so the next pipeline step reads it with jq without parsing text again. The key distinction against result is that result is still the natural language answer and guarantees no shape at all.

RULE: With --json-schema the validated output arrives in structured_output; result is still free text with no shape guarantee.

TRAP: Assuming asking for a schema changes what result carries, when what it does is add a new field to the run object.

TRY IT: Run claude -p with --output-format json and a single-field --json-schema, and compare what result and structured_output carry in the same output.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference
option_feedback: result carries the answer as text; when you ask for a schema that text may still be there, but the validated output does not live in that field.
Correct: with that flag the run returns the usual object plus structured_output, already validated against the schema you passed.
Separate files appear when an MCP tool result exceeds the output limit, not for the run's structured response.
The transcript is saved to disk, but the json format already delivers a single object on stdout: there is no need to walk messages.

question: Your team is starting to use plan mode before big changes. Which TWO statements about how plan mode behaves in Claude Code are correct? (Select TWO)
options: Claude can run shell commands to explore while planning, although it does not edit the source code.
The plan is presented for approval with the ExitPlanMode tool, which is what triggers the dialog.
Plan mode is only activated from permissions.defaultMode; there is no way to enter it mid-session.
On approving a plan the session switches to bypassPermissions, because the plan has already been reviewed by a person.
The files Claude read while planning are discarded from the context when the plan is approved.
answer: Claude can run shell commands to explore while planning, although it does not edit the source code.
The plan is presented for approval with the ExitPlanMode tool, which is what triggers the dialog.
explanation:
The general rule is that plan mode restricts writes, not investigation: Claude reads files, runs exploration commands, writes a plan and waits for your decision. That plan arrives through the ExitPlanMode tool, which is what asks for permission and is why it can be automated with a hook. The key distinction against the idea of a fully read-only mode is that exploration commands remain available, with the auto mode classifier reviewing them when it is enabled.

RULE: In plan mode Claude investigates, shell commands included, and only changes files after you approve the plan that ExitPlanMode presents.

TRAP: Reading plan mode as a mode with no tools: what it blocks are the edits, not the exploration.

TRY IT: Put the session in plan mode, ask it to find out how many tests fail and observe that it runs shell commands to investigate while the approval dialog does not arrive until it calls ExitPlanMode.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands
option_feedback: Correct: in plan mode Claude reads files and runs commands to investigate; what it does not do is touch your code.
Correct: that is why plan approval can be automated with a PermissionRequest hook on that tool.
defaultMode is one route, but you also enter with Shift+Tab, with the /plan prefix or by starting with --permission-mode plan.
On approving you choose how to continue, between auto mode and approving each edit by hand; neither of those options is bypassPermissions.
The exploration context is preserved, unless you enable the option that approves the plan and clears the planning context.

question: Northlane Outfitters sends twelve supplier invoices in a single request so Claude can build a purchasing summary with verifiable provenance. To save tokens, Nora enabled citations only on the four largest invoices and left the other eight without that option. The API rejects the request with a validation error. What should you do?
options: Enable citations only on the large invoices, but move them to the end of the request, after the other documents and the instructions.
Turn the remaining eight invoices into plain text inside the prompt, so they do not count as document blocks of the request.
Enable citations on all twelve documents: the documentation requires it to be enabled on every document in the request or on none.
Leave citations disabled and ask in the prompt for every figure in the summary to state the file name and the source page number.
answer: Enable citations on all twelve documents: the documentation requires it to be enabled on every document in the request or on none.
explanation:
The general rule is that citations is configured for the whole request: the documentation states it must be enabled on every document or on none. Mixing four documents with citations and eight without is what causes the rejection, and the fix is to enable it on all twelve. The reason for the trimming does not hold either, because quoted text does not count as output tokens. Against asking for the references in the prompt, the difference is that the feature returns guaranteed pointers into the document, while a written reference can point anywhere.

RULE: Citations is a request decision, not a per-document one: enable it on every document or on none.

TRAP: Assuming citations is enabled document by document to save; the saving does not exist either, because cited_text does not count as output tokens.

TRY IT: Send two documents in the same request with citations enabled on only one and read the validation error the API returns; repeat with the option on for both and check the response now carries citation blocks.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations
option_feedback: The position of the documents affects quality with long inputs, and the recommendation is to put them at the top, not the bottom; in any case, mixing documents with and without citations is still invalid.
That text stops being citable by the citations feature: you avoid the validation error, but you lose in eight invoices exactly the provenance you were after.
Correct: citations is a whole-request decision; today it must be enabled on every document or on none, and that mix is the cause of the rejection.
A reference written by the model may point at nothing; besides, the saving that motivated the trimming does not exist, because quoted text does not count as output tokens.

question: The Kestrel Pay support agent has a p95 latency target of two seconds per turn and a cost cap per conversation. Marcus needs two checks before running issue_refund: a numeric one, that the amount does not exceed the customer's plan limit, and a judgement one, deciding whether the note the agent writes reveals data that should not go out. He wants to enforce both without inflating the main model's context or adding expensive calls. Which two measures best fit those constraints? (Select TWO)
options: Add both checks to the system prompt with examples and mark them as mandatory, so the model applies them without adding new infrastructure.
Resolve both checks with an agent-type hook, which launches a full agent capable of reasoning about the amount and the note in a single pass.
Enforce the amount limit in a deterministic PreToolUse hook, which runs in your process, consumes no context window and needs no model call.
Delegate the note review to a prompt-type hook, which resolves the judgement with a small model such as Haiku instead of loading it onto the main agent.
Lower the agent's effort to low and disable extended thinking, to offset the time the two new checks will add to the turn.
answer: Enforce the amount limit in a deterministic PreToolUse hook, which runs in your process, consumes no context window and needs no model call.
Delegate the note review to a prompt-type hook, which resolves the judgement with a small model such as Haiku instead of loading it onto the main agent.
explanation:
The general rule is that hooks run in your process and not inside the agent's context window, so moving a check into a hook takes it out of the turn's token budget. From there, the choice depends on the nature of the check: what can be expressed as a deterministic rule is resolved in code, with no model call at all, while what requires judgement is delegated to a prompt-type hook using a small model. Both measures are independent and each covers a different check. The key distinction against the agent-type hook option is proportionality: paying for a full agent to compare an amount against a limit spends exactly what the constraint forbids.

RULE: The deterministic goes in a code hook; what requires judgement goes in a prompt-type hook with a small model, never in the main agent's prompt.

TRAP: Assuming every quality check has to go through the main model: hooks run outside the context window and can use their own model.

TRY IT: Configure a prompt-type hook on PreToolUse and compare its latency in the logs with that of a command-type hook doing the same numeric check.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks
option_feedback: An instruction reduces the error rate but does not eliminate it, and those tokens are paid on every request of the turn, which is exactly the cost Marcus wants to avoid.
Agent-type hooks exist for decisions that call for judgement, but using one to compare a number against a limit adds the latency and cost of a whole agent needlessly.
Correct: this is the check that can be written as a rule, it runs outside the agent's context window and it is the documented way of guaranteeing something on every tool call.
Correct: the documentation offers prompt-type hooks precisely for decisions requiring judgement rather than deterministic rules, and they run with a cheap model outside the main thread.
Effort regulates how much the model deliberates, not whether the checks run: lowering it degrades response quality and provides no guarantee about the refund.

question: The Cedar Ridge Health team is finalizing the JSON schema of the tool that extracts data from medical authorizations. Grant goes over with the team what structured outputs and strict tool use support before freezing the schema. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?
options: You can include the patient's medical record number among the values of an enum, if the request already contains that data.
The schema accepts internal $ref and $defs for reusing definitions, but external $ref references are unsupported and return a 400 error.
A field accepting string or null is declared with anyOf or with an array of types, and union types are expensive to compile.
The pattern field accepts character classes, anchors and alternation, but not backreferences or lookbehind.
answer: You can include the patient's medical record number among the values of an enum, if the request already contains that data.
explanation:
The general rule is that the schema is metadata compiled and cached separately from the message content, and that is why the documentation forbids putting protected health information in its definitions: not in property names, not in enum or const values, not in pattern expressions. The fact that the data already travels inside the patient's document does not change the rule, because message content does accept that data and the schema does not. The other three statements describe precisely what the schema supports: internal $ref and $defs but not external, union types with anyOf or arrays of types, and a regular expression subset without backreferences or lookbehind.

RULE: Sensitive data may travel in the message content, never in the schema: not in properties, not in enum or const, not in pattern.

TRAP: Assuming that if the data is already in the request, repeating it in the schema is harmless; the schema is compiled and cached separately from the content.

TRY IT: Open your current schema and look for patient data in property names, in enum or const values and in pattern expressions, and contrast that list with the strict tool use page to see where that data may travel.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: Correct as the answer: this is the false statement. The documentation forbids including protected health information in the schema definitions, whether in property names, in enum or const values, or in pattern expressions.
True statement: internal $ref, $defs and definitions are supported and only external references are left out, with a 400 error if you use them.
True statement: nullable fields are expressed that way, and the documentation warns that union types are especially costly because they drive up the compilation cost.
True statement: pattern supports classes, anchors, groups, alternation and quantifiers, and leaves out backreferences, lookbehind and named groups.

question: Marcus works in five different Falcon Labs repositories and in all of them he writes tests with the same personal convention: one case per behaviour and no mocks for the database. It is his preference, not the team's, and it only makes sense when he touches test files. Today he repeats it by hand in every session. What is the cleanest way for Claude to apply it on its own, in any of the five repositories and only in those files?
options: Create ~/.claude/rules/tests.md with paths frontmatter pointing at the test files: user rules apply across all his projects.
Add the convention to each repository's CLAUDE.md, in a tests section, and keep the five files in sync by hand when it changes.
Create .claude/rules/tests.md in each repository with the same paths frontmatter and commit them to version control so they do not have to be repeated each session.
Save the convention in a per-repository CLAUDE.local.md, which stays out of git and imposes nothing on the rest of the team.
answer: Create ~/.claude/rules/tests.md with paths frontmatter pointing at the test files: user rules apply across all his projects.
explanation:
The general rule is to choose the scope along two axes: who should see the instruction and when it should load. A personal convention applying across all his repositories goes to user scope, in ~/.claude/rules/, and the paths frontmatter resolves the second axis, because the rule enters context only when Claude reads files matching the glob. The key distinction against copying the rule into each repository is that the project file is versioned and becomes an obligation for the whole team.

RULE: What is yours and applies across all your repositories goes to ~/.claude/rules/; the paths frontmatter decides when it enters context.

TRAP: Confusing the scope with the filter: paths chooses when the rule loads, but the directory chooses who it exists for.

TRY IT: Create ~/.claude/rules/tests.md with paths covering your test files, open another project, edit a code file first and then a test file, and compare with /context when the rule appears.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: Correct: user rules load in every project on the machine and the paths frontmatter makes them enter only when Claude opens a test file.
It works, but it puts a personal preference into a shared file and forces you to maintain five copies that drift apart.
The paths scoping is fine, but it is still one copy per repository and, living in the project, it becomes a team rule and not his.
CLAUDE.local.md is private, yes, but it always loads, cannot be limited by file type and has to be created repository by repository.

question: At Northlane Outfitters, Dana wants the main agent to delegate reading supplier invoices in PDF to a subagent defined in code, which returns only the extracted fields. She works with the Agent SDK and today two things happen: either the main agent never invokes it, or when it does the call asks for permission and the subagent replies it cannot find the files. What is the correct order of steps to get it working?
options: Declare the subagent in agents with its description and its prompt → include Agent in allowed_tools → name it in the prompt along with the PDF paths → read its final message in the tool result
Save the PDF paths in the project CLAUDE.md → declare the subagent in agents with its description → wait for automatic matching to pick it → read its transcript from disk
Include Agent in allowed_tools → ask the main agent to summarize its conversation for the subagent → declare the subagent in agents → read its final message in the tool result
Declare the subagent in agents → give it access to the parent's history with setting_sources → name it in the task prompt → read the intermediate tool results it produced
answer: Declare the subagent in agents with its description and its prompt → include Agent in allowed_tools → name it in the prompt along with the PDF paths → read its final message in the tool result
explanation:
The general rule is that a subagent starts with a fresh context window and the only thing crossing from the parent is the prompt string of the Agent tool, so everything it needs to know (paths, formats, prior decisions) has to go there. Before that, two conditions are needed: that the subagent is declared in agents, because if it does not exist there is no subagent_type to invoke, and that Agent appears in allowed_tools, because otherwise each invocation opens a permission request. Naming it explicitly in the prompt avoids depending on description matching. The key distinction is that no configuration option transfers the parent's history: setting_sources decides what is loaded from the filesystem, not what the subagent sees of the conversation.

RULE: Declare the subagent, auto-approve Agent, name it in the prompt and put everything it needs there: it sees nothing else of the parent's conversation.

TRAP: Assuming the subagent can reach the parent's context through configuration: the only thing that crosses is the Agent tool prompt.

TRY IT: Define a subagent in agents, invoke it by naming it in the prompt and check in the messages with parent_tool_use_id that it only received the text you passed.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: Correct: the subagent exists once declared, listing Agent avoids the permission request, naming it skips automatic matching and the paths travel through the only channel that crosses, the tool prompt.
CLAUDE.md provides project context, not the parameters of a specific task, and automatic matching is still probabilistic; besides, the parent already receives the final message as a tool result.
Asking for a summary burns tokens and is still fragile free text; besides, the order inverts the declaration, which must exist before the Agent tool can invoke that subagent_type.

setting_sources controls what filesystem configuration is read (CLAUDE.md, skills, agents), it does not open the parent's history, and the parent only sees the subagent's final message, never its intermediate steps.

question: At Cascade Power, the billing system client is regenerated on every build inside the generated/ folder, which is listed in .gitignore. Maya asks Claude to check whether any generated file still points at the old rates endpoint, and Claude answers that it finds no matches, even though the files are on disk. What should you do so the review looks at those files?
options: Locate the files with Glob, which does not respect .gitignore by default, and ask Claude to read them and search inside them.
Take generated/ out of .gitignore for the duration of the review, so content searches include that folder again.
Add the folder with --add-dir, because the search tools only reach directories declared in the session.
Repeat the search with Grep in content mode and a type filter, which widens the set of files the tool walks on each pass.
answer: Locate the files with Glob, which does not respect .gitignore by default, and ask Claude to read them and search inside them.
explanation:
The general rule is that the two search tools do not see the same universe of files: Grep, built on ripgrep, respects .gitignore, while Glob does not respect it by default and finds ignored files by name. When what you are looking for lives in an ignored folder, the route is to list the paths with Glob and then read or search inside those specific files. The key distinction against changing Grep parameters is that the .gitignore filter is not an output option: it is part of how it walks the tree.

RULE: Grep respects .gitignore and Glob does not: if the file is ignored, find it with Glob and read it afterwards.

TRAP: Reading an empty result as proof the text does not exist, when it can mean the tool never looked at those files.

TRY IT: Add to a test repository's .gitignore a folder with a file containing a unique word, ask for a content search and then a name search with Glob, and compare the results.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
option_feedback: Correct: Grep skips what is in .gitignore, while Glob does not respect it by default; with the paths in hand, reading or searching those files works.
Touching .gitignore changes the repository for the whole team and affects the build; the problem is solved by choosing the right tool.
--add-dir is for when the file is outside the working directory; here the folder is inside the project and access was never the problem.
Those parameters change how results are filtered and displayed, but they do not change the underlying rule: Grep still respects .gitignore.

question: Hannah planned the template migration of the Brightwater Press site with Claude: they explored twenty files, discussed alternatives and she approved a six-step plan. Halfway through the implementation the context window hits its limit and automatic compaction fires. What can you expect of the approved plan after that compaction?
options: It is lost along with the rest of the summarized conversation, so it is worth pasting it again before continuing.
It survives only if you saved it in a repository file, because compaction does not preserve what was generated in the session.
It is reinjected from disk, just like the root CLAUDE.md, so Claude keeps the plan's pending steps.
It survives in full and the twenty files read come back too, because compaction only summarizes the user's messages.
answer: It is reinjected from disk, just like the root CLAUDE.md, so Claude keeps the plan's pending steps.
explanation:
The general rule is that compaction summarizes the conversation but not the configuration: there are pieces Claude Code reloads from disk. Among them are the root CLAUDE.md, the rules without paths and the approved plan, plus a handful of recently modified files. That is why the implementation can continue without repeating the plan. The key distinction against the exploration is that the twenty files read are indeed summarized: what is preserved is the instruction, not the research material.

RULE: Compaction summarizes the conversation, but the approved plan and the project memory are read again from disk.

TRAP: Assuming everything in the window is lost equally on compacting, without distinguishing what is reread from disk.

TRY IT: Approve a multi-step plan, force compaction with /compact halfway through the implementation and then ask which steps are pending: it lists them without you repeating them, but it no longer remembers the detail of the explored files.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes
option_feedback: That is what happens to much of the conversation, but the plan is one of the pieces Claude Code brings back after compacting.
Saving it to a file is good practice for working across sessions, but for this one it is not needed: the approved plan is reinjected on its own.
Correct: among what is restored after compacting are the root CLAUDE.md, the rules without paths and the written plan, which comes back from disk.
Up to five recently modified files come back, not the twenty that were read, and the summary affects the whole conversation, not only your messages.

question: Kestrel Pay implemented the tool use loop against the Messages API by hand for an agent answering rate queries. Besides its client tools it enabled web_search. The code walks the response, executes every block it finds, builds a tool_result for each one and sends it all back in the next message. On normal turns it works, but when the turn includes a search the API responds 400 and the agent gets stuck. What is the most likely cause?
options: The response arrived with stop_reason pause_turn, and the whole request has to be rebuilt with the same user message before continuing through the loop.
The tool_result blocks of client tools must come after the assistant's text in the content, and the code is placing them before that text.
web_search is a server tool executed by Anthropic, its results already come in the same response and your code must never build a tool_result for it.
tool_choice is missing being set to auto so the model can combine client tools with server tools within the same conversation turn.
answer: web_search is a server tool executed by Anthropic, its results already come in the same response and your code must never build a tool_result for it.
explanation:
The general rule is that there are two classes of tools and only one asks anything of you: client tools you execute and return a tool_result block for each tool_use, while server tools such as web_search, web_fetch or code_execution are run by Anthropic and their results come back inside the same response, in server_tool_use blocks. That is why a hand-written loop cannot treat every block the same: by fabricating a tool_result for the search, the continuation stops being valid. The key distinction against the pause_turn distractor is that this stop_reason describes a turn left paused and resumed by returning the response untouched, whereas here the error comes from a block the code should never have tried to answer.

RULE: A server tool is executed by Anthropic and its result already comes in the response: never build a tool_result for web_search, web_fetch or code_execution.

TRAP: Treating every tool use block the same: server_tool_use is not tool_use and expects nothing from your code.

TRY IT: Enable web_search alongside a tool of your own, print the type of each block of the response and confirm the server_tool_use blocks already arrive with their result.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/handling-stop-reasons
option_feedback: pause_turn indicates the server loop reached its iteration limit and is continued by returning the response untouched, rebuilding nothing; besides, it does not produce a 400.
It is the other way round: tool_result blocks have to come first in the content and any text afterwards; putting them at the start is exactly right.
Correct: server_tool_use blocks are resolved by the server and come back with their result; fabricating a tool_result for one of them breaks the continuation of the turn.
auto is already the default when you send tools, and tool_choice decides whether the model can or must use tools, not who executes each one or what you must return.

question: The nightly pipeline at Riverbank Financial extracts clauses from contracts and has a four-hour window to finish. On any failure, the code retries the same request immediately up to five times and then marks the contract as unprocessed. At peak times, the logs show many 429 errors accompanied by a retry-after header and dozens of abandoned contracts. Which adjustment fits that time window?
options: Keep the immediate retry and raise it from five to fifteen attempts, so no contract is left unprocessed within the window.
Move the whole pipeline to the Message Batches API, so the platform handles the retries of failed requests.
Raise max_tokens and enable streaming on each request, so long connections do not drop during load peaks.
Let the SDK client retry with exponential backoff respecting the retry-after header, and raise its retry limit.
answer: Let the SDK client retry with exponential backoff respecting the retry-after header, and raise its retry limit.
explanation:
The general rule is that a 429 carries a retry-after header and that retries before that deadline always fail. Retrying immediately, and more often, burns the nightly window without processing anything new. The SDKs already implement the correct behaviour: they retry transient failures with exponential backoff, twice by default, honour retry-after and expose an option for raising that maximum. Against moving everything to Batches, the key distinction is that Batches is cheaper but does not retry for you and can take up to 24 hours, which does not fit a four-hour window.

RULE: On a 429 do not retry earlier than retry-after says: leave the exponential backoff to the SDK and adjust its retry maximum.

TRAP: Reading retry more times as if it meant retry sooner; an early retry after a 429 fails by definition and burns the window.

TRY IT: Trigger a 429 with a large batch, read the retry-after header of the response and compare how many contracts finish in an hour retrying immediately against leaving the SDK's exponential backoff and raising its retry maximum.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits
option_feedback: Retries earlier than the deadline retry-after states always fail: fifteen immediate attempts consume the window without processing a single extra contract.
Batches halves the cost of the work and is right for what can wait, but it does not retry for you: the documentation asks you to implement your own logic, and a batch can take up to 24 hours.
Streaming and a high max_tokens avoid timeouts on long requests, which is a different problem: here the connection does not drop, the request is rejected by the rate limit.
Correct: the SDKs retry transient failures with exponential backoff, twice by default and respecting retry-after, and accept an option for raising that maximum.

question: Nora needs Claude to compare how three different libraries resolve cache invalidation, with each one's up-to-date documentation. She asks for a web search and receives a list of titles and links, without the technical detail she expected, and concludes the tool is misconfigured. What should you do to obtain that content?
options: Repeat the search narrowing it with allowed_domains and blocked_domains in the same call, to keep only the official sources.
Raise the per-session search limit, because the response was trimmed when the results budget ran out.
Ask it to use WebFetch on the chosen URLs, because search returns titles and links and does not download the pages.
Give WebFetch the search engine URL so it walks the results and brings the content of each page in a single pass.
answer: Ask it to use WebFetch on the chosen URLs, because search returns titles and links and does not download the pages.
explanation:
The general rule is that the two web tools have different, chained jobs: WebSearch discovers, WebFetch reads. WebSearch returns titles and URLs without bringing the pages, so the technical detail appears only when you ask for the content of a specific URL. The key distinction against adjusting the search filters is that no domain filter changes what WebSearch delivers: it changes which links it delivers, not their depth.

RULE: WebSearch finds links and WebFetch brings the content: the detail arrives only in the second step.

TRAP: Reading a shallow result as a misconfigured tool, when it is that tool's documented contract.

TRY IT: Ask for a web search on a technical topic and look at what arrives, titles and links; then ask for WebFetch on one of those URLs and compare how much technical detail each step provides.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
option_feedback: Both parameters exist, but they cannot be combined in the same call and, even narrowing domains, the search would still return titles and links.
The per-session cap is high and its symptom would be different, running out of results; what Nora received is exactly what WebSearch returns.
Correct: WebSearch discovers links without bringing their content, and WebFetch is the tool that retrieves and processes a specific URL.
WebFetch processes a single URL with a small model and returns redirects to another host instead of following them: it does not walk result lists.

question: Maya is debugging an automated tutor at Lakeside Online University built with the Agent SDK. The conversation goes well for fifteen turns and from one specific message onwards, in which the tutor misjudged the student's level, it goes off track. She wants to try another path from just before that message, without paying again for the tokens of the fifteen previous turns and without altering the original session, which the teaching team is still reviewing. Which option meets all three conditions?
options: Resume with resume passing resume_session_at with that message's uuid and fork_session, to branch from that point into a new session.
Resume with resume without forking and ask the tutor in a new turn to discard what it had assumed about the student's level and start again from there.
Start a new session and paste the full transcript of the fifteen turns into the first prompt, trimming by hand the message that derailed the conversation.
Use continue_conversation to pick up the most recent conversation in the directory and then call rewind_files with the uuid of the message that caused the problem.
answer: Resume with resume passing resume_session_at with that message's uuid and fork_session, to branch from that point into a new session.
explanation:
The general rule is that resuming and branching are different things: resume continues the same session and everything new stays in its transcript, while fork_session creates a new session starting with a copy of the history and leaves the original unchanged. When you also want to go back to an earlier point and not the end, resume_session_at gives the uuid of the message to branch from, and it is normally used together with fork_session. That meets all three conditions at once: it reuses the history, does not pay for it again as new input and preserves the original session. The key distinction against rebuilding the context by hand is that the session stores the conversation as the model saw it, tool results included, something a manual paste does not reproduce.

RULE: To go back to an earlier point without touching the original session, resume with resume_session_at at that message and fork_session.

TRAP: Confusing resuming with branching: resume continues the same session and everything new stays in its transcript.

TRY IT: Run three turns, save the uuid of the second message, resume with resume_session_at and fork_session, and check that the original session keeps its id and its history.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/python
option_feedback: Correct: resume_session_at sets the branching point and fork_session creates a session with its own id, so the original stays intact and the previous history is reused.
Resuming without forking continues the same session: the new turn is added to the transcript the team is reviewing, and the model still sees the message you want to discard.
Rebuilding the history by hand pays for those tokens again as new input, loses the tool results as the model saw them and throws away the prompt caching the session already had.
continue_conversation only takes the most recent conversation in the directory, and rewind_files reverts files with checkpointing, not the conversation: neither branches the history.

question: Summit Mutual Insurance runs its triage with a model that has thinking enabled. The example block in the prompt has this shape: {{TEXT}}water damage. The final category is almost always right, but the preceding reasoning jumps from one criterion to another and sometimes skips reviewing the policy exclusions. Dana wants that reasoning to always follow the same order: coverage, exclusions and amount. What should you do with the examples?
options: Add to the system prompt the instruction to explain its reasoning step by step in the response text before giving the category.
Include inside each example a thinking block showing the reasoning in the desired order: coverage, exclusions and amount.
Raise the call's effort to xhigh, so the reasoning is longer and gets as far as covering the policy exclusions.
Go from one to eight claim-and-category examples, covering a different policy in each of the new examples.
answer: Include inside each example a thinking block showing the reasoning in the desired order: coverage, exclusions and amount.
explanation:
The general rule is that examples teach what they show. An input-output pair fixes the format and the label, but it contains no intermediate reasoning the model can imitate. The documentation states that multishot examples work with thinking and that using thinking tags inside the examples shows it the reasoning pattern, which it then generalizes to its own blocks. The distinction against asking for the reasoning in the response text is that this technique belongs to when thinking is off; with thinking on you read the blocks rather than asking for them to be recited.

RULE: If you want the reasoning to follow a pattern, show it: put thinking tags inside your few-shot examples.

TRAP: Assuming an input-output pair teaches the process; it only teaches the result.

TRY IT: Duplicate the prompt, add to a single example a thinking block with the three criteria in order, run ten claims with each version and compare whether the thinking blocks respect the sequence.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/thinking
option_feedback: Asking for the reasoning in the text is the manual chain-of-thought device for when thinking is off; with thinking on you read the thinking blocks, and asking it to recite its internal reasoning can prompt a refusal.
Correct: multishot examples work with thinking, and putting thinking tags inside each example shows it the reasoning pattern, which the model generalizes to its own blocks.
Effort regulates how much the model thinks, not in what order: longer reasoning can still jump from one criterion to another.
More input-output pairs teach the format and the cases better, but none shows an intermediate reasoning to imitate; besides, the documented useful range is three to five.

question: The nightly pipeline at Heartland Agronomics runs each report with claude -p and stores the session_id from the ResultMessage, to pick up the previous analysis the next day. So the ephemeral containers do not accumulate files, Tyler recently added the CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY variable to the job environment. Since then every resumption fails saying the session does not exist, even though the recorded id is exactly the one the previous run returned. What is the most likely cause?
options: That variable suppresses writing the transcript, so the id exists in the result but no session file was left on disk to resume.
Sessions created with claude -p are hidden from the interactive picker, and that is why the system says it cannot find the session when asked for it.
The transcript is saved under a path derived from the encoded working directory, and each pipeline run starts in a container with a different directory.
The default cleanupPeriodDays retention has already deleted those transcripts, and the pipeline is asking for them after the retention period expired.
answer: That variable suppresses writing the transcript, so the id exists in the result but no session file was left on disk to resume.
explanation:
The general rule is that the session is the transcript on disk, and the session_id is merely its name: the ResultMessage always returns it, on success or failure, without that proving anything was written. The options suppressing persistence, such as the job's environment variable, the CLI flag or persistSession set to false, mean precisely that no file is left, and resuming stops being possible. The diagnosis also rests on the chronology: the failure appears right after the configuration change. The key distinction against the directory distractor is that such a problem would also affect runs from before the change, whereas here everything worked until history writing was disabled.

RULE: If you suppress session persistence, the session_id still comes back but there is nothing to resume.

TRAP: Reading the session_id in the result as proof the session was saved: it always comes, even when the transcript was not written.

TRY IT: Run a query with CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY enabled, note the session_id in the result and look for its .jsonl file under the projects folder to see it was not created.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions
option_feedback: Correct: the session_id comes back in the ResultMessage whatever happens, even when persistence is disabled; with no transcript there is no conversation to pick up.
It is true that -p and SDK sessions do not appear in the claude --resume picker, but they remain resumable by id, so that does not produce this error.
Transcripts do live under a folder derived from the encoded cwd and in another case it would be a reasonable hypothesis, but here the failure started exactly when the environment variable was added.
cleanupPeriodDays cleans old transcripts with a default of thirty days; a pipeline resuming the next day comes nowhere near that deadline.

question: After two failed attempts you press Esc twice with the input line empty and the rewind menu opens. Which option returns the files to the state of the chosen checkpoint and leaves the conversation as it is?
options: The Restore conversation option of the rewind menu.
The Restore code and conversation option of the rewind menu.
The Summarize up to here option of the rewind menu.
The Restore code option of the rewind menu.
answer: The Restore code option of the rewind menu.
explanation:
The general rule is that Claude Code's rewind treats code and conversation as two independent axes: you can restore both, only one, or keep a summary. Every prompt you send creates a checkpoint, so rolling back the files does not force you to lose what was discussed. The key distinction between the options is which of the two axes you want to undo; it is also worth remembering that checkpoints do not record changes made by shell commands.

RULE: Rewind separates code and conversation: choose which axis to undo, and remember that what a shell command changed does not come back.

TRAP: Reading the rewind menu as a single undo, without seeing that each option acts on a different axis.

TRY IT: Ask Claude to edit a file, press Esc twice with the input line empty, choose Restore code and check with git diff that the file rolled back while the conversation keeps everything discussed.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing
option_feedback: It is the symmetric option: it restores the thread and does not touch the code, exactly the opposite of what the stem asks for.
It is the complete option, the one that does both; if you only want to roll back the files, it reverts too much.
Summary options compress the conversation to free context; they do not touch the repository files.
Correct: the menu explicitly separates the two axes and this option acts only on the files.

question: Southline Logistics defines a fleet query subagent with this frontmatter: --- name: fleet-query tools: Read, Grep, Bash, mcp__fleet__* disallowedTools: Bash, mcp__fleet__update_route --- Ben wants to anticipate which tools the subagent starts with before giving it real work. Which set is available?
options: Read, Grep, Bash and every fleet tool: tools is the explicit list and therefore wins over disallowedTools.
None: declaring a tool in both lists is a conflict and the subagent fails to load.
Read, Grep and the fleet tools minus update_route: disallowedTools is resolved first, so Bash disappears.
Read, Grep, every fleet tool and Bash, which stays available but asks for permission on each call.
answer: Read, Grep and the fleet tools minus update_route: disallowedTools is resolved first, so Bash disappears.
explanation:
The general rule is that the two frontmatter fields do not compete at the same level: disallowedTools is applied first and tools is resolved against the surviving set. That is why a tool listed in both is left out, and a pattern such as the fleet server's loses only the denied tool, not the whole server. The key distinction against the intuition that the explicit list rules is the order: denial comes before granting, just as in permission rules, where deny is evaluated before allow.

RULE: In a subagent, disallowedTools is applied first and tools is resolved with what remains: what is in both lists does not exist.

TRAP: Assuming an explicit tools list reverses a denial, when the denial is evaluated first.

TRY IT: Write a subagent with Bash in tools and also in disallowedTools, ask it to run a command and observe it answer that it does not have that tool.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
option_feedback: It is the intuitive reading, but the documentation says the opposite: when both fields are set, disallowedTools takes precedence.
There is no load error: the two fields are designed to be combined, and the resolution order exists precisely for cases like this.
Correct: what is in disallowedTools is removed first and then tools is resolved against what is left, so Bash does not enter even though it is listed.
A bare name in disallowedTools does not leave the tool available with a warning: it removes it from the subagent's context, which does not even see it.

question: A Kestrel Pay MCP tool returns this when a value is missing: {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Traceback (most recent call last): KeyError: 'account_id'"}], "isError": true}. The agent retries with the same arguments and fails again. Which TWO statements describe how this tool should respond? (Select TWO)
options: This case should travel as a JSON-RPC protocol error with code -32602, since it concerns invalid parameters.
The text should say what is missing and in what shape, for example that account_id is required and goes as a ten-digit string.
It is worth adding errorCategory and isRetryable fields to the result, which is how the protocol classifies errors.
Input validation errors go in the result with isError set to true, so the model reads them and retries differently.
Leaving the traceback is enough: the client summarizes it and hands the model an actionable version.
answer: The text should say what is missing and in what shape, for example that account_id is required and goes as a ten-digit string.
Input validation errors go in the result with isError set to true, so the model reads them and retries differently.
explanation:
The general rule separates two channels: problems with the request itself, which are protocol errors, and problems with execution, which travel inside the result with isError set to true. The specification clarifies that input validation belongs to the second group, precisely so the model sees the failure and can correct itself. The second axis is the content: the text has to name what is missing and what to try next. The key distinction against inventing fields such as errorCategory or isRetryable is that the protocol does not define them, so everything the model must read goes in the result content.

RULE: Input validation is an execution error, not a protocol one: it goes in the result with isError set to true and text saying what to fix.

TRAP: Inventing classification fields the client does not read, and sending through the protocol channel an error the model could fix.

TRY IT: Make one of your tools return first a traceback and then a message naming the parameter and its format, and compare how many attempts the agent needs to get it right.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls
option_feedback: Protocol errors are reserved for unknown tools, malformed requests and server failures; the specification clarifies that input validation goes in the result so the model can correct itself.
Correct: an actionable error names the cause and the next step, with the expected format and an example, instead of dumping the exception.
They are generic names from a pattern, not protocol fields: the client does not interpret them, so the category and the retry window have to go in the content.
Correct: reporting it inside the result is what makes the error reach the model and stops the conversation being cut off by a recoverable failure.
The client does not rewrite the error: the model reads what the tool put in the result, and a traceback tells it little about which argument to fix.

question: The Brightwater Press site repository already has an AGENTS.md with the project conventions, maintained by another team and read by other tools. Now they are adopting Claude Code and Evan wants those conventions loaded in every session without duplicating the content across two files. What should you do?
options: Rename AGENTS.md as CLAUDE.md and ask the other team to point their tools and documentation at the new name.
Nothing: Claude Code looks for AGENTS.md at the root when it finds no CLAUDE.md, so it is already covered.
Add AGENTS.md to claudeMdExcludes so Claude Code treats it as the project's memory file.
Create a CLAUDE.md that imports it with an @AGENTS.md line, or leave a symlink from CLAUDE.md to the existing file.
answer: Create a CLAUDE.md that imports it with an @AGENTS.md line, or leave a symlink from CLAUDE.md to the existing file.
explanation:
The general rule is that Claude Code loads its memory from specific names, and AGENTS.md is not one of them. The recommended bridge is a minimal CLAUDE.md importing the existing file with the at-sign syntax, because imports are expanded and loaded at the start of the session; a symlink serves the same purpose. The key distinction against renaming the file is that the bridge leaves the other team's workflow intact and avoids two copies that drift apart.

RULE: Claude Code does not read AGENTS.md: bridge it with a CLAUDE.md that imports it with an at-sign, or with a symlink.

TRAP: Assuming any instructions file at the root is loaded on its own, without checking the list of names Claude Code looks for.

TRY IT: Create a CLAUDE.md whose only content is the line @AGENTS.md, open a new session and ask about a convention written only in AGENTS.md to confirm it knows it without anything being duplicated.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: It solves Claude Code's problem by breaking the other team's; the documentation proposes a bridge that leaves the file where it is.
Claude Code does not read AGENTS.md: its memory files are CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md and CLAUDE.local.md, plus the files in .claude/rules/.
claudeMdExcludes does the opposite: it is for skipping memory files by path pattern, useful above all in monorepos.
Correct: the import is expanded at the start of the session and the symlink achieves the same, without maintaining two copies of the same text.

question: The operations agent at Cascade Power builds maintenance reports from four sources: the manufacturer's manual, two field reports and an internal standard. The four texts are concatenated into a single block before the question, and the prompt asks it to answer based on the available information. The model is Claude Sonnet 5. In the latest report, a figure from the manual appears attributed to a field report and a regulatory limit is cited that is in none of the four sources. What are the two most likely causes? (Select TWO)
options: The four sources do not fit in the model's context window and the first ones are truncated before reaching the prompt.
The sources arrive concatenated in a single block, with no document tag per source with content and origin subtags.
The temperature was left at its default value and a high value makes the model invent figures when summarizing several sources.
The documents' title and context fields are empty, and without them the model cannot attribute any fact to the source it came from.
The prompt does not restrict the answer to the provided sources, so the model fills the gaps with its general knowledge.
answer: The sources arrive concatenated in a single block, with no document tag per source with content and origin subtags.
The prompt does not restrict the answer to the provided sources, so the model fills the gaps with its general knowledge.
explanation:
The general rule is that provenance is built with structure and with limits: each source in its own document tag, with subtags for the content and the origin, and an explicit instruction to answer only from what was provided. Without the first, the model has nothing to separate where each figure comes from; without the second, it fills the gaps with its general knowledge. The two symptoms in the report correspond to those two causes and are independent of each other. The title and context option is the most tempting: they are passed to the model, but they do not count as cited content and do not replace the per-document structure.

RULE: One source per document tag and an instruction forbidding it to go outside them: without both, the synthesis mixes origins and invents data.

TRAP: Reading answer based on the available information as if it were a source restriction; it does not exclude the model's general knowledge.

TRY IT: Send the same report twice, once with the four sources concatenated and once with a document tag per source plus the instruction to answer only from what was provided, and count how many figures are misattributed in each output.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations
option_feedback: That model has a one-million-token context by default, with no beta header; and if the input exceeded it, the API would return a prompt-too-long error, not a report with mixed-up data.
Correct: the documentation recommends wrapping each document in its document tag, with subtags for the content and the source, precisely so the model can distinguish where each fact comes from.
Temperature is not the provenance lever, and in recent models it does not even accept values other than the default; the invented figure appears because nothing bounds the sources.
The title and context fields are passed to the model and help identify it, but they are not what separates provenance and they do not count as cited content.
Correct: the documentation recommends explicitly instructing Claude to use only the information in the provided documents and not its general knowledge.

question: The post-purchase agent at Northlane Outfitters holds conversations of dozens of turns and the team enabled server-side compaction. The thread stays coherent, but since the change the bill has gone up: the usage report shows almost every request after a compaction writes new cache instead of reading it. The system prompt, long and stable, has no breakpoint. What should you do?
options: Raise the compaction trigger to 400,000 input tokens, so compaction happens far less often in each conversation.
Put a cache_control breakpoint at the end of the system prompt, so only the compaction summary is written as new input.
Replace compaction with context editing using clear_tool_uses, which clears old tool results without rewriting the conversation.
Stop resending the compaction block in subsequent requests, so the thread's cached prefix does not change on every turn.
answer: Put a cache_control breakpoint at the end of the system prompt, so only the compaction summary is written as new input.
explanation:
The general rule is that compaction rewrites the thread, so what was cached before the summary stops matching. The documentation therefore recommends placing a cache_control breakpoint at the end of the system prompt: the stable prefix is preserved and only the freshly generated summary is written as new input. Delaying compaction with a higher trigger does not change the mechanism and lets the context grow. The most dangerous option is to stop resending the compaction block, because the API ignores all content before that block and without it the summarized conversation is lost.

RULE: With compaction, the cache breakpoint goes at the end of the system prompt: that way each compaction only pays for writing the summary.

TRAP: Assuming compaction and prompt caching work together on their own; without a stable breakpoint before the summary, every compaction rewrites the whole cache.

TRY IT: Send a turn after a compaction with no breakpoint and another with cache_control at the end of the system prompt, and compare cache_creation_input_tokens against cache_read_input_tokens in each response.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
option_feedback: Compacting less often postpones the problem and lets the context grow to where retrieval degrades, but it does not change the fact that every compaction rewrites the prefix.
Correct: this is the documented recommendation for combining compaction with prompt caching, because the stable prefix is preserved and only the freshly generated summary is paid for as a write.
Clearing tool results also invalidates the cached prefix from the point where it clears, so switching technique does not solve the cost; besides, compaction is the recommended primary strategy.
The compaction block must be returned to the API: without it you lose everything summarized, because on receiving it the API ignores the content before that block.

question: To digitize scanned case files, the City of Fairview builds a request where each case file is a document block with "citations": {"enabled": true} and which also carries output_config with a json_schema format to receive the fields already structured. Derek wants the JSON and the verbatim quote of each field in a single call. What happens when that request is sent?
options: The request is processed and each JSON field arrives accompanied by the citation block pointing at the fragment of the case file.
The API returns a 400 error: citations and structured outputs are incompatible, because citations are interleaved with the text.
The request is processed, but the citations are silently discarded because the schema defines no field to place them in.
The API returns 200 with stop_reason refusal, because the model cannot cite text inside an output constrained by a grammar.
answer: The API returns a 400 error: citations and structured outputs are incompatible, because citations are interleaved with the text.
explanation:
The general rule is that citations and grammar-constrained outputs do not coexist in the same request: citations require interleaving citation blocks with the text and that is incompatible with a strict JSON schema. Enabling citations on any document together with output_config.format produces a 400 error, not a silent degradation. To get both, the work should be split into one call that extracts with citations and another that structures that result. The distinction against the refusal option is that this stop_reason arrives with 200 and corresponds to a refusal by the model, not to invalid parameters.

RULE: Citations and structured outputs do not coexist in one request: extract with citations first, then structure in another call.

TRAP: Assuming cited output and grammar-constrained output can be requested together; citations are interleaved with the text and the grammar prevents it.

TRY IT: Send a request with a document with citations enabled and output_config.format at the same time, confirm it responds 400, and repeat without output_config to see the citations return.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: It is what you would expect, but the API rejects that combination: to have JSON and provenance you have to separate the cited extraction from the structuring into two calls.

Correct: enabling citations on any document together with output_config.format returns 400, because citations require interleaving citation blocks with the text and that clashes with schema-constrained output.
The API does not silently disable features on an unsupported combination: it returns a 400 with the detail of the problem.
The refusal stop_reason exists and arrives with 200, but it corresponds to a content refusal by the model, not to an invalid combination of parameters.

question: Brightwater Press requires every AI-assisted text to carry a human review note before publication, and the rule must be present in every Claude Code session across the four newsrooms, with nobody able to disable it from their own configuration. The platform team already distributes files to each machine's policy folder, for example /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md on macOS. Where should the rule live?
options: As a managed CLAUDE.md in that policy folder: it loads before the user's and the project's and nobody can exclude it.
In each machine's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, placed by the same script that already distributes the rest of the team's configuration files.
As a permissions.deny rule in managed-settings.json, which is the way to impose a policy the client always applies.
In each repository's CLAUDE.md, with a line importing with an at-sign a shared file on a company network path.
answer: As a managed CLAUDE.md in that policy folder: it loads before the user's and the project's and nobody can exclude it.
explanation:
The general rule for organizational policies is to distinguish what is enforced with configuration and what is enforced with memory: blocking tools or paths is the job of permissions.deny, while a style, compliance or behaviour rule is distributed as a managed CLAUDE.md. That file loads before the user's and the project's and, unlike any other memory file, cannot be excluded from individual configuration. The key distinction against copying the text into the user file is exactly that: one is policy, the other is an editable copy.

RULE: What must be in every session and nobody can remove goes in the managed CLAUDE.md; blocking tools or paths is the job of permissions.deny.

TRAP: Confusing distributing a file with enforcing it: a copy in the personal folder gets edited, a managed CLAUDE.md cannot be excluded.

TRY IT: Place a CLAUDE.md in your system's policy folder, start a session and check with /context that it appears among the memory files, ahead of the project one.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings
option_feedback: Correct: the managed CLAUDE.md heads the load order and the documentation clarifies it cannot be excluded from individual configuration.
It leaves the rule in a file each person can edit or delete, and it forces you to trust the script is rerun on every new machine.
Permission rules block tools and paths, which is a different thing: a style or process rule is not expressed as a tool denial.
An import resolving outside the working directory opens an approval dialog the first time, and whoever declines it is left without the rule forever.

question: Dana works with Claude Code in the Summit Mutual Insurance coverage rules repository, a large monorepo. To avoid filling her context, she delegates every task to a subagent, even changing a constant in a file she already has open or renaming a two-line function. The work moves slower than before, the subagents return summaries without the detail she needed and she ends up repeating instructions. What should you recommend?
options: Keep delegating everything, but write fuller delegation messages, with paths, previous errors and decisions already taken.
Work directly on single-file edits and sequential steps, and delegate only parallel or isolated work.
Raise the subagents' effort to xhigh, so they return more complete summaries and fewer instructions have to be repeated.
Compact the main context after each delegation, to recover in the thread the detail the subagent saw during its exploration.
answer: Work directly on single-file edits and sequential steps, and delegate only parallel or isolated work.
explanation:
The general rule is that subagents are reserved for parallel tasks, with isolated context or independent flows, and that simple, sequential or single-file work is done directly. Every delegation costs an outbound message with all the context the subagent cannot see and a summary back that loses detail, so applying it to a two-line change worsens both time and quality. Writing better delegation messages is good advice, but it does not fix the fact that the task did not deserve delegating. And compaction summarizes your own thread, it does not recover what the subagent saw.

RULE: Delegate the parallel and what needs a clean context; the sequential and the single-file is done directly.

TRAP: Confusing looking after your context with delegating always: every delegation pays an outbound message and a summary back.

TRY IT: Take three one-line changes, do one yourself directly in the session and delegate the other two to subagents, and compare total time and how often you have to repeat instructions on each route.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/effort
option_feedback: A subagent does not see your conversation, so a good delegation message always helps; but writing that message to change a constant costs more than making the change.
Correct: the documentation reserves subagents for parallel tasks, with isolated context or independent flows, and recommends working directly on what is simple, sequential or single-file.
The recommendation runs the other way, lowering effort in subagents; and the problem here is not how much they think, but which tasks they are being given.
Compaction summarizes your own thread: it cannot bring back what happened inside a subagent's isolated context, which only returns its summary.

question: Grant instruments the nightly agent at Heartland Agronomics to record the full cycle of a run made with the Agent SDK. He needs to anticipate in what order the messages the library emits will arrive during a task that uses a single tool. What is the correct order?
options: ResultMessage with the session_id → AssistantMessage with the tool_use block → UserMessage with the tool_result → SystemMessage closing the run
SystemMessage of subtype init → UserMessage with the tool_result → AssistantMessage with the tool_use block → ResultMessage with the total cost
AssistantMessage with the tool_use block → SystemMessage of subtype init → ResultMessage with the total cost → UserMessage with the tool_result
SystemMessage of subtype init → AssistantMessage with the tool_use block → UserMessage with the tool_result → ResultMessage with the total cost
answer: SystemMessage of subtype init → AssistantMessage with the tool_use block → UserMessage with the tool_result → ResultMessage with the total cost
explanation:
The general rule is that the Agent SDK loop always opens with a SystemMessage of subtype init, carrying the session metadata, and closes with a ResultMessage, carrying the final text, the token usage, the cost and the session_id. In between, AssistantMessages alternate, emitted per content block and where tool_use appears, with UserMessages, which the SDK emits after executing each tool with the tool_result going back to the model. That cycle repeats until the model answers without requesting any tool. The key distinction is that a tool's result does not travel inside the assistant's message: the SDK delivers it as a separate user message.

RULE: The SDK cycle opens with an init SystemMessage and closes with a ResultMessage; the tool_result travels in a UserMessage in between.

TRAP: Assuming a tool's result comes back inside the same AssistantMessage that requested it: the SDK emits it as a separate UserMessage.

TRY IT: Run a query that uses Read and print the type of each message that arrives, to see the init, assistant, user and result sequence.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: The ResultMessage closes the cycle and carries the cost, the token usage and the session_id, so it cannot be the first thing the library emits.
The tool_result can only exist after the model requested the tool: the UserMessage carrying it always arrives after the AssistantMessage that prompted it.
The SystemMessage of subtype init opens the cycle with the session metadata, before any model response, and the ResultMessage leaves no task messages behind it.
Correct: first the init with the session metadata, then the AssistantMessage blocks per content block, then a UserMessage per executed tool and finally the ResultMessage.

question: The research system at Lakeside Online University launches search subagents defined in code. Most finish in minutes, but every so often one fixates on looking for sources that do not exist and keeps working without stopping; the coordinator waits for it and the team only finds out when somebody looks at the dashboard. Erin wants a per-subagent cap that cuts that case without penalizing the ones making progress. What should you configure?
options: max_turns on the coordinator's query, which counts the tool use turns of the whole run and includes those the subagents consume.
max_budget_usd in the query options, which also covers the subagents' spend and stops those running in the background on reaching the cap.
maxTurns in each subagent's AgentDefinition, which bounds how many turns it can spend before returning its output marked as partial.
CLAUDE_ASYNC_AGENT_STALL_TIMEOUT_MS, which watches asynchronous subagents and cuts off the one running too long in total without returning anything.
answer: maxTurns in each subagent's AgentDefinition, which bounds how many turns it can spend before returning its output marked as partial.
explanation:
The general rule is that SDK hosting offers no wall-clock deadline per subagent, and the documentation fills that gap with maxTurns in each one's AgentDefinition. That cap is the only one applied to the individual delegation: on reaching it the subagent returns what it has, marked as partial and resumable, while the rest of the run continues with its budget intact. The query caps, both max_turns and max_budget_usd, are global brakes and correct for other reasons, but they do not distinguish between the derailed subagent and the ones working well. The key distinction against the watchdog is that it measures inactivity, not duration: the described failure consists precisely of staying active without progressing.

RULE: There is no wall-clock deadline per subagent: the per-subagent cap is maxTurns in its AgentDefinition.

TRAP: Confusing an inactivity watchdog with a total time limit: the subagent working badly never goes idle.

TRY IT: Define a subagent with maxTurns at 3, give it a task needing more steps and watch it return its output marked as partial instead of continuing.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hosting https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: max_turns bounds the whole run, not each delegation: a single derailed subagent can exhaust the turn budget all the others needed.
It is a good production default and does cover subagents, but a spend cap stops the entire run when reached, instead of bounding just one.
Correct: it is the only cap applied per subagent, it leaves the ones that finish quickly untouched and the partial output remains available and resumable.
That variable is an inactivity watchdog, not a total time limit: a subagent still producing activity, however useless, never triggers it.

question: Falcon Labs exposes an internal MCP server with a tool called falcon.build.status that works without trouble in Claude Code. Tyler wants to reuse the definition as a custom tool in a Messages API integration and copies it verbatim: {"name": "falcon.build.status", "description": "Checks the build status of a service.", "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"service": {"type": "string"}}}}. The API rejects the request. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The name: the Messages API only accepts letters, digits, underscore and hyphen in name, so it has to become falcon_build_status.
The description: a single sentence is not enough and the API rejects any definition with fewer than three or four sentences per tool.
The input_schema: the API requires the required field even when the parameter is optional, and without it the definition fails validation.
The dot in the name forces strict to be set to true, because only that mode accepts names with hierarchical separators.
answer: The name: the Messages API only accepts letters, digits, underscore and hyphen in name, so it has to become falcon_build_status.
explanation:
The general rule is that MCP and the Messages API share concepts but not validation rules. Tool names in MCP accept letters, digits, underscore, hyphen and dot, while a custom Messages API tool must comply with a narrower expression, with no dots, of one to 128 characters. That is why a definition travelling unchanged from an MCP server can be rejected. The key distinction against the description guidance is that those affect the quality of selection, while the name is a hard validation that returns an error.

RULE: A dot is valid in an MCP tool name, but not in a Messages API tool: there only letters, digits, underscore and hyphen.

TRAP: Extrapolating MCP naming rules to the Messages API, which validates name against a narrower expression.

TRY IT: Send the Messages API a tool with a dot in the name and then the same one with an underscore, and compare the API response in each case.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
option_feedback: Correct: MCP accepts dots in tool names, but the expression the Messages API validates against does not, with a 128-character limit.
Three or four sentences is a strong recommendation so the model chooses well, not a validation: a short description does not cause a rejection.
required is optional in a JSON Schema and its absence means no parameter is mandatory; that does not invalidate the definition.
strict constrains sampling so the arguments comply with the schema; it does not change which characters are accepted in the tool name.

question: The operations agent at Cascade Power will be able to issue work orders and schedule supply outages in the real systems, deciding for itself how many steps each case needs. Derek already has the prompt and the tools ready and wants to take it to production this week. The team knows that in an autonomous agent an error carries into the following steps and that every step costs money. What should you do before giving it access to the real systems?
options: Move the agent to the most capable model available and expand the system prompt with warnings in capitals about the actions it must never take.
Let it run against the real systems with an operator watching the logs live, ready to cancel the run as soon as an inappropriate action appears.
Register a PostToolUse hook that writes every call and its result into the audit system, so you can reconstruct afterwards what the agent did.
Test it in a sandbox environment with test data, with guardrails on the dangerous tools and a maximum number of iterations as a stop condition.
answer: Test it in a sandbox environment with test data, with guardrails on the dangerous tools and a maximum number of iterations as a stop condition.
explanation:
The general rule is that autonomy is paid for with cost and with errors that compound step by step, and Anthropic's guidance answers that with three measures that go together: testing extensively in sandboxed environments, putting appropriate guardrails around dangerous actions and including stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations. All three act before the agent touches the real system, which is exactly what a tool capable of scheduling a supply outage demands. The key distinction against auditing with PostToolUse is timing: a later record serves to explain what happened, not to prevent it, and with irreversible actions that difference is the whole problem.

RULE: An autonomous agent is tested first in a sandbox, with guardrails and a stop condition: its errors compound step by step.

TRAP: Assuming auditing afterwards equals controlling: a PostToolUse hook documents the irreversible action that already happened.

TRY IT: Point the write tools at a test copy of the systems, run twenty real cases against that copy and count how many times the agent attempted an action it should not have.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: A better model and a more emphatic prompt reduce the error rate, but neither bounds an autonomous loop nor stops an irreversible action reaching the real system.
Live supervision is reactive and does not scale to several simultaneous runs: by the time the outage order appears in the log it has already executed against the real system.
Auditing is necessary and worth having, but PostToolUse runs after the tool: it documents the irreversible action instead of preventing it.
Correct: this is the explicit recommendation for autonomous agents, because their errors compound and the cost grows with every step taken unchecked.

question: The Falcon Labs team is going over the tool descriptions of its internal MCP server before publishing it to the rest of the company, because several look alike and the agent often confuses them. Which of these design recommendations is NOT correct?
options: Aim for at least three or four sentences per description, and more if the tool is complex or has conditions of use.
Say when the tool should be used, when it should not, and what information it does not return, to mark its boundaries.
Name the parameters unambiguously, for example user_id instead of user, and describe what effect each one has.
Create one tool per API endpoint, so each description stays short and selection becomes simpler.
