answer: Create one tool per API endpoint, so each description stays short and selection becomes simpler.
explanation:
The general rule is that more tools do not mean better results: bloated sets create ambiguous decision points and degrade selection. The documentation recommends consolidating related operations into one tool with an action parameter, instead of one tool per endpoint, and reserving the effort for detailed descriptions stating what it does, when to use it, when not to and what it does not return. The key distinction is that the brevity of each description does not compensate for the ambiguity of having many similar tools.

RULE: Fewer tools and better described: consolidate related operations instead of wrapping every API endpoint in its own tool.

TRAP: Assuming splitting the functionality across many small tools simplifies the choice, when it multiplies the ambiguous decision points.

TRY IT: Take two similar tools from your server, merge them into one with an action parameter and a description that also says when not to use it, and count across ten real requests how often the agent chooses wrong before and after.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents
option_feedback: It is the documentation's explicit recommendation: detailed descriptions are the single biggest factor in a tool's performance.
Also correct: saying when not to use it and what it does not return stops the model picking it by elimination.
Correct: a parameter called user_id instead of user removes a frequent ambiguity before it happens.

This is the one that does not apply: the documentation flags wrapping every endpoint in its own tool as a frequent mistake and recommends consolidating related operations into fewer tools, with an action parameter if needed.

question: Brightwater Press installed a plugin from its CMS provider that brings, among other things, a publishing skill. Claude invokes it on its own as soon as anybody mentions publishing, although the team only wants to use it by hand and at the end of the flow. The skill file comes with the plugin and is overwritten on every update. What should you do?
options: Set that skill to user-invocable-only in skillOverrides, in the project configuration.
Edit the plugin skill's frontmatter and set disable-model-invocation to true there.
Deny Skill with that skill's name in permissions.deny of the project configuration.
Disable the whole plugin and copy its useful skills by hand into the repository's .claude/skills/ directory.
answer: Set that skill to user-invocable-only in skillOverrides, in the project configuration.
explanation:
The general rule is to touch what is yours: a skill's frontmatter is controlled by whoever writes it, and when the skill arrives from a plugin or from the built-in set, the control point is the configuration. skillOverrides sets a skill's visibility by name, and the value reserving it for manual invocation takes it out of the model's reach without removing it from the menu. The key distinction against denying it with a permission rule is that this blocks it for people too, which is exactly what the team wants to keep doing.

RULE: To change the behaviour of a skill that is not yours, use skillOverrides in the configuration instead of editing the plugin file.

TRAP: Confusing taking the skill away from the model with taking it away from everybody: denying Skill also blocks manual invocation.

TRY IT: Declare that skill as user-invocable-only in skillOverrides in the project configuration, mention publishing in the session and check that Claude no longer invokes it on its own, while you can still call it by hand.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
option_feedback: Correct: skillOverrides adjusts a skill's visibility from the configuration, without touching plugin files, and that value leaves it outside the model's reach but available to people.
It would be right for a skill of your own, but this file belongs to the plugin: the change is lost on the next update.
Denying the skill blocks it for everybody, including the manual invocation the team does want to keep.
It solves the symptom at the cost of losing the rest of the plugin and of maintaining copies the provider keeps updating on their side.

question: The compliance assistant at Riverbank Financial can read and also edit the regulatory reports. When an analyst writes something ambiguous, such as look at the October report, the assistant interprets that it should correct it and modifies the draft that was under review. Audit requires every change to a report to originate from an explicit request, even if that means more back and forth. What should you add to the system prompt?
options: A policy asking it to infer the most useful action when intent is unclear and to discover with its tools any details that are missing before acting.
A conservative policy: on ambiguous intent, inform, investigate and recommend, and edit only when the analyst asks explicitly.
An instruction for it to estimate its confidence on each request and edit only when that confidence exceeds a high threshold.
A list of the write tools along with the instruction never to use them without prior authorization from the audit team.
answer: A conservative policy: on ambiguous intent, inform, investigate and recommend, and edit only when the analyst asks explicitly.
explanation:
The general rule is that behaviour in the face of ambiguity is decided with a written policy, and the documentation offers two opposite stances. Proceeding by default fits where getting it wrong is cheap: the model infers the most useful action and discovers what is missing with its tools. The conservative one fits where the cost of an unwarranted change is high: inform, investigate and recommend, and act only on an explicit request. In a regulatory report under audit the second applies, and the trap is that the first sounds more helpful and is precisely the one generating the problem.

RULE: Ambiguity is resolved by written policy: infer and proceed where mistakes are cheap, inform and wait for the explicit request where there is an audit.

TRAP: Applying the infer-and-proceed stance in a domain where every change must originate from an explicit request.

TRY IT: Write the two policies into different system prompts, send each agent the same ambiguous request about a report and check with git status which one edits the draft and which merely informs and recommends.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: It is the opposite stance, also documented, and it fits where getting it wrong is cheap; here it produces exactly the behaviour audit wants to eliminate.
Correct: the documentation offers that conservative stance for ambiguous intent, with the criterion of giving information and recommendations and acting only on an explicit request.
Self-reported confidence has no documented threshold to serve as an action criterion, and the official recommendation is to validate critical information, not to trust the number the model declares.
Forbidding the use of a tool through the prompt is not a guarantee; if you really want to prevent the write, you remove the tool or block it in code.

question: Cedar Ridge Health uses the Python SDK with a Pydantic model to extract authorizations. The model declares the authorized days field with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 30, and the service code with a maximum length of 12 characters, and the team passes it to the SDK's parsing helper. Nobody touches the schema by hand at any point. One day the extraction returns 45 authorized days. What happens?
options: The API rejects the request with a 400 error, because minimum and maxLength are not among the restrictions the schema supports.
The API accepts the schema and the grammar prevents the value leaving the range, so that 45 is never generated.
The SDK removes those restrictions before sending and the response arrives unchecked, so you have to validate the range in your own code.
The SDK sends the schema without those restrictions, and it is the SDK that rejects the response when validating it against your original model with all its rules.
answer: The SDK sends the schema without those restrictions, and it is the SDK that rejects the response when validating it against your original model with all its rules.
explanation:
The general rule is that the grammar guarantees shape and types, never ranges or lengths, because minimum and maxLength are not among the supported restrictions. What is usually overlooked is what the SDK does: it transforms your schema before sending, strips those restrictions, moves them into the descriptions, adds additionalProperties false and then validates the response against your original schema with all its rules. That is why you do not see a 400 from the API and do see a validation failure in your own client. The distinction against the option saying the range goes unchecked is exactly that last step: the SDK does check it.

RULE: The SDK strips from the schema what the grammar does not support and validates the response against your original schema: the range fails in your client, not in the API.

TRAP: Assuming removing a restriction from the schema is the same as no longer checking it; the SDK still checks it when parsing the response.

TRY IT: Print the schema the SDK helper generates from your Pydantic model and compare it with the model: you will see the minimum and the maximum length moved into the descriptions and additionalProperties set to false.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: That would happen if you sent the raw schema with those restrictions; the Python, TypeScript, Ruby and PHP SDKs do the transformation for you, so that 400 never occurs.
The grammar guarantees shape and types, never ranges: minimum and maxLength do not even reach the server, so they restrict nothing.
The first half is true and the second is not: validating the response against your original schema is part of what the SDK does, and that is where the 45 is caught.

Correct: the SDK transforms the schema before sending, strips what is unsupported, moves it into the descriptions and adds additionalProperties false, and then validates the response against your original schema.

question: Erin has spent two hours migrating templates on the Brightwater Press site. Every time automatic compaction fires, Claude loses sight of the acceptance criteria they had agreed and proposes changes that were already ruled out. The repository CLAUDE.md has three lines: "Use the components in templates/", "Run npm run lint before committing" and "Do not touch public/legacy". What should you do before the context fills up again?
options: Run /clear and start again with an initial prompt including the acceptance criteria and the current state.
Compact manually with /compact and focus instructions stating what must survive the summary.
Lower the auto-compaction threshold so compaction arrives sooner and the summary is shorter.
Ask Claude to repeat the criteria at the end of every response so they stay among the recent messages.
answer: Compact manually with /compact and focus instructions stating what must survive the summary.
explanation:
The general rule is that compaction can be steered: /compact accepts focus instructions stating what to preserve, and CLAUDE.md also supports a compaction instructions section so that criterion always applies. Compacting manually at the right moment, with those instructions, preserves the acceptance criteria and the already-discarded decisions without losing the work in progress. The key distinction against /clear is that there is no summary to steer there: everything is lost and you start over.

RULE: Compaction is steerable: give /compact focus instructions with what must survive, instead of accepting the default summary.

TRAP: Confusing when compaction happens with what is preserved: moving the threshold does not change the summary's criterion.

TRY IT: In a long session run /compact with a specific focus instruction, check with /context what was kept and compare it with a compaction without instructions.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs https://code.claude.com/docs/en/context-window
option_feedback: It is the right advice after two failed corrections on the same thing, but here the work in progress is long and /clear throws it away entirely.
Correct: /compact accepts focus instructions, so you can tell it what to preserve instead of leaving it to the default criterion.
Compacting sooner does not change what is preserved, only how much context the summary is made from: the problem is the criterion, not the timing.
Repeating text consumes context on every turn and accelerates exactly what you want to avoid; besides, the summary can trim it all the same.

question: Cascade Power publishes an outage lookup tool with this definition: {"name": "lookup_outage_window", "outputSchema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"start": {"type": "string"}, "zone": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["start", "zone"]}}. The system feeding it goes into maintenance and responds 503, so the handler is left with no data for start or zone. Ethan has to decide what the tool returns while the outage lasts. What shape should that response have?
options: A JSON-RPC protocol error with the server's error code, so the client cuts the call before passing anything to the model.
A result with isError set to true and text saying the outage system is not responding and when it is worth trying again.
A schema-conforming result with start and zone as empty strings, which is the only way not to break the client's validation.
A result without isError carrying the raw body of the 503 response, because it already describes the failure with all available detail.
answer: A result with isError set to true and text saying the outage system is not responding and when it is worth trying again.
explanation:
The general rule is that errors the model can make use of travel inside the result with isError set to true, and that only those preventing the call from being dispatched travel as a protocol error. A failure of the system being queried is an API failure, that is, an execution error: the result goes out with isError set to true and with text naming what failed and what to do next. Declaring an outputSchema does not change that split, because it requires a successful result to carry schema-conforming structuredContent, not to fill in fields when there is no data. The key distinction against returning an empty object that does validate is what the model reads next: an actionable error makes it wait or change route, while a blank window makes it carry on with invented data.

RULE: A failure of the API the tool queries goes in the result with isError set to true and actionable text, never disguised as a schema-conforming object.

TRAP: Assuming declaring an outputSchema forces you to always return a conforming object, even if you have to invent the fields the tool could not obtain.

TRY IT: Make the handler of a tool with an outputSchema simulate a 503: return first the raw body without isError and then isError set to true with actionable text, and compare what the agent does in each case.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/custom-tools
option_feedback: The protocol channel covers unknown tools and malformed requests; if the API failure travels there, the model does not see it and cannot change course.
Correct: failures of the API the tool queries are execution errors, and that actionable text leaves the model to decide whether to wait, retry or report.
Meeting the schema with empty values invents an outage window that does not exist, and the model will use it as if it were real data.
The raw body describes the failure for whoever reads logs, but without isError the client treats the call as successful and the model carries on as if it had the data.

question: The Cedar Ridge Health agent normalizes billing records and must leave them valid against an internal validator. When a record does not pass, Hannah discovers the agent writes the expected value directly into the normalizer code so that test passes, instead of reporting that the rule cannot be met. Which system prompt instruction corrects that behaviour?
options: Add a second pass with another instance that reviews each produced record and flags the values that were hardcoded.
Add five examples of well-normalized records to the prompt, so the agent sees how each difficult case is resolved.
Write in capitals that it must NEVER modify the normalizer or touch the internal billing validator's tests.
Ask for a solution valid for every input, with no hardcoded values, and for it to report when the task is unworkable or a test is wrong.
answer: Ask for a solution valid for every input, with no hardcoded values, and for it to report when the task is unworkable or a test is wrong.
explanation:
The general rule is that the model needs an honest way out as well as an objective. The documented instruction asks it to implement a correct solution for every valid input, with no hardcoded values, and to report when the task is unworkable or when a test is wrong, instead of working around the problem. That attacks the cause: the agent invents the shortcut because it is not allowed to fail. Against the prohibition in capitals, the distinction is twofold: the documentation asks you to tone down that imperative register and prefers saying what to do over what not to do, and a prohibition with no alternative only pushes towards the next workaround.

RULE: Give it an honest way out: a general solution with no hardcoded values and explicit permission to report that the task is unworkable.

TRAP: Assuming forbidding the shortcut is enough; without permission to report the problem, the model looks for another shortcut.

TRY IT: Run the same batch of records with the current prompt and with one asking for a solution valid for every input and allowing it to report unworkable tasks, and count the hardcoded values in the normalizer diff of each run.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: A review pass detects the shortcut after the fact and doubles the cost; the preventive instruction is cheaper and is what the documentation recommends.
Examples teach format and criteria, but none gives it permission to say a rule cannot be met, which is precisely what is missing.

It is a prohibition rather than an objective, the documentation recommends toning down that register in capitals, and forbidding the shortcut without offering an honest way out leaves the agent looking for another workaround.
Correct: the documentation proposes exactly that instruction, solve for all valid inputs without hardcoding and report instead of working around the problem when the task or a test is not right.

question: The Southline Logistics pipeline asks the agent for an incident summary with output_format of type json_schema and feeds the fleet system with structured_output. Rachel observes it almost always works, but one run in twenty reaches the system with that field empty and breaks the load, even though the ResultMessage carries subtype success and the result text is complete and well written. What is the most likely cause?
options: The schema uses JSON Schema 2020-12 keywords and the SDK validator works with draft-07, so it silently discards the fields it does not recognize.
The agent used tools before answering, and that invalidates the structured output, which is only produced when the model answers without calling any tool.
A run with subtype success may not carry structured_output, so the pipeline must treat its absence as a failure instead of taking it for granted.
The agent exhausted the schema validation retries, and in that case the result arrives with subtype error_max_structured_output_retries and the field empty.
answer: A run with subtype success may not carry structured_output, so the pipeline must treat its absence as a failure instead of taking it for granted.
explanation:
The general rule is that a ResultMessage's subtype describes how the run ended, not whether the structured output met the schema: they are two different things. The structured outputs documentation says so plainly, a result with subtype success may still not carry structured_output, and it recommends treating that absence as a failure. That is why the fix is not in the schema but in the pipeline, which must check the field is present before feeding the fleet system and decide whether to retry or escalate. The key distinction against the exhausted-retries distractor is that this case has its own subtype, error_max_structured_output_retries, and here the result reports success.

RULE: A success result does not guarantee structured_output: if it is missing, treat it as a failure before passing it to another system.

TRAP: Reading the success subtype as if it validated the structured output: the subtype describes the run, not the schema.

TRY IT: Run the same query with a schema asking for a field the agent cannot fill and check in how many runs success arrives without structured_output.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/structured-outputs
option_feedback: The validator does work with draft-07 and mixing drafts is a real problem, but an invalid schema fails when the query starts, not on one run in twenty.
The agent can use as many tools as it needs before finishing: the structured output is produced all the same when the run closes, so tool use does not explain the empty field.
Correct: the documentation explicitly warns that a successful result can arrive without structured_output and that it must be treated as a failure before being used downstream.
That subtype exists and is the explicit failure route when retries are exhausted, but here the result reports success, so that is not what happened.

question: A provider's documentation carries a configuration block with the mcpServers key and, inside, the entry for their server. You want to register it in Claude Code with claude mcp add-json. What do you pass to the command?
options: The complete block as is, with the mcpServers key included as the outer wrapper.
Only the object inside mcpServers for that server, without the wrapper.
The path to the provider's configuration file, which the command reads and expands.
Only the server's url, because the command infers the rest of the fields.
answer: Only the object inside mcpServers for that server, without the wrapper.
explanation:
The general rule is that MCP configuration files have two levels: the mcpServers map and, inside it, one object per server with its transport and connection details. The add-json command works at the inner level, so you pass it that server's object and not the wrapper. The key distinction against --mcp-config is that this flag does accept files or strings with the complete structure.

RULE: claude mcp add-json takes the server object, not the mcpServers map wrapping it.

TRAP: Copying whole a configuration written for another client, without seeing that the command expects one level deeper.

TRY IT: Pass claude mcp add-json the provider block as is, with the mcpServers key, to see the error; repeat passing only that server's inner object and check with claude mcp list that it is now registered.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: It is the most common mistake when copying configuration written for another client: the command expects the server definition, not the map containing it.
Correct: add-json receives that server's object, with its type and url, or its command and arguments.
For loading servers from files there is --mcp-config in the CLI; add-json expects the JSON on the command line itself.
An entry with url and no type is read as a stdio server and fails: type is precisely one of the fields you have to pass.

question: Lakeside Online University built on top of an orchestration framework a six-agent system for answering student questions from a fixed corpus of course notes per subject. Each answer takes almost a minute, costs considerably more than forecast and, when something goes wrong, the team cannot see which prompt each agent actually received. Reviewing a sample, the questions turn out to be direct and are answered with a search in the corpus. Which two diagnoses does Anthropic's effective agents guidance support? (Select TWO)
options: The task is solved by an LLM augmented with retrieval over the corpus and a handful of tools; orchestration trades latency and cost for performance that is not needed here.
The coordinator needs a more capable model to distribute work better among the six agents and thereby cut the response time of each query.
Few-shot examples are missing from the coordinator's prompt, which is what makes the distribution of subtasks inconsistent from one query to the next.
The number of agents running in parallel has to be increased so total time is that of the slowest rather than the sum of all of them.
The framework adds abstraction layers that hide the real prompts and responses, which is why it is worth starting by calling the API directly.
answer: The task is solved by an LLM augmented with retrieval over the corpus and a handful of tools; orchestration trades latency and cost for performance that is not needed here.
The framework adds abstraction layers that hide the real prompts and responses, which is why it is worth starting by calling the API directly.
explanation:
The general rule of the guidance is to start with the simplest solution and raise complexity only when the result justifies it, because agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance. The basic building block is the LLM augmented with retrieval, tools and memory, and a query answered by searching a fixed corpus falls exactly there, with no need for a coordinator or workers. The second diagnosis is independent of the first and explains the debugging part: frameworks add abstraction layers that hide the real prompts and responses, which is why the guidance recommends starting by using the APIs directly. The key distinction against the model or parallelism options is that both try to optimize an architecture that is unnecessary.

RULE: Start with the augmented LLM and the direct API; move up to multi-agent only when the task justifies it, because you pay latency and cost for that performance.

TRAP: Assuming more agents always means a better answer: agentic complexity is bought with latency, cost and opacity.

TRY IT: Rewrite one of those queries as a single call with retrieval over the corpus and compare latency, cost and quality against the six-agent run.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Correct: the basic building block is the LLM augmented with retrieval, tools and memory, and the recommendation is to look for the simplest solution and raise complexity only when needed.
A better model improves each step, but it does not correct a disproportionate architecture: the latency and the cost come from the number of agents, not from the quality of the distribution.
Few-shot examples help when the criterion is hard to describe; here the problem is not how the coordinator distributes work, but that the distribution exists at all.
Parallelizing helps when the subtasks are genuinely independent and necessary; adding agents to a query answered by a search multiplies the spend without adding anything.
Correct: the guidance warns that this abstraction makes debugging harder and recommends starting from the direct APIs, because many patterns are implemented in a few lines of code.

question: Summit Ridge Insurance's triage is currently a single call that, in the same prompt, classifies the claim, estimates the amount and flags possible signs of fraud. Fraud detection is the part that fails most often, and the cost per case has grown with volume. Megan can redesign the flow, but she does not want to turn it into an autonomous agent. Which TWO changes does the documentation recommend? (Select TWO)
options: Turn the triage into an autonomous agent with tools, letting it decide on its own how many steps to take and when to stop on each claim.
Run the same prompt five times on each claim and keep whichever classification gets the most votes.
Run in parallel one instance that classifies and another that reviews the same claim looking for signs of fraud, each with its own prompt.
Append a section to the current prompt asking it to review its own conclusions before giving the answer.
Route simple, frequent claims to a smaller, faster model, and unusual or hard ones to a more capable model.
answer: Run in parallel one instance that classifies and another that reviews the same claim looking for signs of fraud, each with its own prompt.
Route simple, frequent claims to a smaller, faster model, and unusual or hard ones to a more capable model.
explanation:
The general rule is that when a single call carries several considerations, each one gets partial attention, and performance improves when each consideration gets its own call. That is sectioning: one instance classifies and another screens the same case for fraud, in parallel, which is the guardrail example the documentation gives. Routing attacks the other symptom, sending easy, frequent cases to a small, fast model and hard ones to a more capable model. Turning it into an autonomous agent contradicts the principle of starting with the simplest solution, and voting five times multiplies the cost that was already the problem.

RULE: When one call carries three considerations, split them up: one call per consideration and one model per difficulty tier.

TRAP: Confusing improving triage with making it autonomous; the documentation asks for the simplest solution that works.

TRY IT: Take fifty already-reviewed claims, run them through the single prompt and then through two parallel instances, one classifying and one screening for signs of fraud, and compare the findings and the cost per case.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Agents are for open-ended problems where you cannot predict the steps; they cost more, compound errors, and the guidance asks you to start with the simplest solution.
Voting is a real pattern and helps when you need several perspectives on the same question, but it multiplies by five the cost that was already part of the problem.
Correct: this is the sectioning pattern, and the documentation uses exactly the case of one instance processing while another screens, noting that each consideration performs better in its own call.
Self-review inside the same call competes for the same attention already split across three tasks; real review belongs in a separate pass.
Correct: routing sends the easy and common to a cheaper model and the hard to a more capable one, which is the documented way to cut cost without losing quality.

question: Cedar County sent a batch of 40,000 case files to the Message Batches API. Twenty minutes later, Rachel discovers the prompt has an error that invalidates the classification of every case. The batch still shows processing_status in_progress and the department's budget is tight. What should you do?
options: Delete the batch with the delete endpoint, which stops it immediately and also frees its slot in the processing queue.
Resubmit the corrected batch with the same batch_id, so the new params replace the ones already being processed.
Cancel the batch: it moves to canceling and then to ended with partial results, and requests that were never sent are not billed.
Wait for it to finish and discard the results, since the batch is billed at 50% of standard pricing anyway.
answer: Cancel the batch: it moves to canceling and then to ended with partial results, and requests that were never sent are not billed.
explanation:
The general rule is that a submitted batch cannot be modified: the only way to stop it is to cancel it. On cancel, processing_status moves to canceling and then to ended, partial results from what was already processed are kept, and requests that never reached the model are not billed. The delete endpoint exists, but the documentation makes clear that to delete an in-progress batch you must cancel it first, so it does not work as a brake. Waiting for it to finish only adds forty thousand useless classifications to the bill.

RULE: A submitted batch is not modified: it is canceled, and whatever never reached the model is not billed.

TRAP: Confusing delete with cancel: to delete an in-progress batch you must cancel it first.

TRY IT: Send a small batch, call the cancel endpoint while it shows in_progress and follow processing_status through to ended to see that partial results remain and unprocessed requests add no usage.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing
option_feedback: The delete endpoint exists, but the documentation states that to delete an in-progress batch you must cancel it first: it is not a stop button.
Once submitted, a batch cannot be modified: to fix the prompt you have to cancel this one and create a new one.
Correct: on cancel the status moves to canceling and then to ended, keeping what was already processed, and requests that never reached the model are not billed.
Requests that do get processed are billed, and waiting for forty thousand useless classifications is exactly the spend that canceling avoids.

question: Riverton State University's multi-agent system launches a coordinator and six search subagents. At peak hours, the logs mix two failures: several subagents get 429 with a retry-after header, and others get 529 with type overloaded_error and no such header. Derek dropped concurrency from six subagents to three and the 429s nearly disappeared, but the 529s keep showing up just the same. What is the correct reading of those logs?
options: Both errors are the same quota problem, and the only real fix is moving up a usage tier to raise the limit.
429s are your own rate limit and lowering concurrency reduces them; 529s signal general API overload and are handled with backoff.
529s appear because the workspace hit its monthly spend cap, which does not depend on how many subagents run at once.
Subagents do not return failures as tool_result with is_error, so the coordinator retries them without learning the real cause.
answer: 429s are your own rate limit and lowering concurrency reduces them; 529s signal general API overload and are handled with backoff.
explanation:
The general rule is that 429 and 529 have different origins: the first is your own rate limit, comes with a retry-after header and responds to lowering concurrency; the second is overloaded_error and means the API is overloaded by traffic from all users, so it does not depend on how many subagents you run. Derek's experiment confirms that asymmetry, and the right response to a 529 is retrying with exponential backoff. The spend-cap option is the closest one and fails on a precise detail: that case shows up as a 429 without retry-after that keeps failing, not as a 529.

RULE: 429 is your quota and carries retry-after; 529 is platform overload: lower concurrency for the first, add backoff for the second.

TRAP: Reading every availability error as your own: trimming concurrency does not move a 529, which depends on the platform's global traffic.

TRY IT: Split one peak hour's errors by whether they carry the retry-after header, halve the concurrency, rerun and check that only the 429 count drops while the 529s stay the same.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits
option_feedback: They are different errors: one is produced by your own consumption and the other by the platform's global load, which does not change because you move up a tier.
Correct: 429 is your rate limit and its retry-after header says how long to wait, while 529 overloaded_error appears when the API is overloaded by traffic from all users.
The spend cap does exist, but it shows up as a 429 without a retry-after header that keeps failing until access is restored, not as a 529.
Returning tool failures to the model with is_error is the right practice so it can adapt, but these are API errors, not tool results.

question: The operations desk at Cascade Power gets very different requests: simple meter-status questions and planned-outage schedules that require several steps and validations. Brandon wants each type handled with its own prompt, its own model and its own tools, without a simple request paying the cost of the complex path. What is the correct order of the routing pattern?
options: Classify the incoming request into a category → route it to that category's specialized chain → run it with its own model and tools → return the result
Run every chain in parallel on the same request → compare the outputs against each other → vote on which one answers best → return the winner
Send the request to the most capable model → let it discover along the way which subtasks it needs → delegate them to workers → synthesize their results into an answer
Chain every possible step in a fixed order → put a code gate between each pair of steps → skip the ones that do not apply → return the result
answer: Classify the incoming request into a category → route it to that category's specialized chain → run it with its own model and tools → return the result
explanation:
The general rule is that routing classifies the input and directs it to a specialized follow-up, and it works well on complex tasks where there are clearly distinct categories better handled separately. Classification comes first because it is what picks the path, and only then is that category's chain run with the model and tools that suit it, which lets you send easy queries to a cheap model and reserve the expensive one for the hard ones. The key distinction from orchestrator-workers is who defines the subtasks: in routing the categories are defined in advance, while in orchestrator-workers the orchestrator discovers them because they cannot be predicted.

RULE: If input categories are better served separately, classify first and route: routing optimizes each path without paying for the most expensive one every time.

TRAP: Confusing routing with orchestrator-workers: in routing the categories are defined in advance; in orchestrator-workers the orchestrator discovers them.

TRY IT: Classify a hundred real requests into two or three categories, send the simple ones to Haiku and the complex ones to Sonnet, and compare cost and quality against sending them all to the same model.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Correct: routing classifies the input and directs it to a specialized follow-up, which lets you optimize each category separately and send easy queries to a cheaper model.
That is voting, a variant of parallelization: it helps when you want several perspectives on the same task to gain confidence, not when each category is better handled separately.
That is orchestrator-workers, and the difference is that there the subtasks are not known in advance, while here the request categories are perfectly defined.
That is prompt chaining with gates: it fits when the task decomposes into fixed chained subtasks, not when there are distinct categories requiring distinct paths.

question: At Northgate Labs, the repository's .claude/settings.json contains {"permissions": {"defaultMode": "plan"}} and Aaron also has, in his .claude/settings.local.json, {"permissions": {"defaultMode": "auto"}}. He opens a session by typing claude, with no flags. Which mode does it start in, and why?
options: In auto: settings.local.json has higher precedence than the shared project file, so its value wins.
In Manual: two conflicting defaultMode values cancel each other out and the session falls back to the account's default mode.
In plan, but only until the first prompt, because a mode declared in the project applies only once per session.
In plan: auto does not take effect from project or local settings, so the shared file's value stands.
answer: In plan: auto does not take effect from project or local settings, so the shared file's value stands.
explanation:
The general startup rule is a clear order: first the command-line flag, then permissions.defaultMode, and last the client's default value. On top of that order there is a security exception: the auto and bypassPermissions modes do not take effect from project or local settings, so a repository cannot elevate permissions for whoever clones it. Since the local value is discarded, the shared file's plan wins. The key distinction from ordinary precedence is that here the more specific file does not win: what wins is the only value that source is allowed to apply.

RULE: The startup mode comes from the flag and then from defaultMode; but auto and bypassPermissions are never applied from project or local settings.

TRAP: Applying settings precedence without its exception: the more specific file cannot grant a mode its source is forbidden to apply.

TRY IT: Set defaultMode to auto in .claude/settings.local.json and to plan in .claude/settings.json, open a session and check the mode in the status bar or with /status.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings
option_feedback: That is the general precedence, but there is a documented exception: auto and bypassPermissions do not take effect when they come from project or local settings.
The values do not cancel out: they are resolved by precedence, and here the highest-precedence one simply is not applicable from that file.
The initial mode holds for the whole session until someone changes it with Shift+Tab or a command; it does not expire at the first prompt.
Correct: with the local file's auto discarded, the only applicable defaultMode is the shared file's plan, and a command-line flag would have overridden it.

question: Cedar County's case-file agent runs on Claude Opus 5 with thinking and tools, in sessions lasting several hours. To remind it of the day's priorities, the team started editing the top-level system field mid-conversation and resending the full history. Since that change, some requests fail with 400 and the ones that go through no longer hit the cache. What is the most likely cause?
options: A thinking block stays valid only while the system, the tools and the preceding messages do not change; editing the system invalidates them.
The full history exceeded the model's context window, so the API started rejecting the longer requests with a 400 error.
The history's thinking blocks expired when the five-minute cache lapsed between one turn and the next.
The thinking display is set to summarized, so the blocks you receive can no longer be passed back verbatim on the next turn.
answer: A thinking block stays valid only while the system, the tools and the preceding messages do not change; editing the system invalidates them.
explanation:
The general rule is that the history of a conversation with thinking is append-only: a thinking block stays valid only while the system prompt, the tools and the messages that precede it do not change, and a misaligned or modified block is rejected with a 400. Editing the system field mid-conversation changes that prefix, invalidates the blocks and also drops the cache, which is built over tools, system and messages in that order. The supported way to add instructions on the fly is appending a system-role message at the end of messages. Against the context-window hypothesis, the difference is that an overflow would fail on every request, not on some.

RULE: A thinking block is bound to what precedes it: for new mid-conversation instructions, append a system-role message at the end, do not edit the system field at the top.

TRAP: Assuming the system field can be edited like a global variable; changing it invalidates the earlier thinking blocks and the whole cache.

TRY IT: Send a turn with thinking, edit the system field and resend the full history to see the 400; repeat leaving the system intact and appending the instruction as a final message, and check that it reads the cache again.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/thinking https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching
option_feedback: Correct: thinking blocks are bound to the prefix that precedes them, and the supported way to add instructions mid-conversation is appending a system-role message at the end of messages, leaving that prefix intact.
An overflow produces a prompt-too-long 400 on every request, not on some of them, and this model has a one-million-token context window by default.
The cache is a cost optimization: when it expires you pay the write again, but it does not invalidate any history block or cause a 400.
The display controls what you see of the reasoning; summarized or omitted, you return the blocks exactly as received, with their signature, and that causes no error.

question: Willow Creek Clinic's scheduling assistant has a tool that queries the internal drug formulary, a slow service billed per query. Its description ends with the line CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool whenever you have the slightest doubt about a medication. The logs show the tool is invoked in nearly every conversation, even when the patient asks about office hours, and the monthly cost has tripled. On that budget, what should you do?
options: Leave the line as it is and cap spend with a per-conversation call limit in the code that runs the tool.
Replace the tool with a version that returns fewer fields per query, so each formulary call costs considerably less.
Tone the description down to use this tool when you need formulary data, and remove the phrase about doubt.
Add three examples to the prompt where the assistant answers questions about office hours without calling the formulary tool.
answer: Tone the description down to use this tool when you need formulary data, and remove the phrase about doubt.
explanation:
The general rule is that the prompt's register changes behavior: the documentation asks you to replace formulas like CRITICAL, you must use this tool, with a plain use this tool when, and explicitly warns that instructions of the when in doubt, use the tool kind cause over-triggering. That is exactly what the call log shows, and fixing the description attacks the cause without losing the legitimate queries. A code-level cap puts a ceiling on spend but leaves the bad selection untouched, and it may cut off precisely the query that was needed.

RULE: Write a tool description in a normal register, use this tool when; all-caps register and when in doubt, use it cause over-triggering.

TRAP: Confusing emphasis with precision: the more imperative the instruction, the more the tool fires where it does not belong.

TRY IT: Run twenty office-hours queries with the current description and twenty more with the normal-register version, without the doubt phrase, and count in the logs how many times the formulary tool is called in each batch.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
option_feedback: A cap puts a ceiling on spend but leaves the over-triggering intact: the assistant still picks badly when to query and may run out of calls right when one was needed.
More compact responses are good practice and save context, but the problem is not how much each query returns, it is how many unnecessary queries fire.
Correct: the documentation asks you to swap the imperative register for a normal one and explicitly warns that instructions like when in doubt, use the tool cause over-triggering.
Examples can nudge behavior, but they compete against an all-caps instruction still alive in the tool description: fix the instruction first.

question: Prairie Yield Analytics generates a report per farm field every night: the same call reads the sensor data, computes the indicators, writes the diagnosis and drafts the recommendations. Quality is uneven, especially on the indicators. Reports are delivered at seven in the morning, so there are several hours of slack and per-report latency is not a problem. The steps are always the same. Which redesign is right?
options: Keep a single call and raise effort to max, so the model devotes more reasoning to the indicators.
Launch three parallel instances with the same prompt and merge the three reports into one at the end of the process.
Chain calls, one per step, so each one solves an easier task, trading latency for accuracy.
Set up an orchestrator-workers where a coordinator decides on each report which subtasks are needed and hands them to workers.
answer: Chain calls, one per step, so each one solves an easier task, trading latency for accuracy.
explanation:
The general rule is that prompt chaining fits when the task decomposes cleanly into fixed subtasks, and its stated goal is trading latency for accuracy by making each call easier. The nightly report meets both conditions: the steps are always the same and there are hours of slack. The distinction from orchestrator-workers is predictability, because that pattern exists for when the coordinator has to decide the subtasks based on the input. Parallelization, in turn, is for gaining speed or gathering perspectives, not for a sequence where each step depends on the previous one.

RULE: If the steps are fixed and there is time to spare, chain calls: each one easier and more accurate, and you pay the latency overnight.

TRAP: Choosing orchestrator-workers for a pipeline whose steps you already know; that pattern exists for when you cannot predict them.

TRY IT: Split the report into one call per step, run both versions over the same ten fields and compare the indicators against the real values to see how much accuracy you gain and how much extra time you pay.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Raising effort improves reasoning within the call, but it does not reduce the difficulty of asking for four different jobs at once, and it makes every report more expensive.
Parallelization is for gaining speed or gathering perspectives on the same task; here the steps are sequential and each depends on the previous one.
Correct: prompt chaining is for tasks that decompose into fixed subtasks and its stated goal is trading latency for accuracy, which the overnight slack pays for easily.
That pattern exists for tasks where you cannot predict the subtasks; here they are always the same four, so a coordinator adds cost and variability without contributing anything.

question: At Lakeshore Bank, the regulatory-review coordinator delegates to a subagent the extraction of verbatim quotes from the regulation, which must return the section number and the paragraph word for word. The subagent complies: its final message carries the exact quotes. But the report the coordinator delivers to audit paraphrases them and loses the literal wording. Sophia checks the logs and confirms the Agent tool result arrived complete and untrimmed. What is the most likely cause?
options: Since the version that hardened subagents, the harness rewrites the final message to neutralize instruction-like patterns, and in doing so it alters verbatim quotes.
Compaction on the main thread summarized the tool result before the coordinator wrote the report, and that is what stripped the quotes of their literalness.
The subagent hit its maxTurns and its output was marked partial, so the coordinator filled in the missing part of the text on its own.
The coordinator receives the final message as a tool result but may summarize it in its own response, and to get it reproduced verbatim you have to ask for that in its prompt.
answer: The coordinator receives the final message as a tool result but may summarize it in its own response, and to get it reproduced verbatim you have to ask for that in its prompt.
explanation:
The general rule is that the parent receives the subagent's final message as the result of the Agent tool, but what it delivers to the user is its own response, and nothing forces it to copy that text: the documentation explicitly says it may summarize it and that, if you need verbatim output, you have to instruct the main agent to reproduce it. That is why the fix lives in the coordinator's prompt, not in the subagent's or in the delegation config. The key distinction from the harness distractor is what that mechanism actually does: in recent versions it scans the final message and prepends a marker or escapes turn markers, but it never removes or rewords the subagent's text.

RULE: The parent receives the subagent's final message, but rewrites it as it sees fit unless you ask it to reproduce it word for word.

TRAP: Blaming the harness for a wording change: what it does is prepend a marker and escape turn markers, never rewrite the subagent's text.

TRY IT: Ask a subagent to return a block with a unique identifier and compare the coordinator's response with and without the instruction to reproduce it word for word.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: The harness does inspect the final message, prepends a marker and escapes turn markers, but the documentation clarifies it never removes or rewords the subagent's text.
Compaction leaves a SystemMessage with subtype compact_boundary and would affect far more than the quotes; besides, the logs show the tool result arrived complete.
On reaching maxTurns the output is marked partial and left resumable, which would show in the result; here the subagent's final message contains the complete quotes.
Correct: the parent decides how to write its response from the tool result, and the documentation says to instruct the main agent when the output must be preserved word for word.

question: Bluebird Goods runs two workloads on the same account: the post-purchase support agent, synchronous and latency-sensitive, and supplier invoice extraction, which can deliver results the next day. During afternoon peaks the agent starts getting 429s and the team sees that extraction is consuming a good share of the same model's ITPM. The budget does not allow moving up a tier. What should you do?
options: Schedule invoice extraction for three in the morning, when the support agent gets almost no traffic.
Mark the extraction documents with cache_control, because tokens read from cache do not count toward ITPM.
Move extraction to the Message Batches API: its usage does not affect Messages API rate limits and it costs half.
Split extraction into batches of a hundred requests spaced out with pauses, to stay under the per-minute limit during afternoon peaks.
answer: Move extraction to the Message Batches API: its usage does not affect Messages API rate limits and it costs half.
explanation:
The general rule is that Message Batches API usage does not affect Messages API rate limits, so moving the deferrable load off the synchronous path gives the agent its full quota back and also halves the cost of that work. The other options relieve the symptom without changing the counter: rescheduling keeps the requests on the same API, and spacing them only stretches the work out. The cache option is the subtlest and is half true, because tokens read from cache do not count toward ITPM, but cache writes and each invoice's new content do, and that is where most of the consumption is.

RULE: Whatever can wait goes to Batches: it does not touch Messages API rate limits and costs half.

TRAP: Assuming rescheduling or caching solves a quota contention; only Batches takes that work off the Messages API counter.

TRY IT: Send the same extraction job once through the Messages API and once through the Message Batches API, and compare the rate-limit headers to see how much ITPM is left after each.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits
option_feedback: Moving the schedule relieves today's peak, but the requests still compete for the same quota: one delayed extraction run and the problem is back.
It is true that tokens read from cache do not count toward ITPM, but every invoice is different: only the common prefix would be shared, and cache writes and new content do count.
Correct: the documentation states that Batches usage does not affect Messages API rate limits, so the agent keeps its full quota and the deferrable work is billed at 50%.
Spacing the requests avoids 429s on the extraction itself and the documentation does recommend ramping traffic gradually, but the agent still shares the same ITPM and the work takes far longer.

question: Southbound Freight versions in its .mcp.json the tracking server, which points at production and carries a long timeout meant for heavy queries. Months ago Brandon had added, with local scope, another server also named tracking that points at the test environment. Today the team updates .mcp.json and Brandon notices no change on his machine. What is going on?
options: Claude Code connects only once, using the local entry, which has higher precedence, and does not merge fields across sources.
Both servers load and Claude Code renames the second with a numeric suffix so they can be told apart in the list.
The project entry wins because it is versioned, though the local definition's timeout is kept for being more specific.
The local entry was left pending approval when the project file changed, which is why nothing updates.
answer: Claude Code connects only once, using the local entry, which has higher precedence, and does not merge fields across sources.
explanation:
The general rule is that MCP servers are resolved by name and by precedence: local, then project, then user, then plugin servers and claude.ai connections. When the name matches, Claude Code connects only once and uses the complete entry from the highest-precedence source, without merging fields, so neither the url nor the timeout from the versioned file is ever applied. The key distinction from field-by-field merging is exactly that: the winning source contributes all or nothing, which is why a forgotten local entry can mask months of team changes.

RULE: With duplicate names, an MCP server is resolved by precedence and used whole: local masks project and fields are not merged.

TRAP: Assuming scopes combine field by field, when the winning source supplies the complete definition.

TRY IT: Add with local scope a server named the same as one in your .mcp.json but with a different url and timeout, run /mcp and verify that only the local entry connects and that no field from the project file is mixed in.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: Correct: with duplicate names the definition from the highest-precedence source is used, and the order starts with local, then project, then user.
The numeric suffix appears when importing servers from Claude Desktop and the name already exists, not when two scopes define the same name.
The documentation says the opposite on both counts: the highest-precedence source wins and its entry is used whole, with no field merging across scopes.
Approval applies to project servers and shows as a pending state in claude mcp list; the local server does not go through that dialog.

question: Bluebird Goods reviews each morning the products its suppliers uploaded the night before. For that, Renee built a fixed four-step chain: verify photos, verify sizes, verify prices and write the report, with a programmatic check between each pair of steps. In practice every batch arrives different: some products only have a price problem, others carry both sizes and inconsistent descriptions at once, and every few days a case appears that none of the four steps looks at. What will happen as long as the decomposition stays that fixed chain?
options: The batches will come out fine anyway, because the programmatic check between steps halts the flow whenever a product does not fit the next step.
The anticipated batches will come out fine and the rest will slip through, because a fixed chain only covers the subtasks someone anticipated when designing it.
The batches will come out fine but increasingly slowly, because the chain runs all four steps even on products that have no problem at all.
The batches will fail completely as soon as a new case appears, because the intermediate check breaks the chain and discards what was already verified.
answer: The anticipated batches will come out fine and the rest will slip through, because a fixed chain only covers the subtasks someone anticipated when designing it.
explanation:
The general rule is that the shape of the decomposition is decided by the predictability of the subtasks: when they are known in advance and stable, a chain of fixed steps with checks between them is the cheapest option and the easiest to audit; when they cannot be predicted, you need an orchestrator that determines them from each input and distributes the work. Each morning's batch is the second kind, because its composition changes and it brings cases no step covers, so the chain handles what fits and leaves the rest unreviewed. The key distinction from a step-quality problem is where the failure sits: each step does its job well, and what is missing is the step nobody wrote.

RULE: A chain of fixed steps when the subtasks are known in advance; an orchestrator that determines them from each input when they cannot be predicted.

TRAP: Assuming the checks between steps cover the cases the decomposition did not anticipate, when they only validate the previous step's output.

TRY IT: Take a real batch, count how many products fit none of the four steps and run in parallel a version where an orchestrator decides the steps product by product.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Those checks are real and useful for halting when a step fails, but they only review what the previous step produced: they do not invent the missing step.
Correct: prompt chaining fits when the task decomposes cleanly into fixed subtasks, and here the subtasks change with every batch.
A fixed chain trades latency for accuracy and that is expected, but what the case describes is not slowness, it is products whose problem no step looks at.
An intermediate check stops that product at that point, it does not tear down the batch or erase what was verified before: the real risk is the case that passes unreviewed.

question: Northgate Labs runs PR reviews unattended and wants only the github MCP server's tools to be auto-approved. The step uses this configuration: {"permissions": {"allow": ["mcp__*"]}} and starts with claude -p and no other flags. During runs, some calls sit waiting for an answer nobody will give. Which TWO changes fix the configuration? (Select TWO)
options: Start in acceptEdits, which auto-approves MCP tools along with file edits.
Write the rule as mcp__github__*, because in allow the glob is only valid after the server's literal prefix.
Run with --permission-mode dontAsk, so anything not on the allowlist is denied instead of waiting.
Write the rule as mcp__github(*) to cover all of that server's tools with parentheses.
Start with bypassPermissions, which avoids any waiting because it does not consult the permission rules.
answer: Write the rule as mcp__github__*, because in allow the glob is only valid after the server's literal prefix.
Run with --permission-mode dontAsk, so anything not on the allowlist is denied instead of waiting.
explanation:
The general rule has two layers: what gets auto-approved and what happens to the rest. At the rule layer, allow globs are only accepted after the server's literal prefix, so an entry with a loose wildcard is discarded with a warning and leaves the server without effective permission. At the mode layer, an unattended run needs dontAsk, which denies whatever is not pre-approved instead of opening a dialog nobody will answer. The key distinction from bypassPermissions is that that mode also removes the waits, but by approving everything.

RULE: In allow, an MCP glob is only valid after the server prefix; and with nobody watching, dontAsk turns the unapproved into a denial, not a wait.

TRAP: Writing an unanchored wildcard and assuming it applies, when the rule is discarded as the configuration loads.

TRY IT: Put an allow rule with a loose wildcard and start claude with --debug to see the ignored-rule warning, then repeat anchoring the server prefix.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions
option_feedback: acceptEdits auto-approves file edits, not MCP tools; it is a frequent mix-up when looking for fewer interruptions.
Correct: an unanchored allow entry is ignored with a warning at startup, so today the server has no effective permission.
Correct: in that mode anything not approved is denied, so the run does not sit waiting for an impossible answer.
Claude Code skips any mcp__ rule containing parentheses when loading the configuration, so that entry would never apply.
That mode removes the waits but approves everything else too, which is the opposite of limiting auto-approval to a single server.

question: Cedar County classifies permit applications automatically, and today the only metric the team watches is the percentage of cases escalated to human review, which has been dropping month over month. Rachel wants to decide whether she can shrink the review team, but she does not know whether that drop means the classifier improved or that it is under-escalating. What should you set up before making the decision?
options: Ask the classifier for a 0-to-1 confidence on each case and send to human review only what falls below 0.9.
Manually review a random five percent sample each week and use its error rate as the single quality metric.
Add a second classifier with a different prompt and treat as safe the cases where both agree on the category.
Measure accuracy, consistency, edge cases, bias and cost per classification against a labeled set.
answer: Measure accuracy, consistency, edge cases, bias and cost per classification against a labeled set.
explanation:
The general rule is that a single aggregate metric does not tell you whether a classifier improved. The classification guide lists several dimensions worth tracking, among them routing accuracy, consistency, edge-case handling, bias mitigation, explainability, cost per classification and escalation rate, and measuring them requires a labeled set to compare against. Without those labels, a falling escalation rate is ambiguous: it could be a better classifier or one that stopped asking for help. The second-classifier option is tempting, but agreement between two prompts measures coincidence, not correctness.

RULE: Before cutting human review, measure against a labeled set and across several dimensions: one aggregate metric hides which one you are failing.

TRAP: Reading a falling escalation rate as a sign of improvement; it may mean the classifier is letting the hard cases through.

TRY IT: Hand-label a hundred already-classified applications, measure per-category accuracy, cross-run consistency and cost per case on that set, and check whether the drop in escalation lines up with fewer errors or more.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/ticket-routing https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests
option_feedback: The confidence the model reports itself has no documented threshold to use as a criterion, and the underlying problem is that you still do not know whether the classifications are correct.
A human sample is valuable and worth keeping, but a single aggregate rate does not tell you which dimension the classifier fails on or what each classification costs.
Two prompts agreeing measures agreement, not correctness: both can be wrong the same way on the same kind of case, and without labels there is no way to notice.

Correct: the classification guide lists those dimensions along with explainability and escalation rate, and only a labeled set lets you tell whether escalating less meant improving or letting errors through.

question: Southbound Freight shows on an internal dashboard the progress of each run of the coordinator that delegates to tracking and rate subagents. Nick needs to attribute, while the run is in progress, which activity belongs to which subagent and when each delegation starts and ends. He works with the Agent SDK in Python. Which two mechanisms give you that attribution? (Select TWO)
options: Read parent_tool_use_id on messages: it is populated when the message comes from inside a subagent and empty when the main agent produced it.
Ask the coordinator in its prompt to announce in text which subagent it is about to launch and which just finished, and parse those announcements in the dashboard.
Read model_usage from the ResultMessage, which breaks down consumption per subagent and lets you reconstruct who did each part of the run's work.
Register SubagentStart and SubagentStop hooks, which mark the beginning and end of each delegation and identify the subagent with agent_id.
Open the main session's .jsonl file, where the complete conversations of every subagent the run launched are interleaved.
answer: Read parent_tool_use_id on messages: it is populated when the message comes from inside a subagent and empty when the main agent produced it.
Register SubagentStart and SubagentStop hooks, which mark the beginning and end of each delegation and identify the subagent with agent_id.
explanation:
The general rule is that the SDK already exposes subagent attribution two independent ways, and neither depends on the model cooperating. The first is the parent_tool_use_id field, which is populated on messages emitted from inside a subagent and points to the Agent tool call that launched it, letting you tag activity in real time. The second is the SubagentStart and SubagentStop hooks, which mark the boundaries of each delegation and identify the subagent with agent_id, and of the two it is the SubagentStop payload that also carries its transcript path. The key distinction from model_usage is what it measures and when: it accounts for the whole tree, but broken down by model and only when the run closes, so it is no use for a live dashboard.

RULE: Attribute live with parent_tool_use_id on messages and with the SubagentStart and SubagentStop hooks; model_usage breaks down by model and only at the end.

TRAP: Mistaking model_usage's per-model breakdown for a per-subagent breakdown.

TRY IT: Launch a query that delegates to two subagents and print parent_tool_use_id for each incoming message, to see which ones come from inside a delegation.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks
option_feedback: Correct: that field points to the Agent tool call that launched the subagent, so it lets you attribute each message live, without waiting for the run to finish.
A text announcement depends on the model always writing it and on your parser getting it right: it is not an SDK mechanism and fails exactly when the coordinator improvises.
model_usage gives token and cost accounting for the whole tree, but broken down by model rather than by subagent, and it only arrives at the end of the run.
Correct: those events mark the boundaries of each delegation and identify the subagent, and the SubagentStop payload also carries the path to its transcript.
Subagent transcripts are stored in separate files and persist independently of the main thread, so they are not inside the session's .jsonl.

question: The records-digitization team at the City of Fairview extracts case data with structured outputs, using output_config.format and its own JSON schema. Before moving the pipeline to production, Thomas reviews with the team what the feature guarantees and what stays on their side. Which of the following statements about structured outputs is NOT correct?
options: The first request with a new schema takes longer because the grammar has to be compiled, and compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use.
If the response ends with stop_reason max_tokens or refusal, the output still conforms to the schema because the grammar constrains sampling.
Changing the output_config.format parameter invalidates that conversation thread's prompt cache, and the input token count rises slightly.
Including constraints like minimum, maximum or maxLength in the schema returns a 400 error, because those keywords are not supported.
answer: If the response ends with stop_reason max_tokens or refusal, the output still conforms to the schema because the grammar constrains sampling.
explanation:
The general rule is that structured outputs guarantees the shape of the output only as long as generation ends normally. The grammar constrains sampling token by token, but it cannot complete a response cut off by max_tokens nor override a refusal: in both cases the documentation warns the output may not match the schema, which is why the first step when parsing is to read stop_reason. The other three statements describe documented behaviors: grammar compilation and caching, prompt-cache invalidation when the format changes, and the 400 on unsupported keywords.

RULE: Structured outputs guarantees the schema while generation ends normally: with max_tokens or refusal the output may fall outside the schema.

TRAP: Reading "schema-guaranteed output" as if it also covered truncated or refused responses: what rules in that case is stop_reason.

TRY IT: Send a request with output_config.format and max_tokens at 16, and check that the response comes back with stop_reason max_tokens and truncated JSON that does not validate against your schema.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/handling-stop-reasons
option_feedback: This one is correct: the documentation describes that initial compilation latency and the 24-hour cache, which is invalidated if the schema structure or the request's tool set changes.

Correct as the answer: this is exactly what the documentation denies. With max_tokens the output is incomplete and may not conform to the schema, and on a refusal the refusal message takes priority over the constraints.
This one is correct: the API adds an extra system prompt explaining the expected format, and changing that parameter invalidates the thread's cache.
This one is correct: numeric and string-length constraints are supported in neither JSON outputs nor strict tool use, and using one returns a 400 with the details.

question: Prairie Press runs a nightly job that reviews the site. The CI step is: claude -p "Install the dependencies and run the suite" --permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools "Bash(npm test *)" --output-format json. In the run, Claude emits a single command, npm ci && npm test, the job executes nothing and the result reports a denied permission. What is the correct explanation?
options: The allow rule must match each subcommand separately: npm ci is not on the allowlist and in dontAsk the whole call is denied.
Project allow rules do not apply without the trust dialog, which never appears under -p, so the allowlist ends up empty.
Claude Code splits the compound command and runs only the permitted half, npm test, silently discarding npm ci.
The pattern Bash(npm test *) requires an argument after test, so not even npm test matches the rule as written.
answer: The allow rule must match each subcommand separately: npm ci is not on the allowlist and in dontAsk the whole call is denied.
explanation:
The general rule is that permission rules are evaluated against each subcommand separately: Claude Code splits the command on the &&, ||, semicolon and pipe operators, and an allow rule only pre-approves the call if it covers every part. In dontAsk, anything not pre-approved is denied, so the presence of npm ci drags down the entire call. The distinction from the untrusted-workspace diagnosis is where the allowlist comes from: rules in the project settings file need the trust dialog, but --allowedTools on the command line always applies.

RULE: In a compound command the allow rule must cover every subcommand; a single unpermitted one denies the whole call.

TRAP: Assuming an allowlist covering the main command is enough when the model chains another subcommand with &&.

TRY IT: Start claude --permission-mode dontAsk --allowedTools "Bash(npm test *)", ask it to run npm ci && npm test and confirm the call is denied entirely; then repeat asking only for npm test.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless
option_feedback: Correct: Claude Code splits the compound command and requires every part to be covered; since npm ci matches no rule, in dontAsk the whole call is rejected.
It is true that allow rules stored in project settings do not apply in untrusted sessions, but here the allowlist arrives on the command line via --allowedTools, which does apply.
The command is split for permission evaluation, but the evaluation decides on the whole call: Claude Code does not run one half and discard the other.
An asterisk preceded by a space also covers the bare command, so Bash(npm test *) does match npm test; the problem is in the other half of the command.

question: At Lakeshore Bank, the regulatory-analysis subagent queries the search_regulations tool on an internal MCP server. So that legacy-service outages would not interrupt the review, Jordan wrapped the call in three silent retries and, when all of them fail, the tool returns an empty list as a normal result. Since then, several reports state that no applicable regulation exists for the product under review, and the coordinator incorporates that conclusion without caveats. The logs show the legacy service was down in those cases. What is the most likely cause of this error propagation?
options: The tool turns a failure into a valid empty result, so the model never learns the tool is failing and cannot adapt.
The model hallucinates the conclusion because the question requires information that never made it into the conversation's context.
Three attempts are too few for an unstable legacy service, so the retry count and the wait between attempts should be raised.
A system prompt instruction is missing that forbids concluding no regulation applies without having checked the primary source.
answer: The tool turns a failure into a valid empty result, so the model never learns the tool is failing and cannot adapt.
explanation:
The general rule is that an agent can only adapt to what it sees: tool errors are returned to the model as a tool_result with is_error and an actionable message, and Anthropic reports that telling the agent when a tool is failing works surprisingly well.
