The general rule is that a subagent cannot talk to the person: the runtime removes AskUserQuestion from all subagents, so any human decision point has to live in the main conversation. The correct design turns the doubt into part of the deliverable, with the subagent returning the contradiction, the alternatives and the question, and the coordinator taking it to the advisor before continuing. The key distinction from running the subagent in the foreground is that the foreground changes who waits for whom and which permission prompts are seen, not which tools exist inside the subagent.

RULE: A subagent does not ask: it returns the question. The human decision point always lives in the main conversation.

TRAP: Assuming that listing a tool in the tools field makes it exist: the ones the runtime removes from subagents do not come back through configuration.

TRY IT: Define a subagent whose prompt explicitly tells it to use AskUserQuestion on an ambiguity, launch it with an ambiguous case and watch what it does instead of asking.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents
option_feedback: The tools field trims what the subagent can use, but it does not restore a tool the runtime removes from all subagents, and AskUserQuestion is on that list.
Foreground subagents block the conversation and let permission prompts through, but AskUserQuestion is removed from all subagents, whether they run in the foreground or the background.
Correct: the human decision point lives in the main conversation, and the subagent contributes the question and the alternatives as part of the result it delivers.
More turns help when the subagent still has work to do, but here the contradiction is real and what is needed is a criterion only a person can set.

question: At Northgate Labs, Brandon wants a guarantee that no maintenance session modifies the deployment script. The team proposes always working in plan mode, arguing that there Claude proposes changes without editing the code. What should you do to get that guarantee?
options: Add a deny rule on that path in permissions, or a PreToolUse hook that blocks it: plan mode is not a permission control.
Work in plan mode and review the plan before approving it, which is the documented way to avoid unwanted edits.
Set permissions.defaultMode to plan in the project settings so every session starts by planning.
Write a line with IMPORTANT in the root CLAUDE.md forbidding touching that file in any session.
answer: Add a deny rule on that path in permissions, or a PreToolUse hook that blocks it: plan mode is not a permission control.
explanation:
The general rule is that plan mode organizes the work, it does not restrict permissions: it is for investigating and agreeing on an approach before touching code, and it ends precisely when someone approves the plan. A guarantee that must always hold is written where Claude Code enforces it on its own, that is, in a deny rule or a PreToolUse hook, which are evaluated on every call regardless of mode. The distinction from planning and reviewing is what each protects: plan mode protects while it lasts, the rule protects always.

RULE: Plan mode is a way of working, not a permission; what must never happen is written as a deny rule or a hook.

TRAP: Confusing a mode you leave on approving the plan with a permission control applied on every call.

TRY IT: Start in plan mode, approve any plan and confirm that from then on Claude can edit; then add the deny rule and repeat the exercise.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions
option_feedback: Correct: deny rules and hooks are applied by Claude Code on every call, even in the most permissive modes, and do not depend on which mode the session is in.
Reviewing the plan is the right practice when the approach is uncertain, but the protection disappears as soon as someone approves a plan and the session moves to executing.
It is a valid and useful setting as a starting point, but it fixes the initial mode; it does not prevent leaving it or approving a plan that touches that file.
CLAUDE.md is loaded as context and emphasis helps with a single rule, but it remains advice the model may not follow.

question: At Lakeshore Bank, clause extraction returns JSON that always validates against the strict schema, but in 9% of contracts the amount comes back expressed in a currency the contract never mentions. Today the code detects the inconsistency against the core system, discards the response and repeats the same request with exponential backoff up to four times; each retry costs a full call and the nightly processing window is three hours. What should be done?
options: Raise retries to eight with exponential backoff, which is the policy the documentation recommends for API failures.
Add the currency to the schema as an enum and a minimum for the amount, so the grammar blocks the invalid value at sampling time.
Send to human review every contract where the currency does not match, because it is a business rule the model cannot resolve on its own.
Return an error tool_result stating which rule was violated and what value is expected, so the model corrects on the next turn.
answer: Return an error tool_result stating which rule was violated and what value is expected, so the model corrects on the next turn.
explanation:
The general rule is that a retry only makes sense if something changed: with transient failures, time changes, and with content errors, what has to change is the information the model receives. The documentation is explicit that errors returned as tool_results should say what happened and what should be tried next, because that is what lets the model recover without guessing. The detail that decides against backoff is the nature of the failure: the output validates against the schema and the conflict is with a business rule, so resending the same request burns the nightly window without changing anything.

RULE: A blind retry repeats the error; an error that names the violated rule and the expected value turns the retry into a correction.

TRAP: Applying exponential backoff, which is for transient network or quota failures, to a deterministic content error that will repeat identically.

TRY IT: Take twenty contracts that fail the currency check, first return a generic error and then one naming the rule and the expected value, and compare how many are corrected on the next turn.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/errors
option_feedback: Exponential backoff is right for transient failures like 429 or 5xx, where waiting changes the result; a deterministic content inconsistency will repeat identically on the eighth attempt.
An enum narrows which currency codes are valid, but it cannot know which one that contract mentions; and minimum is not supported in structured outputs, so the schema would return a 400.
It is a safe and sometimes necessary escape hatch, but it spends human time on an error the model itself can fix if told which rule it violated and what is expected.

Correct: the documentation asks for instructive errors, with what went wrong and what to try next, instead of generic messages; that way the retry arrives with new information rather than repeating the same call.

question: During an incident, two on-call engineers at Cascade Power resumed the same operations-agent session by identifier, each from their own terminal. The next day the audit finds a transcript where one engineer's questions are mixed with the other's answers, and on top of that a work order the agent had started to issue right when the session crashed was never recorded anywhere. Which two explanations apply? (Select TWO)
options: Resuming the same session in two terminals without forking interleaves both terminals' messages into a single transcript.
The session was resumed from a different working directory, and transcripts are stored by encoded cwd.
A tool that was executing when the session crashed is not re-executed on resume: the order was left half-done.
On resume the bypassPermissions mode is not restored, so the agent asked for a confirmation nobody answered.
The retention configured in cleanupPeriodDays deleted the transcript before the audit could review it.
answer: Resuming the same session in two terminals without forking interleaves both terminals' messages into a single transcript.
A tool that was executing when the session crashed is not re-executed on resume: the order was left half-done.
explanation:
The general rule is that a session is a single thread written to disk: resuming it from two terminals does not create two conversations but one, where both terminals' messages interleave, and what separates the branches is forking. Besides, resuming returns the conversation and not the state of the world: a tool that was running when the process died is not relaunched, so the half-done order has to be reconciled from the application. The key distinction from the other causes is that none produces both symptoms at once, because an encoded directory prevents finding the session, retention deletes it, and the permission mode only changes who gets asked.

RULE: One session, one thread: to work in parallel from the same point you have to fork, and resuming brings back the conversation, never the work left half-done.

TRAP: Reading resume as if it were sync: two terminals on the same identifier share a transcript instead of each keeping its own.

TRY IT: Open the same session with resume in two terminals, type something different in each and inspect the session file to see how the messages ended up ordered.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation warns about exactly that; to work in parallel from the same point you have to fork and keep two independent sessions.
Storage does depend on the directory, but that results in the session not appearing or not being found, not in two conversations blending into one.
Correct: resuming restores the conversation, it does not relaunch work in flight, so the interrupted step has to be detected and repeated from the application.
It is true that mode is not restored on resume, but that would explain a pause waiting for permission, not an interleaved transcript or an unrecorded order.
Periodic cleanup removes old sessions, but then there would be no transcript to review; here the problem is what it contains, not that it is missing.

question: At Willow Creek Clinic, the authorization-extraction prompt mixes instructions, the scanned form's text and two worked examples into a single block. When the form carries phrases of its own such as "all fields in capital letters", the model sometimes obeys them and returns the data that way. Brandon wants it to be clear which part of the prompt is instruction and which part is data. What should you do?
options: Move the instructions to the end of the prompt, after the form and the examples, so they are the last thing the model reads.
Wrap each type of content in its own XML tag, with descriptive names used consistently across prompts.
Add an all-caps warning at the start telling it to ignore any instruction appearing inside the form's text.
Split the work into two calls, one that cleans up the form's text and another that extracts the fields from the cleaned text.
answer: Wrap each type of content in its own XML tag, with descriptive names used consistently across prompts.
explanation:
The general rule is that when a prompt mixes instructions, context, examples and variable inputs, each type of content should go in its own XML tag, with descriptive names used consistently. That gives the model an explicit boundary between what it must obey and what it should merely read, which is exactly what is missing when the form contains command-shaped sentences. The key distinction from reordering the prompt is that position helps the model attend better to a long input, but it does not declare the role of each block.

RULE: When a prompt mixes instructions, data and examples, each type of content goes in its own XML tag with consistent names.

TRAP: Answering the confusion with more emphasis: an all-caps warning does not mark the line between instruction and data; structure does.

TRY IT: Take a form containing an imperative sentence, run the current prompt and one that wraps the form in its own tag, and compare whether the printed instruction is still obeyed.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: Putting the long document up top and the question at the end improves quality with large inputs, but order does not distinguish your instruction from a phrase printed inside the form.
Correct: XML tags let Claude interpret without ambiguity a prompt that mixes instructions, context, examples and variable inputs, and they reduce exactly this kind of confusion.
Emphatic language is something to use sparingly, and a warning does not mark the boundary between instruction and data: it still depends on the model guessing where each begins.
Chaining calls is useful when the task decomposes into fixed subtasks, but here it adds a call and latency to solve something fixed by structuring the same prompt.

question: Prairie Press needs a compliance instruction to travel inside the system prompt of every Claude Code session, and not as context that arrives after it. Which mechanism achieves that?
options: The --append-system-prompt flag, or its file variant, which appends text to the session's actual system prompt.
The organization-managed CLAUDE.md, which is loaded before the user's and the project's.
A file in .claude/rules/ without a paths frontmatter, loaded at startup with the same priority as .claude/CLAUDE.md.
A SessionStart hook whose stdout output is added to the context when the session begins.
answer: The --append-system-prompt flag, or its file variant, which appends text to the session's actual system prompt.
explanation:
The general rule is that CLAUDE.md and rules are context: they are delivered as a user message after the system prompt, they are not part of it. When an instruction must live in the system prompt, the documented path is --append-system-prompt or its file variant. The distinction from the managed CLAUDE.md is subtle and very tempting: that file is loaded before all the others and cannot be excluded, but before does not mean inside the system prompt. The same goes for a SessionStart hook, which adds text to the initial context.

RULE: CLAUDE.md and rules are context delivered after the system prompt; to write into the system prompt use --append-system-prompt.

TRAP: Reading "is loaded first" as if it meant "is part of the system prompt": load order does not change where the text lives.

TRY IT: Start claude with --append-system-prompt and a test phrase, put that same phrase in CLAUDE.md in another session and compare how Claude answers when asked about its instructions.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference
option_feedback: Correct: it is the documented mechanism for system-prompt-level instructions, exactly what CLAUDE.md cannot offer.
It loads first and nobody can exclude it, but it is still delivered as context after the system prompt, just like any CLAUDE.md.
It is true that a rule without paths enters every session, but it enters as context: it changes what Claude reads, not where the instruction lives.
That hook does inject text at startup, and it is useful for reminders, but it adds it to the conversation's context, not to the system prompt.

question: An agent on Lakeshore Bank's platform team walks a legacy repository of thousands of files to build an inventory of dependencies between modules, and needs to keep comparing what it finds in one file with what it read much earlier. To keep the context from growing, Derek enabled the clear_tool_uses_20250919 strategy with keep at 3. Since then the agent rereads the same files over and over, sometimes mentions that a previous result was removed, cost per session has risen and cache_read_input_tokens have fallen to nearly zero. What is the most likely cause?
options: The repository exceeds the model's context window, so the API returns the prompt-too-long error and the agent restarts exploration from the beginning.
The agent does not have the memory tool enabled, so it cannot store what it discovers and needs to reread the files on every attempt.
The keep value ended up too high: keeping three tool results leaves too much context alive and forces clearing on every turn.
Clearing removes exactly the results the inventory still needs and invalidates the cache from that point on; this task calls for compaction.
answer: Clearing removes exactly the results the inventory still needs and invalidates the cache from that point on; this task calls for compaction.
explanation:
The general rule is that the two context strategies solve different problems: context editing deletes tool results that are no longer needed, and compaction summarizes the conversation when the work accumulates information that remains relevant. Here the task needs to compare what was read at the start with what turns up later, so deleting the oldest results forces rereading them, and each clearing invalidates the cached prefix from the point where it occurs, which explains the drop in cache reads and the rise in cost. The key distinction is what happens to the information: clearing removes it and leaves a notice, while compaction condenses it into a summary that remains available.

RULE: Clear tool results when you will no longer need them; when the work accumulates findings across many files, summarize with compaction.

TRAP: Confusing the two context strategies: deleting results the task still uses forces rereading them and breaks the cache from the clearing point onward.

TRY IT: Run the same exploration twice, once with clear_tool_uses and once with compaction, and compare file rereads and cache_read_input_tokens across the two runs.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-editing https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction
option_feedback: An input exceeding the window fails with an explicit 400 and does not leave the agent working; here the session progresses and what appears are gaps where read results used to be.
External memory is the right answer when findings must persist across sessions, but it explains neither the replacement text nor the drop in cache reads within this session.
Lowering keep would clear even more aggressively and worsen the symptom; the problem is not how much is kept, but that what the task still needs is being deleted.

Correct: tool-result clearing replaces the oldest ones with a notice text and invalidates the cached prefix, and the documentation recommends compaction for long tasks that accumulate information from many files.

question: A team is working with Claude Code and, halfway through an attempt, sees the implementation heading down the wrong path. They want to redirect it right away, without discarding what Claude has already written or starting the session over. What does the documentation recommend?
options: Press Esc to interrupt the action in progress and give the corrected instruction right there.
Wait for Claude to finish the whole attempt and ask for the correction on the next turn.
Press Esc twice on an empty line and restore the code to the previous checkpoint.
Run /clear and repeat the request from scratch with a more specific prompt.
answer: Press Esc to interrupt the action in progress and give the corrected instruction right there.
explanation:
The general rule of iterative refinement is to correct early and often: each pass should start from the best that already exists and not from zero. Interrupting the moment the course goes wrong preserves the work done so far and lets you give the new instruction on top of that state, which is the cheapest way to improve progressively. The other options are real tools from the same box, but they belong to another moment in the cycle: rewind returns the code to a checkpoint when the attempt is beyond saving, and starting over with a more specific prompt is what is advised after two failed corrections on the same thing. The key distinction is how much work you are willing to throw away: interrupting preserves, restoring and clearing discard.

RULE: Correct early: interrupt as soon as you see the deviation and redirect on top of what Claude already did; undoing or starting over are for when the attempt is beyond saving.

TRAP: Assuming you have to let the attempt finish before correcting: the further the wrong course runs, the more work has to be discarded.

TRY IT: Ask for a long change, press Esc halfway through and review the diff: the files Claude had already modified stay as it left them before the interruption.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices https://code.claude.com/docs/en/interactive-mode
option_feedback: Correct: the documentation recommends course-correcting early and often, and interrupting with Esc keeps the work done up to that point, so the new instruction starts from there.
Letting the attempt finish is the comfortable option, but the documentation advises the opposite: the sooner you interrupt, the less wrong work has to be undone later.
Double Esc opens the rewind menu, useful when the attempt is beyond saving; here restoring the code discards exactly what the team wants to keep.
Starting over is the advice for when you have already corrected the same thing twice without success, not for the first deviation within an attempt in progress.

question: Northgate Labs maintains .claude/rules/api.md with the frontmatter paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"] and its handler conventions. A nightly review job runs: claude -p "Review src/api/pricing.ts and report deviations" --setting-sources user --output-format json. What will happen with that rule in that run?
options: It loads anyway, because rules live in the repository and are not a setting: --setting-sources does not decide which rules enter.
It loads as soon as Claude reads pricing.ts, because the file matches the paths glob.
It loads, but below the user rules, which under -p take priority over the project's.
It does not load: by excluding project from --setting-sources, Claude Code skips the project rules even though the file matches.
answer: It does not load: by excluding project from --setting-sources, Claude Code skips the project rules even though the file matches.
explanation:
The general rule is that the paths glob decides when a rule that has already been discovered is loaded, not whether the file gets discovered at all. Discovery depends on the enabled setting sources: with --setting-sources user, the project source is left out and the repository's .claude/rules/ rules are skipped entirely. The distinction from the most tempting alternative is one of order: first it is decided which sources load and then which files match the pattern, and here the job stopped at the first step.

RULE: First it is decided which setting sources load and then which globs match: without project, the repository's rules do not exist.

TRAP: Assuming a repository rule loads because of the glob even when its setting source is excluded from the run.

TRY IT: Repeat the request in an interactive session with and without --setting-sources user and check with /context whether the rule appears among the loaded memory files.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference
option_feedback: Project rules are discovered together with the project settings, so excluding that source leaves them out too.
That is exactly the behavior in a normal session, which is why it is the most tempting answer, but the rule was never even discovered.
The real order is the opposite, user rules load first and project rules weigh more, and besides there are no project rules loaded here.
Correct: if the project source is not enabled, project rules are skipped, and the glob is never evaluated.

question: Summit Ridge Insurance's claim triage prompt lives in prompts/triage.md and its criteria section ends with this line: IMPORTANT: when in any doubt, flag the claim as possible fraud. The fraud team currently receives three times more cases than it can review and, on auditing a sample, 80% show no indicator at all. Which change attacks the cause of the problem?
options: Add six examples of legitimate claims that were flagged by mistake to the prompt, so the model learns not to flag them.
Lower the triage call's temperature so the model is more conservative when applying the fraud criterion.
Replace that line with the concrete indicators that count as fraud and allow answering that there is not enough information.
Raise the classifier's effort so it analyzes each claim more deeply before deciding whether to flag it.
answer: Replace that line with the concrete indicators that count as fraud and allow answering that there is not enough information.
explanation:
The general rule is that a "when in doubt, act" instruction over-triggers: the documentation warns that such phrasing makes the model activate the action far too often, and recommends toning down the imperative and describing precisely when it applies. The fix has two halves: listing the indicators that count as fraud, which is the explicit criterion that does not exist today, and giving it permission to say there is not enough information, a documented technique for reducing unsupported claims. The key distinction from adding examples is that no number of examples contradicts a rule the prompt still states.

RULE: A "when in doubt, flag" instruction manufactures false positives: write what counts as an indicator and allow saying there is not enough information.

TRAP: Papering over an over-triggering instruction with examples or more reasoning: as long as the rule says flag when in doubt, the model will follow it.

TRY IT: Run the same batch of a hundred claims with the original line and with the version that lists indicators and permits admitting missing information, and compare how many are flagged in each run.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations
option_feedback: Examples steer format and criteria when the problem is one of pattern, but here they compete against an explicit rule in the prompt itself ordering it to flag when in doubt: the instruction wins.
Temperature affects sampling variability, not the criterion; besides, models after Claude Opus 4.6 reject with a 400 any value other than the default.
Correct: listing what counts as an indicator supplies the explicit criterion that is missing, and permission to admit uncertainty keeps doubt from automatically becoming a flag.
More effort improves tasks requiring multi-step reasoning, but here the model reasons well and obeys: the result is what the instruction asks for.

question: At Prairie Press, the file .claude/rules/publishing.md opens with the frontmatter paths: ["content/**/*.md"] and continues with 120 lines describing the publishing procedure step by step: generate the index, run the copy editor, request editorial approval and deploy. Every time someone edits an article those 120 lines enter the context, and Claude applies the procedure halfway even though nobody asked for it. Which reorganization applies?
options: Split it into several .claude/rules/ files with the same paths, one topic per file, as the documentation recommends.
Move it to an invokable skill and leave in the rule only the conventions that must be present whenever an article is touched.
Move it to the root CLAUDE.md so the procedure is available in every session without depending on the glob.
Turn it into a PostToolUse hook on Edit that verifies each step of the procedure after every edit.
answer: Move it to an invokable skill and leave in the rule only the conventions that must be present whenever an article is touched.
explanation:
The general rule splits the work across three places: conventions that must be present when touching certain files go in a rule with paths, multi-step procedures that are launched when needed go in a skill, and what must hold without exception goes in a hook. Here the content is a procedure, and its symptom gives it away: it loads without anyone asking and gets applied halfway. The distinction from a hook is who fires it: a hook guarantees a check on every event, while publishing is a task someone decides to start.

RULE: Permanent conventions to the rule with paths, procedures to a skill you invoke, guarantees to a hook: the symptom tells you which one is missing.

TRAP: Using a rule with paths as if it were a procedure manual, when its job is to accompany editing with conventions.

TRY IT: Move the procedure to .claude/skills/publish/SKILL.md, open an article and check with /context that the rule now takes only a few lines.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory https://code.claude.com/docs/en/features-overview
option_feedback: One topic per file is the recommended practice, but since they all share the same glob the context that enters is the same and the procedure still fires on its own.
Correct: a multi-step procedure is loaded on demand as a skill, and the rule keeps the conventions that really should accompany every edit.
It makes the problem worse: it goes from loading when content is touched to loading always, and it competes with the rest of the file for the model's attention.
A hook is the right answer when something must be checked on every edit without exception, but these are steps a person decides to launch, not an automatic verification.

question: Summit Pay's support agent sends a request with manual extended thinking enabled and, to make sure it always checks the balance before answering, sends it with tool_choice: {"type": "any"}. The team also expects the model to explain in text why it chose that tool before calling it. What happens with that request?
options: It works, but the model will not be able to emit text before the tool_use block, because any prefixes the assistant's response with the call.
It works and additionally guarantees exactly one call per response, which is what any adds over auto.
It works, but the thinking block is silently discarded and the response arrives with only the tool_use.
The request fails: with manual extended thinking, any and tool are not supported; you have to use auto and ask for the tool in the prompt.
answer: The request fails: with manual extended thinking, any and tool are not supported; you have to use auto and ask for the tool in the prompt.
explanation:
The general rule is that forcing a tool and enabling manual extended thinking are incompatible: with manual thinking only the auto and none values of tool_choice are accepted, and any or tool return an error instead of running. That is why the way to get what the team wants is tool_choice auto plus an explicit prompt instruction to use the tool. The distinction from the most tempting option is that it describes a real effect of any, the suppression of preceding text, but applied to a request that in this case never runs.

RULE: With manual extended thinking, tool_choice accepts only auto or none: to insist on a tool, ask for it in the prompt.

TRAP: Reasoning about any's effects while forgetting that, with manual thinking, the request is rejected before producing any effect at all.

TRY IT: Send the same request with manual thinking and tool_choice any, and then with auto plus the instruction to use the tool, and compare the two responses.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/define-tools
option_feedback: That is exactly what happens with any when manual thinking is not enabled, which is why it is the trap: here the request never even runs.
Limiting to a single call per response depends on disable_parallel_tool_use, not on any, which only forces using some tool.
There is no silent discard: the combination is rejected up front and the API returns an error.
Correct: with manual thinking only auto and none are accepted, so the way to insist on the tool is to instruct it in the prompt with tool_choice auto.

question: The agent that builds Cascade Power's weekly maintenance plan walks the fault notices, cross-references crew availability and writes the final document, all in a single open-ended run. The runs end with subtype error_max_turns; the team already raised max_turns from 40 to 120 and spend grew without the plan improving. What should you do?
options: Raise max_turns to 300 and add max_budget_usd as a safety net so the run can complete.
Split the work into stages with defined input and output, survey, prioritization and drafting, and run each with its own cap.
Switch to a larger model and raise effort to high so the agent resolves the plan in fewer turns.
Launch ten subagents in parallel, one per section of the plan, to spread the turns among them.
answer: Split the work into stages with defined input and output, survey, prioritization and drafting, and run each with its own cap.
explanation:
The general rule is that max_turns is a safety net and not a dose: if a run always hits the cap, what is missing is decomposition. The documentation recommends writing a staged flow when the steps can be named in advance, and here they can, because first you survey, then you prioritize and finally you draft. Each stage runs with its own cap and its verifiable output, so a failure is localized in one stage instead of consuming the whole run. The key distinction from raising the limit is the pattern: raising the cap rescues a run that ended one step from the finish, not one that never converges.

RULE: If the run always hits max_turns, the problem is decomposition: split into stages with verifiable output before raising any cap.

TRAP: Treating a limit that is always reached as a badly calibrated limit, when it is the symptom of a task with no stages and no termination criterion.

TRY IT: Take a task that exhausts max_turns, split it into three chained prompts with intermediate outputs and compare total turns and cost against the single run.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Resuming with a higher cap is right when the run ended one step from the finish, but here the limit is hit over and over without progress: the cap is not what is missing.
Correct: a limit that is always hit signals a badly decomposed task, and with bounded stages each run has a verifiable objective and a clear ending.
More capacity per turn helps on reasoning-dense tasks, but it does not add structure to work that has no stages or termination criterion.
Parallelizing helps when the subtasks are independent; here prioritization depends on the survey and the drafting on the prioritization, so work would be duplicated.

question: Prairie Press's website team iterates with Claude Code on the homepage. The prompt they keep repeating is: Fix the homepage layout until it looks right, and the project's CLAUDE.md carries the line: The layout must be flawless. After five passes they are still arguing about whether it looks right. Which TWO changes will make the iteration converge? (Select TWO)
options: Attach the design image and ask it to take a screenshot of the result, compare it with the original and list the differences.
Switch to a larger model and repeat the same prompt, because the problem is capacity and not criteria.
Rewrite the CLAUDE.md line in capitals with IMPORTANT so Claude does not overlook it.
Define what looks right means with a command that returns an exit code and ask for its output as evidence.
Open three parallel sessions with the same prompt and keep whichever version the team likes best.
answer: Attach the design image and ask it to take a screenshot of the result, compare it with the original and list the differences.
Define what looks right means with a command that returns an exit code and ask for its output as evidence.
explanation:
The general rule is that an iteration converges when Claude has a way to verify its own work and is asked for evidence rather than a claim of success. The two correct measures attack independent planes: one gives an executable criterion with an exit code and the other a visual comparison against the original design. Neither depends on the prompt being more emphatic. The distinction from underlining the CLAUDE.md line is that an unverifiable instruction does not improve by being written in capitals: what is missing is not emphasis, it is a definition of done.

RULE: Give Claude a way to check the result and ask for the evidence; without a verifiable criterion no iteration converges.

TRAP: Believing a more emphatic prompt or a larger model substitutes for a checkable definition of what done means.

TRY IT: Replace the CLAUDE.md line with a checkable criterion, ask Claude to run the command and paste its output, and count how many passes it takes now.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Correct: it turns looking right into an observable comparison and gives Claude a way to verify its own work on each pass.
A larger model does not invent the missing criterion: without a definition of success, the iteration still has nowhere to stop.
Emphasis helps with a concrete rule that gets skipped, but flawless is not verifiable: underlining it does not make it checkable.
Correct: a checkable criterion plus the requirement to show the evidence closes the loop, instead of trusting Claude's claim that it is done.
Parallel sessions are useful for exploring different approaches, but they multiply the work without resolving the missing acceptance criterion.

question: A team publishes on its MCP server a tool that takes no parameters. How should its inputSchema look according to the specification?
options: The field can be omitted: inputSchema is only required when the tool declares at least one input parameter.
It must be declared as null, which is the way to indicate that no arguments are possible.
It must be a JSON Schema object of type object; the recommended form adds additionalProperties set to false.
It must declare type object and required as an empty list, which is what the specification requires.
answer: It must be a JSON Schema object of type object; the recommended form adds additionalProperties set to false.
explanation:
The general rule is that inputSchema is part of every tool's contract and must always be a valid JSON Schema object, never null and never an absent field. For a tool with no parameters, that translates into a schema of type object with no properties, and the recommendation adds additionalProperties set to false to make clear that no extra fields are accepted. The distinction from the empty required list option is that that form also works, but it is not what the specification requires: what is mandatory is the object, not the list.

RULE: Every tool declares an inputSchema that is a valid JSON Schema object; with no parameters, type object and additionalProperties set to false.

TRAP: Treating the absence of parameters as the absence of a schema and omitting the field or declaring it as null.

TRY IT: Declare a parameterless tool with that schema on your server, list it from the client and confirm it appears with no arguments instead of failing.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools
option_feedback: The field is part of every tool's definition; omitting it leaves the definition incomplete against the specification.
The specification is explicit that inputSchema must be a valid JSON Schema object and not null.
Correct: an object of type object with no properties describes a tool with no parameters, and additionalProperties set to false is the recommended form.
An empty required list is harmless, but it is not a requirement: what is asked for is a valid JSON Schema object of type object.

question: At Northgate Labs, Megan opens a session in a repository she does not yet know and asks Claude Code to inspect the src/reports directory to understand which reports are generated there. The folder has eight files and one of them, the main generator, runs past 12,000 lines. Which TWO things describe what will happen? (Select TWO)
options: Read will return the content without line numbers, so the model does not spend context on the numbering.
Read will skip files ignored by .gitignore, just as Grep does in its searches.
An .ipynb file would come back with only its cells' code, without the outputs, to save context.
Read does not list directories: to see what is in the folder, Claude will use a shell command such as ls.
The long file will come back as a partial view and the reading has to be continued with offset and limit.
answer: Read does not list directories: to see what is in the folder, Claude will use a shell command such as ls.
The long file will come back as a partial view and the reading has to be continued with offset and limit.
explanation:
The general rule is that Read is a file tool, not a directory or search tool: it reads one file by absolute path, returns the content with line numbers and, when the file is large, delivers a partial view that is continued with offset and limit. Listing a folder is outside its scope and is handled with a shell command. The two correct statements describe independent mechanisms, one about the tool's scope and the other about content size, and both show up in the same task.

RULE: Read opens files, not folders, and large ones arrive in segments: listing the directory is the shell's job.

TRAP: Extrapolating other tools' behaviors to Read, such as respecting .gitignore or listing a directory's contents.

TRY IT: Ask Claude to read a folder and then a file of more than 2,000 lines, and watch in the transcript which tool it uses in each case.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
option_feedback: Read returns content with line numbers, which are exactly what later lets it point to where a change goes.
Grep respects .gitignore, but Read opens whatever file it is pointed at, ignored or not.
Notebooks come back with all their cells and also with their outputs, which are usually the part that explains the problem.
Correct: Read only reads files, so the directory listing arrives via a shell command.
Correct: large files come back trimmed with a partial-view notice and are read on in segments.

question: Summit Ridge Insurance evaluates with an LLM judge the responses its agent sends to policyholders. The judge's prompt says: evaluate whether this response to the policyholder is good and return {"verdict": "good"} or {"verdict": "bad"}. The judge approves 94% of responses, but on a sample of two hundred cases reviewed by analysts, agreement with the people is 55%. What is the most likely cause?
options: The judge has no rubric: with no defined dimensions and no comparable scale, its verdict measures nothing verifiable.
The judge uses the same model that generates the responses, and a model tends to approve its own output out of bias.
The evaluation needs to be repeated several times and decided by majority, because a single judge run is too unstable.
The sample reviewed by analysts is too small to compare, and at that size the observed disagreement could be noise.
answer: The judge has no rubric: with no defined dimensions and no comparable scale, its verdict measures nothing verifiable.
explanation:
The general rule is that an automated evaluator is only useful if it has an explicit criterion: a rubric with named dimensions, a defined scale and a passing threshold, so its output is comparable across cases. A prompt asking it to decide whether the response is good and return a binary label declares no dimension at all, so its 94% approval represents nothing measurable and disagreement with people is to be expected. The key distinction from repeating the evaluation is that voting attacks instability across runs, not the absence of criteria: three runs of the same vague prompt agree with each other and still fail to agree with the analysts.

RULE: Before repeating or averaging an automated judgment, check that criteria exist: without a rubric or a scale, voting three times repeats the same bias.

TRAP: Confusing instability with missing criteria: voting reduces variance, it does not invent the rubric the judge never received.

TRY IT: Rewrite the judge's prompt with three named dimensions, a 0.0 to 1.0 score and a passing threshold, rerun the same sample and compare agreement with the analysts.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests
option_feedback: Correct: the evaluation guide asks for detailed rubrics and specific outputs, and the reported practice is a single call with a score and verdict on named criteria.
A model evaluating itself is documented as viable and usually works well; the problem here is not who judges but that it was never told by what criteria.
Voting reduces variance across runs and is useful when the criterion is clear; without a rubric, repeating the evaluation just produces the same vague judgment three times.
It is good practice to start evaluating with small samples, but two hundred cases at 55% agreement is not noise: it is a clear signal that the judge is not measuring what the people are.

question: At the City of Fairview, two reviewers validate the case files the pipeline flags as doubtful, about 20% of the total. Each review takes around nine minutes because you have to go through the forty pages of the scanned file to check the twelve extracted fields, and the queue keeps growing anyway. Rachel wants to cut the time per review without taking people out of the loop. What should you do?
options: Raise the confidence threshold so fewer files reach the queue and reviewers see only the most doubtful cases.
Run a second extraction with a different prompt and send to human review only the fields where the two runs disagree.
Review a random 10% sample of the flagged files and approve the rest by default to drain the queue.
Show alongside each extracted field the quoted fragment of the file that supports it, using citations on the document.
answer: Show alongside each extracted field the quoted fragment of the file that supports it, using citations on the document.
explanation:
The general rule is that a human-review flow is designed along two axes: which cases get reviewed and how much each review costs. Here the routing already works and the problem is on the second axis, so the improvement comes from giving the person the evidence next to the data: with citations, each field arrives accompanied by the exact fragment of the document, with guaranteed pointers into what was sent and no output-token cost for the quoted text. The key distinction from a second extraction is what it attacks: comparing runs helps decide what to review, but it leaves the minutes per review untouched and doubles the extraction spend.

RULE: To speed up human review do not change its volume: put the evidence next to the data, with the verbatim quote that supports it.

TRAP: Attacking the queue's volume when the bottleneck is time per review: filtering more cases does not shorten checking a single one.

TRY IT: Time ten reviews with the current view and ten more where each field is shown next to its cited_text, and compare the average time per file.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests
option_feedback: Adjusting the routing changes how many cases come in, but not the minutes it costs to review one, which is the described bottleneck; besides, it lets doubtful cases through unchecked.
Comparing runs is a documented technique for spotting inconsistencies, but it doubles the extraction cost and does not protect against cases where both runs agree and both are wrong.

Sampling is valid for monitoring quality when per-case risk is low, but here every flagged file is already doubtful and has administrative effect: approving without looking passes the error to the citizen.

Correct: citations returns valid pointers into the source text and cited_text does not count as output tokens, so the reviewer verifies the field against its fragment instead of rereading the whole file.

question: Bluebird Goods' post-purchase coordinator launched twelve subagents to extract the data from twelve supplier invoices and has already incorporated their summaries into the main thread. Hours later, the main conversation is compacted automatically. Brandon asks what happens to those subagents' work. What should you tell him?
options: Compaction reconstructs any missing detail by reading the subagents' transcripts before summarizing.
The subagents are relaunched automatically after compaction to recover the data that was summarized.
What remains in the main thread is the summary of what each subagent returned; their full transcripts live in separate files.
Since each subagent had its own context window, the main thread never approaches the limit and is never compacted.
answer: What remains in the main thread is the summary of what each subagent returned; their full transcripts live in separate files.
explanation:
The general rule is that only the final message travels from subagent to parent: the main conversation never contained the full detail of what each subagent read, only its summary. Compaction acts on that thread and may compress those summaries further, while the subagents' transcripts are stored in their own files and do not depend on the main thread's compaction. The key distinction from the idea that isolation protects the parent is that the parent accumulates anyway: twelve summaries take up context and eventually trigger compaction.

RULE: What comes back from a subagent is the summary, not the transcript: if you will need the detail, persist it when it arrives and not once the thread has been compacted.

TRAP: Assuming compaction can recover what was never in the main thread, or that context isolation keeps the parent from filling up.

TRY IT: Launch two subagents that read long files, force a compaction in the main conversation and then ask for a detail that only existed inside what they read.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: Compaction summarizes what is in the main conversation; it does not go looking for subagent transcripts to fill in what is no longer there.
Nothing relaunches subagents as an effect of compaction: if the detail is needed again, the coordinator has to delegate again explicitly.
Correct: the parent only took in each subagent's final message and compaction may compress it further, but the subagents' transcripts are stored separately.
Isolation keeps the parent from absorbing everything the subagent read, but the summaries it does take in accumulate and the main thread fills up anyway.

question: Sophia is using Claude Code on the repository of Willow Creek Clinic's administrative system, some 4,000 files. She has been working for two hours in the same session, in which she already fixed a billing bug and answered a question about the scheduling module. She started the new task by asking it to read the entire authorizations directory. Now the /context command shows 82% of the window occupied before editing anything, and Claude makes claims about files it never opened. What are the two most likely causes? (Select TWO)
options: The project's CLAUDE.md is approaching 200 lines, and that size fills the context window from the start of the session.
The subagents return summaries of one to two thousand tokens, too long for a session already loaded with work.
Asking to read an entire directory loads files the task does not need, instead of searching and opening only those that match.
The session carries two previous tasks without clearing, so old corrections and outputs still occupy the context window.
Extended thinking is not enabled, so Claude compensates for the missing reasoning by reading more files than necessary.
answer: Asking to read an entire directory loads files the task does not need, instead of searching and opening only those that match.
The session carries two previous tasks without clearing, so old corrections and outputs still occupy the context window.
explanation:
The general rule is that context is a finite resource with diminishing returns: as the token count grows, the model's ability to recall precisely what is inside degrades, which is why curating what goes in matters. The two causes are independent and add up in the same direction: a massive preload by directory instead of searching and opening what matches, and a session accumulating two finished tasks that no longer contribute. The claims about unopened files are the classic symptom of that degradation. The key distinction from blaming the subagents is that their condensed summary is the technique that relieves the problem, not the one that causes it.

RULE: Two context leaks when exploring code: reading whole directories up front and staying in the same session after finishing another task.

TRAP: Assuming "have it read the whole module" is a good exploration instruction: the up-front load burns the window before you know which file matters.

TRY IT: Open a fresh session with /clear, ask it to search by pattern and open only matching files, and compare the percentage /context shows with the previous session's.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Two hundred lines is precisely the recommended target for CLAUDE.md; a file that size is a minimal fraction of the window and does not explain 82% occupancy.
That range is precisely the benefit of delegating: the subagent explores with its own context and returns a condensed summary, so it reduces consumption instead of increasing it.
Correct: just-in-time retrieval means navigating with lightweight identifiers and loading content when needed; preloading a whole directory burns the window before you know which file matters.
Correct: the recommendation is to use /clear between unrelated tasks, because a clean session with a good prompt outperforms a long session with accumulated corrections.
Thinking adds reasoning tokens, it does not save them, and there is no documented mechanism by which its absence triggers extra file reads.

question: At Bluebird Goods, Abigail configured at once a PreToolUse hook, deny and allow rules in the project settings, the permission mode and a can_use_tool callback. Before calling the work done she wants to know in what order a call to the tool mcp__shipping__cancel_shipment is evaluated. What is the correct order?
options: Hooks → deny rules → ask rules → permission mode → allow rules → can_use_tool callback
Permission mode → hooks → allow rules → deny rules → can_use_tool callback
Allow rules → deny rules → hooks → permission mode → can_use_tool callback
can_use_tool callback → hooks → deny rules → permission mode → allow rules
answer: Hooks → deny rules → ask rules → permission mode → allow rules → can_use_tool callback
explanation:
The general rule is that permission evaluation runs from strongest to weakest: first the hooks, which run before everything and whose denial holds even under bypassPermissions, then the deny and ask rules, then the permission mode, then the allow rules and, at the end, the can_use_tool callback. That order explains two facts that often surprise people: that a deny rule beats an auto-approval and that auto-approved tools never reach the callback. The key distinction from the intuition of putting the mode first is that the mode approves what is not already settled, not what a deny rule blocked earlier.

RULE: Hooks first, then deny and ask, then the mode, then allow and the callback last: what is denied above is not rescued by anything below.

TRAP: Assuming the permission mode is the first filter: bypassPermissions does not enable what a deny rule or a hook already blocked.

TRY IT: Add a deny rule for a tool and auto-approve that same tool in allowed_tools; ask Claude to use it and see which of the two configurations prevails.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks
option_feedback: Correct: hooks run first and their denial is absolute, deny rules are evaluated before the mode and before any allow, and the callback is left as a last resort.
It puts the mode ahead of everything, which is the usual intuition, but then bypassPermissions would approve calls a deny rule forbids, and that is not what happens.
It inverts the priority between allow and deny: if allow were evaluated first, auto-approving a tool would override its prohibition, when in fact the deny rule always wins.
The callback is not an entry filter: it is invoked only when evaluation ends in a question, and in modes like dontAsk it is never even called.

question: Prairie Press wants to upload to its claude.ai account a skill it already uses in Claude Code. Its SKILL.md frontmatter declares name, description, argument-hint, allowed-tools and disable-model-invocation. The upload fails with the message Unexpected key(s) in SKILL.md frontmatter. What should be done?
options: Remove allowed-tools from the frontmatter, because permissions belong to Claude Code and do not travel to other environments.
Rename the skill's directory so it matches the name value exactly, which is what the loader validates.
Remove argument-hint and disable-model-invocation: outside Claude Code only a few frontmatter fields are accepted.
Move the long instructions into supporting files and keep SKILL.md under 500 lines.
answer: Remove argument-hint and disable-model-invocation: outside Claude Code only a few frontmatter fields are accepted.
explanation:
The general rule is that a skill's frontmatter has two audiences: Claude Code accepts many of its own fields, while outside it only a reduced set is accepted, and any additional key causes a hard error instead of being ignored. The upload message says so literally, so the fix is removing the Claude Code-specific keys. The distinction from the most tempting option is which keys those are: allowed-tools is part of the accepted set, while argument-hint and disable-model-invocation are not.

RULE: Outside Claude Code a skill's frontmatter accepts few fields and the rest are a hard error, not ignored fields.

TRAP: Assuming anything permission-related is exclusive to Claude Code and deleting allowed-tools, which is portable.

TRY IT: Remove the Claude Code-specific fields from a copy of the SKILL.md, upload it again and confirm it is now accepted.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
option_feedback: allowed-tools is precisely one of the fields accepted outside Claude Code, so removing it solves nothing and loses useful information.
Inside Claude Code the directory name defines the command, but that is not what the external upload rejects: the error names frontmatter fields.
Correct: outside Claude Code the frontmatter accepts a reduced set of fields and any other one causes a hard error like the one in the message.
It is good progressive-disclosure practice, but the rejection has nothing to do with file size and everything to do with the frontmatter keys.

question: Riverton State University's automated tutor currently handles student questions with a single agent, and nine out of ten are specific questions about dates, prerequisites or reading lists. The team proposes turning it into a coordinator with five subagents to improve answer quality. The semester's token budget is already fixed and cannot be increased. What should be done?
options: Keep the single-agent tutor for the bulk of the work and reserve multi-agent for broad, parallelizable searches.
Turn it into a coordinator but with Haiku subagents, so the quality improvement is not paid for out of the token budget.
Turn it into a coordinator and enable prompt caching over the course material to cushion the extra cost.
Turn it into a coordinator and lower each subagent's max_tokens to bound how much each one can write.
answer: Keep the single-agent tutor for the bulk of the work and reserve multi-agent for broad, parallelizable searches.
explanation:
The general rule is to size the architecture to the shape of the task: multi-agent systems consume on the order of fifteen times more tokens than a conversation, and that cost is paid in volume, because each subagent maintains its own context and makes its own calls. That spend pays off when the work splits into broad search subtasks that can run at once, not when the job is answering a specific question a single agent resolves in a few calls. The key distinction from the idea of making subagents cheaper is that switching models lowers the price per token, but it does not reduce the number of tokens five contexts working in parallel generate.

RULE: A cheap subagent lowers the price per token, not the volume: the multi-agent multiplier is paid in tokens and only parallelizable work pays it back.

TRAP: Believing multi-agent cost is a pricing problem rather than an architecture one: the spend comes from multiplying contexts, not from the chosen model.

TRY IT: Measure the total cost of answering ten simple questions with a single agent and with a coordinator of three subagents, and compare the input tokens of each run.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Correct: a multi-agent system spends on the order of fifteen times more tokens than a chat, and that spend only pays off when the task genuinely splits into independent subtasks.
Routing work to a cheaper model is a documented cost-control technique, but the multi-agent multiplier comes from token volume, not from price per token.
Caching makes repeated prefixes cheaper and is worth having, but it does not reduce the tokens five contexts generate working at once on simple questions.
Trimming the output limits part of the spend, but a multi-agent system's cost lies mostly in the input and tool tokens of each additional context.

question: At Southbound Freight, Derek registers the rates MCP server with: claude mcp add rates --transport stdio -- npx -y rates-mcp-server --env RATES_API_KEY=abc123. The server starts, but all its calls fail with 401 because it cannot find the credential. What is the problem?
options: The --env ended up after the double dash, so it is passed as an argument to the server instead of defining the variable.
--scope project is missing: without it the server stays in local scope and does not inherit the project's variables.
A stdio server cannot receive credentials through the environment; they have to be passed with --header as in HTTP servers.
The stdio type is not declared in .mcp.json: without that field the entry is read as a remote server and ends up unauthenticated.
answer: The --env ended up after the double dash, so it is passed as an argument to the server instead of defining the variable.
explanation:
The general rule is that the double dash marks the boundary between the command's own options and the command that launches the server: everything after it is handed to the process uninterpreted. Written this way, --env RATES_API_KEY=abc123 arrives as just another argument to the server executable, which ignores it, and the variable is never defined. The distinction from the other causes is that the server did start: the transport and the registration are fine, and the only thing missing is the credential in the process's environment.

RULE: Everything after the double dash is for the server; claude mcp add's options go before the separator.

TRAP: Writing --env next to the server command because that is where the credential is needed, instead of before the double dash.

TRY IT: Re-register the server with --env before the double dash and compare the output of claude mcp get rates in both cases.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: Correct: everything following the double dash travels intact to the server process, so the option has to be written before the separator.
Scope decides where the definition is stored and who shares it, not where the process's environment variables come from.
Headers are the path for HTTP servers; a stdio server receives its credentials through environment variables.
The real rule is the opposite: an entry with a url and no type is read as stdio, and besides the transport was already given on the command line here.

question: At Summit Pay two similar tools coexist: lookup_transaction, which searches by transaction number, and search_transactions, which searches by date range. Both have a one-line description and the agent picks the wrong one about one time in five. The team proposes moving all lookup tools to a specialized subagent and leaving the main agent with only the conversation. What is most likely to happen?
options: The hit rate will rise because each agent will see fewer tools and choosing between them becomes simpler.
The subagent will keep confusing them and latency and tokens will be added: the cause is in the descriptions.
The main agent will return a permission error because the Agent tool is not in allowed_tools.
Cost will drop because the main agent's context no longer carries those two tools' schemas.
answer: The subagent will keep confusing them and latency and tokens will be added: the cause is in the descriptions.
explanation:
The general rule is that tool design is part of the architecture: a poor description sends the agent down the wrong path, and that flaw follows the tools to whichever agent receives them. Moving the two confusable tools to a subagent does not separate them from each other, so the ambiguity remains intact and on top of it you pay the cost of delegating, because the subagent starts with a fresh context that has to gather information from scratch. The key distinction is when splitting tools does work: when the confusion happens between distinct families and the split leaves each agent with a non-overlapping set.

RULE: Before adding agents, fix the descriptions: splitting tools only helps if the split separates exactly the ones the model confuses.

TRAP: Treating a tool-interface problem as an architecture one: delegating moves the ambiguity somewhere else, it does not resolve it.

TRY IT: Rewrite both descriptions with three or four sentences saying when to use each and when not to, and rerun twenty ambiguous requests counting the hits.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/implement-tool-use
option_feedback: Splitting tools across agents helps when the confusion is between distinct families, but these two end up together inside the same subagent and keep competing with each other.
Correct: a poor description sends the agent down the wrong path and that flaw travels with the tools; the documented repair is writing descriptions of at least three or four sentences.
If you do not auto-approve the Agent tool you get a permission prompt, not a confusion between tools, and that is solved with one line of configuration.
The parent's context is relieved, but each delegation adds a new context with its own calls: on the whole you spend more, not less.

question: Willow Creek Clinic uses strict tool use on the record_authorization tool. Its schema has eighteen fields, fourteen of them optional, several declared as unions with null, and objects nested four levels deep. Every time the team changes the schema, the first call takes noticeably longer, and now they want to add new fields without making grammar compilation heavier. They cannot drop strict from this tool because the billing system depends on its types. Which two changes reduce the schema's complexity? (Select TWO)
options: Add a description to each property so the model better understands what each schema field means.
Make required the fields that always have a sensible value and ask the model to write that default value.
Declare minItems and maxLength on the arrays and strings to bound what the grammar has to generate.
Replace the optional fields with unions with null, so every field is always present in the output.
Flatten the nested objects and keep strict only on this tool, without marking it on the simpler tools in the same request.
answer: Make required the fields that always have a sensible value and ask the model to write that default value.
Flatten the nested objects and keep strict only on this tool, without marking it on the simpler tools in the same request.
explanation:
The general rule is that the structured-outputs grammar is compiled from the schema, and its cost grows with whatever it leaves open: each optional field multiplies part of the state space, unions are especially expensive and deep nesting compounds both effects. The two correct measures are independent: one reduces optionality by turning it into an explicit default value, and the other reduces structure and limits strict's scope to the tool that really needs it. The key distinction from unions with null is that they are a valid, supported way to model nulls, but precisely the one the documentation flags as most expensive: using them to eliminate optionals simplifies nothing.

RULE: To simplify a grammar: fewer optional fields, fewer unions and less nesting, and strict only on the tools that really need it.

TRAP: Swapping optionals for unions with null believing it simplifies: unions cost as much as or more than the optional field they replace.

TRY IT: Measure the first call's latency with the current schema, convert four optionals into required with a default value, flatten one level of nesting and measure again.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use
option_feedback: Per-property descriptions improve the quality of what the model fills in and do not even invalidate the grammar cache, but they do not reduce the state space the grammar has to compile.
Correct: the guide notes that each optional parameter multiplies part of the grammar's state space, and recommends exactly this conversion when a sensible default exists.
maxLength is not supported and minItems only accepts the values 0 and 1, so the schema would be rejected with a 400 instead of simplified.
Unions are supported and seem to simplify, but the documentation flags them as especially costly because they generate exponential compilation cost: you trade one problem for an equal or worse one.
Correct: the guide asks you to simplify nested structures, because deep objects with optional fields compound the complexity, and to mark as strict only the critical tools.

question: In Riverton State University's research system, a PreToolUse hook blocks the publish_summary tool when the synthesis subagent has not yet attached the source citations, and returns as its reason the word denied. Since that change, those subagents try other tools, go in circles and exhaust their turn limit without delivering the summary, even though the citations were available. What is the most likely cause?
options: The subagent does not receive the hook's decision, so it retries blindly until it runs out of available turns.
The block's reason comes back to the model as a tool result: if it does not say what to do, the subagent tries alternative paths.
The tool should be removed from the subagent's tools list, because a hook cannot stop the model from choosing it over and over.
The subagent's turn limit was set too low for a task that includes attaching the citations before publishing the summary.
answer: The block's reason comes back to the model as a tool result: if it does not say what to do, the subagent tries alternative paths.
explanation:
The general rule is that, in a system with agents, a block is not an invisible event: the denial and its reason reach the model as the call's result, and from there the model typically tries another approach or reports that it cannot continue. That is why the reason's text is the recovery interface: if it says only denied, the subagent has nothing to correct with and explores alternatives until it burns its turns. The key distinction from removing the tool from its definition is the nature of the block: restricting the tool set is right when the access should never exist, while a conditional permission calls for a message naming the missing condition.

RULE: The reason a hook returns is read by the model: write it as an instruction for what to do next, not as a rejection label.

TRAP: Assuming a block explains itself: the model receives the denial as a tool result and, with no exit indicated, tries any other path.

TRY IT: Change the hook's reason to a sentence saying what is missing and what to do next, repeat ten runs and compare how many end up publishing the summary.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls
option_feedback: It does receive it: the hook's decision and its reason come back to the model as the call's result, which is exactly why the subagent changes strategy instead of repeating the same tool.
Correct: the rejection reason arrives as the tool's result and the model usually tries another approach; a reason telling it to attach the citations and publish again closes the loop.
Removing the tool is right when the subagent should never have it, but here the block is conditional: it is expected to publish the summary, just after attaching the citations.
Raising the limit would give it more turns to keep guessing; the problem is not how much room it has, but that nobody told it which condition to meet.

question: Prairie Press moves its style guide to each person's personal folder and references it from the project's CLAUDE.md with an import pointing to a path under the home directory, outside the repository. Sophia opens the project for the first time after the change. What will happen?
options: The import counts as external: the first time it asks for approval and, if she rejects it, external imports are disabled.
It loads without asking, just like imports written in the user's CLAUDE.md, which never show that dialog.
It does not load: imports only resolve paths relative to the file containing them and never leave the repository.
It loads, but only when Claude reads a file matching the glob the style guide declares.
answer: The import counts as external: the first time it asks for approval and, if she rejects it, external imports are disabled.
explanation:
The general rule is that an import written in a project memory file that resolves outside the working directory is treated as external: the first time an approval dialog appears and, if someone rejects it, external imports are permanently disabled for that person. The distinction from the most tempting alternative is not in the imported path but in the file that writes it: user-scope files load their imports without a dialog, project files do not. That is why the same line behaves differently depending on where it lives.

RULE: An external import is approved once and only when a project file writes it; user-scope ones do not ask.

TRAP: Looking at where the import points instead of which file contains it, which is what decides whether the dialog appears.

TRY IT: Add to your project CLAUDE.md an import to a file in your personal folder, open the session and watch the dialog; then write the same import in your user CLAUDE.md.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: Correct: an import in a project file that resolves outside the working directory shows a dialog the first time, and rejecting it disables them permanently.
That is true for user-scope files, which is why it is tempting, but here the import is written in the project's CLAUDE.md.
Resolution relative to the file containing the import is real, but paths under the home directory are contemplated and do resolve.
That conditional loading belongs to rules with paths frontmatter; imports are expanded when the session starts.

question: Southbound Freight's nightly agent recalculates fleet assignments and writes them to the legacy system through an MCP. It runs unattended and, the next morning, a supervisor reviews and approves the changes from the internal console. Today the apply_changes tool writes directly, and there was already a night when it applied a hundred and twenty reassignments nobody wanted. What should you do?
options: Instruct in the system prompt that the agent always show the full change plan and wait for sign-off before applying it.
Run the nightly session in plan mode so the agent investigates and proposes changes without writing anything to the legacy system.
Split the operation into two tools: one computes and returns the plan, and another applies it with the identifier of an approved plan.
Register a PreToolUse hook that returns ask before every write, so a person confirms each change.
answer: Split the operation into two tools: one computes and returns the plan, and another applies it with the identifier of an approved plan.
explanation:
The general rule is that what must not be able to happen is made impossible by design, not improbable by instruction. Separating computation from application turns approval into data the write tool requires: without an approved plan's identifier no write is possible, and the supervisor reviews a concrete artifact in the morning instead of trusting that the agent stopped. The key distinction from plan mode and from a hook that asks lies in who is present: both mechanisms assume a person in the session approving in the moment, and this run is unattended.

RULE: Design tools so the dangerous action requires the approval as an argument: what cannot be asked for wrongly is not asked for wrongly.

TRAP: Choosing plan mode or a per-call confirmation for an unattended run: both wait for a person who is not there that night.

TRY IT: Split a write tool into compute_plan and apply_plan, make the second reject any identifier that did not come from the first, and ask the agent to apply changes without computing first.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions
option_feedback: An instruction lowers the error's frequency, but it does not prevent it: what must hold without exception is enforced in code or in tool design, never by prompt.
Plan mode is right when there is a person in the session approving the plan before proceeding, and it is designed for file edits; in an unattended run there is nobody to approve.
