Independently, a subagent starts with a fresh context and the only thing that travels from the parent is the Agent prompt string, so shared inputs are re-fetched by every worker unless the parent writes them into each prompt. The fix is smaller batches with the shared data in the brief, not a bigger dispatch.

RULE: Dispatch subagents in batches and put the shared data in each brief: nothing you already fetched travels to a subagent on its own.

TRAP: Reading concurrent subagent limit reached as a crash: it arrives as a normal tool result, so the run carries on with silent gaps.

TRY IT: Ask an agent to spawn thirty subagents at once and read the Agent tool results one by one: count how many carry the limit message instead of a report.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hosting
option_feedback: Correct: there is a documented limit on how many subagents run at once, and past it the Agent call returns the limit message as an ordinary tool result, which is why the run continues with holes in it.
A subagent never inherits the parent tool results, compaction or not: it starts with a fresh context and the reloading happens on every run.
Correct: the only content that crosses from parent to subagent is the prompt of the Agent call, so shared data such as the fleet list has to be placed there or each worker rediscovers it.
Each subagent has its own context window, which is the point of delegating; a shared window would make parallel research impossible rather than merely wasteful.
The message is produced by the runtime that spawns subagents, not by an MCP server; a server refusing a connection surfaces as a tool error inside one subagent, not as a failed spawn.

question: Willow Creek Clinic has just automated the extraction of authorization forms and wants to know where human review is still needed. Rachel proposes waiting until the administrative team has hand-labelled 500 forms so that the first measurement is statistically solid, and meanwhile the pipeline runs unmeasured. Aaron wants to start measuring this week. What does the documented practice recommend?
options: Start this week with a few dozen real forms, graded automatically where the answer is checkable, and grow the set over time.
Wait for the 500 hand-labelled forms, on the grounds that a small sample cannot support any decision about where review is needed.
Ask the reviewers to score a sample of outputs from one to five on overall quality and track the weekly average.
Ask the model to grade its own extractions and route to humans only the ones it grades below its usual score.
answer: Start this week with a few dozen real forms, graded automatically where the answer is checkable, and grow the set over time.
explanation:
The general rule for evaluations is to be task-specific, automate whatever can be automated and start immediately: the documentation recommends small-scale testing right away with a few examples and states that more questions with slightly lower-signal automated grading is better than fewer hand-graded questions. Dates, amounts and identifier formats have a verifiable answer, so they can be graded by code over dozens of forms today and thousands later. The tempting alternative is to wait for a large hand-labelled set, which applies the most expensive grading method before anyone knows which fields actually fail.

RULE: Measure this week with what you have: a small automated eval that exists beats a large hand-graded one that does not.

TRAP: Confusing statistical comfort with usefulness: waiting for the perfect sample leaves the pipeline unmeasured in the meantime.

TRY IT: Pick twenty forms whose correct values you already know, write a script that compares five checkable fields, and run it against today's pipeline before adding a single new example.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system
option_feedback: Correct: the guidance is to start small-scale testing right away with a few examples, to be task-specific and to automate grading where possible, since more questions with slightly lower-signal automated grading beat fewer hand-graded ones.
Waiting buys precision at the price of running blind for weeks, and the documented advice prioritizes volume and immediacy over a perfect first sample.
A one-to-five human score is flexible but slow and expensive, and a single overall number does not say which field or which kind of case needs review.
Self-grading is useful once it has been checked against ground truth; as the only gate it decides where review happens using the same judgment that produced the error.

question: To stop Claude from finishing a task with red tests, Northgate Labs adds a Stop hook that runs the suite and exits with code 2 whenever it fails, writing "tests still failing" to stderr. On a stubborn refactor the suite keeps failing and Claude keeps trying. What happens as the session continues?
options: The loop continues indefinitely, since an exit code of 2 on Stop always prevents Claude from finishing.
After eight blocks in a row without progress, Claude Code overrides the hook and the turn ends.
The hook stops blocking as soon as Claude reports that it is unable to fix the remaining failures.
Exit code 2 is not honored on Stop, so the hook only logs its message and Claude finishes the task.
answer: After eight blocks in a row without progress, Claude Code overrides the hook and the turn ends.
explanation:
The general rule is that a Stop hook is a verification gate, not an unlimited guarantee: it keeps Claude from ending the turn while the check fails, and Claude Code overrides it after eight consecutive blocks without progress so that a session cannot loop forever. That makes the content of each block decisive, because the reason written to stderr is what Claude reads before its next attempt, and a bare failure message spends the eight retries on the same wrong idea. The alternative that sounds right is an endless loop, which the cap exists to rule out.

RULE: A Stop hook buys a bounded number of retries: write a reason that tells Claude what to change, because after eight blocks the gate gives way.

TRAP: Assuming an enforcement hook can hold the loop open forever, and therefore not investing in the message it returns.

TRY IT: Add a Stop hook that always exits 2 with a reason, run a short task, and count how many times Claude retries before the session finishes anyway.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices
option_feedback: Exit 2 does prevent Claude from stopping, but not without end: the docs describe a cap precisely so that a session cannot be trapped by its own gate.
Correct: the Stop hook is a gate with a loop cap, so it buys a bounded number of retries and the reason it writes has to tell Claude what to change.
A hook does not read Claude's explanation: only the hook's own exit code and JSON output decide, and a claim of impossibility does not change the suite result.
Exit 2 is honored on Stop and prevents Claude from stopping; the event where it is not honored is PermissionRequest, which decides through its own JSON object.

question: Prairie Yield Analytics closes every night with an agent that pulls yield figures, builds a report and publishes it to the client portal through a publish_report tool. Publishing is irreversible and the client sees whatever goes up. Twice this month the agent published a report whose totals had not been validated, even though the system prompt states that validation comes first. Brandon has to make the order impossible to skip. Which sequence should he build?
options: Keep one query with every tool available → repeat the required order in the tool descriptions → add a reminder about validation to CLAUDE.md → review what was published each morning
Run the analysis in a query whose tools do not include publishing → validate the totals in your code → publish in a second query that adds publish_report → store the run id next to the file
Keep one query with every tool available → register a PostToolUse hook on publish_report that recomputes the totals → let the hook flag the reports that do not match → correct them in the portal
Keep one query with every tool available → ask the agent to print its plan before acting → have an analyst approve that plan by hand → let the run continue through to publication
answer: Run the analysis in a query whose tools do not include publishing → validate the totals in your code → publish in a second query that adds publish_report → store the run id next to the file
explanation:
The general rule is that a mandatory order is enforced by code, and the cheapest code is the tool list itself: what is not in the session cannot be called on any turn, at any temperature, however the prompt is worded. Splitting the night job into an analysis query without the publishing tool and a publishing query that only starts after your own validation passes turns the ordering into a property of the pipeline, and passing the run id forward keeps the two stages linked for the audit. The closest wrong answer adds a PostToolUse hook, which is the right mechanism at the wrong moment: it can only describe an action that already happened.

RULE: Enforce an order by what exists, not by what you ask for: the irreversible tool appears only in the stage that runs after the gate.

TRAP: Assuming that listing a tool and telling the agent to use it last constrains the order: an available tool can be called on any turn.

TRY IT: Run the same prompt twice, once with publish_report in the tool list and once without it, and confirm that the second run cannot publish even when you ask it to.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/custom-tools https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Tool descriptions and CLAUDE.md are advice the model follows most of the time, which is why the failure is rare rather than absent, and a morning review arrives after the client has already read the report.

Correct: a tool that is not in the session cannot be called at all, so the order is enforced by availability instead of obedience, the code between the two queries is the gate that decides when publishing becomes possible, and the run id makes the handoff auditable.
PostToolUse runs after the tool has executed, so the hook would notice the bad report only once it was public; an irreversible action has to be checked before the call, not after it.
Approving a plan is a reasonable control for a one-off task, but it approves an intention: nothing prevents the agent from publishing later in the same run when validation turns out badly.

question: Riverton State University now has two versions of its tutor: one agent that does everything itself and a coordinator that splits the work across three subagents. Sophia has to decide which decomposition goes to production, and the team wants an answer this week rather than after a semester of usage. Which order should she follow?
options: Ship the coordinator version to every course at once → watch the support tickets for a month → keep it if the complaints do not go up → write a rubric afterwards
Assemble about twenty representative questions → score both versions with a model judge and a written rubric → read a sample of the runs by hand → adopt the winner
Write the ideal step by step path for each question → compare both versions against those prescribed steps → keep the one whose runs match the path → sample the answers later
Collect several hundred questions before measuring anything → wait until every department agrees on the rubric → run the whole set once → adopt the winner
answer: Assemble about twenty representative questions → score both versions with a model judge and a written rubric → read a sample of the runs by hand → adopt the winner
explanation:
The general rule is that a decomposition is a hypothesis, so you test it early, cheaply and on results. Anthropic recommends starting evaluation immediately with small samples of around twenty queries, because the effect sizes of early agent changes are large enough to see, then scoring with a model judge against an explicit rubric and keeping humans in the loop for a sample of runs. The distinction that decides this item is what gets graded: agents reach the same correct answer by different valid paths, so the end state is what you compare, never the sequence of steps you imagined in advance.

RULE: Test a decomposition on a small sample and on its end state: about twenty cases, a rubric a model can apply, and a human reading some runs.

TRAP: Grading the steps instead of the result: two agents reach the same correct answer by different valid routes.

TRY IT: Take twenty past student questions, score both versions with a rubric of accuracy, completeness and tool efficiency, then read five runs yourself and note what the score missed.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
option_feedback: Production is the slowest and most expensive place to learn, and ticket counts move for many reasons at once; the documented advice is to start measuring immediately on a small sample.

Correct: early agent changes produce large effect sizes, so roughly twenty cases already separate two designs, a model judge with a rubric makes the scoring repeatable, and a human pass catches what the judge misses.
Grading the path is the classic mistake with agents: two runs can take completely different valid routes to the same correct answer, so the score would punish good runs.
A large set and a perfect rubric are not free, and they delay the only question that matters now, which is whether splitting the tutor into subagents helps at all.

question: Two engineers at Summit Ridge Insurance are migrating the policy engine over several days with Claude Code. Each morning they open a new session and spend the first hour re-explaining which modules are already migrated, which tests pass and which decisions were taken the day before. What is the best way to stop paying that hour every day?
options: Keep a progress file in the repository with state, decisions and open items, and have Claude read it first and update it at the end.
Keep a single session open for the whole migration and rely on compaction to carry every detail from one day to the next.
Paste the transcript of the last two days into the first message of each session so that nothing from the earlier work is lost.
Ask Claude to re-read every migrated module at the start of each session and infer the current state of the work from the code itself.
answer: Keep a progress file in the repository with state, decisions and open items, and have Claude read it first and update it at the end.
explanation:
The general rule for work that spans sessions is that anything which must survive a new context window has to live outside it, in a file. The documented multi-session pattern is a progress log plus a checklist that the agent reads before starting and updates before finishing, which turns an hour of re-explaining into a single read. Compaction is the alternative for one long conversation, not across days, and it produces a summary, so precise state such as which tests pass is exactly what it keeps worst.

RULE: What must survive a new session goes in a file the agent reads first and updates last, never in the conversation alone.

TRAP: Expecting a summary to hold precise state: compaction keeps the thread, not the checklist.

TRY IT: Write a progress file with migrated modules, pending items and decisions, start a fresh session that reads only that file, and time how long it takes to resume the work.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents
option_feedback: Correct: structured note-taking persists state outside the context window, and the documented multi-session pattern is exactly this, a progress log the agent reads before starting and updates before finishing.
Compaction keeps one long conversation alive, but it summarizes, and details that must survive precisely belong in a file rather than in a summary.
A transcript is the least curated form of context: it fills the window with tool output and dead ends, and recall degrades as the token count grows.
Models are good at discovering state from the filesystem and that is a useful complement, but code does not record why a decision was taken or what is still pending.

question: The extraction service at Willow Creek Clinic has always closed its requests with an assistant message containing only the character { so that the answer starts as JSON. After moving to a current model, those same requests fail with a 400 error. The team still needs the same JSON object out of every call. What should they do?
options: Replace the prefill with output_config.format and a JSON schema, which constrains the response to the shape they need.
Move the opening brace into the system prompt and ask the model to continue from it in its first line.
Keep the prefill and add a stop sequence so the trailing text after the JSON object is cut off.
Keep the prefill and retry the request on a model released before the change, since the shape cannot be guaranteed otherwise.
answer: Replace the prefill with output_config.format and a JSON schema, which constrains the response to the shape they need.
explanation:
The general rule is to use the feature designed for the job: structured outputs exist to constrain a response to a schema, and the documentation states that prefilled assistant messages on the last turn are no longer supported on the newer models and return a 400 error, recommending structured outputs or system-prompt instructions instead. Replacing the brace with output_config.format keeps the guarantee and removes the failure. The tempting alternative is to reproduce the trick somewhere else, in the system prompt or with a stop sequence, but neither constrains the output and neither fixes a request that is now rejected outright.

RULE: The opening-brace prefill is gone on current models: constrain JSON with output_config.format and a schema instead.

TRAP: Reproducing a removed technique in another field: an instruction to start with a brace is advice, while a schema is a constraint.

TRY IT: Send one request with a trailing assistant message to a current model and read the 400 error, then send the same request with output_config.format and compare the output.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs
option_feedback: Correct: prefilled assistant messages are no longer supported on the newer models, and the documented replacement is structured outputs, which constrains the response to a schema instead of pushing it with a partial turn.
An instruction in the system prompt is a request, not a constraint, and it brings back the preamble and trailing-text problems the prefill was hiding.
Stop sequences trim what comes after the JSON, but the request itself is now rejected with a 400 before any generation happens.
Pinning a pipeline to an older model to keep a removed feature trades every later improvement for a technique the documentation has already replaced.

question: Prairie Yield Analytics gives its reporting agent an in-process tool, load_parcel_series. When a parcel has no readings the handler raises an exception. Rachel expects the run to fail fast; instead the agent carries on, calls the same tool again with the same parcel two or three times, and finally writes a report that quietly leaves that parcel out. The logs show the raw exception text arriving as the result of each of those calls. What explains the behaviour and what is the fix?
options: The agent loop treats a handler exception as a transient failure and retries it on its own, so the handler needs its own retry wrapper with a backoff around it.
The raised exception never reached the model at all, so the agent had no result to read; returning the error as a plain text block would let it react.
An exception aborts the current turn but not the run, so the fix is a lower turn cap that stops the agent before it repeats the same call.
An uncaught exception comes back as an error result with the raw message, which guides nothing: catch it and return an error result that says what to do next.
answer: An uncaught exception comes back as an error result with the raw message, which guides nothing: catch it and return an error result that says what to do next.
explanation:
The general rule is that a tool error is a message addressed to the model, not a failure of the runtime. An uncaught exception in a handler is converted into an error result carrying the raw exception text, and the agent loop keeps going, so the only thing steering the recovery is what that text says. A stack trace says nothing actionable, which is why the agent retries and then improvises by dropping the parcel. Catching the error and returning an instructive result, saying what happened and what to do instead, is the documented practice. The tempting answer is to add retries, which treats a deterministic empty-data case as if it were a transient network failure.

RULE: A tool error is a message to the model: catch it, mark the result as an error and write what happened and what to do next.

TRAP: Expecting an exception inside a tool to stop the run: the loop turns it into an error result and the agent improvises from whatever text it contains.

TRY IT: Raise an exception inside a custom tool and watch what the agent does next, then catch it and return an error result with a clear instruction and compare the two runs.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/custom-tools https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls
option_feedback: The SDK does retry transient API failures such as rate limits with backoff, but a tool handler exception is not one of them: here the model is choosing to call again, because nothing told it the call was pointless.
It did reach the model, which is why the raw text shows up in the logs as the result of the call; the issue is not that the message is missing but that it says nothing the agent can act on.
A lower cap would only shorten the run and hide the missing parcel: the report would still be wrong, and the agent still would not know why the parcel failed.

Correct: a handler error does not stop the agent loop, so recovery depends entirely on the message; catching the exception and returning an error result that says the parcel has no readings and should be recorded as missing is what lets the agent do the right thing.

question: A repository still carries an old .claude/commands/deploy.md from before custom commands were merged into skills, and someone has since added .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md. What happens when a developer types /deploy?
options: The skill runs: both files define /deploy and the skill takes precedence when the names collide.
The command file runs, because the older .claude/commands/ format keeps its priority for compatibility.
Neither runs: a duplicate name disables both entries until one of the two files is removed.
Both appear in the menu, as /deploy for the command and /deploy:skill for the skill.
answer: The skill runs: both files define /deploy and the skill takes precedence when the names collide.
explanation:
The general rule is that custom slash commands have been merged into skills: a file at .claude/commands/deploy.md and a skill at .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy and behave the same way, and existing command files keep working. When the two names collide the skill is the one that runs, which is also why the docs recommend writing new work as a skill, since only skills support supporting files next to the instructions. Both wrong answers assume the older format is either privileged or broken, and it is neither.

RULE: Commands and skills are one mechanism: the same name from both sources runs the skill, and new work belongs in .claude/skills/.

TRAP: Assuming that the older .claude/commands/ format either wins by seniority or has stopped working.

TRY IT: Create a command file and a skill with the same name, give each a different first line, type the command and see which body Claude loads.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
option_feedback: Correct: commands and skills are one mechanism now, and the docs state that the skill is the one that runs when a skill and a command file share a name.
Existing command files do keep working, which is the compatibility guarantee; the tie between the two is nevertheless resolved in favor of the skill.
A duplicate name is resolved rather than rejected; Claude Code picks a winner instead of dropping the command from the menu.
There is no such suffix: subdirectories under commands produce names like /frontend:component, and a skill keeps the plain name of its directory.

question: Prairie Press's repository has a CLAUDE.md at the root with the build and test commands, and a second one at packages/cms/CLAUDE.md with the conventions of that package. Victoria starts a session from the repository root and asks a question about the release process. Which memory files are in context for that first answer?
options: Both files, since Claude Code concatenates every CLAUDE.md found anywhere in the repository at launch.
Only packages/cms/CLAUDE.md, because the most specific file replaces the broader one.
Neither one, until she references a file with an @ mention that pulls the memory in.
Only the root CLAUDE.md; the one in packages/cms loads when Claude reads a file in that directory.
answer: Only the root CLAUDE.md; the one in packages/cms loads when Claude reads a file in that directory.
explanation:
The general rule is that CLAUDE.md discovery has two halves. At launch Claude Code loads the memory files from the working directory and every directory above it, concatenated from the filesystem root down, while files that live in subdirectories below the working directory are included later, when Claude reads files in those subdirectories. A first answer about the release process therefore sees the root file only. The tempting answer is that the nested file overrides the root one, but memory files are additive: they are concatenated rather than overriding each other.

RULE: Upwards from the working directory memory loads at launch; downwards into subdirectories it loads when Claude reads files there.

TRAP: Reading a nested CLAUDE.md as an override that is always active, instead of an addition that arrives when Claude works in that folder.

TRY IT: Put a distinctive line in a nested CLAUDE.md, run /context at the start of a session, then ask Claude to read a file in that folder and run /context again.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: Concatenation is right, but the launch sweep covers the working directory and the directories above it, not the whole tree underneath.
Memory files never replace each other, they are concatenated from the filesystem root down, and nothing makes a nested file load before Claude works there.
The root file loads automatically at the start of the session; @ mentions add files to the conversation and are not what activates project memory.
Correct: files above the working directory load at launch, while files in subdirectories are pulled in on demand as Claude works there.

question: Bluebird Goods writes 4,000 product descriptions a month. A proposal on the table replaces the current single call with a three-stage pipeline: one instance drafts, a second scores the draft against a rubric and a third rewrites it. A pilot on 200 products raised the editors' acceptance rate from 91 to 93 percent and multiplied token use by about fifteen. Budget is tight and there is no quality crisis. What should Derek decide?
options: Adopt the pipeline and lower effort on the drafting stage so that the extra calls stay inside the current budget.
Adopt the pipeline but cap the loop at one review round, since evaluator-optimizer only pays off with several iterations.
Keep the single call and invest in retrieval and better in-context examples, adding stages only if the evals demand it.
Adopt the pipeline and run it as a nightly batch, since the discount offsets most of the extra tokens it consumes.
answer: Keep the single call and invest in retrieval and better in-context examples, adding stages only if the evals demand it.
explanation:
The general rule from the effective-agents guidance is to find the simplest solution that works and to add complexity only when it buys something: optimizing a single call with retrieval and good in-context examples is usually enough, and agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance. Here the measured trade is roughly fifteen times the tokens for two points of acceptance on a workload with no quality crisis, so the pipeline is not earning its price. The closest alternative, capping the review loop, is the right instinct aimed at the wrong question: evaluator-optimizer belongs where criteria are clear and iterative refinement provides measurable value.

RULE: Add an instance only when the measurement asks for it: the first optimization of a single call is retrieval plus better examples.

TRAP: Buying an architecture for the pilot's best number without pricing it: fifteen times the tokens for two points is a cost decision, not a quality one.

TRY IT: Rerun the same 200 products through a single call with four strong examples and a retrieval step, then compare acceptance and token use against the three-stage pilot.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system
option_feedback: Lower effort does cut cost per token, but it cannot absorb a fifteenfold rise in tokens for two points of acceptance, and the architecture is what is being questioned.

The cap is sensible engineering and the pilot already measured a single round; evaluator-optimizer earns its cost when criteria are clear and refinement adds measurable value, which two points barely show.
Correct: the guidance is to find the simplest solution possible and to increase complexity only when needed, since optimizing single calls with retrieval and in-context examples is usually enough.
The batch discount halves the price of tokens the design did not need to spend, and it adds delay to a workload that was never the bottleneck.

question: A tutoring agent at Riverton State University holds sessions that run for hours and span several days per student. Sophia needs the agent to keep working past the context limit without losing the diagnosis it made in the first hour or the study plan it agreed with the student. Which two measures does the documentation support? (Select TWO)
options: Raise max_tokens so that each response has room and the conversation reaches the limit later.
Enable the memory tool so the agent records the diagnosis and the plan in files it checks before each task.
Set the compaction trigger to 20,000 input tokens so the history is summarized long before anything is at risk.
Rely on the one-million-token window and keep the whole history, since nothing is lost while everything still fits.
Enable server-side compaction and pass the returned compaction block back on every later request.
answer: Enable the memory tool so the agent records the diagnosis and the plan in files it checks before each task.
Enable server-side compaction and pass the returned compaction block back on every later request.
explanation:
The general rule is that a long-running agent needs two different things: a way to keep the conversation going when the window fills, and a place to keep what must not be summarized away. Server-side compaction covers the first, provided the compaction block is passed back on every later request, since all content before it is ignored; the memory tool covers the second, because its files live in your application and Claude checks them before starting a task. The distractors get the mechanism right and a detail wrong: the compaction trigger has a documented minimum of 50,000 input tokens, and a larger window does not stop recall from degrading as it fills.

RULE: Compaction keeps the conversation alive and memory files keep the facts; send the compaction block back or the earlier history is gone.

TRAP: Configuring compaction below its documented 50,000-token minimum, or trusting a big window to preserve early detail.

TRY IT: Run a session with compaction enabled and confirm the compaction block in the response, then send the next request without it and check which earlier facts the agent can still name.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool
option_feedback: max_tokens caps the length of one response; it does not change how much history fits, and a longer answer actually consumes the window faster.
Correct: memory files live in your application outside the context window, Claude checks its memory directory before starting a task, and it is told to assume the context may be reset at any moment.
Compaction is the right mechanism, but the trigger value must be at least 50,000 input tokens, so this configuration is rejected.
More context is not automatically better: accuracy and recall degrade as the window fills, and this session is meant to survive past the limit anyway.
Correct: server-side compaction is the primary strategy for long-running conversations, and the compaction block must be sent back on subsequent requests because everything before it is ignored.

question: The prompt that reads authorization letters at Willow Creek Clinic is already long, and the team has agreed not to add more tokens to it than strictly necessary. Two of the proposals below are small, documented ways to make the model follow the intent of the instructions more closely. Which two? (Select TWO)
options: Add one sentence of role in the system prompt, stating what kind of reader the model is.
Add twelve more examples of correct letters at the end of the prompt so that the pattern becomes unmistakable.
Write the two most important rules in capital letters and prefix them with the word CRITICAL.
Explain briefly why an instruction matters, so the model can generalize it to cases the prompt never lists.
List the fifteen mistakes seen in production and instruct the model to avoid every one of them.
answer: Add one sentence of role in the system prompt, stating what kind of reader the model is.
Explain briefly why an instruction matters, so the model can generalize it to cases the prompt never lists.
explanation:
The general rule is that precision comes from clear, well-motivated instructions rather than from volume or emphasis. A single role sentence in the system prompt focuses behavior for the use case, and one line of motivation lets the model generalize a rule to cases nobody enumerated, which is exactly what a list of prohibitions cannot do. The distractors are all real techniques pushed past their point: more examples of the same kind, capitalized emphasis that the guidance now asks you to dial back, and negative framing where positive framing is recommended.

RULE: Two cheap lines beat a long list: say who the model is, and say why the instruction matters.

TRAP: Treating emphasis and volume as precision: capital letters and longer prohibition lists add tokens without adding criteria.

TRY IT: Add the role sentence and one line of motivation to your prompt, rerun thirty letters and compare the errors against the version without them.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: Correct: setting a role in the system prompt focuses behavior and tone for the use case, and the documentation notes that even a single sentence makes a difference.
Examples help, but twelve more of the same kind is the opposite of the agreed constraint and risks teaching an unintended pattern; three to five diverse ones do the work.
That is the aggressive phrasing the current guidance asks you to dial back: normal wording works, and shouted rules tend to cause overtriggering elsewhere.
Correct: providing the motivation behind an instruction helps Claude understand the goal, and the documentation says it is smart enough to generalize from the explanation.
Telling the model what not to do is the documented anti-pattern; describing the behavior you want instead is both shorter and more effective.

question: Summit Pay exposes an internal MCP server over HTTPS with twelve tools, four of which move money. A read-only assistant that answers support questions reaches it through the Messages API MCP connector, and the team must make those four tools unreachable for the assistant without deploying a second server. What should they configure?
options: Instruct the assistant in its system prompt to never call the four write tools under any circumstances.
Send tool_choice none so the model cannot use tools that it should not be calling in this assistant.
In the MCP toolset for that server, disable tools by default and enable only the eight read tools.
Give the assistant a separate API key whose scope on the MCP server excludes the four write tools.
answer: In the MCP toolset for that server, disable tools by default and enable only the eight read tools.
explanation:
The general rule is that what an agent must not do belongs in configuration rather than in wording. The Messages API MCP connector separates the server connection from the toolset that governs it: disabling tools in the default configuration and listing the ones you want produces an allowlist, while disabling specific tools produces a denylist, which the documentation recommends when building read-only assistants. The closest wrong answer is tool_choice none, a real setting that removes every tool from the turn instead of removing four from the catalog.

RULE: Shape an MCP tool catalog in the toolset configuration, disabling by default and enabling what you need, rather than asking the model to abstain.

TRAP: Reaching for tool_choice, which decides whether tools are used in a turn, when the question is which tools exist for the assistant at all.

TRY IT: Point a test request at an MCP server with the default configuration disabled and two tools enabled, then ask for something only a disabled tool could do and watch the model work without it.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector
option_feedback: A prompt instruction lowers the frequency of an unwanted call but cannot make a tool unreachable, and the connector offers a configuration switch that does.
That switch turns off every tool, including the eight the assistant needs; it is the setting for a turn that should use no tools at all.
Correct: an allowlist built from a disabled default configuration plus per-tool entries is the documented way to expose a subset of a server.
Server-side authorization is a sound second layer, but it lives outside the connector and does not answer how the toolset itself should be configured.

question: Northgate Labs commits this to .claude/settings.json so that risky refactors always start with a proposal: {"permissions": {"defaultMode": "plan"}}. Which TWO statements about the effect of that setting are correct? (Select TWO)
options: A user-level settings.json with defaultMode acceptEdits overrides it, since user settings are read last.
The same key set to auto or bypassPermissions in this file would take effect in exactly the same way.
Sessions start in plan mode, but a permission-mode flag on the command line still wins over the setting.
Claude can still run shell commands to explore while planning; what it cannot do is edit the source.
Once a plan is approved the session returns to plan mode next turn, so every change needs a new plan.
answer: Sessions start in plan mode, but a permission-mode flag on the command line still wins over the setting.
Claude can still run shell commands to explore while planning; what it cannot do is edit the source.
explanation:
The general rule is that permissions.defaultMode chooses where a session starts, not what it can become. The startup order is the command-line flag, then defaultMode, then the built-in default, so a session launched with another permission mode ignores the file; and inside plan mode Claude reads files and runs shell commands to explore while edits wait for your approval. Two documented details make the wrong answers tempting: auto and bypassPermissions cannot be set from project or local settings, and settings precedence puts the project file above the user file rather than below it.

RULE: defaultMode sets the starting mode and a command-line flag overrides it; plan mode limits edits, never exploration.

TRAP: Reading a mode written in settings as a lock, and assuming every mode can be set from a project file.

TRY IT: Set defaultMode to plan in .claude/settings.json, start a session and read the status bar, then start another session with an explicit permission-mode flag and see which one wins.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings
option_feedback: Precedence runs the other way: managed settings, then the command line, then project local, then shared project, then user, so the project file wins over the user file.
Those two modes are the documented exception: auto and bypassPermissions do not take effect from project or local settings, so the key would be ignored.
Correct: the startup order is the flag first, then permissions.defaultMode, then the built-in default, so the file sets a default and not a lock.
Correct: plan mode restricts changes and not research, which is why the plans it produces are grounded in the actual code.
Approving a plan moves the session into execution, with edits either auto-accepted or approved one by one; it does not bounce back into planning after each turn.

question: Prairie Press vendors a third-party theme under vendor/theme/, and that folder ships its own CLAUDE.md whose instructions contradict the team's. Whenever Claude opens a theme file those instructions arrive too. Jordan adds this to .claude/settings.json: {"claudeMdExcludes": ["**/vendor/**/CLAUDE.md"]}. What does the setting do?
options: It keeps Claude from reading or editing any file under vendor/theme, which is where those instructions live.
It filters the imports of that file, so the vendored CLAUDE.md loads without the sections it pulls in.
It skips the matching CLAUDE.md files when Claude works there, leaving the project's own memory untouched.
It also lets the team exclude a managed policy CLAUDE.md that is pushed by their organization.
answer: It skips the matching CLAUDE.md files when Claude works there, leaving the project's own memory untouched.
explanation:
The general rule is that claudeMdExcludes filters the memory hierarchy and nothing else. It takes absolute-path globs, the arrays merge across settings layers, and matching CLAUDE.md and rule files simply stop being loaded, which is the documented remedy for vendored code and monorepos where a foreign memory file would otherwise arrive whenever Claude opens a file there. Its one documented limit is the managed policy CLAUDE.md, which an individual settings file cannot exclude, and because the key is about memory it changes nothing about which files Claude may read or edit.

RULE: claudeMdExcludes drops memory files by path glob: it is not a permission rule and it cannot remove the managed policy CLAUDE.md.

TRAP: Reading a memory filter as an access control, and assuming it can override what the organization pushes.

TRY IT: Add a CLAUDE.md with a distinctive line inside a vendored folder, open a file there and check /context, then add the claudeMdExcludes glob and repeat the check.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
option_feedback: Excluding memory is not a permission rule: file access is governed by Read and Edit rules, and this key never touches them.
The key skips whole memory files by path glob rather than editing their contents; there is no per-section or per-import filtering.
Correct: the key takes absolute-path globs and drops those memory files from the hierarchy, which is the documented fix for vendored and monorepo directories.
Managed policy memory is the one thing this key cannot remove: the docs state that those files cannot be excluded by individual settings.

question: Lakeshore Bank writes its compliance audit record from a Stop hook: when the review agent finishes, the hook stores the findings, the files that were reviewed and the session id. The internal auditor reports that roughly one run in twenty leaves no record at all. Megan inspects those runs and finds that their result messages carry the subtype error_max_turns, that the agent did real work before ending, and that the hook itself logged nothing. The hook has no matcher, and it fires normally on the other nineteen runs. What is the most likely cause?
options: Stop is filtered by matcher just like the tool events are, so a hook registered without a matcher is skipped on the runs that end early.
The hook ran past its timeout on those runs, and a hook that times out has its output discarded and its pending write lost.
Hooks may not fire when a run hits the turn limit, so a record needed on every run has to be written by your code from the result message.
The audit write belongs in a PreCompact hook instead, which runs earlier in the session and therefore survives the runs that a limit cuts short.
answer: Hooks may not fire when a run hits the turn limit, so a record needed on every run has to be written by your code from the result message.
explanation:
The general rule is that a hook is part of the run it observes, so it is reliable exactly while the run behaves. The documentation is explicit that hooks may not fire when the agent hits the max_turns limit, and that is the one thing the failing runs have in common: they end with the error_max_turns subtype. Anything the auditor requires for every run therefore belongs in the application, which reads a result message on every run, successful or not, and can write the record from there. The closest wrong answer blames the matcher, but Stop ignores matchers, so that mechanism cannot select one run in twenty.

RULE: A hook lives inside the run: whatever must exist for every run is written by your code from the result message, which always arrives.

TRAP: Treating a Stop hook as a guaranteed final step: a run cut short by the turn limit may never fire it.

TRY IT: Set max_turns to two on a task that clearly needs five and check whether your Stop hook leaves any trace for that run.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: Stop ignores matchers entirely, so a missing matcher cannot explain why the hook runs on nineteen runs out of twenty and not on the twentieth.
A Stop hook that exceeds its timeout produces a warning and the agent stops normally, and in any case the hook logged nothing on those runs, so it never got as far as writing.

Correct: the documentation warns that hooks may not fire when the agent hits the max_turns limit, which is exactly the subtype those runs carry, so the audit write has to come from the application, which always receives a result message.
PreCompact only fires when a compaction happens, so short runs would produce no record at all, and the event says nothing about how the run ended.

question: Prairie Press runs a nightly migration in CI with claude -p "upgrade the deprecated API calls in src/api" --output-format json --max-turns 4 > out.json, and the next step publishes the result field of out.json as the job summary. The job has been green for a week, the migration is half done, and last night Claude hit the turn limit. Which change makes the pipeline report that failure?
options: Add the verbose flag so that the run prints the detail revealing whether it finished.
Switch to the stream-json output format and treat the last line, the result message, as the job outcome.
Fail the step on a non-zero exit code and on is_error true in the envelope, before publishing result.
Raise the turn limit so that the job has enough turns and the limit stops being reached at night.
answer: Fail the step on a non-zero exit code and on is_error true in the envelope, before publishing result.
explanation:
The general rule for headless runs is that success is a signal, not a string. claude -p exits non-zero when the run fails and the JSON envelope carries is_error next to the result text, so a pipeline that publishes result alone cannot tell a finished migration from a run that stopped at the turn limit, which ends with an error. The closest alternative is changing the output format: stream-json gives a finer-grained view and needs the verbose flag, but the verdict still comes from the same fields, so reading them is the actual fix.

RULE: In CI, gate on the exit code and on is_error, never on the presence of result text: a turn limit ends the run with an error, not with an empty answer.

TRAP: Treating any output as proof of success, so an error envelope gets published as the job summary.

TRY IT: Run claude -p with a turn limit of 1 on a task that needs several turns, then print the exit code and read is_error in the JSON envelope.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference
option_feedback: Verbose output is what stream-json requires and what you want while developing; it adds text without giving the job any condition to fail on.
Streaming changes the shape of the output and still needs the verbose flag; the final message carries the very fields the step is already ignoring.
Correct: the run ends with a non-zero exit code and an is_error flag, while result holds text either way, so the check belongs on those two signals.
More turns may finish more work, but it removes one symptom instead of detecting failures, and the next unfinished run would be green again.

question: Northgate Labs connects Claude Code to an internal HTTP MCP server whose bearer token is issued by a helper binary and rotates every hour. The token currently sits in .mcp.json as a static Authorization header, and everybody's session starts failing with 401 an hour after it begins. What is the right configuration?
options: Write the token into an environment variable and reference that variable from the headers entry.
Configure headersHelper with a command that prints a JSON object of header names and values.
Re-add the server with claude mcp add and a fresh header value after every rotation of the token.
Raise the per-server timeout so that the connection survives until the next valid token arrives.
answer: Configure headersHelper with a command that prints a JSON object of header names and values.
explanation:
The general rule is that a credential which changes belongs behind a command, not inside the file. Environment expansion in .mcp.json happens when the configuration is read, so a variable reference freezes whatever value existed at startup, while headersHelper runs a command that must write a JSON object of string key-value pairs to stdout, and those dynamic headers override the static ones. That difference, read once versus fetched on demand, is what separates the keyed answer from the tempting environment-variable option.

RULE: Static headers and variable expansion are resolved once at load; a rotating credential needs headersHelper, whose output overrides static headers.

TRAP: Assuming an environment variable is re-read during the session, when expansion happens when the configuration loads.

TRY IT: Point headersHelper at a script that echoes a JSON object with a timestamped header value, connect, and use claude mcp get to see the value change between runs.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: Expansion reads the variable when the configuration loads, so the session keeps the value it picked up at startup and goes stale exactly as before.
Correct: Claude Code runs that command to obtain headers dynamically, and the values it returns override any static header entry.
It works for one person for one hour and can be neither committed nor automated; the configuration should fetch the credential instead of being rewritten.
A timeout bounds how long a call may take; it has nothing to do with authentication, and an expired token fails fast rather than slowly.

question: For six months the clinic has audited its automated extraction by hand. Every week reviewers take a five percent sample of the cases the pipeline flagged as uncertain and check them field by field, and the audit has reported accuracy above 99 percent throughout. Meanwhile the billing team keeps finding wrong authorization numbers in records nobody ever reviewed. What explains the gap?
options: The sample comes only from the flagged queue, so errors the pipeline was confident about never reach the audit.
Five percent is too small a sample to detect the error rate the billing team is seeing in production.
The reviewers check field by field, which is slower and lets attention drift on the last fields of each case.
The audit measures the reviewers' corrections rather than the pipeline's output, so it reports the queue's accuracy.
answer: The sample comes only from the flagged queue, so errors the pipeline was confident about never reach the audit.
explanation:
The general rule of a human review workflow is that its numbers describe only the population it draws from. Here the sample is taken from the flagged queue, so the audit answers whether the pipeline is right when it already doubted itself, and says nothing about the far larger set of confident extractions that go straight to billing. Humans are kept in the loop precisely to catch what automated signals miss, and that requires a slice of the unflagged traffic as well. The tempting alternative, a bigger sample, improves precision on the same biased population and can never surface an error class it does not see.

RULE: An audit measures only what it samples: always include a slice of the traffic nobody flagged.

TRAP: Reading a high audit score as system accuracy when the sample was drawn from the cases the system already doubted.

TRY IT: Pull fifty cases the pipeline never flagged, check them by hand and compare that error rate with the one your current audit reports.

SOURCE: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests
option_feedback: Correct: an audit can only measure the population it samples from, and drawing exclusively from the flagged queue makes confident errors invisible, which is where the billing team is finding them.
Sample size affects the precision of an estimate, not which population it describes; five percent of the wrong population would still miss these cases.
Field-by-field checking is slower but it is also what makes the review useful; the audit's problem is what it looks at, not how carefully it looks.
Reviewers do correct the cases they see, and those corrections are valuable data, but the reported figure does come from checking pipeline output, just on a biased subset.

question: Mateo is setting up two subagents for the support agent at Summit Pay: a refund reviewer declared in the agents option of the SDK and a knowledge searcher declared as a file in the agents folder of the project. Which statement about how those subagents get invoked is NOT correct?
options: Claude spawns a subagent through the Agent tool, formerly named Task, and listing that tool in allowed_tools auto-approves the spawn so no prompt interrupts the run.
The refund reviewer declared in the agents option takes precedence over a file based agent that happens to carry the same name.
If Claude calls the Agent tool without naming a subagent type, the call fails with an error and the whole main run stops there.
Messages produced inside a subagent carry parent_tool_use_id, so Mateo can attribute them to the Agent call that spawned them.
answer: If Claude calls the Agent tool without naming a subagent type, the call fails with an error and the whole main run stops there.
explanation:
The general rule is that the Agent tool always produces a subagent: if the call does not name one of the definitions, Claude gets the built-in general-purpose agent, with the full subagent tool set and none of the instructions Mateo wrote. That is silent behaviour, not a failure, and it is how a delegation that was supposed to be restricted ends up running with everything available. The other three statements are documented facts about invocation: the Agent tool and its auto-approval, code definitions taking precedence over filesystem ones, and parent_tool_use_id for attribution.

RULE: An Agent call without a subagent type does not fail: it runs the built-in general-purpose agent, with none of your restrictions.

TRAP: Expecting a missing subagent type to raise an error, when the runtime quietly falls back to a default agent.

TRY IT: Ask the agent to delegate something without naming any of your agents, then read the input of the Agent tool call and see which subagent type it used.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/subagents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents
option_feedback: True: the subagent tool is the Agent tool, and auto-approving it is the documented way to stop every delegation from asking for permission.
True and documented: programmatically defined agents win over filesystem agents with the same name, which is what makes code the source of truth in an SDK application.
This is the statement that is not correct, so it is the answer: a call with no subagent type falls back to the built-in general-purpose agent, which runs normally and is easy to miss.
True: the parent tool use id is how work and cost coming from inside a delegation are attributed to the call that started it.

question: A skill in Prairie Press's repository bundles a script next to its SKILL.md and declares this in the frontmatter: allowed-tools: Bash(${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/render.sh *). The body of the skill tells Claude to run that same script. What does ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} do here?
options: It points at the project root, so the path resolves from wherever the session was started.
It expands to the skill's own directory, in the body and in the allowed-tools rule alike.
It works in the body but not in permission rules, so allowed-tools needs the literal path.
It must be exported in the env block of settings.json before the skill is able to use it.
answer: It expands to the skill's own directory, in the body and in the allowed-tools rule alike.
explanation:
The general rule is that a skill should be relocatable: enterprise, personal, project and plugin copies of the same skill live at different paths, so anything that refers to a bundled file has to be written relative to the skill itself. ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} expands to that directory and is substituted both in the skill body and inside allowed-tools Bash rules, which keeps the permission rule and the command in agreement. It should not be confused with the project-directory variable, which points at the project root where the session started.

RULE: Reference bundled scripts with ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}: it resolves in the body and in allowed-tools, so the rule always matches the command.

TRAP: Mixing up the skill directory with the project directory, and hard-coding a path that breaks as soon as the skill is installed somewhere else.

TRY IT: Add scripts/hello.sh to a skill, allow it with a Bash rule built on ${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}, invoke the skill and confirm the command runs without a permission prompt.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills
option_feedback: That is what the project-directory variable does; the skill variable resolves to the skill's own folder, which is what makes a bundled script portable.
Correct: the substitution works in both places, so the permission rule matches the very command that the body asks Claude to run.
The docs give that allowed-tools Bash rule as an example of the substitution; a literal path is what breaks when the skill is installed elsewhere.
Claude Code substitutes these variables itself; the env block sets process environment values and is not where they come from.

question: The claims assistant at Summit Ridge Insurance shows, beside each decision, the policy clause it relied on, using the citations returned by the API. Last week the team started attaching the customer's previous policy as an extra document placed ahead of the current policy, in that same first turn. Since then the interface highlights clauses from the wrong policy, although the reasoning is right. The code maps each citation onto the document list it sent in the last message. What is the cause?
options: Citations were enabled on only one of the two documents, so the indices reported for the other one are not reliable.
PDF citations report page numbers starting at one, and the interface treats the first page as page zero.
The two policies overlap in wording, so the model cited the older clause that matched the text best.
document_index counts every document block in the request across all messages, not the list of the last message.
answer: document_index counts every document block in the request across all messages, not the list of the last message.
explanation:
The general rule is that a citation is only as good as the mapping back to its source, and that mapping is defined by the request, not by the caller's convenience. The documentation defines document_index as zero-indexed from the list of all document content blocks in the request, spanning across all messages, so inserting the previous policy ahead of the current one shifts every index by one and the interface resolves them against the wrong list. The near-miss is the page-number rule, which is real but would misplace a highlight inside one document instead of swapping policies.

RULE: document_index counts document blocks across the whole request, not the ones in the message you happen to be reading.

TRAP: Rebuilding the document list per message: any document added earlier in the request renumbers everything after it.

TRY IT: Send a request with two documents, confirm that each citation's document_index matches the position in the full request, then insert a third document first and watch the indices move.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations
option_feedback: The documentation requires citations to be enabled on all documents of a request or on none, so this is not a valid state to be in, and it would not shift a mapping by one position.
Page numbering is a real trap, since page_location is one-indexed with an exclusive end, but it would move a highlight inside a document rather than across policies.
Citations are not written by the model from memory: they are guaranteed pointers into the documents of the request, so a cited clause always sits where the citation says it does.
Correct: document_index is zero-indexed over all document content blocks in the request, spanning all messages, so adding an earlier document shifts every later index by one.

question: Bluebird Goods submits a single batch of 90,000 supplier-invoice extractions at ten in the evening. The pipeline polls the batch and downloads the results once processing ends. Twenty-four hours later 71,000 requests have completed and the rest have not been sent to the model yet. What will Brandon find?
options: The batch keeps processing past the deadline and ends only when the last request has finished, some hours later.
The batch expires, the unsent requests return as expired and unbilled, and the 71,000 results are available.
The whole batch is discarded, no results can be downloaded and nothing is billed for any of the requests.
The unsent requests are requeued automatically into a new batch and processed in the next window.
answer: The batch expires, the unsent requests return as expired and unbilled, and the 71,000 results are available.
explanation:
The general rule is that the Batches API promises a price and throughput, never a deadline: most batches finish in under an hour, but the contract says results are accessible when everything completes or after 24 hours, whichever comes first, and that a batch expires if it does not finish in that time. Requests that never reached the model come back with result type expired and are not billed, while everything already processed stays downloadable and is billed at the batch price, with results available for 29 days from creation. The prediction to avoid is a soft deadline that merely delays completion.

RULE: Twenty-four hours is a wall, not a target: unsent requests come back expired and unbilled, and resubmitting them is your job.

TRAP: Reading the batch window as a typical wait time: expiry cancels what has not been sent instead of finishing late.

TRY IT: Read request_counts on a finished batch and confirm that the four states, succeeded, errored, canceled and expired, add up to the number of requests you submitted.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing
option_feedback: The documentation is explicit that batches expire if processing does not complete within 24 hours, and there is no grace period that lets the remainder finish.

Correct: results become available when all messages complete or after 24 hours, whichever comes first, requests never sent to the model end with result type expired and are not billed, and the finished results stay downloadable for 29 days from creation.
Completed requests are not thrown away: their results are in the results file, and the ones that did run are billed normally at the batch price.
Nothing is requeued automatically; resubmitting the expired requests, preferably split into smaller batches, is the caller's job.

question: Cascade Power keeps one operations session open for an entire shift, and the regulator requires that every work order the agent issued during the shift can be reconstructed exactly as it was sent. Long sessions get compacted, and Paula notices that after a compaction the beginning of the shift survives only as a summary: the exact parameters of the first work orders are missing from the transcript the team exports at the end. What should she add?
options: A Stop hook that copies the whole conversation into the audit store when the shift session finally ends.
A PreCompact hook that archives the full transcript into the audit store before the summary replaces it.
A UserPromptSubmit hook that injects the earlier work orders back into the context on every new prompt.
A PostToolUse hook that shortens the output of the work order tool so the session reaches compaction much later.
answer: A PreCompact hook that archives the full transcript into the audit store before the summary replaces it.
explanation:
The general rule is that compaction rewrites the conversation, so anything that must survive it has to be copied out before it happens and stored outside the context. PreCompact is the event created for that purpose: it fires before the summary is produced and the hook runs in the application process, so archiving the transcript costs the session nothing. The closest wrong answer waits for the end of the session, which is too late by definition, since by then the only thing left of the early shift is the summary that replaced it.

RULE: Whatever must survive compaction is archived before it happens: PreCompact is the moment, and the archive lives outside the context.

TRAP: Waiting until the session ends to save a transcript that compaction has already rewritten.

TRY IT: Register a PreCompact hook that dumps the transcript to a file, force a compaction in a long session and compare that file with what the session still shows.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: Stop fires every time Claude finishes responding, not once when the shift ends, and each firing sees the conversation as it stands at that moment: after the first compaction that is already the summary, so the archive would hold the summary and never the parameters the regulator asks for.
Correct: PreCompact fires before the conversation is summarized, which is the documented moment to archive the full transcript, and the hook runs in your own process so it costs no context.
Re-injecting old orders keeps them in front of the model but creates no record, and it makes the context grow faster, so compaction arrives sooner rather than later.
Trimming tool output is a good way to slow context growth, but it discards the very parameters that have to be preserved, and compaction still comes eventually.

question: Summit Pay' assistant answers policy questions with the web_search server tool and with the team's own client tools. A developer is writing try and except blocks around web_search so that its failures come back as a tool_result with is_error true, the way the team handles their own tools. What should the team do?
options: Wrap it as planned, since every tool result that Claude reads has to be produced by the application.
Retry the search two or three times inside the loop before returning is_error to the model.
Map the search error codes onto the team's own error categories before handing them to Claude.
Drop the wrapper: server tools are executed by Anthropic and their errors are handled transparently.
answer: Drop the wrapper: server tools are executed by Anthropic and their errors are handled transparently.
explanation:
The general rule is that the two halves of tool use have different error contracts. Client tools run in your application: you execute them, and a failure comes back as a tool_result with is_error true and a message Claude can act on. Server tools such as web_search, web_fetch and code_execution run on Anthropic's infrastructure, which handles their errors transparently and reports them through its own error codes, so there is nothing for your loop to catch. The tempting answer treats every tool as one that your code executes.

RULE: is_error is for the tools your code runs; server tools are executed and error-handled on Anthropic's side.

TRAP: Extending the client-tool error contract to server tools that your application never executes.

TRY IT: Send a request that uses web_search with a deliberately overlong query and inspect the response blocks: the error arrives inside the server tool result, not through your handler.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview
option_feedback: That holds for client tools, which run in your code; a server tool executes on Anthropic's infrastructure and never passes through your handler.
Retrying is reasonable for your own integrations, but there is no result of yours to return here, and the API already reports search failures with its own error codes.
Those codes, such as max_uses_exceeded or query_too_long, already arrive attached to the server tool result; re-mapping them adds a layer without adding information.
Correct: the docs say plainly that you do not need to handle is_error results for server tools, because is_error is for the client tools your application runs.

question: The extraction prompt for scanned municipal files carries four examples that Paula typed by hand from clean transcriptions. Production inputs are OCR output from decades-old paper: broken accents, split words, headers repeated in the middle of a page. Accuracy is good on recent files and poor on the old ones. Paula has one afternoon to improve it. Where should she spend it?
options: Adding eight more hand-typed examples so the set covers every document type the office receives today.
Adding a sentence that warns the model the input may contain OCR noise and asks it to read with extra care.
Rewriting the four examples so their inputs are real OCR text from old files, with the expected output.
Raising effort for the whole prompt so that the model reasons for longer over each difficult page.
answer: Rewriting the four examples so their inputs are real OCR text from old files, with the expected output.
explanation:
The general rule of few-shot prompting is that examples teach what they show, so they have to mirror the real inputs: the documentation asks for examples that are relevant to the actual use case and diverse enough to cover edge cases. Clean typed transcriptions describe a world the pipeline never sees, which is why accuracy collapses precisely on the old files. With one afternoon, replacing four unrepresentative examples with four real ones buys more than adding eight more of the same kind and more than a general warning, which names the problem without demonstrating the expected output.

RULE: Examples must look like the inputs you actually receive: clean examples for dirty data teach the wrong task.

TRAP: Growing an example set instead of making it representative: twelve clean examples still describe a document you never get.

TRY IT: Swap two examples for real OCR pages with their correct output, rerun twenty old files and compare the field-level errors.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices
option_feedback: More examples of the same clean kind teach the same thing again; the documentation asks for examples that mirror the actual use case, and these do not.
A warning is cheap and harmless, but an abstract caution does not show what a broken line looks like or what the correct extraction from it is.
Correct: examples should be relevant, mirroring the real use case closely, and diverse enough to cover edge cases, and four built from real OCR text teach exactly the inputs that fail.
More reasoning per page can help, but it costs on every document and still does not tell the model how a damaged header should be read.

question: Northgate Labs adds the Claude Code GitHub Action to review pull requests. The workflow checks the code out, grants contents, pull-requests and issues write, and passes a prompt, but every run fails while the action authenticates as the GitHub App. The repository stores no key because the team wants the action's default authentication. What is missing?
options: The id-token write permission in the workflow, which the action's default app authentication requires.
A personal access token passed as github_token, since the default token cannot post reviews.
An anthropic_api_key secret, because the action cannot run without a static model credential.
A trigger_phrase input, because without it the action never authenticates on a pull request event.
answer: The id-token write permission in the workflow, which the action's default app authentication requires.
explanation:
The general rule is to keep the two credentials of a CI run apart: one reaches the model and one acts on the repository. The Claude Code action authenticates to GitHub as an app by default and that flow mints an OIDC token, so the workflow's permissions block must include id-token write beside contents, pull-requests and issues. The model credential is the other axis, an API key or an OAuth token from claude setup-token stored as a secret, and adding it would not repair a failing GitHub authentication.

RULE: Give the action id-token write when it authenticates as the GitHub App; repository scopes and the model credential are separate concerns.

TRAP: Reading every authentication failure in CI as a missing Anthropic key, when the side that failed is the workflow's GitHub permissions.

TRY IT: Remove id-token write from a working Claude Code workflow, re-run it, and compare the failure with the run that has the permission in place.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/github-actions
option_feedback: Correct: the example workflow lists id-token write next to the content permissions precisely because the default app auth mints an OIDC token.
The github_token input does accept another token when you need one, but the default token can post comments, and swapping it does not fix an authentication step that never ran.
A key or an OAuth token is how you pay for the model, not how the action authenticates to GitHub, and the team deliberately relies on app authentication.
The trigger phrase decides which comment wakes the interactive mode; with a prompt the action runs on the workflow event, and neither setting touches credentials.

question: Southbound Freight runs a nightly reconciliation through Claude Code. Claude calls Bash with node scripts/import-manifest.js --verbose, and instead of the output it receives a short notice naming a file that holds the whole result; the script itself exited 0. Renee asks what happened and how to keep this from eating context every night. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO)
options: Running it again in the background would stream the output instead of writing it to a file.
Bash keeps output inline up to roughly 30,000 characters and past that returns a file path Claude can read.
Making the script print only the records that failed keeps the result inline and the context cheap.
The notice means the command failed, since a successful command always returns its output inline.
Raising MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS would let the whole result come back inline again.
answer: Bash keeps output inline up to roughly 30,000 characters and past that returns a file path Claude can read.
Making the script print only the records that failed keeps the result inline and the context cheap.
explanation:
The general rule is that the built-in tools protect the context by truncating or offloading large results, and that the durable fix belongs at the source. The Bash tool keeps output inline up to roughly 30,000 characters and then hands back the path of a file holding the whole thing, which is a change of delivery and not a failure, since the exit code still reports whether the command worked. Making the command print less keeps the answer inline and cheap, while raising a limit only moves more low-signal text into the conversation, and the MCP output variable does not apply to Bash at all.

RULE: Large Bash output arrives as a file path rather than as a failure: read the part you need and make the command print less next time.

TRAP: Reading an offloaded result as an error, and reaching for the MCP output limit to fix a Bash limit.

TRY IT: Run a command that prints a hundred thousand characters and watch the file path come back, then pipe the same command through a filter and see the output return inline.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference
option_feedback: Background execution is for long-running processes such as servers and watchers: it changes when you get output, not the size at which inline output stops.
Correct: the notice is the documented behavior for large results, and the file can be read in ranges when only one part of it matters.
