Correct: filtering at the source is the documented way to keep tool output small, and it is what stops the same notice from returning every night.
The exit code, not the delivery of the output, reports success: here the script exited 0 and only the size of its output changed the shape of the answer.
That variable governs MCP tool results and not the Bash tool, whose own limits are the Bash output length variables.

question: Cascade Power runs an unattended maintenance workflow at three in the morning inside an isolated container: the agent reads telemetry, writes a report and files work orders. Two constraints hold at once. Nobody is awake, so a run that stops to ask for approval is a run that dies at the timeout. And the feeder cut tool, which can leave a town without power, must be unreachable even by accident. Which permission setup satisfies both?
options: Use bypassPermissions so that nothing ever prompts, and tell the agent in its prompt that the feeder cut tool is out of scope for the night run.
Use acceptEdits so the report writing is approved automatically, and leave every other tool to the standard permission prompt at run time.
Use plan mode for the whole run so the agent touches nothing, and have the morning shift file by hand the work orders it proposed.
Allow-list the tools the night job needs, deny the feeder cut tool by rule, and run in dontAsk so anything else is refused rather than queued.
answer: Allow-list the tools the night job needs, deny the feeder cut tool by rule, and run in dontAsk so anything else is refused rather than queued.
explanation:
The general rule for unattended work is that every permission decision has to resolve without a person, and that a dangerous tool is blocked by a rule rather than by a mode. In dontAsk anything not pre-approved is denied and the permission callback is never invoked, so the run finishes instead of hanging, while the allow-list states exactly what the night job may do. Deny rules sit above the mode in the evaluation order and block a matching call even in bypassPermissions. The tempting answer is bypassPermissions, which also never prompts, but it removes the prompt by approving rather than by refusing, which is the opposite of what an autonomous night run needs.

RULE: For an unattended run, pre-approve a short list and use dontAsk: what is not on the list is denied, never queued for a human who is not there.

TRAP: Reading bypassPermissions as the mode for automation: it removes the prompt by approving, while dontAsk removes it by refusing.

TRY IT: Run a task in dontAsk with only Read and Grep allowed, ask it to write a file, and confirm the write is denied and the run ends on its own.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/permissions https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop
option_feedback: bypassPermissions approves everything that no rule blocks, so the only thing between the agent and the feeder would be a sentence of prompt; the mode exists for isolated environments, not as a safety measure.
acceptEdits auto-approves file operations only; every other call falls through to a prompt, and a prompt at three in the morning is a stalled run that ends at the timeout.
Plan mode is the right choice when a person will read the plan, but here nobody is awake and the point of the night job is that the orders get filed: the run would produce work, not results.

Correct: this is the documented locked-down pattern, where the allow-list says what the job may do, dontAsk denies anything else without ever calling for a human, and a deny rule blocks the dangerous tool in every mode.

question: A tool at Lakeshore Bank is defined without strict, and Claude calls it with a required parameter missing. According to the documentation, what happens next?
options: The API rejects the response with a 400 error and no tool_use block reaches the caller.
The call arrives with the parameter set to null so the application can decide how to continue.
Claude retries two or three times with corrections and then apologizes to the user if it still fails.
The response ends with a stop reason of invalid_tool_use and the caller is expected to resend it.
answer: Claude retries two or three times with corrections and then apologizes to the user if it still fails.
explanation:
The general rule is that without schema-constrained sampling a tool call is a best effort. The documentation states that if a tool request is invalid or missing parameters, Claude will retry two to three times with corrections before apologizing to the user, and that setting strict to true eliminates invalid tool calls entirely by constraining sampling to schema-valid outputs. This matters in production because those silent retries cost tokens and latency and can end in an apology rather than a result.

RULE: Without strict, an invalid tool call costs two or three silent retries and may end in an apology; strict removes the whole class.

TRAP: Expecting the API to validate tool arguments for you: the schema is guidance until strict turns it into a constraint.

TRY IT: Define a tool with two required fields, prompt for a case that omits one and watch the retries in the transcript, then set strict to true and repeat.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use
option_feedback: A malformed tool call is not a request validation failure: the request itself was valid, so nothing is rejected with a 400.
Nothing fills a missing parameter for you; that is exactly the class of runtime error strict tool use was introduced to remove.

Correct: without strict, an invalid or incomplete tool request leads Claude to retry two to three times with corrections before apologizing, and strict tool use is the documented way to eliminate those calls entirely.
There is no such stop reason: a tool call comes back with stop_reason tool_use whether or not its arguments are complete.

question: Prairie Press's repository already holds a 120-line CLAUDE.md written by hand, plus a .cursor/rules directory left over from another editor. A new teammate runs /init, expecting it to set the project up. What does /init do here?
options: It refuses to run, since /init only creates a CLAUDE.md when the project does not have one yet.
It replaces the file with a freshly generated one, which is why the docs suggest committing first.
It writes a second file at .claude/CLAUDE.md so that the handwritten one stays untouched.
It analyzes the codebase and suggests improvements to the existing file, reading the Cursor rules too.
answer: It analyzes the codebase and suggests improvements to the existing file, reading the Cursor rules too.
explanation:
The general rule is that /init is a bootstrap that respects what you already wrote: it analyzes the codebase and produces the build commands, conventions and layout a session needs, and when a CLAUDE.md is already there it suggests improvements rather than overwriting it. It also reads configuration written for other assistants, such as Cursor rules and Copilot instructions, so an existing setup is folded in instead of ignored. Both tempting answers assume the command is all or nothing: refusing when a file exists, or replacing that file outright.

RULE: /init proposes improvements to an existing CLAUDE.md instead of replacing it, and folds in Cursor and Copilot rule files.

TRAP: Assuming a generator always overwrites, when /init treats the file you wrote as its starting point.

TRY IT: Run /init in a repository that already has a CLAUDE.md and compare the proposal with the file on disk before accepting anything.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory https://code.claude.com/docs/en/commands
option_feedback: A missing file is the simple case rather than a precondition: with a file present the command still runs and turns its analysis into a proposal.
Overwriting is exactly what the docs say it avoids: the existing file is treated as something to improve, not as a draft to discard.
Both paths are valid locations for project memory, but /init does not split them; it works with the file the project already has.
Correct: with a CLAUDE.md present /init proposes changes instead of overwriting, and it picks up Cursor and Copilot rule files while it does.

question: Renee has spent forty turns with Claude Code chasing a rate mismatch at Southbound Freight: the fleet data is loaded, three tool outputs sit in the conversation and she has a working theory. She now wants a side investigation of one legacy tariff table without losing that thread. She can spawn a regular subagent with the Agent tool, or start a fork subtask, which inherits her conversation. Which TWO statements about the fork are correct? (Select TWO)
options: A fork starts from the whole current conversation, with its system prompt, tools and model, so Renee does not have to restate the background in a prompt.
A fork runs in the background by default, so the main conversation stays usable while the side investigation is still going.
A fork shares one context window with the main conversation, so every file it reads also lands in the main thread as well.
A fork is how you give a delegated task a different system prompt and a reduced list of tools than the main session has.
Because a fork copies the conversation, the file changes it makes are rolled back when the fork finishes its work.
answer: A fork starts from the whole current conversation, with its system prompt, tools and model, so Renee does not have to restate the background in a prompt.
A fork runs in the background by default, so the main conversation stays usable while the side investigation is still going.
explanation:
The general rule is that a fork trades context isolation for context inheritance. A regular subagent starts fresh and receives only the prompt string of the Agent call, which is ideal for a self-contained task but expensive to set up when forty turns of background matter; a fork copies the conversation, the system prompt, the tools and the model, and runs in the background so the main thread keeps moving. What a fork does not do is share a live context window with the main conversation or undo anything on disk: its own work stays isolated, and branching a conversation leaves the filesystem exactly as it was.

RULE: Fork when explaining the background costs more than copying it; spawn a fresh subagent when the task is self-contained and the context should stay clean.

TRAP: Expecting a fork to behave like a transaction: it branches the conversation, so nothing it wrote to disk is undone when it ends.

TRY IT: Start a fork subtask after a long debugging session, ask it what it already knows about the bug, and compare its answer with what a fresh subagent says to the same question.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/sessions
option_feedback: Correct: inheriting the entire conversation is the defining property of a fork, and the reason to prefer one when the side task needs more background than you could write into a brief.
Correct: forks run in the background unless told otherwise, so the thread Renee is working in does not block while the tariff table is examined.
The opposite holds: a fork copies the history but its own work stays isolated and only its result comes back, which is what keeps the main context from filling up.
A different system prompt and a restricted tool list come from an agent definition; a fork deliberately inherits both from the conversation it copies.
Forking branches the conversation, never the filesystem: whatever the fork edited stays edited, and undoing it needs file checkpointing.

question: Cascade Power builds shutdown procedures from three maintenance manuals passed as documents with citations enabled. Every manual has an edition number that auditors require beside each quoted fragment, and the team put that number in the context field of each document block. The answers cite the manuals correctly, but no citation ever contains the edition, and the model sometimes states the wrong edition in its prose. What is the cause?
options: Citations were enabled on some documents only, so the metadata of the others never reaches the response.
The context field is passed to the model but is not citable content, so nothing in it can be quoted.
Plain-text documents are chunked into sentences, and a short metadata line is dropped when the chunks are built.
The edition sits in the document title, which the API returns only when the citation covers the first page.
answer: The context field is passed to the model but is not citable content, so nothing in it can be quoted.
explanation:
The general rule of the citations feature is that only the content of a document is citable: the documentation says the title and context of a document are passed to the model but are not used toward cited content. Metadata placed in context is therefore visible to the model, which is why it can talk about the edition and occasionally get it wrong, but it can never appear inside a cited fragment. If auditors need the edition beside the quote, it belongs in the document content, or it can be read from the document_title that accompanies every citation. The near-miss is chunking, which governs how large a citation is, not what may be cited.

RULE: Only document content is citable: title and context are read by the model but never quoted back.

TRAP: Putting audit metadata in a metadata field and expecting it inside the citation: context informs the model, it does not become evidence.

TRY IT: Move the edition line into the first sentence of one manual's content, rerun the query and check whether cited_text can now include it.

SOURCE: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations
option_feedback: Citations must be enabled on all documents of a request or on none, and the symptom here is uniform across the three manuals rather than partial.

Correct: the documentation states that the title and context of a document are passed to the model but are not used toward cited content, so anything that must be quoted has to live inside the document content.
Automatic sentence chunking changes the granularity of a citation, not whether a field is citable; custom content documents are the tool for controlling granularity.
Every citation carries document_title regardless of which part of the document was cited, so no page condition is at work here.

question: An MCP server at Southbound Freight answers a call for a tool name it does not implement with this result: {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Unknown tool: freeze_route"}], "isError": true}. The agent then calls the same missing name twice more before giving up. How should the server report this case?
options: Keep isError true, which is the channel the model actually reads and its only way to pick another tool.
Return a normal result with that text and no flag, so the transcript stays free of error states.
Answer with an HTTP error from the transport so that the client drops the connection and reconnects.
Answer with a JSON-RPC error, code -32602: finding a tool is a protocol matter, not an execution failure.
answer: Answer with a JSON-RPC error, code -32602: finding a tool is a protocol matter, not an execution failure.
explanation:
The general rule is a two-way split. Failures inside a tool that ran, such as validation, business rules or an upstream API that is down, go in the result with isError true and actionable text, because the model can adjust and retry. Failures in finding or dispatching the tool, such as an unknown name, a malformed request or a server that does not support tool calls, are JSON-RPC protocol errors, and the specification names -32602 for an unknown tool. Labelling a missing tool as an execution error invites exactly what happened here: the model reads a recoverable failure and tries the same name again.

RULE: isError is for a tool that ran and failed; an unknown tool name is a protocol error, reported as a JSON-RPC error with code -32602.

TRAP: Applying the rule to report errors inside the result so broadly that even a tool which does not exist looks like something the model can retry.

TRY IT: Call a tool name your server does not implement and inspect what your framework returns: a result with isError true, or a JSON-RPC error object with code -32602.

SOURCE: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/tools
option_feedback: Execution errors are indeed the channel that reaches the model, but a name the server does not implement is not something the model can fix by adjusting its arguments.
Hiding the failure is worse than mislabeling it: the model reads a plain result as success and has no reason to change course at all.
Transport-level failures break the session instead of answering the request, and the protocol already has a JSON-RPC error for a request it cannot fulfil.
Correct: unknown tools, malformed requests and server errors are protocol errors, while isError is for failures inside a tool that actually ran.

question: Cascade Power's operations team uses a desktop assistant that speaks MCP, and they want it to reach the file and search tools that Claude Code already exposes on the same machine, without rebuilding any of them. What should they do?
options: Add the assistant to .mcp.json as a project-scoped server so that the two share one tool catalog.
Run claude mcp serve, which starts Claude Code as a stdio MCP server, and register it in the assistant.
Wrap claude -p with the JSON output format in a small script and call that script from the assistant.
Import the servers with claude mcp add-from-claude-desktop so that both clients end up with the same setup.
answer: Run claude mcp serve, which starts Claude Code as a stdio MCP server, and register it in the assistant.
explanation:
The general rule is to ask which side is the server. Claude Code is normally an MCP host that connects to the servers listed in .mcp.json, but claude mcp serve turns it around: it starts Claude Code as a stdio MCP server so another client can call its tools, and the documentation notes that the client is then responsible for confirming individual tool calls with the user. The distractors all move configuration in the opposite direction, importing or wrapping servers instead of exposing the tools the team already has.

RULE: claude mcp serve turns Claude Code into a stdio MCP server for another client, which then owns the per-call confirmation.

TRAP: Assuming every MCP task is solved by adding a server to .mcp.json, when the goal is to expose Claude Code's own tools.

TRY IT: Add an entry whose command is claude with the arguments mcp serve to another MCP client's configuration and list the tools that client discovers.

SOURCE: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp
option_feedback: The .mcp.json file lists the servers Claude Code connects to, so it points the wrong way for making Claude Code's own tools available elsewhere.
Correct: that subcommand exposes Claude Code's tools to any MCP client, which then has to implement its own confirmation for each tool call.
A shim gives the assistant one opaque prompt endpoint instead of the individual tools, and it loses the per-tool descriptions and confirmations.
That command copies server definitions out of Claude Desktop into Claude Code; it neither exports tools nor runs on every platform.

question:
Scenario: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. The agent handles high-ambiguity requests such as returns, billing disputes, and account issues. It has access to backend systems through custom MCP tools such as get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, and escalate_to_human. Your target is 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.

Question: During testing, the agent correctly returns a tool_use request for lookup_order, but your orchestration code immediately sends the assistant's visible text back to the customer without executing the tool. In other cases, the loop runs the same fixed sequence of support tools even when Claude has already completed the response.   

Which implementation approach correctly handles the agentic loop?
options: Continue the loop until the assistant response contains no tool names, then return the final visible text to the customer.
Inspect stop_reason; when it is tool_use, execute the requested tool, append the tool result to the conversation, and continue until Claude returns an end_turn.
Execute get_customer, lookup_order, and process_refund in a fixed order for every support request, then ask Claude to summarize the results.
Stop after exactly three turns to prevent infinite loops, then return whichever response Claude generated most recently.
answer: Inspect stop_reason; when it is tool_use, execute the requested tool, append the tool result to the conversation, and continue until Claude returns an end_turn.
explanation:
Correct option:

Inspect stop_reason; when it is tool_use, execute the requested tool, append the tool result to the conversation, and continue until Claude returns an end_turn.

The loop should be controlled by Claude's response state, not by visible text inspection. When Claude returns a tool-use stop reason, the application must execute the requested tool and provide the result back to Claude before expecting the final answer.

This keeps the model-driven decision process intact. Claude can inspect the returned tool result and decide whether another tool call, clarification question, escalation, or final answer is appropriate.

This also prevents the two failures described in the question: returning too early before executing a tool, and running a fixed backend sequence when Claude has already completed the task.

Incorrect options:

Continue the loop until the assistant response contains no tool names, then return the final visible text to the customer. - This approach relies on parsing natural language output or visible text. Tool-use state is represented structurally, so the loop should not infer completion from whether a tool name appears in assistant text.

It can also fail when Claude describes a tool in a final explanation or when a tool call exists as a structured block without the tool name appearing in normal prose.

Execute get_customer, lookup_order, and process_refund in a fixed order for every support request, then ask Claude to summarize the results. - A fixed sequence of tools turns the agent into a pre-configured decision tree. The task requires an agentic loop in which Claude chooses the next action based on the current context and prior tool results.

This option also increases unnecessary tool usage and can cause risky actions, such as invoking refund operations when the user only asked a status question.

Stop after exactly three turns to prevent infinite loops, then return whichever response Claude generated most recently. - An iteration cap may be useful as a safety guard, but it should not be the primary completion signal. The main loop should respond to structured stop reasons.

Stopping after an arbitrary number of turns can cut off a valid tool-use cycle before the agent has enough information to answer accurately.

https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

It has access to backend systems through custom MCP tools such as get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, and escalate_to_human. Question: Your support system uses a coordinator agent and three specialized subagents: billing, returns, and account recovery. Production traces show that the coordinator sends every ticket through all three subagents, even when the customer has a simple billing question. This increases latency, creates contradictory recommendations, and makes the final response harder to audit. 

What is the most appropriate orchestration change?
options: Allow the subagents to call each other directly so they can resolve disagreements without involving the coordinator.
Replace the specialized subagents with one general support subagent that has access to all support tools.
Require the coordinator to always invoke the billing subagent first because billing issues are the most common support category.
Have the coordinator analyze the request, select only the relevant subagents, route all communication through itself, and aggregate the results.
answer: Have the coordinator analyze the request, select only the relevant subagents, route all communication through itself, and aggregate the results.
explanation:
Correct option:

Have the coordinator analyze the request, select only the relevant subagents, route all communication through itself, and aggregate the results.

The coordinator should own task decomposition, routing, aggregation, and error handling. It should decide which subagents are needed based on the actual customer request.

This preserves the hub-and-spoke pattern. Subagents remain specialized, but the coordinator controls the flow of information and produces a single final resolution.

This also improves observability. Since all subagent communication passes through the coordinator, the team can inspect why a subagent was invoked and how its result influenced the final answer.

Incorrect options:

Allow the subagents to call each other directly so they can resolve disagreements without involving the coordinator. - Direct subagent-to-subagent communication weakens central control. It makes error handling, auditability, and attribution more difficult.

In a support environment, the coordinator should remain the control point so that customer context, policy decisions, and escalation logic are consistently applied.

Replace the specialized subagents with one general support subagent that has access to all support tools. - A general subagent with all tools reintroduces the same complexity the multi-agent design was supposed to reduce. It also increases the chance of tool misuse outside a focused role.

Specialization is valuable when each subagent has a clear responsibility and limited tool access.

Require the coordinator to always invoke the billing subagent first because billing issues are the most common support category. - A fixed first step is not adaptive orchestration. It may help common billing tickets, but it adds unnecessary work for returns, account recovery, and mixed cases.

The coordinator should select subagents dynamically rather than assume that one category is always the correct starting point.

Question: A coordinator agent verifies a customer, retrieves two related orders, and then delegates a billing-dispute investigation to a subagent. The billing subagent repeatedly asks for the customer ID and order numbers again, even though the coordinator already found them. Your team assumed the subagent would automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history.

What change best addresses the issue?
options: Pass a structured prompt to the billing subagent that includes the verified customer ID, relevant order details, prior findings, and the investigation goal.
Increase the coordinator's context window so the subagent can inspect more of the parent conversation when it starts.
Add a system prompt telling the billing subagent to trust that the coordinator has already verified the customer.
Run the billing subagent after the returns subagent so that more investigation context exists by the time billing starts.
answer: Pass a structured prompt to the billing subagent that includes the verified customer ID, relevant order details, prior findings, and the investigation goal.
explanation:
Correct option:

Pass a structured prompt to the billing subagent that includes the verified customer ID, relevant order details, prior findings, and the investigation goal.

Subagents should receive the context they need explicitly. The coordinator should pass the verified customer ID, order IDs, facts already discovered, and the billing-specific objective in the subagent prompt.

A structured handoff also reduces ambiguity. Separating facts, metadata, and the requested task helps the subagent avoid redoing work or mixing up order-level details.

This is the most production-ready design because it treats subagent execution as isolated work with a deliberate input contract.

Incorrect options:

Increase the coordinator's context window so the subagent can inspect more of the parent conversation when it starts. - A larger parent context window does not guarantee that the subagent receives the parent's conversation history. The problem is not only capacity; it is explicit context passing.

Even if more context is available in the coordinator session, the subagent still needs the relevant facts included in its invocation.

Add a system prompt telling the billing subagent to trust that the coordinator has already verified the customer. - Telling the subagent to trust the coordinator does not give it the concrete facts it needs. The subagent still lacks the customer ID, order numbers, and details of the billing issue.

Trust guidance is not a substitute for passing the actual state required to complete the task.

Run the billing subagent after the returns subagent so that more investigation context exists by the time billing starts. - Changing the order of subagent execution does not solve the missing-context problem. It may even add irrelevant context if returns data is unrelated to the billing dispute.

The issue is the handoff contract, not the sequence in which subagents are invoked.

Generate a structured handoff summary that includes customer ID, order ID, root cause, refund amount, actions already attempted, and recommended next step.

answer: Generate a structured handoff summary that includes customer ID, order ID, root cause, refund amount, actions already attempted, and recommended next step.
explanation:
Correct option:

Generate a structured handoff summary that includes customer ID, order ID, root cause, refund amount, actions already attempted, and recommended next step.

The escalation should carry the operational facts a human agent needs to continue the case. A structured handoff prevents the human agent from starting over.

Ask the customer to restate all important details immediately before calling the escalation tool. - Asking the customer to repeat information increases friction and weakens the automation experience. The agent has already collected or retrieved these facts.

It has access to backend systems through custom MCP tools such as get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, and escalate_to_human. Question: Production logs show two reliability issues. First, the agent sometimes tries to call process_refund for amounts above the company's $500 autonomous-refund limit. Second, different backend tools return dates and statuses in inconsistent formats, causing the agent to misread whether an order is still eligible for return.

Which TWO changes should you implement?
options: Add a pre-tool-call interception hook that denies process_refund calls above $500 and redirects the case to escalation.
Add a prompt instruction saying that refunds above $500 are not allowed unless the customer has provided strong evidence.
Add a post-tool-use hook that normalizes tool outputs such as Unix timestamps, ISO dates, and numeric status codes before Claude reasons over them.
Remove the process_refund tool entirely and require every refund request to be escalated to a human agent.
Increase max_tokens so Claude has more room to reason through inconsistent backend responses.
answer: Add a pre-tool-call interception hook that denies process_refund calls above $500 and redirects the case to escalation.
Add a post-tool-use hook that normalizes tool outputs such as Unix timestamps, ISO dates, and numeric status codes before Claude reasons over them.
explanation:
Correct options:

Add a pre-tool-call interception hook that denies process_refund calls above $500 and redirects the case to escalation.

A refund limit is a deterministic business rule. A pre-tool-call interception hook can block or deny the tool call before the action is executed.

This is stronger than relying on the model to remember a prompt instruction. The hook enforces the rule even if the model attempts the wrong action.

It also supports a safe alternate workflow. The case can be redirected to human escalation when the refund exceeds the autonomous limit.

Add a post-tool-use hook that normalizes tool outputs such as Unix timestamps, ISO dates, and numeric status codes before Claude reasons over them.

A post-tool-use hook is appropriate for transforming tool results after the backend call completes. It can normalize heterogeneous fields before the model uses them.

This reduces reasoning errors caused by inconsistent formats. For example, the agent should not have to infer whether 2, RETURNABLE, and return_eligible=true mean the same thing.

This pattern improves reliability without changing the backend systems or overloading the prompt with format-specific reminders.

Incorrect options:

Add a prompt instruction saying that refunds above $500 are not allowed unless the customer has provided strong evidence. - A prompt instruction can reduce some mistakes, but it does not guarantee compliance. For financial limits, the system needs deterministic enforcement.

The phrase "strong evidence" is also ambiguous. It introduces a subjective exception to a business rule that should be enforced consistently.

Remove the process_refund tool entirely and require every refund request to be escalated to a human agent. - Removing the refund tool would reduce risk, but it would also undermine first-contact resolution for straightforward refunds under the limit.

The better design is to keep the tool available within controlled boundaries and escalate only cases that violate policy.

Increase max_tokens so Claude has more room to reason through inconsistent backend responses. - More tokens do not normalize inconsistent data. The agent may still misinterpret heterogeneous formats even with more space to reason.

The issue is data shape and enforcement, not response length or context capacity.

https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/handle-tool-calls

answer: The tool descriptions are not sufficiently differentiated; expand them with expected inputs, outputs, example requests, edge cases, and when to use each tool versus the other.

The tool descriptions are not sufficiently differentiated; expand them with expected inputs, outputs, example requests, edge cases, and when to use each tool versus the other.

A combined tool could still make poor internal decisions unless its own contract is carefully designed.

Question: The process_refund MCP tool returns the same text response, "Operation failed," for timeouts, invalid order IDs, expired return windows, and permission failures. The agent retries some non-retryable failures and gives vague explanations to customers.

Which response design best supports reliable recovery?
options: Return an MCP tool error result with structured metadata such as errorCategory, isRetryable, and a customer-facing explanation.

Throw a server exception for every failed refund attempt and let the top-level orchestrator terminate the case.

answer: Return an MCP tool error result with structured metadata such as errorCategory, isRetryable, and a customer-facing explanation.
explanation:
Correct option:

Return an MCP tool error result with structured metadata such as errorCategory, isRetryable, and a customer-facing explanation.

Structured error responses help the agent distinguish transient, validation, permission, and business-rule failures. That distinction is necessary for deciding whether to retry, clarify, explain, or escalate.

The isRetryable flag prevents wasted retries for policy or validation failures. It also allows the agent to retry only failures that might succeed on a later attempt.

A customer-facing explanation lets the agent communicate clearly without exposing low-level backend details.

Incorrect options:

Return an empty successful result whenever the refund cannot be processed, so the agent does not expose backend errors to customers. - An empty successful result hides the failure. The agent may incorrectly conclude that there was no refund issue or that there were no matching results.

This makes recovery harder because the coordinator cannot distinguish a valid empty result from a failed operation.

Throw a server exception for every failed refund attempt and let the top-level orchestrator terminate the case. - Terminating the entire case on every failure is too aggressive. Some failures can be retried, clarified, or routed to a human.

The orchestrator needs structured information to choose the right recovery path rather than treating all failures as fatal.

Return "Operation failed" plus a timestamp so the support team can inspect the logs later. - A timestamp helps log investigation, but it does not help the agent decide what to do next. The response still lacks the reason and retryability of the failure.

The customer-facing interaction remains vague because "Operation failed" gives no meaningful explanation.

explanation:
Correct options:

Add explicit criteria that require immediate escalation when the customer clearly asks for a human agent.

An explicit request for a human should be honored as an escalation trigger. The agent should not continue troubleshooting after the customer clearly asks to stop.

This is a clear decision boundary, not a case where the agent needs to infer sentiment or complexity. The customer's instruction itself is enough.

Adding this criterion makes behavior more predictable and avoids frustrating users who have already chosen the human-support path.

Instruct the agent to ask for additional identifiers when multiple customer records match instead of choosing heuristically.

Multiple matching customer records create an identity ambiguity. The agent should ask for additional identifiers such as email, phone, order ID, or another safe verification detail.

Choosing heuristically can lead to account mix-ups, privacy issues, and incorrect actions on the wrong customer record.

Clarification is the reliable pattern because it resolves ambiguity before downstream tools are used.

Incorrect options:

Add a sentiment threshold so all angry customers are automatically escalated before any investigation starts. - Sentiment is not the same as case complexity or escalation need. A frustrated customer may still have a straightforward issue the agent can resolve.

Automatic sentiment-based escalation can reduce first-contact resolution and overload human agents.

Instruct the agent to select the most recently active customer record when multiple customer matches are returned. - Choosing the most recently active record is a heuristic. It may be wrong if multiple customers share a name or if the real customer has not ordered recently.

The agent should not guess identity when backend results are ambiguous.

Use the agent's self-reported confidence score to decide whether the request is too complex to resolve. - Self-reported confidence is not a reliable proxy for complexity. Agents can be confident in cases that actually require policy review or clarification.

The escalation decision should be based on explicit criteria, policy gaps, inability to progress, customer requests, and ambiguity signals.

answer: Have the coordinator create an adaptive investigation plan that can spawn new targeted subtasks when intermediate findings reveal gaps.

What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Append the tool result to the conversation history before the next model call so Claude can reason over the returned evidence.
Suppress repeated tool calls by blocking the search tool after it is used once.
Parse the assistant's visible text and stop the loop when it mentions that a search has been performed.

answer: Append the tool result to the conversation history before the next model call so Claude can reason over the returned evidence.
explanation:
Correct option:

Append the tool result to the conversation history before the next model call so Claude can reason over the returned evidence.

Tool results must be returned to Claude as part of the next turn. Otherwise, the model has no evidence that the requested action was executed.

Appending the result lets the coordinator decide whether to search again, analyze the evidence, or synthesize a response.

This preserves the agentic loop: Claude requests a tool, the application executes it, and the result becomes new context for the next model decision.

Incorrect options:

Suppress repeated tool calls by blocking the search tool after it is used once. - Blocking the tool after one use hides the real bug. The coordinator may need multiple searches for different subtopics.

The problem is missing tool-result context, not excessive tool availability.

Parse the assistant's visible text and stop the loop when it mentions that a search has been performed. - Visible text is not the reliable control signal for tool-use loops. Tool calls and stop reasons are structured.

Stopping based on a phrase can fail if the model mentions search in a different context or repeats the phrase without actual tool evidence.

Increase the number of search results returned by the tool so Claude has more evidence available. - More search results do not help if the application never returns them to Claude. The result must be appended to the conversation.

The issue is loop state management, not the quantity of retrieved evidence.

Question: You are configuring the coordinator so it can launch subagents and pass context correctly. The research system must spawn a web-search agent and a document-analysis agent in parallel, then provide both result sets to the synthesis agent with source metadata preserved.

options: Include the Task tool in the coordinator's allowed tools so it can invoke subagents.

Pass search results and document findings explicitly to the synthesis subagent in a structured format that separates claims from source metadata.

answer: Include the Task tool in the coordinator's allowed tools so it can invoke subagents.
Pass search results and document findings explicitly to the synthesis subagent in a structured format that separates claims from source metadata.
explanation:
Correct options:

Include the Task tool in the coordinator's allowed tools so it can invoke subagents.

The coordinator needs the subagent-invocation mechanism available to it. If the Task tool is not allowed, it cannot spawn the specialized agents.

This is a configuration requirement before orchestration logic can work. The coordinator cannot delegate work using a tool it is not permitted to call.

Including Task enables the coordinator to create web-search, document-analysis, synthesis, or report-generation subagent work as needed.

Pass search results and document findings explicitly to the synthesis subagent in a structured format that separates claims from source metadata.

The synthesis agent should receive the evidence it needs directly. Structured context should keep claims, source URLs, document names, dates, and page references distinct.

This preserves attribution through synthesis. It also prevents the model from blending evidence without knowing which source supports which claim.

The pattern is especially important for cited reports, where provenance is part of the output quality.

Incorrect options:

Assume the synthesis subagent can automatically read the coordinator's full conversation history. - Subagents do not automatically inherit all parent context. Assuming they can read the coordinator history leads to missing facts and repeated questions.

The synthesis agent needs explicit inputs, not implicit access to prior turns.

Force every subagent to use the same system prompt so they share a common memory. - Sharing the same system prompt does not create shared memory. It can also weaken role specialization.

Each subagent should have role-specific instructions and receive the task context it needs.

Emit only one Task tool call per coordinator response so parallelism does not confuse the model. - Parallel subagent work can be initiated through multiple Task calls when appropriate. Restricting to one call per response unnecessarily serializes independent work.

The issue is proper context passing and aggregation, not avoiding parallelism.

answer: Evaluate intermediate synthesis for coverage gaps and re-delegate targeted follow-up tasks before generating the final report.
explanation:
Correct option:

Evaluate intermediate synthesis for coverage gaps and re-delegate targeted follow-up tasks before generating the final report.

The coordinator should assess whether the evidence covers the user's requirements. If gaps exist, it should launch targeted follow-up work before final synthesis.

It also improves reliability because the final report can distinguish well-supported findings from areas that remain weak or incomplete.

Ask the report generator to make the final report sound more confident. - A more confident tone does not improve evidence coverage. It can actually hide uncertainty and make the report less reliable.

The issue is missing evidence and caveats, not wording style.

The task requires comprehensive cited research, so some iterative refinement is appropriate.

Have every subagent write a complete report independently and concatenate the outputs. - Concatenating complete reports creates duplication and inconsistency. It does not give the coordinator a controlled way to resolve conflicts or fill gaps.

Aggregation should be structured, not a raw merge of independent outputs.

Question: Your research system reports 96% overall extraction accuracy from a validation set, so the team wants to remove human review for all high-confidence outputs. A closer look shows that the validation set contains mostly policy briefs, while financial filings and scanned contracts are rare.

options: Measure accuracy separately by document type and field before reducing review for high-confidence outputs.

Remove human review because 96% aggregate accuracy is high enough for a foundation-level workflow.

answer: Measure accuracy separately by document type and field before reducing review for high-confidence outputs.
Use stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to continue detecting hidden error patterns.
explanation:
Correct options:

Measure accuracy separately by document type and field before reducing review for high-confidence outputs.

Aggregate accuracy can hide weak segments. Measuring accuracy by document type and field reveals whether performance is consistent across policy briefs, filings, contracts, and specific extracted fields.

This prevents the team from over-automating rare but high-risk segments. A strong overall metric is not enough if one document type performs poorly.

It also helps set review policies that reflect actual risk rather than a single headline score.

Use stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions to continue detecting hidden error patterns.

Stratified sampling keeps a controlled review channel open for high-confidence outputs. It can detect novel failure modes that confidence thresholds may miss.

Sampling by segment makes the monitoring more useful. It avoids letting common document types dominate the error-rate estimate.

This is important when document formats evolve or new edge cases appear after deployment.

Incorrect options:

Remove human review because 96% aggregate accuracy is high enough for a foundation-level workflow. - Overall accuracy alone is not enough. It may hide poor performance on underrepresented document types or critical fields.

Removing review solely because the aggregate number looks strong can create hidden operational risk.

Route all records with high model confidence directly to downstream systems without calibration. - Model confidence should be calibrated using labeled data. Uncalibrated confidence can be misleading.

High-confidence outputs still need sampling or segment validation before full automation.

Use a single global confidence threshold for every document type and field. - A single global threshold ignores differences in risk and accuracy across fields and document types. Some fields may require stricter review.

Review routing should be calibrated, segmented, and monitored.

Give the subagent forced access to the deployment tool first so it understands deployment context.

answer: Restrict the subagent to tools needed for codebase exploration, such as Read, Grep, Glob, and narrowly scoped MCP documentation tools.
explanation:
Correct option:

Restrict the subagent to tools needed for codebase exploration, such as Read, Grep, Glob, and narrowly scoped MCP documentation tools.

Subagent tools should align with the subagent's role. A codebase exploration agent needs search and reading tools, not calendar or customer-support actions.

Reducing the tool set lowers decision complexity and prevents cross-domain misuse. It also narrows the blast radius if the model chooses poorly.

This preserves the architecture's separation of responsibilities while still allowing the subagent to complete its intended work.

Incorrect options:

Keep all tools available and add a prompt sentence saying the subagent should focus on code. - A prompt reminder does not remove irrelevant tools from the action space. The subagent can still select them.

The described issue is tool overexposure, not only insufficient instruction.

Give the subagent forced access to the deployment tool first so it understands deployment context. - Deployment is outside the subagent's role and can be risky. Forcing deployment context first would increase the chance of inappropriate actions.

Exploration should start with code understanding, not operational changes.

Specific tools with clear contracts are better for reliable model use.

answer: Create .claude/rules/ files with YAML frontmatter paths entries such as infra/**/* and **/*.spec.ts.

explanation:

options: Do not let a blocking CI review directly execute this architectural refactor; use plan mode or a planning workflow to produce a reviewable migration plan instead.
Use direct execution because CI should always apply the fastest possible fix.
Ask Claude to choose any valid design and commit it automatically if tests pass.

answer: Do not let a blocking CI review directly execute this architectural refactor; use plan mode or a planning workflow to produce a reviewable migration plan instead.
explanation:
Correct option:

Do not let a blocking CI review directly execute this architectural refactor; use plan mode or a planning workflow to produce a reviewable migration plan instead.

Large architectural changes require exploration and human review before implementation. A blocking CI review should not directly restructure a service on its own.

Plan mode or a planning workflow lets Claude analyze dependencies and propose options without immediately changing the codebase.

This preserves safety while still using Claude to accelerate the migration design.

Use direct execution because CI should always apply the fastest possible fix. - Speed is not the main requirement for architectural refactoring. Direct execution is best for simple, well-scoped changes.

Here, the task affects service boundaries and build configuration, so the risk of costly rework is high.

Ask Claude to choose any valid design and commit it automatically if tests pass. - Passing tests does not prove that a service decomposition is architecturally correct. Multiple designs may pass tests but differ in maintainability and operational impact.

The team should review the plan before implementation.

The workflow needs planning, not isolated per-file execution.

Question: The automated review prompt says, "Be conservative and only report high-confidence issues." The reviewer still flags many harmless naming differences and local style choices. Developers are starting to ignore the comments.

options: Replace vague confidence wording with explicit criteria that define which categories to report and which categories to skip.
Ask Claude to assign a confidence score to every finding and hide findings below 7 out of 10.
Tell developers to manually dismiss false positives until the model learns from their actions.
Make the review comment more polite so developers trust the findings.
answer: Replace vague confidence wording with explicit criteria that define which categories to report and which categories to skip.
explanation:
Correct option:

Replace vague confidence wording with explicit criteria that define which categories to report and which categories to skip.

Explicit criteria are stronger than vague instructions. The prompt should define reportable categories such as bugs, security defects, and broken behavior, and skip categories such as minor style preferences.

This targets the root cause: the model lacks a precise boundary for what counts as a valuable finding.

Clear criteria also make review output more consistent across pull requests and improve developer trust.

Incorrect options:

Ask Claude to assign a confidence score to every finding and hide findings below 7 out of 10. - Self-reported confidence is not a reliable filter. A model may be confident about low-value or incorrect findings.

The better control is to define the categories and examples that should be reported.

Tell developers to manually dismiss false positives until the model learns from their actions. - Manual dismissal may provide operational feedback, but it does not improve the prompt immediately. Developers will still see low-value comments.

The prompt should prevent predictable false-positive categories upfront.

Make the review comment more polite so developers trust the findings. - Politeness affects tone, not precision. A polite false positive is still a false positive.

The team needs sharper review criteria.

Scenario: You are integrating Claude Code into your Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment pipeline. The system runs automated code reviews, generates test cases, and provides feedback on pull requests. You need to design prompts that provide actionable feedback and minimize false positives.

Question: The review system has two recurring problems: it flags many minor style preferences as high severity, and it continues reporting a flaky false-positive category that developers always dismiss.

Which TWO changes should you make first?
options: Define explicit severity criteria with concrete examples for each severity level.
Temporarily disable the high false-positive category while you refine the prompt for that category.
Ask Claude to report only findings it feels extremely confident about.
Route every finding to human review before posting so developers never see model mistakes.
Increase the number of files reviewed per prompt so Claude sees more style patterns.
answer: Define explicit severity criteria with concrete examples for each severity level.
Temporarily disable the high false-positive category while you refine the prompt for that category.
explanation:
Correct options:

Define explicit severity criteria with concrete examples for each severity level.

Severity criteria need concrete examples. They show Claude what qualifies as critical, high, medium, or low severity.

This reduces arbitrary severity assignment and helps align comments with developer expectations.

It also makes the review system easier to audit because severity decisions are tied to defined examples.

Temporarily disable the high false-positive category while you refine the prompt for that category.

A high false-positive category can damage trust in the entire reviewer. Temporarily disabling it can restore confidence while the prompt is improved.

This is a practical calibration strategy. Accurate categories can keep running while the weak category is repaired.

It also prevents developers from training themselves to ignore all automated comments.

Incorrect options:

Ask Claude to report only findings it feels extremely confident about. - Self-reported confidence is not a precise control. Claude can be confident about issues that developers consider low value or incorrect.

Specific criteria and examples are stronger than confidence wording.

Route every finding to human review before posting so developers never see model mistakes. - Human review for every finding may reduce user-facing mistakes, but it defeats much of the automation value. It is also not the first prompt-level fix.

The better approach is to reduce predictable false positives at the source.

Increase the number of files reviewed per prompt so Claude sees more style patterns. - More files can add context, but it does not define severity or false-positive boundaries. It may increase attention dilution.

The problem is review criteria, not lack of surrounding examples.

options: Add targeted few-shot examples that demonstrate extraction from varied document structures and ambiguous cases.

answer: Add targeted few-shot examples that demonstrate extraction from varied document structures and ambiguous cases.
explanation:

Add targeted few-shot examples that demonstrate extraction from varied document structures and ambiguous cases.

Few-shot examples help Claude understand how to handle variety. They can show invoices, contracts, and lab reports with different layouts and wording.

Examples are especially useful for ambiguous cases because they demonstrate judgment, not just formatting.

This improves consistency without forcing the model to fabricate values when information is absent.

Examples can be targeted to avoid overfitting while still improving consistency.

Question: The extractor returns JSON that passes syntax validation, but a semantic validator detects that invoice line items sum to $980 while the stated total is $1,080. The source document includes both values clearly.

What is the best retry approach?
options: Send a follow-up request with the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error about the mismatch.
Retry the same extraction prompt silently and hope the second attempt gives a different result.
Accept the extraction because JSON syntax validation succeeded.
Drop the document from processing because any mismatch proves the source is unusable.
answer: Send a follow-up request with the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error about the mismatch.
explanation:
Correct option:

Send a follow-up request with the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error about the mismatch.

The retry should include the original evidence, the failed output, and the specific validation error. That gives Claude the information needed to correct the semantic issue.

This pattern works when the required information exists in the source and the error is in placement, calculation, or interpretation.

It also preserves auditability because the correction is tied to a concrete validation failure.

Incorrect options:

Retry the same extraction prompt silently and hope the second attempt gives a different result. - A silent retry gives Claude no information about what went wrong. It may repeat the same mistake.

Error feedback makes the retry targeted and more likely to succeed.

Accept the extraction because JSON syntax validation succeeded. - Schema syntax validity is not the same as semantic correctness. Values can be well-formed but wrong.

Downstream systems need both structural validity and domain validation.

Drop the document from processing because any mismatch proves the source is unusable. - A mismatch does not always mean the source is unusable. The extraction may be correctable if the source clearly contains the values.

The system should retry with feedback before discarding the document.

Question: You need to process 20,000 archived documents for a monthly analytics report. The result is not needed for users in real time, but the report must be ready within 30 hours. Some documents may exceed context limits and need chunking on retry.

options: Use the Message Batches API, track each request with custom_id, and resubmit only failed documents with modifications such as chunking.
Use synchronous API calls for all documents because batch results cannot be mapped back to inputs.
Submit one batch every 29 hours so all processing finishes just before the deadline.
Use batch processing only for documents that have already failed synchronous processing.
answer: Use the Message Batches API, track each request with custom_id, and resubmit only failed documents with modifications such as chunking.
explanation:
Correct option:

Use the Message Batches API, track each request with custom_id, and resubmit only failed documents with modifications such as chunking.

The workload is large and latency-tolerant, so batch processing is appropriate. The 30-hour SLA can accommodate asynchronous processing if submission timing is planned.

custom_id lets the system correlate each result with its source document. That enables targeted resubmission instead of reprocessing the whole corpus.

Failed oversized documents can be modified, such as by chunking, before being resubmitted.

Incorrect options:

Use synchronous API calls for all documents because batch results cannot be mapped back to inputs. - Synchronous calls are not required when the work is not user-blocking. They may cost more and complicate large-volume throughput.

Batch results can be correlated to requests using identifiers.

Submit one batch every 29 hours so all processing finishes just before the deadline. - Submitting one batch every 29 hours leaves almost no buffer if processing takes longer than expected. The system should submit early enough to account for the processing window and retries.

The timing strategy should be based on the SLA and maximum processing window.

Use batch processing only for documents that have already failed synchronous processing. - Using batch only after synchronous failure loses the cost and throughput benefits for the main workload.

Batch processing is suitable as the primary approach for this latency-tolerant archive job.

question:
Scenario: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JSON schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.

Question: The extraction system produces structured records from long contracts. You want to reduce subtle errors before records enter the downstream system, especially when the same model generated the initial extraction.

Which TWO review architecture choices are most appropriate?
options: Use an independent Claude instance to review the extracted record without the extractor's prior reasoning context.
Split long-document review into focused passes, such as field-level checks and cross-field consistency checks.
Ask the same Claude session to confirm that its own extraction is correct.
Skip review when the JSON schema validates successfully.
Use only one full-document pass so the reviewer sees everything at once.
answer: Use an independent Claude instance to review the extracted record without the extractor's prior reasoning context.
Split long-document review into focused passes, such as field-level checks and cross-field consistency checks.
explanation:
Correct options:

Use an independent Claude instance to review the extracted record without the extractor's prior reasoning context.

An independent review instance is less influenced by the extractor's prior reasoning. It can challenge choices that the generating session might overlook.

This is useful when subtle extraction errors have downstream consequences.

The reviewer can compare the record against the source with a fresh perspective.

Split long-document review into focused passes, such as field-level checks and cross-field consistency checks.

Focused passes reduce attention dilution. Field-level checks can verify local extraction, while cross-field passes can catch inconsistencies such as totals, dates, and party roles.

This is better than asking one pass to catch every possible issue in a long document.

It also creates clearer review outputs for routing and remediation.

Incorrect options:

Ask the same Claude session to confirm that its own extraction is correct. - The same session may be biased by its own earlier reasoning. It may be less likely to question assumptions it already made.

Self-review can help in some cases but is weaker than independent review for subtle errors.

Skip review when the JSON schema validates successfully. - JSON schema validation does not guarantee semantic correctness. A record can be valid JSON and still contain wrong or inconsistent values.

Review should consider field accuracy and cross-field consistency.

Use only one full-document pass so the reviewer sees everything at once. - A single full-document pass can suffer from attention dilution. Long contracts often need focused review structure.

The goal is reliable verification, not merely maximum context.
